summary: The paper presents a simple posterior approximation for Bayesian testing of control and experimental groups, intended for treatment-effect analysis in online experiments. It bins each group’s observed metric values and treats the bin counts as categorical data with a Dirichlet prior, producing a Dirichlet posterior for each group. Posterior draws are mapped from bin proportions to metric values and used to estimate the chance that one group has a higher average, expected loss, and quantile differences. The authors assess the method in simulations of complex bounded data and compare it with bootstrap and normal-based estimates. They report that the method performs well with sufficient bins and is practical enough to use as their standard internal analysis method.
key_results: The authors ran 10,000 simulations, with the number of visitors in each simulated group ranging from 8,000 to 25,000. For average differences, chance to beat, and expected loss, roughly 32 bins were enough for offsets from the ground truth to be near zero and have variance similar to the comparison methods. Quantile estimates required more resolution: the Dirichlet-Categorical approximation was similar to bootstrapping at roughly 256 bins. With a few dozen bins or more, the reported 99% credibility intervals contained the ground-truth mean difference in about 99% of simulations; the normal-based intervals for the mean were narrower than the bootstrap or Dirichlet-Categorical intervals.
key_equations:
Binned Dirichlet posterior: \[\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{*}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\boldsymbol{n},\quad n_i=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}(d_j\in B_i)\] Alpha is the prior concentration-parameter vector, alpha-star is the posterior vector, n is the vector of bin counts, n sub i is the count in bin i, N is the number of observations, d sub j is observation j, B sub i is bin i, and the indicator is one when the observation belongs to that bin.

Monte Carlo estimate of a posterior metric: \[\mathbb{E}[w(X_A,X_B)]\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}w(x_{A,j},x_{B,j})\] The expectation is over the joint posterior, w is the metric function, X sub A and X sub B are posterior proportion vectors for groups A and B, N is the number of paired draws, and x sub A comma j and x sub B comma j are draw j for the two groups.
limitations_stated: The authors say the approximation is best suited to metrics with known, guaranteed minimum and maximum values. Nonuniform values within a bin can make the chosen bin-to-value mapping biased, although more bins can reduce this issue; they also caution that the method is unlikely to work well with sparse or rare data. They acknowledge that their simulation parameters may have happened to cover a well-behaved part of the possible parameter space.
limitations_unstated: The simulations use a particular tripartite hurdle-model family, visitor-count range, and uniform prior, so their results do not establish performance for other data-generating processes or informative priors. The method assumes the two groups can be analyzed independently, and the paper does not quantify its performance on operational experiments or provide a broad comparison across experimental settings. Bin choices and the need for bounded metrics may also limit direct use for metrics with long tails or changing practical bounds.
future_work_stated: The authors encourage readers to run simulations on data resembling their own before adopting the method. They also say the framework can be extended beyond the metrics presented and adapted to other business needs, and invite feedback on calculating theoretical bounds for uncertainty intervals.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the approximation on additional metric types, data-generating processes, and informative-prior choices, with prospective validation against real experimental outcomes. It could also develop practical guidance for selecting bin boundaries and mapping values, and evaluate how the method behaves under operational constraints such as sparse outcomes or interacting experiment groups.

summary: This paper develops foldover screening designs for experiments that need to identify important main effects while accounting for second-order effects and estimating error variance before model selection. The method is developed for numeric or categorical factors under a second-order response model, with the objective of improving main-effect detection while preserving information for later interaction and quadratic-effect analysis. It constructs a half design, appends its sign-reversed runs, and characterizes the resulting pure-error and fake-factor degrees of freedom. A search algorithm uses the expected confidence interval criterion to choose designs, and an augmentation method adds runs when the run budget or model-estimation needs make a complete foldover unsuitable. The simulations show that these designs can perform similarly to traditional designs under sparse, hierarchical effects and can perform better when those principles do not hold; a 20-run chemical-process experiment illustrates their use.
key_results: In simulations with five two-level factors and 16 total runs, the traditional half-fraction design had true-positive rates below 0.10 when ten effects were active, while the three augmented foldover designs had main-effect true-positive rates from 0.710 to 1.000 across the reported scenarios. In the seven-factor, 24-run comparisons, for the largest simulated model the R0.a75.n20 design detected two-factor interactions at a rate of 0.908 versus 0.826 for ADSD.n24, and quadratic effects at 0.635 versus 0.539; SM.n22 had the highest quadratic-effect rate, 0.712, but an interaction rate of 0.777. Each simulation setting used 500 generated responses. In the real 20-run ethylene experiment with eight factors, the chosen design had one fake-factor degree of freedom, two pure-error degrees of freedom, three variance-estimation degrees of freedom, and an ECI value of 0.791; the first-stage analysis selected factors 1, 2, and 4, and the final model included the interaction between factors 1 and 4 with an R-squared value of 0.967.

Foldover construction: \[D_{\pm}=\begin{pmatrix}H\\-H\end{pmatrix}\] The foldover design D± is formed by stacking the half design H and the same design with every factor setting sign-reversed.

Degrees of freedom characterization: \[f=v-n_0-\sum_{g=1}^{G}(n_g-1),\qquad p=\max(0,2n_0-1)+2\sum_{g=1}^{G}(n_g-1)\] Fake-factor degrees of freedom f and pure-error degrees of freedom p are determined by v, the number of center runs n0, the number ng of rows in each noncenter group g, and the number G of such groups.

Foldover expected confidence interval criterion: \[\mathrm{ECI}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c(g_X)t_{\alpha/2,g_X}\sqrt{v_j/2}\] The criterion averages over m factors the product of the adjustment factor c(gX), the t critical value t(alpha/2,gX), and the square root of half the design variance vj for factor j; the design search minimizes this quantity.
limitations_stated: The authors state that a foldover requires an even number of runs and that a complete foldover with many runs can create unnecessarily many variance-estimation degrees of freedom, reducing the rank available for estimating second-order effects. They recommend augmentation when the run count is odd or the complete foldover would be too large, while requiring the initial foldover to have adequate power for screening.
limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence covers selected factor counts and effect patterns, including settings built around effect heredity, so it does not establish performance across a broad range of response behavior or severe model misspecification. The real-data illustration is a single experiment, and the paper does not report independent confirmation runs or validation of the selected model on new experimental data.
future_work_stated: The authors describe a possible sequential strategy: run and analyze the foldover first, then use the results to refine the second-order model for augmented runs. They note that this strategy would generally require adding a block effect to the augmentation criterion. They also suggest comparing candidate designs with secondary criteria, such as a reduced lack-of-fit criterion, when the screening criterion alone produces designs with more power than needed.
future_work_unstated: Future work could assess robustness when the assumed second-order model or normal, constant-variance error assumptions are inaccurate, and evaluate constrained designs that reflect practical limits on factor combinations, cost, or run order. summary: The paper develops procedures for identifying effects on the mean and variance in replicated regular two-level factorial experiments. It addresses the individual error rate (IER) and experimentwise error rate (EER) under a normal response model with a linear mean model and a log-linear variance model. For mean effects, it derives the test statistic's distribution when variances differ among runs and uses Monte Carlo sampling to obtain critical values. For variance effects, it replaces an approximate variance with the exact variance of the log sample variance to calibrate tests. Simulations show that the proposed procedures control both error rates well across the studied settings, and the authors illustrate them with a putting experiment dataset.
key_results: The simulations used three- and four-factor designs, three to six replications per treatment, and 20,000 repetitions per setting. For heterogeneous variances in the mean model, the proposed method kept simulated IER values close to the five percent target, while the Wu and Hamada approach produced values as high as 8.5 percent; for heterogeneous-variance EER, the proposed method gave 4.9 to 5.4 percent, compared with 6.0 to 8.7 percent for Wu and Hamada and 2.3 to 3.0 percent for Lenth's method. In the variance model, the proposed method's simulated IER values for null effects were generally near five percent, while the existing Wu and Hamada and jackknife approaches were anticonservative and Lenth's method was conservative. For variance-model EER, the proposed method gave 5.1 to 5.5 percent, compared with 10.9 to 26.4 percent for Wu and Hamada; Lenth's method gave 4.3 to 4.8 percent. Under homogeneous variances, the existing Wu and Hamada method also controlled the mean-model error rates well, and the proposed method had similar power in the reported comparisons.

summary: The paper develops online experiment-design methods that choose system inputs to identify linear and nonlinear dynamic models efficiently. It adapts active learning for regression to nonlinear autoregressive models with exogenous inputs and recurrent neural network state-space models, updating model parameters recursively with a Kalman filter. At each step, the method chooses an admissible input using a criterion that balances predicted uncertainty and exploration, with optional penalties for predicted output-constraint violations. The authors test the approach on simulated two-tank, ethylene oxidation, and industrial robot arm systems, comparing it with random excitation and other active-learning strategies. Their inverse-distance-based approach generally improves prediction as samples are collected, although its computation can be slower than the comparison methods.
key_results: In the two-tank benchmark, the nonlinear autoregressive model was run for 1,000 samples after 80 initial samples, over 30 runs; without output constraints, the mean test coefficient of determination was 98.17% for the proposed method and 97.92% for passive sampling, while the greedy input-space method also reached 98.17%. In the ethylene oxidation benchmark, the proposed method reached 92.96% for the nonlinear autoregressive model without constraints, compared with 92.57% for passive sampling. For the robot arm recurrent neural network, the proposed method reached 95.79% without constraints, compared with 92.04% for passive sampling; the experiments used 500 samples after 40 initial samples and 10 runs. Computation was a trade-off: in the two-tank nonlinear autoregressive experiment, the proposed method averaged 90.8 milliseconds per sample, compared with 22.8 milliseconds for the input-space greedy method and 25.2 milliseconds for the incremental greedy method; the authors also report that penalties reduced output-constraint violations.

State-space model: \[x_{k+1}=f_x(x_k,u_k,\theta_x),\qquad y_k=f_y(x_k,\theta_y)\] The hidden state at time k plus one is given by state function f sub x of the current hidden state, input, and state-model parameters theta sub x; the output at time k is given by output function f sub y of the current hidden state and output-model parameters theta sub y.

limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses noisy synthetic data from three benchmarks rather than data from physical experiments, so the reported performance does not establish effectiveness under unmodeled plant behavior or operational disturbances. future_work_stated: The authors propose integrating the active-learning strategies with closed-loop control, such as model predictive control. They also identify instrumental-variable methods as a possible way to address closed-loop effects in parameter estimation.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on physical systems and under model mismatch, disturbances, and strict safety requirements, while reporting whether constraint compliance is guaranteed. summary: This paper designs a fast-and-slow experimentation framework for optimizing long-term outcomes in online systems with Bayesian optimization. It is intended for tuning parameterized systems such as recommendation and ranking policies, where treatment effects can change over time and reliable measurement may take weeks. The design runs a long experiment to measure long-term outcomes while running shorter experiments in parallel to test candidate settings. Gaussian process models link short-term measurements and other proxy data to the long-term objective, with a target-aware model that can downweight unhelpful proxies. The authors report that this approach improves optimization in their benchmark studies and can reduce experimentation wall time by over 60 percent compared with sequential experimentation.
key_results: Across four real-world-based simulation benchmarks, the parallel design significantly outperformed sequential optimization, and including additional proxies with the target-aware model further improved results in some tasks. In a video playback and a retrieval benchmark, reported out-of-sample prediction log-likelihoods were -298275 versus -831 and -952 for sequential, intrinsic-coregionalization, and target-aware models in video playback; for retrieval, the corresponding values were -22799742, -461, and -456. In a real deployment example, retrieval-system tuning saved over 2 megawatts of capacity while improving ranking performance; the authors also report more than 30 major launches per year from the framework’s broader deployment. The authors report over 60 percent lower experimentation wall time than a traditional sequential design, and accounting for time-of-day effects improved log-likelihood on 12 of 14 engagement metrics and mean squared error on 6 metrics.

limitations_unstated: Most quantitative optimization comparisons use simulations built from benchmark functions or fitted surrogates, including time-varying transformations, rather than prospective head-to-head deployments on live systems. summary: The paper designs an adaptive acquisition procedure for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), using sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) to choose which k-space measurements to acquire. Its objective is to select measurements with high expected information gain (EIG) about the image being reconstructed and, where relevant, a downstream analysis such as segmentation. The method represents feasible sampling patterns with a design parameter and optimizes that parameter using diffusion-based posterior sampling and stochastic optimization. In tests on MRI datasets, the method attained a mean structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 91.34 on the fastMRI knee test set when sampling 25% of k-space. The paper also presents segmentation examples and reports that this task can be inferred from less sampling than is needed for high-fidelity image reconstruction.
key_results: At 25% k-space sampling, corresponding to four times acceleration, the method achieved a mean SSIM of 91.34 on the fastMRI knee test set. The reported comparison scores were 91.26 for active diffusion subsampling, 91.08 for sequential MRI sampling, 90.2 for random sampling, 90.13 for fixed-mask diffusion posterior sampling, 89.52 for LOUPE, and 87.97 for PG-MRI. On brain fastMRI data, at iteration 9 the paper reports 15.6789% k-space sampling, a PSNR of 20.6784, and an SSIM of 0.9104. For white matter hyperintensity segmentation, the paper provides visual examples but no numerical segmentation score; it reports that segmentation can be inferred from less data than detailed image reconstruction requires.

Expected information gain criterion: \[\operatorname{EIG}(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta,y\mid\xi)}[\log p(\theta\mid y,\xi)-\log p(\theta)]\] EIG is the expected information gain, xi is a candidate design, theta is the unknown target, y is a possible measurement, p denotes the relevant probability distribution, and log is the natural logarithm; the criterion averages the change from prior to posterior log probability.

limitations_stated: The described procedure is limited to single-coil acquisition and two-dimensional images. The authors also state that performance depends on the quality of learned priors and on having sufficiently large training datasets; task-aware use requires enough paired image and segmentation examples.
limitations_unstated: The reported numerical comparison focuses on reconstruction scores for the knee test set, while the segmentation results are shown visually without reported numerical segmentation outcomes. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to multiple coils and three-dimensional imaging, and investigating other subsampling schemes, including variable-density trajectories.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate task-aware acquisition quantitatively across held-out patients, reporting segmentation scores as sampling increases and comparing them with reconstruction-focused designs. The authors evaluate the methods through mathematical results and numerical comparisons, including integration, physics-informed neural network training, and computer-model emulation. They report better space-filling and prediction performance in their tests, together with substantial savings in design-search and model-fitting computation.
key_results: For lattice-based designs, the new evaluation formulas reduce the cost of assessing design criteria from quadratic in run size to linear, or to logarithmic in run size for the bivariate projection criteria. summary: This paper proposes a way to estimate variance components for response surface analyses of multi-stratum experiments, including split-plot and split-split-plot designs. The method, called pure error residual maximum likelihood (PE-REML), fits the full treatment model when estimating variance components, rather than relying on the assumed polynomial response surface model. Those estimates are then used with generalized least squares (GLS) to estimate response surface effects, with a Kenward-Roger adjustment available for their standard errors. The authors compare the method with standard response surface residual maximum likelihood (RS-REML) using three examples and simulations. They find that both methods perform similarly when the response surface model is correct, while PE-REML is more robust when it is misspecified.
key_results: In simulations of 10,000 data sets where the assumed model was correct, fixed-effect estimates were similar between methods, and empirical standard errors for the quadratic effects differed by less than 0.001 in the reported table. With a large omitted third-order effect in the whole-plot stratum, PE-REML standard-error biases were no greater than about 10%, while RS-REML biases exceeded 40% for several whole-plot effects; the mean whole-plot variance estimate was 4.0358 with PE-REML and 9.6323 with RS-REML. When the omitted effect was in the subplot stratum, PE-REML variance estimates were close to the true values, while RS-REML standard-error biases for several subplot effects were about 76% to 89%. In the ceramic-pipe experiment, which had 12 whole plots with four runs each, PE-REML gave smaller standard errors for some effects and larger ones for others than RS-REML.

Response surface model: \[X_t\tau = X\beta\] Xt is the full treatment design matrix, tau is the vector of treatment means, X is the response surface design matrix, and beta is the vector of response surface parameters.

Pure error residual projection: \[K^{\prime}X_t=0,\qquad \operatorname{rank}(K)=n-t\] K is the matrix defining the residual projection, K transpose is its transpose, Xt is the full treatment design matrix, n is the number of runs, and t is the number of treatments; the method applies residual maximum likelihood to the projected responses.
limitations_stated: The authors state that pure error estimation is infeasible for many multi-stratum designs, including many D-optimal designs, so the method can be used only when the design provides the necessary information. They also report that PE-REML standard errors are consistently negatively biased by up to about 10%, and that the Kenward-Roger correction helps only a little.
limitations_unstated: The results rely on a limited set of examples and simulations, including a particular split-plot design with 12 whole plots and selected forms and sizes of model misspecification; performance across a wider range of designs and variance structures is not established. Because the method needs pure-error information from replicated treatments, it may offer little or no usable estimate for designs with few treatment replications or very limited residual degrees of freedom.
future_work_stated: The authors identify the search for better corrections to standard errors, p-values, and confidence intervals as a useful direction for further research, since the Kenward-Roger correction helps only a little.
future_work_unstated: Further work could quantify when a design has enough replicated-treatment information for stable pure-error variance estimates, and compare design choices that increase this information against their run cost. It could also test the method in real experiments with broader variance structures and develop a practical workflow for applying it alongside model checks.

summary: The paper develops an optimal experimental design procedure for identifying the anode rate constant in a lithium-ion cell electrochemical model. The procedure uses a reduced-order electrochemical cell model and a data-driven estimator of cathode surface concentration as an input to the controller. The authors compare the resulting experiment with constant-current discharge tests and a relaxation current interrupt discharge test. The adaptive design identifies the parameter with low drive-cycle voltage prediction error in a much shorter experiment than the relaxation current interrupt discharge test.

summary: This paper presents an input-design method for nonlinear dynamic system identification that aims to improve model prediction by filling the relevant regions of the model-input space with data. It uses a surrogate model and a receding horizon control (RHC) procedure to choose inputs, repeatedly selecting the next input from an optimized future sequence. Its objective is to make supporting points spread through the region of interest while respecting input and model-space constraints. The procedure can run offline with a fixed surrogate model or online with a model updated from process observations. In a simulated nonlinear example, the authors report better space-filling performance than the comparison methods they tested.
key_results: The evaluation used a simulated Hammerstein process and compared the proposed method in adaptive and fixed-surrogate modes with incremental dynamic space-filling design (IDS-FID) and amplitude-modulated pseudo random binary signals (APRBS). For each method, the study generated 50 signals, each with a dataset size of 300. The paper reports that the proposed method outperformed the comparison methods on both the largest-empty-ball radius and distribution uniformity measures, but does not give numerical summary values for those metrics in the text. The adaptive version increasingly improved on the fixed-surrogate version as data accumulated, while the IDS-FID comparison used the same fixed linear time-invariant surrogate as the proposed offline method.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the method's effectiveness depends on surrogate-model quality and that the relationship between model accuracy and input-signal quality needs systematic analysis. limitations_unstated: The demonstrated evaluation is limited to one simulated Hammerstein process, so it does not establish performance across different process dynamics or real experiments. The fixed offline surrogate is given the process time constant, and the evaluation focuses on space-filling metrics rather than directly reporting prediction or generalization error.
future_work_stated: The authors propose evaluating the method on more complex and realistic processes and systematically studying how surrogate accuracy affects the resulting input design. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method on real processes with practical safety, actuator, and operating constraints, and report prediction performance alongside space-filling measures. They could also assess whether sequential use remains effective when observations are noisy or when online optimization must meet strict computation-time limits.

summary: The paper develops a sequential design of experiments (DoE) method to estimate seismic fragility curves when only a binary indicator of state (BIS) is observed for each intensity measure (IM). It uses a Bayesian probit-lognormal model and a constrained reference prior to estimate failure probability while addressing degenerate likelihoods that can arise with small samples. At each step, the method selects an intensity measure value expected to have a large effect on the posterior estimate, then tests or simulates the structure and records its outcome. The authors evaluate the strategy using simulated responses for a nuclear-industry piping system, with peak ground acceleration and pseudo-spectral acceleration as the intensity measures. They report that the sequential method usually estimates the curve more efficiently than standard sampling, particularly with fewer than 100 observations, while reducing likelihood degeneracy.
key_results: In 100 replications, the authors compared standard sampling with sequential selections for sample sizes up to 250; the sequential approach reduced estimation error more quickly, with its clearest advantage below about 50 observations. With pseudo-spectral acceleration, estimation bias approached the probit-lognormal model-bias level by about 50 observations, and decreased little beyond about 100; the paper reports that around 80 observations gave a reasonable estimate. With peak ground acceleration, the method outperformed standard sampling up to about 100 observations, but its performance degraded beyond that point because of model bias and the limited range of that measure. The proposed stopping indicators suggested about 60 observations for pseudo-spectral acceleration and about 40 for peak ground acceleration at the stated information-index threshold; the authors caution that such thresholds depend on the case study.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the influence of the seismic signal generator is outside the scope of the study. They also note that the probit-lognormal model can be biased, that peak ground acceleration does not fully describe the fragility curve in their case, and that their proposed stopping thresholds are case-specific rather than established guidance. The constrained prior does not guarantee against estimates whose spread parameter tends toward zero in very small samples.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation centers on one piping-system model and synthetic seismic signals calibrated to a limited collection of real accelerograms, so it does not establish performance across other equipment or seismic settings. The sequential selection procedure is assessed through simulations using an existing signal database rather than a prospective physical testing campaign, leaving practical execution and transfer to operational experiments unvalidated.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method on additional structures, seismic scenarios, and real experimental campaigns, including constraints on which signal levels can actually be produced or tested. summary: The paper introduces BLADE, a Bayesian method for discovering sparse governing equations of dynamical systems from measurements. It assumes the system can be represented as a linear combination of candidate functions and estimates coefficient uncertainty using replica-exchange stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. For limited-data settings, it chooses additional observations by combining predictive uncertainty with a space-filling criterion, then refits the model as data are added. The authors test the method on simulated Lotka–Volterra, Lorenz, Burgers, and convection–diffusion systems, comparing it with sparse regression, a Bayesian sparse-regression method, and alternative samplers. In the active-learning tests, the combined selection strategy reaches the reported error target with substantially fewer measurements than random sampling.
key_results: For the Lotka–Volterra system, the hybrid uncertainty and space-filling strategy reduced the number of measurements needed to bring the total error bar below 10 to the power of minus 2 from 70 with random sampling to 30, a reduction of about 60%. For Burgers’ equation, the same target required 50 measurements with the hybrid strategy versus 90 with random sampling, a reduction of 44%; at 50 points, the hybrid strategy identified the correct candidate functions while the other strategies retained extra terms or an incomplete model. In the convection–diffusion test, the hybrid strategy recovered the correct equation structure with 50 points and reported coefficient estimates of 1.002 and minus 0.996, while random sampling missed the diffusion term. In a matched-throughput test on the Lorenz system, replica-exchange sampling achieved 25.29 steps per second compared with 1.14 for the No-U-Turn Sampler.

Sparse system model: \[\dot{U}=\Theta(U)\Xi\] U is the matrix of measured system states, its dotted form is the matrix of time derivatives, Theta is the library of candidate functions evaluated at U, and Xi is the coefficient matrix.

Langevin coefficient update: \[\tilde{\xi}_{k+1}=\tilde{\xi}_k-\eta_k\nabla\tilde{L}(\tilde{\xi}_k)+\sqrt{2\eta_k\tau}\,\zeta_k\] The coefficient vector at iteration k plus one is updated from its value at iteration k using step size eta, the gradient of the approximate negative log-posterior L, temperature tau, and Gaussian random noise zeta.

Hybrid acquisition score: \[C(u_i)=\alpha\tilde{\sigma}^{2}(u_i)+(1-\alpha)\tilde{d}(\Theta(u_i))\] C is the candidate-point score, u_i is a potential design point, alpha weights normalized predictive variance, sigma squared is predictive variance, d is normalized space-filling distance in the candidate-function feature space, and Theta maps the point to that feature space.
limitations_stated: The authors state that replica-exchange sampling costs more computation than deterministic optimization and may be prohibitive for very large systems or real-time applications. The candidate-function library is specified in advance, and finite-difference derivative estimates can be fragile for noisy partial differential equation data. They note that the partial differential equation tests used lower noise levels than the ordinary differential equation tests, so those results do not comprehensively test robustness to high noise.
limitations_unstated: The active-learning evaluations use simulated data pools, and the authors calculate response derivatives from the original regular data even in scenarios framed as having difficult or costly derivative acquisition. Thus, these tests do not establish the full real-world cost or feasibility of acquiring each selected measurement. The evaluation also covers a small set of known benchmark systems and does not show how performance changes when the candidate library or the assumed sparse model is wrong.
future_work_stated: The authors propose improving sampling through adaptive temperature scheduling and parallel chains, and exploring neural operators or manifold-learned features to discover candidate bases automatically. For noisy partial differential equation problems, they suggest weak-form or integral methods, transformed-domain methods, filtering, and neural-network-based denoising with automatic differentiation.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test BLADE on physical experiments where each selected measurement has a recorded acquisition cost and derivatives are not available from a full underlying trajectory. It would also be useful to test alternative design constraints and acquisition criteria, and to evaluate sequential use when observations arrive over time and the system may change.

summary: This paper studies Bayesian optimization (BO) for finding the minimum of intrinsically noisy response surfaces, such as those encountered in physical experiments. It models the response with a Gaussian process (GP) and compares choices of initial sample size, replication, acquisition function, and covariance function. The study varies the problem, noise magnitude, and noise form using simulated functions, and evaluates performance by the gap between the selected and true optimum. Across the tested settings, the Matérn covariance function performs best, while the available experimental budget strongly affects other design choices. The authors provide recommendations for selecting initial samples, replicates, and acquisition functions according to that budget.
key_results: The study reports 18,225 experiments, using five repetitions of each unique experimental setting, and evaluates results after 25, 37.5, and 50 times the problem dimension in samples. The Matérn covariance function performs better on all test problems than the Gaussian and power exponential alternatives. A larger initial sample size generally improves the optimum gap, while replication has a minor overall effect but becomes more useful as the experimental budget grows. The preferred acquisition function also depends on budget: probability of improvement is favored for smaller budgets, while the upper confidence approach is more suitable for larger budgets. The authors report that objective-function type and the studied noise properties do not interact with the controllable choices in the way that total budget does.

limitations_stated: The study considers normally distributed experimental noise and only a limited set of noise-variance forms. It does not investigate batch acquisition, and it estimates Gaussian process hyperparameters by maximum likelihood rather than accounting for their uncertainty.
limitations_unstated: The comparisons use only three low-dimensional simulated objective functions, so the reported rankings may not transfer to more complex or higher-dimensional physical experiments. future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating Bayesian approaches that account for uncertainty in the emulator’s hyperparameters and developing problem-specific acquisition functions. They also call for new statistical methods for optimizing noisy response surfaces when data are sparse.
future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the recommendations in physical experiments and test them on a wider range of response surfaces and noise distributions. It could also assess whether the design guidance remains effective under practical constraints such as restricted or costly input settings.

summary: The paper designs a more efficient sampling step for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), which approximates a complex model locally with a linear explanation. summary: This paper develops active hypothesis-testing methods for situations where a valid test statistic is costly to obtain but an inexpensive, possibly invalid proxy is available. summary: The paper presents an R package for constructing and analyzing covariate-balanced assignments in randomized treatment-control experiments. Its objective is to improve treatment-effect precision while preserving design-based inference conditional on assignment acceptance. The package batches assignment generation and balance checks, can use graphics processing units (GPUs) or tensor processing units (TPUs), and stores compact random-number keys rather than all accepted assignment vectors. It supports exact enumeration when feasible and Monte Carlo generation for larger problems, with randomization tests and optional fiducial intervals. The paper reports faster pool generation in its benchmarks and derives how stricter acceptance can reduce the imbalance contribution to estimation error under its stated model assumptions.
key_results: For 100 units, 100 covariates, and an acceptance probability of 0.005, the authors report that pool generation takes about 5 seconds on the GPU backend, compared with 112 seconds for a baseline R workflow, a speedup of about 24 times. For 1,000 units and 1,000 covariates at the same acceptance probability, generation takes 7 seconds on the GPU and 91 seconds on the package's CPU backend; GPU runtime reductions reach 96% at 1,000 covariates. The authors report speedups over baseline implementations exceeding 42 times in some high-dimensional, high-unit-count, stringent-acceptance settings, while noting that baseline results are shown only where those implementations finish in a reasonable time. Under the paper's theoretical example with an outcome variance share of 0.5, acceptance probability 0.01 yields an estimated root mean squared error reduction of about 15% at 30 covariates and about 3% at 1,000 covariates.

limitations_stated: The paper does not provide a dedicated limitations section. limitations_unstated: The precision analysis relies on standardized or whitened covariates, an approximately Gaussian covariate-mean difference, and a linear outcome model; its predictions may therefore be inaccurate with strong model misspecification or important nonlinear outcome relationships. future_work_stated: The authors propose multi-device parallelism for candidate generation and richer balance criteria designed for structured text, image, or network covariates.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess the package on real randomized experiments and compare assignment quality and inference calibration across a wider range of outcome models and balance metrics. summary: The paper develops an optimal experimental design for learning how to rank a large set of items from a limited number of human comparisons. key_results: In synthetic experiments on three datasets, the paper reports lower ranking loss for DopeWolfe than for uniform sampling and, generally, the clustering baselines; it evaluated each setting over 100 random runs. With real feedback from two public datasets, DopeWolfe also had lower ranking loss than uniform sampling, with results averaged over 10 trials. For one runtime comparison, DopeWolfe took 1,646.70 seconds for 1,000 iterations, compared with a reported total of 4,927.38 seconds for the DBSCAN baseline; the authors note these runtimes are not directly comparable because their tuning parameters differ. They report that DopeWolfe typically reached similar performance in about 100 iterations, taking 164.67 seconds in that comparison. For 100 items and comparisons of 10 at a time, the paper estimates about 17 trillion possible subsets, illustrating why enumerating all candidate groups is impractical.

summary: This paper develops an approach to optimize thermoelectric performance by adjusting antimony and tellurium contents in silver antimony telluride. summary: This paper develops a determinant-based D-optimal design method for discretizing norms and recovering functions from samples. For a finite-dimensional space of continuous complex-valued functions, it constructs points and nonnegative weights that exactly reproduce the L2 norm using a Marcinkiewicz–Zygmund identity. The construction maximizes a Gram-matrix determinant and uses a convex-geometric reduction to bound the number of points. The method also constructs tight frames and provides a deterministic sampling recovery procedure for functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space when leading eigenfunctions are available. The authors establish general bounds and test the construction numerically for trigonometric polynomials, while also showing that lattice designs cannot have a point-count bound based only on the number of frequencies in complete generality.
key_results: For a space of dimension n, the paper proves an exact weighted L2 discretization with at most n squared plus 1 points; for trigonometric frequencies in a finite index set, the bound is the size of the difference set, at most the frequency count squared minus the frequency count plus 1. In the recovery setting, the method uses at most n squared plus 1 samples and gives worst-case squared L2 error at most 3 times the tail sum of squared singular values. The paper reports recovery computation requiring order n cubed arithmetic operations for its direct implementation, and notes that prior sharp probabilistic approaches can have a large sampling constant and do not construct verifiable point sets. In numerical tests, the authors obtained a discretization with 41 points for a 41-frequency set and 45 points for a 33-frequency set; for a challenging 10-frequency example, they found a 91-point design and did not find one with fewer points, which they present as numerical evidence for sharpness rather than a proof.
key_equations:
D-optimal design criterion: \[\rho^*=\arg\max_{\rho}\det\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\rho_i\,\phi(x_i)\phi(x_i)^*\right)\] The optimal design rho-star maximizes the determinant of a weighted sum over design points; rho denotes the design measure, rho_i its weights, M the number of candidate points, phi the basis-function vector, x_i a point, and the asterisk the conjugate transpose.

Exact weighted norm discretization: \[\int_{\Omega}|f(x)|^2\,d\mu(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_i|f(x_i)|^2\quad(f\in V)\] The integral of the squared magnitude of any function f in the space V over domain Omega under measure mu equals the weighted sum at N design points, with weights w_i.

General point-count bound: \[N\leq\dim\operatorname{span}\{fg:f,g\in V\}\leq n^2\] The required number of points N is bounded by the dimension of the span of products of pairs of functions in V, which is at most n squared when V has dimension n; the probability-weighted construction may use one additional point.

Sampling recovery error: \[\sup_{\|f\|_{H(k)}\leq1}\|f-S_{n,N}^{k,\mu}f\|_{L_2(\mu)}^2\leq3\sum_{j\geq n+1}\sigma_j^2\] For functions f in the unit ball of the Hilbert space H(k), the worst-case squared L2 error of the sampling recovery operator S is at most three times the tail sum of squared singular values sigma_j, beginning at index n plus one; n is the truncation dimension, N is the sample count, and mu is the target measure.
limitations_stated: The authors state that equal-weight exact discretization for every trigonometric frequency set with a number of points depending only on the set’s cardinality remains an open question. They also show that lattice rules cannot, in general, have a point-count bound depending only on that cardinality without additional structure on the frequency set. For function recovery, their deterministic construction uses a quadratic-in-dimension sample bound, while some earlier probabilistic methods have better sample scaling but nonconstructive or unverifiable point sets.
limitations_unstated: The numerical construction relies on iterative optimization and repeated initializations, so the theoretical existence result does not ensure that a practical search will find a design efficiently or reliably for large problems. The method assumes a specified function space and target measure and permits unequal weights; the paper does not establish performance when experiments impose run costs, restricted feasible settings, measurement noise, or other operational constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors leave open whether equal-weight exact discretizations can be obtained for arbitrary trigonometric frequency sets using a number of points depending only on the frequency count. They also note that constructive subsampling could reduce the recovery design to a number of samples proportional to the dimension, while retaining the error bound up to constants.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to adapt the construction to practical design constraints such as forbidden settings, unequal run costs, replication limits, and noisy responses, then validate it in real experiments. Further work could also compare the optimization’s runtime and reliability with alternative design algorithms across larger spaces and test whether sequentially adding runs preserves the exactness or recovery guarantees.

summary: The paper develops alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithms to compute convex relaxation bounds for the 0/1 D-optimality problem (D-Opt) and maximum-entropy sampling (MESP). D-Opt selects a fixed number of design points to maximize information for parameter estimation, while MESP selects variables to maximize the information in a covariance submatrix. The algorithms split the relaxations into simpler updates, including bounded least-squares steps and closed-form matrix updates based on eigenvalues; the factorization-bound update is supported by new theoretical results. Numerical tests show strong performance for the natural D-Opt bound, the MESP factorization bound, and the MESP Boolean quadratic programming bound, with the linear-algebraic MESP bound less competitive. The authors position these methods as tools for faster upper-bound calculations within branch-and-bound optimization.
key_results: For the natural D-Opt bound, the algorithm solved random instances with 15,000 candidates in 1.0 second, compared with 35.5 seconds for KNITRO and 27.3 seconds for MOSEK; on the quadratic-response instances with 50,000 candidates, it took 219.1 seconds, compared with 430.0 and 1,226.7 seconds, respectively. For the factorization bound on MESP instances with 2,000 variables and covariance rank from 150 to 300, the algorithm was faster than KNITRO on most tested ranks; when varying the selection size from 50 to 150 at rank 150, it took about 0.6 to 2.5 seconds and was faster than KNITRO throughout. For the Boolean quadratic programming bound, it solved tested instances up to 400 variables in 3,279.3 seconds, while SDPT3 ran out of memory above 300 variables and MOSEK ran out of memory at 250 variables. In a 100-step D-Opt diving test, warm-starting reduced cumulative time from about 600 seconds to about 100 seconds, a reported speedup of about six times; the computed relaxations used a target duality gap of 0.05.
key_equations:
Natural relaxation for D-optimal design: \[\max\{\log\det(A^T\operatorname{Diag}(x)A): e^Tx=s,\ x\in[0,1]^n\}\] The vector x gives fractional selection weights, s is the required total selection, n is the number of candidate points, e is the all-ones vector, A is the design matrix, and log det is the natural logarithm of the determinant.

Factorization bound for maximum-entropy sampling: \[\max\{\Gamma_s(F^T\operatorname{Diag}(x)F): e^Tx=s,\ x\in[0,1]^n\}\] The vector x gives fractional selection weights, s is the selection size, n is the number of variables, e is the all-ones vector, F is a factor of the covariance matrix, and Gamma sub s is the spectral function that defines the factorization bound.

Closed-form eigenvalue update for the log-determinant matrix step: \[\lambda_i=\frac{\theta_i+\sqrt{\theta_i^2+4\rho}}{2\rho}\] The updated eigenvalue lambda sub i is calculated from input eigenvalue theta sub i and positive penalty parameter rho.
limitations_stated: The authors report that their ADMM algorithm for the linear-algebraic MESP bound is not competitive because its matrix update is a bottleneck. They also note that their practical one-gradient-step approximation for bounded least-squares updates and other speed modifications mean the standard ADMM convergence guarantees do not apply to the numerical implementations.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation covers generated design matrices and a limited set of covariance benchmarks, so performance on other design structures and applied data settings is uncertain. The paper does not test a full branch-and-bound solver end to end; its warm-start evidence comes from a D-Opt diving experiment rather than a complete exact optimization study.
future_work_stated: The authors identify developing a fast first-order method for the MESP nonlinear-programming bound as a challenge, and explain that a particular version can be obtained through the natural bound for a related D-Opt instance. They also propose incorporating the algorithms into branch-and-bound, investigating parent-solution warm starts, and adapting the penalty parameter during solution.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be an end-to-end branch-and-bound evaluation that reports total runtime, node counts, and solution gaps against established exact methods. Further work could also test the algorithms on real experimental-design applications with practical selection constraints and make an implementation available for independent validation.

summary: This paper proposes Bootstrap Matching for estimating treatment effects when an A/B test or observational comparison does not have truly random treatment assignment. The method is intended for treatment and control groups with pre-treatment response data and measured features. It repeatedly samples subsets of subjects, performs matching within each subset, and averages the treatment-effect estimates; the authors suggest correcting the replicate significance results for multiple testing. In a real online advertising example, the treatment assignment used an identifier-ending rule and the groups were imbalanced before treatment. The paper reports that matching across bootstrap samples reduced this pre-treatment imbalance, but does not provide a numerical post-method treatment-effect result.
key_results: The advertising dataset contained approximately 400,000 observations over 12 days, with 6 days before and 6 days after treatment. The pre-treatment comparison showed imbalance, with a reported p-value below 0.01. The authors used 300 bootstrap replicates and sampled 10,000 observations per replicate; they describe the resulting pre-treatment balance as improved, while noting that some replicates remained substantially imbalanced. The raw-scale figure reports a treatment effect of -0.005 and a treatment p-value of 0.566, but the paper gives no numerical post-matching effect estimate, runtime measurement, or quantitative comparison against another method.

limitations_stated: The authors note that some bootstrap samples can still have substantial imbalance after matching. limitations_unstated: Repeated sampling and matching do not by themselves remove bias from unmeasured confounders, so causal interpretation still depends on assumptions the paper does not evaluate. future_work_stated: The authors propose improving computational efficiency for very large datasets, including exploring distributed computing and graphics processing unit acceleration. They also suggest improving matching criteria with machine learning and extending the method to time-varying treatments and longitudinal data.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test the procedure under controlled simulations with known treatment effects, unmeasured confounding, and varying degrees of overlap, and compare it with standard matching and other adjustment methods. Practical guidance is also needed on choosing the sample fraction and replicate count, defining acceptable balance, and validating the approach in additional operational experiments.

summary: This paper develops a sequential design method for maximum a posteriori (MAP) parameter estimation in linear structural dynamics, using frequency response data. To reduce costly evaluations of the structural model, it represents each response with a rational polynomial chaos expansion (RPCE), constructed as a ratio of polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs). Sparse Bayesian learning estimates the surrogate coefficients and their uncertainty, while Bayesian optimization adds new model evaluations at points selected using expected improvement (EI). The method is demonstrated on a two-degree-of-freedom system with simulated measurements and on a cross-laminated timber plate using measured data. In both examples, adaptive sampling produces more accurate MAP estimates than a fixed experimental design at comparable run sizes.
key_results: For the three-parameter two-degree-of-freedom example, with 15 initial evaluations and a budget of 50, the active method's global reward estimate had a median relative MAP error of 2.8 × 10^-5, compared with 2.2 × 10^-2 for the fixed-design RPCE estimate. The global reward estimate reached an error on the order of 10^-4 from about 35 training samples, while the simple reward estimate converged less accurately. In the four-parameter timber-plate example, with a budget of 35 evaluations, the global reward estimate had a median error on the order of 10^-4, compared with about 10^-2 for fixed design. The authors report that including surrogate-model error in expected-improvement sampling slightly improves accuracy, with little added cost.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the method trains a separate surrogate for every scalar response entering the likelihood, which can be computationally demanding for many observations. limitations_unstated: The demonstrations cover only two structural models, and the real-data application uses one timber plate and selected frequency intervals; the results therefore do not establish performance across a wide range of structural systems or measurement conditions. future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on additional structures, measurement setups, and independently collected datasets to assess robustness beyond the two demonstrations. It could also evaluate practical restrictions on where parameters or model evaluations may be chosen, and assess whether the sequential design remains effective when model evaluations are parallelized or performed under operational constraints.

summary: The paper develops a collaborative analysis method for estimating treatment effects in two A/B experiments conducted on a shared group of users. It models each outcome as an experiment-specific intercept and treatment effect, a shared user effect, and random error. For fully paired data, the method combines the separate-experiment and paired-difference estimates; it also adapts that combination to partially paired data. The authors derive large-sample properties and show that the method is asymptotically a best linear unbiased estimator under stated assumptions. key_results: The simulations used 100 replications and included sample sizes from 1,000 to 1,000,000 for the computational comparison; the proposed method had similar accuracy to the linear mixed-effects model and a growing computation-time advantage as sample size increased. In further simulations, with missing rates of 0.1 and 0.3 and sample sizes of 1,000 and 10,000, the proposed method generally had lower mean squared error than separate and paired analyses across the examined user-effect settings and continuous, binary, and count outcomes. future_work_unstated: Further work could test the estimators on real paired experiments with binary and count outcomes, and assess sensitivity to treatment-by-user variation and informative missingness. summary: The paper develops a method to reduce the input and output dimensions of a nonlinear model together, with particular attention to Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED). Its design objective is to find sensors that maximize information about a specified parameter quantity, using a computable lower bound on expected information gain (EIG). The method forms diagnostic matrices from model gradients and uses their eigenvectors to construct reduced subspaces; for coordinate sensor selection, it ranks diagonal entries of the output diagnostic matrix. An alternating eigendecomposition updates the input and output subspaces, while goal-oriented sensitivity analysis is another application of the framework. Simulations show that the method identifies useful sensors and produces coupled reductions that capture model relationships missed by separate principal component analysis (PCA).
key_results: For the conditioned-diffusion example, the authors estimated diagnostic matrices using 10,000 prior samples and found that the alternating procedure converged after three iterations across 10 random initializations. In that example, the coupled method had error and upper-bound values similar to the joint reduction method, and both improved more quickly as subspace dimensions increased than the compared PCA and canonical-correlation approaches. For the Burgers’ equation sensor study, they used 1,000 prior samples, selected 10 sensors, and evaluated EIG using 30 inner samples and 1,000 outer samples; the proposed sensor sets almost always had higher EIG than 250 random placements. The proposed selections generally performed similarly to sensors from the Fedorov–Wynn method, and outperformed that comparison for two of the reported goals where model linearization could be inaccurate. The paper also reports that derivative-based bounds closely tracked total Sobol’ indices in the conditioned-diffusion example.

summary: This paper develops methods for causal inference and experimental design when people’s outcomes can be affected by other people’s treatments through a network, but the network is only partly observed. The approach uses a structural causal model for outcomes and estimates the missing network structure with a generative graph model. It averages estimating equations over possible networks to estimate outcome-model parameters and supports inference for effects such as the global average treatment effect. For experimental design, it uses Bayesian optimization to select cluster treatment saturation levels that reduce estimator variance, and it also constructs model-based seeding strategies. Semi-synthetic studies based on village networks in India and Malawi show that partial-network methods can estimate effects and improve treatment allocation, although results depend on the assumed outcome and network models.
key_results: In semi-synthetic studies of the global average treatment effect, the aggregated relational data approach reduced estimation bias and error compared with difference-in-means and Horvitz–Thompson estimators, although regression using the full network performed best. For estimating the diffusion parameter alpha one, optimized designs using partial network data reduced root mean squared error by 38% (plus or minus 12%), compared with an 11% (plus or minus 2%) reduction for optimized designs with complete network data, both relative to uniform random designs. Across all model parameters, the corresponding reductions were 45% (plus or minus 10%) and 18% (plus or minus 2%). summary: This paper develops fixed-budget experimental designs for multi-fidelity computer experiments that use an autoregressive Gaussian process model. It extends the model to infinitely many fidelity levels by representing each level as the previous level plus an independent response increment whose variance decreases geometrically. The proposed multi-level Gaussian process (MLGP) design allocates runs across nested fidelity levels to reduce integrated prediction error under a cost budget. Its run allocations are derived from an error bound and use a simple construction rather than a numerical search over designs. The authors’ theoretical analysis and simulation studies support lower cost or improved prediction accuracy compared with the single-fidelity and other multi-fidelity designs they examine.
key_results: The authors prove that, asymptotically, the proposed design reaches a given prediction accuracy with lower cost order than any single-fidelity design under their assumptions. In the one-dimensional misspecification studies, mean root mean squared error (RMSE) was 0.2831 for MLGP versus 0.3441 for the classical multi-fidelity method and 0.3789 for the single-level method with a misspecified variance-decay parameter; with a misspecified smoothness parameter, the respective errors were 0.1652, 0.2127, and 0.2064. limitations_stated: The authors state that their theoretical analysis assumes quasi-uniform nested designs and that it is unclear how to obtain such designs efficiently. They use Halton sequences as computationally efficient, approximately quasi-uniform designs instead.
limitations_unstated: The empirical comparisons are based on simulated Gaussian-process response functions, with a limited set of dimensions, parameter settings, and competing designs; the paper does not validate the method on real computer-code experiments. limitations_unstated: The simulation comparisons use a particular balanced design and a limited family of generated potential-outcome patterns, so they do not establish performance across the range of block structures and outcome behavior encountered in practice. limitations_unstated: The evaluation is a synthetic case study and compares the proposed placement only with random placement, so the results do not establish performance against a wider range of design methods or in field deployments. summary: This paper develops a Bayesian design method for nonlinear models when the experiment is intended to improve predictions rather than estimate model parameters for their own sake. Its objective is to choose the design with the greatest expected information gain about predictive quantities of interest. The method uses nested sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo to draw parameter samples after simulated observations, kernel density estimation to approximate predictive densities, and Bayesian optimization to search the design space. The results show that designs selected for predictions can differ substantially from designs selected to learn parameters.
key_results: The standard nested-sampling settings were 1,000 outer and 1,000 inner samples; in one-dimensional tests, increasing both counts to 2,000 and 3,000 reduced variation while preserving the general utility trends and optimal design locations. In a non-bijective prediction example, the parameter-information optimum was at design value 1.0, while the prediction-information optimum was around 0.2, demonstrating that the two objectives can select different designs. For the convection-diffusion example, the neural-network surrogates had reported testing mean-squared errors around 10^-6 and 10^-7 for the two modeled times and accelerated each forward-model evaluation by about 10^5 times compared with the finite-volume solver. In the computational cost tests, at 1,000 outer and inner samples, the sampling share of per-iteration cost exceeded 65% and increased toward 100% as dimension increased; in the one-dimensional sample-size test, that share fell from about 80% at 1,000 inner samples to about 40% at 4,000.

Optimal design: \[d^*=\arg\max_{d\in\mathcal{D}}U(d)\] The optimal design d star is the design in the design space D that maximizes expected utility U.
limitations_stated: The method depends on Markov chain Monte Carlo and kernel density estimation. Sampling can be slow for complex posterior distributions and high-dimensional parameter spaces, leading to high estimator variance; finite density-estimation error and imperfect bandwidth tuning can bias utility estimates and shift the selected design, while frequent bandwidth retuning is expensive.
limitations_unstated: The sensor-placement examples use simulated model outputs and a trained surrogate, so they do not establish performance with field measurements or model error in an operating environmental system. future_work_unstated: Future studies could incorporate installation costs, inaccessible regions, and minimum distances between sensors directly into the design search, then test the resulting designs in real monitoring systems. summary: The paper develops a cost-efficient batch-sequential design for estimating two parameters in a binary response model with a complementary log-log link. It is motivated by switching measurements on Josephson junctions, where changing the current-pulse setting takes substantial time compared with a measurement. The authors use the dynamic programming principle (DPP) to choose when to update covariates, using a two-point D-optimal design and an approximate model for information growth. They formulate scheduling both to maximize information by a fixed final time and to reach a target information level in minimum time. Simulations show that the proposed scheduling can reduce time cost compared with earlier methods.
key_results: In the reported simulation, the authors ran 100 simulated paths for the proposed design and compared it with the approximate cost-efficient method of Karvanen (2009) and the earlier ad hoc method. The DPP design reduced time cost by 13.58% relative to the Karvanen (2009) method in that comparison. For the illustrative design, the final time was 3500 and the reported total time cost was 14.77313 seconds. The reported stages used 100, 98, and 2944 measurements, with accumulated D values of 0.14, 161.54, and 4945.63, respectively.

limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison centers on one simulated Josephson-junction setting and does not validate the scheduling method in real experiments. future_work_stated: The authors suggest applying the approach to other applications with batch data collection and update costs. They also mention considering the DPP approach with other optimality criteria; they note that information-growth functions have been estimated for logit and probit links.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the schedules in real switching measurements and assess sensitivity to errors in the assumed information-growth function and initial parameter estimates. summary: This paper designs sequential experiments to improve Gaussian process (GP) surrogates used in Bayesian inverse problems, where costly computer models link unknown inputs to observed outputs. Its objective is to reduce prediction uncertainty in regions that matter to the posterior distribution of the inputs. It proposes Inverse Problem Stepwise Uncertainty Reduction (IP-SUR), which minimizes the expected future value of a posterior-weighted uncertainty measure, and Constraint Set Query (CSQ), which maximizes predictive uncertainty within a region near the posterior maximum. The methods are intended to refine an existing surrogate rather than build its initial training set. Across three simulated test cases, both methods generally outperform standard D-optimal and I-optimal designs; IP-SUR also has a theoretical guarantee of almost sure convergence for its uncertainty measure.
key_results: The methods were tested for 20 added points per design strategy, with 100 repetitions and an initial training set of 10 input-output pairs. Average runtime per test case was 16, 14, and 18 seconds for CSQ, versus 235, 265, and 1,676 seconds for IP-SUR; the corresponding D-optimal runtimes were 3, 2, and 16 seconds, and the I-optimal runtimes were 136, 92, and 440 seconds. Both proposed methods generally improved the reported uncertainty and posterior-comparison measures more than D-optimal and I-optimal designs, particularly for the bimodal and four-dimensional neutron-noise cases. Against the Bayes-risk design of Sinsbeck and colleagues, the authors report broadly similar performance for the banana-shaped and neutron-noise cases, and more reliable results for their methods in the bimodal case; IP-SUR alone has the stated convergence guarantee among these compared methods.

limitations_stated: The authors say the proposed methods are for fine-tuning a surrogate and should not be used to construct its initial training set. IP-SUR is computationally more intensive than CSQ, while CSQ has no convergence guarantee and its performance can depend substantially on the chosen region-width parameter. The methods are developed for GP surrogates; the authors note that approximating the criterion for other surrogate types could jeopardize the convergence guarantee.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation uses simulated examples, including an analytical approximation for the neutron-noise application, rather than a real experiment or a full transport-model run. The comparisons cover three cases, only 20 added points per strategy, and a limited set of competing designs, so the results may not establish performance across other model structures, input dimensions, or operational constraints. IP-SUR also depends on posterior sampling and costly optimization, which may limit its practicality when those computations are themselves difficult.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring the method with surrogate models other than Gaussian processes, including approximate evaluation of the criterion, and investigating the robustness of such approximations and their effect on convergence guarantees. They also present a tempered version connecting the inverse-problem criterion to integrated mean squared prediction error as a possible extension.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate both designs on real engineering experiments and on cases where observations, priors, or the surrogate model are misspecified. It would also be useful to study practical constraints such as restricted or batch runs, sequential updating with changing observations, and ways to reduce the posterior-sampling and optimization burden.

summary: This paper develops a Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) method for selecting a fixed number of observations from a larger candidate set. Its objective is to maximize mutual information (MI) between the selected observations and unknown model parameters, which is also an expected measure of information gained about the parameters. The proposed logarithmic Sobolev inequality greedy (LSIG) method uses an inequality to bound information gain and then selects observations greedily using score and covariance matrices. This avoids repeatedly estimating MI during selection, a costly step for nonlinear, non-Gaussian models. Simulations show that LSIG is competitive with greedy selection based on nested Monte Carlo (NMC) MI estimates, and can outperform a Gaussian approximation in the nonlinear examples.
key_results: For the linear Gaussian example with 50 parameters and 50 candidate observations, LSIG produced MI values nearly indistinguishable from standard greedy selection, while random selection performed worse. In the epidemic example, the goal was to select 10 of 50 time points; LSIG and NMC-greedy had similar MI, and both outperformed the Gaussian approximation, which was only comparable to or slightly better than random selection. In the spatial Poisson example, which had 25 candidate cells and selected up to 10, LSIG’s MI exceeded the Gaussian approximation for every tested design size and exceeded NMC-greedy except at sizes 1 and 2. The reported leading costs are O(Mm) sample draws and model evaluations and O(nk³) linear algebra for LSIG, compared with O(nkMinMout) sample draws and model evaluations for NMC-greedy and O(nk⁴) linear algebra for the Gaussian approximation; for the nonlinear experiments, LSIG used 1,000 joint samples and 1,000 prior samples, whereas NMC used 10,000 inner and 1,000 outer samples.
key_equations:
Information-based design objective: \[A^\ast=\arg\max_{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\,|A|=k} I(X;Y_A)\] A is the selected index set, n is the number of candidate observations, k is the number to select, X is the unknown parameter, Y_A is the subset of observations indexed by A, and I denotes mutual information.

Logarithmic Sobolev information bound: \[I(X;Y)\leq\frac{\kappa}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\!\left[\left\|\nabla_y\log\pi_{X\mid Y}(X\mid Y)\right\|_{\Gamma}^{2}\right]\] I is mutual information, X is the parameter, Y is the observation vector, κ is the logarithmic Sobolev constant, the expectation is over the joint distribution of X and Y, ∇ with subscript y is the gradient with respect to observations, π is the conditional density of X given Y, and Γ defines the weighted squared norm.

Greedy matrix selection: \[i^\ast=\arg\max_{i\in A^c}\operatorname{diag}\!\left(F_{A^c}S_{A^c\mid A},i\right)\] i-star is the next candidate index, A is the set already selected, A-complement is the set of remaining indices, F is the score outer-product matrix restricted to those remaining indices, S is their covariance conditional on the selected observations, and diag of a matrix with index i denotes its ith diagonal entry.
limitations_stated: The bound relies on reference distributions satisfying the assumptions of the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, and the paper notes that determining the relevant reference measure and constants can be difficult in general. The method also requires gradients of the likelihood and estimates the observation-density score using Monte Carlo; the authors report that neural-network score estimates can make the score-matrix rankings sensitive. The authors state that they do not focus on theoretical optimization guarantees for the greedy procedure.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons cover three simulated models, with candidate pools of 50 observations or 25 spatial cells, so performance in larger or real industrial experiments is not established. The method’s rankings depend on estimated score and covariance matrices, but the paper does not provide a systematic study of how sampling error in those matrices changes the selected design or its achieved information.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to implicit models, where only samples are available and the likelihood and its gradient are intractable. They plan to use score-estimation tools that are more consistent and stable.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method on real experiments and candidate sets with practical constraints, such as costs, forbidden combinations, or limited measurement capacity. Further work could also evaluate sequential updating and compare alternative design objectives, while quantifying how score-estimation error affects design quality.

summary: The paper develops rerandomization methods for randomized experiments designed to improve covariate balance while preserving randomization-based inference. It focuses on experiments with covariates grouped by importance, stratified assignments, and multiple treatment arms, with treatment-effect estimation as the objective. The proposed method orthogonalizes contrast groups, calculates a squared Mahalanobis distance for each group, and accepts assignments using a weighted sum of those distances. Under stated asymptotic symmetry conditions, conditionally affinely invariant balance rules have equal percent variance reduction within each group. The authors show that their weighted-distance method is admissible, while common intersection rules can be inadmissible, and illustrate the method using a stratified factorial experiment dataset.
key_results: The theory shows that conditionally affinely invariant balance rules reduce variance equally across linear combinations within each relevant contrast group, under the paper’s asymptotic assumptions. The authors establish that weighted sums of the group-specific squared Mahalanobis distances form an admissible complete class for minimizing their conditional means, and show that intersection rules using separate thresholds are inadmissible when there is more than one group. In the dataset example, after 1,000,000 rerandomizations with an asymptotic acceptance probability of 0.001, the proposed weighted rule had lower mean distances than the intersection rule in all six groups: 2.16 versus 2.65, 85.34 versus 88.60, 18.86 versus 23.25, 0.99 versus 1.04, 38.13 versus 45.57, and 7.78 versus 12.46. The corresponding means under complete randomization were 8.41, 110.51, 33.89, 4.34, 55.90, and 15.36, respectively.
key_equations:

Squared distance for a canonical contrast: \[D_m = c_m^\top c_m\] For tier m, D_m is the squared Euclidean length of canonical contrast vector c_m, and the superscript T denotes vector transpose.

Asymptotic distance distribution: \[(D_1,\ldots,D_M) \overset{d}{\longrightarrow} (\chi^2_{k_1},\ldots,\chi^2_{k_M})\] As the sample size grows, the distances D_m converge jointly in distribution to independent chi-square variables, with k_m degrees of freedom for tier m.
limitations_stated: The authors evaluate balance criteria at a fixed asymptotic acceptance probability and note that finite-sample imbalance can remain when perfect balance is not achieved. They also note that collecting more covariates adds to experiment costs and identify the trade-off between covariate-collection cost and efficiency gain as future work.
limitations_unstated: The theoretical guarantees depend on asymptotic central limit and conditional ellipsoidal-symmetry assumptions, so their performance under substantial departures from those assumptions is not established here. The numerical illustration uses one dataset and focuses on the first blocking variable; it does not provide broad comparisons across varied sample sizes, covariate structures, or practical assignment constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing a framework for studying the trade-off between the efficiency gain from covariates and the cost of collecting them.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method under departures from the assumed limiting distributions and under uncertainty in the weights used to prioritize balance groups.
