Two-dimensional interference model: \[y_{ijk}=\mu+\beta_k+\tau_{d(i,j,k)}+\gamma_{d(i-1,j,k)}+\gamma_{d(i+1,j,k)}+\gamma_{d(i,j-1,k)}+\gamma_{d(i,j+1,k)}+\epsilon_{ijk}\] Here, y is the plot response, mu is the overall mean, beta is the block effect, tau is the direct treatment effect, gamma is the neighboring-treatment effect, epsilon is the error, and d assigns a treatment to row i, column j, and block k.

Treatment-effect information matrix: \[C_d=C_{d00}-C_{d01}C_{d11}^{-}C_{d10}\] Here, C_d is the information matrix for direct treatment effects, C_d00 is the direct-effect information component, C_d01 and C_d10 are cross-information components, and C_d11 is the information component for neighboring-treatment effects; the superscript minus denotes the generalized inverse used in the paper.

Scalar criterion for a design measure: \[q_{\xi}(x)=c_{\xi00}+2c_{\xi01}x+c_{\xi11}x^2,\qquad q_{\xi}^{*}=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}q_{\xi}(x)\] Here, xi is a design measure, x is a real scalar, q is the quadratic criterion, c with the indicated subscripts are its coefficients, and q-star is its minimum over real x.

Universal optimality condition: \[C_{\xi}=y^{*}\frac{B_t}{t-1}\] Here, C-xi is the treatment-effect information matrix under design measure xi, y-star is the maximum attainable scalar criterion, B-t is the treatment-contrast centering matrix, and t is the number of treatments.
limitations_stated: The authors identify the large number of possible block arrays as a major computational challenge and note that the number of symmetric block sets can grow rapidly. They also state that when the number of treatments is at least the number of plots per block, exact universally optimal designs rarely exist because the relevant scalar value is typically irrational, although highly efficient designs can be constructed.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes the neighboring effect depends on treatment but not on direction, so it does not distinguish effects from different directions. It also assumes no guard plots or edge effects, which may not reflect field experiments where boundaries matter; the paper's explicit theoretical description of the supporting arrays is limited to a special covariance structure.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future work could extend the design theory to direction-specific neighboring effects and to explicit boundary or guard-plot arrangements. It could also investigate construction methods under practical randomization and resource constraints, and validate the proposed designs in real field experiments.

summary: This paper develops sequential experimental designs for fitting sparse polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs) to computational models. Its objective is accurate prediction across the input space while limiting the number of model evaluations. The method begins with a space-filling design, uses least angle regression (LAR) to select a sparse polynomial basis from the observed responses, and then adds points selected using regression optimality criteria, including the S-value criterion. The authors compare the approach with space-filling and other sequential designs on four numerical models ranging from three to sixty-two input dimensions. The sequential S-value design generally gives the most accurate and stable predictions in those comparisons.
key_results: The study compares designs over 50 replications on four benchmarks: the three-dimensional Ishigami function, an eight-dimensional Sobol function, a ten-dimensional truss model, and a sixty-two-dimensional diffusion model. The sequential S-value design is reported to outperform the alternatives in prediction accuracy and to show less variability between replications; it also has a consistently smaller information-matrix condition number in the Ishigami comparison. The reported sequential runs start with 40 points and add 20 at a time for Ishigami, 100 and 50 for the eight- and ten-dimensional examples, and 100 and 20 for the diffusion example; the plotted design sizes reach 160, 1,500, 450, and 300, respectively. Sequential D-optimal designs perform poorly in the reported comparisons, while sequential maximin designs are useful at low to moderate dimensions but erratic at high dimension.
key_equations:
Polynomial surrogate model: \[f(x)\approx\sum_{j=1}^{K}c_j\psi_j(x)\] The response f at input x is approximated by a sum of K polynomial terms psi_j evaluated at x, each multiplied by its coefficient c_j, with j indexing the terms.

S-value criterion: \[S(A)=\left(\frac{\sqrt{\det(A^{\mathsf T}A)}}{\prod_{j=1}^{K}\|a_j\|}\right)^{1/K}\] The S-value S(A) for model matrix A combines the determinant of A transpose times A with the lengths of its columns a_j, and K is the number of columns.

Sequential design update: \[X_{t+1}=X_t\cup Z_t,\quad Z_t=\arg\max_{Z\subset X_L\setminus X_t,\ |Z|=N_{\rm new}}S(A_B(Z))\] At iteration t, the next design X at t plus one is the union of the current design X_t and selected batch Z_t; the batch contains N_new points chosen from candidate pool X_L outside the current design to maximize the S-value of model matrix A_B for selected basis B.
limitations_stated: The authors report that no reliable rule of thumb determines the initial design size or the number of points added per iteration; suitable choices may depend on the model and its sparsity. They also report erratic sequential maximin behavior in high dimensions and poor performance for the sequential D-optimal design in their tests.
limitations_unstated: The comparison covers four benchmark models and does not validate the method on data from real industrial experiments, so the reported advantage may not carry over to other response types or operating conditions. The procedure also depends on an initially adequate basis estimate and on searching a candidate pool, which may add design-selection effort beyond the cost of evaluating the model.
future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating other basis-selection methods, including orthogonal matching pursuit, and applying the approach to low-rank approximations. They also propose studying sequential adaptive designs for reliability analysis.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the design with noisy model evaluations and with dependent or constrained inputs, which are not part of the reported comparisons. It could also assess practical stopping rules and compare total computational effort, including the cost of selecting points, in real engineering experiments.

summary: The paper presents a method for predicting quantitative outcomes when high-resolution measurements are costly but threshold-based, categorical measurements are easier to obtain. It is demonstrated on molecular features for predicting antimalarial potency and aqueous solubility. The method extracts eigenvectors of feature correlations within coarse-label groups, then uses the quantitative measurements to fit the importance of those features in a quadratic model. This combines a linear model fitted to quantitative data with interactions informed by the coarse data. The authors report improved prediction over quantitative-only models in their examples and show how the method behaves in simulated energy landscapes.
key_results: For antimalarial potency, the dataset included 1,528 active compounds and quantitative potency measurements for 1,189 compounds; the authors report that combining coarse and quantitative data could achieve similar predictive accuracy with about an order of magnitude fewer quantitative measurements. For aqueous solubility, the method achieved a mean absolute error of 0.61 and a coefficient of determination of 0.85 using 90% of the 1,144-molecule dataset; the paper compares this favorably with a reported coefficient of determination of 0.83 for kernel partial least squares. In a simulated stratified-sampling example, using 500 quantitative measurements with the combined method recovered the interaction matrix with a mean absolute error of 0.12, compared with 0.31 using quantitative measurements alone. In that example, random-matrix cleaning alone did not recover the interaction matrix.
key_equations:
Quadratic prediction model: \[y=h^T f+f^T Jf+\epsilon\] Here y is the predicted quantitative outcome, h is the vector of individual-feature coefficients, f is the sample feature vector, J is the feature-interaction matrix, T indicates transpose, and epsilon is random measurement error.

Interaction matrix from coarse-data eigenvectors: \[J=\sum_k c_k u_k u_k^T\] Here J is the interaction matrix, the summation adds contributions over included eigenvectors indexed by k, c_k is the fitted weight for eigenvector u_k, u_k is an eigenvector derived from a coarse-label group, and T indicates transpose.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their Letter considers only an Ising-type model. They also show that eigenvalues can mis-rank informative eigenvectors when sampling is stratified or when energy-basin depth is not proportional to basin width, so eigenvalue-based cleaning alone may fail in those settings.
limitations_unstated: The paper does not quantify the relative costs of coarse and quantitative assays, so its claimed cost advantage depends on the actual cost difference in a given application. Its real-data demonstrations are limited to molecular prediction, and it does not evaluate how the method performs under practical experiment constraints such as restricted factor settings or run-order requirements.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest using overlaps between samples and the coarse-data eigenvectors as inputs to nonlinear models, such as an artificial neural network.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the approach in prospective experiments with realistic assay costs, thresholds, and constraints on which samples can be measured. It could also test sequential selection of quantitative measurements and assess performance across additional domains and model types.

summary: This paper develops methods for designing order-of-addition experiments, which study how the sequence of applying components affects a response. Its objective is to estimate effects efficiently while using fewer runs than a full set of component orders. The design represents each order through pairwise ordering factors and seeks balance among those factors, including through a new order-of-addition orthogonal-array definition. The author uses D-optimal search algorithms to find designs and also considers secondary balance measures, process factors, and restrictions on allowable orders. The paper reports useful balanced designs in 4, 5, and 6 components, and near-balanced designs in 7 components.
key_results: For 5 components and 15 runs, the paper found designs with a mean variance-inflation factor of 2.17 and D-efficiency of 0.96, compared with Van Nostrand’s design, which had a mean variance-inflation factor of 3.28 and D-efficiency of 0.79. The paper reports 12-run order-of-addition orthogonal arrays for 4 and 5 components and 24-run arrays for 5 and 6 components. For 7 components, no 24-, 36-, or 48-run orthogonal arrays were found in the reported searches; the best 24-run design had D-efficiency 0.990 and an average strength-2 chi-square measure of 0.07. The paper also demonstrates augmenting a 24-run, 5-component design with process factors and adapting the search to restricted component orders.
key_equations:
Main-effects model matrix: \[X=[\mathbf{1}\mid P]\] The model matrix X consists of a column of ones, written 1, and the pairwise ordering-factor matrix P.

D-optimal design criterion: \[\max \det(X^{\mathsf T}X)\] The search selects a candidate design to maximize the determinant of X transposed, written with T, multiplied by X.
limitations_stated: The author says the D-criterion is limiting for very small designs when the model matrix lacks full column rank. The paper does not provide a closed-form construction method and does not prove that D-efficiency of 1 is equivalent to D-optimality. The reported searches did not find orthogonal arrays for 7 components at the run sizes investigated.
limitations_unstated: The searches rely substantially on the main-effects model for pairwise ordering factors, while interactions may matter; the paper suggests interaction-aware analysis but does not evaluate how the proposed designs perform under such models. The failure to find larger-component orthogonal arrays in a finite search does not establish that none exist, and the numerical comparisons cover selected examples rather than a broad range of real experimental settings.
future_work_stated: The author proposes investigating whether D-efficiency of 1 implies D-optimality, finding closed-form constructions, and determining the largest component count for which arrays exist at given run sizes and strengths. The paper also calls for catalogs covering restricted orders and process factors, accessible software, structural study of non-isomorphic designs, and efficient chi-square search algorithms.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the designs in real experiments and compare their estimation performance when pairwise-order interactions or other response models are important. Research could also examine practical randomization and operational constraints, and assess whether designs can be augmented sequentially as experimental knowledge changes.

summary: The paper designs geographic clusters for randomized experiments in which users may move between regions, causing treatment interference. It introduces GeoCUTS, an algorithm that uses anonymized search-query locations and user movement patterns to build a weighted geographic graph and partition it into regions. The partitioning seeks to limit interactions across regions while keeping region sizes balanced. The authors also define the Q-metric for interference and the B-metric for balance, and connect the Q-metric to bias under a linear treatment-dose response model. On Google Search data, GeoCUTS performs comparably to hand-designed regions in the United States and better than a simple grid baseline on the reported interference measures.
key_results: The evaluation used one percent of Google Search data collected over 28 days, with about 11,000 United States grid nodes in one reported configuration; comparisons used about 200 clusters for the United States and about 50 for France. The query-weighted Q-metric for GeoCUTS was 92 percent for highly active and 85 percent for highly mobile United States data, matching the DMA results; the grid results were 91 percent and 81 percent. In France, GeoCUTS had query-weighted scores of 89 percent for highly active data and 79 percent for highly mobile data, compared with 86 percent and 77 percent for the grid. In the United States cut-size comparison, GeoCUTS had cut sizes 4 percent of the reported reference for both highly active and highly mobile data, compared with 7 percent for DMA and 15 percent or 14 percent for the grid, respectively; the paper also reports that GeoCUTS and linear embedding had the best cut sizes among the compared methods.

Q-metric and estimator bias relationship: \[Q_k=\sum_i\frac{a_{ik}^2}{a_{:k}a_{i:}},\qquad \bar Q=\frac{1}{M}\sum_k Q_k,\qquad \mathbb{E}_Z[\hat\tau]=TE+\beta(\bar Q-1)\] Q_k is the quality of region k, a_ik is the query count for user i in region k, a_:k is the total query count in region k, a_i: is the total query count for user i, Q-bar is the average region quality, M is the number of regions, the expectation is over treatment assignments Z, tau-hat is the difference-in-means estimate, TE is the treatment effect estimand, and beta is the dose-response coefficient.

GeoCUTS graph edge weight: \[w(AB)=\sum_u\sqrt{n_{uA}n_{uB}}\] w(AB) is the edge weight between location nodes A and B, u indexes users, and n_uA and n_uB are that user's visit counts at the respective locations.
limitations_stated: The authors note that query locations are approximate bounding boxes and that a small number of location samples may not reconstruct a cookie's movement path. They also point out that cookie churn and low query frequency can cause some users' movements to be underrepresented, so they evaluate separate highly active and highly mobile subsets.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses search-query cookies as proxies for users, so it may not capture movement or interference for other services or populations. The Q-metric's bias justification uses a linear dose-response model, and the paper does not validate that model or the method's treatment-effect performance in a prospective randomized experiment; the empirical comparison is also limited to two countries and a small set of partitioning baselines.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate GeoCUTS in prospective randomized experiments and test whether its interference and balance measures predict actual estimator bias and variance under different response patterns. Extend the method and comparisons to other services, locations, practical geographic constraints, and alternative treatment-effect models.

summary: The paper develops theory for weighted optimal experimental design in a linear model with parameters of interest and nuisance parameters. Its objective is to estimate a chosen system of estimable functions, possibly assigning different importance to those functions, using eigenvalue-based criteria such as A-optimality and E-optimality. The paper proves that this weighted objective is equivalent to ordinary optimality for an appropriately defined system of functions, and gives a construction that also works from a specified weight matrix. It extends the weight-matrix definition to singular matrices and systems that span only part of the estimation space. The main finding is theoretical equivalence, allowing methods already available for standard optimal design of functions to be used for weighted design.
key_results: For eigenvalue-based criteria, the paper proves that the information matrix for a system of estimable functions and its corresponding weighted information matrix have the same nonzero eigenvalues, including multiplicities. It also shows how to construct a system of estimable functions from a specified weight matrix so that the weighted and standard criteria are equivalent. The proposed weight matrix for a system of interest is the product of its coefficient matrix and its transpose; it applies even when the system is rank-deficient or the weight matrix is singular. The paper interprets weighted E-optimality as minimizing the largest weighted variance over functions in the weighted space, and weighted A-optimality as minimizing an average variance for an appropriately sized system of functions. It reports theoretical results and illustrative examples, but no numerical efficiency, run-size, or prediction comparisons.
key_equations:
Linear model: \[y = X(\xi)\tau + L\beta + \varepsilon\] The response vector y is modeled using the design matrix X under design ξ, the parameters of interest τ, the nuisance-effect matrix L and parameters β, and the error vector ε.

Information matrix for functions of interest: \[N_Q(\xi) = (Q^T C(\xi)^+ Q)^+\] The information matrix N_Q for the functions defined by coefficient matrix Q is formed from the design information matrix C, with the plus superscript denoting a generalized inverse.

Weight matrix for a system of functions: \[W_Q = QQ^T\] The weight matrix W_Q is formed from the coefficient matrix Q of the functions of interest.

Equivalence of weighted and standard criteria: \[\Phi(C_{W_Q}(\xi)) = \Phi(N_Q(\xi))\] For an eigenvalue-based criterion Φ, the weighted information matrix C_W under the weight matrix W_Q gives the same criterion value as the information matrix N_Q for the functions of interest, under the paper's feasibility conditions.
limitations_stated: The authors note that in rank-deficient systems the implied weights on the functions of interest need not equal their assigned primary weights. They also distinguish primary weights specified by experimenters from secondary weights implied for other functions, and limit the stated equivalence results to eigenvalue-based criteria.
limitations_unstated: The paper establishes equivalences theoretically but does not benchmark the proposed constructions in computation or compare their practical performance on real experiments. Its conclusions are developed for the stated linear model with uncorrelated errors and a fixed common estimation space, so the paper does not establish how robust the approach is to model misspecification or changing practical constraints.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to implement and benchmark the equivalent formulations for exact-design algorithms under realistic run-size, blocking, and resource constraints. Further work could also test the approach in real experiments and examine sequential design or settings with correlated errors and model misspecification.

summary: This paper reviews Bayesian experiment design and develops an approach for finding designs for multivariable generalized linear models (GLMs). It focuses on approximate coordinate exchange (ACE), which uses a Gaussian process emulator to smooth simulated estimates of design performance and searches one design coordinate at a time. The authors apply the method to logistic and Poisson regression designs that aim to reduce uncertainty about model parameters, and to a Gamma regression model for predicting paper-helicopter flight time. The helicopter model combines physical relationships from dimensional analysis with prior distributions for unknown parameters. In the examples, the Bayesian designs generally performed better than the selected comparison designs, with the size of the improvement depending on the model and objective.
key_results: For the 16-run logistic regression example, the design minimizing self-information loss (SIL) had about 10% lower negative expected Kullback-Leibler divergence than the pseudo-Bayesian determinant-based design, and both outperformed the central composite design. In the Poisson regression examples, the SIL designs and minimally supported pseudo-Bayesian designs performed very similarly for both prior settings tested. In the four-run paper-helicopter example, the squared-error loss (SEL) prediction design had average expected posterior variance around 8% lower than the V-optimal design, 11–12% lower than the two fractional factorial designs, and 11–17% lower than the maximin Latin hypercube designs. The comparisons used repeated Monte Carlo evaluations; the paper reports 20 repetitions with 20,000 simulations for these evaluations.
key_equations:
Generalized linear model: \[\eta(x)=f(x)^T\beta,\qquad g(\mu(x))=\eta(x)\] The input setting is x, the linear predictor is eta, the known model functions are f, the regression coefficients are beta, the link function is g, and the mean response is mu; the superscript T denotes transpose.

Bayesian expected-loss design criterion: \[\xi^*=\arg\min_{\xi\in X^n}\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\int_{\Psi}l(\xi,y,\psi)p(\psi,y\mid\xi)\,d\psi\,dy\] The optimal design is xi star; xi is a design in the design space X for n runs; y is the response in response space Y; psi is the model parameter; l is the loss; and p is the joint density of parameters and responses conditional on the design.

ACE coordinate update: \[x_{ij}\leftarrow\arg\min_{x\in X_j}\widehat{\Phi}_{ij}(x\mid\xi)\] The current coordinate x at run i and variable j is proposed to be replaced by the value minimizing the emulated expected loss; X sub j is the allowed range for variable j, Phi hat is the emulator, and xi is the current design.
limitations_stated: The authors state that Bayesian design remains computationally challenging for larger examples. They also caution that a single generic loss summary may not capture an experiment’s aims and that using prior information to shape a design may be unwelcome in some applications.
limitations_unstated: The examples rely on specified model forms and prior distributions, so the reported advantages may not hold if those assumptions poorly represent a real process. The paper evaluates a small set of examples through simulation-based comparisons; the four-run helicopter design, in particular, is assessed for prediction over a specified grid rather than validated in a new physical experiment.
future_work_stated: The authors do not state a specific future research project. They note that ACE can be used with different approximations to expected loss and report that it is implemented in the acebayes R package.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the designs in real industrial or scientific experiments and check whether their benefits persist when the assumed models and prior distributions are imperfect. Further work could also examine how practical restrictions, such as run costs or restricted randomization, affect the designs and their performance.

summary: The paper develops condition-number optimal designs, called K-optimal designs, for estimating regression parameters in linear models driven by Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes and sheets. It compares these designs with determinant-optimal, or D-optimal, designs for temporal sampling and spatial regular grids. The designs are constructed by deriving the information matrix from the OU covariance structure and optimizing either its condition number or determinant. The paper also studies equidistant designs, including grid refinement and expansion of the sampling region. Its main finding is that K-optimal designs can give lower estimation error than D-optimal designs for large covariance parameter values, when a non-collapsing K-optimal design exists.
key_results: For the restricted three-point temporal design, the D-optimal point is always at the midpoint, while a non-collapsing K-optimal design exists only when the covariance parameter is below 0.5718 or above 4.9586. For two-point temporal designs, the paper proves that a unique K-optimal design exists; for increasing-domain equidistant designs, the determinant criterion increases with spacing while the condition-number criterion has at least one global minimum. In the simulations, 10,000 samples were used for each example; for the temporal design, K-optimal performance was similar to D-optimal performance at small covariance values and superior in the upper parameter range. For the spatial nine-point designs, reported relative efficiencies of K-optimal versus D-optimal mean squared errors ranged from 88.90% to 115.33% in the displayed large-parameter table, with values below 100% indicating lower error for the K-optimal design. For sufficiently dense equidistant designs, doubling the grid density on a fixed region gives limiting criterion ratios of 1 for both criteria.

Design criteria: \[K(\xi)=\operatorname{cond}(I(\xi)),\qquad D(\xi)=\det(I(\xi))\] ξ is the sampling design, I(ξ) is its Fisher information matrix, K is its condition number, and D is its determinant; the K criterion is minimized and the D criterion is maximized.
limitations_stated: The paper assumes that the covariance parameters of the driving OU process and sheet are known. It focuses on linear regression trends and particular temporal designs and spatial regular grids, and presents the results as an initial investigation of K-optimality with correlated errors.
limitations_unstated: The simulations and numerical comparisons cover a small set of restricted designs and parameter settings, so they do not establish performance for general design spaces or other regression functions. The paper does not evaluate sensitivity to covariance-model misspecification or practical constraints such as inaccessible sampling locations and unequal measurement costs.
future_work_stated: The authors identify estimation of the OU covariance parameters, rather than treating them as known, as a direction for further research. They also suggest extending the results to other regression basis functions and covariance structures.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess K-optimal designs under realistic constraints on location, cost, and measurement availability, and test their performance using real experiments. It could also develop sequential design procedures that update sampling locations as covariance and regression parameters are learned.

summary: This paper studies whether experimenters can monitor A/B tests continuously and stop them early when using Bayesian hypothesis testing. It considers a normal-mean model, first with a specified treatment effect and then with a composite alternative that assigns a normal prior to the effect. The method calculates the Bayes factor using all observations collected up to the stopping time, with a stopping rule based only on information already observed. The authors prove that the posterior odds retain their Bayesian interpretation under any such proper stopping rule that stops in finite time with probability one. Simulations illustrate the result and show that early stopping can reduce the amount of data collected while changing rejection rates and power.
key_results: In simulations with 100,000 runs, a sample size of 100, and a Bayes-factor cutoff of 9, the fixed-horizon design had a false rejection rate of 0.018, power of 0.465, and false discovery rate of 0.037. With one-sided early stopping, these were 0.060, 0.599, and 0.09; two-sided early stopping gave 0.060, 0.598, and 0.09. The average run length with early stopping was about 55 rather than the fixed sample size of 100; early stopping occurred in 59.5% of runs under the alternative in the one-sided design and in 64.9% under the alternative and 65.0% under the null in the two-sided design. The paper also reports a simulation for a composite alternative with sample size 1,000 and a normal prior with standard deviation 0.1; its figures illustrate that the observed ratios between alternative and null runs track the calculated Bayes factors under both fixed-horizon and early-stopping designs.
key_equations:

Bayes factor for the specified-effect model: \[BF_N=\exp\left\{\frac{N}{2}\delta(2\bar X-\delta)\right\}\] BF sub N is the Bayes factor after N observations, exp is the exponential function, delta is the specified effect, and X-bar is the sample mean.

Posterior odds: \[O_{\mathrm{post}}=O_{\mathrm{prior}}\,BF\] O-post is the posterior odds of the alternative relative to the null, O-prior is the corresponding prior odds, and BF is the Bayes factor.

Posterior-odds interpretation at stopping: \[\frac{P(H_1\mid O_{\mathrm{post},\tau}=K)}{P(H_0\mid O_{\mathrm{post},\tau}=K)}=K\] P denotes probability, H1 and H0 are the alternative and null hypotheses, O-post at tau is the posterior odds at the stopping time, tau is the stopping time, and K is the observed posterior-odds value.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their result depends on using a proper stopping rule based only on present and past information and on calculating the Bayes factor from all observations available at stopping. They caution that the theorem does not cover peeking into future data, selecting only some observations, or repeatedly testing new experiments while ignoring evidence from earlier runs. They also take the models’ assumptions as given and note that Bayesian testing requires choices about the prior and the alternative distribution.
limitations_unstated: The simulations use simplified normal-mean models and a limited set of stopping rules and cutoffs, so they do not establish how the reported efficiency and performance would transfer to varied real-world A/B-test metrics or constraints. The paper supplies theoretical results and simulated examples, but no validation on real experiments or broad numerical comparison across alternative design choices.
future_work_stated: The authors identify properly combining evidence from repeated, nonidentical experiment runs as a challenge and point to preliminary work on the topic. They also describe learning prior settings from historical experiments as a practical approach, while noting that the general problem of objective prior learning is outside this paper’s scope.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method with real A/B-test data, non-normal outcomes, and operational constraints such as delayed metrics or required minimum run durations. Comparisons across stopping rules and priors, along with accessible software for calculating the sequential Bayes factors, would help engineers apply and validate the approach.

summary: This paper develops methods for placing a fixed number of design points to cover a design region as uniformly as possible in the worst case. The target is a minimax design for computer experiments and other coverage tasks, including sensor placement. The authors construct the design by repeatedly assigning representative region points to their nearest design point and updating each cluster center to reduce its largest distances; particle swarm optimization is added to search beyond local solutions. They also refine these designs to improve coverage when projected onto lower-dimensional subspaces. Simulations and a Georgia air-monitoring example show better worst-case distance results than the compared methods, while the projection refinement improves projected coverage.
key_results: For design sizes from 20 to 100 on the tested hypercubes, simplex, ball, and Georgia region, the proposed method generally had the lowest reported minimax distance among the compared methods: binary integer programming, principal points, and fast flexible space-filling designs. For a 7-point two-dimensional design, its minimax distance was within 0.001 of the reported global minimum. With 100,000 representative points, reported computation time ranged from 15 to 90 seconds in two dimensions and from 4 to 8 minutes in eight dimensions; binary integer programming took nearly 30 minutes per design, while principal points and fast flexible space-filling designs were faster but generally had worse minimax results. For 60-point designs in eight dimensions, the projection refinement improved projected minimax and average-distance measures relative to the compared designs, but performed worse on the projected maximin measure.
key_equations:
Minimax design criterion: \[\min_{D\subseteq X,\ |D|=n}\ \sup_{x\in X}\ \min_{m\in D}\|x-m\|_2\] Here X is the design region, n is the number of design points, D is their set, x is any region location, m is a design point, and the Euclidean norm measures distance.

Cluster-center update: \[C_q(Z)=\arg\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^p}\frac{1}{|Z|}\sum_{z_i\in Z}\|z-z_i\|_2^q\] Here C_q(Z) is the center for cluster Z, z is a candidate center, z_i are points in that cluster, q is the distance exponent, p is the dimension, and the Euclidean norm measures distance.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the clustering method is developed for convex and bounded regions, although they demonstrate its use on Georgia because they judge that region to be convex enough for the center updates. They note that minimax designs on irregular regions can look visually non-uniform, and that the projection refinement can slightly increase the measured minimax distance when distances are estimated from a finite representative set.
limitations_unstated: The method optimizes geometric distance rather than prediction error under a specified response or emulator model, so its value for prediction depends on whether Euclidean distance reflects the experiment’s input effects. The comparisons cover selected algorithms, dimensions up to eight, and a small set of regions; the Georgia example evaluates geometric coverage rather than actual monitoring performance or prediction accuracy.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying minimax designs under norms other than Euclidean distance, including whether alternatives could improve high-dimensional projected coverage. They also suggest testing more sophisticated ways to combine particle swarm optimization with clustering to obtain better designs with fewer computational resources.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the designs using emulator prediction errors on simulators with different response surfaces and degrees of input sparsity. It would also be useful to evaluate practical constraints such as forbidden or costly locations, unequal input scaling, and sequential addition of runs, and to validate sensor allocations against observed environmental measurements.

summary: The paper develops a randomization-based method for estimating causal effects in a two-factor, two-level split-plot experiment. It targets the population average effects of each factor and their interaction, including when treatment allocations are unbalanced. The design assigns one factor at the block level and randomizes the other factor among units within each block; the authors derive sampling variances from between-block and within-block potential-outcome covariances. They also construct conservative variance estimates and corresponding interval estimates. Simulations report better coverage than the comparison methods in many of the settings studied, particularly where those methods under-cover.
key_results: The method gives unbiased estimates and a closed-form sampling variance that separates between-block and within-block contributions; under strict additivity, balanced designs minimize the reported sampling variances. Simulations used 1,000 randomizations per setting, a nominal 95% interval level, and block and within-block sizes of 40 and 80. For potential-outcome type II under strict additivity with sizes 40 and 40, coverage for the whole-plot effect was 95.0% for the proposed method, compared with 0.0% for complete-randomization, generalized linear model, and mixed-model intervals; the other two effects had 100.0% coverage for all four methods. Under type II with no additivity assumption, proposed-method coverage was 99.3%, 99.7%, and 98.7% for the whole-plot, sub-plot, and interaction effects, compared with 33.9%, 42.3%, and 36.8% for complete-randomization intervals. The authors report similar overall patterns for sizes 80 and 80, though those results are not shown.

Estimated factorial effect: \[\hat{\tau}_F=\frac{1}{2}g_F^\top(\bar{Y}_{obs}(1),\bar{Y}_{obs}(2),\bar{Y}_{obs}(3),\bar{Y}_{obs}(4))^\top\] τ̂_F is the estimated effect for F, g_F is its contrast vector, and Ȳ_obs(k) is the observed outcome average among units assigned to treatment k, for treatments 1 through 4.

Split-plot sampling variance: \[\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_F)=\frac{(W-1)M}{4}g_F^\top(C_{btw}\circ S^2_{btw})g_F+\frac{W(M-1)}{4}g_F^\top(C_{in}\circ S^2_{in})g_F\] Var is the sampling variance under the split-plot randomization, τ̂_F is the estimated effect, F identifies the effect being estimated, g_F is its contrast vector, W is the number of blocks, M is the units per block, C_btw and C_in are coefficient matrices, S²_btw and S²_in are the corresponding between-block and within-block potential-outcome covariance matrices, and ◦ denotes entrywise multiplication.
limitations_stated: The authors do not give a formal limitations section. They state that space limitations constrained further development and identify extensions to other split-plot forms as areas for further exploration.
limitations_unstated: The simulations use balanced factor allocations, even though the method is intended to handle unbalanced allocations, and use only two reported block and within-block sizes; they do not validate the method on a real experiment. The analysis assumes equal block sizes, so its results do not directly establish performance for unequal-sized blocks, and the interval justification is asymptotic as the numbers of blocks and units per block increase.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending Bayesian causal inference to split-plot designs while preserving frequency properties, developing randomization tests for sharp unit-level null hypotheses, and extending the results to multi-level factors, more factors, and more complex split-plot designs.
future_work_unstated: Further work could develop and validate variance estimates for unequal block sizes and for practical constraints beyond the allocation imbalance treated here. summary: The paper develops Bayesian optimal designs for experiments whose statistical models depend on solutions to nonlinear ordinary differential equations. At 7 placentas, the parameter-estimation designs generally used early observation times and treatments unlike the experimenters’ original treatments, while the model-selection design placed most observation times later in the interval. summary: This paper studies two-stage adaptive dose-response designs for Phase II pharmaceutical studies, with the aim of estimating the full dose-response curve efficiently. It compares updating the second-stage allocation using a maximum likelihood (ML) point estimate with updating it using the full posterior distribution of the parameters. The model used for design is a four-parameter sigmoid Emax model, and the design objective is D-optimality. To make Bayesian design calculations faster, the authors approximate posterior samples with a weighted set of k-means cluster centers. In simulations, Bayesian updating generally performed better than ML updating, especially when the interim analysis occurred early, while the benefit of adaptation depended on the starting design.
key_results: The evaluation covered 448 scenarios, with 5,000 simulated trials per scenario and total sample sizes of 150 or 250. Bayesian updating generally had higher second-stage design efficiency and lower variability than ML updating, with the clearest advantages at early interim analyses; the two approaches became more similar as the first-stage sample increased. The advantage of adapting was strongly dependent on the starting design: starting design C had efficiencies from 0.03 to 0.22 across the four simulated dose-response profiles, while several other starting designs had efficiencies above 0.8 in some profiles. For the posterior approximation, the reported average relative efficiencies were 0.915, 0.961, and 0.976 for first-stage sample sizes of 15, 60, and 150, respectively; in one scenario, its average design-calculation time was 7.7 seconds versus 124.9 seconds using the full posterior.
key_equations:
Assumed sigmoid dose-response model: \[Y_{ij}=\theta_1+\theta_2\frac{x_i^{\theta_4}}{\theta_3^{\theta_4}+x_i^{\theta_4}}+\epsilon_{ij},\quad \epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\] Yij is the response for patient j at dose xi; theta1 is the placebo effect, theta2 the maximum treatment effect, theta3 the half-maximum dose, theta4 the steepness parameter, epsilonij the independent normal error, and sigma the error standard deviation.

Information matrix: \[M(w,\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{q}w_i g_i(\theta)^Tg_i(\theta)\] M is the information matrix, w_i is the proportion allocated to dose i, theta is the parameter vector, q is the number of available doses, and g_i(theta) is the gradient of the dose-response model at dose i.

Bayesian D-optimality criterion: \[\Psi_B(w)=E_{\theta\mid y^{(1)}}[\log\det M(w,\theta)]\] PsiB is the Bayesian design criterion, w is the allocation vector, theta is the parameter vector, y^(1) is the first-stage data, M is the information matrix, and the expectation is over the posterior distribution of theta given that data.

Cluster approximation of the Bayesian criterion: \[\Psi_B(w)\approx\sum_{l=1}^{K}\alpha_l\log\det M(w,a_l)\] PsiB is the approximated Bayesian criterion, w is the allocation vector, K is the number of posterior clusters, alpha_l is the posterior-sample proportion in cluster l, a_l is that cluster's center, and M is the information matrix.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their focus is parameter uncertainty rather than model uncertainty, and they use the sigmoid Emax model for design updating. They also note that Bayesian updating depends on the prior, especially with an early interim analysis, and that adaptation does not improve performance in every setting.
limitations_unstated: The design update assumes the sigmoid Emax form even when the simulated true response is linear or quadratic, so the results do not establish performance when the working model is more seriously misspecified. The evaluation is based on simulated dose-response settings with fixed dose grids and allocation changes; it does not establish how the approach performs under practical constraints such as safety limits, recruitment changes, or restricted randomization.
future_work_stated: The authors propose evaluating an update-on-demand strategy: assess the starting design's efficiency at interim and update only when it falls below a threshold. They also suggest that accurate, valid informative priors could further improve Bayesian updating.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the procedure with operational and safety constraints, including restricted dose use and allocation rules, and to validate it in real pharmaceutical studies. Further work could also test design updating under explicit model uncertainty and compare whether the results hold for objectives other than estimating the full curve with D-optimality.

summary: The paper develops universally optimal block designs for estimating direct treatment effects when treatments can affect plots immediately to their left and right. It also studies a model in which the left- and right-neighbor effects are equal. The design calculations allow an arbitrary positive definite within-block covariance matrix and cover general numbers of treatments and plots per block. The author derives conditions for universal optimality and a system of linear equations for finding sequence proportions that meet those conditions. The paper also shows that, for persymmetric covariance matrices, a design’s efficiency under the equal-neighbor model is at least its efficiency under the separate-neighbor model.
key_results: For a four-treatment, four-plot example with 10 blocks, the reported A-, D-, E-, and T-efficiencies are 0.9943, 0.9946, 0.9682, and 0.9949. A design with 24 blocks is reported to be universally optimal for four treatments and five plots per block. With five treatments and five plots per block, a particular symmetric-block design has efficiency 0.9999 under all four criteria when the adjacent-plot covariance parameter is 0.5, while the compared type-I orthogonal-array design has efficiency 0.8232; at parameter value 0.9, that array design’s efficiency falls to 0.3395. For four treatments and three plots per block, the figure reports exact-design efficiencies for block counts from 5 to 50, illustrating that the proposed equations can produce efficient designs at different run sizes.

summary: The paper develops block designs for experiments with naturally ordered treatments when the goal is to estimate differences between consecutive treatments. They allow nonbinary blocks, in which a treatment can appear more than once within a block, when needed. The examples show that small exact designs can have high efficiency and that some can be nested for experiments conducted in stages.

For seven treatments, block size five, and nine blocks, the constructed design has efficiency 0.9992 and includes nonbinary blocks. For six treatments and block size three, nested designs with 10, 11, and 12 blocks have efficiencies 0.9547, 0.9578, and 0.9785, respectively. limitations_unstated: The method assumes fixed block size and the stated additive model with homoscedastic, uncorrelated errors; its performance under model misspecification or unequal error variances is not evaluated. summary: The paper introduces a general way to represent practical experimental-design restrictions as limits on the use of multiple resources. Their numerical results show that the heuristic produces highly efficient designs and often matches or outperforms methods tailored to narrower constraint types.
key_results: For a block model with 16 treatments and run sizes from 15 to 120 blocks, the heuristic generally matched or exceeded simulated annealing, with reported exceptions at sizes 28, 36, 53, 54, 55, and 78; it also found theoretically D-optimal designs for the listed run sizes from 64 through 120. summary: The paper studies exact designs for estimating parameters of a shifted Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) sheet, a stationary Gaussian field with exponential correlation, when measurement locations must increase in both coordinates. For covariance-parameter estimation alone and for joint estimation of trend and covariance parameters, the authors prove that an optimal design does not exist within the admissible monotonic class. In the thermal-field example, the reported efficiencies are 0.99, 0.978, and 0.999 for the three listed correlation-parameter settings. summary: The paper develops graph cluster randomization for estimating the average effect of a treatment when people’s outcomes can be affected by their neighbors’ treatment assignments. It models exposure as a set of assignments under which an individual’s outcome is assumed to match the outcome in the all-treatment or all-control universe. The method groups nearby vertices into clusters, randomizes treatment at the cluster level, and uses exposure probabilities to construct an unbiased Horvitz-Thompson estimate when the exposure model is correctly specified. The authors give an exact dynamic program for probabilities under several neighborhood exposure conditions and propose a three-net clustering procedure for graphs with restricted neighborhood growth. Their main theoretical finding is that this clustering can give variance that grows linearly, rather than exponentially, with vertex degree under the stated graph and outcome conditions.
key_results: For a cycle graph, the derived variance is minimized when clusters contain three vertices, matching the size of a vertex’s neighborhood in that graph. For powers of a cycle with degrees from the tested cases, simulations used 5,000 vertices and one million cluster randomizations; the cluster size giving the reported linear-in-degree behavior was 2k + 1, where the degree is 2k. The authors prove a linear-in-degree variance upper bound for their three-net clustering on restricted-growth graphs, while vertex-level randomization under full-neighborhood exposure has a variance lower bound that grows exponentially with degree. For neighborhood exposure probabilities under cluster randomization, the exact dynamic program runs in O(dmax s) time, where dmax is the maximum degree and s is the number of clusters connected to the vertex.
key_equations:
Average treatment effect between the two universes: \[\tau=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[Y_i(\mathbf{1})-Y_i(\mathbf{0})\right]\] The average treatment effect τ is the mean over n vertices indexed by i of each vertex’s outcome Yᵢ when everyone is treated, denoted by the all-ones assignment, minus its outcome when everyone is in control, denoted by the all-zeros assignment.

Horvitz-Thompson effect estimate: \[\hat{\tau}(Z)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{Y_i(Z)1[Z\in\sigma_i^1]}{\pi_i^1}-\frac{Y_i(Z)1[Z\in\sigma_i^0]}{\pi_i^0}\right]\] The estimated effect τ̂ averages across n vertices the observed outcome Yᵢ under randomized assignment Z, weighted by an indicator that Z is in the vertex’s treatment or control exposure set σᵢˣ and divided by that exposure probability πᵢˣ.

Restricted-growth graph condition: \[|B_{r+1}(v)|\leq\kappa|B_r(v)|\] For every vertex v and positive radius r, the number of vertices in its neighborhood of radius r plus one is at most κ times the number in its radius-r neighborhood.

Three-net cluster construction: \[D(u,v)>2\ (u\ne v,\ u,v\in S),\qquad V=\bigcup_{v\in S}B_2(v),\qquad C_v=\{w\in V:v\in\arg\min_{u\in S}D(u,w)\}\] The centers u and v in S are more than two graph steps apart, their radius-two neighborhoods cover the vertex set V, and each vertex w is assigned to the closest center v to form cluster Cᵥ, with ties resolved consistently.
limitations_stated: The authors provide variance guarantees for restricted-growth graphs but state that they do not give guarantees for arbitrary graphs clustered using general partitioning or community-detection methods. They also note that efficient exact computation of core-exposure probabilities is unclear and do not pursue a direct Monte Carlo estimate of those probabilities.
limitations_unstated: The estimate’s unbiasedness depends on the chosen exposure conditions matching the outcome process; the paper itself notes that misspecification can introduce bias. The empirical evaluation is limited to simulated cycle-based examples, while the main guarantees rely on restricted-growth structure and specified outcome conditions, so performance in real experiments and under practical allocation constraints remains untested.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing a computationally tractable objective for minimizing estimator variance and exploring whether clusterings that minimize variance in an A/A experiment can help with treatment-effect experiments. They also suggest using continuous exposure-response structure and adding methods to analyze bias from exposure-model misspecification.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method in real online experiments and compare estimates and uncertainty against existing network-experiment designs. Further work could also adapt the clustering and estimator to operational constraints such as unequal cluster assignment probabilities, limited treatment capacity, or changing networks.

summary: This paper develops simulation-based Bayesian design methods for models that can be simulated but whose likelihood is not available in analytical form. The goal is to choose design settings that maximize expected utility, including expected information gain, while using prior observations to update beliefs about model parameters. The authors combine approximate Bayesian computation with Markov chain Monte Carlo design search, and describe both a direct augmented-target approach and a two-stage approach that first estimates the parameter posterior. They test the methods on a quadratic regression example where the exact answer is also available. The two-stage approach recovers the known optimal designs in one and two dimensions, while the direct approach becomes difficult when the utility target is raised to higher powers.
key_results: In the direct method, chains of 10^8 iterations took 2.25 to 3 minutes; across the tested tolerance values, acceptance rates ranged from 0.0048 to 0.0170 and integrated autocorrelation times ranged from 44.01 to 12.28. For the two-stage method, posterior particle sets of 5,000, 10,000, and 20,000 gave results close to the exact posterior; in the one-dimensional example, computing 20,000 particles took 13.71 minutes compared with 3.41 minutes for 10,000, with little reported gain from the larger set. In the two-dimensional example, posterior sets of those sizes took 0.85, 3.35, and 13.39 minutes, respectively, and the design samples for J = 200 concentrated near the exact optima, (0, 1) and (1, 0); the longest second-stage run took 1.19 minutes. In the one-dimensional example, the known optimum is the design setting 1, and the two-stage sampler concentrated near it as J increased to 200, although acceptance fell to 0.0078 and the integrated autocorrelation time rose to 524.14.

Augmented target for utility search: \[h_J(z_{1:J},d,\theta_{1:J})\propto\left[\prod_{j=1}^{J}u(z_j,d,\theta_j)p(z_j\mid\theta_j,d)p(\theta_j\mid y,\xi)\right]\mu(d)\] h is the augmented target distribution, J is the number of utility contributions, j indexes those contributions, z_j and theta_j are simulated data and parameters, d is the design, u is utility, p denotes probability densities, y and xi are prior data and its design settings, and mu is a measure over designs.

ABC approximation to the posterior: \[p_\epsilon(\theta,x\mid y)\propto p_\epsilon(y\mid x,\theta)p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\] p with tolerance epsilon is the approximate posterior density, theta is the parameter, x is simulated data, y is observed data, and p denotes the model and prior densities.
limitations_stated: The authors note that choosing the ABC tolerance and its schedule, the number of simulations per update, and the schedule for increasing J can strongly affect performance; a sufficiently large simulation count may be computationally prohibitive. They also report that the direct augmented-target approach is unsuitable for higher-dimensional design problems when a large J is needed, and that the population Monte Carlo posterior-estimation step has computational complexity of order N squared.

The study does not validate the method with real experimental data or examine practical restrictions such as run costs, discrete settings, or constrained randomization.
future_work_stated: The authors say they expect to compare their likelihood-free design variants with the independently developed approach of Drovandi and Pettitt. They also describe sequential Monte Carlo extensions as a way to support adaptive design.
future_work_unstated: Further work could benchmark the methods on real experiments and on nonlinear or stochastic models with genuinely unavailable likelihoods, measuring whether the chosen design improves outcomes under realistic operating constraints. summary: This paper develops space-filling Latin hypercube designs (LHDs) for computer experiments, starting from nearly orthogonal arrays (NOAs) constructed from stars in finite projective geometry. Its construction connects the randomization restrictions represented by randomization defining contrast subspaces (RDCSSs) to the columns of an array, then converts that array into an LHD. The authors give conditions guaranteeing that these arrays exist and propose three guidelines for choosing the generators that produce them. In a worked example, designs following all three guidelines have larger reported distance measures than examples violating one or more guidelines. The paper considers deterministic simulators and does not assume a particular response or prediction model.

For a 16-run, three-factor example, the design following all three guidelines has a minimum interpoint distance (MID) of 0.2724 and an average interpoint distance (AID) of 0.6910; examples violating the first or second guideline report MID values of 0.1875 and AID values of 0.6896 or 0.6867, while the example violating the third reports 0.1531 and 0.6793. The simulation generates 100 random arrays for each of the three single-guideline violations and the no-violation case, and both distance measures favor designs satisfying all guidelines. In that comparison, violating the third guideline is most damaging, while the relative damage from violating the first or second is not consistent across both measures.

limitations_stated: The authors state that their three guidelines are not exhaustive and are somewhat ad hoc rather than designed to optimize either distance measure. future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare prediction accuracy and space-filling performance against conventional orthogonal-array and optimized maximin designs across a wider range of run sizes and dimensions. summary: This paper evaluates how dependence between users and items affects uncertainty estimates in online experiments that aim to estimate treatment effects. It develops a crossed random-effects framework and compares independent-observation, one-way, and multiway bootstrap methods for constructing confidence intervals. The evaluation uses Facebook click data for advertisements, search results, and News Feed stories to create same-versus-same (A/A) tests, along with simulations from a probit random-effects model. The authors find that ignoring dependence can substantially inflate false positives, while accounting for dependence among users assigned to conditions is often adequate under the sharp null. When treatment effects interact with items, accounting for both users and items can be important for reliable coverage.
key_results: Across all three datasets, the independent-observation bootstrap performed poorly, and its nominal 95% confidence intervals became increasingly anti-conservative as data accumulated. After two weeks, the paper reports that a search comparison between equivalent user groups could reject the null nearly 50% of the time using that method. In the A/A evaluations, each bootstrap method was assessed using 500 comparisons and 500 reweightings per comparison; user-level intervals had advertised or conservative error rates under the sharp null, while multiway intervals were conservative. In simulations, a nominal 95% interval from the user bootstrap covered the true value only 87.5% of the time for item-effect standard deviation 0.5 and treatment-control item-effect correlation 0.75, whereas the multiway bootstrap remained mildly conservative.

limitations_unstated: The operational data come from one company and concern click-through outcomes in three product areas, so the empirical findings may not transfer to other industries, outcome types, or dependence patterns. The synthetic tests and simulations also cover selected assignment structures and modeled item interactions, rather than a broad range of real treatment effects and operational constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing more sophisticated ways to perturb existing data and using additional parameters estimated from real experiments to make evaluations more like field outcomes. future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the bootstrap comparisons in randomized field experiments across different industries and outcome types, including settings with more than two dependent unit types. In the detergent example, three products are ranked as P1 first and P2 and P3 tied second; the example describes four replications. In the classroom example, the ranking is classrooms 1 and 2 tied first, with classroom 3 third, using 25 pupils per classroom and 75 pupils in total. summary: This study examines how compiler options affect the energy use and execution time of embedded software. summary: This paper derives a minimal Markov basis for conditional exact tests of main effects in half-fraction factorial designs with two-level factors, where the design resolution equals the number of factors. summary: This paper develops gradient-based methods for Bayesian experimental design when the objective is expected information gain about unknown model parameters. It presents Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation and sample average approximation combined with the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno method. The methods use gradients derived from a nested Monte Carlo estimate, with a polynomial chaos surrogate to make repeated model evaluations and gradient calculations less costly. The authors test the methods in a simulated environmental-monitoring problem: choosing one sensor location to infer a contaminant source location from measurements generated by a diffusion model. In that example, both methods tend to identify domain corners as informative sensor locations, and Robbins-Monro generally obtains lower error than the sample-average approach at comparable computational effort.
key_results: The comparison used 1,000 independent optimization runs for each method across outer sample counts of 1, 11, and 101 and inner sample counts of 2, 11, 101, and 1,001. The polynomial chaos surrogate used a total-order polynomial of degree 12 and 1,000,000 forward-model evaluations; reported relative L2 errors ranged from 6 × 10^-3 to 10^-6. In the sensor-placement example, the four corners of the square domain were optimal and the center was worst; with the largest sample counts, approximately 250 runs selected each corner. The authors report that Robbins-Monro consistently achieved lower mean square error than sample average approximation with Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno at comparable computational effort, while noting that the advantage was small and could depend on the problem and implementation. Deterministic Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno runs usually found a local maximum in fewer than 10 iterations, whereas Robbins-Monro runs could continue to the 50-iteration maximum used in the experiments.

limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison is limited to one simulated two-dimensional source-inversion problem with one sensor, a uniform prior, and a specific noise model; it does not establish performance across other physical systems, parameter dimensions, or design constraints. summary: The paper develops a method for selecting experiments to infer parameters in nonlinear models that may be expensive to simulate. The method uses a Bayesian objective: choose the experimental conditions expected to provide the greatest information about the parameters. It estimates this objective with nested Monte Carlo sampling and uses polynomial chaos surrogates to reduce the cost of repeated model evaluations. key_results: For the combustion example, the single-experiment optimum was around 975 K and equivalence ratio 0.5; inference at that setting produced a tighter posterior than at the two alternative settings tested. For two-experiment optimization, the Nelder–Mead nonlinear simplex method performed better overall than simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation in the reported study of 100 independent optimization runs. A design with two experiments on the favorable design ridge produced a tighter posterior than the tested four-experiment factorial design. With 5,000 noisy-objective evaluations and 10,000 inner samples per evaluation, using the full model would require 50,000,000 model evaluations, compared with 10,000 evaluations to construct the surrogate; the authors estimate a speedup of roughly 3.5 orders of magnitude and a saving of 49,990,000 model evaluations, or roughly four months of serial computation. A lower-order surrogate with order 6 and 10,000 quadrature evaluations still found reasonable designs, but its parameter-inference posteriors were substantially less accurate than those from the higher-order surrogate with order 12 and 1,000,000 quadrature evaluations.

limitations_unstated: The demonstrations use simulated data and a single combustion mechanism, targeting only two kinetic parameters, so performance on real experiments or broader chemical systems is not established. future_work_stated: The authors propose more efficient construction of polynomial chaos expansions, including construction that adapts alongside stochastic optimization. future_work_unstated: A practical extension would incorporate equipment limits, operating windows, experiment costs, and restrictions on which combinations of settings are feasible. summary: The paper develops conditional exact tests for factor effects in two-level fractional factorial experiments with discrete responses. It considers independent Poisson models for counts and logistic models for binomial responses, where the response is a count out of a known total. The method fixes the sufficient statistics for a chosen null model and uses a connected Markov chain to sample from the resulting conditional distribution when direct enumeration is infeasible. A Markov basis supplies the moves that keep samples within that conditional space, and sampled test statistics are used to estimate p-values. In the wave-soldering example, the estimated conditional p-value differs substantially from the large-sample result, showing why exact conditional calibration can matter for these data.
key_results: For the wave-soldering data, the paper reports an estimated conditional p-value of 0.032 for the likelihood-ratio test, compared with the asymptotic p-value of 0.0040. The estimate used 100,000 burn-in steps followed by 1,000,000 Monte Carlo samples, and its estimated standard deviation was 0.0045. The authors report that the asymptotic distribution understated the upper-tail probability and overstated the evidence against the null model in this example. Their design-to-contingency-table correspondences also identify settings where existing Markov-basis results apply; for the illustrated 16-run null model, a minimal basis has 35 moves.
key_equations:
Poisson log-linear model: \[\log(\mu_i)=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{r}\beta_j x_{ij}\] The expected response for run i is μ_i, the intercept and model coefficients are β_0 and β_j, covariate j for run i is x_ij, and r is the number of covariates.

Conditional distribution for Poisson responses: \[f(y\mid X_0^{\mathsf T}y=s)\propto\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{y_i!}\] The conditional distribution is f, the response vector is y with run-level counts y_i, X₀ is the null-model covariate matrix, s is the fixed sufficient-statistics vector, and k is the number of runs.

Moves preserving the sufficient statistics: \[X_0^{\mathsf T}z=0,\qquad z\in B\] The null-model covariate matrix is X₀, z is an integer move, zero is the zero vector, and B is a Markov basis whose moves preserve the conditioned statistics.
limitations_stated: The authors state that calculating a Markov basis can be problematic and that current algorithms may take a very long time for experiments with 64 runs or more. They report that algebraic software works well and is practical for Poisson models with 16 or 32 runs.
limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstration is concentrated on one Poisson example, so the paper provides limited empirical evidence about performance across different designs, response distributions, or factor-effect patterns. The reported Monte Carlo standard error does not, by itself, establish that the chain has mixed adequately; the paper gives no broad assessment of convergence or mixing across applications.
future_work_stated: The authors propose considering more complicated designs and developing appropriate Markov bases, including designs with three levels and balanced incomplete block designs.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate mixing, convergence diagnostics, and p-value accuracy systematically across designs and null models, including the logistic examples. It could also develop accessible software workflows and assess the approach in additional real manufacturing experiments with practical constraints on runs, randomization, or blocking.

summary: The paper develops optimal measurement designs for estimating spherical harmonic coefficients used to describe three-dimensional shapes. It studies a linear regression model for the measured radius over directions on the unit sphere, with the objective of estimating all or selected coefficients and supporting principal component analysis. The authors show that the uniform distribution on the sphere is optimal for several parameter-estimation criteria and for a criterion focused on principal components. They construct practical discrete designs by combining a polar-angle quadrature rule with equally spaced azimuthal points, giving the same information matrix as the continuous uniform design. In the examples, these designs outperform commonly used sampling patterns, including a design previously applied to citrus shapes.
key_results: The proposed discrete designs reproduce the identity information matrix and are therefore optimal for the criteria considered in the paper. In the degree-seven citrus example, the existing 360-point design sampled in 10 circles had efficiencies of 0.003 for the first principal-component criterion, 0.019 for the criterion using seven components, 0.149 for the trace-based criterion, and 0.840 for the determinant-based criterion. The authors’ proposed 360-point design had efficiencies of 0.958 for each of the reported principal-component criteria, 0.987 for the trace-based criterion, and 0.992 for the determinant-based criterion. For the degree-two model, one of the proposed discrete designs can be represented by 12 points on the sphere.
key_equations:
Spherical harmonic regression model: \[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\theta,\phi]=c^{\mathsf T}f_d(\theta,\phi),\qquad \operatorname{Var}[Y\mid\theta,\phi]=\sigma^2\] Y is the measured response, theta and phi are the polar and azimuthal angles, c is the coefficient vector, f_d is the spherical harmonic basis vector of degree d, and sigma squared is the constant error variance.

Target information matrix: \[M(\xi)=\int f_d(\theta,\phi)f_d(\theta,\phi)^{\mathsf T}\,d\xi(\theta,\phi)=I_{(d+1)^2}\] M is the information matrix for design xi, f_d is the basis vector of degree d, theta and phi are the measurement angles, and I is the identity matrix of dimension (d plus 1) squared; the paper constructs discrete designs with this same matrix as the uniform spherical design.

Polar-angle quadrature and product design: \[\sum_{i=1}^{r}w_i x_i^k=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}x^k\,dx\quad(k=0,\ldots,2d),\qquad \xi=\mu\otimes\nu,\quad t\geq 2d+1\] The quadrature nodes x_i and weights w_i integrate powers through degree 2d exactly, with k the power index and r the number of nodes; xi is the product of the polar design mu and the azimuthal design nu, which uses t equally spaced points.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their covariance calculations rely on uncorrelated observations, an assumption that may need to be checked or incorporated into the design for measurements taken from one object. They also note that finding equal-weight quadrature rules becomes numerically more difficult as the expansion degree increases, and that the sample size limits the degree that can be fitted.
limitations_unstated: The optimality results depend on the specified truncated spherical harmonic regression model and its constant-variance error assumption; the paper does not test robustness to model mismatch or uneven measurement error. The numerical comparisons cover selected conventional designs and model degrees, with the degree-seven illustration drawn from one previously published application, so performance under other measurement constraints or real-world acquisition systems remains uncertain.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending design methods to alternative classification tools, including independent component analysis, and developing criteria for shape reconstruction based on expected mean squared error. They also identify correlated observations and two-dimensional image reconstruction using Zernike polynomials as directions for further research, and call for suitable software to support higher-degree equal-weight quadrature construction.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess the proposed designs in real shape-measurement experiments, including sensitivity to inaccessible surface regions, sensor limits, and location-dependent measurement precision. It would also be useful to develop practical software for constrained finite-run designs and to evaluate sequential design strategies as additional measurements become available.
