summary: The paper develops a joint design and inference method for multifactor online experiments with treatment effects, nuisance block effects, and treatment-by-block interactions. Its objective is to stop early when effects are practically negligible while controlling errors under continuous monitoring and retaining precise treatment-effect estimates. The method pairs block-orthogonal allocations with a radial e-value, and uses an isotropic allocation that spreads treatment information evenly across directions. Orthogonal arrays provide explicit ways to construct these allocations, and repeating the same design across batches produces an anytime-valid evidence process. The authors show theoretically that the design is optimal for worst-case evidence growth and for several standard estimation criteria, and illustrate its performance in simulations and a prompt-design experiment.
key_results: In simulations with 32 runs per batch, 8 batches, and 1,000 replications, the proposed procedure had expected log-growth 3.704 and average stopping batch 1.406, compared with 0.165 and 7.733 for the safe-testing competitor. Its treatment-effect mean squared error was 0.0080 versus 0.0257, and its block-effect mean squared error was 0.0163 versus 0.0341; the proposed procedure’s empirical type-I error was 5.8%, compared with 3.8% for that competitor. In the prompt experiment, using 128 responses, the proposed method stopped at batch 4 with log e-value 3.14, while the other procedures reached the full horizon without rejecting. The theoretical results establish that the isotropic block-orthogonal allocation is minimax-rate optimal for evidence growth and simultaneously achieves A-, D-, and E-optimality for treatment-effect estimation; the paper also notes that an orthogonal array can reduce a seven-factor example from 128 full-factorial runs to 16 runs while retaining the required properties.
key_equations:
Assumed linear model: \[Y=X\psi+Z\lambda+J\theta+\epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_n)\] Y is the response vector; X, Z, and J are the treatment, block, and treatment-by-block interaction design matrices; psi, lambda, and theta are their respective coefficient vectors; epsilon is the error vector; N denotes a normal distribution; and I_n is the identity matrix for n runs.

Worst-case evidence-growth bound and isotropic allocation: \[\Gamma_n(A_n,\rho_n)\leq \frac{n\rho_n^2\lambda_{\min}(A_n)}{2}\leq\frac{n\rho_n^2}{2},\qquad A_n=I_q\] Gamma is the optimal worst-case expected log-evidence growth; A_n is the scaled treatment information matrix; rho_n is the separation from the practical-effect boundary; n is the run count; lambda_min is the smallest eigenvalue; and I_q is the identity matrix for q treatment factors.

Block-orthogonal isotropic design: \[X^{\top}X=nI_q,\qquad X^{\top}Z=0,\qquad X^{\top}J=0\] X is the treatment design matrix, Z is the block design matrix, J is the interaction design matrix, n is the run count, q is the number of treatment factors, I_q is the identity matrix, and the zero equalities express orthogonality.

Radial e-value: \[E_n^*=\frac{f_{q,n(\Delta-\rho_n)^2}(Q_n)}{f_{q,n\Delta^2}(Q_n)},\qquad Q_n=\frac{\|S_n\|^2}{n}\] E_n* is the proposed e-value; f is the noncentral chi-square density with q degrees of freedom and the indicated noncentrality; Delta is the minimum practically meaningful effect size; rho_n is its separation parameter; Q_n is the squared length of score S_n divided by n; and n is the run count.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the framework currently assumes Gaussian errors. They also note that the block-orthogonal design protects main-effect inference but does not generally identify interaction effects, although a separate construction can identify them at a greater run-size cost.
limitations_unstated: The method depends on being able to allocate treatments in carefully balanced, block-orthogonal patterns and repeat them across batches; real platforms with changing traffic, incomplete blocks, or allocation constraints may not be able to do this exactly. The empirical evidence is also limited to a simulation with two treatment factors and one prompt experiment, so performance under other response distributions, larger treatment systems, or operationally changing online environments is not established here.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to generalized linear models for non-Gaussian outcomes, developing designs that preserve main-effect robustness while allowing estimation of prespecified interactions, and validating the approach in prospective large-scale deployments.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess how to retain valid evidence growth when traffic constraints or missing treatment-block combinations prevent exact orthogonality. Prospective evaluations could also test robustness to changing user populations and response variance, and provide practical software for generating feasible allocations and monitoring evidence.

scope_reason: The paper studies rerandomization as a design-stage method for restricting treatment allocations to improve precision under interference.
design_type_evidence: “rerandomization, a design procedure that restricts the assignment space to allocations with sufficiently small covariate imbalance.”
glossary: EATE = Expected average treatment effect: the average direct treatment effect, averaged over a specified distribution of other units’ assignments.|SUTVA = Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption: each unit’s outcome depends only on its own treatment assignment.|M_n = The squared Mahalanobis distance used to measure covariate imbalance.|a = The prespecified maximum imbalance accepted by the rerandomization procedure.|τ̂_x = The vector of treated-minus-control covariate imbalances.|τ_x = The expected value of the covariate imbalance vector under the baseline assignment mechanism.|Σ_xx = The covariance matrix of the covariate imbalance vector under the baseline assignment mechanism.|v_p = The variance factor for a truncated normal distribution, determined by the covariate dimension and acceptance threshold.|R² = The squared multiple correlation between the treatment effect estimator and the covariate imbalance vector.|τ̂ = The Hájek estimator of the expected average treatment effect.
summary: The paper extends rerandomization to randomized experiments in which units’ outcomes can depend on other units’ treatment assignments, rather than assuming the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA). It targets the expected average treatment effect (EATE), estimated with the Hájek difference-in-means estimator, under a Bernoulli reference assignment. The design repeatedly draws assignments and accepts only those with sufficiently small covariate imbalance; the balanced information can include both pre-treatment covariates and assignment-dependent exposure summaries. The authors establish that this procedure can preserve asymptotic unbiasedness and reduce the estimator’s asymptotic variance under limited dependence, without correctly specifying the interference mechanism. They also propose conservative variance estimation and confidence intervals for inference after rerandomization.
key_results: The theory gives an asymptotic variance ratio of 1 − (1 − v_p)R² relative to Bernoulli randomization, so rerandomization is asymptotically no worse and its gain depends on covariate association with the estimator and the balance threshold. In simulations with 2,000 units and a network generated using preferential attachment, each rerandomization strategy was calibrated to a 5% acceptance rate. For the linear outcome setting, balancing pre-treatment covariates reduced variance to roughly 0.21 times the Bernoulli variance when baseline signal dominated, while balancing assignment-dependent covariates reduced it to 0.04 or less when interference signal dominated. Joint balancing produced variance ratios of about 0.22 across signal regimes in the linear setting with the smaller exposure set, and about 0.24–0.55 in the nonlinear setting; adding a weakly predictive exposure summary yielded ratios of 0.36–0.39 and 0.37–0.65, respectively. Across the reported settings, confidence-interval length ratios were at most 1, and all three compared variance-estimator constructions were conservative in the simulations.
key_equations:
Rerandomization acceptance criterion: \[M_n=(\hat{\tau}_x-\tau_x)^\top\Sigma_{xx}^{-1}(\hat{\tau}_x-\tau_x)\le a\] The design accepts an assignment when the squared Mahalanobis distance M_n between the observed covariate imbalance vector τ̂_x and its baseline expectation τ_x, scaled by the inverse covariance matrix Σ_xx, is no greater than the threshold a.

Asymptotic variance under rerandomization: \[\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}\mid M_n\le a)=\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau})\{1-(1-v_p)R^2\}\] The conditional asymptotic variance of the Hájek estimator τ̂ given acceptance is its baseline variance multiplied by a factor determined by v_p, the threshold-related truncated-normal variance factor, and R², the squared multiple correlation with the balanced covariates.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the proposed variance estimator can be conservative, particularly for nonlinear outcome models or highly heterogeneous networks, which can make confidence intervals wider than necessary. They also note that an excessively small acceptance threshold can make assignment generation costly, and that thresholds shrinking too quickly may require separate asymptotic analysis.
limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence centers on a single 2,000-unit preferential-attachment network, with treatment-dependent covariates constructed from the true network, so performance with estimated or misspecified networks and in real experiments is not demonstrated. The design also requires repeated assignment draws and recalculation of assignment-dependent covariates, while its inference procedure relies on access to a suitable dependence graph; the practical burden of these requirements is not evaluated in the reported comparisons.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method beyond the EATE to spillover and total effects, and beyond Bernoulli assignment to settings such as cluster randomization. They also identify combining rerandomization with regression adjustment, selecting useful covariates before the experiment, and developing sharper conservative variance estimators as directions for future work.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess design and inference when the interaction network is estimated, partially observed, or changes during an experiment, including how uncertainty in that network affects guarantees. Field evaluations and computational comparisons could also quantify assignment-generation cost and coverage in realistic settings, and investigate sequential or constrained assignment procedures where repeated unrestricted draws are impractical.

summary: The paper introduces Latinized aperiodic tiling (LAT), a space-filling design for computer experiments that can use any sample size. It targets efficient coverage of the input space and integration with fewer model evaluations, including when the available run budget is not a power of two. The method recursively cuts the unit hypercube along its longest edge using golden-ratio-based integer splits, puts one point in each equal-volume cell, and matches cells to bins to create Latin margins while keeping points inside their cells. The authors evaluate discrepancy and integration errors on analytical functions and engineering emulators, comparing LAT with Monte Carlo sampling, Latin hypercube sampling (LHS), Halton and Sobol’ sequences, and a lattice rule. They find that LAT performs consistently across sample sizes, beats Monte Carlo and LHS on integrands with interactions, and supports local refinement and other uses of its cell partition.
key_results: The construction cost scales as dimension times sample size times the logarithm of sample size; its cell partition itself is built in a single pass. At 1,000 runs on the type A function in two dimensions, LAT has a reported root-mean-square error of 1.7 × 10⁻⁴, compared with 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ for a truncated Sobol’ sequence, 1.6 × 10⁻³ for LHS, and 1.1 × 10⁻² for Monte Carlo sampling. At powers of two, Sobol’ is generally more accurate, but truncating its sequence to 1,000 rather than using 1,024 points increased its error by a factor of three in the reported comparison; LAT’s accuracy was stable across sample sizes. On the pure-interaction test function, LAT reduced error by a factor of 60 relative to LHS, and on the engineering emulators its variance reduction relative to Monte Carlo ranged from three to 1,000.
key_equations: Golden-section split rule: \[j_1=\min\{\max(\operatorname{round}(j/\varphi),1),j-1\}\] Here j is the number of points in the cell being split, φ is the golden ratio, and j₁ is the number assigned to one child cell, with rounding and bounds ensuring both children receive at least one point.
limitations_stated: The authors report that the inexpensive greedy cell-to-bin matching is slightly biased, with bias up to 2.6% of its root-mean-square error in the tested cases; their unbiased matching costs more. Filtering cells to sample non-rectangular regions is biased when cells have unequal intersections with the region and performs several times worse than rejection sampling for the five-dimensional ball example. They also note that adding a point to a whole-cube design changes its Latin-bin matching and can move existing points.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation uses selected analytical functions and five engineering emulators rather than results from physical experiments, so performance on real systems is not established. The main construction assumes a uniform input distribution over a hypercube; its behavior for correlated inputs or practical parameter constraints is not validated in the reported comparisons.
future_work_stated: The authors propose allocating further runs to cells that contribute most to variance, using probability mass rather than volume to split cells for nonuniform input distributions, and weighting boundary cells to remove bias when sampling constrained regions. They also identify making unbiased Latinization practical at the cost of a sort as a direction for further work.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate LAT in real engineering campaigns and compare total computational cost, including design generation and model evaluations, against commonly used alternatives. It would also be useful to test whether the design can support sequential additions while preserving useful properties such as Latin margins without relocating existing runs.

summary: The paper develops Optimal Multi-way Stratification Trees (OMST), a method for constructing strata to reduce the variance of estimates in online controlled experiments. It targets estimation of a population mean within each treatment or control group, so that the difference between group means can estimate the treatment effect. The method represents possible strata as paths through features and selects paths by minimizing an objective based on stratified-sampling variance. It uses outcome-informed binning for numerical features and reduces computation by removing redundant paths and grouping units with identical assignment patterns. Tests on one real-world and one simulated dataset show that the method can provide substantial estimation-error reduction with shallow, interpretable trees.
key_results: With a sample size of 100, the experiments repeated sampling 10,000 times and compared estimation error against simple random sampling (SRS). On the bike-sharing dataset, OMST with optimal binning reduced root mean squared error (RMSE) by 30.9% under proportional allocation and 35.9% under optimal allocation, the largest reductions among the compared stratification methods. On the customer-purchase dataset, the Controlled Experiments Using Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED) method reduced RMSE by 68.4%, while OMST with optimal binning achieved 63.1% and 64.8% under the two allocation rules, comparable to other tree and stratification methods. In the bike-sharing depth comparison, OMST with optimal binning reached reductions of 36.8% and 43.9% at depth three; on that dataset, the problem reductions also lowered runtime from 69.3 to 29.0 seconds under proportional allocation and from 67.3 to 33.5 seconds under optimal allocation.
key_equations:
Variance of the stratified mean: \[\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\mu}_{\mathrm{strat}})=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{N_h^2S_h^2}{n_h}-\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{h=1}^{H}N_hS_h^2\] The variance of the stratified estimate is determined by population size N, number of strata H, stratum index h, stratum size N_h, within-stratum standard deviation S_h, and stratum sample size n_h.

Path-selection objective under proportional allocation: \[\min_z\sum_{j\in P}N_jS_j^2z_j\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{j\in P}a_{ij}z_j\leq1,\ \sum_{j\in P}N_jz_j\geq\rho N,\ \sum_{j\in P}z_j\leq L\] The method selects binary path indicators z_j from candidate paths P to minimize the sum of path size N_j times within-path variance S_j squared, while a_ij indicates unit membership, rho sets required population coverage, and L limits the number of selected strata.

Path-selection objective using Neyman allocation: \[\min_z\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{j\in P}N_jS_jz_j\right)^2-\sum_{j\in P}N_jS_j^2z_j\] The Neyman-type surrogate minimizes an objective over the same feasible path selections, where n is total sample size, P is the candidate-path set, z_j selects path j, N_j is its population size, and S_j is its within-path standard deviation.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the evaluation uses only one real-world and one synthetic dataset, and that held-out resampling does not fully reproduce a live online experiment. They also note that distribution shifts require monitoring and retraining, feature-wise discretization may miss interaction-specific thresholds, and exhaustive path enumeration limits scalability in high dimensions.
limitations_unstated: The reported comparisons use a fixed sample size of 100, so the performance of the selected strata at other run sizes is not established. The optimal-allocation path objective uses a continuous Neyman allocation as a surrogate before integer allocation is computed, so integer allocation constraints or operational assignment quotas could change which design is best.
future_work_stated: The authors propose broader validation on real-world data, comparisons with modern machine-learning regression-adjustment methods, sensitivity analyses of model parameters, and detailed ablations of the reduction procedures. They also propose joint feature discretization and dynamic path generation, including column generation.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method under practical assignment restrictions such as minimum per-group counts, capacity limits, and missing covariates. Research could also test whether periodically updating strata during an experiment, rather than applying fixed historical rules, preserves reliable treatment-effect estimates.

summary: This paper designs a sequential experimental-design method for selecting genetic controllers for biological systems with uncertain dynamics. It considers a finite set of candidate plant hypotheses and a finite library of implementable controllers. After each experiment, the method updates the probabilities assigned to the hypotheses and selects the controller with the lowest expected regret. It chooses the next experiment to reduce that regret and stops when the remaining expected regret is below a specified threshold. In three simulated mechanistic cases, the method reached the stopping criterion in fewer experimental rounds than model-uncertainty and random-selection policies, with similar success rates.
key_results: Across 50 seeds, the proposed method averaged 3.14 rounds in Case 1, 2.86 in Case 2, and 3.59 in Case 3; its success counts were 50/50, 49/50, and 49/50. The model-uncertainty method averaged 3.65, 4.24, and 4.50 rounds, with success counts of 49/50, 49/50, and 50/50; random selection averaged 5.62, 5.66, and 5.81 rounds, with success counts of 48/50, 47/50, and 48/50. The paper reports significantly fewer rounds for the proposed method than for model-uncertainty selection in all three cases, with mean reductions of 0.57, 1.39, and 0.90 rounds in Cases 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Success required both reaching controller regret below 0.05 and selecting the correct optimal controller.

summary: The paper develops a method for planning clinical validation studies of binary predictive tests and fixed-horizon survival outcomes. It starts with sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), and disease prevalence (pi), then derives the risks among test-positive and test-negative patients and the contrast between those risks. Fisher information and the delta method give Wald-type variance, power, and sample-size calculations for several risk scales, with safeguards for small samples and rare events. The authors also use optimal-design criteria to show how prevalence and test thresholds affect efficiency. Simulations generally support the approximations, and a coronary artery calcium example illustrates how to use the method for a real clinical prediction problem.
key_results: In simulations with 2,000 replicates per configuration, the binary-outcome estimators had relative bias within plus or minus 10 percent across the evaluated design grid, and standard-error calibration was near one for small-to-moderate effects. For the coronary artery calcium example, the fixed-horizon estimate was a log hazard ratio of 2.19, compared with 2.13 for the reported adjusted Cox estimate; their standard errors were 0.31 and 0.34, respectively, though the estimates target different quantities. The calculated sample size was 155 for 80 percent power and 207 for 90 percent power, compared with about 100 from a naive Schoenfeld calculation at the example operating point. In a threshold-only efficiency sweep for that example, the uncorrected required sample size fell from 155 to 87, while the safeguarded final size fell only to 139 because the minimum-events rule then governed.

summary: This paper designs a sequential way to decide which large language model should serve each workload when prices and traffic are known but model quality is uncertain. The objective is to maximize workload-weighted quality under a serving budget, while also accounting for the possibility that observed scores are biased by selective assignment or by an imperfect evaluator. The method, causal active sequential experimentation (CASE), uses production logs and randomized re-evaluations to form a range of plausible quality tables, then checks whether the same allocation remains optimal across that range. If the decision is not settled, it directs further randomized evaluation to model-workload pairs where the current and adverse allocations disagree, and repeats the test. The paper finds that allocation can be solved exactly, but the evidence often does not identify a robust decision because evaluator error remains after correcting for selective assignment.

At the measured evaluator-error width, the exact certificate settled only 1 of 210 tested instances; the median decision margin on LLMRouterBench was 0.0456 at 1.25 times the cheapest feasible spend and 0.0026 at 8 times that spend. In a separate LLMRouterBench comparison, target quality rose from 0.4798 using raw logs to 0.4924 using selection-adjusted scores and 0.5255 using designated outcomes, while deployment cost rose from USD 3,109 to USD 3,850 and USD 4,386 per million requests.

summary: This paper extends Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED) to improve treatment effect estimation in switchback and other clustered experiments. In the taxi data, basic CUPED reduced variance by 78.7% and had a standard error of 4.23; the best enriched version reduced variance by 85.9% and had a standard error of 2.81. Across the taxi-data enriched configurations, standard errors ranged from 2.81 to 3.16, and adding spatial indicators to the prediction model worsened performance relative to omitting them. In a simulation adding noise features, in-sample prediction fit appeared to improve while cross-fitted fit declined, illustrating why the authors regard cross-fitting as necessary.

summary: This paper develops a finite-sample theory for recovering smooth functions with Matérn regression on a periodic domain. Their main finding is that resolution and information at both relevant lengthscales determine whether error can decrease, while smoothness determines the subsequent rate of decrease.

summary: The paper designs a randomized experiment to estimate how deployment of a trading strategy erodes its returns as capital accumulates. Its proposed design assigns parallel implementations, called sleeves, to different deployment levels and compares treated and control sleeves on the same dates to remove common market shocks. Because erosion builds over time, the paper derives how finite holding periods attenuate the measured effect and how to correct for that attenuation. It also shows that same-date comparisons identify a sleeve’s own response at a fixed average deployment, not the crowding effect of scaling the whole strategy. The authors find that the design can be very costly in calendar time, while the proposed comparisons and simulations clarify which effects it can estimate and what assumptions those estimates require.

In simulations, contemporaneous assignment reduced contrast variance as sleeves were added, whereas staggered assignment reached a variance floor; with 100 sleeves, the reported variance ratio was 12.1 and the calendar-time requirement was 23.9 times higher under staggered assignment. For 100 sleeves and two-year holds, the study required 509 months in the uncorrected block-average scenario; comparing deployment levels 0 and 1 cost 228 cumulative percentage points of forgone edge, compared with 11 points for levels 1.5 and 2.0 at nearly the same duration. The paper also reports that impact-only capacity estimates overstate capacity by 10% to 51% in scenarios where crowding accounts for 15% to 50% of total erosion.

summary: The paper develops a method for constructing large Orthogonal Minimally Aliased Response Surface (OMARS) designs for three-level quantitative factors. It also uses partial enumeration and vertical concatenation of weighing designs to extend the available run sizes. The authors report complete enumeration through 24 rows and construct OMARS designs with up to 156 runs; comparisons show competitive results against definitive screening designs for selected 96-run cases.

At 16 rows, partial enumeration retaining 2%, 5%, or 10% of candidates recovered the best design and the top 5 and top 10 designs from the complete 6-column results; coverage of the complete set was 6.1%, 21%, and 39.9%, respectively. Complete enumeration of the 16-row, 6-column case took 9.6 days, and peak memory across fully enumerated cases reached about 32 GB. In the 96-run comparison, OMARS designs with 5 and 8 factors had higher D-, A-, and G-efficiencies than the corresponding definitive screening designs: for 5 factors, the values were 44.68%, 9.27%, and 86.39% versus 36.65%, 3.16%, and 40.32%; for 8 factors, they were 37.25%, 2.79%, and 84.42% versus 33.38%, 0.58%, and 81.60%.

summary: This paper develops a sequential design for longitudinal experiments in which treatment is assigned at multiple stages and the goal is to estimate one or more statistical targets efficiently. summary: This paper designs a method for choosing between two algorithms in randomized online A/B testing, using a contextual bandit model and aiming to reduce incorrect algorithm selections. The method, called Middle-In-Difference (MID), introduces a hypothetical middle algorithm and estimates the difference in performance in two steps using shared data within each step. The authors derive a middle policy that minimizes a component of the estimator’s variance and show when the estimator is unbiased. They evaluate the method with theoretical analysis and simulated A/B tests based on the public KuaiRec video recommendation dataset. In those experiments, MID reaches comparable selection error rates with substantially fewer samples than the conventional sample-mean approach.
key_results: In a reported setting, the average-reward sample-mean estimator (AVG) had a 27.49% selection error rate, compared with 9.05% for the inverse propensity scoring estimator (IPS). With algorithm similarity fixed at 0.5, AVG required a sample size of 350–400 to reach a 5% error rate, while MID reached that rate at a sample size of 100–200. The authors describe this as requiring one-half to one-quarter as many samples as conventional A/B testing; their abstract also reports achieving the same selection error rate with half the A/B testing data. Across their simulated comparisons, MID had lower selection error and higher statistical power than AVG and IPS, including at low algorithm similarity.

limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated A/B tests constructed from KuaiRec rather than a live deployment, so it does not establish that the reported gains transfer to operational online experiments. summary: The paper develops a framework for designing sequential experiments that efficiently estimate causal effects, including comparisons among multiple treatments. The framework summarizes each design by its average propensity, the average probability of assigning each treatment at each covariate value, and uses this quantity to define an efficiency benchmark. The authors give two batched ways to approach that benchmark: regression adjustment and covariate balancing. Their theory and numerical studies show that both routes can improve precision, while the performance of covariate balancing is more sensitive to the dimension of the balancing partition.
key_results: The theory establishes a lower bound: a regular, locally unbiased estimator cannot have variance below the independent-assignment efficiency benchmark evaluated at the design’s induced average propensity. For general smooth targets, the regression-adjustment route reaches the benchmark under a nuisance-estimation rate faster than the paper’s one-quarter threshold; for linear functionals, it allows any positive nuisance-estimation rates and gives a minimax-sharp second-order rate up to logarithmic factors. In synthetic experiments with 10,000 units and 3,000 replications per setting, regression adjustment improved normalized mean squared error over uniform assignment in all reported settings; covariate balancing improved it in most, but tied uniform assignment for one average treatment effect setting and performed worse for the quantile effect at dimension eight with the default partition. In the HELPMed data study, the vector-effect normalized trace error was 5.43 under uniform assignment and 5.03 under adaptive covariate balancing at 1,200 units; at 2,400 units, the reported values were 5.27 and 4.84 for the full-feature version, and 5.27 and 4.87 for the top-two-covariate version.

Efficiency lower bound: \[\operatorname{Var}(T)\geq \frac{V(\bar e)}{n}\] The variance of estimator T is at least the efficiency benchmark V evaluated at the induced average propensity e-bar, divided by the number of units n.

Allocation objective: \[L(e)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a}\frac{m_a(X)}{e_a(X)}\right]\] The allocation objective L for propensity rule e is the expectation over covariates X of the sum across treatment arms a of the arm-specific conditional second moment m divided by that arm’s propensity.

summary: The paper designs a sequential measurement method for X-ray scanning probe tomography, aiming to improve reconstruction quality while limiting the number of acquired beams. It derives a relationship between object boundaries and features in the sinogram, so the method can identify edge-aligned beams without first reconstructing the image. A Gaussian process interpolates unmeasured parts of the sinogram, and its uncertainty and estimated edge strength are combined to choose measurements while discouraging redundancy. The authors evaluate both individual-beam selection and whole-angle selection using simulated data and compare them with uniform raster scans and a Bayesian design baseline. Across the tested samples, individual-beam selection generally gives the fastest improvement in reconstruction accuracy, and the proposed method is reported to require substantially less computation than the Bayesian baseline.
key_results: The evaluation uses five simulated samples at 128 by 128 pixels, with 128 new beams per iteration and a five-angle raster initialization for sequential methods. The authors report that both proposed selection variants generally reduce reconstruction root mean square error faster than the uniform raster scan and the Bayesian angle-selection baseline, especially early in acquisition; individual-beam selection is generally best, though the angle variant is briefly surpassed by the Bayesian baseline on the biological sample. The method remains more accurate than the baseline in the reported additive-noise test at noise levels up to 5 percent. The authors report orders-of-magnitude faster per-iteration runtime than the Bayesian baseline, whose computation depends strongly on image resolution; they do not state a specific runtime ratio in the text.
key_equations:
Tomography measurement model: \[y(\theta,r)=\mathcal{R}[f](\theta,r)\] Here, y is the measured sinogram value, theta is the beam angle, r is the beam offset, R is the Radon transform, and f is the sample image.

Gaussian process posterior mean: \[\hat{y}_k(u)=K(u,\Phi_k)^\top[K(\Phi_k,\Phi_k)+\sigma^2 I]^{-1}Y_k\] Here, the predicted sinogram value at iteration k and beam location u is formed from the covariance function K, measured locations Phi, observed values Y, observation-noise standard deviation sigma, and identity matrix I.

Per-beam acquisition score: \[\psi(u)=\hat{\Sigma}_k(u)\,\hat{E}[\hat{y}_k;\alpha](u)\] Here, psi is the beam acquisition score, Sigma-hat is the confidence-interval width, E-hat is the estimated edge score evaluated from the predicted sinogram, and alpha controls edge sensitivity.

Batch selection: \[U_k^*=\arg\max_{U\subseteq\Phi\setminus\Phi_k,\ |U|=n_b}\sum_{u\in U}\psi(u)\] Here, the selected batch U at iteration k maximizes the sum of beam scores psi over candidate locations in Phi that have not been measured, and nb is the batch size.
limitations_stated: The authors note that independently positioning individual beams introduces experimental overhead. They also report that sinogram interpolation can miss sparse or rapidly varying edge features, and that high image resolution may oversmooth small features unless kernel length scales and the minimum-distance parameter are tuned.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated measurements rather than acquisitions from physical tomography equipment, and it tests only five samples, so its performance on real samples and experimental noise conditions remains unverified. The method also relies on the assumed Radon forward model and a Gaussian process interpolation scale; misspecification of either could misidentify edges or uncertainty. Its greedy selection over a finite candidate grid may not transfer directly to hardware with restricted beam positioning or other acquisition constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors identify advances in adaptive scanning hardware as a direction for future work, given the experimental overhead of independent beam positioning.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation on real tomography data and hardware, including measurement-time and radiation-dose comparisons at equal reconstruction quality. Further work could test alternative sinogram models and design criteria, and adapt the selection procedure to practical beam-positioning constraints or sequential stopping decisions.

summary: The paper develops a distributed Bayesian method for choosing one common experiment across multiple sites when each site can send only its locally preferred experiment to a fusion center. The objective is to maximize expected information gain about an unknown parameter, as a centralized designer would do with access to all sites’ information. The fusion center uses the observed recommendation pattern to choose the experiment with the largest conditional expected centralized information gain, rather than simply following the majority. The authors derive an optimality rule and information-loss bounds, including conditions for agreement with the centralized choice as the number of sites grows. Simulations for Gaussian and binary-response models show that this fusion method can perform close to the centralized benchmark, while majority voting can perform poorly when sites differ in informativeness.
key_results: In the scalar Gaussian simulation with 25 sites, Bayes fusion had mean regret of 0.010 and agreement with the centralized oracle of 0.876; majority voting had mean regret of 0.166 and agreement of 0.263, while random fusion had mean regret of 0.111. In the binary-response simulation with 25 sites, Bayes fusion had mean regret of 0.0060 and oracle agreement of 0.9421, compared with 0.3344 regret and 0.1324 agreement for majority voting. As the number of sites increased, Gaussian Bayes-fusion regret fell to 0.002 at 81 sites, while its oracle agreement rose to 0.954. In the binary-response model, regret fell to 0.0010 and oracle agreement rose to 0.9864 at 51 sites; majority voting’s agreement fell to 0.0284.
key_equations:
Centralized information utility for a common experiment: \[U(a)=I(\theta;Y_1,\ldots,Y_M\mid \xi_1=\cdots=\xi_M=a)\] U is the centralized expected information gain, a is the common experiment label, I is mutual information, θ is the unknown parameter, Y denotes the observations at the sites, M is the number of sites, and ξ denotes each site’s design.

Local recommendation: \[D_m=\arg\max_{e\in\{0,1\}} I_m(e)\] D_m is site m’s recommendation, e is a candidate experiment label, and I_m(e) is the local expected information gain for that experiment.

Bayes-optimal fusion rule: \[\delta^*(d)=\arg\max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\mathbb{E}[U(a)\mid D=d]\] δ* is the optimal fusion rule, d is the observed vector of recommendations D, a is a candidate common experiment, and U(a) is its centralized expected information gain.

Information loss: \[L(a,b)=U(b)-U(a)\] L is the information loss from choosing experiment a when b is the centralized information-optimal experiment, and U is centralized expected information gain.
limitations_stated: The main theoretical development uses two candidate experiments, and the numerical studies consider binary choices. The authors state that the paper assumes a finite set of candidate designs and a common experiment across sites; continuous designs and relaxing the common-choice restriction remain open directions.
limitations_unstated: The fusion rule depends on knowing or estimating how local recommendation patterns relate to the centralized information-optimal experiment, so performance may be sensitive to inaccurate calibration of that relationship. Evaluation is limited to simulations of two model families and constructed heterogeneous site types; the paper does not report validation on real experiments or operational constraints such as site-specific feasibility.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to multiple candidate experiments and richer local messages, such as ranked recommendations or quantized information gains. They also identify sequential distributed design, coded experimentation that relaxes the common-experiment requirement, and continuous design spaces as future directions.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the fusion rule in real multi-site experiments and under practical restrictions such as unequal costs, unavailable designs, or privacy constraints. Further work could also measure robustness when the assumed recommendation probabilities or statistical models are misspecified, and provide software for fitting and applying the fusion rule.

summary: The paper introduces Goal-driven Bayesian optimal experimental design (GoBOED), a method for choosing experiments to improve a downstream decision rather than simply reduce uncertainty about every model parameter. It considers decisions made under uncertain parameters, with the decision obtained by solving a constrained convex optimization problem. The method trains an amortized variational posterior model offline, then optimizes the experimental design by differentiating through that posterior model and the decision problem. The authors evaluate it using simulated source-localization, epidemic-management, and pharmacokinetic examples, with mean, chance-constraint, and conditional value-at-risk formulations. They report that designs focused on the decision can have broader near-optimal windows than designs chosen by expected information gain alone.
key_results: In the epidemic example, the expected-information-gain design selects day 5, while the robust-control objective has a reported near-optimal window of approximately days 7–11; the qualitative pattern also holds for chance constraints and conditional value-at-risk. In the pharmacokinetic example, expected information gain selects hour 17, while the robust-control window is about hours 15–23, with later observations generally reducing the dose needed to meet therapeutic targets. Online robust-objective evaluations take approximately 387–395 seconds for the epidemic model and 5.4 seconds for the pharmacokinetic chance-constraint case or 16.1 seconds for its conditional value-at-risk case; the paper excludes offline amortizer training from these timings. Gradient-based search converges in 3–5 projected steps, compared with an estimated 5,805 seconds for exhaustive evaluation of the 15 epidemic candidate days.
key_equations:
Observation model: \[y=f(\theta,\xi)+\epsilon\] The observation y is generated by the forward model f from unknown parameters theta and design xi, with noise epsilon.

Robust decision problem: \[J^*(y,\xi)=\min_{g\in G} J(g)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \rho_{\theta\sim p(\theta\mid y,\xi)}[c_j(g,\theta)]\leq 0\] The optimal robust cost J star minimizes cost J over decisions g in the allowed set G, subject to each constraint c evaluated under the posterior distribution p using risk functional rho.

Goal-driven design criterion: \[\xi^*=\arg\min_{\xi\in\Xi}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(y\mid\xi)}[J^*(y,\xi)]\] The chosen design xi star minimizes the expected optimal robust cost J star over observations y drawn from the design’s marginal distribution p.
limitations_stated: The method is presented for a single-step, non-adaptive design setting, and its differentiable decision layer assumes a convex downstream problem. The authors also note that performance depends on variational-posterior accuracy, that non-convex problems generally have only local guarantees, and that they use a non-principled cost padding rule for infeasible prior samples.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence comes from simulated examples and compares the method primarily with expected-information-gain design; it does not establish performance in real experiments or against a broad set of adapted decision-focused methods. In the design gradient, importance weights and the selected chance-constraint scenario set are held fixed during backpropagation, which may affect gradient accuracy when those quantities change sharply with the design.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to fully sequential adaptive designs, richer posterior families such as diffusion- and flow-based models, and end-to-end joint training. They also identify a formal extension of the gradient result to nonlinear task-relevant parameter structure as future work.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on real experimental data and compare it with other decision-aware design approaches adapted to the same robust-control objectives. Further work could test sensitivity to scenario selection, importance-sampling accuracy, and infeasibility handling, and develop designs that accommodate practical sampling, safety, or scheduling constraints.

summary: The paper develops a method for Bayesian inference over factorial-design models, where each model groups treatment cells into permissible pools with shared expected outcomes. Its objective is to estimate cell means and their uncertainty while averaging across the full set of possible partitions, rather than relying only on a small set of high-scoring models. The method uses a Rashomon Partition Set of high-evidence partitions to initialize annealed importance sampling, mixing those partitions and their neighbors with a uniform component over the model space. It then gradually shifts the sampling distribution toward the full posterior and uses importance weights to correct the estimates. The authors report that this approach recovers posterior summaries more accurately and efficiently than restricted inference in their simulations and real-data analyses.
key_results: In the simulation with 36 cells, the authors used approximately 10^6 iterations of Markov chain Monte Carlo as a reference and compared methods over 50 replications; seeded annealing produced posterior summaries close to the reference and was robust to the size of the seed set. In that simulation, seeded annealing took approximately 180 seconds on average, about 70% less time than the Markov chain Monte Carlo benchmark, while the PAC-Bayesian competitor took over 800 seconds. For the charitable-donation data, seeded annealing had an absolute-error score of 0.01 and interval overlap of 0.991, with a runtime of 1199.2 seconds, compared with 2911.2 seconds for the Markov chain Monte Carlo reference. For the NHANES telomere data, seeded annealing had a reported absolute-error score of 0.000 and interval overlap of 0.965, with a runtime of 2914.8 seconds; it also changed conclusions suggested by the restricted partition set, whereas the PAC-Bayesian approach gave results largely like the restricted analysis.

Seed-based initial distribution: \[q_0(M;S)=\alpha_1\frac{\widetilde p(M\mid D)\mathbf{1}_S(M)}{\sum_{M'\in S}\widetilde p(M'\mid D)}+\alpha_{2+}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{L_1(S)}(M)}{|L_1(S)|}+(1-\alpha_1-\alpha_{2+})\] Here q zero is the initial distribution for candidate model M, S is the seed set, p tilde is the unnormalized posterior score given data D, alpha one weights sampling from the seed, alpha two plus weights sampling from the one-move neighborhood L one of S, and each indicator marks membership in its set; alpha two plus is zero if that neighborhood is empty and otherwise equals alpha two.

Self-normalized posterior summary: \[\widehat\psi_J=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^J w_j\zeta(M_j)}{\sum_{j=1}^J w_j}\] Here psi hat with subscript J is the estimated posterior summary from J trajectories, w sub j is the importance weight, zeta is the quantity of interest evaluated at terminal model M sub j, and M sub j is the terminal model for trajectory j.
limitations_stated: The authors limit the factorial-design analysis to partitions within a single profile chosen in advance; learning profiles is described as an NP-hard problem outside their scope. They estimate the residual variance separately and then treat it as fixed. They also note that applying the framework to other model spaces requires a suitable distance metric and efficient proposal distributions.
limitations_unstated: The estimates depend on the Gaussian outcome model, the prior that penalizes the number of pools, the chosen profile, and a separately estimated but fixed residual variance; sensitivity to these assumptions is not established in the reported evaluations. The empirical comparisons cover two simulation settings and two datasets, and the larger simulation uses a long Markov chain Monte Carlo run as a surrogate reference rather than an exact posterior, so performance in larger or differently structured model spaces remains uncertain.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to other structured model spaces, including trees and directed acyclic graphs, when suitable distances and sampling proposals are available. They also identify applications to discrete optimization and structure learning as natural future research directions.
future_work_unstated: Further work could measure sensitivity to outcome-model misspecification, uncertainty in the residual-variance estimate, and alternative partition priors or criteria. It could also test the method under practical factorial-design constraints and sequential experiments, and validate its uncertainty summaries on additional operational or field datasets.

summary: This paper develops nearly balanced treatment-cardinality-constrained (TCARD) designs for experiments in which every run must activate exactly a fixed number of factors. It uses a balanced incomplete block design as a reference and defines near balance through even factor replication and even pairwise co-occurrence. The authors introduce the Balanced Concurrence Deviation (BCD) objective, which combines penalties for both kinds of imbalance, and construct designs with a coordinate-exchange search that preserves the fixed run size. They also propose choosing the objective’s weights by simulation to match a planned downstream analysis. The method is theoretically linked to established design criteria and performs competitively in simulations; a prompt-screening case study shows that task-aware weight tuning can improve screening and held-out validation results.
key_results: The theoretical results show that nearly balanced designs minimize the first two generalized word-length pattern components, and that the proposed objective is connected to the centered UE(s2) criterion and to Bayesian D-optimality in stated settings. The simulation comparison covered 20 to 80 factors, run-to-factor ratios of 1.5 and 3, and active-factor ratios of 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5; no method dominated every diagnostic, while the proposed criterion was generally competitive in balance and projected information quality. In the prompt case study, the design used 21 runs, 15 components, and 3 active components per run; the three tuned BCD designs had replication imbalance of 0 and pairwise-dispersion values from 24 to 46. Their refit R-squared values ranged from 0.61 to 0.91 and full-model R-squared values from 0.84 to 0.95, while the closest comparison methods recovered fewer components supported by both screening and full-model analysis. On held-out problems, the tuned designs calibrated for active-set sizes 4 and 5 improved accuracy over baseline by 1.10% ± 1.26% and 1.80% ± 1.61%, respectively; the untuned default and most comparison designs did not show positive improvement.
key_equations:
Fixed-cardinality constraint: \[\sum_{j=1}^{p} x_{ij}=k,\quad i=1,\ldots,n\] Here x_ij is the zero-or-one activation of factor j in run i, p is the number of factors, k is the fixed number active per run, and n is the number of runs.

Balanced Concurrence Deviation objective: \[\Phi_{BCD}(X)=\frac{w_1}{p}V_1(X)+\frac{w_2}{\binom{p}{2}}V_2(X),\quad V_1=\sum_j(r_j-\bar r)^2,\quad V_2=\sum_{j< l}(\lambda_{jl}-\bar\lambda)^2\] Here Phi_BCD is the objective to minimize, w1 and w2 are positive weights, V1 and V2 measure dispersion in replications and pairwise concurrences, r_j and lambda_jl are the corresponding counts, and their barred forms are the arithmetic average counts.

Within-run exchange used in construction: \[x_{ia}\leftarrow 0,\quad x_{ib}\leftarrow 1,\quad x_{ia}+x_{ib}=1\] Here a is an active factor and b is an inactive factor in run i before the exchange; the swap preserves that run's fixed number of active factors.
limitations_stated: The authors state that explicit algebraic constructions of nearly balanced designs remain open for most cases with 3 ≤ k ≤ p − 2, and that exact reconstruction becomes impractical as the number of possible factor subsets grows. They characterize the coordinate-exchange procedure as a practical descent method rather than a guarantee of global or exact optimality, and describe the prompt case study as a worked example rather than a benchmark.
limitations_unstated: The simulations cover factor counts only up to 80 and do not establish how search time or design quality scales beyond that range; the exchange search can also stop at a local minimum. Weight tuning depends on the simulated sparsity, effect, and noise scenarios representing the actual study, so misspecified scenarios may select weights poorly. The empirical application uses one language model, one task, a fixed prompt-component order, and a limited run budget, which constrains how broadly its findings can be generalized.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to continuous-factor, mixed-factor, and grouped-factor designs. They also identify richer downstream objectives, adaptive or sequential weight calibration, faster search methods, and other constrained-design settings as directions for future work.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method across multiple real engineering screening studies and compare its recommendations with subsequent confirmation runs. It would also be valuable to develop robust weight choices that perform reliably across uncertain scenario assumptions, and to study designs that directly protect against higher-order interactions or operational restrictions such as blocks and unavailable factor combinations.

summary: The paper designs a sequential sensor-placement method for simulated, two-dimensional bearing-only localization of multiple sources. It combines a maximum-entropy reweighting step with D-optimal placement based on the Fisher information matrix. The reweighting shifts particle weights toward the current estimate while satisfying a bound on sliced Wasserstein distance, then the placement step optimizes sensor positions using those weights. The method is evaluated against conventional D-optimal placement in simulations with different numbers of sources and sensors and two noise levels. On average, reweighting lowers localization error, especially when there are more sensors than sources and measurements are relatively informative.
key_results: The study evaluated 64 source-and-sensor-count configurations at two noise levels, using 1,000 particles per source, 10 sequential iterations, and 20 simulation seeds. Compared with D-optimal placement using the current particle weights, the proposed method reduced mean root-mean-square error by 7.9% at a bearing noise standard deviation of 15 degrees and by 17.2% at 8 degrees; individual changes ranged from a 21% degradation to a 25% improvement at 15 degrees, and from a 7% degradation to a 34% improvement at 8 degrees. Its reported equivalent sensor saving averaged 2.8 sensors at 15 degrees and 5.5 sensors at 8 degrees. The gains were strongest when the sensor count exceeded the source count, while reweighting sometimes reduced performance when sensors were scarce relative to sources.
key_equations:
Bearing measurement model: \[\beta_{r,m}=\operatorname{atan2}(p_{m,y}-s_{r,y},p_{m,x}-s_{r,x})+\eta_{r,m},\quad \eta_{r,m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\] The bearing beta from sensor r to source m is the angle from sensor position s to source position p plus Gaussian noise eta with standard deviation sigma.

D-optimal placement criterion: \[\max_{s_1,\ldots,s_R\in D}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\log\det F^{(m)}(s_1,\ldots,s_R;w^{(m)})\] The design maximizes the sum of log determinants of the source-specific Fisher information matrices F over sensor positions s in the allowed region D, for M sources and their particle weights w.

Maximum-entropy reweighting: \[w_i^{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda)=\frac{w_i^-\exp(-\lambda g_i)}{Z(\lambda)},\quad Z(\lambda)=\sum_j w_j^-\exp(-\lambda g_j)\] The reweighted particle weight w_i opt is the previous weight w_i minus multiplied by an exponential tilt based on particle cost g_i and tilt parameter lambda, then normalized by Z.

Accuracy constraint: \[\sum_i w_i g_i\leq\epsilon^2\] The reweighted weights w_i must keep the weighted particle costs g_i within the squared accuracy budget epsilon.
limitations_stated: The method assumes known data association between bearings and sources, and the synthetic experiments do not model effects such as multipath, clutter, model mismatch, or intermittent communications. The experiments are limited to two-dimensional source positions. The authors also note that sensor placement is non-convex and the sequential procedure is greedy, so it has no global or multi-step optimality guarantee.
limitations_unstated: The simulations use a fixed reweighting budget and a Dirac target at the current weighted mean, so performance may be sensitive to these choices when the posterior shape differs from the tested cases. The study does not establish performance under practical placement constraints such as minimum separation between sensors or restricted deployment locations beyond the rectangular region.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to moving-target tracking and integrating it with data-association methods. They also suggest comparisons with other information criteria and Bayesian design baselines, testing alternative posterior targets, adapting the accuracy budget over time, and jointly optimizing sensor noise precision and position.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method with field data and realistic sensor constraints, including sensor separation, communication limits, and nonuniform noise. It would also be useful to evaluate how robust the sequential design is to errors in the assumed bearing model and to compare different reweighting budgets across repeated experiments.

summary: Dynamic Adaptive Rerandomization via Thompson Sampling (DARTS) is a sequential design for randomized controlled trials that need to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) when measuring pretreatment covariates is costly. Before each batch, it uses Thompson sampling to select covariates under a total measurement budget, learning which features predict control outcomes from earlier batches. The selected covariates guide rerandomization to improve treatment-control balance and are also used in regression adjustment when estimating the batch effect. The authors prove that choosing covariates using only past batches preserves batch-level randomization validity and establish asymptotic coverage for the combined estimate under stated conditions. In simulations, DARTS often improves precision over methods that do not learn which covariates are useful, while remaining less efficient than an oracle that knows the prognostic covariates in advance.
key_results: In the comparison with variable costs, based on 1,000 replications with 200 batches of 1,000 units, 100 candidate covariates, and a budget of 2,000, DARTS had a relative root mean squared error of 1.415 versus 1.018 for ARMM and 1.036 for MADCovar; the oracle value was 1.812. Across the simulation grid, DARTS achieved a reported relative efficiency of up to 3.56 over the difference-in-means baseline, compared with up to 1.26 for randomly selected covariates. In the Liang simulation with 100 covariates, a budget of 2,000, and batches of 1,000 units, the mean final posterior inclusion probability was 0.34 for signal covariates and 0.11 for noise covariates. The authors report confidence interval coverage near the nominal level in their fixed-horizon simulations; their theoretical regret upper and lower bounds have matching polynomial rates up to logarithmic factors.
key_equations:
Budgeted covariate-selection objective: \[\max_{a_{jt}\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{p}a_{jt}\theta_j\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{p}a_{jt}c_j\le B,\quad\sum_{j=1}^{p}a_{jt}\le K\] The indicator a_jt is one when covariate j is selected in batch t; theta_j is its unknown mean reward and proxy for prognostic value; c_j is its measurement cost; B is the total budget; T is the number of batches; p is the number of candidate covariates; and K is the per-batch selection limit.

Beta posterior update for Thompson sampling: \[\alpha_j(t)=\alpha_j(t-1)+r_j(t),\qquad\beta_j(t)=\beta_j(t-1)+1-r_j(t)\] Alpha and beta are the parameters of covariate j’s Beta posterior, t is the batch index, and r_j(t) is the observed binary reward for that covariate in the binary-reward formulation.

Rerandomization balance criterion: \[z_t^*=\arg\min_z(\bar X_1(t)-\bar X_0(t))^\top\hat\Sigma(t)^{-1}(\bar X_1(t)-\bar X_0(t))\] The selected assignment z_t^* is the candidate assignment z that minimizes the Mahalanobis imbalance; the two X-bar terms are the covariate means in the treatment and control arms of batch t, and Sigma-hat is the pooled sample covariance matrix for that batch.

Inverse-variance weighted cumulative estimate: \[\hat\mu_T=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat\tau_t/\hat v_t}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}1/\hat v_t}\] Mu-hat is the cumulative treatment-effect estimate through batch T; tau-hat-t is the adjusted treatment-effect estimate for batch t; and v-hat-t is its estimated variance, so batches with smaller estimated variance receive greater weight.
limitations_stated: The theoretical regret results use an idealized Beta-Bernoulli model; the guarantee for fractional rewards depends on an unobservable posterior approximation error and is less informative in dense-signal settings. The inferential guarantee is for the fixed-horizon estimate, so sequential peeking or early stopping invalidates the stated coverage. The comparison with ARMM and MADCovar is informationally asymmetric: those methods receive randomly preselected covariates, whereas DARTS learns from the full candidate pool.
limitations_unstated: The acquisition reward measures predictiveness of control outcomes, so it may not prioritize covariates that are chiefly useful for explaining treatment-effect heterogeneity or predicting treated outcomes. The evidence is based on simulations rather than real trials, and the reported computational burden—including about 35 CPU minutes per replication in the main method comparison—may limit practical use at larger scales.
future_work_stated: The authors propose methods that account for dependence among covariates, including group LASSO rewards when covariate clusters are known and bandit methods with correlation structure. They also propose confidence-sequence inference to make the cumulative estimate valid for sequential monitoring and early stopping.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate DARTS in real experiments, including studies where covariate measurement costs and availability vary across participants or sites. Further work could also assess acquisition policies that target treatment-effect modifiers directly and compare methods under matched access to candidate covariates.

summary: This theory paper develops bounds on the covering radius of binary orthogonal arrays (OAs) with even strength. The objective is to bound how far any point in the binary space can be from its nearest array row. The authors improve linear programming (LP) bounds by using Krawtchouk polynomials and signed measures, with different bounds depending on whether farthest points have array rows at their antipodes. They also construct three infinite families of arrays related to BCH, Melas, and Zetterberg codes, and derive lower bounds using algebraic curves over finite fields. Their improved bounds are better than earlier bounds for non-tight arrays, and some examples have closely matching upper and lower bounds.
key_results: The new LP bounds improve on the Fazekas–Levenshtein bounds for non-tight arrays, subject to the paper’s stated cases concerning farthest points and their antipodes. For the first constructed family with length 15, the authors give a lower bound of 3 and an improved upper bound of 4, compared with the earlier upper bound of 5; at length 31, the lower bound is 10 and the improved upper bound is 11, compared with 12. For the Zetterberg-related family at length 17, the lower and upper bounds both equal 5, giving the exact covering radius; at length 65, the lower bound is 25 and the improved upper bound is 27, compared with the earlier upper bound of 28. The paper gives theoretical derivations and numerical comparisons for selected small lengths, rather than evaluating experimental designs on data.
key_equations:
Orthogonal-array moment condition: \[\sum_{j=1}^{M} f(t_j(y))=f_0M,\quad \deg(f)\le 2k\] Here M is the number of array rows, f is any polynomial of degree at most twice k, t_j(y) is the transformed distance from point y to array row j, and f_0 is the constant coefficient of f in its Krawtchouk-polynomial expansion.

Combined covering-radius bound: \[\rho(C)\ge \min\{t_{k,k}^{0,\ell},q_k(n,|C|)\}\] Here rho(C) is the normalized covering-radius quantity for array C, t_{k,k}^{0,ell} is the largest zero of the paper’s modified orthogonal polynomial for degree k and threshold ell, q_k(n,|C|) is the cardinality-dependent bound, n is the array length, and |C| is the number of rows.

First constructed family: \[n=2^m-1,\quad M=2^{me},\quad \tau=2e,\quad R(O)\ge 2^{m-1}-1-(e-1)2^{m/2}\] Here n is the array length, m and e are positive integer construction parameters, M is the number of rows, tau is the strength, R(O) is the covering radius of the constructed array O, and the displayed inequality is the family’s lower bound on that radius.
limitations_stated: The authors state that finding the exact covering radii of the three constructed families is a natural and difficult problem that remains open in general. They also note that obtaining analytical expressions for the cardinality-dependent bound is difficult when k is greater than 1.
limitations_unstated: The improved bounds rely on conditions about the farthest points, including whether their antipodes belong to the array; applying the strongest conditional bound may therefore require structural information that is not readily available. The numerical comparisons cover selected small lengths and constructed code families, so they do not establish performance across a broad range of arrays or real design settings.
future_work_stated: The authors identify determining the exact covering radii of the three constructed families as an open direction. They also suggest that more detailed study of some examples could determine their exact radii.
future_work_unstated: It would be useful to develop practical procedures for identifying which conditional bound applies and for optimizing the cardinality-dependent bound at larger values of k. Further work could also assess these bounds for arrays with practical run constraints and test their usefulness in actual designed experiments.

summary: This paper develops an adaptive discretization algorithm for locally optimal experimental design with constraints. It minimizes a convex design criterion, most often the D-criterion, while satisfying finite sets of convex inequality and affine equality constraints; a different design criterion can also be imposed as a constraint. The algorithm repeatedly optimizes the design on a finite set of candidate experiments, then adds an experiment that violates a sensitivity-based optimality condition. The authors prove convergence to an optimal design for the zero-tolerance version and finite termination at an approximately optimal design for the positive-tolerance version, under stated regularity and feasibility assumptions. Numerical examples use an exponential growth model and a chemical reaction-kinetics model, including constraints on average product return and measurement time.
key_results: The paper proves that the zero-tolerance algorithm either terminates at an optimal design or has accumulation points that are optimal, with criterion values converging monotonically to the optimum; its positive-tolerance version terminates finitely at a design meeting the specified optimality tolerance. In the exponential-growth examples, the algorithm required 2, 4, and 3 iterations, with reported runtimes of 0.1244, 0.2399, and 0.7182 seconds; the computed designs had 2, 4, and 3 support points. In the reaction-kinetics examples, the unconstrained and constrained designs each had 6 support points and required 8 and 9 iterations, with runtimes of 301.01 and 302.72 seconds; their reported approximation-error bounds were 2.6459 × 10⁻⁶ and 3.3856 × 10⁻⁵. The algorithm’s sensitivity-minimization subproblems have the dimension of the experiment space, compared with larger nonlinear subproblems in two of the cited methods, and the general version needs approximate global sensitivity minimization only when its preliminary search finds no violating experiment; these comparisons are analytical rather than head-to-head runtime tests.
key_equations:
Constrained design problem: \[\min_{\xi\in\Xi(X)}\Psi_0(\xi)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\Psi_i(\xi)\le 0\ (i\in I_{\mathrm{ineq}}),\quad\Psi_i(\xi)=0\ (i\in I_{\mathrm{eq}})\] Here xi is a design, Xi(X) is the set of designs on design space X, Psi_0 is the objective, Psi_i are constraint functions, and I_ineq and I_eq index the inequality and equality constraints.

D-criterion and information matrix: \[\Psi_0(\xi)=-\log\det M(\xi),\qquad M(\xi)=\int_X m(x)\,d\xi(x)\] Here Psi_0 is the D-criterion, xi is the design measure, M is its information matrix, m(x) is the information matrix for experiment x, and X is the design space.

Sensitivity optimality condition: \[\inf_{x\in X}\psi^L(\xi^k,\lambda^k,x)\ge -\epsilon\] Here psi^L is the Lagrangian sensitivity function, xi^k is the design at iteration k, lambda^k is its vector of constraint multipliers, X is the design space, and epsilon is the optimality tolerance.

Discretization update: \[X^{k+1}=X^k\cup\{x^k\}\] Here X^k is the finite set of candidate experiments at iteration k, x^k is the experiment added at that iteration, and X^{k+1} is the expanded set.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the zero-tolerance version is not guaranteed to terminate after finitely many iterations. Its sensitivity minimization problem is generally nonconvex and may require computationally expensive global optimization. The convergence and termination results require regularity assumptions, including an initially strictly feasible discretized problem and a non-one-sidedness condition for the equality constraints.
limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstrations use finite candidate grids, so they do not establish how performance or design quality changes when the continuous experiment space is discretized differently. The reaction-kinetics examples take about 301 to 303 seconds even on the reported grid-based implementation, and the paper does not provide direct runtime comparisons against the cited algorithms on the same problems. The examples also use locally specified parameter values and a limited set of model types and constraints, leaving robustness to parameter uncertainty or model misspecification untested.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method against competing algorithms on shared constrained-design benchmarks, especially for very large candidate sets and continuous experiment spaces. Further work could also test robustness under parameter uncertainty and model misspecification, and extend the design formulation to practical restrictions such as exact run counts, replication limits, or sequential experiment selection.

summary: The paper proposes a three-phase adaptive design for screening factors and optimizing a response within one experimental program. In the first phase, a modified definitive screening design and a screening statistic identify important factors and two-factor interactions using Elastic Net regression. In the second phase, the design adds experiments chosen according to the number and structure of the identified factors and interactions. In the third phase, a Gaussian process model guides optimization and selects six refinement runs in regions of high uncertainty. In simulations covering six scenarios, the method achieved 97.08% mean factor detection accuracy, with a mean prediction error of 3.61, while using an average of 41.5 runs.
key_results: Across six simulated scenarios and 540 evaluations, the method achieved 97.08% mean detection accuracy, compared with 83.33% for traditional sequential methods, 82.22% for augmented definitive screening designs, and 73.61% for standard definitive screening designs. The reported mean prediction error was 3.61, compared with 4.31 for traditional sequential methods; space-filling methods had lower errors, including 0.83 for Latin hypercube sampling and 1.45 for Sobol sequences, but provided no factor screening. The method maintained at least 90% detection accuracy in every scenario, including 90.0% in the interaction-heavy scenario. It used an average of 41.5 runs versus 29 for traditional sequential methods, a 43% increase, and the authors report statistically significant detection comparisons at below 0.001.
key_equations:
Phase 1 run count: \[n_1=2k+3\] Here n1 is the number of Phase 1 runs and k is the number of factors.

Screening statistic: \[\mathrm{CWESS}_i=\frac{|\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{main},i}|}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{main},i})+\epsilon}\times\mathrm{SNR}\] Here CWESS with subscript i is the score for factor i, beta-hat-main,i is its estimated main effect, SE is the estimated standard error of that effect, epsilon is a small positive constant, and SNR is the signal-to-noise ratio.
limitations_stated: The authors state that validation used synthetic response functions and that industrial case studies are needed. The study focused on six continuous factors; higher dimensions, categorical factors, and mixture constraints need further investigation. They also note that Gaussian process computation may limit use when cumulative run counts are very large.
limitations_unstated: The detection metric counts the proportion of true active factors found, but does not penalize identifying inactive factors as important; consequently, the reported accuracy does not fully describe screening specificity. Prediction error is measured at the true optimum, so it does not by itself establish how well the method predicts across the response surface or how close the selected operating point comes to the optimum.
future_work_stated: The authors propose industrial case studies, extension to higher-dimensional screening and categorical or mixed factors, and work on constrained and multi-response optimization. They also identify adaptive Bayesian sequential decision-making and an open-source software implementation as future directions.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could report false-positive screening rates alongside detection accuracy and assess how threshold choices affect both measures. Testing the design under explicit blocking, restricted randomization, and practical run constraints would also clarify how readily it can be used in industrial experiments.

summary: The paper presents ALMAB-DC, a framework for sequential experimental design and optimization using a Gaussian process (GP) model and asynchronous parallel computing. It is intended for tasks such as response optimization, dose selection, and spatial sampling, with objectives including finding a high-performing setting and reducing prediction uncertainty. The method combines an acquisition rule, a multi-armed bandit (MAB) that allocates evaluations across regions, and a Kriging Believer (KB) update to diversify parallel proposals. Completed evaluations trigger new selections without waiting for every worker, using an event-driven dispatch rule. The authors report improved design performance over selected baselines and faster progress in wall-clock rounds, while noting that the results rely substantially on simulated evaluations.
key_results: In the polymer response-surface simulation, with 20 evaluations per run, ALMAB-DC using the upper confidence bound (UCB) had median final regret of 0.18% and an 85.4% success rate, compared with 0.41% and 78.0% for sequential Bayesian optimization. In the dose-response case, the reported median regret for the single-worker method was 0.00263; with four workers it reached zero within the same ten-round wall-clock budget. For spatial sampling, final integrated posterior variance (IPV) was 0.072 for ALMAB-DC and greedy maximum-variance selection, compared with 0.107 for Latin hypercube sampling and 0.098 for random selection; the rounds to reach the stated IPV threshold fell from 13 to 6 with two workers and to 4 with four. At four workers, asynchronous dispatch reached the stated thresholds in 7 versus 10 rounds for the response-surface case, 6 versus 8 for dose selection, and 4 versus 6 for spatial sampling; terminal regret was not statistically distinguishable from the synchronous versions in those comparisons.

Regional bandit priority: \[I_m(t)=\hat{\rho}_m(t)+\sqrt{\frac{2\log t}{N_m(t)}}\] Here, I is the priority for region m at decision stage t, rho with a hat is the running mean reward for that region, and N is the number of times that region has been selected.

Candidate selection within a selected region: \[x_{t+1}=\arg\max_{x\in R_m}\left[\mu_t(x)+\sqrt{\beta}\,\sigma_t(x)\right]\] Here, x at stage t plus one is the next candidate, R is the selected region m, mu is the GP posterior mean, sigma is its posterior standard deviation, and beta controls the exploration contribution.
limitations_stated: The authors state that exact GP computation scales cubically with the number of observations and limits practical budgets to about 200 unless a sparse GP or neural surrogate is used. They also note that their simulations use calibrated surrogates, that they have not conducted prospective randomized comparisons on physical processes, and that they did not provide a direct wall-clock comparison with batch GP methods on a unified time axis.
limitations_unstated: The primary examples use specified kernels and relatively small, structured candidate spaces, so the results do not establish how well the method works when the response surface is poorly matched by the surrogate or the design space has many factors. The regional allocation and diversity procedures are evaluated in selected settings, leaving their performance under practical constraints on allowable combinations, costs, or feasible locations unclear.
future_work_stated: The authors propose using sparse GP or neural surrogates to support larger evaluation budgets, adapting the framework to heterogeneous workers with different latencies, and conducting prospective randomized comparisons with classical central composite designs on physical processes. They also propose direct wall-clock comparisons with batch GP methods such as q-EI.
future_work_unstated: Further studies could test the method on constrained, mixed-factor designs where some combinations are infeasible or have different evaluation costs. It would also be useful to assess sequential adjustment of the worker count and region partition as experiments progress, and to validate the resulting recommendations prospectively in industrial or laboratory studies.
