summary: This paper introduces uMaxPro, a space-filling design method for computer experiments that aims to cover low-dimensional projections well while also avoiding bias in sampling the bounded design domain. It modifies the MaxPro criterion by replacing ordinary coordinate distances with periodic distances based on the minimum image convention. Designs are constructed as Latin hypercubes and optimized using simulated annealing with coordinate swaps. The authors compare the method with MaxPro and other sampling approaches using numerical integration, projection assessments, and structural engineering examples. They report that uMaxPro retains strong projection performance while producing statistically uniform samples and unbiased integration estimates.
key_results: Across 10,000 independent optimized designs, the authors report that MaxPro undersamples parts of the domain, with the reported undersampled volume reaching 34.77% in five dimensions; for uMaxPro, the reported value is 0.41%. In tests across two to five dimensions, uMaxPro has wrap-around discrepancy close to the Halton sequence, and its root mean square integration error decreases at a rate close to one divided by the number of points, with lower error than Halton on the tested interacting function. The integration comparisons use 500 independent runs and show biased estimates for MaxPro but unbiased estimates for uMaxPro. In engineering prediction tests averaged over 500 design realizations, uMaxPro performs well against the compared sampling methods; in the finite element concrete example, it improves estimation relative to MaxPro, while the paper notes that Halton can have a steeper error decrease at larger sample sizes.

limitations_unstated: The evidence is based on dimensions up to five, selected integration functions, and a small set of structural engineering applications, so performance in higher dimensions or other model classes is not established. future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Further studies could test uMaxPro with other design restrictions and objectives, and assess it on additional engineering models with different input distributions and domain constraints. summary: This paper develops a Bayesian optimal experimental design framework for identifying parameters in history-dependent constitutive models, with the goal of reducing parameter uncertainty. It uses expected information gain (EIG) to evaluate candidate experiments and derives a faster approximation based on the Fisher information matrix (FIM) and a Gaussian approximation to the posterior. To make optimization practical for batches of experiments, the authors train a neural-network surrogate of the FIM and reuse it across different batch sizes. Numerical studies design uniaxial tests for linear and nonlinear viscoelastic materials by choosing specimen hole geometry and loading paths, using simulated force and image data. The optimized designs generally improve parameter identifiability over random designs, including for parameters governing stress relaxation and other memory effects.
key_results: For linear viscoelasticity, the optimized single-test designs produced about 10% higher EGA utility than random designs and reduced average 95% credible-interval widths by 47% to 48%. Their marginal utility improvement was largest for stress-relaxation parameters, at 10.4% to 11.2%; the study also found a Spearman correlation of 0.67 between EGA utility and stress-state entropy. For nonlinear viscoelasticity, optimized batches improved utility by approximately 7% to 9% over random batches of the same size; average credible-interval reductions were 44% without loading-rate regularization and 29% with regularization. The FIM surrogates achieved over 97% mean relative accuracy for predicting the logarithm of the FIM and over 99.6% and 99.4% accuracy for approximate information gain in the linear and nonlinear studies, respectively. In the linear study, EGA evaluations were reported to cost four orders of magnitude less than the nested Monte Carlo comparison, which became impractical with the high-dimensional image data.
key_equations:

Gaussian approximation to the design utility: \[\operatorname{EIG}(z)\approx\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim\pi_\Theta}\left[\log\det\left(\operatorname{FIM}(\theta,z)-\nabla^2\log\pi_\Theta(\theta)\right)\right]+H(\pi_\Theta)\] EIG is expected information gain, theta is a parameter value drawn from prior pi, z is the design, FIM is the Fisher information matrix, the Hessian term is the second derivative of the log prior with respect to parameters, and H is prior information entropy.

Design optimization objective: \[z^\dagger\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{z}\left\{\operatorname{EIG}(z)-P(z)\right\}\] The optimal design z dagger maximizes expected information gain EIG over candidate designs z after subtracting the design penalty P.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the Gaussian posterior approximation introduces bias in estimating expected information gain and can fail when the Fisher information matrix is singular or the likelihood is multimodal. They also note that their numerical studies focus primarily on uniaxial loading of planar specimens under simplified conditions.
limitations_unstated: The results come from simulated experiments rather than physical tests, so they do not establish that the selected geometries and loading paths deliver the same gains in a laboratory. The comparisons also rely on specified parameter priors, noise models, and a restricted family of planar specimens and loading controls, which may limit transfer to other materials or practical test constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose using more general non-parametric posterior density estimation to reduce approximation bias and to incorporate nuisance uncertainty, such as uncertain boundary and initial conditions. They also propose extending the work to complex three-dimensional geometries and loading scenarios, with joint optimization of specimen topology and multiaxial protocols and possible use of three-dimensional volumetric data.

summary: This paper develops space-filling lattice designs for computer experiments, with the aim of supporting accurate prediction while maintaining adequate separation between runs. It presents an explicit rank-1 lattice construction based on algebraic numbers and a Korobov lattice construction that searches for a parameter using the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovasz basis reduction algorithm. The explicit construction determines its run sizes from the chosen algebraic parameters, while the Korobov construction can target a chosen prime run size. The authors prove that both approaches generate quasi-uniform families, balancing coverage and point separation. Their numerical results show that the lattice designs maintain the optimal separation-radius rate and can improve Gaussian process regression performance in lower dimensions.
key_results: The theory establishes that both constructions have covering and separation radii of order N to the power minus one over d; the explicit construction also has isotropic discrepancy of order N to the power minus one over d. In tested dimensions 2, 3, 5, and 7, the proposed lattices showed this optimal separation-rate behavior, unlike the compared random, Halton, and Sobol’ point sets, whose separation radii decayed faster. The Korobov construction generally had lower and more stable theoretical mesh-ratio bounds than the explicit construction; its search checks N minus 1 candidate parameters and has cost polynomial in dimension and quasi-linear in run size. In Gaussian process regression tests repeated over 100 noise realizations, both lattice designs generally performed better for sufficiently large run sizes in dimension 2 and had smaller asymptotic mean errors in dimension 3; no distinct prediction advantage appeared in dimensions 5 and 7 over the tested range.
key_equations:
Mesh-ratio design criterion: \[\rho = h/q\] The mesh ratio rho is the covering radius h divided by the separation radius q; a bounded ratio indicates that coverage and separation are balanced.

Optimal radii for a quasi-uniform design: \[h = \Theta(N^{-1/d}), \qquad q = \Theta(N^{-1/d})\] The covering radius h and separation radius q both have order N to the power minus one over d, where N is the number of points and d is the dimension.

Korobov lattice generating vector: \[z = (1,a,a^2,\ldots,a^{d-1}) \pmod N\] The generating vector z has components given by powers of the integer parameter a reduced modulo N, where N is the run size and d is the dimension.
limitations_stated: The explicit construction does not allow arbitrary run sizes: its run sizes are determined by the Diophantine properties of its chosen algebraic parameters. The authors also note that the high-dimensional prediction comparisons are limited to a pre-asymptotic range by the computational cost of fitting Gaussian process models. Fixed algebraic parameters can produce poor low-dimensional projections, including overlaps or alignments that caused prediction-error spikes in one five-dimensional test.
limitations_unstated: The prediction comparison uses a limited set of synthetic benchmark functions and a single fixed Matérn smoothness setting, so the results do not establish performance for a broad range of real simulator responses or kernel choices. The Korobov search examines every candidate parameter, which may become burdensome at run sizes beyond those tested, and the evaluation does not compare against a broad range of established optimized space-filling designs.
future_work_stated: The authors propose optimizing the algebraic parameter vector to improve the quality of low-dimensional projections and avoid structural anomalies in the explicit construction.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate both constructions under practical input constraints, such as restricted factors or nonrectangular feasible regions, and compare them with optimized classical designs on real computer experiments. It could also investigate sequential ways to add runs while retaining the space-filling and separation properties.

summary: The paper develops a framework for using sample splitting to evaluate analysis methods and launch rules in A/B testing when the true impact of each test is unknown. It applies the method to per-test impact estimates assumed to be unbiased and normally distributed, with known sampling variances. Each test is partitioned so that one split applies the method and a separate split supplies an independent estimate of the true impact. The authors derive estimators and asymptotic confidence intervals for average performance, and examine choices of split fraction and number of partitions. Their theory and simulations show that sample splitting estimates performance on the split rather than full-test performance, creating a bias and variance tradeoff.
key_results: The authors show that average performance estimates are unbiased for the sample-split target, and derive asymptotic normality and valid confidence intervals as the number of tests grows. In simulations with 5K tests, the estimates had negligible bias for the sample-split target and the 95 percent confidence intervals covered it approximately 95 percent of the time. The simulations used 30 partitions as their benchmark and found minimal additional variance reduction beyond 30; increasing the number of independent tests consistently reduced variance. Allocating more than half the data to the methodology split reduced bias for full-test performance, but could increase variance; the mean-squared error optimum depended on the comparison being evaluated. For plug-in methods, resampling split estimates from their conditional distribution avoids repeated unit-level partitioning and, according to the authors, can reduce computational costs by orders of magnitude.
key_equations:
Assumed impact-estimate model: \[\hat{\Delta}_i\mid\Delta_i=\delta_i\sim\mathcal{N}(\delta_i,\tau_i^2)\] The estimated impact for test i, conditional on its true impact δᵢ, follows a normal distribution with mean δᵢ and sampling variance τᵢ².

Sample-split performance target: \[\theta(\kappa,\alpha)=\mathbb{E}\left[p\left(\kappa(X_{ia}),\delta_i\right)\right]\] The target θ is the expected score p when methodology κ is applied to training-split data Xᵢa, with split fraction α and true impact δᵢ.

Unbiased squared-error score: \[\widehat{Y}_{is}=\left(\kappa(X_{ia})-\hat{\delta}_{ib}\right)^2-\tau_{ib}^2\] The estimated score Ŷᵢs for partition s is the squared difference between the methodology output and the split-b impact estimate, minus the sampling variance of that estimate.

Asymptotic distribution of average performance: \[\sqrt{I}\left(\hat{\theta}-\theta\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,\zeta^2)\] As the number of tests I grows, the estimated average performance θ-hat, centered at θ and scaled by the square root of I, approaches a normal distribution with mean zero and variance ζ².
limitations_stated: The authors state that sample-split estimates are generally biased for performance on the full sample because the methodology is applied to only part of the data. Their asymptotic inference may be unreliable with a small number of tests; they caution that confidence-interval coverage can be poor in that setting.
limitations_unstated: The framework relies on unbiased, normally distributed impact estimates with known variances and on tests being independent and identically distributed, assumptions that may not fit every testing system. The empirical validation is simulation-based and focuses on two specific comparisons, so it does not establish performance across real experiments, other methodology classes, or a broad range of performance measures.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the approach on historical or prospective experiments where the normality and known-variance assumptions are less plausible, and evaluate methods that change how impact estimates are constructed. It would also be useful to assess split choices under practical allocation constraints and to compare additional performance objectives beyond the examples studied here.

summary: This paper introduces Hyperparameter-Informed Predictive Exploration (HIPE), an adaptive method for choosing initial experiment batches in Bayesian optimization and active learning. It is designed for Gaussian process models and aims to reduce uncertainty in predictions while also learning the model hyperparameters that affect later optimization. HIPE combines Expected Predictive Information Gain, which targets predictive uncertainty, with Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement, which targets information about hyperparameters. The authors construct a batch criterion whose balance weight is determined by the information hyperparameters provide about test-point predictions, and optimize the criterion jointly over candidate batches. In the reported benchmarks, HIPE generally improves the balance of predictive accuracy, model calibration, and subsequent optimization performance, particularly when only a few large batches are available.
key_results: In batch active learning, using batches of 16 points for 4 rounds across 100 seeds, HIPE was the only method that consistently ranked among the top two for both predictive error and predictive calibration across the tested tasks. In two-batch optimization experiments with batches of 24 points, HIPE matched or exceeded the best method on the noisy synthetic benchmarks; on five benchmark optimization tasks tested across 200 seeds each, it had the highest final performance on four and was competitive on the fifth. On the 40-dimensional support vector machine task, HIPE achieved the highest optimization performance, narrowly ahead of the alternatives, and identified the two important input dimensions more effectively than space-filling initialization. In a reported 4-batch runtime comparison with batches of 8 points, HIPE acquisition optimization took 19.61 seconds, compared with 8.62 seconds for negative integrated posterior variance; initial model fitting took 21.91 seconds and model fitting during the optimization loop took 181.79 seconds for HIPE.
key_equations:
Combined predictive and hyperparameter information criterion: \[\mathrm{HIPE}_{\beta}(X)=\mathrm{EPIG}(X;p_*)+\beta\,\mathrm{BALD}(X)\] HIPE is the proposed batch criterion; X is the candidate batch; EPIG is Expected Predictive Information Gain under test-point distribution p*; BALD is Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement; and β is the weight balancing the two terms.

Information-based balancing weight: \[\beta=I(y(x_*);\theta\mid D),\qquad x_*\sim p_*\] β is the balancing weight; I is mutual information; y(x*) is the response at test input x*; θ denotes model hyperparameters; D is the data already collected; x* is drawn from test-point distribution p*.
limitations_stated: The authors state that HIPE can be computationally expensive, especially for large batches in higher dimensions. The paper focuses on Gaussian process surrogates; applying the method to other Bayesian models requires deriving a suitable acquisition function for those models.
limitations_unstated: The empirical study relies on synthetic functions and benchmark or surrogate tasks, rather than reporting validation in a physical or operational experiment. Most optimization comparisons use only two batches, so the results provide limited evidence about performance over longer sequential campaigns or under practical constraints on which input combinations can be tested.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending HIPE to transfer learning, including use with a multi-task Gaussian process and data from related problems. They also propose incorporating expert knowledge through a non-uniform test-point distribution and studying multi-objective settings with multiple surrogates that share input locations.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test HIPE in real experiments and assess how it performs when inputs have operational restrictions, such as discrete choices, forbidden combinations, or limited resources. It would also be useful to study cheaper approximations for large batches and repeated sequential use when observations arrive over many rounds.

summary: The paper introduces mutual transport dependence (MTD), a geometric criterion for optimal experimental design that aims to select experiments useful for estimating an unknown quantity. Unlike mutual information (MI), the MTD compares the joint distribution of the unknown quantity and the outcome with the product of their marginal distributions using optimal transport. Its transport cost can be chosen to reflect the parameter scale, a transformed representation, or a task-specific priority. The authors estimate the criterion from samples and optimize designs with gradient-based methods when the experiment simulator is differentiable. In simulated benchmarks, the method often gives lower parameter-estimation errors than the MI-based comparison and can be tailored to prioritize a specified decision.
key_results: For the Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) benchmark after 10 sequential experiments, MTD had lower reported root mean squared errors than posterior contrastive estimation (PCE) across all reported parameter metrics; for example, error for rho was 0.018 with MTD versus 0.047 with PCE, and error for alpha was 0.009 versus 0.036. In source location finding over 25 experiments, MTD produced lower error through most of the rollout, although the MI-based designs had similar error by the final iteration. In that location-finding comparison, optimizing one design took about 30 seconds for MTD and about 120 seconds for PCE under the reported implementation. A weighted transport cost reduced the reported zero-one loss more quickly when the task included identifying whether a source was in a specified region.
key_equations:
Assumed experiment model: \[p(\theta,y\mid d)=p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,d)\] Theta is the unknown target quantity, y is the observed outcome, d is the experiment design, p(theta) is the prior distribution, and p(y given theta and d) is the outcome model.

Mutual transport dependence: \[\mathcal{T}_c(d)=\operatorname{OT}_c[p(\theta,y\mid d),p(\theta)p(y\mid d)]=\min_{\gamma\in\Pi}E_\gamma[c(\theta,y,\theta',y')]\] T sub c of d is the MTD for design d; OT sub c is the optimal transport cost using sample-level cost c; the two distributions are the joint and the product of the marginals; gamma ranges over valid couplings Pi; and the expectation averages the cost between paired samples, where primes mark the second sample.

Design selection: \[d^*=\arg\max_d\mathcal{T}_c(d)\] The selected design d star is a design d that maximizes the MTD under cost c.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the empirical transport estimate has positive finite-sample bias, which decreases as the sample count grows, and that MTD estimates can have high variance. Gradient-based optimization also relies on differentiable sampling with respect to the design.
limitations_unstated: The empirical comparisons use simulated CES and source-location tasks, so they do not establish that the gains transfer to real industrial experiments or other model families. The criterion depends on choosing a suitable cost, and the reported implementation uses 1,000 samples per gradient step and 250 gradient steps, which may be demanding for large models or costly simulators.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method in real experiments and under practical restrictions such as discrete candidate settings, safety limits, and fixed run budgets. Further studies could also test how sensitive design performance is to misspecified costs and models, and compare computational scaling across larger problems.

scope_reason: The paper develops methods for choosing sequential experiments and when to stop, making experimental design its central subject.

summary: The paper develops a method for deciding both which experiment to run next and when to stop a sequential campaign. It frames sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) as a finite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP), with expected information gain (EIG) balanced against experimental cost. The stopping decision compares the reward from stopping now with the expected value of continuing, while a policy-gradient method learns continuous design choices. A training curriculum gradually shifts from forced continuation to the learned stopping rule to reduce premature stopping during learning. Simulations show that the approach can learn cost-aware design and stopping policies, with the clearest benefit when earlier design choices affect later experimental opportunities.
key_results: In the linear-Gaussian benchmark, the analytical best utilities were 2.892 for four experiments at zero cost, 1.703 for one experiment at cost −0.5 per experiment, and 2.047 for two experiments at cost −0.25 per experiment. The tested maximum horizons were 3, 4, and 5 experiments; at zero cost the learned policy continued to the allowed maximum, while at negative costs it learned earlier termination. In the source-detection example with a cost of −0.5 per experiment and maximum horizon 4, vanilla training settled at an average stopping stage of about 2.4, while curriculum training stopped slightly after stage 3 and attained substantially higher reward. On one illustrative source-detection trajectory, the vanilla policy stopped after two experiments and earned −0.564, whereas the curriculum-trained policy continued for three experiments and earned 2.198. The source-model surrogate had test mean-squared error on the order of 10⁻⁶ and was approximately 10⁵ times faster than the numerical solver.
key_equations: Value-based stopping rule: \[\text{Stop at state }s\text{ when }r_T(s)\ge Q(s)\] Here s is the current state, r_T(s) is the immediate reward for stopping there, Q(s) is the expected value of continuing with another experiment, and the comparison means stop when the immediate reward is no smaller.
limitations_stated: The authors state that evaluating rewards can be costly when posterior updates or Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence calculations are expensive, especially for high-dimensional parameters. They also note a circular dependence between the learned continuation value and the training data distribution, and that the paper focuses on information gain rather than other scientific objectives.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulations rather than real experimental campaigns, so practical performance under real measurement noise, logistics, or operational constraints is not demonstrated. The examples use short maximum horizons of 3 to 5 experiments and selected model settings; the paper does not establish how results scale to longer campaigns or compare performance across a broad set of methods and repeated real-world studies.
future_work_stated: The authors propose combining the framework with scalable posterior approximations, amortized inference, or surrogate models for information gain. They also suggest direct stopping-policy parameterizations or offline pretraining of continuation values to improve robustness, and extending the objective to predictive performance or other task-specific scientific goals.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the learned policies in real experiments and test them under practical constraints such as hard budgets, safety limits, and unavailable or costly design settings. Further work could also assess transfer to longer campaigns and sequential retraining as new data arrive, and provide reusable software and reproducible benchmarks.

summary: This paper develops a method for choosing the path of a moving sensor to reduce uncertainty in a Bayesian inverse problem governed by a linear partial differential equation (PDE). The sensor makes continuous or frequent measurements of the evolving state, and the unknown parameters have a Gaussian prior while measurement errors have a Gaussian noise model. The authors derive the posterior covariance as a function of the path, then optimize trace-based or determinant-based uncertainty criteria while enforcing path and control constraints. They represent feasible paths through an ordinary differential equation for sensor motion and use a time discretization designed to remain consistent as it is refined. Simulations of pollutant transport show that optimized paths can reduce posterior uncertainty, and that coarser solutions can provide useful starting points for finer optimization.
key_results: In the two-parameter pollutant example, the A-optimal utility fell from 0.791 to 0.493 for initial path 1, and from 1.149 to 0.729 for initial path 3; path 2 instead rose from 1.090 to 1.119. For path 1, refining the sensor time step through six halvings to about 1.5 × 10^-4 led to an optimization that reached the reported optimum in one iteration, using two objective and two gradient evaluations. In the 25-dimensional parameter-reduced example, the reduced space captured 99.01% of prior sample energy, and optimization lowered the A-optimal utility from 6.359 × 10^-3 to 5.461 × 10^-3, a relative factor of 0.859, in 184 seconds. The study compares starting paths and measurement setups within its simulation, rather than benchmarking against other design algorithms; source code and data are reported as publicly available.
key_equations:
Posterior covariance for a sensor path: \[\Sigma_{\mathrm{post}}(p)=\left(G(p)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}^{-1}G(p)+\Sigma_{\mathrm{pr}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\] The posterior covariance Σpost for path p is computed from the measurement map G, the noise covariance Σnoise, and the prior covariance Σpr; the superscript T denotes matrix transpose.

A-optimal and D-optimal design criteria: \[\Psi_A(\Sigma_{\mathrm{post}})=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{post}}),\qquad \Psi_D(\Sigma_{\mathrm{post}})=\det(\Sigma_{\mathrm{post}})\] The A-optimal utility ΨA is the trace of the posterior covariance, and the D-optimal utility ΨD is its determinant; the design seeks a path that minimizes the selected utility.
limitations_stated: The authors restrict the main formulation to linear parameter-to-observable maps and a single moving sensor. Their parameter-field example uses a 25-dimensional parameter-reduced posterior, and they state that an efficient, scalable extension to parameter fields remains future work.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is limited to simulated pollutant transport in one domain, so performance with real sensor data, model error, or different environmental systems is not established. The objective is non-convex and the reported outcomes depend on initial paths; the paper does not establish global optimality or compare the method broadly with alternative design algorithms. Fine time discretizations also make gradient calculations costly, and the high-dimensional result depends on a specific prior-based reduction.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the design criteria, including expected information gain, to nonlinear parameter-to-observable maps, and developing scalable approaches for infinite-dimensional parameter fields using model reduction and multifidelity techniques. They also propose improving robustness to aleatoric uncertainty and finding cheaper ways to generate initial paths; they note that extending the approach to multiple sensors is straightforward.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation with a physical mobile-sensing experiment, including measured navigation error and noise-model calibration. It would also be valuable to evaluate practical operational constraints such as battery limits, communication loss, and restricted flight corridors, and to assess whether the optimized paths remain effective when those constraints or the transport model are imperfect.

summary: The paper develops a method for removing candidate points that cannot belong to any optimal exact design without changing the best achievable design. It addresses finite candidate sets and the D-optimality objective for estimating model parameters. The method uses an optimal approximate design and a known nonsingular exact design to screen candidates with an augmentation condition, followed by a more computationally involved exchange condition. The authors apply the screening before exact-design optimization using mixed-integer second-order cone programming. Their examples show that this preprocessing can shrink very large candidate sets enough to make exact-design computation feasible, while the paper also proves that sufficiently large designs have support within a maximum-variance set.
key_results: In simulated Gaussian-regressor examples with candidate sets from 10^4 to 10^8 points, the augmentation screen reduced the sets to about 100 or fewer candidates; the exchange screen gave moderate additional reduction in this model class. In the constrained mixture example, screening reduced 9,991 candidates to 1,644 after augmentation and then to 390 after exchange. For the mixture problem, the exact-design solver was stopped after 60 seconds with a reported gap of 0.87%; the returned design had a D-criterion value of 1.495 × 10^-4, compared with 1.169 × 10^-4 for the previously reported design. For the discretization with 981,901 candidates, the authors report that exchange screening reduced the remaining set by more than a factor of ten beyond augmentation, with the number retained depending non-monotonically on design size.
key_equations:
Information matrix: \[M(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i f_i f_i^{\top}\] The information matrix M for design w is the sum over candidate indices i from 1 to N of each weight w_i times the regressor vector f_i and its transpose.

D-optimality criterion: \[\Phi(M)=\det(M)^{1/m}\] The criterion Phi of information matrix M is its determinant raised to the reciprocal of m, the number of model parameters.

Augmentation screening condition: \[v_\ell^* \ge mn\left(\operatorname{eff}_{\infty}(w_n^+)-\frac{n-1}{n}\right)\] For candidate index ell to be eligible for an optimal exact design, its optimal-approximate-design variance value v_ell star must be at least m times n times the difference between the efficiency of the known exact design w_n_plus and the quantity n minus 1 divided by n.

Single-point exchange condition: \[\Phi\left(M(w_n^*)-\frac{1}{n}f_\ell f_\ell^{\top}+\frac{1}{n}f_i f_i^{\top}\right)\leq\Phi\left(M(w_n^*)\right)\] For an optimal exact design w_n_star, replacing one trial at supported candidate ell with one trial at any candidate i must not increase the criterion Phi; M is the information matrix, f denotes the corresponding regressor vector, and n is the trial count.
limitations_stated: The authors state that candidate reduction is impossible in certain highly symmetric models where criterion-preserving transformations map any candidate to any other, so every candidate supports some optimal exact design. They also note that the exchange condition is more complex and computationally demanding than the augmentation condition, so its usefulness should be assessed for each problem.
limitations_unstated: The method depends on having an optimal approximate design and a nonsingular exact design available; the paper's practical results therefore do not establish equal performance when either input is difficult to obtain. The numerical evidence covers a limited set of simulated Gaussian models and one constrained mixture example, and the mixture solver was stopped before proving optimality in that demonstration.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to multivariate responses and to exact designs with additional constraints. They also propose developing candidate-removal methods for other criteria, particularly A-optimality, and studying the computational complexity of determining the set of candidates that support optimal exact designs.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test screening under errors in the approximate-design calculation and establish safe numerical tolerances for candidate elimination. It could also evaluate the method on a broader range of industrial experiments and incorporate practical restrictions such as costs, blocking, or forbidden run combinations.

summary: This review introduces Bayesian optimization as a way to choose experiments iteratively when the objective is costly to measure and its functional form is unknown. It is written for bioprocess engineering, including tasks such as optimizing reaction conditions, media, strains, and scale-up. The authors describe a workflow using initial experiments, a probabilistic surrogate model, an acquisition function to choose subsequent experiments, and a stopping rule. They give practical guidance on experimental coverage, model choices, measurement noise, batch effects, and calibration, alongside illustrative simulated examples. The review finds that methods accounting for biological and measurement complications can improve the guidance provided by the model, while also identifying barriers to wider use and areas needing further development.
key_results: In the illustrative simulated pH optimization, the paper reports that the procedure identifies the global optimum at pH 7.2 by iteration 6. The associated figure shows the model fitted to five initial data points; this is an example, not a general run-size result. In a separate simulated biocatalysis example, a hybrid model accounting for first-order reaction kinetics and batch effects learns more efficiently from seven observations per reaction than a naive Gaussian process model, although no numerical error or efficiency measure is reported. As practical guidance rather than a comparative finding, the authors suggest that initial experiments may use roughly half the total experiment budget and that an appropriate kernel length scale may be one-quarter to one-half of the parameter-space width.
key_equations:
Upper confidence bound acquisition score: \[A(x)=\mu(x)+\gamma\sigma(x)\] A is the acquisition score, x is an experimental input, mu is the predicted mean response, gamma sets the exploration weight, and sigma is the predicted standard deviation.

Mechanistic model with a residual response: \[y(x)=m(x)+r(x)\] y is the modeled response at input x, m is the output of the mechanistic or empirical model, and r is the residual response.
limitations_stated: The authors state that real-world use of Bayesian optimization in bioprocess engineering remains nascent and that more experience is needed to establish standards for selecting models, priors, and acquisition functions. They also note that some approaches are computationally demanding and that specialized algorithms are needed for complex parameter spaces.
limitations_unstated: The review does not report a systematic literature search or a reproducible method for selecting and evaluating the cited studies, so its guidance is not presented as a formal evidence synthesis. Its examples are illustrative simulations rather than prospective comparisons in real experimental campaigns, and it gives no shared quantitative benchmark for performance against conventional design of experiments.
future_work_stated: The authors call for domain scientists to test, evaluate, and further develop the recommendations, and for machine learning researchers to develop methods tailored to bioprocess challenges. They also identify the need for more user-friendly tools, reusable model components, and stronger practices for sharing data, software, and documentation.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective, multi-site studies comparing the recommended approaches with conventional experimental designs under realistic budget, batch, and measurement constraints. Shared benchmarks could also test sensitivity to model misspecification and measurement drift, while reporting both optimization quality and the number and cost of experiments.

summary: The paper proposes the data-pooling treatment roll-out (DPTR) framework to help online platforms decide which policies to deploy when each randomized experiment has limited data. It targets positive average treatment effects across multiple experiments and can also guide heterogeneous treatment effect decisions for groups within one experiment. The method combines each experiment's own effect estimate with the average estimate across experiments, using a data-driven scale to control shrinkage and applying the resulting lower decision bound to select policies. The authors analyze the method theoretically for non-overlapping linear experiments and evaluate other settings through simulations and real datasets. They find that pooling often improves deployment reward over individual treatment roll-out, especially with small samples and many experiments, while noting important limits under strong interactions and tight deployment capacity.
key_results: In simulations of non-overlapping linear experiments with covariates, for noise variance 9, the optimality ratio was 0.1003 for individual treatment roll-out, 0.7123 for DPTR with a shared scale, and 0.7612 for DPTR with personalized scales when there were 100 experiments; with 5 experiments, the corresponding values were 0.0990, 0.3726, and 0.5882. In a real overlapping-experiment dataset, DPTR exceeded individual treatment roll-out for every estimator and sample size reported: for the double machine learning estimator at sample size 1,000, the values were 0.3654 and 0.0080, respectively, and at sample size 20,000 they were 0.5474 and 0.2145. The paper's theory establishes weak improvement over the individual method in its analyzed setting and strict improvement under a positive pooled anchor as the number of experiments grows. In the Criteo subgroup analysis, which used 1,744 groups and repeatedly sampled 10 to 30 users per group, the authors report higher reward for DPTR than for individual roll-out at each tested sample size, alongside higher recall and lower specificity.

Pooled anchor: \[\hat{\tau}_0=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{\tau}_k\] Here, tau-hat-zero is the anchor, K is the number of experiments, k indexes an experiment, and tau-hat-k is that experiment's individual effect estimate.

DPTR roll-out rule: \[\hat{A}_{\mathrm{DPTR}}=\left\{k:\frac{N}{N+\beta}\hat{\tau}_{k,lb}+\frac{\beta}{N+\beta}\hat{\tau}_0>0\right\}\] Here, A-hat is the set of selected policies, k indexes a policy, N is its sample size, beta is the shrinkage scale, tau-hat-k-lb is its estimated lower decision bound, and tau-hat-zero is the pooled anchor; a policy is selected when the shrunken lower bound is positive.
limitations_stated: The authors state that formal guarantees cover non-overlapping experiments with linear specifications, while other settings are assessed empirically. They report that performance may deteriorate when interactions reverse treatment-effect signs and that the method may underperform under stringent capacity constraints.
limitations_unstated: The approach pools toward a single average anchor, which may be a poor match when experiments belong to distinct populations or have markedly different effect patterns; the paper does not establish a general rule for detecting when pooling should be restricted. The real-data evaluations use resampling and full-sample estimates as benchmarks rather than prospective deployment outcomes, so they do not directly measure realized business effects after rollout.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the approach to continuous treatments, observational data, and optimization problems with uncertain objectives. They also identify capacity-constrained deployment as requiring additional analysis.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to develop diagnostics or clustered anchors that identify which experiments are sufficiently comparable to pool, then assess those choices on new datasets. Prospective validation in live randomized rollouts, including checks for changes in effects over time, would clarify how well the estimated reward gains transfer to deployment.

summary: The paper develops an estimator and an adaptive assignment strategy for sequential experiments with binary treatment, focusing on estimating the average treatment effect. Its adaptive-design-likelihood-based targeted maximum likelihood estimator uses the average of the experiment's treatment assignment rules to update an outcome model, rather than relying on each unit's individual assignment probability. The authors show theoretically that this estimator is asymptotically normal and semiparametrically efficient under conditions requiring positivity and stabilization for the average assignment rule. They also propose an adaptive design that steers this overall average toward an estimated variance-minimizing Neyman allocation. Simulations find lower estimator variance for the proposed estimator than for the earlier adaptive-design estimator, and lower variance for the proposed assignment strategy than for standard Neyman adaptation.

The paper reports that the proposed estimator had lower variance than the earlier estimator under both adaptive designs, and that the proposed average-design-driven strategy consistently had lower variance than standard Neyman adaptation and moved closer to the oracle design. summary: The paper studies the multiplicative algorithm (MA) for optimal experimental design (OED), where a probability distribution over a finite set of design points is chosen to maximize an information-based criterion for parameter estimation. It gives an optimization-based proof that the algorithm's objective values do not decrease under conditions on a transformed version of the criterion and on the gradient at the current design. The proof uses a matrix Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and also yields sufficient conditions for strict improvement. Two examples show that the choice of the algorithm's power parameter can strongly affect behavior, and that zero gradient components can prevent the algorithm from continuing. The paper also discusses open questions about applying the algorithm to a generalized design formulation that permits estimation of parameter subsystems.
key_results: The monotonicity result applies when the transformed criterion is differentiable, isotonic, and concave, and the gradient is positive on the current design's support; it covers criteria including D-, A-, and certain pth-mean criteria. With a power parameter strictly between zero and one, the objective strictly increases whenever the current design is not unchanged, under the theorem's conditions. In a two-point, two-parameter A-criterion example, a power parameter of one causes cycling, while one-half reaches the optimum in one step; the example's objective-gap contraction factor is the absolute value of one minus twice the power parameter. In a three-point, three-parameter c-criterion example, a zero gradient component makes the next design have objective value minus infinity, so the algorithm cannot proceed. These are theoretical examples rather than empirical comparisons or run-size evaluations.
key_equations:
Moment matrix and design objective: \[M(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iA_i,\qquad f(w)=\phi(M(w))\] The weight w_i for design point i multiplies its Fisher information matrix A_i; summing over n design points gives the moment matrix M(w), and the criterion ϕ evaluated at that matrix gives the objective f(w).

Multiplicative update: \[w_i^{k+1}=\frac{w_i^k\bigl(\nabla_i f(w^k)\bigr)^{\lambda}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_j^k\bigl(\nabla_j f(w^k)\bigr)^{\lambda}}\] At iteration k, each weight w_i is multiplied by the corresponding gradient component raised to the power parameter lambda, then normalized by the sum over design points j to form the next weights.

Transformed criterion: \[\psi(M)=-\phi(M^{-1})\] The transformed criterion ψ at a positive definite matrix M is the negative of the original criterion ϕ evaluated at the inverse of M.

Monotonicity guarantee: \[f(w^{k+1})\geq f(w^k)\] Under the paper's assumptions on the transformed criterion and positivity of the gradient on the current design's support, the objective at iteration k plus one is at least the objective at iteration k.
limitations_stated: The authors state that monotonicity does not by itself ensure convergence to an optimum when the original criterion is nonconcave. They also show that if gradient components are zero, as can occur for the c-criterion, the algorithm may leave the feasible region on which its objective is finite and fail to continue. For the generalized formulation, they leave open whether dropping coordinates preserves feasibility and monotonicity and whether an optimal solution has the dropped coordinates equal to zero.
limitations_unstated: The analysis is for a finite design space and locally specified information matrices, so its conclusions do not establish performance when the assumed statistical model or the locally chosen parameter value is inaccurate. The paper provides theoretical examples but no computational benchmarks, real-experiment validation, or assessment of the practical cost of reaching a useful solution on larger design problems.
future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating coordinate dropping for the generalized design formulation. They identify feasibility after a coordinate becomes zero, objective monotonicity across the support change, and existence of an optimal solution with that coordinate zero as open questions.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test variants that handle zero gradient components and other practical constraints, then compare their performance with alternative design algorithms on representative finite design problems. Further analysis could also examine robustness to locally misspecified information matrices and validate the method in actual experiments.

summary: This paper develops sample size calculations for split-plot factorial longitudinal cluster-randomised trials with continuous outcomes. The method addresses a cluster-level treatment assigned through a longitudinal cluster-randomised design and an individual-level treatment assigned within cluster-periods. It derives treatment-effect variances for models that include or omit an interaction, and extends the calculations to unequal cluster-period sizes. The calculations combine the individual-treatment variance expressions with the variance for the corresponding single-factor longitudinal cluster trial. In an application to the SharES breast cancer trial, the required observations per cluster-period differed according to the assumed correlation structure and whether the model included an interaction.
key_results: For the SharES design, which had 25 clusters across six periods, targeting an effect size of 0.35 standard deviations with 80% power and a 0.05 significance level required 4 observations per cluster-period for the cluster-level effect and 2 for the individual-level effect without an interaction under an exchangeable correlation structure. With an interaction, the corresponding requirements were 6, 3, and 6 observations for the cluster-level effect, individual-level effect, and interaction; under the block-exchangeable structure these were 7, 3, and 5. Without an interaction, the block-exchangeable requirements were 5 observations for the cluster-level effect and 2 for the individual-level effect. At an effect size of 0.2, the block-exchangeable requirements for the cluster-level effect rose to 71 observations with an interaction and 61 without one, compared with 21 for either model under the exchangeable structure; the individual-level and interaction requirements were 11 and 21, respectively.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the method assumes continuous outcomes and either an exchangeable or nested exchangeable correlation structure. It also assumes block randomisation of the individual-level treatment, so that the treatment allocation proportion is fixed within each cluster-period.
limitations_unstated: The worked numerical evaluation focuses on one healthcare trial and a limited set of correlation assumptions, so it offers little evidence about performance across other longitudinal designs or practical allocation patterns. The calculations also depend on specified variance and correlation parameters, but the paper does not evaluate how errors in those inputs affect the resulting sample sizes.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to binary and time-to-event outcomes, to other within-cluster correlation structures such as decay structures, and to designs with more treatment factors. They also identify designs in which eligibility for one treatment depends on allocation to another as a direction for generalisation.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess the accuracy of these sample size calculations through simulation across a broader range of longitudinal designs and parameter misspecification. Practical tools could also evaluate constrained allocation patterns and help trial teams compare designs using realistic recruitment and cluster-size information.

summary: The paper develops interleaved lattice-based maximin distance designs for mixed continuous, ordinal, and binary variables. The objective is to spread computer experiment runs through the input space by maximizing the minimum Euclidean distance between design points; no response model is specified. The design construction combines a lattice structure with choices of levels for each variable, then selects a translation to bring the number of runs close to the target. The authors provide separate construction algorithms for lower, middle, and higher numbers of variables. Their numerical comparisons show that the method often produces larger separation distances than existing methods for mixed-variable designs, while performing similarly to the continuous-variable method it extends when all variables are continuous.
key_results: For mixed continuous and ordinal inputs, the reported separation distances are typically two to ten times those from the constrained-design method of Stinstra and colleagues. For all-ordinal inputs, the new method generally outperforms the methods of Sun and colleagues and Stinstra and colleagues, although Stinstra’s method is sometimes equally good. For all-continuous inputs, the new method and the continuous-variable method of He have nearly identical separation distances in most cases, with occasional slight improvements by the new method. limitations_unstated: The method’s distance calculation treats ordinal levels as numerical values, so its results depend on whether the numerical gaps between levels appropriately represent their practical differences. summary: This paper develops a method for testing whether a new policy improves outcomes over a standard control in A/B experiments. It targets the average treatment effect and covers both independent observations and experiments with effects that carry over between time periods. The method constructs doubly robust pseudo-outcomes, applies an adaptive two-armed bandit rule to form test statistics, and combines results from randomly permuted sample orders. For dynamic experiments, it uses a reinforcement-learning estimator to construct pseudo-outcomes from daily trajectories. The authors report controlled type-I error and higher power than comparison tests in theoretical results, simulations, and evaluations using ridesharing data.
key_results: In the passenger-subsidy datasets, the permutation-based two-armed bandit test produced p-values of 0.482, 0.044, and 0.023; the corresponding bandit-only values were 0.571, 0.086, and 0.041, and the double machine learning values were 0.574, 0.055, and 0.027. The tests did not reject on the A/A dataset, while the permutation-based test and double machine learning test rejected at the 5% level on the other two datasets; the bandit-only test did not reject on the second dataset. In simulations with unconfounded and confounded treatment assignment, the authors report that the permutation-based test generally had the highest power among the proposed test, the bandit-only test, and double machine learning, while maintaining appropriate type-I error in most tested settings. For dynamic experiments, the study used 1,000 simulation replications; in real-data-based bootstrap environments, all three tests kept type-I error below the nominal 0.05 level, and the permutation-based test outperformed the bandit-only test in most scenarios. The paper also evaluated five ridesharing datasets in total, but the dispatch-policy power assessment used bootstrap-generated data based on two A/A datasets rather than a live randomized dispatch-policy experiment.

limitations_stated: The authors identify two limitations of the oracle bandit test: its statistic depends on sample ordering, and it requires both potential outcomes even though only one is observed for each subject. summary: The paper introduces Goal-Oriented Causal Bayesian Experimental Design (GO-CBED), a sequential method for choosing interventions in structural causal models. Rather than seeking information about every part of a model, it chooses interventions to learn a user-selected causal quantity, such as a causal effect or graph structure. It plans across a sequence of experiments and approximates expected information gain with a variational lower bound. The authors jointly train an intervention policy and a posterior estimator, using a transformer policy and flexible probability models for the target. Simulations and semi-synthetic gene-network studies show that targeting the stated research goal can improve information gain and causal estimates compared with the tested baselines.
key_results: For causal-reasoning tasks on synthetic networks, the authors report that GO-CBED targeting the causal quantity generally achieves higher expected information gain than a policy targeting graph structure, especially with nonlinear mechanisms; the comparison used 10-node networks, 10 stages, and three interventions per stage. In the nonlinear E. coli semi-synthetic reasoning example, the targeted policy improved rapidly after stage 3 and outperformed the graph-learning and random policies by stage 10. For causal discovery, tests included linear synthetic models with 30 variables and 15 stages, and nonlinear synthetic models with 20 variables and 10 stages; the paper reports an F1-score as high as 0.75 on scale-free graphs. On a 20-variable linear E. coli benchmark with 10 stages, GO-CBED performed better than the tested baselines on information gain, graph distance, and edge-prediction score; discovery results were averaged over 10 random seeds.

summary: The paper develops a new criterion for Bayesian optimal experimental design that scores an experiment by the expected Wasserstein distance between the prior and posterior distributions. summary: This paper develops a sequential experimental-design framework for multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems in which one unit’s treatment can affect other units through a network. In the simulation, the network had 101 units, two actions, and a central unit connected to five peripheral clusters; each method was run 1,000 times, with results plotted through 10,000 rounds. UCB-TSN was compared with Standard (no initial uniform-exploration phase) and Uniform (uniform exploration throughout): the paper reports that Standard and UCB-TSN had the lowest cumulative regret, while Uniform had the highest; UCB-TSN and Uniform had lower and more compact ATE estimation errors than Standard.

limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation uses one simulated network structure, with 101 units and two actions, so it does not establish how performance changes across other network topologies, treatment spaces, or real experiments. summary: The paper develops algorithms for choosing a fixed-size set of experiments that maximizes information for regression models that are linear in their parameters but may be nonlinear in factor levels. It focuses on first- and second-order models with constraints on allowable experiments, including knapsack constraints. The design is constructed through pricing-based local search, which searches for beneficial experiment replacements, and column generation, which solves a continuous relaxation to provide an upper bound. The local search can use integer optimization when simple bit-change heuristics fail, and the methods accommodate large candidate sets that are not listed explicitly. Numerical tests show that the approach often matches or improves on JMP solutions, while also showing substantial computation time for some larger instances.
key_results: For the first-order model with a cardinality constraint and factor dimensions 11 through 20, the local-search value at dimension 20 was 41.115, compared with 40.221 from JMP and a convex-relaxation upper bound of 41.528. For first-order models with knapsack constraints at dimension 19, local search starting from JMP improved the value from 42.518 to 42.598; for the second-order knapsack model at dimension 20, the corresponding values were 161.097 and 161.298. The second-order local search took 6,926.83 seconds at dimension 20, and first-order column generation with knapsack constraints took 45,500.13 seconds at dimension 20. The authors prove a conditional performance guarantee for local search when its pricing subproblem has an approximation algorithm, and show that approximating a particular second-order pricing problem better than one-half is computationally hard.
key_equations:
Regression model: \[y\approx\theta^{T}p(x)\] Here y is the response, theta is the vector of unknown model parameters, T means transpose, x is a factor-level vector, and p(x) is the vector of model-term values at x.

D-optimal design criterion: \[\max\det(S),\quad S=\sum_{v\in P}\lambda_v vv^{T},\quad \sum_{v\in P}\lambda_v=k,\quad \lambda_v\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\] The design maximizes the determinant of information matrix S; P is the set of feasible design vectors, v is a vector in that set, lambda_v is its replication count, k is the total run budget, T means transpose, and Z+ denotes nonnegative integers.

Pricing problem for a design-point search: \[\max_{x\in Y}p(x)^{T}Gp(x)\] The pricing problem maximizes a quadratic score over allowed factor vectors x in Y, where p(x) is the model-term vector and G is a matrix determined by the current design or relaxation.
limitations_stated: The authors show that, for a special second-order pricing problem, achieving an approximation ratio better than one-half is computationally hard. They also report that solving pricing problems with integer programs can be computationally burdensome, particularly for second-order models and larger instances.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons cover selected simulated constraint instances with factor dimensions from 11 through 20, rather than a broad range of experimental settings or repeated real-world studies. The reported results therefore provide limited evidence about performance under other model structures, constraint types, noise conditions, or substantially larger designs.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying what approximation guarantees are possible for the second-order pricing problem with a general positive semidefinite matrix. They also suggest combining local search and column generation with branch-and-bound to seek integral optimal designs.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the algorithms on real experiments and on a broader range of factor-level restrictions, including operational constraints beyond the reported knapsack examples. It could also investigate other design criteria and sequential procedures that update the design as new observations become available.

summary: The paper develops reliability acceptance sampling plans (RASPs) for life tests with competing failure causes and progressive Type-I interval censoring (PIC-I). Its general framework covers independent and dependent competing risks, and it derives Fisher information and large-sample properties for maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs). For a specific design, the authors use Weibull failure times with a shared gamma frailty, which represents dependence and includes the independent model as a limiting case. They choose inspection timing and withdrawal proportions to improve the precision of estimated reliability, with and without a test-budget constraint. The paper reports that accounting for dependence can materially change the required sample size, inspection schedule, and acceptance limit, and demonstrates the method on electronics reliability data and simulations.
key_results: In a budget-constrained illustration using the transmitter-receiver data, with a withdrawal proportion of 0.2, the dependent plan used a sample size of 73, 5 inspections, and an interval of 0.115 time units, with an acceptance limit of 0.538; the independent plan used 78 units, 5 inspections, an interval of 0.079, and a limit of 0.563. In the numerical study, stronger modeled dependence generally increased the required sample size and acceptance limit, while optimal inspection intervals became longer. The finite-sample evaluation simulated 5,000 data sets for each plan; estimated producer’s risks were 0.049 to 0.054 and consumer’s risks were 0.111 to 0.128, compared with specified risks of 0.05 and 0.1. The authors report that average estimated reliability was close to its true value and that its precision changed little as the withdrawal proportion increased.

Fisher information for interval-censored competing risks: \[I(\theta\mid\zeta)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{E[N_i]}{q_{ij}}\nabla_\theta q_{ij}\nabla_\theta q_{ij}^{T}+\frac{E[N_i]}{1-q_i}\nabla_\theta q_i\nabla_\theta q_i^{T}\right]\] I is the Fisher information matrix; theta is the parameter vector; zeta denotes the design; M is the number of inspection points; i indexes intervals; J and j identify the number and index of failure causes; E[N_i] is the expected number at risk; q_ij and q_i are the cause-specific and all-cause interval failure probabilities; nabla_theta denotes a parameter gradient; T denotes transpose.

Reliability-focused c-optimality criterion: \[\phi(\zeta)=S^2=C_T^{T}[I_1(\theta\mid\zeta)]^{-1}C_T\] Phi is the design criterion and S squared is the variance for estimating reliability at the target time; zeta is the design; C_T is the gradient of reliability with respect to the parameters; I_1 is Fisher information per test unit; theta is the parameter vector; the superscript T denotes transpose and the exponent minus one denotes a matrix inverse.

Sample size for specified producer's and consumer's risks: \[n=\left[\frac{S_1z_\beta-S_0z_{1-\alpha}}{\pi_0-\pi_1}\right]^2\] n is the required sample size; S_0 and S_1 are the standard deviations of the reliability estimator under the acceptable and rejectable hypotheses; z_beta and z_(1-alpha) are standard normal quantiles; alpha is producer's risk and beta is consumer's risk; pi_0 and pi_1 are the acceptable and rejectable reliability limits.
limitations_stated: The authors do not explicitly identify limitations. They note that dependence is represented through a frailty model and propose investigating copula models and Bayesian plans as extensions.
limitations_unstated: The specific dependent model assumes a common Weibull shape across failure causes and a shared gamma frailty, which restricts the dependence patterns represented. The c-optimal designs rely on guessed parameter values and asymptotic approximations, and the practical designs further focus on equally spaced inspections and uniform withdrawal proportions; the numerical and real-data comparisons cover a limited set of examples and scenarios.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing plans for competing risks represented by copula models. They also suggest Bayesian reliability acceptance sampling plans when useful prior information is available.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the plans on more real manufacturing and electronics studies, including settings with unequal failure-mode shapes or dependence structures beyond shared positive frailty. It could also develop designs for irregular inspection schedules, operational withdrawal constraints, and sequential decisions, and check performance when the assumed lifetime model is misspecified.

summary: This paper presents a toolbox for designing and analyzing experiments for energy-system simulations and laboratory tests. Its objective is to help users use limited experiment resources to study how changes in model or system inputs affect selected outputs. Users describe the experiment, factors, and target metrics in an object-oriented configuration; the toolbox generates run configurations and provides analysis and visualization after runs are completed. It supports several design and sensitivity-analysis approaches, including space-filling sampling and screening methods. Two energy-system applications illustrate its use, and the authors show how it can identify influential inputs and interactions.
key_results: In the multi-energy co-simulation case, the authors used 1,024 samples for global sensitivity analysis: photovoltaic scaling had the greatest first-order effect on electricity self-consumption, while heat-profile scaling had the greatest first-order effect on minimum supply temperature. For the hybrid energy storage system, the analysis used 512 parameter combinations, from which the toolbox generated 3,072 parameter sets; after adding reset blocks and five power-profile samples per set, 23,040 simulation runs were executed. Analysis of variance identified the restoration factor and capacity fraction as significant factors, and multivariate analysis confirmed their effects. The paper presents these as demonstrations of toolbox functionality, not as a performance ranking against other software or designs.
key_equations: Not applicable
limitations_stated: The authors state that some parts of the toolbox may need to be made more general for other experiment types, and that support for additional execution-framework adapters could broaden its use. They also note that using the toolbox requires clear identification and description of uncertainty.
limitations_unstated: The paper does not report a quantitative comparison of the toolbox with alternative packages or an evaluation of how consistently different users can configure the same study. The hybrid-storage demonstration required 23,040 simulation runs, which may be impractical when each run is costly or laboratory-based; the applications also cover only a limited set of energy-system cases.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the toolbox with more sampling and analysis methods and adding specific handling for known, controllable nuisance factors. They also suggest making experiment components and execution adapters more general, and integrating uncertainty information from existing sources such as holistic test-description templates.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the toolbox on physical laboratory experiments with run budgets and operational constraints defined in advance, and compare its generated designs with established alternatives. It could also support sequential designs that use early results to select later runs, with validation of the resulting sensitivity estimates on additional energy-system models.

summary: This paper develops an adaptive experimental-design method for learning reward functions in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). It targets a linear reward model with pairwise preference responses and allows a teacher’s rationality to differ across both teachers and types of prompts. At each step, the method uses a determinant-based information criterion to select both a prompt-and-completion comparison and a teacher, then estimates the reward parameters from the collected preferences. It uses the resulting estimate in a pessimistic offline policy-learning procedure to reduce risks from limited coverage of actions. The authors prove asymptotic design optimality and give a sub-optimality bound; simulations and public language-model datasets show better reward-estimation or prediction performance than the tested alternatives.
key_results: In simulations with a sample budget of 1,000, the proposed method had the lowest reported generalized variance and mean squared error across batch sizes 1, 50, and 100; for batch size 1, the reported values were 1.52 in units of 10^-11 and 1.147, compared with 41,600 in units of 10^-11 and 2.808 for random selection. The authors report that the pessimistic policy’s sub-optimality decreases at a parametric rate of order 1 divided by the square root of the sample budget, up to logarithmic factors, while a greedy policy can retain a nonzero gap. In the public-data experiments, the feature representation came from Gemma-7b-it with dimension 3,072; the feedback budget was 5,000 from 32,000 training examples, and reward accuracy was higher for the proposed method than for the benchmark methods in the reported figures. The paper reports reward-accuracy improvements of 1.77%–9.06% on Anthropic and UltraFeedback datasets. For the proposed batch method, reported runtimes on one Nvidia A100 were 6.06 and 2.70 hours on Anthropic for batch sizes 50 and 100, and 6.05 and 2.68 hours on UltraFeedback.

Linear reward and pairwise preference model: \[r_{\theta}(x,a)=\theta^{\top}\phi(x,a),\quad P(Y=1\mid z,\beta,\theta)=\mu(\beta\theta^{\top}z)\] The reward r at context x and action a is parameterized by θ and feature map φ; Y is the binary preference, z is the feature vector for the second action minus that for the first, β is the selected teacher’s rationality, and μ is the logistic function.

Information matrix: \[M(\xi_T,\theta)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\dot{\mu}(\beta_t\theta^{\top}z_t)\beta_t^2z_tz_t^{\top}\] M is the information matrix for design ξ over T queried comparisons; t indexes a query, β_t is its teacher rationality, z_t is its feature difference, θ is the reward parameter, and dot μ is the derivative of the logistic function.

D-optimal design criterion: \[\xi^{*}=\arg\max_{\xi}\det\sum_{z,\beta}\xi(z,\beta)\dot{\mu}(\beta\theta^{\top}z)\beta^{2}zz^{\top}\] The optimal design ξ* maximizes the determinant of the information matrix, where ξ assigns design weight to feature differences z and teacher rationalities β, θ is the reward parameter, and dot μ is the derivative of the logistic function.

Sequential selection rule: \[(z_t,\beta_t)=\arg\max_{z,\beta}\det\{H_{t-1}(\hat{\theta}_{t-1})+\dot{\mu}(\beta\hat{\theta}_{t-1}^{\top}z)\beta^2zz^{\top}\}\] At step t, the method selects the available feature difference z and compatible teacher rationality β that maximize the updated determinant; H is accumulated sample information and θ-hat is the current reward-parameter estimate.
limitations_stated: The authors note that single-step batch selection is prohibitively computationally costly for their large-language-model experiments, so they omit batch size 1 in those experiments. Their theoretical results also rely on boundedness and identifiability assumptions for the reward parameters and features.
limitations_unstated: The public-data evaluation uses synthetic language-model teachers rather than a study with human teachers, so it does not establish that the teacher-selection gains carry over to costly human feedback. The method also relies on a linear reward representation and a logistic preference model, and the demonstrated large-model setting uses one pretrained model and a finite, pre-collected candidate pool. Reward accuracy on held-out dataset labels is a proxy for downstream alignment quality; the paper does not report a real deployment evaluation with users.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to more general ranking problems. They also suggest studying infeasible tasks and integrating causal reasoning into large language models using the dual active-learning framework.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method with human raters and assess whether its estimated teacher expertise remains reliable across changing tasks and populations. It would also be useful to evaluate nonlinear reward models, operational constraints on which prompts and teachers can be queried, and sequential deployment with new prompts and feedback beyond a fixed candidate pool.

summary: The paper introduces the Wasserstein Homogeneity Partition (WHOMP) for splitting a sample into equal-sized groups for controlled experiments and A/B tests. It aims to make each subgroup resemble the full sample in its distribution, using squared Wasserstein-2 distances rather than balancing only subgroup averages. The authors show that finding an optimal partition is equivalent to balanced K-means, then propose randomized and transport-matching procedures based on an estimated balanced K-means solution. Their theoretical results relate subgroup distributional similarity to treatment-effect estimation under stated assumptions. In simulations and tests on tabular, image, and graph data, WHOMP generally produces more homogeneous and stable subgroups than the reported random and covariate-adaptive methods.
key_results: In the Gaussian-mixture experiment, with 60 observations and 100 repetitions, average Wasserstein-2 distance for two groups was 1.642 for WHOMP random and 1.651 for WHOMP matching, compared with 3.481 for random partitioning and 3.589 for covariate-adaptive randomization. For six groups, logistic-regression accuracy was 0.980 with WHOMP random and 0.984 with WHOMP matching, compared with 0.944 for random partitioning; support-vector-machine accuracy was 0.999 and 1.000, respectively, compared with 0.987. At six groups, linear-regression mean squared error was 2.282 for WHOMP random and 2.320 for WHOMP matching, versus 2.548 for random partitioning and 2.383 for covariate-adaptive randomization. In the 500-repetition NPI dataset experiment, two-group average Wasserstein-2 distance was 2.148 for WHOMP random and 2.179 for WHOMP matching, versus 2.222 for random partitioning. The paper also proves that optimal WHOMP partitions correspond to balanced K-means solutions and gives a variance bound for treatment-effect estimation when the outcome function satisfies its Lipschitz assumption.
key_equations:
WHOMP partition criterion: \[\mathcal{Q}^*=\arg\min_{\mathcal{Q}\in\mathcal{P}(N,c),\ |q|=K}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}W_2^2(X_q,X)\] Here, the optimal partition is Q star, Q is a partition of the N observations into c groups, each group q has K observations, X is the full empirical sample, X_q is the empirical distribution in group q, and W_2 is Wasserstein-2 distance.

Equivalent balanced K-means criterion: \[\mathcal{P}^*\in\arg\min_{\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{P}(N,K),\ |p|=c}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\operatorname{Var}(X_p)\] Here, P star is an optimal balanced K-means partition, P is a partition of N observations into K groups, each group p has c observations, and Var of X_p is the within-group variance.

WHOMP matching construction: \[q_i=\{T_k(\bar{x}_i):k\in[K]\}\] Here, q_i is the i-th output subgroup, x bar i is a point in the Wasserstein barycenter of the balanced K-means clusters, T_k is the optimal transport map from that barycenter to cluster k, and K is the number of clusters.

Assumed outcome regularity: \[\|Y(x,c_q)-Y(x',c_{q'})\|_2\leq L\|x-x'\|_2\] Here, Y is the outcome as a function of covariates and control factor, x and x prime are covariate values, c_q and c_q prime are control factors, L is the Lipschitz constant, and the norm measures Euclidean distance.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the WHOMP optimization problem is computationally hard because it is equivalent to balanced K-means, so their algorithms estimate solutions rather than guarantee a global optimum in practice. They describe the method as efficient for moderate- or low-dimensional Euclidean data and use embeddings for high-dimensional image and graph data. They also note that the sample size, number of groups, and Gaussian-mixture parameters in the experiments were chosen arbitrarily and encourage testing other settings and datasets.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons use selected synthetic settings and specific public datasets; they do not demonstrate improved treatment-effect estimates in a real clinical trial or operational A/B test. Results for image and graph data depend on embedding representations, so the reported distances and subgroup quality may not transfer if those representations distort relevant structure. The paper does not report runtime or scaling results that would help assess use on large, high-dimensional experimental datasets.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing WHOMP assignment methods for data arriving sequentially, such as participants enrolled over time in a clinical trial. They also suggest using a specified acceptable range for the WHOMP objective to generate training and test splits for cross-validation or holdout sets.
future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate WHOMP with real experimental outcomes and compare treatment-effect bias, precision, and decision quality against established trial designs. It could also test alternative outcome-relevant distances and practical constraints, such as stratification requirements, restricted assignments, or unequal group sizes, while measuring computation time and performance as dataset size grows.
