summary: This paper develops a pilot-scan method for choosing scan angles in computed tomography (CT) to improve image reconstruction while reducing the number of scans. It uses a deep image prior (DIP) fitted to a sparse set of measurements, then linearizes the network around that fit to create a data-dependent Gaussian prior. The method selects additional angles sequentially by estimating uncertainty in measurements for the remaining candidate angles. The authors evaluate it on simulated images with preferential directions and compare it with equidistant and random angle selection, as well as simpler prior models. Their main finding is that the data-dependent design can match equidistant reconstruction quality with roughly 30% fewer angles in the early scan regime, including when reconstruction uses traditional total variation (TV) regularization.
key_results: On 30 simulated images with 5% noise, the linearized DIP design improved reconstruction peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by over 1.5 decibels over equidistant selection at 10 to 15 total angles, and required roughly 30% fewer angles to match the equidistant baseline in that early regime. Retraining the network every 5 angles provided gains greater than 0.5 decibels after 20 angles; the authors report significant improvement over the equidistant baseline through 20 scanned angles without retraining and through 35 scanned angles with retraining. Benefits were also observed when reconstruction used TV regularization, and remained significant though smaller with 10% noise. Expected squared error (ESE) selection performed better than expected information gain (EIG) across the tested models; isotropic and Matérn models performed similarly to or worse than random selection. On an NVIDIA A100 graphics processing unit, a design step using 3,000 samples took 9 seconds, and a complete design took 5 minutes.
key_equations:
Linear Gaussian measurement model: \[y=Ax+\epsilon,\quad \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_y^2 I),\quad x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{xx})\] The image is x, the measurements are y, A is the forward operator, epsilon is Gaussian measurement noise with standard deviation sigma_y, I is the identity matrix, and Sigma_xx is the Gaussian prior covariance of the image.

Linearized neural-network prior: \[x=J\theta,\quad \theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_\theta),\quad \Sigma_{xx}=J\Sigma_\theta J^\top\] The image x is represented by the Jacobian J times network parameters theta, theta has Gaussian covariance Sigma_theta, and the resulting image covariance is Sigma_xx.

Angle acquisition criteria: \[\mathrm{EIG}(\beta)=\log\det(\sigma_y^2 I+A_\beta\Sigma_{x|y}(A_\beta)^\top)+C,\quad \mathrm{ESE}(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}(A_\beta\Sigma_{x|y}A_\beta^\top)+C\] For candidate angle beta, EIG uses the log determinant and ESE uses the trace of the predicted measurement covariance; sigma_y is the noise standard deviation, I is the identity matrix, A_beta is the forward operator at that angle, Sigma_x|y is the image covariance after previous measurements, and C is an angle-independent constant.

Greedy angle selection: \[\beta_t=\arg\max_{\beta\notin B_t}\mathrm{ESE}_t(\beta)\] At design step t, beta_t is the next angle selected to maximize ESE among candidate angles beta not already in B_t, the set of previously selected angles.
limitations_stated: The experiments use synthetic rectangle images rather than real CT measurements, and the authors identify application to real measurements as future work. They also report that prior and hyperparameter choices can overfit sparse pilot data, and that model misspecification can degrade EIG estimates. The authors note that the 30-image evaluation limits the strength of their statistical conclusions.
limitations_unstated: The synthetic image class has a narrow structure: a small number of rectangles with edges aligned around a preferential direction, so it does not establish performance for varied real-world objects or anatomy. The study also assumes a fixed set of selectable angles and does not evaluate scanner-specific constraints such as acquisition time, motion, dose limits, or changing measurement quality. Its reported computing time and reliance on pilot fitting may make the workflow burdensome in settings with limited computation or strict scan-time requirements.
future_work_stated: The authors propose applying the linearized DIP design to real measurements, investigating alternative ways to set model hyperparameters, and running more experiments to strengthen the statistical claims.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the approach on real industrial and medical CT datasets with varied object classes, scanner geometries, and realistic dose or motion constraints. Study sequential updating beyond the initial pilot design and compare objectives that directly target image reconstruction error or explicitly account for scan cost. Assess whether the method remains reliable under model mismatch and whether computation can be reduced enough for practical deployment.

summary: This paper develops optimal experimental design methods for estimating linear functionals of an unknown function in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). The model uses noisy point evaluations, while the target may be a lower-dimensional quantity such as a gradient, integral, or solution characteristic. The authors construct interpolation and ridge-regression estimators and choose experiment allocations using bias-aware information criteria. They also derive finite-sample confidence sets for both fixed and adaptive data collection. Their main finding is that uncertainty can be controlled in terms of the target dimension and the geometry of available experiments, rather than requiring estimation of the entire function.
key_results: The method provides confidence guarantees for fixed and adaptive designs under sub-Gaussian noise, with confidence parameters that scale with the dimension of the target functional. In a two-dimensional gradient example, the optimized allocation over the five candidate evaluations was (0.37, 0.09, 0.08, 0.09, 0.38), and the authors report that the best step sizes follow the proposed bias-variance trade-off as the query budget changes. In the pharmacokinetic simulation, the optimized design reduced the mean squared error for estimating model parameters by a factor of 10 compared with equally spaced sampling. In the controller-stability simulation, with 500 queries and 10 repetitions, the proposed confidence sets gave tighter bounds and enabled faster certification than the classical confidence sets; the paper also derives a finite-action linear-bandit regret bound that is a factor of the square root of the parameter dimension tighter than the standard bound discussed there.

limitations_unstated: The guarantees rely on a specified kernel and parameter-norm operator, and on sub-Gaussian noise with a known variance proxy; performance under misspecification of these assumptions is not established. future_work_stated: None stated.

summary: The paper introduces Gauss-Dantzig Selector Aggregation over Random Models (GDS-ARM) for screening experiments with many two-level factors and relatively few runs. Its goal is to identify important factors while considering both main effects and two-factor interactions. The method repeatedly applies the Gauss-Dantzig Selector (GDS) to models containing all main effects and a randomly chosen subset of interactions, ranks the resulting models using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and aggregates effects found among the top models. A final stepwise regression removes selected effects that do not fit and gives main effects another chance to enter. In the reported simulations and two real-data examples, the method generally performs better than analyses using only main effects or all two-factor interactions at once, particularly when interactions are active.
key_results: The authors evaluated screening power and error over 1000 simulated datasets per scenario, comparing GDS-ARM with GDS using only main effects and GDS using main effects plus all two-factor interactions. Across the reported scenarios and designs, GDS-ARM generally performed better when interactions were active; the all-interactions approach could perform poorly with small run sizes, while the main-effects-only approach did well mainly when there were no active interactions. For the cast fatigue experiment with 12 runs and 7 factors, GDS-ARM identified A, E, F, and G as important; for the grape-composition experiment with 12 runs and 8 factors, it identified A, C, and D, matching the conclusion cited from earlier analysis. For 18 runs and 22 factors, the authors report that an individual GDS application took about one tenth of a second and the full method took about 24 seconds on their specified desktop computer.
key_equations: Assumed regression model: \[y = X\beta + \epsilon\] The response vector y is modeled as the model matrix X multiplied by the effect-parameter vector beta, plus the error vector epsilon.
limitations_stated: The authors focus their tuning recommendations on scenarios with zero to two active interactions and say that a larger interaction subset may be needed when more interactions are expected. They note that some designs performed poorly and that further investigation is needed to determine which designs work best. Extending the method to factors with three or more levels is possible, but its tuning would require more work.
limitations_unstated: The evaluations rely mainly on simulated sparse models with normally distributed errors and effect sizes, plus two real examples, so performance under other error patterns or substantial model misspecification is not established. The repeated random model fits and data-driven selection steps may also produce results that vary across random selections, and the paper does not report uncertainty intervals for that variability.
future_work_stated: The authors call for further investigation to identify designs that work best with the method. They also state that tuning needs further work for factors with three or more levels, and that the interaction-subset size should be adjusted if more active interactions are expected.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method under non-normal errors, weaker effects, and higher-order interactions, and to report the stability of selected factors across repeated random interaction subsets. Further study could also assess practical constraints such as restricted randomization and evaluate the method prospectively in additional industrial and agricultural experiments.

summary: This paper designs low-cost interventions for identifying a chosen causal effect when observational data alone are insufficient. It assumes a known causal graph, which may include hidden confounding, and initially assumes that intervention costs add across variables. For a target set forming one c-component, the authors show that the design problem can be expressed as finding a least-cost set that hits every hedge obstructing identification. They give an exact algorithm, approximation and heuristic approaches, and methods for targets with multiple c-components. The problem is computationally hard in general, but the simulations show that the proposed heuristics often find solutions close in cost to the exact solution on the graphs tested.
key_results: The minimum-cost intervention problem is proved NP-complete, and the paper establishes hardness for approximation better than a logarithmic factor under the stated complexity assumption. For a target in one c-component, the exact algorithm is optimal but has exponential worst-case runtime; its approximation version has a logarithmic-factor guarantee when it discovers polynomially many hedges. For a target with k c-components, the minimum-cost-flow method returns an identifiable intervention collection costing at most k times the optimum. In simulations using random graphs with directed-edge probability 0.35, bidirected-edge probability 0.25, and intervention costs sampled from 1 through 4, results averaged over 40 trials showed negligible regret for the heuristics in most cases; graphs ranged from 10 to 200 vertices, and the comparisons included the exact, approximate, and greedy approaches.

limitations_unstated: The methods assume the causal graph is known, so errors in graph structure or unrecognized confounding could invalidate the intervention choices. future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the tree-structure results to graphs where the number of paths between each pair of vertices is bounded by a constant. They note that their proposed hedge-enumeration approach for more general graphs can still require exponential time.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test these designs when the graph is uncertain and when estimated effects must meet a specified precision with limited experimental samples. summary: The paper develops a way to monitor randomized treatment-control experiments, or A/B tests, for changes in representation across specified groups. Its deviation from equal representation (DER) statistic measures how far group means for a non-negative metric are from parity, and estimates whether treatment moves groups closer to or further from parity. The authors derive an asymptotic variance for the statistic and use a multiple-comparison correction to generate alerts across many experiments and metrics. They also use causal trees to search for cohorts with differing treatment effects, helping investigate experiments flagged by the alerts. Simulations and a LinkedIn case study show how the approach can detect representation changes and support follow-up analysis, while the authors emphasize that representation differences do not by themselves establish unfairness.
key_results: In simulations of 1,000 A/B tests, with group-treatment interactions added in 5% of tests and results averaged over 100 runs, DER alerts had a 3.9% rejection rate and no false discoveries on those interactions. DER power was 73.9% for interactions generally, 85% for interactions at least 1% of the control metric mean, and 96% for the top 2.5% of the absolute expected DER change. The comparison based on differences in group treatment lifts had an 80.9% false discovery rate, versus 0% for DER; its corresponding power figures were 78.3%, 82.5%, and 100%. For experiments with 40,000 members, the asymptotic variance estimates differed from resampling estimates by up to a factor of 2.5, and the estimates approached one another as sample size increased. In the LinkedIn case study, an initiative involving over 100 experiments was flagged using a holdout of 2% of members; causal-tree analysis identified a worse session response among dormant women than dormant men during the alert period, while their confidence intervals overlapped in the later period.
key_equations:
Deviation from equal representation: \[D(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k)=\frac{k}{k-1}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left(\frac{\mu_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_j}-\frac{1}{k}\right)^2\] Here D is the deviation from equal representation statistic, k is the number of groups, i and j index groups, and mu_i is the mean metric value for group i.

Treatment-control change in representation: \[\widehat{\Delta}=D(\widehat{m}^{1}_1,\ldots,\widehat{m}^{1}_k)-D(\widehat{m}^{0}_1,\ldots,\widehat{m}^{0}_k)\] Here Delta-hat is the estimated treatment-minus-control change, D is the deviation from equal representation statistic, m-hat_i is the observed mean for group i, and superscripts 1 and 0 denote treatment and control.

Asymptotic variance for two groups: \[\sigma^2=\frac{16(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{(\mu_1+\mu_2)^6}\left(\frac{\mu_2^2\sigma_1^2}{p_1}+\frac{\mu_1^2\sigma_2^2}{p_2}\right)\] Here sigma squared is the asymptotic variance for the statistic with two groups, mu_1 and mu_2 are their population means, sigma_1 squared and sigma_2 squared are their outcome variances, and p_1 and p_2 are their population fractions.

Bonferroni alert threshold: \[p_c\leq\frac{\alpha}{N}\] Here p_c is the p-value for a comparison, alpha is the significance level, and N is the total number of comparisons.
limitations_stated: The authors assume non-negative metrics for the DER statistic and present the asymptotic derivation for two groups, noting that the extension to more groups is omitted for simplicity. They report that the asymptotic variance estimate can differ from resampling estimates by as much as a factor of 2.5 in experiments with 40,000 members. They also state that gender monitoring was limited to men and women because of data availability, and that causal-tree pruning often returns no split because heterogeneous effects can be difficult to detect.
limitations_unstated: The statistic measures parity in group means for a chosen metric; it may therefore miss important group differences in outcome distributions or in metrics that were not selected. The simulation evidence is based on a LinkedIn-shaped data generator and a specified experiment setup, so it does not establish performance for other outcome patterns or experimentation systems; the strict correction may also make alerts hard to obtain in smaller experiments.
future_work_stated: The authors propose considering other ways to quantify equity and fairness in large-scale A/B testing. They also identify expanding gender alerts to include other gender identities as an important future step.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test the alerts and causal-tree findings on operational data from other organizations and under a wider range of outcome distributions, group sizes, and experiment designs. Further work could also assess how to account for network interference and practical experiment constraints, and develop a sequential alerting approach for continuously monitored experiments.

summary: The paper proposes a way to interpret effects of a primary factor in a factorial experiment without first testing for interaction. It considers qualitative factors, including unbalanced designs, and focuses on the primary factor both separately at each level of a secondary factor and pooled across those levels. The procedure combines the relevant multiple contrasts into one simultaneous analysis, using confidence intervals or adjusted p-values to control the family-wise error rate. It can be applied with different model types and outcome distributions, including nonparametric methods. Examples from medical trials and plant science illustrate how the joint analysis can reveal effects that separate or pooled analyses alone may miss.
key_results: In the irritable bowel syndrome trial, the joint analysis found adjusted p-values of 0.019 and 0.026 for pooled comparisons of doses 3 and 4 with placebo; for dose 4, analysis of pooled data alone gave a p-value of 0.01, illustrating the conservatism of the joint procedure. In the plant-science example, the pooled heteroscedastic Williams-type contrast had an estimate of 11.3594 and a reported p-value of 0.0000, while the separate analysis for the wild type had a p-value of 0.0023 for its corresponding plateau-shaped contrast. In the reocclusion example, the pooled aspirin-versus-control comparison had an estimate of -1.3 and a reported p-value of 0.0000, while the pooled aspirin-plus-dipyridamole comparison had a p-value of 0.1474. These are illustrative real-data examples, not a comparison of competing run-allocation designs.
key_equations: Combined family of contrasts: \[T_{\mathrm{joint}} = T_{\mathrm{pooled}} \cup T_1 \cup \cdots \cup T_J\] T_joint is the full family analyzed together, T_pooled is the set of pooled contrasts, T_j is the set of contrasts at secondary-factor level j, and J is the number of secondary-factor levels; the union symbol means all these sets are included.
limitations_stated: The authors say the procedure is conservative compared with unadjusted analysis of variance tests and defers the pre-test decision problem to interpreting many individual comparisons. They recommend it mainly for designs with few factor levels, especially few secondary-factor levels. They also caution that variance heterogeneity combined with unbalanced data can make Dunnett-type inference liberal, reduce power, be conservative, or produce comparison-specific bias.
limitations_unstated: The paper does not give a prospective run-size or power-planning method for the joint contrast family, even though it notes that small samples and imbalance matter in its examples. Its illustrations cover a limited collection of real datasets and selected contrast types, so they do not establish how well the procedure performs across a broad range of practical factorial designs or under model misspecification.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate power, coverage, and family-wise error control across systematically varied run sizes, imbalance patterns, and degrees of interaction, including outcomes where the assumed model is misspecified. It would also be useful to develop guidance for selecting contrasts and planning sample sizes under practical run constraints, then validate that guidance in prospective experiments.

summary: The paper introduces differential property classification (DPC), a machine-learning method to help manufacturing researchers choose between two sets of process parameters. The authors demonstrate it using real data from 20 aluminum 7075 tube experiments made with Shear Assisted Processing and Extrusion (ShAPE). summary: The paper develops a method for choosing which units to treat and how to weight control units when panel outcome data are available before an experiment. The designs are constructed by jointly selecting treatment assignments and weights to optimize how well pre-treatment outcomes match, while penalizing variable weights; the resulting problems can be formulated as mixed-integer programs (MIPs). summary: The paper develops variance-reduction methods for estimating treatment effects in online randomized experiments, covering both count metrics and ratio metrics. The methods use pre-treatment covariates to predict outcomes, correct prediction error with a debiasing step, and use cross-fitting so that each unit’s prediction is produced without fitting on that unit. Flexible machine-learning models can be used, and the authors establish asymptotic inference and semiparametric efficiency when the prediction functions are consistent. For ratio metrics, the paper gives separate procedures depending on whether the denominator can change under treatment, as well as a computationally efficient linear adjustment. Simulations and two LinkedIn experiments show reduced variance compared with difference-in-means and linear adjustment approaches.
key_results: In simulations with 10,000 units and 1,000 repetitions, the count-metric method reduced variance by about 88% to 92% in the nonlinear settings with random forests or gradient boosting, compared with 34.11% to 37.62% for the linear CUPED comparator; reported empirical confidence-interval coverage was generally near the nominal 0.95. For ratio metrics, simulations reported up to 71.39% variance reduction when the denominator was stable, while the method for a changing denominator reduced variance by 39.64% to 41.30% in the non-stable-denominator cases and maintained coverage of 0.941 to 0.942. Ratio-metric treatment-effect targets: \[\delta=\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]}{\mathbb{E}[Z(1)]}-\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]}{\mathbb{E}[Z(0)]},\qquad \delta_0=\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]}{\mathbb{E}[Z]}\] Delta is the treatment effect when the numerator and denominator may both change under treatment, while delta-zero is the target under the stable-denominator assumption; E denotes population expectation, Y is the numerator metric, and Z is the denominator metric, with zero and one indicating control and treatment potential outcomes.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the consistency condition for the machine-learning prediction functions may fail when the selected function class cannot represent the true conditional mean. limitations_unstated: The efficiency guarantees rely on randomized assignment, independent randomized units, and consistent outcome prediction, so the paper does not establish comparable performance under interference, substantial departures from randomization, or severely misspecified prediction models. future_work_stated: The authors propose adding a linear regression step to improve robustness when machine-learning predictions are inaccurate, and studying optimal variance reduction under limited model capacity when consistency may fail. future_work_unstated: Further work could benchmark compute time and memory use across cross-fitting choices and prediction methods, and provide software that helps practitioners select and validate the appropriate ratio target. The computation took about 2 hours on a MacBook Pro with a 2.3 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7 processor, whereas the earlier Groebner basis calculation for this problem was reported not to finish in one week on a standard PC. summary: The paper develops a two-stage design for survey experiments that aims to estimate the population average treatment effect while improving both the representativeness of the sample and the balance between treatment groups. The method, called rerandomized survey experiments using Mahalanobis distances (ReSEM), first repeatedly samples units until their covariates meet a balance threshold, then repeatedly assigns treatment until a second balance threshold is met. The authors derive asymptotic results for the difference-in-means estimator and for regression adjustment of remaining covariate imbalance. Their theory shows that both stages of rerandomization can improve estimation precision, and that regression adjustment can improve it further when additional covariates are available. Simulations and an election-study illustration support the theoretical findings, with confidence-interval coverage close to its nominal level.
key_results: The theory shows that the reduction in asymptotic variance relative to a completely randomized survey experiment is nonnegative and adds contributions from sampling-stage and assignment-stage rerandomization; the gain depends on how strongly the covariates relate to outcomes and treatment effects. In the main simulation, the population had 10,000 units, sample sizes ranged from 100 to 1,000, and each design used 10,000 rerandomizations; when both stage acceptance probabilities were 0.01, rerandomization at both stages improved precision over rerandomization at only one stage, and regression adjustment produced the shortest confidence intervals. The reported 95% interval coverage probabilities in that simulation were close to 95%. In the election-study illustration, the authors used a population of 49,452 and a sample of 1,000, split evenly between treatment and control; with acceptance probabilities of 0.001, both-stage rerandomization and regression adjustment reduced estimator variability and interval lengths relative to the completely randomized survey experiment, while coverage remained approximately nominal.

Sampling-stage imbalance distance: \[M_S=(\bar W_S-\bar W)^T\{(1/n-1/N)S_W^2\}^{-1}(\bar W_S-\bar W)\] M_S is the sampling-stage Mahalanobis distance, bar W_S is the sample covariate mean, bar W is the population covariate mean, n is the sample size, N is the population size, and S_W^2 is the population covariance matrix of covariates W.

Treatment-assignment imbalance distance: \[M_T=(\bar X_1-\bar X_0)^T\{(n/(n_1n_0))s_X^2\}^{-1}(\bar X_1-\bar X_0)\] M_T is the assignment-stage Mahalanobis distance, bar X_1 and bar X_0 are the treatment and control covariate means, n is the sample size, n_1 and n_0 are the treatment and control group sizes, and s_X^2 is the sample covariance matrix of covariates X.

The goal is to estimate failure-time quantiles under normal-use conditions as precisely as possible, particularly the median, when measurement times are fixed in advance. The authors model repeated degradation measurements with aggregate regression effects, unit-to-unit random effects, and measurement errors, then connect failure-time quantiles to the model parameters. They show that choosing stress settings reduces to an extrapolation design problem for the response at the normal-use stress condition. Their examples show that these designs can be more efficient than uniform stress allocations, including for tests with two stress variables.
key_results: For the single-stress example with normal-use stress at -0.056, the optimal approximate design assigns 0.95 of units to stress 0 and 0.05 to stress 1; the equal-allocation endpoint design has efficiency 0.55, so it requires 81% more units for comparable precision. In the two-stress example with interactions, the optimal weights at the four stress combinations are 0.58, 0.17, 0.19, and 0.06, while equal allocation has efficiency 0.61 and requires 64% more units for comparable precision. For the example with two non-interacting stress variables, the equal-weight design has efficiency 0.49 relative to an optimal design, implying that it needs more than twice as many units for comparable precision. The paper derives these comparisons theoretically and evaluates them numerically; it does not report a real experimental validation or a specific total run size for the optimal designs.
key_equations:
Repeated-measures mixed effects model: \[Y_{ij}=(f_1(x_i)\otimes f_2(t_j))^\top\beta+f_2(t_j)^\top\gamma_i+\epsilon_{ij}\] The response for unit i at measurement j is modeled using the stress regression vector, the time regression vector, aggregate coefficients, unit-specific random effects, and measurement error.

Failure-time quantile relation: \[h(t_\alpha)=z_\alpha,\qquad h(t)=\frac{\mu(t)-y_0}{\sigma_u(t)}\] The failure-time quantile at probability alpha solves this relation, where h is the standardized aggregate degradation, z alpha is the standard normal quantile, mu is the aggregate path, y zero is the threshold, and sigma sub u is the standard deviation of a future unit's degradation.

Stress-design criterion: \[\xi^*=\arg\min_{\xi} f_1(x_u)^\top M_1(\xi)^{-1}f_1(x_u)\] The optimal approximate stress design minimizes the extrapolation variance criterion, where f one is the stress regression vector at normal-use stress x sub u and M one is the stress-model information matrix for design xi.

Product construction for two stress variables: \[\xi^*=\xi_1^*\otimes\xi_2^*\] In the paper's two-stress example with a product regression structure, the combined optimal design is the tensor product of the optimal marginal designs for the first and second stress variables.
limitations_stated: The main results assume constant stress within each unit, complete interactions between stress and time, and random effects associated with time but not stress. The authors note that independent optimization of stress and time may fail for models without interaction terms or with random effects for stress, and propose further study of robust designs and criteria for jointly estimating multiple failure-time characteristics.
limitations_unstated: The recommendations depend on the assumed linear degradation form and normal random effects and errors, so departures from these assumptions could change the optimal allocations and the estimated failure-time distribution. The designs are given as approximate proportions, and the paper does not report how rounding them for a particular total sample size affects performance; practical restrictions on stress settings and allocation are not evaluated.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying how optimal designs change when stress and time cannot be optimized independently, including models with additive stress and time effects or random effects for stress. They also identify robust maximin or Bayesian designs and criteria for simultaneous estimation of multiple failure-time characteristics as future research.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the proposed allocations in real accelerated degradation experiments and compare their observed precision with the theoretical predictions. Further work could also develop allocation procedures for practical constraints such as limited stress combinations, unit-specific costs, or sequentially updated experiments.

summary: The paper develops a way to estimate whether the effect of a feature in an online randomized experiment changes as users learn about it. It models the metric as a combination of a time effect, a treatment effect, and a user-learning effect, which can represent novelty or primacy. The proposed method uses difference-in-differences (DID): it compares the treatment group’s change over time with the control group’s change, without adding cohorts or changing the usual experiment setup. The authors compare it with an existing staggered-cohort experimental design through theoretical derivation, Microsoft experiment data, and simulation. They conclude that the proposed method is easier to deploy and can have greater statistical power, but may mistake other treatment-by-time interactions for user-learning.
key_results: Under the paper’s variance assumptions, the proposed estimator has variance 8 times one minus the within-unit correlation, multiplied by the metric variance and divided by the sample size; the existing experimental estimator has variance 2 times k times the metric variance divided by the sample size. The authors say this favors their method when the within-unit correlation exceeds one minus k divided by 4, a condition guaranteed when k is greater than 3. In a 14-day simulation repeated 1,000 times, the proposed method estimated alpha as 1.001 with standard error 0.049 and beta as 0.339 with standard error 0.052, close to true values of 1 and one third; the experimental method gave 1.013 with standard error 0.105 and 0.581 with standard error 2.107. In one Microsoft application experiment with about 300,000 users in each group, the estimated learning effect was 30.30 percent in week 1 with p-value 7e-22, while by week 3 neither the treatment effect nor the learning estimate was statistically significant. For the msn.com example, the quick test detected a negative learning effect for total clicks with p-value 0.0083.

Assumed metric model: \[\mu_t = \alpha + \beta_t + (\tau + \delta_{t-t_0})I_\tau\] The expected metric in time window t is modeled using intercept alpha, time-window effect beta, treatment effect tau, user-learning effect delta since exposure began at t0, and treatment indicator I tau.

DID estimate of user-learning: \[\hat{\delta}_t = (T^t - T^1) - (C^t - C^1)\] The estimated learning effect at time window t is the treatment cohort’s change from its first-window mean minus the control cohort’s change from its first-window mean.
limitations_stated: The proposed method cannot distinguish user-learning from other treatment interactions with time, such as seasonality, and those interactions can bias the learning estimate. The authors also identify limitations shared by both methods: estimates can be biased by non-durable experimental units, interference between units, future feature or competitor changes, and external behavior changes not captured in the experiment.
limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence is limited to selected Microsoft examples, and the simulation uses data from one of those examples, so performance across other products, organizations, and metrics is not established here. The long-term estimate can depend on fitting an extrapolation model when learning has not stabilized; the paper illustrates an exponential model, but does not establish how reliably that choice works for other learning patterns.
future_work_stated: The authors recommend using the observational method to test for user-learning, then running the experiment longer if learning is significant. If learning continues to change, they recommend constructing a learning time series and extrapolating it to estimate long-term impact; for strong suspected seasonality interactions, they suggest the more complex experimental approach or time-series decomposition and related methods.
future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the method across products and organizations, and assess its performance for metrics and user behavior patterns beyond those in the paper’s Microsoft examples and simulation. It could also evaluate practical adjustments for constraints such as changing exposure dates, missing observations, and limited experiment duration, and compare alternative extrapolation approaches when learning has not converged.

summary: The paper designs CherryPick, a family of unsupervised methods for separating endogenous messages, driven by social-network interactions, from exogenous messages, driven by outside influences. The methods are built on the SLANT opinion-dynamics model and aim to select messages that yield precise estimates of the model’s opinion parameters. They formulate message selection as a cardinality-constrained experimental-design problem, using four criteria based on the parameter-estimation covariance and greedy selection algorithms. The authors evaluate the methods using Twitter datasets and synthetic data, comparing resulting predictions and parameter estimates with robust-regression and outlier-removal baselines. The reported results show that CherryPick often improves opinion forecasting, though performance differs by criterion and dataset.
key_results: On five Twitter datasets, with gamma fixed at 0.2 and a 4-hour prediction horizon, CherryPick’s best variant had MSE values of 0.037 on Club, 0.069 on Verdict, 0.056 on Sports, and 0.035 on Delhi; the corresponding robust hard-thresholding baseline values were 0.038, 0.070, 0.069, and 0.037. Elections was an exception: the hard-thresholding baseline had MSE 0.049, compared with 0.051 for the best CherryPick variant. On Sports, the D-optimal CherryPick variant had an FR of 0.079, compared with 0.090 for the hard-thresholding baseline. Synthetic tests used networks of 512 nodes, varied training data from 20 to 400 events per node, and included 20% exogenous messages; D-optimal and T-optimal variants generally had the strongest parameter-estimation performance, while the hard-thresholding baseline was often comparable. The authors prove that the selection task is computationally intractable in general and establish greedy approximation guarantees: the D-optimal and T-optimal objectives receive the standard one-minus-one-over-e guarantee, with separate bounds for the weakly submodular A-optimal and E-optimal objectives.

Opinion model using the combined message history: \[\mathbf{x}^*(t)=\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\int_0^t g(t-s)\mathbf{A}[\boldsymbol{\zeta}(s)\odot d\mathbf{P}(s)]\] The latent opinion vector x at time t equals the baseline opinion vector alpha plus the accumulated influence of messages; A is the influence matrix, g is the time-decay kernel, zeta is the message-sentiment vector, and P counts all messages, including endogenous and exogenous ones.

Parameter-estimation covariance for a selected message set: \[\mathbf{\Sigma}(H_T)=\operatorname{diag}_u\left[c\mathbf{I}+\sigma^{-2}\sum_{e_i\in H_T}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{iu}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{iu}^{T}\right]^{-1}\] Sigma is the parameter-estimation covariance for selected set H sub T; the diagonal blocks are indexed by user u, c is the regularization constant, I is the identity matrix, sigma is the sentiment-noise standard deviation, and phi is the feature vector for event i and user u.

Cardinality-constrained design objective: \[\max_{S\subseteq U_T,\ |S|=N_H} f_X(S),\qquad f_X(S)=-\Omega_X(S)\] The method selects set S from all observed messages U sub T, requires its size to equal N sub H, and maximizes f for criterion X; f is the negative of the corresponding covariance-based complexity measure Omega.

Greedy event selection: \[S_{k+1}=S_k\cup\arg\max_{e\in U_T\setminus S_k}\left[f_X(S_k\cup\{e\})-f_X(S_k)\right]\] At selection step k, the algorithm adds event e with the largest marginal increase in objective f for criterion X; S is the selected event set and U sub T is the full message set.
limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a dedicated limitations section. They report that the A-optimal and E-optimal variants can perform poorly on high-SNR synthetic data because their objectives are only weakly submodular, and that the E-optimal and T-optimal variants can incur computational inefficiency in their optimization.
limitations_unstated: Real-message labels are unavailable, so the real-data evaluation uses forecasting performance as an indirect test rather than measuring classification accuracy against known labels. The method also requires the user to specify how many messages to select, and its findings depend on the assumed SLANT dynamics, sentiment measurements, and observed social network; the paper does not establish performance when these assumptions are violated.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the selection method under other opinion-dynamics models and to assess how sensitive its results are to an incorrectly specified endogenous-message fraction. Evaluation on datasets with independently verified message labels, and on real operational applications beyond the studied Twitter topics, would also clarify how reliably the selected messages represent endogenous dynamics.

summary: The paper develops nonparametric tests for factorial repeated-measures studies with missing observations and potentially ordinal outcomes. It tests hypotheses about differences among outcome distributions, including group effects, time effects, and group-by-time interactions. The method estimates relative effects from pooled ranks and uses quadratic test statistics with critical values obtained by multiplying centered rank vectors by random bootstrap weights. The authors prove asymptotic validity under a missing-completely-at-random assumption and evaluate the methods through simulations and two clinical datasets, also examining selected missing-at-random scenarios in simulations. They recommend the bootstrap analysis-of-variance-type test because it generally controls false positives well while retaining useful power and requiring less restrictive conditions than some alternatives.
key_results: The simulations used 10,000 runs per setting and 999 bootstrap runs, with sample sizes including group sizes of 5, 10, or 20 and designs with four or eight measurement times. In a normal-data example with four times, group sizes of 5 and 5, and 10% missing completely at random, the classical Wald-type test had a 25.5% false-positive rate for the no-time-effect hypothesis, compared with 7% for the classical analysis-of-variance-type test and 5.2%, 5.0%, and 6.1% for the bootstrap Wald-type, bootstrap analysis-of-variance-type, and bootstrap modified analysis-of-variance-type tests. Across the broader simulations, the classical Wald-type test was often liberal; bootstrap Wald-type and analysis-of-variance-type procedures generally kept false-positive rates closer to the nominal 5%, while bootstrap Wald-type tended to have the lowest power and the bootstrap analysis-of-variance-type and modified analysis-of-variance-type tests had power similar to the classical analysis-of-variance-type test. In the fluvoxamine data, all five tests reported p-values below 0.00001 for both therapeutic and side-effect changes; in the skin-disorder data, all five rejected the group and time hypotheses, and reported interaction p-values ranged from 0.009 to 0.032.
key_equations:
Distributional null hypothesis: \[H_0: CF=0\] H_0 is the null hypothesis, C is the contrast matrix defining the effect to test, and F is the vector of outcome distributions across groups and measurement times.

Rank-based relative effect estimate: \[\hat p_{ij}=\frac{1}{N\lambda_{ij.}}\sum_{k=1}^{n_i}\lambda_{ijk}\left(R_{ijk}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\] The estimated relative effect for group i and time j is p-hat with indices i and j; N is the number of observed measurements, lambda indicates whether subject k's measurement is observed, n_i is the number of subjects in group i, and R is its pooled mid-rank.

Analysis-of-variance-type statistic: \[T_A=\frac{n\hat p^{T}T\hat p}{\operatorname{tr}(T\hat V_n)}\] T_A is the analysis-of-variance-type statistic, n is the total number of subjects, p-hat is the vector of estimated relative effects, T is the contrast projection matrix, V-hat_n is the estimated covariance matrix, and tr denotes the matrix trace.

Wild bootstrap rank construction: \[Z_{ik}^{*}=W_{ik}Z_{ik},\qquad P(W_{ik}=-1)=P(W_{ik}=1)=\frac{1}{2}\] Z-star is the bootstrap centered rank vector for subject k in group i, Z is the original centered rank vector, W is an independent random weight, and P denotes probability.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the theoretical development assumes measurements are missing completely at random. They examine selected missing-at-random cases in simulations, but do not establish the method's validity for those cases theoretically.
limitations_unstated: The simulations examine selected distributions, covariance patterns, factor layouts, and missingness scenarios; they do not test missingness that depends on the unobserved outcomes. The empirical applications are both clinical studies, so performance in industrial experiments or other settings is not demonstrated. The bootstrap calculations require repeated resampling, and the paper does not report runtime or assess the computational burden for larger designs.
future_work_stated: The authors plan to include the methodology in the R package nparLD. They also propose extending the investigation to general multivariate analysis-of-variance settings with missing values.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess validity under missingness that depends on the unobserved outcome and under more complex practical constraints, such as unequal measurement schedules or restricted treatment allocation. Evaluations in real quality-engineering experiments and studies of how the method performs when used sequentially during an ongoing experiment would help establish its practical value.

summary: The paper presents a computational framework that chooses experimental inputs and polynomial model bases together for discrete biological-network data. It focuses on minimal polynomial models, in which terms representing unobserved interactions are excluded, and on whether the data can identify a model. The authors construct the framework by grouping input data sets related by coordinate-wise affine shifts and annotating each group with the model bases identifiable from its members. They also select a representative data set for each group and provide a searchable database for a limited set of network sizes and state counts. In an example based on an epidermal derived growth factor receptor signaling model, the framework identifies experiments for a specified interaction and shows which additional interactions may also be identifiable.
key_results: For the epidermal derived growth factor receptor example, the authors consider 56 possible input sets of five points and report that these form seven shift-equivalence classes. Requiring the model basis to include the interaction between Rkip and Kras reduces the possibilities to 32 data sets in four classes; one class, containing eight data sets, identifies the specified basis uniquely. In a point-addition example, adding one of the three possible points to the starting data set can identify additional interactions; adding the point 111 yields two distinct bases, involving different additional interactions. The paper provides no measured runtime or quantitative efficiency comparison; its database covers cases with two states and two to four nodes, and cases with three states and two nodes.
key_equations:
Identifiability by evaluation: \[\operatorname{rank} X(f,S)=q\] Here X is the matrix evaluating the monomials of polynomial f on input data set S, q is the number of monomials in f, and rank denotes matrix rank; the polynomial is identifiable when this matrix has full column rank.

Representative of a shift-equivalence class: \[S_{\mathrm{rep}}\in\arg\min_{T\in[S]}D(T,0)\] Here S_rep is a representative data set, [S] is the class of data sets related to S by linear shifts, T is a member of that class, D is the sum of the Euclidean distances of its points from the origin, and 0 denotes the origin; ties are resolved by the paper’s lexicographic ordering.
limitations_stated: The authors do not give a formal limitations section. They state that their database covers only selected combinations of state counts, node counts, and data-set sizes, and say that expanding the database and its contents would make the approach more accessible.
limitations_unstated: The database relies on exhaustive enumeration and algebraic computations, so its demonstrated coverage may not scale readily to larger networks or richer state spaces. The method treats discrete states over prime-sized finite fields and only groups designs under coordinate-wise affine shifts; it does not address practical restrictions such as randomization, costs, or feasibility of particular experimental settings, nor does the example validate the framework with newly collected experimental data.
future_work_stated: The authors propose further theoretical and computational study of the number and sizes of linear-shift equivalence classes and how these properties inform the relationship between data and modeling. They also propose growing the database and expanding the information it provides.
future_work_unstated: Future work could extend the framework to other model families and design criteria, and incorporate constraints such as costs, forbidden settings, or required randomization into the search for identifiable experiments. It could also evaluate sequential design and test the proposed designs against new biological experiments, while assessing computational scaling as network size increases.

summary: The paper examines how to measure mobile app performance in randomized online controlled experiments, with the goal of making performance results more useful for product decisions. It compares performance summaries calculated across events with summaries that give each user equal weight, and describes how event-based summaries can overrepresent heavily engaged users with higher-end devices. It treats missing performance values as a possible source of selection bias and proposes a proportion-based check followed by imputation or matching. The methods rely on missingness being explainable by experiment group, device model, and users’ pre-experiment engagement. Simulations and Snap experiments show that these methods can reduce misleading results, while also identifying cases where they do not fully correct bias.
key_results: Across 8,338 performance metrics from 152 A/B tests, about 10% of event-level and user-level results were inconsistent in significance or estimated effect direction. In a separate analysis of 11 metrics across 61 A/B experiments, more than 20% of the experiments had most performance metrics fail the self-selection check. In simulations averaged over 100 iterations, imputation and matching produced estimates close to the true effect and generally avoided the false conclusions seen without correction; in the paper’s real examples, the methods removed misleading significant results in two cases but did not fully correct another. Both methods ran in under one hour for 6 million users, 100 subgroups, and 100 iterations on the reported laptop.

Treatment effect estimand: \[\mathrm{ATE}=\mathbb{E}[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)]\] ATE is the average treatment effect, E is the expected value, i indexes a user, and Y_i(1) and Y_i(0) are that user's potential outcomes under treatment and control.

Missingness assumption: \[\Pr(M\mid Y,X_1,X_2,X_3)\approx\Pr(M\mid X_1,X_2,X_3)\] Pr is probability, M indicates whether a user has a performance event, Y is the performance value, X_1 is experiment group, X_2 is device model, and X_3 is pre-treatment engagement; the relation assumes missingness is nearly independent of the performance value within these groups.

Self-selection check: \[H_0:p_T=p_C,\qquad H_1:p_T\ne p_C\] H_0 is the null hypothesis that p_T and p_C, the proportions with observed performance events in treatment and control, are equal, and H_1 is the alternative that they differ.

Imputation and matching construction: \[\tilde Y_i\sim F_g,\qquad w_i=\begin{cases}1&i\in T\\N_g^T/N_g^C&i\in C\end{cases}\] F_g is the empirical distribution of observed performance values in subgroup g, tilde Y_i is an imputed value for user i, w_i is the matching weight, T and C are treatment and control users, and N_g^T and N_g^C are their respective subgroup counts.
limitations_stated: The methods depend on the missing-at-random assumption, which cannot generally be verified, so they do not completely remove self-selection bias and may fail to correct false positives. The authors also report that user-level high-percentile metrics can be underestimated for users with few events, potentially misleading results when treatment changes event counts. They say that extending scalable bias correction to event-level metrics remains a challenge.
limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from Snap’s user population and operational experiments, so the results may not transfer directly to apps with different device mixes, engagement patterns, or event logging. The subgroup rules, including grouping less-common device models as “Other” and splitting engagement at the mean, may leave meaningful differences within subgroups that affect the correction.
future_work_stated: The authors leave scalable methods for reducing self-selection bias in event-level performance metrics to future research. They also suggest that more accurate imputation for user-level P90 metrics among users with very few events may help, while noting that it would require additional assumptions.

summary: This paper develops covariate-adjusted Fisher randomization tests (FRTs) for testing the average treatment effect (ATE) in randomized experiments. It compares adjustment based on covariate-only outcome residuals with adjustment based on regression models that include treatment and covariates. The recommended approach fits an ordinary least squares (OLS) model with centered covariates and treatment-by-covariate interactions, then uses the treatment coefficient's robustly studentized statistic. The authors derive its properties for complete, cluster, and stratified randomization, as well as rerandomization based on covariate balance. They find that the recommended test is exact for the null of no individual effects and asymptotically valid for the null of zero average effect, while improving power under alternatives.
key_results: In theory, the recommended robustly studentized Lin statistic is asymptotically valid for testing a zero average treatment effect and is the most powerful of the valid robustly studentized options considered; all the proposed tests remain finite-sample exact under the null of no individual effects. In simulations with 500 units, 1,000 repetitions, and 500 treatment permutations per repetition, only the four robustly studentized statistics controlled error rates under the weak null, and Lin's statistic had the highest power; the Fisher and Rosenbaum adjusted statistics had lower power than the unadjusted robust statistic in the reported alternative. In the application, the experiment included 219 students; for the overall physician-video comparison, the covariate-adjusted estimate was 0.463 with robust standard error 0.190 and randomization-test p-value 0.017, compared with an unadjusted estimate of 0.406, standard error 0.202, and p-value 0.047. The authors also give design-specific recommendations: use cluster totals for cluster randomization, weighted averages across strata for stratified randomization, and use the Lin statistic under rerandomization when covariates are available.

limitations_stated: The asymptotic results require moment and other regularity conditions; the authors note that heavy-tailed outcomes can prevent the tests from controlling error rates even asymptotically. The paper focuses on OLS-based procedures, and it defers extensions to high-dimensional settings, nonlinear models, machine-learning estimators, and experiments with many small strata. The authors also leave rigorous quantification of relative power for future work.
limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence is based on a limited set of generated outcome settings and does not establish performance across the broad range of experimental conditions encountered in practice. The application is one experiment, and its small within-class groups make the large-sample approximations questionable; exact randomization inference may also require many permutations when the assignment set is large.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the theory to high-dimensional covariates, nonlinear models, and machine-learning-based estimators. They also identify general theory for studentized tests, broader use of prepivoting, and rigorous comparisons of power as topics for future research.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate these procedures under practical constraints such as limited covariate availability, missing outcomes, and restricted or unequal-probability assignments. Sequential applications and validation across a wider set of real experiments would help establish how reliably the theoretical power and validity results translate into practice.

summary: This paper compares blocking with complete randomization for estimating treatment effects in randomized experiments. It uses the potential-outcomes framework and distinguishes finite samples from several ways of sampling units and forming blocks. The authors derive variance comparisons for these settings, then examine what happens when treatment proportions vary across blocks and when analysts ignore the blocking in their analysis. Simulations and a teacher professional development data example illustrate the theoretical results. The main finding is that blocking often improves precision and can yield large gains, but its guarantees depend on the sampling framework, block formation, and treatment proportions.
key_results: With equal treatment proportions, blocking is guaranteed not to increase variance under stratified sampling and under two-stage sampling; it can increase variance in finite samples and when complete structural blocks are sampled. In simulations, the worst equal-proportion blocking case increased variance by about 7%, while the most favorable case reduced it by almost 92%; with unequal proportions, the largest increase was 30% and the largest reduction was about 89.8%. In the teacher data example, the existing geographic blocks increased the standard error by 4%, while blocking by a baseline test reduced it to 67.1% of the complete-randomization standard error; a hypothetical highly predictive baseline reduced it to 25.4%. The paper also shows that a complete-randomization variance estimator applied after blocking can underestimate the true blocked-design variance in some finite samples, and that the relative variability of the two designs’ variance estimators has no universal ordering.

limitations_unstated: The simulation results come from selected constructed scenarios, and the applied example evaluates hypothetical designs using one teacher dataset rather than testing the recommendations prospectively across experiments. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying the practical effects of degrees-of-freedom loss from estimating more parameters under blocking, and further assessing variance-estimator stability. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the comparisons under practical allocation constraints that make equal treatment proportions difficult, and assess the results across a broader range of real experiments. It would also be useful to evaluate how the paper’s conclusions extend to rerandomization and other covariate-balancing approaches, which the authors mention but do not investigate.

summary: The paper develops an optimal allocation method for two-treatment A/B tests when subjects have known covariates and are connected in a social network. It models continuous outcomes with treatment and covariate effects, while a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model represents correlation between connected subjects. The design assigns subjects to treatments to improve precision in estimating the treatment effect, balancing covariates and network connections. Because the network correlation is unknown, the method uses a locally optimal criterion evaluated at a chosen value, typically the prior mean, and a hybrid optimization procedure to construct assignments. Simulations and a music-streaming network example show improved precision over a design that ignores network connections, with performance close to designs based on the true correlation value in the tested settings.
key_results: In simulations, the locally optimal design generally outperformed the optimal design that ignored network connections, particularly for smaller, sparser networks and stronger true network correlation. When compared with the design using the true correlation value, the difference in percentage improvement in precision was mostly under 3% in the reported tests. For the network-aware design, the reported precision improvement declined from about 40% at 50 subjects to about 5% at 1,000 subjects, partly because the network edge count dominates the criterion in larger networks. In the real-network study, the proposed design improved precision over the no-network design; in simulated-outcome tests on sampled networks of approximately 1,000 users, its mean squared error was usually better than that of random balanced designs, while the no-network design did not outperform those random designs.
key_equations:
Outcome model: \[y_i=x_i\theta+f_i^\top\beta+\delta_i\] The index i identifies a subject, y_i is its continuous outcome, x_i is its treatment assignment, theta is the treatment effect, f_i contains its intercept and covariates, beta contains the covariate coefficients, and delta_i is its error.

Network error distribution: \[\delta\sim N_n\!\left(0,\sigma^2(D-\rho W)^{-1}\right)\] The vector delta contains the subject errors, N_n denotes an n-dimensional normal distribution, n is the number of subjects, sigma squared is the error variance, D is the diagonal matrix of degrees, rho is the network correlation parameter, and W is the adjacency matrix.

Treatment-effect precision criterion: \[T(x,\rho)=x^\top Kx,\quad K=D-\rho W-(D-\rho W)F[F^\top(D-\rho W)F]^{-1}F^\top(D-\rho W)\] The vector x contains treatment assignments, rho is the network correlation, K is the precision matrix after adjusting for covariates, D is the degree matrix, W is the adjacency matrix, F is the covariate design matrix, and T is the criterion maximized to reduce the treatment-effect variance.

Hybrid construction of the locally optimal design: \[\min_x x^\top(D-\rho_0W)F[F^\top(D-\rho_0W)F]^{-1}F^\top(D-\rho_0W)x,\quad x^\top Wx\le\sqrt{m}z_\alpha,\quad -1\le\sum_i x_i\le1,\quad x\in\{-1,1\}^n\] The vector x assigns the two treatments, rho_0 is the selected network correlation value, W is the adjacency matrix, D is the degree matrix, F is the covariate matrix, m is twice the number of edges, z_alpha is the standard normal percentile used for the network-balance cap, alpha sets that percentile, i indexes subjects, and n is the number of subjects.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the method depends on the CAR additive model and that the network representation is simpler than real social networks; the validity of the model assumptions is important. The model does not apply directly to isolated nodes, which have no network neighbors.
limitations_unstated: The empirical validation is limited to simulations and one social-network dataset; the real-data case study simulates outcomes rather than testing treatment assignments in a live experiment. The construction also depends on the network and covariates being available before assignment, and its optimization settings were evaluated with a 500-second runtime limit rather than across a broad range of operational constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to directional or weighted networks, other models such as spatial autoregressive models, subject-specific correlation, and ways to handle isolated nodes. They also identify selecting subjects and assigning treatments jointly, accounting for uncertain covariates, and extending the design to more than two treatment settings as future research.
future_work_unstated: A prospective study using observed outcomes from a deployed experiment would help validate whether the reported precision gains translate to operational A/B tests. Further work could also assess the design under practical allocation restrictions, such as limits on assignments within service regions or user segments.

summary: The paper develops sequential sampling methods to map regions where multiple environmental measurements jointly cross specified thresholds. It models the responses, illustrated by ocean temperature and salinity, as a vector-valued Gaussian random field and defines uncertainty in the resulting excursion set. The design selects sampling locations to reduce expected integrated Bernoulli variance, with formulas that make the criterion computationally tractable. The authors compare a simple probability-based rule, a greedy rule, a two-step look-ahead rule, and fixed survey paths. Simulations favor the greedy and look-ahead rules for excursion-set uncertainty, and field trials show an autonomous underwater vehicle using the greedy rule to track a river-plume boundary.
key_results: The simulation comparison used 100 replicate runs, each with 10 sampling stages, and compared the adaptive strategies with three fixed paths. The greedy and look-ahead strategies achieved the largest reductions in realized integrated Bernoulli variance and performed similarly; both generally outperformed the simple probability-based rule on that objective. Some fixed paths performed well on prediction measures because they covered more of the domain, while the look-ahead strategy required substantially more computation and was described as nearly impractical onboard. In two field missions, each planned for about 40 minutes and 15 waypoints, the vehicle crossed the plume front multiple times and produced similar final front estimates.
key_equations:
Excursion set: \[\Gamma=\{u\in M: Z_u\in T\}\] Gamma is the excursion set, u is a spatial location in domain M, Z at u is the vector of field responses there, and T is the set of response values defining the excursion.

Integrated Bernoulli variance: \[\operatorname{IBV}=\int_M p(u)(1-p(u))\,d\nu(u)\] IBV is integrated Bernoulli variance, M is the spatial domain, p of u is the probability of excursion at location u, and nu is the measure used to integrate over the domain.

Greedy sampling criterion: \[u_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{u\in J}\operatorname{EIBV}_n(u)\] The next location u at stage n plus one is chosen to minimize expected integrated Bernoulli variance at the current stage n over candidate waypoints J.
limitations_stated: The authors note that their field case study is for an upper-water-column, two-dimensional domain and does not include temporal effects. They identify spatio-temporal and non-Gaussian modeling as extensions, and report that the two-step look-ahead strategy is nearly impractical onboard because of its computational cost.
limitations_unstated: The method’s sampling choices depend on the fitted Gaussian field, trend, covariance structure, and user-specified thresholds; errors in these assumptions could change which locations are selected and how the excursion boundary is estimated. The real-world evaluation is limited to two missions at one river plume, on a waypoint grid and with both temperature and salinity measured, so it does not establish performance across other environments or operating constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to three-dimensional and spatio-temporal settings, including models based on advection and diffusion, and to non-Gaussian phenomena. They also identify volume-uncertainty, hybrid objectives, continuous navigation, multiple vehicles, and value-of-information analysis as possible research directions.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test how the selected paths and excursion estimates change under deliberate covariance-model misspecification, uncertain thresholds, and changing measurement noise. Further field validation could compare the method with fixed and alternative adaptive designs across multiple sites while accounting explicitly for navigation, energy, and safety constraints.

summary: The paper develops a method for testing differences in median survival times in factorial studies with right-censored observations. It applies to general group contrasts, including main effects and interactions, without requiring proportional hazards. The method estimates group medians with Kaplan-Meier estimators and uses studentized Wald-type statistics with permutation testing. The authors establish asymptotic validity and consistency, then assess performance in simulations and a liver-cirrhosis clinical-trial dataset. Their simulations favor the permutation test using a one-sided variance estimator for reliable type-1 error control and competitive power.
key_results: The simulation study used 5,000 runs and 1,999 resampling iterations at a nominal 5% significance level. For the tested 2-by-2 and 2-by-3 designs, the permutation tests generally controlled type-1 error reasonably well; the one-sided permutation test was the authors’ preferred Wald-type procedure, while asymptotic tests sometimes had error rates as high as 13.8% or as low as 1.9%, and the quantile-regression jackknife reached 11.9% in the 2-by-3 design. In the 446-person clinical dataset, the preferred one-sided permutation test reported p-values of .015 for treatment and .012 for the treatment-by-sex interaction; in the female subset it reported .021 for the prothrombin effect, and in the male subgroup aged 60–69 it reported .007 for that effect. The authors’ theory establishes asymptotic validity under their assumptions and finite-sample exactness for randomized tests when the group data are exchangeable.
key_equations:
Median contrast null hypothesis: \[H m=0\] H is the contrast matrix, m is the vector of population group medians, and 0 is the zero vector.

Wald-type test statistic: \[W_n(T)=n(T\hat{m})^{\mathsf{T}}(T\hat{\Sigma}T^{\mathsf{T}})^{+}T\hat{m}\] W_n(T) is the test statistic, n is total sample size, T is the projection matrix for the contrasts, m-hat is the vector of estimated group medians, Sigma-hat is the diagonal matrix of estimated median variances, the superscript T denotes transpose, and the superscript plus denotes the Moore–Penrose inverse.

Permutation test decision: \[\phi_n^\pi=\mathbf{1}\{W_n(T)>c_\alpha^\pi\}\] Phi-n-pi is the permutation test decision, the indicator is one when its condition holds, W_n(T) is the observed Wald-type statistic, and c-alpha-pi is the conditional permutation critical value at significance level alpha.
limitations_stated: The authors focus on median survival times and leave factorial extensions for other effect sizes to future work. Their asymptotic results require positive density at each group median, censoring that permits events after the median, and group sample sizes that do not vanish relative to one another; the pooled permutation analysis also requires its pooled median to be observable and regularity conditions near that median.
limitations_unstated: The simulations cover selected two-factor layouts, a limited set of survival distributions and censoring patterns, and relatively small group sizes, so performance in other factorial structures or more severe censoring is not established by these comparisons. The clinical illustration is a single healthcare dataset rather than validation in other application domains, and the analysis does not demonstrate how the method performs when covariate adjustment is needed.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to ratios of median-survival contrasts, restricted mean survival, and more general survival quantiles in factorial designs. They also plan permutation methods for meta-analysis and report that they are working on an R package and a Shiny web application for the proposed procedures.
future_work_unstated: Further work could examine covariate-adjusted median contrasts and practical design constraints such as unequal allocation or planned censoring, then assess the methods in additional factorial layouts. Comparisons in real experiments outside healthcare, along with accessible software and reproducible implementation details, would help establish practical use for design-of-experiments work.

scope_reason: It develops and characterizes efficient adaptive designs for choosing between policies in online experiments with temporal interference.
design_type_evidence: We use this characterization to propose a consistent, efficient online experimental design that adaptively samples the two Markov chains.
glossary: alpha = The treatment effect: the difference between the two chains’ steady-state average rewards.|P, pi, r = For a chain, its transition probabilities, stationary state probabilities, and expected one-step rewards by state.|ell = The index identifying one of the two chains.|S, x, y = The shared state space and states within that space.|kappa, K = Kappa gives the long-run sampling proportions for each chain and state; K is the set of feasible proportions.|sigma = The state-specific standard deviation term used in the asymptotic variance of the estimator.|p_n, M_n = The probability of choosing a chain at time n and the number of visits to a state by that time.|n = The time step or, in asymptotic statements, the number of observations.|A hat = A mark over a quantity indicates that it is estimated from observed data.
summary: The paper develops an adaptive experiment for comparing two policies when running one policy can change the system state encountered by the other. It models each policy as an unknown, finite-state, irreducible Markov chain and targets the difference in their steady-state average rewards. The method estimates each chain’s transition behavior and rewards using nonparametric maximum likelihood, then selects policies using estimated state-specific sampling allocations. Those allocations are obtained by minimizing an asymptotic variance criterion over proportions that satisfy the system’s flow-balance constraints. The authors show that their online design is consistent and asymptotically efficient under the stated assumptions.
key_results: The theoretical results characterize the minimum asymptotic variance through a convex optimization problem, and show that the proposed online design approaches its optimal allocation while remaining consistent and efficient. The allocation uses forced exploration with a probability term proportional to the number of state visits raised to the power negative one-half. In the paper’s constructed example, running each chain separately gives estimator variance scaling as Θ(s/n), whereas cooperative sampling gives variance scaling as Θ(4/n); the relative improvement can grow without bound as s increases. The paper reports theoretical results and this illustrative example, not empirical evaluations on real systems.
key_equations:
Treatment effect: \[\alpha=\sum_{x\in S}\pi(2,x)r(2,x)-\sum_{x\in S}\pi(1,x)r(1,x)\] Alpha is the treatment effect; S is the state space; x is a state; pi is the stationary probability of a state for chain 1 or 2; and r is that chain’s expected one-step reward in the state.

Feasible sampling proportions: \[\sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\sum_{x\in S}\kappa(\ell,x)P(\ell,x,y)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\kappa(\ell,y),\quad \sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\sum_{x\in S}\kappa(\ell,x)=1,\quad \kappa\geq0\] Kappa gives nonnegative sampling proportions for chain ell in state x; P gives the probability of moving from state x to state y under that chain; S is the state space; and the equations impose flow balance and make the proportions sum to one.

Asymptotic variance criterion: \[\min_{\kappa\in K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\sum_{x\in S}\frac{\pi(\ell,x)^2\sigma(\ell,x)^2}{\kappa(\ell,x)}\] The design minimizes the asymptotic variance over feasible proportions kappa in K; ell indexes the chain, x is a state, pi is its stationary probability, and sigma is the state-specific standard deviation term.

Online chain-selection probability: \[p_n(\ell,x)=\left(1-M_n(x)^{-1/2}\right)\frac{\hat\kappa_n(\ell,x)}{\hat\kappa_n(1,x)+\hat\kappa_n(2,x)}+\frac{1}{2}M_n(x)^{-1/2}\] At time n and state x, p is the probability of choosing chain ell; M is the number of visits to x, and the hatted kappa values are the estimated sampling proportions, with the added term providing forced exploration.
limitations_stated: The authors focus on asymptotic rather than fixed finite-horizon efficiency, and say that optimal finite-horizon design remains an important direction for future work. They also note that full knowledge of the state space may be infeasible in practice.
limitations_unstated: The results assume a finite state space, irreducible chains, bounded rewards, and that the state and policy-specific transitions can be observed and estimated; systems that violate these assumptions are not covered. The paper provides theory and a constructed example rather than validation on real platform data, and it does not evaluate practical constraints such as switching costs or limits on which policy can be run in a given state.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying optimal finite-horizon experimental design and how the forced-exploration tuning parameter affects finite-horizon bias and variance. They also identify applying the approach when the full state space is not known as an active direction for future study.
future_work_unstated: Future research could assess the design in real platform experiments and compare its estimates and run requirements with switchback designs under realistic operational constraints. It could also extend the method to settings with nonstationary transitions, restrictions on switching policies, or state spaces that must be learned or approximated.
