design_type_evidence: This is a novel extension of the model introduced in ref. [27].
design_objective: Information gain or uncertainty reduction|Parameter estimation
glossary: EFT = Effective field theory; in this paper, the predictions are from chiral effective field theory.|GP = Gaussian process, a probability model for smooth functions.|KL = Kullback-Leibler, referring here to a measure of information gained when updating a prior to a posterior.|Sigma 2x and Sigma 2x-prime = The spin asymmetry for circularly polarized photons on a transversely polarized target, and the corresponding recoil-polarization-transfer observable.|gamma E-minus = The spin-polarizability combination gamma E1E1 minus gamma E1M2.|Measurement-model notation: x, a, y_exp, y_k, delta_yk, delta_yexp = The kinematic point, polarizability parameters, measured observable, finite-order theoretical prediction, theory truncation error, and experimental error, respectively.|Kernel notation: omega, theta, l_omega, l_theta, x-prime = Photon energy, scattering angle, energy and angle correlation lengths, and a second kinematic point.|Error-covariance notation: Sigma, c-bar, R_delta, Sigma_exp = Total error covariance, the typical size of theory coefficients, the truncation-error covariance kernel, and experimental-error covariance.|Design and posterior notation: d, U_KL, V, V0, B = Experimental design, expected information gain, posterior and prior parameter covariance matrices, and the matrix of prediction sensitivities to parameters.
summary: The paper develops a Bayesian method for choosing experiments that use chiral effective field theory to estimate nucleon polarizabilities from proton Compton-scattering measurements. The design objective is to maximize expected information gain, measured through reduction in the uncertainty volume for the polarizabilities. The method represents theory truncation errors as smooth, correlated Gaussian-process errors, with their scale adjusted for the changing EFT power counting across photon energies, and combines them with experimental errors. The authors assess one-point and five-point designs at a fixed energy, using assumed experimental precision levels and practical angle restrictions. Their main finding is that accounting for theory error changes the recommended kinematics and identifies spin-asymmetry measurements as especially informative for a key spin-polarizability combination.
key_results: For five-point proton designs, the spin observables Sigma 2x and Sigma 2x-prime can reduce the uncertainty in gamma E-minus by about 50%; the strongest regions are around 140–200 MeV and scattering angles of about 40–120 degrees. Five-point differential-cross-section designs can reduce uncertainty in alpha E1 minus beta M1 by about 25%, and provide information on gamma pi, gamma E-minus, and gamma M-minus, with about 30% combined reduction reported for those spin combinations. Including theory truncation errors shifts optimal designs toward lower energies and moderates their expected information gain compared with designs that omit those errors. The paper compares one-point and five-point designs at three assumed precision levels: cross-section uncertainties of 5%, 4%, and 3%, and absolute spin-observable uncertainties of 0.10, 0.06, and 0.03; which allocation is preferable depends on the observable.
key_equations:
Measurement model: \[y_{\mathrm{exp}}(x)=y_k(x;a)+\delta y_k(x)+\delta y_{\mathrm{exp}}(x)\] At kinematic point x, the measured observable y_exp is the finite-order prediction y_k for parameters a plus theory truncation error delta_yk and experimental error delta_yexp.

Correlated truncation-error kernel: \[r(x,x')=\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\omega-\omega')^2}{2l_\omega^2}-\frac{(\theta-\theta')^2}{2l_\theta^2}\right]\] The correlation r between points x and x-prime decreases with differences in photon energies omega and scattering angles theta, at rates set by the correlation lengths l_omega and l_theta.

Posterior parameter covariance: \[V(d)=\left(V_0^{-1}+B^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}B\right)^{-1},\qquad \Sigma=\bar c^{\,2}R_\delta+\Sigma_{\mathrm{exp}}\] For design d, V is the posterior covariance, V0 is the prior covariance, B contains prediction sensitivities, and Sigma is total error covariance formed from coefficient scale c-bar, truncation covariance R_delta, and experimental covariance Sigma_exp.

Expected information gain and optimal design: \[U_{\mathrm{KL}}(d)=\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{|V_0|}{|V(d)|},\qquad d^*=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{d}U_{\mathrm{KL}}(d)\] The expected information gain U_KL for design d is one half the natural logarithm of the ratio of the prior covariance determinant to the posterior covariance determinant, and d-star is the design that maximizes it.
limitations_stated: The authors say that their prior only approximately represents current knowledge because they did not re-extract polarizabilities from existing data using the same theory-error model. Their analysis omits common-mode correlated experimental errors and acknowledges that the truncation-error estimate for spin observables is less reliable near the pion-production threshold. They also note that the assumed linearization, experimental capabilities, and design restrictions are simplifications, and that neutron precision assumptions are optimistic.
limitations_unstated: The candidate designs are restricted to one photon energy and either one or five angles, with five-point angles required to be separated by at least 10 degrees; this may miss useful designs that jointly allocate measurements across energies or use other constraints. Results depend on the assumed polarizability prior, error levels, and theory model, so the reported reductions do not by themselves establish the information achievable in an actual facility run or under model misspecification.
future_work_stated: The authors propose a consistent Bayesian extraction of polarizabilities from the existing proton Compton database, more detailed treatment of correlated experimental errors, and further study of EFT convergence, especially for spin observables. They also identify facility-specific designs, sequential experimental design, and applications to other EFT-based experiments, including few-nucleon targets, as future directions.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to optimize designs over multiple energies, realistic beam-time and detector constraints, and explicit run-time or cost budgets, then validate the predicted gains against data from completed experiments. It would also be valuable to assess robustness to alternative theory-error models and to compare the planned measurements’ information gain with what is realized after fitting the resulting data.

scope_reason: The paper discusses planning and designing micro-randomized trials, including how to choose experimental allocations for digital interventions.
design_type_evidence: Pages 9–10 and 20: sequential randomization at repeated decision points; availability for later randomization depends on prior survey or task completion.
glossary: JITAI = Just-in-time adaptive intervention: an intervention that adapts its content or delivery to a person’s changing context.|MRT = Micro-randomized trial: a trial that repeatedly randomizes intervention options at prespecified decision points.|MOST = Multiphase optimization strategy: a framework for developing, optimizing, and evaluating interventions.
summary: This tutorial explains how to design a micro-randomized trial (MRT) to develop just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs), which adapt support to a person’s changing context. The objective is to identify intervention options and decision rules that improve outcomes while limiting burden and unnecessary intervention. The design repeatedly randomizes available participants among component options at prespecified decision points, while collecting context and short-term outcomes that can inform future decisions. The authors use three healthcare case studies to explain choices about components, availability, timing, randomization probabilities, and outcomes. They conclude that MRTs can efficiently inform JITAI design and fit within the multiphase optimization strategy (MOST), while noting that optimizing individual components does not by itself optimize the whole intervention.
key_results: The paper is a design tutorial, not a comparative evaluation, and reports no common sample size or pooled effect estimate. The 42-day HeartSteps example used five daily decision points for activity suggestions, with randomization probabilities of 0.30 for a walking suggestion, 0.30 for an anti-sedentary suggestion, and 0.40 for no suggestion. The 30-day SARA example examined four engagement components, while the 120-day BariFit example combined two baseline-randomized factors with two micro-randomized factors. The paper gives design guidance and illustrative trial details rather than ranking designs by measured performance.
key_equations: Not applicable
limitations_stated: The authors state that more work is needed to integrate MRTs into the broader MOST framework and to use their results to optimize the intervention as a whole. Individual component costs and effects may not add up simply, since components can interact or produce economies of scale.
limitations_unstated: The case studies illustrate design choices but do not provide a standardized empirical comparison of design performance, and this paper does not report sample sizes or common effect estimates. Consequently, the examples do not establish how well the recommended choices about randomization probabilities, participant burden, or outcome timing transfer to other populations and settings.
future_work_stated: The authors call for work on integrating MRT findings into optimization of the whole intervention. They also propose conducting MRTs within deployed digital interventions for ongoing improvement, exploring MRTs for pull content, and developing person-specific decision rules.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could replicate these design approaches across clinical and behavioral settings and assess whether proximal outcome improvements translate into meaningful long-term outcomes. Researchers could also develop and validate planning tools that help teams choose decision points and randomization probabilities while accounting for practical constraints such as participant burden and safety.

summary: This paper examines whether transforming a low-discrepancy uniform design produces a low-discrepancy design for a different target distribution. It studies designs evaluated by kernel-based discrepancy, including designs transformed to follow the standard multivariate normal distribution. The authors show that the transformation preserves discrepancy when the target density and transformed kernel meet specific conditions, but that this result need not hold for a practical kernel choice. They demonstrate the problem with examples and propose improving transformed designs using a coordinate-exchange algorithm. In simulations, coordinate exchange generally gave the lowest discrepancy among the compared normal-design generators.
key_results: For a ten-dimensional integration example with 512 points, two uniform designs had similar discrepancy, 0.0285 and 0.0292, but their transformed normal designs had discrepancy 18.57 and 58.82. Their integral estimates were 10.0182 and 11.2238, with relative errors 0.0018 and 0.1224, respectively. In simulations, 500 designs were generated for each tested dimension and sample size; coordinate exchange produced the smallest discrepancy overall, with its advantage over the other low-discrepancy methods more apparent for the sparser designs. For the reported cases, coordinate-exchange construction times ranged from 0.0134 seconds for dimension 2 and 32 points to 3.84 seconds for dimension 10 and 512 points; the authors report convergence within 20 iterations in all simulation examples.

Discrepancy under a transformed design: \[X=\{\Psi(u_i)\}_{i=1}^N,\quad K(t,x)=K_{\rm unif}(\Psi^{-1}(t),\Psi^{-1}(x)),\quad D(X,F,K)=D(U,F_{\rm unif},K_{\rm unif})\] X is the transformed design, Ψ is the transformation, u_i is point i of the uniform design U, N is the number of points, K is the transformed kernel, F is the target distribution, and the subscript unif denotes the corresponding uniform-design distribution and kernel.

Coordinate-exchange update: \[\Delta(x)=D^2(X,F,K)-D^2(X^*(x),F,K),\quad x^*=\arg\max_{x\in\Omega}\Delta(x)\] Δ is the reduction in squared discrepancy, X is the current design, X*(x) is the design after replacing the selected coordinate with candidate value x, F is the target distribution, K is the kernel, Ω is the domain for the candidate value, and x* is the value that maximizes the improvement.

limitations_unstated: The simulations focus on standard multivariate normal targets and a limited set of dimensions and run sizes, so they do not establish performance for other target distributions or dependence structures. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess the method for correlated and nonnormal targets, as well as for experimental constraints that prevent unrestricted coordinate changes. summary: The paper develops a method for choosing internal temperature-sensor locations to reconstruct iron-loss heat sources in an electrical machine. It models the source through a linear heat-conduction equation and uses Bayesian inference to quantify uncertainty in the reconstruction. The source and temperature fields are discretized with finite elements, and sensor locations are selected to reduce the weighted posterior uncertainty using A-optimality. The authors optimize movable internal sensors with a gradient-based procedure and use a low-rank approximation to make boundary-camera data manageable for larger models. In simulations of transformer models, optimized sensor positions improve source reconstruction compared with regular sensor layouts, and the reduced boundary model supports a three-dimensional calculation with tens of thousands of source parameters.
key_results: In the two-dimensional transformer simulation, 18 A-optimized internal sensors reduced relative reconstruction error from 0.243 with regular placement to 0.169; with 26 sensors, the error fell from 0.186 to 0.143. In the three-dimensional simulation, 23 optimized sensors reduced the relative error from 0.317 at the initial locations to 0.262, for a model with 49,310 source degrees of freedom and 7,680 measurements. The boundary measurement representation was reduced from 7,220 data dimensions to rank 120, with no relevant loss of information reported for the reconstruction in the test. In the unit-square study, the A-optimality measure tracked average reconstruction error across 100 random sensor configurations and 200 simulated sources, and the optimized layout performed best among those compared.
key_equations:
Bayesian measurement model: \[y=F(p)X+N\] Here, y is the measurement vector, F(p) is the forward map determined by sensor positions p, X is the random vector of source coefficients, and N is independent measurement noise.

Posterior covariance: \[\Gamma_{post}(p)=\left(\Gamma_{pr}^{-1}+F(p)^T\Gamma_{noise}^{-1}F(p)\right)^{-1}\] Here, Γpost(p) is the posterior covariance at sensor positions p, Γpr is the prior covariance, F(p) is the position-dependent forward map, and Γnoise is the measurement-noise covariance.

A-optimal sensor design: \[p^*=\arg\min_p\operatorname{tr}\left(A\Gamma_{post}(p)A^T\right)\] Here, p* is the selected sensor-position vector, p ranges over candidate positions, tr is the matrix trace, A specifies the error metric, and Γpost(p) is the posterior covariance.

Low-rank boundary representation: \[F_{bdry}^{pr}\approx U_r\Sigma_rV_r^T\] Here, Fbdry^pr is the prior-conditioned boundary measurement map, Ur and Vr are orthonormal factor matrices, Σr contains the retained singular values, and r is the reduced rank.
limitations_stated: The authors describe the work as a preliminary study using a simplified linear model and simulated measurements. They note that practical heat transfer is more complex, that the heat-transfer coefficient is not known precisely, and that source and material properties can depend on temperature. They also state that their prior does not yet capture generic properties of realistic iron-loss fields and that the assumed noise covariance is treated as known.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence comes from a small set of simulated transformer configurations, so it does not establish performance on measured machine data or across a broad range of geometries and operating conditions. The study also does not assess how sensitive the chosen positions are to errors in material parameters or to changes in the assumed source distribution.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing prior distributions that represent generic properties of reasonable iron-loss models and designing statistical tests to assess proposed loss models from temperature data. They also suggest incorporating modeling error through an approximation-error approach or solving a nonlinear inverse problem that includes the uncertain heat-transfer coefficient.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the optimized placements with physical temperature measurements on transformer hardware, including practical installation and sensor-contact constraints. Further work could also compare alternative uncertainty criteria and test whether sequential sensor placement remains effective when new measurements update the prior.

summary: The paper develops a sequential Bayesian experimental design method for estimating parameters in implicit models, where the likelihood cannot be evaluated but the model can be simulated. Its objective is to choose each next experimental setting to maximize the expected information gained about the parameters. The method uses likelihood-free inference by ratio estimation (LFIRE) to estimate density ratios, which support both mutual information (MI) calculation and posterior updating. It uses weighted parameter samples, resampling when the effective sample size becomes small, and Bayesian optimization (BO) to search for informative designs. Simulations on an oscillatory model, epidemiological models, and a cell-spreading model show that the method can produce informative parameter estimates in a few sequential experiments and can retain multimodal beliefs that a precision-based criterion may disfavor.
key_results: For the oscillatory toy model, after four sequential experiments, the MI design gave a frequency estimate of 0.503 with a 95 percent credibility interval of [0.481, 0.527]; the Bayesian D-optimality design gave 0.494 with an interval of [0.468, 0.516]. Their first designs differed: the MI design selected measurement time 2.196 and the D-optimality design selected 1.656; the paper reports that the criteria become similar once the posterior is unimodal. For the Death model, after four iterations, the estimated infection rate was 1.376 with a 95 percent interval of [1.128, 1.621], containing the simulated true value of 1.5. For the susceptible-infected-recovered model, after four iterations, the estimated infection and recovery rates were 0.171 and 0.045, with respective 95 percent intervals [0.112, 0.233] and [0.024, 0.068], containing the true values 0.15 and 0.05. The cell model used 300 initial parameter samples and five sequential iterations; its final estimates for motility and proliferation were 0.394 and 0.00150, with respective 95 percent intervals [0.166, 0.642] and [0.00055, 0.00265], containing the simulated true values 0.35 and 0.001.
key_equations:
Sequential information-gain design criterion: \[U_k(d)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\theta\mid D_{k-1}),\,y\sim p(y\mid\theta,d)}[\log r_k(d,y,\theta,D_{k-1})]\] U_k is the utility at iteration k, d is a candidate design, θ is a parameter draw from the belief given prior data D_{k-1}, y is a simulated observation, p denotes the relevant probability density, and r_k is the estimated posterior-to-belief density ratio.

Density ratio used by LFIRE: \[r_k(d,y,\theta,D_{k-1})=\frac{p(\theta\mid d,y,D_{k-1})}{p(\theta\mid D_{k-1})}=\frac{p(y\mid\theta,d)}{p(y\mid d,D_{k-1})}\] r_k is the density ratio at iteration k, θ is the parameter, y is the observation, d is the design, D_{k-1} is the previous data, and p denotes the posterior, belief, likelihood, or marginal data density indicated by its conditioning variables.

Monte Carlo utility estimate: \[\widehat U_k(d)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log r_k(d,y^{(i)},\theta^{(i)},D_{k-1})\] The estimated utility is the average of log density ratios over N simulated samples indexed by i, where each parameter θ^(i) is drawn from the current belief and each observation y^(i) is simulated at design d.

Accumulated particle weights: \[w_k(\theta;D_k)=\prod_{s=1}^{k}r_s(d_s^*,y_s^*,\theta,D_{s-1})\] The weight w_k for parameter θ after data D_k is the product over iterations s through k of the estimated ratios evaluated at the selected design d_s^* and observed data y_s^*, conditional on previous data D_{s-1}.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their demonstrations use low-dimensional models and that standard Bayesian optimization becomes expensive and less effective for high-dimensional designs. The information-gain objective does not account for experimental or financial costs. They also note that their mixture-based resampling does not exactly preserve the particle distribution.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated data, so it does not establish performance with real experiments, measurement errors, or operational constraints. The method uses chosen summary statistics and a log-linear density-ratio model in its examples, and the paper does not quantify how sensitive design choices and estimates are to those modeling choices or to the limited particle counts.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest using high-dimensional Bayesian optimization or alternatives such as approximate coordinate exchange for higher-dimensional designs. They also propose maximizing information gain relative to estimated experimental cost, and extending the framework to model discrimination or combined model discrimination and parameter estimation.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method in real experiments and measure performance under practical constraints such as restricted or costly measurement schedules. Further work could evaluate robustness to alternative summary statistics and ratio models, and adapt the sequential procedure to settings where observations from successive runs are dependent rather than generated by independent processes.

summary: The paper develops QANOVA, a set of inference methods for quantiles in general factorial designs with univariate outcomes. It tests contrasts of group quantiles, including medians and interquartile ranges, and can address main effects and interactions in potentially heteroscedastic models. The method estimates quantiles and their covariance matrices, then uses studentized Wald-type statistics with permutation-based critical values. Three covariance estimation approaches are considered: kernel density estimation, bootstrap estimation, and an interval-based estimator. Simulations show that the permutation methods generally control false positive rates better than their asymptotic counterparts in the studied small and moderate samples.
key_results: The simulations used 5,000 runs per setting and 1,999 permutation iterations, with a nominal significance level of 5 percent. Across the studied median and interquartile-range tests, permutation methods generally kept false positive rates near the target; for example, the three-quantile setting with group sizes of 8, 13, 12, and 11 had permutation rates from 4.2 to 5.3 percent, while asymptotic rates ranged from 0.6 to 3.9 percent. For interquartile-range tests in smaller samples, asymptotic procedures could be markedly inaccurate: reported rates included 0.3 percent for the bootstrap-based method and 10.2 percent for the kernel-based method, whereas permutation results in that table ranged from 4.6 to 5.2 percent. Power differences among the three permutation variants depended on the setting: interval and bootstrap approaches performed better in the reported interquartile-range comparisons, while the kernel approach had the greatest power for median tests with heavy-tailed distributions. In the children’s growth-data examples, asymptotic p-values ranged from 8.43 to 10.95 percent, while permutation p-values ranged from 3.30 to 6.75 percent.

limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a dedicated limitations section. limitations_unstated: The simulations cover selected one-way and two-by-two layouts and a limited set of distributions and variance patterns, so performance in other factorial structures and operating conditions is not established. The real-data illustrations use observational subgroup comparisons rather than controlled experiments, and the paper does not validate the methods across a broad set of practical experimental constraints or report computational runtime.

summary: The paper develops designs for estimating the coefficients of multiple linear regression when the coefficients vary randomly and may be correlated. It considers one response per experimental unit, a symmetric hypercube of settings, and a covariance structure with a separate random intercept and equally variable, equi-correlated factor coefficients. The authors construct rhombic designs, which group settings into symmetry-related orbits and thereby reduce the number of design choices. Using the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem, they derive conditions for when these designs are optimal and whether their support lies on the hypercube vertices or includes interior settings. They give explicit results for models with 2 through 5 factors and state a conjecture about the pattern in higher dimensions.
key_results: The paper shows that a design with an interior setting is D-optimal if and only if its information matrix equals the dispersion matrix inverse divided by the number of regression coefficients. For vertex rhombic designs, the authors derive an optimality condition that gives a covariance-based boundary between cases where vertex support can be optimal and cases requiring interior support. They provide explicit design results for 2 through 5 factors: for 2 factors, a D-optimal rhombic design is reported throughout the admissible covariance region; for 4 factors, one is reported throughout the model cone. Some parameter settings are not covered by the reported rhombic designs for 3 factors, and only a small region is reported for 5 factors above the specified correlation boundary. The paper reports theoretical conditions and design formulas rather than numerical efficiency comparisons or sample-size performance results.
key_equations:
Variance under the random-coefficient model: \[\sigma^2(x)=f(x)^T D f(x)\] The variance σ²(x) at setting x is obtained from the regression-function vector f(x) and the random-coefficient dispersion matrix D.

Information at a setting: \[M(x)=\frac{f(x)f(x)^T}{\sigma^2(x)}\] The elemental information matrix M(x) is formed from the regression-function vector f(x) and the variance σ²(x) at setting x.

D-optimality equivalence condition: \[\frac{f(x)^T M(\xi^*)^{-1}f(x)}{\sigma^2(x)}\le p\] A design ξ* is D-optimal when, at every setting x, the regression vector f(x), the design information matrix M(ξ*), the variance σ²(x), and the number of coefficients p satisfy this bound.

Information matrix for an interior-point optimum: \[M(\xi^*)=\frac{1}{K+1}D^{-1}\] For an optimal design ξ* with an interior setting, the information matrix M(ξ*) equals the inverse of dispersion matrix D divided by K plus one, where K is the number of factors.
limitations_stated: The detailed explicit design regions are developed for dimensions from 2 through 5, and the authors note that their listed cases do not cover every parameter setting for 3 factors. They also report that some parameter regions have no rhombic optimum identified and present the general-dimensional pattern as a conjecture rather than a proved result.
limitations_unstated: The model requires equal variances and equicorrelation among factor coefficients, an uncorrelated random intercept, and a symmetric hypercube, so the results may not transfer directly to other covariance structures or constrained operating regions. The designs are approximate; the paper does not address converting their weights into feasible exact run counts or assess performance under model misspecification or real experimental data.
future_work_stated: The authors conjecture that for an even number of factors a D-optimal rhombic design exists throughout the model cone. For an odd number of factors, they conjecture existence throughout the cone when the factor-coefficient covariance does not exceed half the factor-coefficient variance.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to prove or test the conjectures for higher dimensions and examine designs under covariance structures that are not equicorrelated. Further work could also develop methods to round approximate weights to practical run sizes and validate the designs in real experiments.

summary: This paper develops estimators for ratio metrics in A/B tests when users contribute repeated, correlated observations and may belong to different segments. It assumes observations within a segment share a common mean and a common within-user correlation, while users are independent of one another. The method estimates that correlation and uses it to weight each user's average, assigning weights according to the estimated precision of the user average. The authors compare this correlation-adjusted estimate with the naive mean, which weights observations equally, and the normalized mean, which weights users equally. Simulations and eBay data show that the correlation-adjusted estimate can reduce variance and increase experiment sensitivity.
key_results: In simulations with correlation values from 0.1 through 0.9, the correlation-adjusted estimate had the smallest reported standard deviation at every value; for example, at correlation 0.1 the standard deviations were 0.00942 for the adjusted estimate, 0.00947 for the naive mean, and 0.01016 for the normalized mean. At correlation 0.9, the corresponding values were 0.01407, 0.01540, and 0.01406. In eBay data, estimated within-user correlations were 9.6% for one United Kingdom metric and 56% for one United States metric, based on five replicas of 500,000 users each. The authors report that the adjusted estimate reduced required sample sizes by up to 15.2% and 40.3%, respectively, compared with the relevant unadjusted approaches; the preferred unadjusted estimate differed with the correlation level.
key_equations:
Variance of a user's average: \[\operatorname{Var}(r_i)=\sigma^2\left(\frac{1-\rho}{n_i}+\rho\right)\] The variance of user i's average, r_i, depends on the observation variance, sigma squared, the within-user correlation, rho, and the number of observations for that user, n_i.

Correlation estimate: \[\hat{\rho}=1+\frac{S_3}{S_1}\] The estimated within-user correlation, rho-hat, is one plus the ratio of statistic S_3 to statistic S_1; the paper also presents an estimator using S_2 in place of S_1.

Minimum-variance user weights: \[w_i\propto\frac{1}{\sigma^2\left((1-\rho)/n_i+\rho\right)}\propto\frac{n_i}{1+(n_i-1)\rho}\] The weight for user i, w_i, is proportional to the inverse variance of that user's average and can be expressed using the observation count n_i and within-user correlation rho.

Correlation-adjusted estimate: \[\bar{R}_{\rho}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i^{1-\rho}r_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i^{1-\rho}}\] The correlation-adjusted estimate, R-rho, averages each user's average, r_i, using an approximate weight based on that user's observation count, n_i, and the within-user correlation, rho, across N users.
limitations_stated: The method assumes a common within-user correlation for different users in the same segment. The authors note that correlation may vary among users within a segment.
limitations_unstated: The evidence is limited to simulations and two metrics from eBay data; the real-data analysis evaluates estimator standard errors rather than validating treatment-effect decisions against known outcomes. The approach also depends on segment definitions and on estimating correlation from the available repeated observations, but the paper does not assess how unstable the estimates or resulting weights may be with sparse data or many segments.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying more flexible settings in which within-user correlation varies among users in the same segment and its distribution may differ across segments.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the estimator across more outcome types, segment structures, and practical experiment constraints, and test its treatment-effect inference in prospective experiments. It could also assess sequential monitoring and provide software that checks correlation estimates and weight stability before use.

summary: This paper extends a quadratic-form inference method for repeated-measures and split-plot designs with multiple groups. It tests linear hypotheses about group means, including group, time, and interaction effects, when the number of groups, measurements, and subjects can grow in different combinations. The observations are assumed to have a multivariate normal distribution and a common covariance matrix, and the method estimates covariance trace quantities to standardize the test statistic. It also approximates critical values using a standardized chi-square distribution, with subsampling proposed to reduce the computation needed for one estimator. Simulations show good control of false rejections for the proposed test across the studied settings, while power depends on the alternative being tested.
key_results: The simulations used 10,000 runs at a nominal significance level of 5%, with dimensions of 5, 50, 200, and 600 and between 2 and 12 groups for the type-I error study. summary: The paper introduces Mendelian factorial design (MFD) to estimate malaria vaccine efficacy when no reliable observable case definition separates malaria illness from other causes of fever. Simulations show that MFD avoids the systematic bias of the conventional approach, while a bounded estimator can improve performance when the genetic factor is weak.

At size 2,000, MFD had proportional absolute bias below 5% in most settings when the factor had protective efficacy of 50%; performance worsened with a weaker factor and lower case specificity, but improved as sample size increased. The conventional estimator's proportional absolute bias was 20% at specificity 0.8 and 50% at specificity 0.5, and its confidence intervals generally had poor coverage; MFD intervals had correct or conservative coverage in most simulated settings. summary: The paper develops a way to optimize policies for a live recommendation system when online experiments are costly and an offline simulator is biased. It models online and simulator outcomes together using a multi-task Gaussian process (MTGP), with a shared policy-space covariance and a learned relationship between tasks. The optimization targets an online objective subject to constraints, using noisy expected improvement to select candidate policies. In the proposed workflow, candidates are first evaluated in the simulator and a selected subset is then tested online. The authors find that simulator data often improve prediction and enable constrained policy searches with substantially fewer online tests.
key_results: Across 11 real policy-search experiments, each with 20 online observations and 100 simulator observations, the authors modeled 99 outcomes and found that the multi-task Gaussian process (MTGP) generally reduced leave-one-out prediction error compared with an online-only Gaussian process (GP); when its prediction error was high, it was no worse than the online-only model in these comparisons. The real optimization examples covered 10–20 parameters and reached improved feasible policies using 40–50 total online observations. In one 13-parameter example, 40 online policies and 160 simulator policies were evaluated, and the optimized batches improved the best feasible objective over the initial search. In the learning-curve analysis, when squared online-simulator correlation was 0.95, 2 online observations combined with 90 simulator observations gave better predictions than 18 online observations; simulator value was much smaller when correlation was low. In the synthetic comparison, interleaving simulator evaluations with online tests outperformed both online-only optimization and a model that used simulator data only at initialization.
key_equations:
Online-simulator covariance model: \[\operatorname{Cov}[f_d(x),f_{d'}(x')] = B_{d,d'}\,\kappa(x,x')\] Cov denotes covariance; f_d and f_d' are response functions for tasks d and d'; x and x' are policy-parameter points; B with task indices is the task covariance; and kappa is the shared covariance function over policy parameters.

Constrained optimization objective: \[\max_x f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad c_j(x)\geq 0,\;j=1,\ldots,J\] The method maximizes the online objective f at policy point x while requiring every constraint c_j at that point to be at least zero, with j indexing the J constraints.

Acquisition rule with online and simulator data: \[\alpha_{\mathrm{NEI}}(x\mid X_T,D_T\cup D_S)\] Alpha NEI is noisy expected improvement evaluated at candidate policy point x, using online policy points X_T and the combined online observations D_T and simulator observations D_S.
limitations_stated: The simulator is biased, and its relationship to online outcomes can be weak for some metrics; the method’s benefit depends on the correlation between tasks and on the shared-covariance and smooth-bias assumptions. The authors also note that their fixed interleaving strategy does not choose whether to run the next batch online or in the simulator, and that developing a decision rule for this trade-off remains open work.
limitations_unstated: The real evidence comes from one company's recommendation system, with 11 modeling experiments and five reported policy-search examples, so it does not establish performance across other operating environments or policy types. The approach may be less reliable when a simulator’s errors have a different structure from the smooth bias represented by the shared-covariance model, or when task relationships change in ways not captured by the modeled task effects.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing an acquisition decision rule that weighs the expected value and resource requirements of online and simulator batches. They identify selecting the experimentation modality while accounting for constraints as an important area for future work.
future_work_unstated: The method could be tested prospectively in independent operational systems, with comparisons that include alternative multi-task models and acquisition rules. Further work could also adapt the procedure to policy spaces with discrete or operationally restricted settings and to sequential decisions under explicit online-test budgets.

summary: The paper extends the linear network effects model (LNM) to construct optimal block designs for experiments on networks. Its network block model (NBM) represents direct treatment effects, differences among blocks, and indirect effects transmitted through connections between units. The authors choose assignments to minimize the average variance of either direct treatment comparisons or network-effect comparisons, using a point exchange on networks (PEN) algorithm to search for good designs. They also use spectral clustering and modularity to define blocks from network communities. Their examples show that designs accounting for blocks and network connections can be substantially more efficient than conventional randomized designs that ignore network effects.
key_results: In the 22-unit example, under the NBM, the optimal design for direct treatment comparisons had a criterion value of 0.1828, compared with 0.3621 for the design optimized without blocks; the latter was reported as 50.4% efficient. For network-effect comparisons in that example, the design optimized without blocks was reported as 39% efficient relative to the block-and-network design. Across randomized designs in the example, median efficiencies for network-effect comparisons were 0.17 for completely randomized designs and 0.18 for randomized block designs. For the 324-unit Facebook network, the optimized designs assigned 161 and 163 units to the two treatments for direct treatment comparisons, and 117 and 207 units for network-effect comparisons.
key_equations:
Network block response model: \[y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_{r(ij)}+b_i+\sum_{g=1}^{\kappa}\sum_{h=1}^{n_g}A_{ij,gh}\gamma_{r(gh)}+\epsilon_{ij}\] Here y is a unit response, mu is the intercept, tau is the direct effect of the treatment r assigned to a unit, b is its block effect, A indicates a connection between units, gamma is the network effect of a treatment received by a connected unit, epsilon is the error, i and j index a block and unit, g and h index a connected unit’s block and unit, kappa is the number of blocks, and n_g is the number of units in block g.

L-optimality criterion: \[\phi(\xi)=\operatorname{Tr}\{M(\xi)^{-1}L\},\qquad L=SS^{T}\] Here phi is the criterion for design xi, M is its information matrix, L is the contrast-weight matrix, S contains the selected parameter contrasts, and Tr denotes the matrix trace.

PEN exchange rule: \[\xi_{t+1}=\begin{cases}\xi'_t,&\phi(\xi'_t)<\phi(\xi_t)\\\xi_t,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\] Here xi at step t is the current design, xi-prime is a design formed by exchanging a unit’s treatment, and the algorithm keeps the exchange only when it lowers the criterion phi.

Modularity for selecting blocks: \[Q=\frac{1}{2l}\sum_{j,h=1}^{n}\left(A_{jh}-\frac{d_jd_h}{2l}\right)\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa}s_{ji}s_{hi}\] Here Q is modularity, l is the number of edges, n is the number of units, A indicates a connection, d is vertex degree, kappa is the number of clusters, and s indicates whether a vertex belongs to a cluster.
limitations_stated: The authors say their methods are intended for small to moderate networks and that generalizing them to networks with hundreds of thousands of nodes is an open research problem. The PEN search is not guaranteed to find the global optimum, and the authors note that network effects cannot be estimated for regular graphs under their model.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes an undirected, unweighted network and independent errors with constant variance, so its designs may not be suitable when connections are directional or have different strengths, or when outcomes remain correlated after accounting for network effects. The paper’s numerical evidence is based on a limited set of network examples, and it does not assess how sensitive the chosen blocks are to uncertainty in the observed network or to practical restrictions on treatment allocation.
future_work_stated: The authors identify generalizing the methods to large-scale networks, including networks with hundreds of thousands of nodes, as an open research problem.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs on directed or weighted networks and assess robustness when the assumed network-effect model is imperfect. It could also study allocation restrictions and randomization procedures that are practical in field experiments, and validate the predicted efficiency gains in real experiments.

summary: This paper extends a holistic testing process for cyber-physical energy systems (CPES) by proposing a practical way to incorporate design of experiments (DoE). It is intended to help researchers plan reproducible tests, from defining the test purpose and factors to selecting an experimental design and analysis approach. The proposed workflow is illustrated with a simulation of fault ride-through (FRT) behavior in a wind power plant, where screening examines control settings and system conditions that affect voltage and frequency responses. The example identifies factors that merit closer study and shows how screening can narrow the scope of a later experiment. The paper provides guidance and a worked example rather than a fully specified optimized design or a quantitative comparison of designs.
key_results: In the simulated example, increasing the additional reactive-current control gain from 0 to 2.0 had a relatively small effect on terminal voltage, while frequency deviation was clearly reduced at gain values of at least 1.0. Prioritizing reactive-axis current was favorable for the frequency response compared with prioritizing active-axis current, so the authors recommend treating the limiting strategy as a block in further analysis. Active-power recovery rates above 10 per-unit per second were considered technically infeasible, while very low rates substantially impaired frequency response. The paper reports no run-count reduction, numerical efficiency comparison, or statistical estimates such as effect sizes or uncertainty bounds.
key_equations: Not applicable
limitations_stated: The authors note that the diversity of statistics and CPES applications prevents them from providing standard application cases. For brevity, the example concentrates on the screening stage rather than demonstrating the complete experimental-design process.
limitations_unstated: The example is a single simulation case and presents screening results mainly through qualitative response plots; it does not report a treatment matrix, run count, replication plan, or inferential statistics. It also does not compare the proposed workflow with alternative designs or validate its recommendations in a real laboratory or field experiment.
future_work_stated: The authors expect to develop more guideline material for applying DoE to CPES testing. They also propose improving the guidelines with discussion of threats to internal validity and to the transferability of results.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could demonstrate a complete designed experiment with a specified treatment set, run budget, randomization or blocking plan, and reported statistical estimates. The workflow could also be tested across additional simulation models and laboratory experiments to assess whether the screening conclusions transfer to practical testing conditions.

summary: This paper develops locally optimal experimental designs for estimating the parameters of the Bradley–Terry model, which describes binary preferences between pairs of alternatives. The authors use the determinant of the information matrix as the design objective and represent comparisons with graphs. They prove that every saturated locally D-optimal design has a path as its graph, and give polynomial inequalities describing when such designs are optimal. For four alternatives, they derive optimality regions and design weights for saturated and several unsaturated designs. Their results provide a way to select a design using approximate parameter values, while leaving one class of four-alternative designs unresolved.
key_results: For any number of alternatives, every saturated locally D-optimal design is a path, and the authors give its optimality region through inequalities involving the pairwise comparison intensities. With four alternatives, there are 20 possible saturated designs: 8 have empty optimality regions, while 12 correspond to labelings of a path and have nonempty regions. Along the paper's illustrated parameter-space line, a five-point design becomes optimal at approximately 1.4, a four-point design around 2.1, and a saturated design from 2.9. In the limit along that line, the uniform design requires twice as many observations as the optimal saturated design.
key_equations:
Bradley–Terry preference probability: \[P(Y(i,j)=1)=\frac{\pi_i}{\pi_i+\pi_j}\] P is probability, Y is the binary response indicating preference for alternative i over alternative j, and π is the positive preference value of the indicated alternative.

Locally D-optimal design criterion: \[\max_{\xi}\ \det M(\xi,\beta)\] The criterion maximizes the determinant of M, the design's information matrix, over ξ, the design, at parameter vector β.

Optimality condition for a path design: \[g(i,j)=\lambda_{ij}\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\frac{1}{\lambda_{k,k+1}}\leq 1\] g is the path-design condition, λ is the information intensity for a comparison, and i, j, and k index alternatives with i less than j.
limitations_stated: The authors leave open Problem 15: proving that a four-point design with two omitted comparisons whose edges are disjoint cannot be locally D-optimal except in a saturated case. They also state that extending the approach to multiple attributes presents formidable computational challenges.
limitations_unstated: The results are local: the selected design depends on parameter values that are not known before experimentation, so the procedure relies on useful initial estimates. The broad arbitrary-alternative result covers saturated designs, while the detailed unsaturated analysis is for four alternatives; the reported numerical efficiency comparison is also limited to one parameter-space line.
future_work_stated: The authors propose using tools from real algebraic geometry to study optimality regions, particularly for fully supported designs. They discuss extending the work to models with more than one attribute and conjecture a rational-function structure for fully supported optimal-design weights as the number of alternatives increases. They also suggest investigating whether the geometry of the regions in parameter space offers further insight.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess designs when parameter estimates are uncertain, rather than treating the screening estimate as fixed. Further work could also translate the continuous design weights into practical integer run allocations and validate the recommendations in real paired-comparison experiments.

summary: The paper designs experiments for learning causal graphs while minimizing the total cost of intervening on variables. It studies nonadaptive interventions for causally sufficient systems, where the undirected components of the observed essential graph are chordal. The authors represent intervention plans as graph-separating sets, equivalently as colorings, and construct a cost-aware greedy coloring method that quantizes vertex costs. For interventions limited to at most k variables, they give a method based on a minimum vertex cover and coloring its induced graph. They prove approximation guarantees, establish that the general minimum-cost problem is NP-hard, and report that the greedy method performs close to an integer-programming optimum in their simulated comparisons.
key_results: The authors prove that minimum-cost intervention design is NP-hard, even for interval graphs with equal vertex costs. Their quantized greedy method has a cost no more than 2 plus epsilon times the optimum when the intervention count is at least the logarithm of the chromatic number plus the logarithm of the logarithm of the vertex count plus 5. For the minimum-size k-sparse problem, their algorithm has an approximation factor of 1 plus k times (maximum degree plus 1) times maximum degree divided by the vertex count; this approaches 1 when k and maximum degree are both little-o of the vertex count to the one-third power. In simulations, for graphs with 10,000 vertices, maximum degree 20, and 5 interventions, the greedy method finished in 5 seconds, compared with 128 seconds for the integer-programming solution; for a separate sparse-intervention example, cost was 0.78 with 561 interventions versus 1.0 with 510, and the reported lower bound was 506 interventions.
key_equations:
Total intervention cost: \[\operatorname{cost}(\mathcal{I})=\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}}\sum_{v\in I}w_v\] The intervention design is the collection of intervention sets, each I is one set in that collection, v is a vertex in a set, and w_v is that vertex's intervention cost.

Cost quantization: \[w'_v=\left\lfloor\frac{w_v n^3}{w_{\max}}\right\rfloor\] The quantized cost w'_v is obtained from the original vertex cost w_v, the vertex count n, and the largest remaining vertex cost w_max; the floor rounds down to an integer.

Greedy approximation guarantee and intervention-count condition: \[\operatorname{cost}(\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{greedy}})\le(2+\epsilon)\mathrm{OPT},\quad m\ge\log\chi+\log\log n+5\] The greedy design has cost at most 2 plus epsilon times the optimal cost OPT, provided the intervention count m meets the stated bound in terms of the chromatic number chi and vertex count n.

Sparse-design size guarantee: \[m_k\le\left(1+\frac{k(\Delta+1)\Delta}{n}\right)\mathrm{OPT}\] The algorithm's number of interventions m_k is bounded using the sparsity limit k, maximum graph degree Delta, vertex count n, and optimal number of interventions OPT.
limitations_stated: The authors frame the work around causally sufficient systems, nonadaptive interventions, and chordal undirected components of essential graphs. They do not explicitly identify these assumptions as limitations; for the weighted k-sparse problem, they describe a penalty-based approach for exploring the cost and size tradeoff rather than stating a comparable approximation guarantee.
limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation uses generated chordal graphs and simulated vertex costs, so it does not establish performance on real experiments or under errors in the learned essential graph and intervention costs. The methods also assume nonadaptive planning and do not evaluate practical constraints beyond a per-intervention size limit.
future_work_stated: For the weighted k-sparse problem, the authors suggest running their penalty-based algorithm with different penalty values to explore the tradeoff between cost and intervention count. They also discuss extending their approach to the weighted version of that problem.
future_work_unstated: It would be useful to evaluate the methods on real experimental systems and test their robustness to uncertain graph structure and uncertain intervention costs. Further work could incorporate practical constraints beyond intervention size and study adaptive or sequential experiment selection.

summary: The paper studies how to assign subjects in a fixed, two-group trial to estimate a treatment effect when some covariates are observed before the trial and other outcome influences are unobserved. It compares completely randomized assignment with forced group-size balance, designs that optimize observed covariate balance, and pairwise matching. The authors assess treatment-effect estimation using average error, worst-case error, and a proposed criterion based on a high percentile of error across possible unobserved influences. Their theoretical argument and simulations indicate that the best design for this upper-tail criterion should combine randomization and balance optimization rather than use either extreme. They do not provide a procedure for finding that best design and conclude that forced-balance randomization is the prudent choice until further research is done.
key_results: In the simulation with 20 subjects, 2,000 draws of unobserved effects, and a 95th-percentile error criterion, pairwise matching had lower estimated tail error than both completely randomized forced-balance assignment and perfect balance. The reported maximum errors were 0.36 for completely randomized forced-balance assignment, 1.65 for perfect balance, and 0.38 for pairwise matching; perfect balance had the lowest average error, while randomization had the lowest worst-case error. In the separate scenario with no effect from observed covariates, randomization had the lowest 95th-percentile error; when observed covariates explained more of the outcome variation, the preferred design moved closer to optimized balance. A simulation with 200 subjects showed the same qualitative pattern, although the perfect-balance allocation was approximated using a repeated greedy search rather than found exactly.
key_equations:
Additive outcome model: \[y=\beta_T w+f+z\] The outcome vector y equals the treatment effect beta_T times the allocation vector w, plus the observed-covariate contribution f and the unobserved contribution z.

Conditional mean squared error: \[\operatorname{MSE}_w=\frac{1}{n^2}(f+z)^T\Sigma_w(f+z)\] The conditional mean squared error MSE_w is calculated for sample size n, observed contribution f, unobserved contribution z, and allocation covariance matrix Sigma_w.

Upper-tail design criterion: \[\inf_{\Sigma_w\in\Omega_\Sigma}\operatorname{Quantile}_z(\operatorname{MSE}_w,q)\] The criterion minimizes, over allowed allocation covariance matrices Sigma_w in Omega_Sigma, the q percentile of the mean squared error as the unobserved contribution z varies.
limitations_stated: The authors do not give a procedure for finding the design that optimizes their upper-tail criterion. They note that such a procedure would require handling the unknown response function and estimating quantities such as the share of response variation explained by observed covariates. They also state that more work is needed on statistical power and hypothesis testing under restricted randomization.
limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence uses a narrow set of scenarios, mainly one observed covariate with a linear contribution and normally distributed unobserved effects; performance under multiple covariates, nonlinear response functions, or other residual distributions is not established. The larger trial example relies on an approximate greedy balance search, and the proposed criterion depends on features of unobserved outcomes that practitioners may not be able to estimate reliably before assigning subjects.
future_work_stated: The authors call for a procedure to find the optimal compromise design and for methods to estimate the quantities on which it depends. They also propose further work on power and hypothesis testing, and note that the analysis could be extended to the ordinary least squares regression estimator.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the proposed criterion across more realistic trial settings, including multiple observed covariates, nonlinear outcome relationships, unequal allocation constraints, and departures from the assumed residual distribution. Develop and validate a practical randomized assignment algorithm that targets the criterion, and test it in real experiments while examining how sensitive its recommendations are to estimates of unexplained outcome variation.

summary: This paper develops locally D-optimal designs for estimating binary-predictor effects in the Rasch Poisson counts model (RPCM) and the Rasch Poisson-Gamma counts model (RPGCM). These models describe count responses, with the predictors representing item features that affect item easiness. The authors derive conditions for when a design using only the basic item and items with one feature present is optimal, assigning equal weights to those settings. For both models, the key condition can be checked using pairs of predictor effects rather than combinations involving all predictors. The proposed design is optimal when the effects are sufficiently strong and negative; when effects are weaker, the optimal weights must be found numerically.
key_results: For K equal to 2, 3, and 6 predictors, the proposed design has reported efficiencies of about 84%, 59%, and 31%, respectively, at the point where all predictor effects are zero. The corresponding minimum efficiencies reported for the standard full factorial design under large negative effects are 75%, 50%, and 11%. The authors give a pairwise condition for the proposed design to be locally D-optimal in the Poisson-Gamma model, and state that the Poisson result follows as a limiting case. A sufficient condition is that each cognitive operation decreases easiness by at least a factor of 0.414; for effects outside the optimality region, designs including items with multiple features require numerical weight determination.
key_equations:
Count response model: \[Y\mid\theta,x\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu(x)),\qquad \mu(x)=\theta\exp\left(\beta_0+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\beta_k x_k\right)\] Y is the count response, theta is person ability, x is the predictor setting, mu is the response mean, beta zero is the intercept, beta k is the effect of predictor k, and K is the number of predictors.

Locally D-optimal criterion: \[\xi^*\in\arg\max_{\xi}\det M(\xi;\beta)\] xi star is a locally D-optimal design, xi is a candidate design, det is the determinant, M is the information matrix, and beta is the regression coefficient vector.

Pairwise condition for the proposed design: \[q_0(\beta)+q_j(\beta)+q_k(\beta)\leq q_{jk}(\beta),\qquad 1\leq j< k\leq K\] q zero is the inverse information weight for the basic item, q j and q k are the weights for items with only predictor j or k present, q jk is the weight for an item with both present, beta is the coefficient vector, and j and k index distinct predictors among K predictors.

Proposed design and equal weights: \[\xi_0=\{x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_K\},\qquad w_i=\frac{1}{K+1}\quad(i=0,\ldots,K)\] xi zero is the proposed design, x zero is the setting with no features, x i is the setting with only feature i present, w i is the weight assigned to setting i, and K is the number of predictors.
limitations_stated: The authors emphasize that the designs are locally optimal and depend on the regression effects. Their results do not account for interactions between predictors, and they note that the sufficient effect-size condition may be unrealistic for tests involving elementary cognitive operations. When effects are below the optimality region, weights for designs including multiple features must be determined numerically.
limitations_unstated: The paper develops theoretical results but does not report validation using a real experiment, so their performance in applied calibrations is not demonstrated here. Because the designs depend on unknown effect sizes, applying them requires effect estimates or assumptions in advance; moreover, equal approximate weights may need rounding to achieve a feasible exact run allocation.
future_work_stated: The authors identify maximin-efficient and weighted, or Bayesian, designs as future work for situations where effect sizes are uncertain. They also propose further research on optimal designs that include interactions and on the broader development of optimal designs for Poisson regression models.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare the proposed designs with other criteria and robust designs across a wider range of predictor counts and effect patterns, including practical restrictions on which feature combinations can be run. Sequential updating of the design as effect estimates improve, supported by accessible software and validation in real test-calibration or process experiments, would also address practical implementation.

summary: The paper develops post-experiment statistical tests to check whether groups created by online A/B testing have the same distribution of user profile data. It assumes categorical columns and independent users, and presents methods for testing differences across multiple columns and their interactions. The methods include distance components (DISCO), propensity-score classification, and a randomized chi-square test that repeatedly samples columns; resampling is used to adjust for multiple tests. The methods are compared in simulations and applied to an operational marketing dataset. The results show that each method can detect imbalances, with the randomized chi-square method particularly useful for finding interaction differences and identifying potentially imbalanced columns.
key_results: In a simulated real-world scenario with 800 observations in each of two groups, the reported detection powers were 0.93 for the propensity-score method, 0.91 for DISCO, and 0.87 for the randomized chi-square test. In simulations varying the data dimension from 10 to 50, DISCO and the propensity-score method generally gained power as dimension increased, while randomized chi-square was comparatively effective for many small differences and for interaction heterogeneity. For the randomized chi-square test, resampling had higher power than Holm’s procedure at all three simulated heterogeneity levels. On the operational dataset, the two groups each had 5,055 rows and 383 columns, with 2 to 50 categories per column; all three methods rejected the hypothesis that the groups had the same distribution.

limitations_stated: The authors assume categorical columns, independent rows, large group sizes, and negligible network effects. They note that randomized chi-square testing is directly applicable only to categorical data, that column flags from random sampling may not be exhaustive, and that the operational data’s encodings and collection details were unavailable to them.
limitations_unstated: The methods depend on the observed profile variables capturing the imbalances that matter; they cannot establish balance on unmeasured characteristics. The paper gives limited practical guidance for choosing the number of sampled columns and sampling rounds across different datasets, and its evaluations do not establish how the procedures perform in experiments with dependent users or changing assignment mechanisms.
future_work_stated: The authors identify testing whether experiments are correctly carried out from the beginning as a promising research area. They point to further work involving multivariate analysis, multiple testing, feature selection, observational data, and sequential analysis, and call for collaboration with data engineers to implement the methods.
future_work_unstated: Future work could assess the tests under alternative dependence structures, noncategorical models, and practical assignment constraints, including repeated users and time-varying traffic allocation. It could also provide guidance or software for selecting the sampling settings and validate the diagnostics prospectively in operational experiments.

summary: This paper develops optimal designs for estimating the parameters of a two-level linear model with main effects and no interactions. It addresses experiments in which settings are restricted to have between a minimum and a maximum number of factors at the high level. The authors use invariance under factor permutations to reduce the design problem to choosing proportions across groups of settings with the same number of high levels. When the allowed range is narrow, an optimal design uses only the two boundary groups; when the range is sufficiently wide, designs can attain the information of the unrestricted full factorial design. The paper gives theoretical conditions and example designs, but does not use experimental data.
key_results: For sufficiently wide allowed ranges, the paper shows that optimal designs can have an identity information matrix and thus match the full factorial design’s efficiency. For narrower ranges, the optimal invariant designs are concentrated on the groups at the lower and upper bounds. In the reported example with 6 factors and bounds of 2 and 4 high levels, a design with 30 runs is provided, and the corresponding optimal design has efficiency 0.9882 relative to the full factorial. The tables also show that efficiencies can be lower for more restrictive ranges; for example, the reported design with 6 factors and bounds of 0 and 1 has efficiency 0.4688.

future_work_stated: The authors propose studying the specific relationship between their designs and orthogonal arrays, and extending the results to models with interactions between rules.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to develop exact-run versions that account for practical constraints on which factor combinations can be tested, then compare their efficiency with the approximate designs. summary: The paper designs a hierarchical strategy for the generalized group testing problem (GGTP), where people have different known probabilities of infection and the objective is to minimize the expected total number of tests. The proposed hierarchical dynamic programming (HDP) method sorts people by their infection probabilities and uses backward induction to choose group sizes and later splits. It assumes error-free tests for its main design, and it also extends the calculations to tests with misclassification. Simulations, comparisons with existing procedures, and an oral human papillomavirus (HPV) screening example are used to assess the method. The authors find that the method can reduce expected testing and be much more computationally feasible than the competing approach they evaluate.
key_results: In simulations with population size 100 and average infection probability 0.01, the proposed algorithm required an average of 8.788 tests, compared with 14.923 for the method proposed by Black and colleagues; at probability 0.10, the corresponding results were 43.714 and 99.885. For population size 20 and probability 0.01, the results were 2.052 and 2.397 tests, respectively. The authors report that the proposed method took less than 1 second for a population of 100 in their stated computing environment, while the competing method could not be run for four stages at that size; its four-stage computation took 3,195 seconds for a population of 60 in one example. In the oral HPV example using 3,883 people from the 2011–2012 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, the proposed design used 1,588 tests compared with 1,894 for the competing method, a reported efficiency gain of 16%.

Expected tests for a defective-set split: \[T(n,l,x)=2-\frac{\Pi_a(1-\Pi_b)}{1-\Pi_{ab}}+\frac{1-\Pi_a}{1-\Pi_{ab}}h_a+\frac{1-\Pi_b}{1-\Pi_{ab}}h_b\] T is the expected number of tests for a split of a set known to contain at least one infected person; n is its first label, l is its size, x is the first part’s size, Π_a and Π_b are probabilities that the two parts contain no infected people, Π_ab is that probability for the entire set, and h_a and h_b are the expected further tests for the respective parts when each is known to contain an infected person.

Optimal split of a defective set: \[h(n:n+l-1)=\min_{1\le x< l}T(n,l,x)\] h is the minimum expected number of further tests for a set known to contain at least one infected person, n is its first label, l is its size, x is the size of the first part tested, and T is the expected test count for that candidate split.
limitations_stated: The method relies on ordering people by their individual infection probabilities; the authors say optimizing over all possible orderings is intractable. They also state that finding an optimal design subject to an arbitrary maximum number of stages is very difficult. For tests with misclassification, minimizing the expected number of tests alone can yield poor sensitivity, so the authors say the objective should also account for classification performance.
limitations_unstated: The simulation comparisons cover selected population sizes and prevalence settings, and the real-data illustration is limited to one oral HPV cohort, so performance in other screening settings is not established. The method also depends on supplied individual infection probabilities being accurate; errors in those inputs could lead to inefficient groupings, but their effect is not evaluated.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing an optimal hierarchical design for tests with errors that includes misclassification in the design criterion, accounting for sensitivity and specificity as well as the expected number of tests.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the design with prevalence predictions estimated from different populations and quantify how prediction errors affect test use and classification. It could also assess operational constraints, such as limits on group size, stage capacity, or geographically restricted pooling, in real screening programs.

summary: The paper develops a method for removing design points that cannot support an E-optimal design, with the aim of making large design problems solvable. It considers linear regression with uncorrelated observations, while stating its main result in a more general information-matrix setting. The method starts with a design having a nonsingular information matrix, constructs a weighted combination of its eigenvectors, and uses a deletion test to identify points that cannot be support points of any E-optimal design. summary: This paper presents automated methods for diagnosing bias and changing treatment effects in online A/B tests, particularly experiments that analyze only users who trigger the experiment. The methods are intended to help experimenters understand whether results are biased, why metrics move together, and whether treatment impact changes over time. The authors construct the methods from experiment summary statistics, historical experiment results, statistical tests, and fitted trend models. They describe checks for sample imbalance and common bias causes, a method for learning related metrics and early indicators, and detection methods for trigger-day and novelty effects. The paper reports that its diagnosis toolkit reduced investigations from weeks to within hours, and that its early-indicator method achieved 0.9 precision and 0.6 recall in its evaluation.
key_results: The authors report that about 10% of LinkedIn's triggered experiments previously suffered from bias, and that automated diagnosis reduced investigation time from weeks to within hours. In an evaluation using day-seven results from experiments that ran for at least three weeks, the early-indicator method achieved 0.9 precision and 0.6 recall. The paper's theoretical analysis shows that including unaffected users in non-triggered analysis can weaken the test signal compared with triggered analysis. The methods were illustrated and assessed using LinkedIn experiments and historical data; the paper does not report a general numerical comparison against alternative diagnostic systems.

Novelty-effect trend model: \[\Delta_t=\beta_0+\beta_1 t^{-\alpha}+\beta_2 t^{-\gamma}\] The single-day treatment impact Δ_t on day t is modeled by an intercept β₀, coefficients β₁ and β₂, and slowly and rapidly decaying terms whose rates are controlled by α and γ.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their novelty-effect detection method cannot distinguish novelty from other time-dependent trends, including day-of-week effects. The paper does not address identifying heterogeneous treatment effects.
limitations_unstated: The detection rules and examples are based largely on LinkedIn's triggered-analysis infrastructure and historical experiments, so performance and diagnosis quality may differ on platforms with different assignment, tracking, or metric systems. future_work_stated: The authors identify heterogeneous treatment-effect detection as an important area they did not address, noting the difficulty of analyzing multiple dimensions. future_work_unstated: Future work could test the diagnosis rules on independent platforms and report accuracy, false-alarm rates, and operational costs across different experiment types. summary: The paper develops nonparametric methods for estimating and testing treatment and interaction effects in factorial studies of time-to-event outcomes subject to independent right-censoring. It defines each group’s effect by comparing its survival time with an independent benchmark drawn from the average survival distribution across groups, with ties counted appropriately and follow-up truncated at a specified time. The effects are estimated using Kaplan–Meier estimates, and contrasts are tested with a statistic whose critical values are obtained by a multiplier wild bootstrap. The method allows different survival distributions and tied event times without requiring a proportional-hazards model. The authors establish large-sample validity and study finite-sample behavior through simulations and a colon cancer treatment example.
key_results: In the simulations, tests with the smallest group sizes, from 10 to 14, were liberal: one-way type I error rates were mostly 13.0% to 17.7%, while two-way rates were mainly 8.1% to 11.7%. In the shift simulations, one-way power reached 0.8 even at the smallest sample sizes and was almost 1 for shifts of at least 0.5 with moderate to larger samples; the two-way tests also gained power as sample size and shift increased. In the colon cancer example, involving 929 patients and six treatment-by-sex groups, the overall group comparison, treatment effect, and treatment-by-sex interaction each had a p-value below 0.001, while the sex main-effect test had a p-value of 0.331.

future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess how sensitive estimated effects and conclusions are to the choice of truncation time, and provide practical guidance for choosing it before data collection.
