summary: The paper develops a method for optimizing Bayesian experimental designs to maximize expected information gain about hidden parameters. The method applies randomized multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) to construct unbiased estimates of the design gradient, which is difficult to estimate because it contains nested expectations. It uses antithetic corrections across increasing inner sample sizes and draws levels randomly, allowing the gradient estimate to have finite expected squared size and finite expected computational cost under stated assumptions. The authors combine this estimator with stochastic gradient optimization and test it on a simple example and a pharmacokinetic (PK) design problem. The simple example shows that fixed-size inner Monte Carlo estimates can lead optimization away from the true optimum, while the proposed method reaches it; in the PK example, it produces a different sampling-time allocation and a slightly higher estimated information gain than the standard Monte Carlo comparison.
key_results: In the simple test case, the estimated decay rates for the squared MLMC corrections were 1.64 and 1.63 at the tested design points, and the randomized estimator used an expected 2.21 inner samples per gradient sample. With the same computational-cost comparison, fixed inner sample sizes from 1 to 64 either moved toward the wrong design or leveled off away from the optimum, whereas the proposed method continued to converge; the reported mean squared error decayed approximately as iteration count to the power of minus 1.12. In the PK problem, the proposed method used an expected 1.34 inner samples and yielded three clusters containing 3, 6, and 6 sampling times, compared with 3, 5, and 7 for standard Monte Carlo. Across 10 runs, the estimated information gain was 4.544 for the proposed method and 4.535 for standard Monte Carlo, versus 3.774 for the initial design.

Expected information gain: \[U(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta,\varepsilon}[\log\rho(f_{\xi}(\theta,\varepsilon)\mid\theta,\xi)]-\mathbb{E}_{\theta,\varepsilon}[\log\mathbb{E}_{\theta'}\rho(f_{\xi}(\theta,\varepsilon)\mid\theta',\xi)]\] U is expected information gain, ξ is the design, θ is the hidden parameter vector, ε is the noise, θ′ is an independent copy of θ, ρ is the likelihood, and each E denotes expectation over the variables shown beneath it.

Antithetic level correction: \[M_{\ell}=M_{0}2^{\ell},\qquad\Delta\psi_{\xi,\ell}=\psi_{\xi,M_{\ell}}-\frac{\psi_{\xi,M_{\ell-1}}^{(a)}+\psi_{\xi,M_{\ell-1}}^{(b)}}{2}\] Mℓ is the inner sample size at level ℓ, M0 is its initial size, Δψξ,ℓ is the correction for design ξ, ψ denotes a gradient estimate, and a and b denote estimates computed from the two disjoint halves of the larger sample.
limitations_stated: In the PK example, the observed correction decay rate at the initial iteration was at most 1, so the theoretical result did not establish a level-weight choice with both finite expected cost and finite expected squared estimator size for that case. limitations_unstated: The method relies on a differentiable design objective, explicitly computable likelihoods, and the moment and bounded-gradient conditions used in its theory; performance is not established for problems that fail these assumptions. summary: The paper develops the cumulative Aalen survival analysis-of-variance approach, called CASANOVA, for comparing groups in factorial studies with possibly right-censored survival times. It tests hypotheses about cumulative hazards, including main effects and interactions, without requiring proportional hazards. The method forms weighted Nelson–Aalen-type integrals and combines weights to address both proportional and crossing hazard patterns. A studentized permutation procedure is used to obtain critical values, with theoretical results establishing its asymptotic validity. Simulations and a lung cancer data analysis show that the combined permutation test can control false positive rates and detect different hazard patterns without selecting just one weight in advance.
key_results: In the simulations, each setting used 5,000 runs and 1,999 permutation iterations, with a nominal false positive rate of 5 percent. For the two-by-three factorial layout, only 4 of 72 permutation-test scenarios fell outside the reported 95 percent interval of 4.4 to 5.6 percent; asymptotic tests were often conservative, with rates around 3 percent for main effects and 2 percent for interactions. In the additional one-way simulations, asymptotic false positive rates reached 25.9 percent, while permutation rates were generally close to the target. In the lung cancer analysis, the permutation combined test gave a treatment p-value of 1.0 percent, compared with 2.8 percent for the log-rank test and 79.1 percent for the crossing-weight test; the reported interaction p-value was 75.0 percent.
key_equations:
Null hypothesis for cumulative hazards: \[H A = 0\] Here, H is the contrast matrix, A is the vector of group-specific cumulative hazard functions, and 0 is the zero vector.

Combined Wald-type statistic: \[S = (T Z)^\top (T \Sigma T)^{+} T Z\] Here, S is the joint Wald-type statistic, T is the projection matrix for the tested contrast, Z is the vector of weighted Nelson–Aalen-type integrals, Sigma is their estimated covariance matrix, superscript T denotes transpose, and plus denotes the Moore–Penrose inverse.
limitations_stated: The authors state that it is unclear whether the permutation method remains valid with more complex filtering mechanisms, such as truncation or certain interval-censoring settings. They also report that implementation in the GFDsurv software package was still in progress.
limitations_unstated: The simulations cover selected distributions, censoring patterns, sample sizes, and weight choices, so they do not establish performance across the full range of factorial survival studies. The method tests cumulative-hazard contrasts, but the paper does not provide a general procedure for translating a rejection into an estimated, practically interpretable treatment effect.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to more complex filtering mechanisms, while noting that multiplier resampling would be their first choice for approximating critical values beyond ordinary right-censoring. They also state that they are working on implementing the combination test in GFDsurv and on encouraging medical and epidemiological applications.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method with additional factorial structures, censoring mechanisms, and weight combinations, and provide guidance for choosing contrasts and planning sample sizes. Testing the procedure prospectively in real factorial clinical studies would also help assess its practical performance.

summary: The paper develops a sequential method for thinning a stream of candidate experimental conditions when only a fixed proportion can be retained. It targets an optimal bounded design measure for parameter estimation, maximizing a concave function of the information matrix, including determinant-based D-optimality. At each step, the method scores a candidate by the directional derivative of the objective and compares that score with a quantile threshold that is updated recursively. The method tracks the information matrix and a small number of scalar quantities rather than storing the full sequence. Under stated regularity conditions, the authors prove convergence to the optimal information matrix and illustrate the method with simulated design problems.
key_results: Theorem 3.1 proves that the information matrix produced by the method converges almost surely to the optimal bounded-design information matrix when the candidate sequence is independent and identically distributed and a fixed positive proportion is selected. In a quadratic-regression example with 100,000 candidates, the method selected 50,000 or 10,000 points and its objective values approached the reported optima. For a fixed target of 100 points from 100,000 candidates in a three-dimensional regression example, adapting the selection proportion avoided the drop in objective value caused by late forced selections. In simulations with dimension 25, 10,000 candidates, and 100 repetitions, the proposed method achieved higher reported D-efficiency than IBOSS, though the authors note that it was substantially slower when it used many repeated passes over the data.
key_equations:
Optimal bounded design: \[\xi_\alpha^*=\arg\max_{\xi\in\mathcal P(X),\,\xi\le\mu/\alpha}\Phi\bigl(M(\xi)\bigr)\] The optimal design measure xi at selection proportion alpha maximizes objective Phi of information matrix M, among probability measures on candidate space X bounded above by candidate distribution mu divided by alpha.

Directional-derivative score: \[Z_k(x)=\operatorname{trace}\{\nabla\Phi(M_{n_k})[M(x)-M_{n_k}]\}\] The score Z for candidate x at iteration k is the trace of the gradient of objective Phi at current information matrix M, multiplied by the difference between candidate information M of x and current information M.

Recursive quantile update: \[\widehat C_{k+1}=\widehat C_k+\frac{\beta_k}{(k+1)^q}\bigl(\mathbf 1\{Z_k(X_{k+1})\ge\widehat C_k\}-\alpha\bigr)\] The estimated threshold C at iteration k plus one equals its current estimate plus step size beta divided by iteration k plus one to exponent q, multiplied by the indicator that the next candidate's score Z meets the current threshold, minus target selection proportion alpha.

Information-matrix update when selected: \[M_{n_{k+1}}=M_{n_k}+\frac{1}{n_k+1}\bigl(M(X_{k+1})-M_{n_k}\bigr)\] When candidate X at iteration k plus one is selected, the updated information matrix M is the previous matrix M plus the candidate information M of that point minus the previous matrix, divided by the new selected count n.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the initialization and tuning parameters have not been optimized. Their convergence theorem relies on assumptions that can fail for discrete components or score distributions with atoms, and fixed-size selection does not have a general performance guarantee as the candidate sequence grows. They also limit the main analysis to models whose information matrix does not depend on unknown parameters and do not address robustness to model misspecification.
limitations_unstated: The guarantees rely on an independent and identically distributed candidate stream and regularity conditions on the score distribution, which may be difficult to verify in production experiments. The non-independent examples use buffer scrambling, but the paper does not establish convergence for that preprocessing, and the simulations cover a limited set of models rather than real experimental streams. The stated storage efficiency also does not remove the computational burden of repeatedly evaluating candidate information and objective gradients, especially for large parameter dimensions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying better initialization and tuning, extending the method to online parameter estimation in nonlinear models, and developing adaptive treatment-allocation procedures. They also identify model-robust design as an open topic and say further work is needed to understand the observed convergence rate.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be testing the method on real industrial streams with practical constraints such as eligibility rules, costs, and limits on randomization, while measuring prediction and estimation performance as well as design efficiency. Further work could also provide maintained software and investigate controlled use with dependent or drifting streams, including criteria beyond the concave information objectives analyzed here.

summary: The paper presents a Bayesian experimental design method for stochastic models whose likelihoods cannot be evaluated, with the aim of choosing experiments that provide information about unknown parameters. It targets the expected information gain measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) between prior and posterior distributions. The authors derive a lower bound for this objective using entropies of simulated outputs, then refine it by partitioning the parameter prior according to clusters of output samples. They estimate the required entropies from simulations using a nearest-neighbor estimator, so likelihood evaluation is not required. In examples, the method selected useful designs for both strongly non-Gaussian and approximately Gaussian posteriors, and improved parameter estimates over a posterior-precision comparison in one example.
key_results: In the mathematical example, the lower-bound design with partition closely matched the expected KLD design and selected d = 5, whereas the posterior-precision method selected d = 100. For the Ricker model, the lower-bound method selected statistics 1 and 2, while the posterior-precision method selected statistics 2 and 3; across 1,000 simulated trials, the reported MSEs for log r were 0.01 versus 0.02, for phi were 0.0046 versus 0.0073, and for sigma were 0.080 versus 0.079, respectively. For the Aphid model, the methods selected similar sampling times: for four observations, the lower-bound design was (13.8, 19.1, 24.5, 30.6), compared with (15.8, 20.4, 25.2, 30.5) for posterior precision. The examples used 3 × 10^4 model simulations for lower-bound utility estimation; the paper does not report quantitative runtime or efficiency comparisons.
key_equations:
Expected information gain: \[U(d)=H[p(y|d)]-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[H(p(y|\theta,d))]\] U is expected information gain for design d, H is entropy, y is the output, theta is the unknown parameter, p denotes a probability distribution, and E denotes expectation over the parameter.

Paired-output entropy bound: \[\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[H(p(y|\theta,d))]\leq H(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[p(z|\theta,d)])-\frac{m}{2}\log 2\] Theta is the parameter, y is an output, d is the design, z is the difference of two independent outputs conditional on theta, p denotes a probability distribution, H is entropy, E is expectation, and m is the dimension of y.

Partitioned lower-bound criterion: \[U_L(d)=H(p(y|d))+\frac{m}{2}\log 2-\sum_{l=1}^{L}w_l H(\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim f_l}[p(z|\theta,d)])\] U_L is the partitioned lower-bound utility for design d; y is output, z is a paired-output difference, m is output dimension, L is the number of groups, w_l is the weight of group l, f_l is the parameter distribution within that group, theta is the parameter, p denotes a probability distribution, H is entropy, and E is expectation.

Prior partition into a mixture: \[p(\theta|d)=\sum_{l=1}^{L}w_l f_l(\theta)\] The prior distribution p of parameter theta at design d is represented as a mixture of L groups, where w_l is the weight and f_l is the parameter distribution for group l.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the lower-bound method may not select the same design as the exact KLD criterion in some circumstances. They also note that their comparisons were limited to the posterior-precision method and that the theoretical choice of partition strategy and number of partitions remains unresolved.
limitations_unstated: The method depends on simulated outputs being available and on choices such as the number of partitions and minimum cluster size; the paper does not establish how sensitive results are to those choices across problems. The examples use particular models and simulation settings, and do not establish the computational cost or design quality for high-dimensional outputs or a broad range of practical experiment constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose comparing the method with other likelihood-free design approaches in terms of effectiveness and efficiency. They also plan to study when the lower-bound approximation is suitable and to develop a theoretically justified partition strategy, including the choice of the number of partitions.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess robustness to model misspecification and to practical constraints such as limited sampling times, costs, or restricted randomization. Sequential design and validation on real experiments would also show whether the simulation-based gains carry over to ongoing quality-engineering studies.

summary: The paper presents Bayesian analysis and decision methods for controlled randomized experiments that compare business variants, especially website offers. It covers one-option conversions, multiple mutually exclusive options, and cases where only overall conversions and revenue are recorded. For each case, the authors specify probability models, update them with observed experiment data, and use posterior samples to estimate which variant is best, expected uplift, and expected loss. In three business examples, the analyses supported changing a product-page discount and adopting a progressive discount for an advertising landing page. The authors report that the aggregated-data analysis reached a similar decision, though it was more uncertain for gain per visitor.
key_results: In the one-product discount experiment, which ran for 53 days, the 40% discount had a 58% probability of being best, a mean improvement of 12% over the 20% baseline, and an expected loss of 1%; the company adopted it. The results matched Google Optimize's results up to insignificant rounding differences. In the multi-product experiment, which ran for 58 days with 8,067 and 8,082 visitors in the two variants, the progressive discount had an 89% probability of being best for gain per visitor, a mean improvement of 53%, and an expected loss of 2%; it was adopted. With aggregated data from that experiment, the progressive option had an 86% probability of being best for gain, a mean improvement of 62%, and an expected loss of 3%; the paper reports greater uncertainty in gain than with the multi-option model.

limitations_unstated: The conclusions depend on the assumed conversion distributions, chosen prior parameters, and the exponential model for individual revenue; departures from these assumptions could change the posterior decision metrics. summary: The paper proposes a Bayesian optimization method for expensive experimental design when experts have knowledge about where the global optimum is likely to lie. It represents that knowledge as a probability distribution over the optimum and combines it with the optimum-location distribution inferred from a Gaussian process model. The method samples possible optima from this combined distribution and evaluates a selected point, repeating the process as observations accumulate. The authors study synthetic optimization problems, classifier hyperparameter tuning, and a laboratory experiment producing short polymer fibers. Their reported results show faster or better optimization than several comparison methods when the prior is useful, while noting that a substantially misleading prior can be harmful.
key_results: For the two-dimensional synthetic problem, experiments began with 3 Latin hypercube observations and were repeated 20 times; posterior sampling generally achieved lower simple regret than standard Thompson sampling and other baselines over 30 evaluations. The authors tested 100, 200, and 500 sampled candidate optima and found little sensitivity to the number, recommending 100 times the input dimension for reliable estimation. On a six-dimensional Hartmann function, results over 50 evaluations favored posterior sampling over Thompson sampling, expected improvement, and prior-based random search. In classifier tuning, each run used 30 iterations and average F-measure from 10-fold cross-validation; posterior sampling performed best in the reported radial-basis-function support vector machine experiments, while comparisons were more mixed for other classifier and dataset combinations. The polymer experiment had 162 discrete combinations and 5 runs with different sets of 3 initial samples; the authors report that using the expert prior helped the method reach higher maximum fiber-quality values during the experiment, but give no exact numerical effect size in the text.

Sampled-function maximizer: \[x_i^*=\arg\max_{x\in X} f_i(x)\] Here x_i* is the maximizer of sampled function f_i, x is an input point, and X is the search space.
limitations_stated: The authors state that choosing a suitable expert prior is nontrivial. They also note that a grossly misleading prior can make the method vulnerable and can require more iterations for convergence.
limitations_unstated: The method’s practical benefit depends on obtaining and encoding a useful prior, but the paper does not provide a systematic procedure for eliciting or calibrating one. future_work_stated: The authors propose developing methods to detect a misleading prior quickly. They also hope the work will inform further use of perceived expert knowledge in experimental design and Bayesian optimization.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test prior-elicitation and prior-calibration procedures with multiple experts, including ways to combine conflicting knowledge and quantify uncertainty in the prior. summary: The paper proposes MINEBED, a method for Bayesian experimental design when a model can generate data by simulation but has an intractable likelihood. Its objective is to choose designs that maximize the expected information the data provide about the model parameters. A neural network learns a lower bound on mutual information, and the method jointly trains that network and optimizes the design using gradients when the simulator provides design derivatives; Bayesian optimization is used when it does not. The trained network also provides an approximation to the posterior distribution, so a separate inference step is not required. Simulation studies show useful designs and posterior estimates, including a linear-model example with 100 design dimensions.
key_results: For the noisy linear model, the reported mutual-information lower bounds were about 2.5 for one measurement and 4.5 for 10 measurements; the 100-dimensional example reached a reference mutual-information value of 5.78. For that 100-dimensional example, the reference values for boundary-only, boundary-and-zero, and equally spaced designs were 4.61, 4.83, and 4.91, respectively; random designs averaged 4.92 across 100 repeats, with a standard deviation of 0.08. In the 10-measurement linear example, posterior estimates were 1.441 plus or minus 0.826 for the offset and 4.949 plus or minus 0.108 for the slope. In the pharmacokinetic example, one measurement identified the absorption-rate-to-volume ratio more effectively than all parameters, while 10 measurements gave narrower and more accurate posterior distributions for all parameters. In the oscillatory toy-model comparison, MINEBED selected a measurement time of 2.19, compared with 1.66 for the covariance-based Bayesian optimality criterion; the authors report that MINEBED reached its optimum in significantly less time in that comparison.

limitations_stated: The gradient-based method requires the Jacobian of the sampling path, or its product with the neural-network gradient, to be computable; this is not guaranteed for every implicit model. They also report that the lower-bound bias is larger in higher dimensions, although it remained reasonably small in their examples.
limitations_unstated: The experiments are simulation studies on a small set of illustrative models, so performance in real experiments and under model misspecification is not established. Training can involve many simulation samples and epochs, and the approach depends on neural-network architecture and optimization choices; the paper does not give a general run-time or resource comparison across models.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying sequential experimental design, where the posterior is updated after each real experiment. They also suggest extending the method to design for model discrimination and for prediction of future observations.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test sensitivity to incorrect priors, simulator mismatch, and measurement noise, and validate the designs in real experiments rather than simulations alone. summary: The paper designs a sequential test for comparing treatments when one system receives a sequence of actions and earlier actions can affect later outcomes. It uses a Markov decision process and reinforcement learning to represent those carryover effects, and defines the long-term treatment contrast as the difference in discounted value averaged over initial states. The method estimates value functions using temporal-difference equations with basis-function approximation, then updates the estimate and test as new observations arrive. A bootstrap procedure sets interim rejection boundaries while controlling the overall false-positive rate. The authors report that their procedure detects delayed treatment effects missed by standard tests, and apply it to a ride-sharing dispatch experiment.
key_results: In a simulated delayed-effect example with 500 observations, the reported power was 0.73 for the proposed test, compared with 0.04 for a two-sample t-test and 0.06 for a double machine learning test; in a no-carryover example, the proposed test and the two-sample t-test had powers of 0.98 and 0.76, respectively. summary: This paper studies fully parallel, one-shot hyperparameter search, where a fixed set of points is used to find a low value of an objective function. It compares space-filling methods with random search and proposes reshaping the search distribution as an additional way to improve optimization. When the distribution of the optimum is known, its recentring method concentrates points toward the center, with the amount of concentration depending on the budget and dimension. When the optimum’s distribution is unknown, the paper proposes Cauchy-based sampling to search farther from the center or nearer to the boundaries. key_results: The theoretical analysis finds that Latin hypercube sampling and jittered sampling have the same stochastic-dispersion rate as random sampling, up to a constant factor, including after projection onto a subset of variables. For a known optimum distribution, recentring—especially the proposed budget- and dimension-based setting—was frequently among the best methods across the tested dimensions and budgets; Cauchy sampling did not help much in that known-distribution setting. In the real-world benchmark tests, which used 7400 repetitions and included dimensions from 10 to 120 and budgets from 25 to 12800, Cauchy variants and boundary-rescaled designs often performed well. Cauchy counterparts also achieved better loss values than their Gaussian counterparts on the Attend, Infer, Repeat task, with the paper reporting a p-value of 0.05 for that comparison; the combined Cauchy and recentring method performed best in the progressive generative adversarial network test.

summary: The paper presents adaptive kernelized maximum-minimum distance (AKM2D), a sequential sampling method for point-based inspection when measuring every location is too costly or time-consuming. It targets accurate, pixel-level quantification of sparse, clustered anomalies while also estimating a smooth background. The method combines initial space-filling measurements with later selections that balance searching unsampled areas and taking measurements near suspected anomalies. After each measurement, robust kernel regression updates the background estimate and sparse kernel regression updates the anomaly estimate. Simulations and a guided-wave inspection of a composite laminate show that the method can quantify anomalies using substantially fewer measurements than the tested alternatives.
key_results: In simulations with 250 measurements, AKM2D achieved recall of 0.78 and an F-measure of 0.72; the best comparison results were 0.27 and 0.39, respectively. With 400 measurements, its recall was 0.88 and its F-measure was 0.80, compared with best comparison results of 0.65 for both measures. In the composite-laminate case study, 300 measurements, or 1.1% of complete sensing, gave an F-measure of 0.8, while the other methods reached at most 0.5; the authors also report that 200 measurements, or 0.7% of complete sensing, reduced inspection time from 4 hours to 2 minutes. In the simulation timing comparison, AKM2D took 0.0046 seconds per sampled point, compared with 0.0025 seconds for grid sampling and 0.473 seconds for the variance-based method.

limitations_stated: The authors assume that the background and anomalies remain static, that anomalies are sparse and clustered, and that the background is smooth for the estimation procedure. They note that the grid-based optimization is practical only when the sampling-space dimension is not too large, and propose more efficient optimization for higher-dimensional settings.

future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to batch sampling, so multiple locations can be selected together. They also propose extending it to higher-dimensional spaces using optimization methods more efficient than grid search.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test robustness to changing backgrounds, correlated or non-normal measurement noise, and anomalies that are not clustered or have different shapes and intensities. summary: The paper extends Bayesian design of experiments to cases where the model used to evaluate the design differs from the model assumed for analyzing the eventual data. The authors derive an asymptotic approximation to this external expected loss and explain how different loss functions balance estimation precision and point-estimation accuracy. Examples show that designs based on the alternative model can encourage replication or spread settings across the design region, depending on the problem and criterion.
key_results: In a 16-run linear regression example with 10 fitted parameters, the design optimized for external self-information loss achieved 85% efficiency under that criterion, while the ordinary D-optimal design achieved 7%; for squared error, the corresponding efficiencies were 84% and 10%. For the 20-run Michaelis-Menten example, the external squared-error design had 100% efficiency under its own criterion and 79.7% under internal squared error; the external trace-variance design had 99.9% efficiency under internal squared error. summary: This paper develops optimal approximate designs for a linear model with treatment effects and covariate effects, where response variances may differ by treatment. The objective is to estimate specified treatment contrasts together with selected linear functions of the covariate effects. The authors show that an optimal design can be found among product designs, which combine a treatment allocation with a covariate allocation, and derive results for Kiefer’s eigenvalue-based criteria, including average-variance optimality (A-optimality) and minimum-eigenvalue optimality (E-optimality). They also give linear constraints that characterize other optimal designs and use linear programming to find designs with fewer supported treatment-covariate combinations. Examples show that these sparse designs can be easier to convert into exact trial plans while retaining high efficiency.
key_results: The theory establishes that for any eigenvalue-based information criterion considered, an optimal product design exists; the treatment and covariate allocations can be optimized in separate marginal problems. In Example 1, the product design has 24 support points, while a linear-programming design has 10; for 48 trials, their rounded efficiencies are 0.9641 and 0.9991, respectively. The sparse design can be rounded for trial counts from 10 through 23, whereas the stated rounding procedure cannot be applied to the product design for counts of 23 or fewer. In Example 2, the E-optimal design has 28 support points compared with 45 for the product design, and the rounded design for 40 trials has efficiency 0.8493.

limitations_stated: The authors note that product designs can have large supports, making them difficult to round into exact designs when the number of trials is small. They also report that rounding a sparse non-product design is not always more efficient than rounding the product design.

summary: The paper studies a sequential adaptive design procedure for parameter estimation in generalized linear models (GLMs) with a univariate response from a one-parameter exponential family. At each stage, the procedure estimates the unknown parameter from the observations collected so far and selects the next experimental setting using the Wynn rule for D-optimal design. The authors establish its asymptotic properties under compactness, continuity, and other stated regularity conditions. They show that the adaptive maximum likelihood (ML) estimates converge almost surely to the true parameter and that the designs become locally D-optimal there. When the true parameter is in the interior of its parameter space and additional smoothness conditions hold, the estimates are also asymptotically normal.
key_results: The paper proves strong consistency of the adaptive ML estimates under its stated assumptions, without requiring that the estimates used to choose settings at each stage are themselves ML estimates. If those estimates converge to the true parameter, the information matrices of the generated designs converge to those of a locally D-optimal design. Each design in the sequence is an exact design of size n at stage n. Under the additional conditions in the asymptotic normality theorem, the scaled ML estimates have a limiting normal distribution, with covariance given by the inverse information matrix of the locally D-optimal design; the paper reports theoretical results, not numerical performance comparisons.

summary: The paper presents a staged method for comparing a new recommendation system with the current system in a randomized treatment-control experiment. Its objective is to determine whether revenue per visit (RPV), calculated from conversion rate and average order value (AOV), has changed, while potentially reducing the sample size needed. The method first uses Lachenbruch’s two-part test to assess differences in purchase incidence and order values, then uses a parametric test on newly collected data if the first test leaves the revenue effect indeterminate. The parametric options use a two-stage model in which visits can result in no purchase or in a purchase whose value follows a log-normal distribution. The authors report that the approach can use smaller samples on average, avoids subjective outlier removal, and provides a confidence interval for revenue per visit, but do not give numerical comparative sample-size results.
key_results: The paper reports that Lachenbruch’s combined test rejects equality of the treatment and control distributions when its statistic exceeds 9.633, using a 95% confidence threshold. They state that their method needs a smaller sample on average than other methods and does not require subjective outlier removal, but provide no numerical sample-size comparison or quantified treatment-effect result. summary: The paper develops a framework for choosing space-filling designs for computer experiments and for estimating integrals of an unknown function. It considers a function modeled as a constant mean plus a Gaussian random field with a specified covariance kernel, and connects Bayesian quadrature to estimation of the mean by a best linear unbiased estimator. The design is constructed by minimizing a kernel-based discrepancy from a target measure, often the uniform distribution, and the paper shows how sequential kernel herding can select points one at a time. Its numerical example in a two-dimensional square shows that the resulting designs can improve covering and packing measures relative to the first points of a Sobol sequence. The paper also explains that discrepancy improvement is not always equivalent to better geometric coverage, so kernel choice and evaluation of the actual design remain important.
key_results: In the example on the unit square with 100 points, sequential kernel herding achieved a covering radius of about 0.0925 and a packing radius of about 0.0262, compared with about 0.1377 and 0.0204 for the first 100 Sobol points. Local maximization of the Bayesian quadrature criterion, initialized from the herding design, improved these measures to about 0.0869 and 0.0364; direct minimization of empirical-measure discrepancy gave about 0.0955 and 0.0359. The authors also give convergence results for the conditional-gradient construction: a prescribed step size gives an energy-error bound of order log n divided by n, while an energy-minimizing step size gives a bound of order 1 divided by n; stronger rates are shown under additional conditions. In a ten-dimensional illustration, covering-radius evaluation is approximate, based on a finite test set.
key_equations:
Assumed location model: \[f(x)=β_0+Z_x\] The unknown function f at point x equals the constant mean β₀ plus the zero-mean Gaussian random-field component Zₓ.

Bayesian quadrature design criterion: \[s_n^2=\min_{w^T\mathbf{1}=1}E_K\left(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\delta_{x_i}-\mu\right)\] The posterior variance factor sₙ² equals the minimum kernel energy of the difference between the weighted design measure and target measure μ, over weights w that sum to one; E_K is kernel energy, δₓᵢ is a point mass, and the design has n points xᵢ.

Reduced kernel: \[K_\mu(x,x')=K(x,x')-P_\mu(x)-P_\mu(x')+E_K(\mu)\] The reduced kernel Kμ is formed from kernel K by subtracting the potential Pμ at each argument and adding the kernel energy E_K of the target measure μ.

Sequential kernel-herding update: \[x_{n+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^{(n)}K(x,x_i)-P_\mu(x)\right],\quad \xi^{(n+1)}=(1-\alpha_n)\xi^{(n)}+\alpha_n\delta_{x_{n+1}}\] At step n, the next point xₙ₊₁ minimizes the current weighted potential minus the target potential over region X, and the current measure ξ⁽ⁿ⁾ is updated toward that point mass using step size αₙ.
limitations_stated: The authors do not aim to tune the kernel to prior knowledge of the response or estimate kernel parameters; they note that correlation lengths can be difficult to choose in advance. limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison of geometric design quality centers on a two-dimensional example and a Sobol-sequence baseline, so it does not establish performance across varied domains, kernels, constraints, or competing design methods. future_work_stated: The authors specifically say that selecting the approximate-design parameters to obtain good space-filling properties for a prescribed number of runs remains difficult and requires further investigation. They also present extensions for simultaneous estimation of several integrals and for Bayesian c-optimal design, but do not identify these as proposed future work.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the methods on real computer experiments and compare them with a broader range of space-filling designs under practical constraints such as forbidden regions, factor bounds, and nonuniform target measures. Evolutionary optimization performs better when traffic is limited and when variables interact, while Taguchi can approach its performance given sufficient traffic when effects are independent.

In the independent [3,3,3,3] setting, Taguchi used 9 runs; evolution performed better at low traffic, and the methods performed similarly after about 500,000 visits. For a setting with 15,552 possible combinations, the Taguchi array used 36 runs, and Taguchi was comparable to evolution only at traffic greater than 5,000,000. With interacting variables, evolution found better candidates at all tested traffic levels, while Taguchi’s predicted candidate was similar to its best tested candidate.

limitations_unstated: The comparison is based on simulated evaluators rather than real website experiments, and the nonlinear evaluator includes pairwise interactions rather than testing a broader range of possible response structures. future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the methods on live website experiments and on response models with higher-order interactions, changing traffic patterns, and practical implementation constraints. summary: This paper develops methods to find heterogeneous treatment effects in online controlled experiments, where treatment effects may differ across user groups or user characteristics. The methods use transformed outcomes to represent individual treatment effects and then apply either the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure or the knockoff method to control false discoveries. The Benjamini–Hochberg version is intended to find subgroups whose effects differ from the overall average, while the knockoff version can identify characteristics associated with effect heterogeneity. The authors evaluate the methods with simulations and two real experiments, and report that they control false discoveries in the tested settings while retaining useful detection power. They also describe a toolkit deployed at Snap and discuss limitations involving model assumptions and scalability.
key_results: In simulations averaged over 100 replicates, the naive approach did not control the false discovery rate, while the Bonferroni method had substantially lower power than the proposed methods. For orthogonal designs, the Benjamini–Hochberg and knockoff methods had similar power; for non-Gaussian outcomes, both controlled the false discovery rate empirically and reached power of 1 when effects were large enough. For non-orthogonal designs, the Benjamini–Hochberg method exceeded its target false discovery rate at relatively small signal sizes, whereas knockoffs maintained a very small false discovery rate. In two real experiments, the methods selected nearly the same subgroups in one case; in the other, Benjamini–Hochberg selected one subgroup and knockoffs selected none. The toolkit completed analyses within one hour on datasets with 24 million observations and 20 predictors, and with 7 million observations and 80 predictors, on the reported laptop.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the knockoff method's theoretical guarantees rely on a linear model with Gaussian errors, and that linearity may be inappropriate when treatment effects relate nonlinearly to user characteristics. They also identify scalability as an unresolved limitation: their attempt to analyze multiple experiments together using a transformed design matrix increased computational complexity.
limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation covers only two real experiments, so the reported operational evidence does not establish performance across a wide range of products, outcome types, or experimental allocation schemes. The subgroup approach tests groups against an estimated overall average, but the authors treat that estimated average as fixed; uncertainty in that reference could affect the resulting tests. future_work_stated: The authors identify model-free knockoffs as a possible route to extending the method beyond linear models. They also propose further research on scalability, especially methods that make it feasible to analyze many experiments without running detection separately for each one.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate calibration and detection performance prospectively across more experiments, including settings with unequal treatment allocation and strongly dependent user characteristics. summary: The paper extends Bayesian optimal design for experiments that distinguish competing models of human behavior in strategic interactions. The method combines an adaptive Gaussian-process search over design parameters with sampling of model parameters to generate representative datasets rather than enumerating every possible dataset. They find the algorithm is much faster than exhaustive computation, and the experiments favor reinforcement learning as the best explanation of participant behavior among the models tested.
key_results: The computation to find the design was reduced from about 72 hours on a supercomputing cluster to about an hour on a standard laptop. The procedure sampled 10,000 datasets per search, and the authors report that about 1,000 were sufficient to identify the optimal design; the predicted optimum was a maximum payout near 2 and a state probability of 0.5. In simulations over 200 runs, the adaptive search had lower regret than random and grid search; its regret was significantly lower than random search from iteration 30, with p < 10^-10. In the real experiment, 79 participants contributed data across five designs, and one 10-player dataset per design was enough for the authors to distinguish model fit; after adding reinforcement learning, it fit better than the other three models in all five designs. future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring informative priors for complex, high-dimensional searches and building an automated online platform that assigns experimental parameters, runs experiments, updates model predictions, and evaluates model differences. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method prospectively in additional games and applied settings, testing whether its predicted information advantage holds with larger and more diverse participant samples. summary: The paper develops an improved method for estimating the sampling variance of factorial effects in full factorial experiments with binary outcomes. It uses the potential outcomes framework and considers completely randomized assignment to all combinations of two-level treatment factors. The construction derives a sharp lower bound on the variance of individual effects from the average effect, then uses that bound to reduce the classic Neymanian variance estimate. The adjustment is nonnegative, so the improved estimate is no larger than the classic estimate for any observed data set. The paper establishes the result theoretically and illustrates it with examples rather than empirical data.
key_results: The paper proves that the sharp lower bound on the variance of individual effects is the number of units divided by one less than the number of units, multiplied by the maximum of zero and a term based on the absolute average effect and its square. The classic estimator’s expected overestimation is the variance of individual effects divided by the number of units; the improved estimator subtracts an estimate of the sharp lower bound’s contribution. In a balanced three-factor example with 40 units, the paper gives two cases where the bound equals the true variance, with reported values of 0.016 and 0.0058. The comparison is theoretical: the paper does not report empirical performance or prediction results.
key_equations:
Sharp lower bound: \[S^2(\bar{\tau}_l) \geq \frac{N}{N-1}\max\left\{2^{-(K-1)}|\bar{\tau}_l|-\bar{\tau}_l^2,0\right\}\] Here N is the number of units, K is the number of factors, l indexes the factorial effect, S²(τ̄_l) is the variance of individual effects, and τ̄_l is the population average effect; the inequality, maximum, and absolute value have their usual meanings.

limitations_stated: The method is developed for binary outcomes. The authors state that extending the result to general outcomes is nontrivial and identify this as an open direction.
limitations_unstated: The method assumes completely randomized assignment, with at least two units in each treatment combination, and the number of combinations grows quickly as factors are added, which may make the full factorial design impractical. The paper guarantees a bias correction but does not establish that the resulting estimated variance is always nonnegative, or validate its performance in real experiments.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to general outcomes, including continuous and time-to-event outcomes. They also suggest studying partial identification for more complex experimental designs, such as Latin square and split-plot designs.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess the method under practical constraints such as limited runs, restricted randomization, or fractional factorial designs. Simulation and real-experiment studies could also examine uncertainty calibration and ways to handle any negative variance estimates produced by the correction.

summary: The paper proposes a sequential method for choosing landmark locations on a compact manifold, with biological surface shapes as its motivating application. It models the response field as a Gaussian process and seeks to reduce the largest mean squared prediction error over the manifold. At each step, it selects the candidate vertex with the greatest conditional prediction variance, using a heat-kernel covariance that can be reweighted to emphasize high-curvature regions. The authors connect this greedy selection rule to reduced-basis approximation and derive convergence bounds. Their examples show landmarks resembling manually placed landmarks on fossil teeth, while their theory establishes rapid error decay under smoothness assumptions.
key_results: For smooth compact manifolds, the authors prove that the maximum prediction error of the greedy design decays faster than any inverse polynomial in the number of selected landmarks; they also relate its rate to the best achievable error for an optimal design. In an example involving 116 second mandibular molars, they varied the number of landmarks from 1 to 150 on meshes with around 5,000 vertices each; the reported prediction error fell approximately linearly on log-log plots for both the reweighted and Euclidean kernels. A visual example compares 22 automatically selected landmarks with 16 manually placed observer landmarks and describes the automatically selected points as strikingly similar in their coverage of tooth features. The algorithm's reported computational cost is cubic in the desired number of landmarks and its storage cost is quadratic in the number of candidate points; the paper does not provide a quantitative benchmark against other selection methods.
key_equations:
Assumed process model: \[Y\sim\mathrm{GP}(m,K)\] Y is the modeled response field, GP denotes a Gaussian process, m is its mean function, and K is its covariance function.

Sequential maximum-uncertainty selection: \[x_{n+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in V}\operatorname{Var}\!\left[Y(x)\mid Y(x_1),\ldots,Y(x_n)\right]\] The next location x sub n plus 1 is chosen from candidate vertices V to maximize the conditional variance of response Y at x, given responses at the n previously selected locations x sub 1 through x sub n.

limitations_stated: The authors state that their current techniques do not establish exponential convergence for the kernels considered on general compact smooth manifolds; stronger conclusions would require additional assumptions on manifold regularity. They also leave a fuller theory explaining why the method identifies biologically meaningful points, especially with relatively few landmarks, for future work.
limitations_unstated: The selection is restricted to vertices in the supplied mesh, so the resulting landmarks depend on mesh resolution and geometry rather than being freely chosen anywhere on the continuous surface. The prediction-uncertainty criterion depends on the chosen covariance kernel and curvature weights, and the reported biological comparisons are mainly visual rather than broad quantitative comparisons with alternative designs or landmarking procedures.
future_work_stated: The authors propose further theoretical work on optimal experimental design for manifold learning and on applications to adaptive matrix sensing and image completion. They also suggest extending covariance structures from individual shapes to pairs or collections of shapes for biological surface registration and collection shape analysis, and studying algorithm variants based on other pivoting methods.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method under noisy observations and assess sensitivity to kernel scale, curvature-weight settings, and mesh resolution. They could also compare prediction error and landmark usefulness quantitatively against uniform, random, and other design strategies on additional real experimental datasets.

summary: This paper develops a faster minimum energy design (MED) method for approximating Bayesian posterior distributions when evaluating the posterior is expensive. The method seeks points that are both well separated and concentrated in high-probability regions, rather than spreading points uniformly as quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) does. It constructs the design in stages, gradually changing from a uniform density to the target density and using inexpensive local approximations to select candidate points. The authors also modify the distance criterion to improve projections and representation of correlated distributions. They demonstrate the approach with simulations and a friction drilling calibration using a finite element model (FEM), and report substantial reductions in posterior evaluations relative to earlier MED construction and the expected cost of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).
key_results: For a 30-dimensional normal distribution, the new algorithm used 1,500 times fewer density evaluations than the generalized simulated annealing algorithm used for the earlier MED method. In a separate 30-dimensional example, generating 241 MED points took about 40 minutes and required 5,302 density evaluations; the resulting designs had lower centered L2 discrepancy than designs from the earlier algorithm, although the Sobol sequence had slightly lower discrepancy. In the friction drilling calibration, a 113-point MED took about 3.4 hours, compared with an estimated 43 hours for a typical MCMC analysis using about 10,000 samples. The calibration posterior means were 0.75 for the friction coefficient and 0.88 and 1.18 for the two adjustment parameters on the original scale, and the calibrated model prediction was closer to the physical measurements.
key_equations:
Generalized MED criterion: \[\max_D\min_{i\ne j} f(x_i)^{1/(2p)}f(x_j)^{1/(2p)}d_s(\Sigma^{-1/2}x_i,\Sigma^{-1/2}x_j)\] The design D contains points x_i in dimension p; f is the target density; d_s is the generalized distance with tuning parameter s; and Σ is the covariance matrix used to transform the points.

Generalized distance: \[d_s(u,v)=\left(\frac{1}{p}\sum_{l=1}^{p}|u_l-v_l|^s\right)^{1/s}\] The distance d_s compares points u and v across p coordinates, l indexes each coordinate, and s controls how coordinate differences are combined.

Density annealing schedule: \[f_k(x)=f(x)^{\gamma_k},\qquad \gamma_k=\frac{k-1}{K-1},\quad k=1,\ldots,K\] The target density is f, x is a parameter point, f_k is the density used at step k, γ_k is the annealing level, and K is the number of steps.

Posterior evaluation budget: \[N_{\mathrm{eval}}=Kn\] The algorithm uses K stages and generates n points per stage, so N_eval is the total number of target-density evaluations under the stated construction.
limitations_stated: The authors say that convergence properties and optimal choices of algorithm parameters remain insufficiently understood. They caution that deterministic samples may be inaccurate for complex distributions and in high dimensions, and that very expensive evaluations can make even deterministic sampling unaffordable. For the friction drilling example, they also state that they ignore uncertainty in the Gaussian-process approximation.
limitations_unstated: The method requires the user to specify a hypercube expected to contain the target density, so an incorrect or overly broad choice could undermine the design. The comparisons and demonstrations cover a limited set of simulated distributions and one manufacturing calibration; they do not establish accuracy or evaluation savings across a broad range of real engineering problems. The iterative procedure also depends on local approximations and tuning choices whose sensitivity is not quantified in these examples.
future_work_stated: The authors identify understanding the algorithm's convergence and finding optimal parameter choices as future research. They also suggest following MED with MCMC or a deterministic approximation method when higher accuracy is needed, and using MED points to make later MCMC or function approximation more efficient.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method on a broader range of manufacturing models and compare posterior estimates and predictive accuracy against reference analyses, not only evaluation counts and discrepancy measures. It would also be useful to study automated selection of the hypercube and tuning settings, and to assess the method under practical constraints such as parameter bounds or other restrictions on candidate runs.

summary: This paper develops multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) trial designs for comparing several treatments with a shared control. It assumes normally distributed outcomes with known variance and aims to reduce sample size while controlling generalized type-I and type-II error rates. The design allows the trial to stop when a chosen number of hypotheses have been rejected, rather than requiring only immediate stopping after the first rejection or continuing until every hypothesis has a decision. The authors construct a method to evaluate error rates, power, and expected sample size, then optimize group size and stopping boundaries using a stochastic search. In a three-treatment example based on the TAILoR trial, the designs met their specified operating-characteristic targets and illustrated how design choices affect expected sample size and power.
key_results: For the TAILoR example, the authors report optimized designs with a first-stage group size of 40 for the conventional 1111 design, compared with 24 for the 1131 design and 13 for the 2132 design. In the reported design searches, 540 runs each took approximately 10 to 15 minutes on a Macbook Pro using seven cores. The examples show that increasing the termination threshold often increased power but could also increase expected sample size; for instance, with b = 1 and c = 2, increasing d from 1 to 3 raised the expected sample size under the target effects from 79.6 to 118.5. The authors also show that exploiting interchangeability among treatments with equal effects, allocations, and variances can substantially reduce the number of outcome scenarios that must be evaluated.
key_equations:

Compound design objective and operating constraints: \[\min_{n,f,e}\left[w_1E(N\mid 0)+w_2E(N\mid\delta^{c,K})+w_3n\sum_{k=0}^{K}r_{k,J}\right],\quad FWER_I(a\mid 0)\le\alpha,\quad FWP(b,c\mid\delta^{c,K})\ge1-\beta\] The design minimizes a weighted sum of expected sample size under the null, expected sample size under the target-effect scenario, and maximum sample size; n is first-stage group size, f and e are stopping boundaries, w values are weights, N is required sample size, r is an allocation ratio, K is the number of experimental treatments, J is the final analysis, and the constraints require the generalized type-I familywise error rate to be at most alpha and familywise power to be at least one minus beta for the specified b, c, and target-effect scenario delta.

Trial termination rule: \[\text{stop if }\sum_{k=1}^{K}I(\psi_k=1)\ge d\text{ or }\sum_{k=1}^{K}I(\omega_k=0)=0\] The trial stops if at least d hypotheses have been rejected or if every treatment has a decision; K is the number of experimental treatments, I is the indicator function, psi indicates rejection, and omega records the analysis at which a decision is made.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the stochastic search is not guaranteed to find the global optimum, so repeated searches from randomized starting points and suitable algorithm settings are important. They note that determining designs may become difficult as the number of treatments or analyses increases. The method assumes known outcome variance; extension to normally distributed outcomes with unknown variance is not straightforward.
limitations_unstated: The examples use a particular normal-outcome, known-variance setup and specified effect scenarios, so performance under misspecified distributions, uncertain variances, or effects different from those scenarios is not established here. The optimization treats group size as continuous before converting it to an integer-compatible choice, and the worked example selects the upper compatible value; the practical consequences of that choice may depend on allocation requirements and trial resources.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest investigating a dynamic-programming approach for finding optimized designs. They also suggest extending a method that reduces the dimensionality of the optimization problem to help retain tractability as the number of treatments and analyses grows.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess these designs under alternative outcome distributions, unknown or changing variances, and practical constraints such as unequal recruitment rates or limits on control-arm enrollment. summary: This paper introduces an adaptive space-filling method for computer experiments with nonlinear models. Its objective is to place design points so that their model outputs represent a desired distribution on the output manifold, rather than being uniform only in the parameter space. The method alternates between resampling outputs according to estimated local sparsity and perturbing parameter points with a smoothed distribution that preserves exploration. When model derivatives are available, a second version uses the model Jacobian directly; otherwise, the method estimates local expansion from nearest-neighbor distances. The paper proves a convergence result under stated regularity conditions and demonstrates the method on illustrative models, including an enzymatic reaction model.
key_results: The authors prove that the derivative-based algorithm approaches the target parameter distribution in Kantorovich–Rubinstein distance as the sample count and iteration count increase, subject to a sufficient condition on the perturbation bandwidth. In the torus examples, 10,000 algorithm-generated samples visually match samples from the exact area formula more closely than samples drawn uniformly in parameter space. In the exponential-model example, 2,000 algorithm-generated samples resemble the area-formula samples, while uniform parameter sampling concentrates on a small boundary region of the output manifold. In the enzymatic model, the method identifies a protruding output region using 4,000 simulations, compared with 5,000 simulations for uniform parameter sampling; the paper reports this as a clearer identification with fewer simulations, not as a measured error or efficiency percentage.

summary: The paper develops a way to evaluate integrated mean-squared prediction error (IMSPE) for computer experiments whose prediction region is a circular disk. It considers a Gaussian covariance model with known hyperparameters and seeks designs that minimize prediction error across the region. The method divides the disk into horizontal sections, represents each section by a rectangle with the same area, and uses analytic integrals for the Gaussian covariance terms within those rectangles. The authors apply the method to one-, two-, and four-run examples. Their four-run example gives a twin-point design on the disk, showing that such designs are not limited to square or otherwise non-round boundaries.
key_results: For one run with both covariance hyperparameters equal to 1, the optimal point is at the disk center and the reported IMSPE is 0.735759. For two runs under the same hyperparameters and with centered inversion symmetry, the points lie at radius 0.546820 and the reported IMSPE is 0.426149; the design is continuously rotatable. For four runs with hyperparameters 0.128 and 0.00016, the putatively optimal disk design has distal points at (±0.69945, 0) and a coincident twin pair at the origin in the infinite-precision limit, with IMSPE 0.000029210. The corresponding putatively optimal square design has IMSPE 0.000066822, and the authors report that the four-in-line and rectangular designs they examined on the disk were suboptimal to the twin-point design.

limitations_unstated: The four-run search imposes centered inversion symmetry and bases its optimality claim on comparisons among selected design families, so it does not demonstrate global optimality over all four-point configurations. future_work_stated: The authors say that their method can be extended to more than two factors, prediction regions beyond squares and disks, and other assumed covariance functions. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test unrestricted optimization for the four-run disk design and quantify how its solution changes when covariance hyperparameters are estimated rather than known. summary: The paper introduces the Modular Optimal Learning Testing Environment (MOLTE), a software package for comparing learning policies that choose among a finite set of alternatives using noisy measurements. It supports both offline ranking and selection, where the goal is to recommend the best alternative after a measurement budget, and online learning, where the goal is to earn high cumulative reward. Users select problems, policies, priors, belief models, objectives, and budgets through a spreadsheet; the package runs simulations and reports graphical and numerical comparisons. Its starter library includes many problem classes and policies, and users can add their own through modular files. The experiments show that policy performance depends on the problem and evaluation objective, so the authors find no single policy that is best in all settings.
key_results: The package includes 23 pre-coded problem classes and 20 pre-coded policies, and its experiments commonly compare policies over 1,000 runs using the same pre-generated observations. For independent-belief bandit problems, the reported measurement budgets are 10, 100, and 500 times the number of alternatives; for correlated-belief comparisons, the budget is 0.2 times that number. In one correlated-belief Goldstein comparison at the 0.2-times budget, tuned interval estimation had a normalized opportunity-cost difference of -0.061 against online knowledge gradient and outperformed it in 0.81 of runs; tuned upper confidence bound with exploration had a difference of -0.097 and outperformed it in 0.92 of runs. summary: This paper develops sequential rerandomization for experiments in which participants arrive in groups rather than all at once. The design aims to balance treatment and control groups on continuous or binary covariates, using Mahalanobis distance, and thereby support estimation of the average treatment effect. At each group, assignments are proposed and accepted if the combined covariate imbalance across groups meets a prespecified threshold. The authors derive an asymptotic rule for allocating randomization effort across groups and compare the method with complete rerandomization. Their main theoretical finding is that, under stated assumptions and with the same expected total number of rerandomizations, sequential rerandomization can achieve lower expected imbalance.
key_results: The authors prove that the treatment-effect estimator is unbiased under the design’s symmetry condition, and that, under an additive treatment-effect model, its variance reduction depends on the reduction in expected Mahalanobis distance and the squared multiple correlation with the covariates. As the expected total number of rerandomizations grows, the expected final distance under sequential rerandomization is asymptotically about n_K/N times the distance under complete rerandomization; with equal group sizes, the improvement ratio approaches the number of groups. In the clinical dataset with 548 participants, 12 covariates, and 2,000 expected rerandomizations, the sequential designs had distance-improvement ratios of 2.25, 3.02, 3.58, and 6.90 compared with complete rerandomization. In simulations with five groups and five covariates, the ratio was 4.42 for the ideal large-sample setting, but fell to 1.89 for group size 20 with either the heavy-tailed Weibull or log-normal covariates.

Acceptance criterion: \[M_k^* < a_k\] M_k^* is the tentative Mahalanobis distance for the first k groups, a_k is the prespecified acceptance threshold, and k identifies the group.

limitations_stated: The theoretical results rely on assumptions including an approximately normal distribution for group-level covariate differences; the authors note that the advantage can weaken for small groups or heavy-tailed covariates. limitations_unstated: The real-data comparison uses one public clinical dataset and simulated assignments, not an implemented clinical trial with observed treatment outcomes. future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method in prospective clinical trials and test how the design performs when enrollment groups, allocation ratios, or practical covariate constraints differ from the paper’s examples. summary: The paper develops an optimal experimental design (OED) method for choosing model outputs or sensor locations that provide information about uncertain model parameters. Simulated examples show the method can identify informative designs in several physical models, including a high-dimensional flow model.
key_results: In the stationary convection-diffusion example, the selected sensor locations were similar when the calculation used 50 prior samples and when it used 5,000; the reported expected information gain for the top location was 2.758 with 50 samples and 2.826 with 5,000. In the 100-parameter porous-media example, the authors report that 1,000 prior samples gave a sufficiently accurate design approximation compared with 10,000 samples; the expected information gain for the leading location was 1.992 and 2.008, respectively. In the inclusion example, a sensor closer to the inclusion gave information gain 1.701, compared with 0.257 for a more distant sensor. For the transient source-location example, the highest expected gains were near the domain corners, consistent with the cited statistical Bayesian design study; the paper does not report a numerical head-to-head comparison of the methods.

Optimal design criterion: \[Q^{opt}=\arg\max_{Q_z\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbb{E}(I_{Q_z})\] The optimal design is the candidate design Q sub z in the design set that maximizes expected information gain.
limitations_stated: The authors limit their demonstrations to selecting designs from discrete candidate sets, noting that their approach does not address efficient optimization over continuous design spaces. limitations_unstated: The method’s results depend on the assumed prior and on the chosen family and spread of possible observed-data densities, so a design that is optimal under those assumptions may not be optimal for actual measurement conditions. future_work_stated: The authors propose pursuing more efficient gradient-based methods for optimization over continuous design spaces. They also identify coupling the method to continuous optimization as future work.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the designs using real experiments and test how robust the selected locations are to misspecified priors, measurement distributions, and model-structure errors. summary: The paper develops adaptive designs for estimating an excursion set: the inputs for which an expensive function meets a specified threshold. It models the function with a Gaussian process and seeks a conservative set estimate that controls the probability of including unsafe or otherwise out-of-set inputs. The design uses sequential uncertainty reduction to choose new evaluations, including batches of locations, by targeting uncertainty in the conservative estimate. The authors derive tractable formulas for the selection criteria and provide an implementation in R. Synthetic studies and a nuclear criticality safety example show that the method, especially its Type II uncertainty criterion, can reduce missed portions of the set effectively compared with the tested alternatives.
key_results: In the synthetic benchmark, strategies tailored to conservative estimation, especially strategy C, reduced expected Type II error faster than integrated mean squared error and targeted integrated mean squared error in the reported batch scenarios; the differences were less pronounced when seven additional space-filling points were included in each batch. In the nuclear safety study, each of 20 iterations selected a batch of three points, for 75 evaluations including the 15-point initial design. At the final iteration, strategy C had a median Type II error 27% lower than integrated mean squared error, while strategies B and A were 25% and 12% lower, respectively. The ground-truth safe-set volume estimated from a 50 by 50 grid was 88.16% of the input-space volume, and strategies B and C showed the strongest relative-volume-error decline in the first five iterations.
key_equations:
Excursion set: \[\Gamma(f)=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:f(x)\ge t\}\] Gamma is the set of inputs in the domain X where function f reaches or exceeds threshold t, and x denotes an input.

Conservative estimate: \[\mathrm{CE}_{\alpha,n}\in\arg\max_{C\in\{Q_{n,\rho}\}}\{\mu(C):P_n(C\subset\Gamma)\ge\alpha\}\] The conservative estimate CE at level alpha after n evaluations is the largest-measure set C among the quantile sets Q indexed by rho for which the conditional probability P sub n of inclusion in Gamma is at least alpha; mu measures set size.

Batch selection by expected uncertainty reduction: \[x^*=\arg\min_{x^{(q)}\in\mathcal{X}^q}\mathbb{E}_{n,x^{(q)}}[H_{n+q}]\] The selected batch x star minimizes the expected future uncertainty H after n plus q evaluations, where q is batch size, X is the input domain, and the expectation is conditional on the existing data and proposed batch.
limitations_stated: The authors state that conservativeness depends on the quality of the underlying Gaussian process model, and that a discrete approximation is currently used to compute the estimator. They also note that the strategies target uncertainty in conservative set estimates rather than overall function-model quality or reliable covariance-parameter estimation; their experiments use a fixed confidence level of 0.95.
limitations_unstated: The empirical comparisons cover a limited collection of synthetic scenarios and one two-input nuclear safety case, so the reported rankings may not hold for other response surfaces, thresholds, or engineering applications. The method also relies on numerically approximating and optimizing an integrated criterion, which may become burdensome in higher-dimensional domains or when the relevant set occupies a small fraction of the input space.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest comparing other confidence levels, such as 0.99 and 0.995, and investigating continuous approximations for the excursion probability. They also identify stopping rules and the limiting behavior of expected errors, sequential behavior of covariance-parameter estimates, and a fully Bayesian treatment of parameter uncertainty as topics for further research.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the approach under operational constraints such as unequal evaluation costs, restricted or infeasible input combinations, and a limited number of parallel workers. Broader validation on real engineering experiments and tests in higher-dimensional problems would help establish when the conservative inclusion guarantee and the observed efficiency gains are practically useful.

summary: This paper develops an active learning method for choosing experiments when the response model is nonlinear in unknown parameters. Experiments are selected to improve either the estimated best alternative or knowledge of the parameters, with the latter objective based on reducing entropy. limitations_stated: The authors state that the earlier fixed-candidate method becomes computationally expensive as the number of candidates grows and depends on the strong assumption that the truth is among those candidates. limitations_unstated: The method's Bayesian probability updates and likelihood-based resampling depend on the assumed response model and noise distribution being appropriate; the paper does not evaluate robustness to model misspecification or unknown noise variance. summary: This paper develops an adaptive experimental procedure to assess path-following performance for an unmanned surface vehicle (USV). summary: This paper proposes a method for finding Bayesian optimal experimental designs when expected loss is difficult to compute. limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstrations cover a small set of specified models and prior distributions, so they do not establish how well the method performs under prior or model misspecification in process experiments. future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating alternative deterministic approximations, particularly expectation propagation, as a way to approximate posterior distributions and marginal likelihoods. They note that this could allow approximation families from the exponential family.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the designs in real chemical or process experiments and assess their sensitivity to prior choices and model misspecification. summary: This paper develops robust designs for complete block experiments that compare treatment means when errors within a block may be correlated. In the contaminant example, the sequential method achieves higher expected reward than the greedy and batch designs in the reported comparisons.

summary: This paper develops large-sample theory for rerandomization in treatment-control experiments that estimate the average causal effect using the difference in treatment and control outcome means. summary: The paper develops a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate method for detecting system failure regions and estimating failure probabilities when simulations of the underlying model are expensive. The reported examples show accurate failure-probability estimates with relatively few model evaluations, and the Branin example reports better performance than stepwise uncertainty reduction on the plotted measures.
key_results: On the Branin example, both limit-state inference (LSI) and stepwise uncertainty reduction (SUR) began with 4 Latin-hypercube design points and then added 9 points sequentially; the authors report that LSI generally had lower detection and failure-probability errors in this example. On the clamped beam, 164 design points produced an estimate of 3.35 × 10^-3, matching the reported standard Monte Carlo estimate; 12 failures were classified as safe and 10 safe cases as failures.
