summary: The paper introduces affinely full-dimensional designs, a class of non-regular two-level fractional factorial designs for estimating the parameters in a main effect model. A design belongs to this class when its points are not contained in any affine hyperplane over the two-element field, or equivalently when it is not a proper subset of a regular fractional factorial design. The authors show that every design in the class makes all main effect model parameters simultaneously identifiable. They examine the class in relation to determinant-based design optimality, focusing especially on saturated designs and on enumerated designs with four or five factors. Their results suggest a pattern by run size modulo eight, but the general pattern remains a conjecture.
key_results: The authors prove that an affinely full-dimensional design has a nonsingular information matrix, and for saturated designs they show that membership in the class is equivalent to the design matrix determinant not being divisible by two raised to the run size. For saturated designs, their conjecture is that determinant-optimal designs are affinely full-dimensional for run sizes congruent to five, six, or seven modulo eight, and are subset designs for the other listed residues; they report no counterexample and say the pattern holds for all proved determinant optima below one hundred runs. For four- and five-factor designs, they enumerate designs with up to ten runs and report the determinant-optimal designs, but find no clear general relation between optimality and class membership. They also report that the saturated determinant-optimal designs for four and five factors shown in their tables are A-optimal and E-optimal as well.

summary: The paper develops sampling-time designs for two nonlinear models that combine a pharmacokinetic compartment model with a pharmacodynamic Emax model. The models use drug-effect measurements over time to estimate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters together. For the four-parameter Emax-PK1 model, the authors prove that the locally D-optimal design has four equally weighted times, including both boundaries of the design interval. For the five-parameter Emax-PK2 model, they give a sufficient condition under which a design uses the minimum number of time points. The paper also proposes expanded designs intended to improve robustness when the parameter values used to construct a design are uncertain, and reports a tradeoff between robustness and efficiency.
key_results: For Emax-PK1, with the stated nominal parameters and a dose of 5 mg/kg, the four-point design on an unbounded time interval uses 0, 13.48, 31.62, and 160.00 hours, with equal allocation and relative efficiency 1. With upper time limits of 72 and 24 hours, the reported designs are 0, 13.26, 31.05, 72 hours and 0, 7.97, 17.83, 24 hours, respectively. For Emax-PK2, the reported five-point design uses 0, 0.275, 2.999, 14.75, and 32.7 hours, also with equal allocation. In the Emax-PK1 comparison, the five-point equally spaced uniform design has efficiency 0.476373989, while the five-point expanded design has efficiency 0.7588; the paper reports that larger locally D-optimal designs can have greater robustness but lower efficiency, and recommends five- or six-point equally spaced designs for practical use.

limitations_stated: The authors note that a locally optimal design may perform poorly if its nominal parameter values are far from the true values. They also treat pharmacokinetic parameters as fixed effects even though these parameters may differ between subjects.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons use selected nominal parameter values and do not validate the proposed designs in real pharmaceutical experiments. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying random effects for selected pharmacokinetic parameters because those parameters are likely to vary between subjects.
future_work_unstated: Further work could compare these designs with Bayesian or other parameter-averaged criteria and evaluate them under practical limits on sampling windows and allocations. Validation using data from real pharmaceutical studies would show how well the theoretical efficiency and robustness results transfer to practice.

summary: This paper develops a bootstrap method for estimating a confidence region for the operating conditions that maximize a response within a specified experimental region. It concerns response surface models and demonstrates the method for two-dimensional quadratic surfaces, including a concave-down surface and a saddle surface. The method resamples standardized model residuals, refits the response surface, finds the maximum within the region, and estimates the distribution of those bootstrap maxima with a boundary-corrected kernel density. A high-density contour enclosing the requested proportion of bootstrap estimates forms the confidence region and stays within the experimental region. The simulations find that coverage improves as the number of runs increases, while the two bandwidth-selection methods have similar coverage.
key_results: The simulation comparison used 500 experiments, with 13 runs per experiment and 2,000 bootstrap samples per confidence region. Normal rule-of-thumb and plug-in bandwidth selection produced statistically indistinguishable coverage; the plug-in bandwidths were slightly larger, while the rule-of-thumb method required less computation. Coverage was below the nominal level at the smallest run count, especially for the concave-down case, and approached the nominal level as the run count increased from 13 to 26 to 208. Increasing the bootstrap count to 4,000 or 6,000 did not significantly improve coverage; the authors report that a single region using 2,000 bootstrap samples took about 2 minutes on their computer.
key_equations:
Response model: \[y_i=g(x_i;\theta)+\epsilon_i\] Here y_i is the observed response in run i, g is the response function, x_i is the setting for run i, theta is the vector of model parameters, and epsilon_i is the unexplained error.

Bootstrap kernel density estimate: \[\hat f(x)=\frac{1}{b h_1 h_2}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\prod_{j=1}^{2}K\left(\frac{x_j-x^*_{cm,i,j}}{h_j}\right)\] Here fhat is the estimated density at setting x, b is the number of bootstrap samples, h_j is the bandwidth for coordinate j, K is the kernel function, x_j is coordinate j of x, and x*_{cm,i,j} is coordinate j of the estimated maximum from bootstrap sample i.

Percentile confidence region: \[C_{1-\alpha}=\{x\in R:\hat f(x)\ge c_{\alpha}\}\] Here C is the confidence region at level one minus alpha, x is a candidate setting, R is the experimental region, fhat is the estimated bootstrap density, c_alpha is the density threshold chosen to enclose the target proportion of bootstrap estimates, and alpha is the tail probability.
limitations_stated: The method relies on the maximizing operating condition being unique; when it is not unique, the estimated optimum may not be consistent. The simulations cover only two-dimensional quadratic surfaces in a rectangular region, and coverage is below nominal for small samples. Residual bootstrapping assumes a correct model with exchangeable errors, and the authors note that a direct analogue of standardized residuals is generally unavailable for nonlinear regression.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated data from only two constructed response surfaces, so it does not show how the method performs on real processes or across a wider range of response shapes. The region is rectangular and the study focuses on two factors, leaving practical performance with more factors, irregular feasible regions, or additional process constraints unverified.
future_work_stated: The authors discuss bootstrap calibration as a way to improve coverage and suggest more robust scale estimates or variable-bandwidth density estimation for difficult or multimodal bootstrap distributions. They also describe extending the approach to higher dimensions and to operating conditions that optimize a combined desirability measure for multiple responses.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluation could test sensitivity to model misspecification and errors that are not exchangeable, and compare coverage and computational effort across a broader set of response surfaces and experimental designs. Validation on real experiments, including studies that add runs sequentially when the estimated region is too large, would help establish practical usefulness.

summary: This paper develops a way to identify regular fractions contained within a two-level fractional factorial design, with factor levels coded minus one and plus one. It represents a design by an indicator polynomial and derives a condition on its coefficients for deciding whether a candidate regular fraction is included. The authors use that condition to search for disjoint regular fractions whose union is the original design. In examples based on Plackett-Burman designs, a five-factor, twelve-run design is decomposed into three regular fractions of four runs each. The paper also uses the structure of these decompositions to construct orthogonal arrays of strength two.
key_results: For the selected five-factor, twelve-run design, the authors found 15 contained regular fractions of four runs and five distinct ways to partition the design into three such fractions. Across the 70 distinct five-factor designs with twelve runs formed from the Plackett-Burman designs, each had 15 contained four-run regular fractions and five decompositions into three regular fractions. The 462 column selections considered were grouped into 81 classes: 70 classes had designs with twelve runs and 11 had designs with eleven runs. The authors generated 192 distinct strength-two orthogonal arrays, the same total reported in the cited prior work; they did not report efficiency or prediction comparisons.

summary: The paper studies randomized sampling designs for estimating the integral of a function over a unit hypercube, as used in computer experiments. It constructs the samples by starting with an orthogonal array of strength two, randomizing the symbols in each column, and adding independent uniform jitter within array strata; it also analyzes orthogonal-array-based Latin hypercube variants. Under smoothness conditions, it proves that the standardized integration estimates from all three design classes converge to the standard normal distribution as the alphabet size grows. The paper also derives their leading asymptotic variances in terms of the integrand's higher-order residual component. The results provide theoretical support for approximate normal inference, including confidence intervals, under the stated conditions.
key_results: Each design uses a run size equal to the square of the number of symbols per array column. For the randomized orthogonal-array design and one orthogonal-array-based Latin hypercube construction, the paper shows that the run-size-scaled variance approaches the integral of the squared residual integrand; it also establishes that the variance of the randomized orthogonal-array estimator and that of the two Latin hypercube variants agree to the reported asymptotic order. For a smooth integrand with positive residual variance and at least three dimensions, the standardized estimates from all three design classes converge in distribution to the standard normal as the alphabet size grows. These are theoretical asymptotic findings; the paper reports no finite-run numerical comparisons.

limitations_unstated: The smoothness condition on the highest-order mixed partial is demanding and may exclude integrands with discontinuities or sharp transitions that arise in computer experiments. future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful extension would establish finite-run normal-approximation bounds and investigate whether weaker smoothness assumptions preserve the results. summary: The paper proposes a way to test main effects and interactions in two-valued input-output systems evaluated across settings of controllable factors. It models the counts in each run as independent binomial observations and represents the system performance through the odds ratio. The method builds covariates from the factor settings, then tests effects by conditioning on sufficient statistics for nuisance parameters; it also accounts for aliasing in fractional factorial designs. In the example of an inspection machine, the method finds evidence for an interaction that the authors’ analysis of variance of the signal-to-noise ratio treats less decisively.
key_results: For the compressor inspection data, the likelihood-ratio statistic for testing the main-effects model against a model that adds the interaction between A and C is 13.06 on 1 degree of freedom, with a p value of 0.000301. The signal-to-noise ratio analysis of variance reported a p value of 0.04482 for that interaction. In an imagined dataset with smaller sample sizes for two runs, the proposed test gives a statistic of 11.56 and a p value of 0.000674. The authors note that the signal-to-noise ratio analysis of variance changes little for this altered dataset, whereas their conditional test accounts for the changed sample sizes.

limitations_unstated: The method assumes independent binomial observations and two-level controllable factors, so its results may not transfer directly to other response types or factor structures. future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the conditional testing procedure across additional manufacturing studies, especially experiments with sparse counts and different sample-size patterns. summary: This paper develops methods to construct blocked regular fractional factorial designs using the minimum aberration (MA) objective. It studies regular main-effect (RME) designs and considers four ways to combine treatment and block wordlength patterns into a single criterion. The construction method uses coding theory and row-coincidence moments, providing a way to compare designs without directly counting all defining words and alias sets. The paper also derives a lower bound on a block wordlength count and gives conditions under which designs built from unblocked MA designs are optimal under all four criteria. It reports MA designs for all 8, 16, 27, and 32 runs, for 64 runs up to 32 factors, and for all 81 runs.
key_results: The authors provide blocked MA designs for all 8, 16, 27, and 32 runs, 64 runs with up to 32 factors, and all 81 runs, considering four combined wordlength patterns. Designs under the four criteria are the same in most examined cases; the paper identifies four types of exceptions, including cases where the Chen–Cheng criterion selects a different design. For 64 runs, the lower bound on the block wordlength count helps reduce searches; for example, it narrows one search to 17 regular designs in a case where searching all designs under the stated cutoff would involve more than 100,000. The paper notes that counting words directly can be cumbersome: its example of a 64-run design with 25 factors in 8 blocks requires counting 4,194,303 words.

limitations_stated: The authors focus on regular designs for simplicity, although they note that most results can be extended to nonregular designs. They also state that the lower bound on the block wordlength count is not always tight and can sometimes be improved.
limitations_unstated: The construction and comparison results are developed for regular designs over finite fields and do not establish how well the criteria perform when the assumed design structure is unsuitable. summary: This paper develops bounds for codes and ordered orthogonal arrays in the Niederreiter–Rosenbloom–Tsfasman (NRT) ordered Hamming space, rather than designs for physical experiments. The space has vectors divided into blocks, and its distance weights a block according to the position of its last nonzero coordinate. The authors construct the associated scheme from a one-block scheme and identify its eigenvalues as multivariate Krawtchouk polynomials. They use these polynomials in linear programming bounds, including an asymptotic bound, and give a sharper analysis for the case of two coordinates per block. The principal finding is that some of their bounds improve on established bounds over stated ranges of distances, with no experimental data or practical design evaluation.
key_results: The paper proves a Bassalygo–Elias asymptotic bound that is better than the Hamming bound for every relative distance from zero through the critical distance. It is also better than the Plotkin bound for all positive distances below the critical distance when the alphabet size is 2 and there are 2 coordinates per block; for alphabet size 3 and 4 coordinates per block, the authors give an improvement range of 0 to 0.54. A general linear programming bound improves on the asymptotic Plotkin bound at large code distances. For 2 coordinates per block, the authors derive a further bound using the zeros of Krawtchouk polynomials and compare it with the Plotkin, Gilbert–Varshamov, Elias, and general linear programming bounds in plots for alphabet sizes 2 and 3 and block lengths 2 and 3.

limitations_stated: None stated.
limitations_unstated: The results are mathematical bounds, not validated procedures for selecting or running physical experiments; the paper gives no empirical comparison or implementation assessment. future_work_stated: The authors identify the characterization of association schemes arising from more general partial orders, and derivation of MacWilliams-type relations for them, as open questions. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess how the bounds behave at practical finite run sizes and to compare them numerically across a wider range of alphabet sizes and block lengths. summary: The paper develops a method for generating all two-level orthogonal arrays with a specified number of factors and force, while allowing any number of replications. The nonnegative integer solutions form the lattice points of a rational cone, and a Hilbert basis gives a finite set of arrays from which every array satisfying the requirements can be assembled. The authors use the 4ti2 software to compute examples. Their results demonstrate the method for small cases, but computation for six factors and force two was too time-consuming.
key_results: For OA(5, 3), 4ti2 found a Hilbert basis of 28 arrays in 0.05 seconds on the authors’ slow laptop; 12 had 16 treatments without replications, and 16 had 24 points with replications. A previously reported classification had 60, 192, and 552 arrays at those respective sizes after complement duplicates were removed; the authors explain that the 390 additional 16-treatment arrays are unions of two disjoint 8-treatment arrays. Its aim is to classify such designs up to row and column permutations and sign changes, with particular attention to orders 21 and 26. The author derives the structure of the optimal designs of order 21 and shows that they arise from a construction based on Hadamard matrices of order 20. summary: This paper develops local designs for estimating parameters in nonlinear regression models that include rational, logistic, and exponential forms. It studies E-optimal designs, which protect estimation of the least-informed parameter direction, and c-optimal designs for specified parameter combinations. The authors replace the nonlinear problem with an equivalent linearized regression model whose functions include derivatives with respect to the nonlinear parameters. When those parameters are sufficiently close, the optimal designs can be constructed at the extrema, or Chebyshev points, of a best equi-oscillating approximation, with weights determined by the design criterion. Across b values at or below negative one, its reported efficiency for estimating the first coefficient ranges from approximately 0.9061 to 0.9595, and for the second coefficient from approximately 0.9805 to 1. In the reported comparison at separation parameter z equal to 0.1, the limiting design has individual-coefficient efficiencies of 1.00, 0.99, 1.00, and 1.00; at z equal to 0.95, these are 0.27, 0.21, 0.08, and 0.07, while the model-specific E-optimal design has efficiencies of 0.78, 1.00, 0.44, and 0.31.

summary: The paper develops a theory for how far mobile sensors may need to move when a signal model changes and the D-optimal sensor placement is recomputed. It considers a fixed mobility graph and determinant-based placement objectives built from a changing subspace projector. The authors measure movement by matching old and new sensor positions to minimize the greatest travel distance, and define a distance margin to quantify how much worse distant placements are under the old objective. They prove that sufficiently small projector changes and a sufficiently large distance margin ensure every new optimum stays within a chosen radius. A weighted-path example shows that perturbation size and eigengap alone cannot guarantee small movement; the paper also gives finite certification methods and extensions to other determinant criteria.
key_results: In the synthetic study, 1,189 of 1,224 one-edge perturbation cases, or 97.1%, met the theorem’s conditions for certification, and the observed movement never exceeded the certified radius in those cases. A nontrivial certificate was obtained in 1,035 cases, or 87.0%; the certified and actual radii were equal in 561 cases, or 47.2%, including 547 cases with no movement. The optimizer moved in 33 eligible cases, and the median gap between certified and actual movement was two hops overall and one hop among cases with positive movement. In a separate example, actual movement was one hop while the certified radius was four hops; the paper cautions that the synthetic cases do not support ranking graph families.
key_equations: Distance-margin movement guarantee: \[M_t(P)>B_t\implies d_{\mathrm{match}}(S_t^*,S)\le P\] Here M_t(P) is the distance margin at time t for radius P, B_t is the perturbation budget, d_match is the bottleneck matching distance, S*_t is a baseline maximizing placement, and S is any maximizing placement after the update; the implication states that a margin exceeding the budget confines every new maximizer to radius P.
limitations_stated: The movement measure treats sensors as interchangeable and does not account for sensor types, trajectory collisions, travel times, or edge-capacity constraints. The experiments use small synthetic instances and exhaustive evaluation, and the authors note that the certificate can be conservative and that computing margins by enumeration limits its use on larger networks. The guarantees concern exact maximizers and local-region feasibility, not whether a particular placement algorithm finds the global optimum.
limitations_unstated: The stability guarantee depends on the chosen subspace model and objective; real sensor data may not be represented well by the assumed projector, and the paper does not validate the guarantees on field measurements. The numerical study covers a limited set of small graph families and perturbation scenarios, so its reported certification frequencies may not predict performance in operational sensor networks.
future_work_stated: The authors propose finding conservative lower bounds on distance margins without enumerating all placements, to make certification practical on larger networks. They also suggest extending the movement geometry to heterogeneous sensors, travel costs, and collision constraints, and extending the stability results to approximate maximizers produced by practical algorithms.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the certificates on real dynamic sensing applications and assess whether the assumed projector drift reflects model changes observed in practice. Further work could also study sequential placement updates with operational constraints, including sensor-specific movement limits and measurement availability during relocation.

summary: Sequential Supersaturated Screening (S3) is a sequential design method for screening many candidate factors with relatively few runs, then optimizing the response using a second-order response surface. It assumes a second-order response with linear, interaction, and quadratic effects, measurement noise, and a batch effect. In Stage 1, it adds two-level runs in rounds, constructs designs by coordinate exchange, and progressively eliminates or commits factors using an importance score and a graduated quantile rule. Its design criterion encourages pairwise column inner products to be positive and balances their spread and magnitude on a scale determined by the Welch lower bound. Simulations and the Borehole benchmark show that it generally selects fewer inactive factors than one-shot cross-validated Lasso while retaining optimization performance, and the paper also gives theoretical bounds for noise-factor commitment and Stage 1 run count.
key_results: Across the recommended operating ranges in the simulations, S3 had lower Type I error in all eight case-and-size settings: 0.0095 to 0.0715, compared with 0.0910 to 0.3029 for one-shot cross-validated Lasso. Its F1 scores ranged from 0.50 to 0.81, compared with 0.30 to 0.47 for the baseline; this came with higher Type II error in all eight settings. At matched factor counts, S3 had a significant optimization-loss advantage in seven of eight settings, from 0.05 to 0.10 lower loss, with a statistical tie in the weak-signal setting at p = 200. Stage 1 took a mean of 34.8, 58.1, 66.9, and 106.2 runs at p = 40, 80, 120, and 200, respectively, and was faster than the one-shot baseline at each tested size, with median-time ratios from 0.85 to 0.95. Welch-calibrated positive-cone design criterion: \[\operatorname{Var}(s_+^W)=s^2-\bar{s}^{\,2}+\eta_W(n,p)\bar{s}^{\,2}+\lambda\sum_{i< j}\min(s_{ij},0)^2\] Here s_ij is the inner product of design columns i and j, s-bar is the mean of the pairwise inner products, s-squared is their mean squared value, eta-W is calibrated from n runs and p factors, and lambda penalizes negative inner products.

limitations_unstated: The main simulation study uses a limited set of synthetic signal patterns, while the benchmark is a single evaluable mathematical function rather than a real industrial experiment. future_work_stated: The authors identify the connection between the graduated elimination schedule and standard high-dimensional regularity conditions as an open question. future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test the method in real industrial experiments and under practical constraints such as restricted factor combinations, run costs, and randomization limits. summary: The paper develops a method for finding which baseline covariates modify which main effects and interactions in a factorial randomized experiment with binary treatment components. It targets linear projection coefficients for the conditional Walsh–Hadamard contrasts, rather than unrestricted conditional effects. The method subtracts a treatment-invariant baseline from an inverse-probability-weighted contrast score, estimates that baseline by cross-fitting, and uses sparse regression with debiasing to estimate modifier coefficients. A multiplier bootstrap supplies simultaneous confidence bands, and a Romano–Wolf step-down procedure selects cells while controlling the familywise error rate (FWER). The authors report that simulations maintained near-nominal coverage and error control across grids of up to 3,150 cells, with accurate cross-fitted baselines improving precision.
key_results: Across the primary simulations, which included grids from 300 to 3,150 cells, the global-null FWER ranged from 0.045 to 0.059; under sparse signals, simultaneous coverage ranged from 0.940 to 0.953 and strong FWER from 0.046 to 0.057. At a sample size of 1,000, the cross-fitted quadratic baseline produced bands about 1.8% to 1.9% wider than the oracle bands when prognostic variation was present. In the Gaussian simulation settings, multiplier-bootstrap bands were only 0.24% to 0.75% shorter than Bonferroni bands on average, and step-down true-positive rates exceeded Holm’s by 0.3 to 1.0 percentage points. At a sample size of 200, fitting the quadratic baseline without cross-fitting yielded coverage of 0.902, compared with 0.942 for the cross-fitted version.

Projection target: \[\theta^*_S=\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb{R}^p}\mathbb{E}\left[(\tau_S(X)-Z(X)^\top b)^2\right]\] The coefficient vector θ for contrast S minimizes expected squared error between conditional contrast τ and a linear combination with coefficient vector b of standardized covariates Z; the expectation is over the covariate distribution, and p is the number of features.
limitations_stated: The target is a projection coefficient tied to the chosen feature dictionary, scaling, and covariate distribution; it is not generally a derivative or a fully nonparametric conditional effect. limitations_unstated: The finite-sample multiplier calibration uses 1,000 draws in the simulations, but the paper does not quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty in the estimated critical values, especially over repeated step-down sets. future_work_unstated: A useful extension would be to evaluate whether the procedure remains calibrated under constrained or blocked randomization schemes used in practical experiments. summary: DeltaSelect is a method for affordable, repeated baseline-versus-candidate comparisons of coding agents, rather than for ranking models. It uses repeated public benchmark runs to identify tasks whose single-run results reliably track full-benchmark performance across observed model and reasoning configurations. For each selected task, it maps fail-to-pass (F2P) results onto the benchmark's full-score scale, then scans the fixed task ranking to select tasks within a specified budget. The selected tasks and scoring rules are frozen, and the system must be baselined in its intended harness before comparisons begin. In a case study of revisions to coding-agent skills and instructions, the adopted version cost less than the initial version, while its higher observed score was not statistically established.
key_results: In the DeepSWE data, only 22 of 113 tasks, or 19.5 percent, had a fifth-percentile one-run correlation of at least 0.50 with the full benchmark score; the median task's fifth-percentile correlation was 0.321. A published-data projection found that nine selected tasks could distinguish two configurations with a projected p-value of 0.0473 at a total cost of USD 113.08, 27.1 times less than the full protocol's recorded cost of USD 3,063.63; this was a projection, not a newly run test. In the target-harness case study, the adopted skills and instructions scored 42.36 percent versus 36.46 percent for the initial version, but the score difference was not statistically significant (p-value 0.326). Recorded cost decreased from USD 4.18 to USD 1.75, a 58.1 percent reduction, and all eight matched task costs were lower for the adopted version.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the selected subset is intentionally narrow and cannot represent every capability of the full benchmark; repeated development on the same tasks may also specialize a system to those tasks or their verifiers. Their experiments do not establish that this selector is better than random, cheapest-first, or median-correlation selection at matched cost, nor do they isolate the effects of fractional scoring, calibration, or weighting. The evidence uses one DeepSWE snapshot, one model family, and one custom harness, and the case-study uncertainty relies on variance transferred from a different harness.
limitations_unstated: The development sequence does not use randomized or counterbalanced assignment of versions to runs, so time-related changes in the evaluation environment could be confounded with version changes. Because only a small number of selected tasks are run in each comparison, task-specific events can also have substantial influence on a development decision even when the aggregate score is calibrated.
future_work_stated: The authors propose matched-cost comparisons with alternative task selectors, nonlinear calibration, equal-weight sensitivity analysis, and methods that account for covariance among related tasks. future_work_unstated: A follow-up study could randomize or counterbalance the order of baseline and candidate runs and repeat both versions to better separate version effects from run and time variation. summary: The paper develops a method for choosing a second-wave experiment to improve a later welfare-maximizing policy choice under constraints. It considers a finite-dimensional parametric model in which policy effects depend on unknown parameters, and assumes that an initial wave of data is already available. The method approximates policy regret with a quadratic function and the information from the experiment with Gaussian estimates, then chooses a design to learn the policy-relevant marginal effects. The authors establish asymptotic optimality under their stated regularity conditions. In a simulation based on the Progresa conditional cash transfer experiment, the tailored second-wave designs substantially reduce expected policy regret compared with repeating the original design.
key_results: In the Progresa simulations, the proposed design reduced expected regret by 50 to 70 per cent relative to the original Progresa design for samples of 500 or 1,000 observations per wave; gains were smaller but remained positive at 250 observations per wave. For example, at the Boys Primary reference point with 500 observations per wave, expected regret was 2.644 percentage points with the Progresa design, 0.957 with the proposed method, and 0.843 with the oracle design. The paper reports that this reduction in regret corresponds to graduation rates about 1.5 percentage points higher than those attainable using policies estimated from the original Progresa experiment. The proposed designs tended to focus on secondary school and use larger experimental subsidies for smaller treatment groups.
key_equations:
Quadratic local regret: \[r(c,b)=c^{\mathsf T}b+\frac{1}{2}c^{\mathsf T}\bar{H}c,\quad c\in G\] The local regret r is the sum of the policy adjustment c dotted with the marginal-effect change b and a quadratic curvature term using the constraint-adjusted curvature matrix H̄, with c restricted to the feasible cone G.

Second-wave design criterion: \[\delta_2^*=\arg\min_{\delta\in\Delta}\mathbb{E}[V(\hat b_2)\mid D_1,\delta]\] The optimal second-wave design δ₂* minimizes the expected approximate policy value V of the posterior mean marginal-effect estimate b̂₂, conditional on the first-wave data D₁ and the chosen design δ, among feasible designs Δ.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their asymptotic optimality result is for Bayes regret and that extending it to minimax regret is left for future work. The method assumes a parametric model, locally strongly concave welfare, and two waves that both grow large; the authors note that these conditions rule out some settings, including binary treatment choice with a linear welfare objective.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation is a simulation based on one structural model and historical Progresa data, with local uncertainty centered on four calibrated reference points; it does not establish that the gains carry over to other settings or to parameter values far from those points. The method's design recommendations depend on the structural model and its estimated information, so misspecification could direct the experiment toward the wrong policy margins; the simulations also report that some optimization replications did not converge.
future_work_stated: The authors leave analysis of minimax regret for future work. They also identify use of their asymptotic representation theorem to study efficiency of estimators and tests in adaptive experiments with continuous treatments as a direction for future research.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the procedure prospectively in a field experiment and test its robustness to misspecified structural models and welfare functions. Further work could also develop operational software and examine sequential or multi-wave implementations under practical budget, ethical, and treatment-assignment constraints.

summary: This paper develops a risk-aware approach to Bayesian optimal experimental design that chooses measurements to improve predictions rather than only estimate model parameters. Its objective combines posterior predictive spread, aggregation across prediction locations, and risk across possible datasets, allowing practitioners to emphasize adverse tails at each stage. The authors construct a differentiable estimator using nested sampling and shared importance weights, then optimize continuous allocation weights over candidate measurement locations. They demonstrate the approach with an analytically tractable linear-Gaussian example and a simulated environmental monitoring problem governed by an advection-diffusion model. In the latter, risk preferences changed sensor allocations, and prediction-focused designs substantially outperformed the parameter-focused baseline on prediction objectives.
key_results: In the advection-dominated environmental monitoring example, the design used 50 candidate sensors and 20 downstream prediction locations, with 4,000 outer and 4,000 inner samples; the authors also assessed design variability using 30 bootstrap resamples. Risk-aware prediction designs concentrated much of their weight on sensor 26, with some objectives assigning it about 0.7, while the expected-information-gain baseline assigned it essentially zero and instead spread weight across other sensors. Under prediction objectives, the parameter-focused baseline performed about as well as random allocations; conversely, prediction-focused designs performed about as well as random allocations under the parameter-focused objective. When comparing different prediction-focused objectives, using a design optimized for another risk preference incurred gaps of up to 20–25%, while the level-two average-value-at-risk choice interpolated between spatial averaging and a worst-component criterion.
key_equations:
Three-level risk-aware prediction objective: \[U(w)=R^{\mathrm{data}}_{p(y\mid w)}\!\left[R^{\mathrm{QoI}}_{\mu}\!\left[\left(D^{\mathrm{pf}}_{p(\theta\mid y,w)}[q_j(\theta)]\right)_{j=1}^{Q}\right]\right]\] The design objective U is evaluated at allocation vector w; the outer risk operator R aggregates across possible datasets y drawn from p, the middle risk operator R aggregates prediction components under measure mu, and the deviation operator D measures uncertainty in component prediction q_j of parameter theta, with j indexing the Q components.

Continuous allocation constraint: \[w_k\geq 0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k=1\] Each candidate condition k has a nonnegative allocation weight w_k, and the weights across all K candidates sum to one.

Advection-diffusion application model: \[\partial_t c+u\cdot\nabla c-D\Delta c=s(x;\theta)\] The contaminant concentration c changes over time t under velocity u and diffusivity D, with source s at location x depending on uncertain parameter theta.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their design parameterization relies on a Gaussian observation model. They also report poor scaling of the nested importance-weighted estimator when sensor noise is extremely large, beyond approximately 100 candidate locations.
limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstration is centered on one simulated environmental transport problem, with a specified source prior, physics model, and candidate layout, so performance across other systems and real monitoring data remains untested. The optimized design is continuous and is converted to integer measurement counts by a rounding rule rather than by directly solving a constrained integer design problem; rounding could change performance at small budgets.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to sequential optimal experimental design and reducing computational cost by replacing importance sampling with amortized generative models, including models based on normalizing flows. They also identify broader support for larger candidate sets and non-Gaussian likelihoods as goals.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation using field measurements and independently specified transport or source models, to test whether the recommended sensor locations remain effective under model mismatch. Further work could also compare the rounding rule with direct integer-budget optimization under practical siting, access, and per-sensor cost constraints.

summary: Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED) is a method for choosing experiments when the goal is to distinguish structural families but persistent nuisance uncertainty can make observations hard to interpret. Instead of maximizing expected information gain (EIG), the method seeks the experiment that can support the smallest nonempty set of structural explanations while controlling the chance of excluding the truth. It allows validity to be required at every nuisance state, on average across nuisance states, or in an adverse upper tail of the nuisance distribution. The authors establish that an experiment can score highly on information measures yet provide poor valid structural resolution when the same observation has different meanings across nuisance states. Simulations and finite-sample calibration studies show that the criterion can change experiment selection and can trade smaller candidate sets for stronger protection against false exclusions.
key_results: In the constrained depositional-architecture benchmark, RAED and model-index EIG clearly selected different experiments in 7 of 16 sensing settings; across all settings, the selected experiments produced mean held-out candidate-set sizes of 2.520 for RAED and 2.658 for EIG. In the constrained Watt reservoir benchmark, the criteria clearly differed in 3 of 16 settings, with mean sizes of 2.092 and 2.111, respectively. In a fluvial benchmark, average-validity RAED selected the symmetric-bank test and achieved a candidate-set size of 1.047, while tail-protected RAED selected a staged-rate test and achieved 1.788; the corresponding worst-five-percent false-exclusion risks were 0.434 and 0.014 for one family, and 0.876 and 0.003 for the other. In methane oxidation, calibration on 10,000 nuisance states per mechanism certified the three familywise tail-risk bounds at 0.048, 0.038, and 0.048 with 95% joint confidence, while the held-out candidate-set size was 1.750.
key_equations:
Observation model: \[Y\mid(M=k,\theta,e)\sim P^e_{k,\theta}\] The observation Y follows probability law P for experiment e, structural family k, and persistent nuisance state theta.

Nuisance-tail validity: \[\rho_{\delta,\mu_k}(L_{k,e})=\inf_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{\delta}\int(L_{k,e}(\theta)-\eta)_+\,\mu_k(d\theta)\right\}\leq\alpha\] The upper-tail risk rho of false-exclusion loss L, under nuisance distribution mu for family k and tail level delta, must not exceed tolerance alpha.

Optimal valid candidate-set size: \[V_e^*(\alpha,\delta)=\inf_{g\in\mathcal{G}_e(\alpha,\delta)}\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim Q_e}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}g_{k,e}(Y)\right]\] For experiment e, V-star is the minimum expected candidate-set size over valid rules g; Q is the predictive observation distribution, K is the number of families, and validity is set by alpha and delta.

Experiment selection: \[e^*(\alpha,\delta)\in\arg\min_{e\in\mathcal{E}}V_e^*(\alpha,\delta)\] The selected experiment e-star minimizes the optimal valid candidate-set size across the available experiment set.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their empirical studies use a restricted learned score family rather than the population-optimal rule. The held-out Watt and WCA results are empirical rather than finite-sample population certificates because their available nuisance samples are too small for the reported positive-tail guarantees. Their finite-sample calibration guarantees cover positive tail levels, not the pointwise-validity endpoint.
limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence comes from simulated benchmarks and declared nuisance distributions, so it does not establish that the selected designs will behave similarly in real experiments or under misspecified physical models. The reservoir studies require large numbers of full-physics simulations, which may make the workflow difficult to apply when simulation or experimental resources are limited.
future_work_stated: The authors propose learning the score model, experiment, and exclusion thresholds more jointly. They also propose sequential designs in which later experiments are chosen to break aliases that remain after earlier observations.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method prospectively in physical experiments and assess how robust its rankings are to changes in the nuisance distribution and model assumptions. It would also be useful to evaluate designs under practical constraints such as budgets, safety limits, and restricted experiment availability.

summary: This paper studies how the purpose of flood monitoring affects where to place a single water-depth sensor. It applies Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) to a simulated flood in metropolitan Detroit, comparing designs that learn model parameters with designs that inform specified flood predictions. The authors use a neural-network surrogate trained on simulations from a six-parameter uncertainty model and evaluate 2,576 candidate locations. They construct expected information gain (EIG) rankings for point, multi-location, regional-average, and regional-maximum predictions, and also examine parameter learning at different observation times. The main finding is that the best location depends on the monitoring objective: point-depth targets favor nearby measurements, while regional targets can favor remote ones.
key_results: The surrogate was trained using 200 flood-model simulations, and its reported root mean square errors for two displayed field comparisons were of order 10^-2 meters. Rankings were evaluated over 2,576 candidate locations, using a common observation-error standard deviation of 0.05 meters. Point predictions had nearby max-EIG locations, whereas regional-average targets had max-EIG locations outside their target regions; regional maximum-depth targets produced both local and remote maxima depending on the region. The authors report qualitative ranking differences rather than numerical EIG values or a numerical ranking against alternative placement methods; public-data feasibility classes counted 782 high, 1,753 medium, and 41 low locations, while context classes counted 938 high, 1,602 medium, and 36 low locations.
key_equations:
Sensor observation model: \[Y=\hat h(\xi,t_o;\Theta)+E,\qquad E\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\epsilon^2)\] Y is the prospective sensor measurement, ĥ is the surrogate water-depth prediction, ξ is the candidate location, t_o is the observation time, Θ is the uncertain parameter vector, E is additive Gaussian observation error, and sigma epsilon is its standard deviation.

Information objective and optimal location: \[U_A(\xi)=I(A;Y\mid\xi),\qquad \xi^*\in\arg\max_{\xi\in D}U_A(\xi)\] U_A is the expected information gain about learning target A at location ξ, I is mutual information, Y is the prospective observation, ξ* is a maximizing location, and D is the candidate set; choosing A as the parameter vector gives parameter-oriented design, while choosing A as a prediction gives goal-oriented design.

Variational estimate for prediction information: \[U_L(\xi;\lambda)=\mathbb E[\log q(A\mid Y,\xi;\lambda)-\log p(A)]\le I(A;Y\mid\xi)\] U_L is the variational lower bound for information about prediction target A at location ξ, lambda parameterizes the conditional density q, Y is the observation, p is the prior-predictive density of A, and I is the mutual information.
limitations_stated: The authors describe the work as an event-specific study of one urban domain, one historical precipitation forcing, and a single-sensor design. It represents uncertainty with six parameters and a neural-network surrogate; uncertain rainfall, topography, boundary conditions, spatial parameter variation, observation-model misspecification, and model discrepancy are not included. The authors also note that repeated calculations are needed to assess ranking stability and that public geospatial proxies require local verification.
limitations_unstated: The results do not establish that the surrogate preserves the EIG rankings: the paper reports field-error comparisons for only two displayed times, rather than direct validation of rankings against the full flood simulator. The study also does not quantify uncertainty in the estimated location rankings or compare the proposed criteria numerically with established placement heuristics or other design criteria.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the workflow to uncertain future rainfall, additional flood events, sensor networks, adaptive schedules, and mobile observations. They also propose broader uncertainty models, validation of the surrogate at high-EIG locations, repeated design calculations to assess ranking stability, stakeholder elicitation of prediction priorities, and field assessment of candidate sites.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test whether the selected sites and their rankings remain reliable when sensor error varies by location or when the flood model is evaluated on independent observed events. The design could also be extended to jointly select multiple sensors under realistic cost, access, power, and maintenance constraints, and then assessed through a field deployment.

summary: The paper extends quantile-stratified (QS) sampling to multivariate distributions, with the aim of generating samples that cover density levels more evenly than independent and identically distributed sampling. For multivariate normal and other elliptically contoured distributions, it stratifies a scalar distance from the distribution’s mode and then generates points on the corresponding density contours. It also describes a general construction for other distributions and an approximate approach, called quasi-QS sampling, when exact contour-based sampling is difficult. The authors assess coverage mainly through plots of ordered log-density values, rather than through numerical performance measures. They report that QS samples have smoother ordered log-density values, while quasi-QS can be computationally costly because it requires a larger base sample.
key_results: For the multivariate normal examples, the plots show smoother ordered log-density values for QS samples than for independent and identically distributed samples of size 30; the scatter plots do not show an obvious visual difference. The paper derives constructions for multivariate normal, multivariate t, multivariate logistic, elliptically contoured, and more general strictly quasi-concave distributions, while noting that some require difficult calculations or contour sampling. In the Dirichlet example, a quasi-QS sample of size 30 uses a multiplier of 40 and a base sample of 1,200 points, compared with an independent and identically distributed sample of size 30 in the plots. The paper concludes that quasi-QS offers space-filling coverage but is not computationally competitive for estimation when direct sampling is available.
key_equations: Stratified distance construction: \[R_s = Q((s-1+U_s)/n), \quad s=1,\ldots,n\] R is the sampled distance, Q is its quantile function, U is a uniform random value within the stratum, n is the sample size, and s indexes the quantile stratum; the construction places one distance in each of the n equiprobable strata.
limitations_stated: The authors state that exact QS sampling can require difficult computation of distance quantiles and simulation from conditional distributions on density contours. They also state that quasi-QS requires a substantially larger base sample and is computationally inefficient relative to direct sampling for estimation.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is primarily visual and illustrative; the paper does not provide systematic numerical comparisons of coverage, estimation error, or computational cost across dimensions and distributions. The usefulness of the contour-based design also depends on knowing the target density and being able to simulate correctly on its contours, which may be difficult in constrained or practically sampled settings.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future work could benchmark coverage and estimation performance against Latin hypercube sampling and other space-filling methods across a broader set of dimensions, sample sizes, and distributions. It could also develop implementations for practical constraints and test whether sequential or constrained sampling can retain the stated coverage benefits in real experiments.

summary: The paper develops a framework for estimating microscopic Hamiltonian parameters and planning measurements for the quantum magnet NiPS3. It uses a differentiable neural surrogate to predict spectra from parameter values for powder and single-crystal inelastic neutron scattering. Bayesian inference represents uncertainty in the parameters, while an observation metric identifies parameter combinations that the spectra constrain weakly or strongly. A posterior-based design rule selects subsequent single-crystal orientations where predicted spectra vary most across the current parameter distribution. The authors demonstrate the approach with simulations and processed experimental spectra, finding that powder measurements can inform subsequent crystal measurements and that joint inference retains uncertainty rather than returning only one fitted model.
key_results: The surrogate was trained on 20,000 sampled Hamiltonians; the paper notes that a grid search using a comparable budget of 18,000 forward calculations would yield only about three grid points per parameter in the nine-parameter model. In a benchmark of 10 trials, Bayesian optimal experimental design reached a low-error regime within the first few measurements, compared with slower improvement from sequential acquisition; random acquisition had a similar mean result but greater variability. In the simulated comparison, powder-only estimates had the largest errors for most parameters, while adding powder information narrowed posterior distributions for some weakly constrained parameters but did not uniformly lower point-estimation error relative to single-crystal-only measurements. For the experimental comparison, the selected posterior Hamiltonian had powder and single-crystal Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.913 and 0.601, compared with 0.905 and 0.596 for the reference Hamiltonian.

Observation metric: \[G(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\Omega)}[\nabla_\theta S(x;\theta)\nabla_\theta S(x;\theta)^T]\] G is the local observation metric, theta is the Hamiltonian parameter vector, the expectation averages over coordinates x sampled uniformly from the accessible domain Omega, S is predicted intensity, nabla is the gradient with respect to theta, and T denotes transpose.

Orientation utility and selection: \[U(\psi)=\frac{1}{N_\psi}\sum_{x\in\Omega_\psi}\mathrm{SD}_{\theta\sim P}[S_{\mathrm{sc}}(x;\theta)],\quad \psi_{\mathrm{next}}=\arg\max_\psi U(\psi)\] U is the utility at rotation angle psi, Npsi is the number of sampled coordinates in the accessible domain Omega sub psi, SD is the posterior standard deviation under distribution P over theta, S sub sc is the predicted single-crystal intensity, and psi next is the angle chosen to maximize utility.
limitations_stated: The surrogate is limited by the assumed Hamiltonian family, the fidelity of the forward solver, and the coverage and computational cost of its training data. The posterior quantifies uncertainty only within the assumed model class, so missing interactions, disorder, domains, or instrumental effects may appear as broad uncertainty or systematic residuals. The powder spectrum also relies on model-dependent source separation and enhancement, and the authors leave systematic comparison of alternative powder-processing methods for future work.
limitations_unstated: The adaptive orientation strategy is demonstrated in simulation rather than through a live experimental campaign, so its practical performance under real instrument operations is not established. The validation is limited to one material and these two related measurement modalities, which does not show how well the framework transfers to other materials or substantially different observation types.
future_work_stated: The authors propose incorporating surrogate uncertainty, for example with Bayesian neural networks or ensembles, and using residuals across modalities to diagnose model inadequacy. They also suggest hierarchical Bayesian models for separating measurement uncertainty from material heterogeneity, extending design to other probes and experimental controls, and ultimately supporting closed-loop laboratory experiments.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to run the adaptive design policy in a real instrument workflow and assess it under practical constraints such as acquisition time, instrument limits, and sample availability. Further validation could compare its uncertainty reduction with alternative design criteria across multiple materials and measurement modalities.

summary: The paper proposes Target-Weighted Neyman Allocation (TWNA), a design for estimating group average treatment effects (GATEs) when an experiment’s population has different group proportions from the population where results will be used. Its objective is to minimize estimation error weighted by each group’s share in that target population. The design first runs a balanced pilot to estimate outcome variability by group and treatment arm, then allocates the final sample across groups and treatment arms using those estimates and the target shares. It also gives rules for uncertain target shares and a stabilized version for noisy or heavy-tailed pilot data. In simulations and benchmarks using real covariates with simulated outcomes, the design often improves on standard allocation alternatives and approaches the oracle design as pilot estimates become more reliable.
key_results: In the simulations with a final sample of 5,000 and a pilot of 1,000, TWNA’s relative target-weighted mean squared error was within 0.005 of the oracle in every scenario; in the aligned shift-and-variance scenario it was 0.693, compared with 1.000 for uniform balanced allocation. In the calibrated benchmark using real covariates and simulated outcomes, TWNA scored 0.837, compared with 0.908 for the Hahn–Hirano–Karlan plug-in design and 0.843 for the oracle. On the infant health development program benchmark, TWNA scored 0.884 compared with 1.017 for the Hahn–Hirano–Karlan design and 0.931 for the oracle. Average design regret fell by 93.5% as pilot size increased from 100 to 1,000; in the main simulation interval comparison, the target-weighted mean interval width was 0.304 for TWNA and 0.324 for uniform allocation at a final sample of 5,000 and a pilot of 1,000.
key_equations:
Target-weighted design criterion: \[B_Q(\rho,e)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{q_k}{\rho_k}\left(\frac{\sigma_{1k}^{2}}{e_k}+\frac{\sigma_{0k}^{2}}{1-e_k}\right)\] The criterion B_Q is the leading variance measure; q_k is group k’s target-population share, rho_k is its experimental sample share, sigma_1k and sigma_0k are the outcome standard deviations in the treatment and control arms, e_k is the treatment probability in that group, and k and K denote the group index and number of groups.

Oracle treatment and group allocation: \[e_k^*=\frac{\sigma_{1k}}{\sigma_{1k}+\sigma_{0k}},\qquad \rho_k^*=\frac{\sqrt{q_k}(\sigma_{1k}+\sigma_{0k})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\sqrt{q_\ell}(\sigma_{1\ell}+\sigma_{0\ell})}\] The starred e_k and rho_k are the optimal treatment probability and sample share for group k; sigma_1k and sigma_0k are its arm-specific outcome standard deviations, q_k is its target share, and ell indexes the sum over all K groups.
limitations_stated: The theory uses fixed-group, finite-dimensional asymptotics and assumes groups are pre-specified. It addresses composition shift, assuming group-specific effects transport, rather than broader changes within groups. The batch analysis does not model recruitment costs, capacity constraints, interference, or multi-wave adaptation.
limitations_unstated: The real-covariate benchmarks pair public covariates with simulated potential outcomes, so they do not demonstrate performance in a completed real randomized experiment. The estimated allocation depends on pilot cells being informative about group-by-arm variability; rare outcomes or extreme values can make those estimates unstable, and the robust version’s performance is demonstrated in constructed stress tests rather than a broad set of field trials.
future_work_stated: The authors identify relaxing the design’s stated scope and learning groups instead of fixing them in advance as natural next steps.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective evaluation in randomized experiments with observed outcomes, including tests of whether group effects remain transportable under within-group population changes. Further work could also study how to choose pilot size and allocation when recruitment costs or minimum group sample requirements constrain the experiment.

summary: The paper develops a sampling-calibrated stratum-imbalance Gaussian approximation (SIGA-S) and a randomization-calibrated version (SIGA-R) for power and sample-size evaluation in two-arm clinical trials using Pocock–Simon biased-coin minimization. Both procedures replace repeated inner-loop regeneration of treatment assignments with reusable allocation-only simulations. Their construction separates a treatment statistic into a joint-stratum imbalance component and an orthogonal within-stratum component. The sampling-calibrated procedure targets repeated-sampling inference for a marginal treatment effect, while the randomization-calibrated procedure targets the conditional distribution of a prespecified fixed-score randomization test. Simulations show close agreement with the corresponding reference tests while substantially reducing computation.
key_results: Across 56 practical simulation scenarios, the largest difference from the reference randomization test was 0.42 percentage points for SIGA-S and 0.32 percentage points for SIGA-R. The practical scenarios had mean randomization-to-sampling variance ratios from 1.000 to 1.042; in deliberately strong sensitivity scenarios, the mean ratio reached about 1.19, and SIGA-R tracked the reference test more closely than SIGA-S. For 100,000 analyses, reported SIGA-S runtimes ranged from 0.050 to 2.259 minutes, compared with 113.04 to 2,625.76 minutes for nested rerandomization. In the trial-inspired example, estimated power was 81.48% for unadjusted SIGA-S, 81.44% for unadjusted SIGA-R, and 81.28% for the reference test; total method-specific times were 0.98, 0.85, and 406.36 minutes, respectively.
key_equations: Variance gap between the two inferential targets: \[v_R(b)-v_S(b)=\frac{1}{16}d(b)^{\mathsf T}\left(\Psi_D-\Pi\right)d(b)\] The conditional randomization variance v_R(b) minus the repeated-sampling variance v_S(b) equals one-sixteenth times the quadratic form of the stratum-deviation vector d(b) with the difference between paired-path covariance Ψ_D and stratum-probability matrix Π.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their results require explicit allocation-limit conditions, and they do not establish the required one-path stability condition for the full class of positive joint-profile distributions. They also note that SIGA-R reproduces any weak-null size distortion of the reference randomization test rather than correcting it, and that finite-sample or discrete-tail discrepancies can remain.
limitations_unstated: The practical benchmarks cover a limited set of simulated settings, principally designs with two or five binary minimization factors and the specified absolute-imbalance rule, so performance in other allocation rules or more complex trial structures is not demonstrated. SIGA-R also relies on stratum-specific boundary deviations supplied by the design model or consistently estimated, which may be difficult to specify reliably in practice.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess the procedures under additional minimization rules, correlated or higher-dimensional factors, and operational constraints such as unequal allocation or restricted enrollment. Evaluation using participant-level data from real trials, together with methods that update calibration during sequential planning, could test robustness beyond the paper's simulated examples.

summary: The paper introduces SCOPE, a benchmark for assessing whether large language models (LLMs) can design complete experimental plans from a research description and method, without access to the original paper’s experiments. It evaluates plans across six parts: main experiments, ablations, analyses, datasets, baselines, and metrics. The benchmark contains 300 research tasks drawn from papers in 19 areas, and scores plans against the original papers’ designs using a rubric and penalties for critical errors. The authors find that models are generally weak at selecting concrete experimental resources, and that unstructured web search does not reliably improve plans. They also introduce OptED, a staged workflow with search, structured editing tools, and behavioral rules, which improves scores across the evaluated models.
key_results: Across seven mainstream models, the average benchmark score was 14.81 out of 30; Claude 4.5 Sonnet scored highest at 18.62, while Grok-4 scored 12.55. Low-level configuration scores were 2.78 points below high-level planning on average, and no model scored above 3 out of 5 in any low-level dimension. Search produced no statistically significant total-score difference for five of seven models, and reduced GPT-5.2’s score from 18.22 without search to 16.77 with search. Compared with the search-enabled baseline, OptED improved high-level scores by 1.6 points and low-level scores by 1.2 points on average across six models; DeepSeek-V3.2 gained 4.22 points and Grok-4 gained 3.67. The authors also report human-to-judge agreement values from 0.726 to 0.803 across the six scoring dimensions.
key_equations: Total benchmark score: \[T=\sum_{j=1}^{6}s_j\] T is the total score, j indexes the six evaluation dimensions, and s_j is the score for dimension j on a scale from 0 to 5.
limitations_stated: The benchmark covers computer science and artificial intelligence research from three machine-learning venues, so its results do not directly represent experimental design in natural sciences involving physical or laboratory procedures. It assesses a one-shot plan and does not test execution, result interpretation, or iterative redesign. The authors also note that the sampled research areas are unevenly represented and that converting papers into structured tasks can lose nuance despite verification and quality review.
limitations_unstated: The benchmark’s reference is the design in each source paper, so a scientifically sound alternative plan may score poorly if it differs from that reference. Most scores rely on one language-model judge, and the human agreement check covers a sample of 60 tasks, leaving uncertainty about scoring consistency across the full benchmark. The paper evaluates plans rather than whether they can be executed successfully or produce useful experimental evidence in practice.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the benchmark to natural-science experimental workflows, including their physical procedures and resource constraints. They also suggest multi-turn planning tasks in which models receive simulated experimental outcomes and revise their plans.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess plans by having independent research teams execute a subset and report feasibility, reproducibility, and the usefulness of the resulting evidence. Future evaluations could also compare multiple independent expert raters and test whether high benchmark scores predict better real-world experimental decisions.

summary: This paper develops a policy-aware way to design and analyze online A/B tests of personalized policies. It targets estimation of the average treatment effect while reducing the variance of estimates when the policies select the same actions in some contexts. The method treats randomized assignment between the two policies as a mixture policy, then uses counterfactual weighting to focus estimation on where the policies differ. The authors also derive a traffic allocation that minimizes estimator variance, propose a reward-model training objective, and extend the approach to ranking policies. Theoretical results and simulations show that the method can reduce variance relative to standard difference-in-means testing, especially when policy overlap is substantial.
key_results: The authors prove that their policy-aware inverse propensity estimator has variance no greater than the difference-in-means estimator for any nonzero traffic split, with strict improvement when overlapping actions have residual outcome variance. In a simulated asymmetric policy comparison, the variance-minimizing allocation assigned about 0.81 of traffic to the exploratory policy and reduced variance by about 18% versus an even split. In a heterogeneous simulation, the proposed reward-model training objective reduced variance by about 75% relative to the policy-aware inverse propensity baseline and about 8% relative to the doubly robust estimator; reported mean squared errors were 0.0100, 0.0027, and 0.0025, respectively. The single-action simulations covered action spaces from 10 to 5,000 actions, while the ranking simulation used 100 items and rankings of 25 positions; the baselined ranking estimator reduced variance across the tested policy-divergence range.
key_equations:
Mixture policy for randomized assignment: \[\pi_0(a|x)=p\pi(a|x)+(1-p)\pi'(a|x)\] Here, π₀ is the logging mixture policy, π and π′ are the two policies being compared, p is the traffic fraction assigned to π, x is context, and a is an action.

Policy-aware importance weight: \[w_{\Delta}(x,a)=\frac{\pi(a|x)-\pi'(a|x)}{\pi_0(a|x)}\] Here, wΔ is the policy-aware importance weight, π and π′ are the compared policies, π₀ is their logging mixture, x is context, and a is an action.
limitations_stated: The empirical evaluation uses synthetic simulations, which require simplifying assumptions and do not establish exact real-world variance reductions. The estimators require policy probabilities, which may be costly or numerically unstable to compute for some models and large action spaces. The allocation analysis also relies on stationarity of the context distribution, and its analytical solution for the inverse propensity estimator assumes homoskedastic outcomes.
limitations_unstated: The simulations do not test how the design behaves when users influence one another or when outcomes are correlated across repeated observations from the same user. The paper establishes variance advantages in its settings, but does not report a real deployment that tests implementation demands, operational constraints on traffic allocation, or the resulting impact on experiment duration.
future_work_stated: The authors propose estimating a full cross-rank covariance matrix to obtain a globally optimal joint baseline for ranking. They also identify dynamically adaptive allocation that converges to the optimal traffic split, evaluating distributional treatment effects, and applying the proposed reward-model objective to offline policy learning as future directions.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the method with practical allocation constraints, including minimum traffic requirements and limits on how quickly traffic can be changed. Validation in live experiments, as well as evaluation under user-level clustering or interference, would help establish when the simulated gains translate into shorter and reliable experiments.

summary: The paper develops an order-of-addition (OofA) approach to prompt engineering: it uses designed experiments to measure how prompt component order and wording affect a large language model (LLM). The demonstration task is to generate two-level fractional factorial designs with maximum resolution and minimum aberration. The authors vary prompt-element order and, in some experiments, wording, then model the probability of a successful design using logistic regression with pairwise-ordering effects. They use fractional OofA designs to study many prompt configurations with fewer tests than a full ordering factorial would require. In confirmation runs, optimized prompts substantially improved success for both tested LLMs on selected design-generation tasks.
key_results: For the first experiment, the authors tested 48 combinations of order and wording, with 40 repetitions for each of six tasks involving 16-run designs with seven to 12 factors; both factors affected gpt-4.1 success, and the wording of the factor-count and run-count phrase was particularly influential for four tasks. For the 16-run, nine-factor task, an 80-test design with 20 repetitions per test was used instead of the 240-test full design; a follow-up test found 98.3% success for the selected prompt versus 11.7% for the base prompt. For gemini-2.5-flash on the 16-run, seven-factor task, the selected prompts achieved 100% success in confirmation runs, compared with about 35% for the original prompt. The fitted interaction models had McFadden pseudo R-squared values of 0.773 for the gpt-4.1 task and 0.789 for the Gemini task; the paper also reports that newer GPT and Gemini models showed order effects in a smaller five-sequence test.

Pairwise-ordering coding: \[z_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&i\text{ precedes }j,\\-1,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\] The symbol z_ij is the pairwise-ordering code for components i and j, taking the value 1 when i precedes j and minus 1 otherwise.

Generalized word length measure: \[A_k=n^{-2}\left\|\mathbf{1}_n^{\mathsf T}X_k\right\|_2^2\] A_k is the generalized word length value for interaction order k, n is the number of design runs, 1_n is a column of n ones, and X_k contains the contrast vectors for the k-factor interactions.

Fractional ordering-factorial construction: \[F_{N,q}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{N_f},\quad \mathbf{1}_N\otimes X\] F_{N,q} is an N-run order-of-addition design for q components, X is an N_f-run two-level design for component versions, 1_N and 1_{N_f} are columns of ones of the indicated lengths, and the Kronecker products combine ordering and version settings.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the reduced logistic model with interactions is less interpretable than the main-effects model. limitations_unstated: The demonstrations cover selected tasks and a small set of LLMs, so the results do not establish that the same prompt effects will hold for other models, tasks, or engineering settings. future_work_stated: The authors propose developing OofA designs and models for nested prompt components, such as phrases within a larger instruction element. They also propose custom optimal OofA designs for logistic pairwise-ordering models and applications to other tasks, including multiple-choice benchmarks and few-shot examples.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test whether the optimized prompts remain effective across model versions, nonzero sampling settings, and independently run replications. It could also compare the method’s cost and predictive performance with alternative prompt-search methods on practical engineering tasks beyond the design-generation examples.

summary: The paper introduces a fine-tuning method for large language models that aims to improve sequential information gathering without doing extra design optimization at inference time. It trains question-asking policies to maximize expected information gain while also rewarding successful completion of the task. The method estimates information gain using plausible target entities and the model’s predicted likelihoods for possible answers, then uses these rewards in multi-turn policy training. The authors train on the 20 Questions game and evaluate on held-out animal and plant categories and on the medical information-seeking benchmark MediQ. The method improves success on the 20 Questions task, greatly reduces inference time relative to an inference-time design baseline, and shows some transfer to MediQ at the 7-billion-parameter scale.
key_results: On the 7-billion-parameter model, success increased from 7.6% to 21.0% for animals and from 6.8% to 16.6% for plants; on the 14-billion-parameter model, it increased from 35.0% to 39.2% for animals and from 11.8% to 13.6% for plants. The method outperformed the inference-time Bayesian design baseline in two of the four model-category settings, while the baseline had higher success in the other two. Inference time was approximately the same as for the base model, whereas the inference-time baseline took 25.7 to 36.1 times as long per episode. On MediQ, the 7-billion-parameter model’s accuracy rose from 46.7% to 47.6%, and its voluntary accuracy rose from 50.1% to 51.8%; the reported general language benchmark scores showed no meaningful change after fine-tuning.

limitations_stated: The authors report weaker behavioral adaptation for the 14-billion-parameter model and mixed MediQ results at that scale, including slightly lower voluntary accuracy and marginally higher overconfidence. They do not provide a separate limitations section.
limitations_unstated: Evaluation of the 20 Questions task uses only two held-out categories and averages over five episodes, so results may not represent broader target domains or run-to-run variation. The training game relies on a language-model oracle and the medical evaluation uses a simulated patient, leaving performance with real people, noisy observations, and operational constraints untested.
future_work_stated: The authors propose separating the effects of the information-gain and outcome rewards, evaluating broader sequential information-gathering benchmarks, and extending the method to reasoning models that generate intermediate reasoning steps.
future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test other experimental-design objectives and models with noisy or costly outcomes, as well as practical constraints such as limited measurement budgets. Testing sequential deployment with real users or experiments, and validating whether the learned policy remains effective as observations accumulate over time, would clarify its practical transfer.
