summary: The paper develops a framework for sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design in dynamic systems described by partial differential equations with uncertain, high-dimensional parameters. Its objective is to select experiments adaptively to maximize expected information gain about those parameters. The authors test it on simulated tumor growth, choosing four MRI observation days from ten candidate days. In that example, the method reduces uncertainty and achieves a reported amortized computational speedup of 180 times compared with finite element calculations.
key_results: For the tumor model, the parameter and full-state observation each had 14,003 dimensions; the authors reduced both to 64 dimensions with reported projection errors below 1%. Across the evaluated time points, the latent attention neural operator's observation prediction error decreased from 8.05% to 2.27%, and its reduced Jacobian error ranged from 4.05% to 1.57%; the neural ordinary differential equation's recursive observation error reached 95.91% at day 10, while the projected neural network's error reached 89.65% at day 6. The operator's mean relative error for maximum a posteriori estimates was 1.52% for daily observations and 1.31% for the sparse observation set, and the reported mean relative eigenvalue error was 0.8%. For information-gain evaluation, its online calculation took 16.0 seconds versus 3,148.9 seconds with the finite element method, a 197-times speedup; including offline data generation and training, the authors report an amortized 180-times speedup. The selected adaptive observation days were 2, 7, 9, and 10, compared with days 2, 8, 9, and 10 for the static design and days 2, 4, 6, and 8 for the uniform design; the adaptive design produced the smallest reported parameter uncertainty in this simulated example.

Assumed dynamic system: \[\partial_t u(t,x)+R(u(t,x),m(x))=0\] Here u is the system state, t is time, x is position, R is the differential operator governing the system, and m is the uncertain parameter field.

Derivative-informed neural-network training loss: \[\ell(\theta)=\sum_{n=1}^{N_t}(\|\beta_F^{(n)}-N^F_\theta(\beta_m^{(n)})\|^2+\|\beta_J^{(n)}-\nabla_\beta N^J_\theta(\beta_m^{(n)})\|^2)\] Here ℓ is the training loss, θ denotes network parameters, N_t is the number of training samples, n indexes a sample, β_F and β_J are its reduced observable and Jacobian coefficients, β_m is its reduced parameter coefficient, N^F and N^J are networks predicting the observable and Jacobian, and ∇_β denotes differentiation with respect to β.
limitations_stated: The authors note that their approach may be less suitable when the posterior is not well approximated by a Laplace approximation or when the posterior covariance is not low rank. They identify variational inference as a possible approach for those cases.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is limited to one simulated tumor-growth application with a specified model, prior, and observation setup, so the reported performance does not establish accuracy for real MRI data or other physical systems. future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring variational inference when Laplace approximation is inadequate or the posterior covariance is not low rank. future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the method with real clinical imaging data and compare its selected schedules with operational constraints such as available scan windows and patient burden. summary: Inspection-Guided Randomization (IGR) is a framework for restricting the treatment assignments available in a randomized experiment. It is designed for experiments with different objectives and estimands, including trials with interference and experiments that form groups with specified compositions. Researchers define design desiderata, translate them into inspection metrics, combine the metrics into a fitness score, and filter a pool of candidate assignments. They evaluate and adapt the resulting design, pre-register accepted assignments and their probabilities, and then randomly select an assignment for the experiment. Simulations show that this approach can improve estimation relative to benchmark randomization designs, although the gains depend on the chosen metrics and restrictions.
key_results: In the interference simulation, the researchers enumerated 100,000 candidate allocations and retained 500, the top 0.5 percent by fitness score. With mirror allocations included and interference weighted at 0.75, the difference-in-means estimator’s absolute bias was 88.31 percent of the CR benchmark’s, with reported variation of 0.56 percentage points; at an interference weight of 1, it was 86.18 percent, with variation of 0.37 percentage points. At an interference weight of 0.125, the difference-in-means variance was 0.003, compared with 0.61 for the CR benchmark; at a weight of 0.875, it rose to 1.01. In the group-formation simulation, IGR with balance and composition criteria reduced RMSE to 56.82, 55.52, and 56.39 percent of the group-formation-randomization benchmark across the three group comparisons using the maximum Mahalanobis criterion; using the sum of maximum absolute standardized mean differences reduced it to 48.83, 47.61, and 47.82 percent.
key_equations:

IGR assignment mechanism: \[P_{\mathrm{IGR}}(Z=z)=\begin{cases}p_z,&z\in Z_{\mathrm{pool}},\ r(f(z,X))=1,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] The probability under the IGR assignment mechanism P_IGR of drawing allocation z is p_z when z is in the candidate pool Z_pool and passes restriction rule r applied to fitness score f using covariates X; otherwise its probability is zero.
limitations_stated: The authors note that IGR uses a hand-crafted fitness function, which may be an imperfect proxy for the true conditional mean-squared error. They also emphasize that choosing and evaluating appropriate metrics and restrictions requires substantial analyst and domain-expert effort, and that flawed choices may produce poor designs.
limitations_unstated: The reported performance evidence comes from simulations rather than a real experiment, and the interference results rely on a particular simulated network and exposure model. The examples use 100,000 candidate allocations and a 0.5 percent acceptance threshold, so the paper does not establish how well the approach scales or performs when the candidate pool misses important assignments or real-world constraints limit feasible randomization.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing theory about how closely the fitness function must approximate conditional mean-squared error to improve estimates. They also suggest using pilot studies, earlier waves, or historical experiments to refine the fitness function, and developing accessible implementation software, potentially with an interactive dashboard.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs in real experiments and assess their sensitivity to misspecified interference networks, exposure thresholds, and outcome models. It could also develop and evaluate ways to incorporate practical constraints, such as treatment-delivery capacity or participant availability, while retaining a sufficiently broad set of randomized assignments.

summary: The paper develops an online framework for choosing among candidate adaptive treatment-allocation designs during an experiment. The framework estimates these outcomes with targeted maximum likelihood estimation and selects the candidate with the highest lower confidence bound. Its motivating application compares adaptive designs that use short-term surrogate outcomes to guide treatment assignment while the long-term outcome is still being collected. Simulations show that the framework can favor early or later surrogates as their value changes over time, while providing estimates with approximately nominal confidence-interval coverage.
key_results: In the main simulations, the authors compared seven designs over 500 runs, with 50 enrollment times and 50 participants enrolled at each time; treatment probabilities were capped at 90%. At time 50 in Scenario 2, the proposed design's average regret was 0.025, close to 0.024 for the design using the best early surrogate and below 0.120 for equal-probability randomization. In Scenario 1, its regret was 0.080 at time 50, compared with 0.071 for the best fixed candidate; the proposed design's regret became second-lowest from time 23. In simulations inspired by the ADAPT-R trial, using data from 215 participants to generate outcomes and 500 simulated runs, the final expected outcome was 0.576 for the proposed design, compared with 0.579 for the best fixed early-surrogate design and 0.565 for equal-probability randomization. Across the reported simulation settings, the estimator generally had low bias and confidence-interval coverage near the nominal 95% level.

Online candidate selection: \[j_t^{*}=\arg\max_{j}\left(\hat\Psi_{t,j}-z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\hat\sigma_{t,j}}{\sqrt{n_t}}\right)\] At time t, j*_t is the candidate design j with the largest lower confidence bound, using its estimated value Ψ-hat, estimated standard error σ-hat, sample size n_t, confidence-level quantile z, and tail probability α.

summary: This article surveys optimal experimental design: methods for deciding what data to collect to support estimation, prediction, or other goals. It covers classical criteria for linear models as well as Bayesian and decision-based criteria that apply to nonlinear and non-Gaussian models. The authors review ways to estimate design criteria and optimize designs, including Monte Carlo, density approximation, dimension reduction, combinatorial selection, and continuous optimization. They also explain sequential design policies that adapt later experiments to earlier observations while accounting for future experiments. The article synthesizes methods and open challenges rather than proposing one new design algorithm or reporting a single winning design.
key_results: The review reports that the standard nested Monte Carlo approach to estimating expected information gain has a mean-square error rate of order computational budget to the power negative two-thirds; reaching mean-square error equal to tolerance squared requires effort of order tolerance to the power negative three. It contrasts this with multilevel nested Monte Carlo, which is reported to reduce the effort to order tolerance to the power negative two. The article also describes a linear-Gaussian example where finite-sample bias in the standard estimator obscures the true best design, while multiple importance sampling performs better without guaranteeing stable maxima at finite sample sizes. These are results from methods and studies covered by the review, not a head-to-head evaluation conducted by the authors.
key_equations:
Expected utility design criterion: \[U(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_{Y,\Theta\mid\xi}[u(\xi,Y,\Theta)]\] The expected utility U for design xi averages the utility u over observations Y and parameters Theta under the model for that design.

Information gain in parameters: \[I(Y;\Theta\mid\xi)=\mathbb{E}_{Y,\Theta\mid\xi}\left[\log\frac{p(Y\mid\Theta,\xi)}{p(Y\mid\xi)}\right]\] The mutual information I between observations Y and parameters Theta for design xi is the expected logarithm of the likelihood density divided by the marginal observation density p.

summary: The paper develops Constrained Row Screening (CRowS), a method for screening many compounds by placing pools of compounds in wells while limiting the number in each well. It targets supersaturated designs for a main-effects model in which the number of compounds can equal or exceed the number of wells. The design is constructed to reduce the average squared off-diagonal values of its information matrix, subject to the pool-size limit, using a coordinate-exchange search. The observed responses are analyzed with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) to identify active compounds. Simulations favor CRowS over one-compound-one-well screening and the existing poolHiTS method, and laboratory experiments identify a known inhibitor in three of four screens.
key_results: In simulations, CRowS had higher true positive rates than one-compound-one-well screening and poolHiTS across the design settings studied, while poolHiTS often had difficulty controlling false positive rates. The compared pooled designs used 88 to 99 wells to screen 96 to 192 compounds, whereas one-compound-one-well screening used one well per compound. The authors constructed designs using 100 randomized algorithm starts and selected the best criterion value. In the laboratory demonstration with 31 compounds, CRowS identified the known inhibitor in three of four experiments, including the experiment allowing 10 compounds per well; it missed the inhibitor when the limit was five per well.

Row-constrained design construction: \[\min_{X\in\{-1,1\}^{n\times k}} UE(s^2)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{j=1}^{k}X_{ij}\le 2c-k,\ i=1,\ldots,n\] The design matrix X has n rows and k columns with entries minus one or plus one, and each row must satisfy the bound set by maximum pool size c.
limitations_stated: The authors state that constructing designs with both the number of wells and compounds in the thousands may take on the order of days. The method may reduce the number of plates relative to one-compound-one-well screening but can require more liquid handling because each well contains multiple compounds. They also report that synergistic interactions can reduce the ability to detect active compounds, and that unpredictable compound interactions require further investigation.
limitations_unstated: The physical demonstration covers one enzyme assay, one known inhibitor, and 30 inert compounds, so it provides limited evidence about performance across different assays, compound libraries, and hit prevalence. future_work_stated: The authors propose testing the method in larger-scale screens and investigating ways to reduce false positives, including use as a secondary screen. They also propose tightening the theoretical bounds and characterizing when row constraints are guaranteed to be tight.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare design criteria that directly optimize hit recovery or false-positive control, rather than relying on the information-matrix criterion as a proxy. future_work_unstated: Further work could test robustness to misspecified priors, noise distributions, and forward models, and validate the method with prospectively collected experimental data. summary: The paper develops a sequential, adaptive method for choosing interventions to discover a causal graph while using fewer interventional samples. It assumes discrete variables, an available faithful observational distribution, and a true directed acyclic graph within the Markov equivalence class represented by the completed partially directed acyclic graph. The method constructs a graph-separating set of intervention targets, enumerates candidate causal effects, and adaptively allocates samples to interventions that best distinguish competing graph structures. It stops when an information-based rule meets a user-specified confidence level. The authors prove a problem-dependent sample-complexity result and report better simulation and benchmark performance than the comparison methods.
key_results: The theoretical analysis shows that the exact algorithm is sound for any confidence level one minus delta and asymptotically matches the stated lower bound, with expected sample size scaling as log of one over delta divided by the instance-dependent information rate. The practical version is also shown to be sound and has an asymptotic information rate no better than the exact version. In simulations on complete chordal graphs with 5, 6, and 7 vertices and random chordal graphs with 10 vertices at density parameters 0.1, 0.15, and 0.2, the authors report that their method achieves lower structural Hamming distance with fewer samples than random interventions, directed clique tree active learning, adaptive sensitivity search, and greedy interventional equivalence search. On the Sachs benchmark, with 13 nodes and 17 edges, the method likewise has lower structural Hamming distance for the same number of samples. A supplementary experiment over 50 generated graphs starting from an incorrect completed partially directed acyclic graph reports faster convergence in sample count, although the methods do not reach zero structural Hamming distance.

limitations_unstated: The experiments use randomly generated chordal graphs and one benchmark network, so the reported comparisons do not establish performance across a broad range of graph structures or real intervention settings. future_work_unstated: Future work could incorporate intervention costs and practical constraints into the allocation criterion, and test whether the resulting designs remain efficient. summary: The paper develops an optimal experimental design (OED) method for nonlinear Bayesian inverse problems, with the goal of choosing sensor locations that reduce posterior uncertainty. It replaces the costly nonlinear forward model with a linear surrogate and uses the Bayesian approximation error (BAE) approach to account for the surrogate’s error. The authors prove that the resulting A-optimal objective is asymptotically independent of the chosen linear surrogate, which allows them to use even the zero map and work from parameter and data samples. They extend the method to designs for primary parameters when other model inputs are uncertain, and use a greedy procedure to select sensors. Simulations for subsurface flow and tsunami source reconstruction show that uncertainty-aware designs can outperform random designs and designs that ignore model error.
key_results: For subsurface flow, the study used 10,000 prior samples to form the error statistics and selected up to 20 sensors from 1,600 candidates; the resulting joint design had lower posterior covariance trace than 100 randomly chosen designs, and it also performed better than random designs in the reported comparison using the full nonlinear model. For marginal estimation of boundary flux, the uncertainty-aware design outperformed the design that ignored permeability uncertainty across the cases considered. In the tsunami study, designs were computed from 500 samples, with 44 fault patches and 214 candidate sensor locations; the uncertainty-aware design reduced posterior covariance trace and average posterior-mean error compared with uncertainty-unaware and random designs. With 13 sensors, relative errors for slip magnitudes were approximately 0.26 for the uncertainty-aware design and 0.44 for the uncertainty-unaware design; for slip rakes, they were approximately 0.13 and 0.17, respectively. The authors also report that reasonable tsunami designs could be obtained with as few as 50 costly forward-model runs, although more samples produced more effective designs.

BAE total-error covariance: \[\Gamma_{\eta|v}=\Gamma_e+\Gamma_{\epsilon\epsilon}-C_{\epsilon v}C_{vv}^{-1}C_{v\epsilon}\] Gamma_eta_given_v is the total-error covariance conditional on v, Gamma_e is the measurement-noise covariance, Gamma_epsilon_epsilon is the approximation-error covariance, C_epsilon_v and C_v_epsilon are error-parameter cross-covariances, and C_v_v is the prior parameter covariance.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the approach may be unsuitable for highly nonlinear parameter-to-observable maps or non-Gaussian priors, and that effective designs for the original problem are not guaranteed in those cases. Their implementation explicitly forms covariance matrices or operators, which may become infeasible for large problems.
limitations_unstated: The designs are selected from fixed candidate sensor sets and use a greedy search, so the results do not establish global optimality or address placement constraints beyond the specified candidates and sensor count. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying control variates to reduce the number of costly model runs needed to estimate error statistics. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the approach on real sensor data and under practical placement, cost, and reliability constraints. key_results: The study conducted 1,920 analyses across 16 benchmark problems, using 3 surrogate types and 4 enrichment methods, with 10 runs per strategy. PCK had the highest overall accuracy: it met the target error tolerance in 84% of cases at tolerance 0.05 and 98% at tolerance 0.25; it also most often required the fewest simulator evaluations among the surrogate types. Against the uniform MD design, AL was not consistently more efficient: for GP, reported efficiency changes ranged from 0% to 67%, while they ranged from negative 43% to 30% for PCE and negative 33% to 22% for PCK. The authors found that PCK is a robust general choice, but recommended uniform designs for PCE and PCK, and AL for GP, while emphasizing that the problem can change which method is best.

limitations_stated: The authors caution that their recommendations are based on 16 benchmarks and may not apply to problems substantially different from those benchmarks. They also note that some examples converge slowly and may require more simulator evaluations or different surrogate settings.
limitations_unstated: The benchmark set covers only 2 to 21 random inputs and includes just 3 FEM examples, so the comparisons provide limited evidence for higher-dimensional or strongly constrained engineering problems. future_work_stated: The authors expect the findings to be relevant to sensitivity analysis, parameter estimation, and reliability-based optimization. They also state that the proposed pool-based maximin-distance method may be promising for applications beyond the distribution-estimation comparison.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the design recommendations on real engineering simulators, especially cases with more inputs, constraints, and pronounced local nonlinearities. summary: This paper introduces a variational approach to Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) that uses normalizing flows to estimate expected information gain (EIG) about uncertain model parameters. In the high-dimensional linear case, both methods used a budget of 1 million forward model runs: the flow method achieved a lower-bound estimate of 20.94 and an NMC estimate of 24.91, compared with 12.07 and 24.28 for the Gaussian and Gamma variational method. In the coating application, the results selected a constant current of 7.5 milliamps as the best of the three candidate designs, and adding a long short-term memory (LSTM) summary network improved the lower-bound estimate and posterior approximation. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the selected coating and measurement designs in real experiments and compare their outcomes with the simulated predictions. summary: The paper proposes a Bayesian optimal experimental design method for choosing which MRI measurements to collect. Its objective is to maximize expected information gain, which the authors connect to maximizing the expected log likelihood of the unknown image given the observations. The method jointly trains a conditional normalizing flow to approximate the posterior and learns a probabilistic binary sampling mask using Bernoulli sampling and a gradient approximation. The demonstration uses a public knee MRI dataset and a sampling budget of 2.5 percent. Against a hand-crafted fixed mask, the learned design yields lower uncertainty and improved image reconstruction measures in the reported tests.
key_results: Training used 1,800 image-observation pairs and a design budget of 2.5 percent of k-space frequencies; evaluation included 100 unseen test samples. Training took 20 hours for the proposed method and 16 hours for the baseline, using the same density estimator. Across the test set, the paper reports consistently reduced uncertainty and lower reconstruction error with the learned design, but does not provide numerical aggregate values in the text. For the example shown in Figure 4, the posterior mean had a structural similarity index measure of 0.68 versus 0.57 for the baseline, and normalized mean squared error of 0.0223 versus 0.1053.
key_equations:
Expected information gain criterion: \[\mathrm{EIG}(M)=\mathbb{E}_{p(y\mid M)}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p(x\mid y,M)\,\|\,p(x)\right)\right]\] Expected information gain is averaged over observations y drawn from distribution p given design M; x is the unknown parameter, p is a probability distribution, and D_KL is the Kullback–Leibler divergence.

Joint posterior-likelihood optimization: \[\max_{\theta,M}\;\mathbb{E}_{p(x,y\mid M)}\left[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid y)\right]\] The method jointly chooses flow parameters theta and design M to maximize the expected natural logarithm of the conditional probability of parameter x given observation y, under their joint distribution p for design M.
limitations_stated: The authors note that their method requires an additional adjoint Fourier transform during training and report a training time of 20 hours, compared with 16 hours for the baseline. They do not otherwise identify formal limitations.
limitations_unstated: The evidence is limited to knee MRI from one public dataset, one sampling budget, and a comparison with a hand-crafted fixed mask rather than a broad set of optimized design methods. The learned mask and posterior model are trained using 1,800 pairs, and the reported numerical reconstruction metrics include a single illustrated example; robustness to other datasets, acquisition conditions, or model misspecification is not established.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the learned design on additional imaging datasets, sampling budgets, and acquisition constraints, and compare it with other optimized design approaches. summary: This paper develops methods for choosing sensor locations in Bayesian linear inverse problems using the D-optimal information-gain objective. It recasts sensor selection as a Column Subset Selection Problem (CSSP) and constructs designs by computing a truncated singular value decomposition (SVD), then selecting columns using the right singular vectors. The authors also introduce randomized methods, including Randomized Adjoint-free Optimal Experimental Design (RAF-OED), and a method for completing measurements at unselected locations. The methods are analyzed theoretically and tested on simulated heat-equation and seismic-tomography problems. The randomized approaches provide competitive designs with fewer forward-model evaluations than the greedy comparison method, while RAF-OED avoids adjoint evaluations during sensor selection.
key_results: For the heat problem with 30 sensors, randomized Golub-Klema-Stewart (RandGKS) achieved a D-optimality value of 6.8017 and relative reconstruction error of 0.1274 in 124.5957 seconds; RAF-OED achieved 6.6441 and 0.1263 in 41.6364 seconds, while the greedy method achieved 7.0857 in 1348.8915 seconds. For the seismic problem with 50 sensors, RandGKS took 1.9811 seconds and RAF-OED took 0.6742 seconds, compared with 66.5252 seconds for the greedy method; their D-optimality values were 5.6962, 5.6760, and 5.9211, respectively. In the heat experiment, RAF-OED required 50 forward-model evaluations at 30 sensors, compared with 200 for RandGKS and 2,565 for the greedy method; on the seismic experiment with 50 sensors, the corresponding counts were 70, 280, and 11,575. Measurement completion improved to about the 2% noise level for heat with up to 20 sensors, and the authors report nearly full-data reconstruction accuracy for seismic after completion.
key_equations:
Linear measurement model: \[d = Fm + \epsilon\] The data d are generated by applying the forward and observation operator F to the unknown parameter m and adding measurement noise epsilon.

limitations_stated: The analysis focuses on linear inverse problems with Gaussian priors and, for most of the paper, uncorrelated noise with scalar variance. The authors leave extensions to general correlated noise and nonlinear inverse problems as future work.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation covers two simulated inverse problems with grids of 4,225 degrees of freedom and candidate sensor sets of 100 or 256 locations, so it does not establish performance on larger or field experiments. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the methods to A-optimal and goal-oriented criteria, nonlinear inverse problems, and correlated noise. They also suggest investigating volume sampling and determinantal point processes.
future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test the methods on real experiments and on larger systems with practical constraints such as sensor accessibility, installation cost, and minimum spacing. summary: The paper tests an adaptive design of experiments (ADoE) method on an industrial injection moulding process for a polyoxymethylene clip. Its objectives are to reduce the temperature difference between a hotspot and an average-temperature location, and to reduce cycle time. Two in-mould thermocouples provide a real-time temperature differential used as a proxy for later shrinkage, while Bayesian optimisation with a Gaussian process and expected improvement selects settings iteratively. key_results: For single-objective temperature-differential optimisation, ADoE used 16 experimental settings, compared with 31 for the central composite design and desirability approach. limitations_unstated: The experimental validation concerns one component and material, so the reported efficiency and temperature-proxy relationship may not transfer to other moulds, materials, or production conditions. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method across additional components, moulds, and material batches, with repeated independent starting datasets, to assess how reliably it transfers. summary: The paper develops a framework for making one product decision from multiple outcomes in randomized online experiments. It distinguishes success metrics, which should improve, from guardrail metrics, which must not decline beyond a chosen margin, and from deterioration and experiment-quality checks. The authors combine tests for these roles into a rule for deciding whether to ship a change, with adjustments to significance levels and statistical power matched to that rule. The framework is designed for two-group experiments and is evaluated through theoretical results and Monte Carlo simulations. The main finding is that controlling false-positive risk alone is not enough: power must also be adjusted when the rule requires all guardrail metrics to pass.
key_results: The theory shows that guardrail non-inferiority tests do not require a multiplicity adjustment to their significance level, while success tests do; the design must also adjust power across the success and guardrail tests. For the complete decision rule, the authors allocate a total significance level across deterioration and quality tests and further adjust power to account for these tests. In simulations with 5 success metrics, 5 guardrail metrics, 2 additional deterioration metrics, and 2 quality tests, using 100,000 replications per setting, the proposed correction produced decision rejection rates of 84.2% to 95.2% under the global alternative across the four dependence settings. The alpha-only correction produced rates of 27.0% to 75.6% in those settings, while the proposed correction kept rejection rates under the status-quo scenario between 1.1% and 4.5%, below the intended 5% false-positive rate.
key_equations:
Success and guardrail hypotheses: \[H_0^S: \delta\le 0\;\text{vs.}\;H_a^S: \delta>0,\qquad H_0^G: \delta\le -m\;\text{vs.}\;H_a^G: \delta>-m\] H₀ and Hₐ are the null and alternative hypotheses, the superscripts S and G identify success and guardrail metrics, δ is the treatment effect, and m is the non-inferiority margin.

Significance-level allocation: \[\alpha_S=\frac{\alpha}{S},\qquad \alpha_G=\alpha\] Alpha is the target type I error rate, alpha with subscript S and alpha with subscript G are the per-test significance levels for success and guardrail metrics, and S is the number of success metrics.

Power allocation: \[\beta_S=\beta_G=\frac{\beta}{G+1}\] Beta is the target type II error rate, beta with subscripts S and G are the per-test type II error rates for success and guardrail metrics, and G is the number of guardrail metrics.
limitations_stated: The authors prioritize simple, explainable Bonferroni-like corrections over statistically optimal procedures, and note that their corrections can be conservative for some dependence structures. They also state that sequential deterioration tests complicate error-rate calculations and that choosing a non-inferiority margin can be challenging.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is simulation-based and does not establish how the proposed rule performs in real product experiments with actual metric distributions or operational constraints. The paper also does not translate the corrections into practical sample sizes or run durations, so the design’s feasibility for particular experiments is not quantified.
future_work_stated: The authors describe Nyholt’s effective-number-of-tests method as a way to improve efficiency when metrics are correlated, and discuss multivariate variance reduction as another possible efficiency improvement. They also describe further efficiency gains under additional assumptions about how deterioration-test rejection regions relate to the other tests.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the decision rule on real online experiments and report the resulting run sizes, durations, and decision behavior. Further work could also examine constrained randomization and settings where sequential decisions are made for both success and guardrail tests.

Rather than searching the full input space continuously, Vorcands generates candidates on boundaries between Voronoi cells of previously evaluated points. Across the reported test problems, Vorcands generally found better solutions than simple candidate sets and was faster than continuous acquisition optimization.

Vorcands achieved better best-observed function values than multi-start continuous optimization on 7 of the 8 problems and took less execution time on every problem. It also outperformed Latin hypercube sample candidates in best-observed value while taking comparable time, and its results were more consistent than those from Sobol sequence candidates. limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses a limited set of eight deterministic benchmark problems, so it does not establish performance on noisy, real industrial experiments or across a broad range of practical design constraints. summary: The paper develops a one-step design framework for choosing which prompts to annotate for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of large language models (LLMs). It studies a 7B LLaMA-2 model, with the goal of maintaining generalization while reducing the number of annotated prompt-response pairs. The methods select prompts using model uncertainty, feature-space coverage, or a facility location objective that favors a diverse and representative subset. Selection uses the pretrained model before responses are collected, avoiding the repeated retraining and pool-wide inference required by active learning. On the evaluated instruction dataset and benchmarks, facility location selection generally improves performance over random selection, with the paper reporting roughly half the annotation budget needed to match random sampling with a larger budget.
key_results: On the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, facility location selection with kernel width gamma equal to 0.002 reached 47.63 at a 45K budget, compared with 45.99 for random selection at the same budget; the reported 90K result was 47.76. On the Big-Bench-Hard (BBH) chain-of-thought benchmark, the same method scored 41.30 at 45K, compared with 39.44 for random selection at 45K and 40.49 for random selection at 90K. In a preference comparison judged by GPT-4, the 45K facility-location model had a 52.81% win rate against the model trained on 90K randomly selected prompts. The authors report that their methods can save approximately 50% of annotation cost while reaching comparable generalization, although the results vary by selection strategy and evaluation.

limitations_stated: The authors restrict their experiments to the 7B version of LLaMA-2. They use curated data and assume accurate prompt responses, so they do not assess noisy annotations. They also evaluate after SFT only and do not study subsequent reinforcement learning with human feedback.
limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from one pretrained model, one 99K prompt pool based on FLAN V2, and a limited set of benchmarks, so performance may differ for other models, domains, or annotation pools. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the selection methods across more model sizes, datasets, and response-quality conditions, and compare their performance under real annotation constraints. summary: This paper develops the Global-Rank-Sum statistic for comparing treatment and control outcomes in randomized online experiments. It targets settings where long-tailed metrics make the normality assumption behind the student t-test unreliable, and where separately reranking users for many experiments is too costly. The method ranks each user's metric once across the full population, then compares the treatment and control groups' average global ranks within each experiment. The authors derive its large-sample behavior under randomized group assignment and evaluate it in simulations, with a real-data example illustrating long-tailed outcomes. They find that it closely matches the traditional rank-sum test in statistical accuracy and power while becoming faster when many experiments are tested.
key_results: In simulations with a population of 1,000,000 users, 5,000 experiments, and 100,000 users in each group, the global-rank method had type I error close to the nominal levels of 1%, 5%, and 10%, much like the traditional rank-sum test. In the table's setting with parameter values negative five and seven, at a nominal 5% level the t-test rejected 0.52% of null cases, while both rank-sum methods rejected 5.16%. With a 5% lift and a nominal 5% level, reported power was 0.92% for the t-test, 33.56% for the traditional rank-sum test, and 33.52% for the global-rank method. For 500 experiments, runtime was 30.057 seconds for the traditional rank-sum tests and 9.025 seconds for the global-rank tests, a reported 70.0% reduction; for one experiment, the global method was slower.
key_equations:
Global ranks: \[R_i=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}(X_j\leq X_i)\] R_i is user i's rank among the full population, X_i and X_j are user metric values, N is the total population size, i and j are user indices, and the indicator is one when the comparison is true.

Global-Rank-Sum statistic: \[\mathrm{GRS}=\frac{\bar R_t-\bar R_c}{s_R\sqrt{1/N_t+1/N_c}}\] GRS is the test statistic, R̄_t and R̄_c are the treatment and control average global ranks, s_R is the sample standard deviation of ranks within the experiment, and N_t and N_c are the two group sizes.

Rank standard deviation: \[s_R^2=\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{i\in J}(R_i-\bar R)^2\] s_R is the sample standard deviation of ranks in the experiment, M is its sample size, J is its set of users, R_i is user i's global rank, and R̄ is the average global rank among users in J.
limitations_stated: The authors say that the rank-sum statistic is less informative about the underlying distribution than conventional tests that report means and variances, and suggest using measures such as medians or quantiles alongside it. They also state that the method does not provide a refined correction for tied values: ties are assigned random ranks, and a tie correction remains to be explored.
limitations_unstated: The theoretical result relies on randomized treatment assignment and the null hypothesis that treatment and control samples follow the same distribution; the paper does not examine how the method performs under allocation or data-selection departures from those conditions. Its accuracy and power comparisons are simulations based on log-normal metrics, while the real-data example illustrates a long-tailed metric rather than validating treatment-effect findings on field experiment outcomes. The runtime results also provide no hardware or implementation details for judging how directly they transfer to other platforms.
future_work_stated: The authors identify a more refined tie correction for the Global-Rank-Sum statistic as an area for further exploration. They also suggest reporting medians or quantiles as intermediate measures to make rank-based results more informative.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the method on field experiments with known or independently assessed treatment effects, and benchmark it on other platforms and data sizes. It would also be useful to assess its behavior under nonrandom assignment, experiment-specific sampling, and metrics with many ties, and to compare it with other robust tests or treatment-effect estimands.

summary: This paper develops theoretical constructions of orthogonal arrays (OAs) and large sets of orthogonal arrays (LOAs), without targeting a particular statistical model or optimization objective. The authors construct LOAs directly and through juxtaposition, Hadamard matrices, finite fields, and difference matrices. They then combine LOAs to derive new classes of OAs, including arrays with higher strength and mixed factor levels. The main finding is a collection of new parameterized existence results, rather than an empirical comparison or a claim of improved experimental performance. The authors note that the resulting arrays have low saturation, while describing the construction methods as efficient.
key_results: The paper establishes LOA(2^n, k, 2, 2) for n ≥ 2 and n ≤ k ≤ 2^n − 1, and LOA(2^(n+1), k, 2, 3) for n ≥ 2 and n + 1 ≤ k ≤ 2^n. For prime powers q ≥ 3, it establishes LOA(q^4, k, q, 3) for 4 ≤ k ≤ q^2 + 1; it also gives strength-2 LOAs with v^3 or v^4 runs when v ≥ 4 and v is not congruent to 2 modulo 4. Combining these and earlier LOA results yields about 16 infinite classes of LOAs and many OA existence results, with detailed examples listed in the paper’s tables. The paper presents theoretical derivations and parameter ranges, not measured run-size savings, estimates, prediction accuracy, or quantitative efficiency comparisons.
key_equations:
Size of a symmetric large set: \[M=\frac{v^k}{N}\] M is the number of arrays in the large set, v is the number of levels per factor, k is the number of factors, and N is the number of runs in each array.

Finite-field LOA existence result: \[\operatorname{LOA}(q^4,k,q,3),\quad q\ge 3,\quad 4\le k\le q^2+1\] LOA denotes a large set of orthogonal arrays; q is a prime-power level count, the arrays have q⁴ runs and strength 3, and k is the number of factors in the stated range.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the saturation of the OAs obtained by their constructions is low. They identify constructing OAs with higher saturation as an important research challenge and say that further applications of LOAs, especially with mixed levels, should be explored.
limitations_unstated: The results are existence theorems and parameter listings, with no reported empirical validation in physical or computer experiments and no supplied software for generating or checking the designs. Practical issues such as constraints on factor settings, run randomization, and whether the stated run sizes are acceptable in a given application are not evaluated; the claim of construction efficiency is not quantified against alternatives.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing constructions of OAs with higher saturation and exploring new applications of LOAs, particularly mixed-level LOAs.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to provide accessible software that generates the arrays and verifies their balance properties, then benchmark construction time and design properties against existing alternatives. Researchers could also study whether these constructions can meet practical randomization and factor-setting constraints, and validate their usefulness in real experimental settings.

summary: This paper proposes an experimental design for estimating treatment and spillover effects when units interfere through an observed network. The method divides units into an independent set, with no links between its members, and an auxiliary set that can influence them. A greedy procedure constructs the independent set, and assignments in the auxiliary set are chosen to control or diversify the independent units’ interference exposures. The design estimates direct effects and, under a linear additive outcome model, spillover and total effects. The authors provide theoretical results and simulations showing that the design can improve estimation compared with several conventional network-experiment designs.
key_results: For an Erdos-Renyi graph with n units and expected average degree s, the authors show that the greedy procedure finds an independent set of size at least n log(s) divided by s with high probability. In the spillover-effect simulation with n = 100 and edge probability 0.10, the independent-set design had bias 0.398 and variance 0.242, compared with 0.598 and 0.468 for randomization on the independent set, and 0.473 and 0.399 for randomization on the full graph. For direct effects at the same graph size and edge probability, its bias and variance were 0.117 and 0.009, compared with 0.262 and 0.035 for randomization on the independent set and 0.261 and 0.023 for randomization on the full graph. The simulations on distinct graph settings were run 2,000 times per configuration, and the independent-set design had the lowest reported bias and variance in the presented comparisons.
key_equations:
Additive outcome model: \[Y_i(Z_i,\rho_i)=\alpha+\beta Z_i+\gamma\rho_i+\epsilon_i\] Y_i is unit i's outcome, Z_i is its treatment assignment, rho_i is its proportion of treated neighbors, alpha is the baseline, beta is the treatment effect, gamma is the spillover effect, and epsilon_i is its error term.

Assignment criterion for direct effects: \[\min_{Z_A\in\{0,1\}^{|V_A|}}\|\Gamma Z_A-\rho\mathbf{1}\|_1\] The design selects the auxiliary assignment vector Z_A to minimize the sum of absolute deviations between the resulting interference exposures and target rho; Gamma maps assignments to exposures, V_A is the auxiliary set, and 1 is a vector of ones.

Assignment criterion for spillover and total effects: \[\max_{Z_A\in\{0,1\}^{|V_A|}}\operatorname{Var}(\Gamma Z_A)\] The design selects binary assignments Z_A for the auxiliary set V_A to maximize the variance of the interference exposures produced by the matrix Gamma.
limitations_stated: The design estimates effects using only the independent set, so its effective sample size is smaller than that of an experiment using the full network. Optimizing auxiliary assignments may be computationally costly, and the method relies on an observed network; its performance with a misspecified network is unknown.
limitations_unstated: The spillover and total-effect regression results rely on the linear additive outcome model, while the exposure mapping assumes outcomes depend on the proportion of treated neighbors; other response forms or exposure definitions are not evaluated. The evidence is based on synthetic simulations rather than real experiments, so the reported comparisons do not establish performance under practical assignment constraints or in a specific application.
future_work_stated: The authors propose improving the computational efficiency of optimizing auxiliary assignments and extending the method to settings with a misspecified network.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the design under nonlinear outcome models and alternative definitions of network exposure, and assess how assignment constraints affect achievable treatment and interference levels. Validation on real network experiments would also show whether the simulation findings carry over to practice.

summary: This paper proposes an expert-guided method for experimental design when the goal is to optimize an expensive, derivative-free system. It uses a Gaussian process model and a utility function to identify a standard next solution, then constructs distinct alternatives for an expert to choose among. The alternatives trade off their total utility against a covariance-based measure of how varied the set is, and the method presents the set at the knee of that trade-off. The expert selects one of the alternatives or the standard solution for evaluation, and the new observation updates the model. In simulations, informed or partly informed choices often improved convergence, while random choices recovered the performance of standard Bayesian optimization in the reported settings.
key_results: The authors tested the method on 50 simulated functions sampled from Gaussian process priors, including one-, two-, and five-dimensional cases, and presented four choices at each iteration. With a practitioner modeled as selecting the best choice 75% or 50% of the time, the reported regret generally improved over the standard Bayesian optimization behavior; the benefit was weaker when the practitioner selected the best choice only 25% of the time. At that 25% rate, which corresponds to random selection among four choices, the authors report recovery of standard Bayesian optimization convergence in the one- and two-dimensional tests and to a lesser extent in five dimensions. A practitioner that consistently selected the worst true objective value performed worse, particularly in higher dimensions; the paper reports no timing or run-cost comparison.
key_equations:
Standard utility maximizer: \[x^* = \arg\max_{x\in X} U(x)\] Here x is a candidate solution, X is the search domain, U is the utility function, and x* is the solution that maximizes that utility.

Total utility of the alternatives: \[\hat U(X;D_t)=\sum_{i=1}^{p-1} U(X_i)\] Here X is the matrix of alternatives, D_t is the observed data at iteration t, p is the number of presented choices, i indexes the alternatives, X_i is one alternative, and U-hat is their summed utility.

Variability of the augmented solution set: \[\hat S(X,x^*)=\det(K_{X_{\rm aug}}),\quad X_{\rm aug}=X\cup\{x^*\}\] Here X is the set of alternatives, x* is the standard utility maximizer, X-aug combines them, K is the covariance matrix for that augmented set, and S-hat is its determinant.

Pareto-front knee selection: \[X_k^*=\operatorname{knee}\!\left(\operatorname{ParetoFront}(\hat U,\hat S)\right)\] Here U-hat is total utility, S-hat is variability, the Pareto front contains trade-off solutions for those two criteria, and X-star-sub-k is the alternative set selected at the front's knee.
limitations_stated: The authors state that they could not benchmark real human behavior because the objective functions are random and because of practical issues. Their evaluation instead represents human behavior with idealized, adversarial, trusting, and probabilistic selection rules.
limitations_unstated: The simulation's idealized decision rules do not capture the range of real expert judgments, so the reported regret results do not establish how actual practitioners would perform. The study also uses simulated objectives and does not compare computational cost or optimization performance against the batch Bayesian optimization methods it identifies as relevant alternatives.
future_work_stated: The authors propose benchmarking the method against existing batch Bayesian optimization approaches, including methods with similar multi-objective formulations. They also propose investigating whether large language models can perform the choice-selection step, and leave evaluation of real human behavior for future work.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method in real experiments with actual practitioners, recording both objective improvement and the time or effort required for each decision. Further studies could test noisy measurements and practical process constraints, and examine whether the method remains useful when the number of choices or the search dimension changes.

summary: The paper proposes using factorial experiments to evaluate business policies that can be broken into separate factors and levels. It applies the approach to DoorDash consumer promotions, with the objective of improving profit while keeping promotional spending efficient. The authors assume that factor effects add together without interactions, then use an orthogonal fractional factorial design to test eight combinations and estimate effects for all 24 possible policies. They add a ninth, held-out combination to compare model predictions with observed results. In this case study, the method identified a predicted policy with 5% higher profit and reduced policy setup cost by 67% compared with the status quo approach.
key_results: The experiment evaluated 24 promotion policies using eight main experimental arms, a reduction the authors associate with 67% lower implementation cost. Their theoretical comparison reports that the design can detect effects as small as 38% of the minimum detectable effect for a policy-by-policy experiment, and reports a 267% increase in speed for measuring the same effect. The held-out arm’s predicted and observed effects were not detectably different in a joint test, with a p-value of 0.80. The selected policy was predicted to increase profit by 5% relative to the control group and by 1% relative to the best of the eight main arms; their heterogeneous-effects analysis estimated a further 2% profit improvement. The broad test for treatment-effect heterogeneity was not significant, with a p-value of 0.2, although a focused analysis using average prior order spend found statistically significant interactions and different predicted policies for different spend ranges.

limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence comes from one company and one promotion campaign, and the held-out validation covers only one randomly selected policy combination; this gives limited evidence about how well the method generalizes to other policy spaces. future_work_stated: None stated.

summary: The paper develops guidance for designing randomized experiments when the goal is to predict treatment effects for individual units, rather than only estimate an average effect. It focuses on a two-group randomized experiment and linear models estimated separately in the treatment and control groups. The authors derive expressions for prediction error and examine how sample size, treatment-effect moderators, and differences between the study and target populations affect that error. They also compare unit-specific predictions with using the same average effect prediction for every unit, and discuss weighting to address population differences. The main finding is that unit-specific prediction often needs larger samples or strong moderators, while differences between study and target populations can make predictions less accurate and increase uncertainty.
key_results: In the paper’s numerical comparisons, with 20 units per group and treatment-effect variation equal to 40 percent of outcome variation, one moderator had to explain 34 percent of effect variation to outperform the adjusted average-effect model; three moderators had to explain 68 percent. With 100 units per group, those thresholds fell to 8 percent and 16 percent. In the ASSISTments planning example, a study of 80 schools had a minimum detectable average effect of 0.22 standard deviations, but prediction intervals could still include both positive and negative effects when treatment-effect variation was moderate or large. For North Carolina schools used to predict effects across the United States, weighting covered 98.3 percent of the target schools and had a variance-inflation multiplier of 1.42; the authors estimate that 113 schools in North Carolina would be needed to match the accuracy of 80 schools sampled from the target population.
key_equations:
Unit-specific treatment-effect model: \[\delta_i=\Delta_A+x_{i|A}^{\prime}\delta+\eta_i\] Here δᵢ is unit i’s treatment effect, ΔA is the average effect in population A, xᵢ|A is the unit’s standardized covariate vector, δ contains the moderator coefficients, and ηᵢ is unexplained unit-specific effect variation.

Mean squared prediction error: \[\operatorname{MSPE}(\hat{\delta}_i)=\left(\frac{\sigma_{0|x}^2}{n_0}+\frac{\sigma_{1|x}^2}{n_1}\right)(1+p)+\tau_{A|x}^2\] Here MSPE is mean squared prediction error, σ₀|x and σ₁|x are the residual standard deviations in the control and treatment groups, n₀ and n₁ are their sample sizes, p is the number of covariates, and τA|x is unexplained treatment-effect variation in population A.

Weighting variance inflation: \[\operatorname{MVIF}=1+\frac{V_A(w_i)}{E_A(w_i)^2}\] Here MVIF is the variance-inflation multiplier, VA is variance in population A, EA is expectation in population A, and wi is the weight for unit i.
limitations_stated: The authors limit their derivations to a simple two-group randomized experiment and linear models estimated by ordinary least squares. They note that the correlation between potential-outcome residuals is unknowable, making unexplained treatment-effect variation difficult to identify, and that predictive-error formulas based on a random sample may not apply when the study sample differs from the prediction population.
limitations_unstated: The derived results depend on a correctly specified linear moderator structure, but the paper does not empirically validate that structure against nonlinear or machine-learning alternatives. Its numerical examples rely on assumed or prior-informed values for important quantities that cannot be identified from the trial alone, so their practical design recommendations may be sensitive to those assumptions.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the design guidance using prospective experiments and compare linear models with nonlinear or machine-learning prediction methods. They could also extend the formulas to constrained and clustered experiments and test whether the predicted error estimates remain calibrated in real target populations.

summary: This paper develops and evaluates a Factorial Adaptive Multi-Arm Multi-Stage (FAST) clinical trial design for comparing fluid therapies and fludrocortisone in patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage. The motivating design combines multiple treatment arms with a factorial comparison and interim decisions: it can drop a newer fluid therapy, stop fluid enrollment for lack of a biomarker signal, and then test retained treatments on the primary clinical outcome. The design is intended to estimate treatment effects while using shared control groups and adapting enrollment across trial stages. Simulations varied the timing of the two Phase II assessments and the treatment effects on biomarkers and the Phase III outcome. The findings show that assessment timing affects operating characteristics and that conducting arm dropping before the feasibility assessment generally gives better overall power.
key_results: The authors generated 1,000 simulated datasets for each simulation condition and varied assessment sample sizes from 90 to 300, in increments of 30. They report that power is generally greatest when the feasibility assessment uses a larger sample and arm dropping uses a smaller sample, supporting the order of arm dropping before feasibility. In the table’s example with arm dropping at 150 outcomes and feasibility at 300, the reported probability of retaining the correct arm is 0.949 in the null condition, and power exceeds 90% in conditions where at least one treatment in each domain has a nonzero effect. The paper describes family-wise Type I error as approximately 5%; its table reports 0.060 for the null condition, and the paper does not present a direct numerical comparison with traditional designs.

limitations_stated: The authors note that pooling the newer fluid arms in the feasibility assessment can underpower the comparison if their effects differ. limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated scenarios rather than patient data, and the paper reports only 1,000 simulated datasets per condition. summary: This paper develops computational methods for Bayesian optimal experimental design when the model has both parameters of interest and uncertain nuisance parameters. The objective is to choose a design that maximizes expected information gain about the parameters of interest, after accounting for nuisance uncertainty. The authors introduce two estimators: one uses nested Laplace approximations, and the other uses Laplace approximations as importance-sampling distributions for Monte Carlo integration. They derive error and computational-work analyses and show how to allocate samples for the standard double-loop Monte Carlo estimator. Four numerical examples demonstrate use in a linear model, pharmacokinetics, and electrical impedance tomography; the proposed methods can substantially reduce the inner sampling required, but the nested approximation can introduce consequential bias.
key_results: In the linear Gaussian example, both proposed estimators identify design ξ = 1 as optimal when only the parameter of interest is targeted; without nuisance uncertainty, the comparison design is ξ = 1/2. For that example, Laplace-based importance sampling reduced the required number of inner samples to one, even at small tolerances. In the pharmacokinetics example, optimizing 15 measurement times increased the reported EIG from 6.12 for geometrically spaced times to 6.25 for the optimized times. In the electrical impedance tomography comparison, the small-noise method was applicable only up to nuisance covariance of approximately 9.03 × 10^-7, while the computational cost of the proposed methods rose sharply at larger covariance; in another example, the nested Laplace estimator was ineffective at tolerance 0.2 because of its bias.
key_equations:
Expected information gain with nuisance uncertainty: \[I(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta,Y}\left[\log\frac{p(Y\mid\theta,\xi)}{p(Y\mid\xi)}\right]\] I is expected information gain, ξ is the design, θ is the parameter of interest, Y is the data, p denotes data densities with nuisance parameters marginalized, and E denotes expectation over the parameter and data.

Marginalized likelihood used in the information criterion: \[p(Y\mid\theta,\xi)=\int p(Y\mid\theta,\phi,\xi)\,\pi(\phi\mid\theta)\,d\phi\] p(Y given θ and ξ) is the data density after marginalizing nuisance parameter ϕ; p(Y given θ, ϕ, ξ) is the conditional data density, and π(ϕ given θ) is the conditional prior density.
limitations_stated: The authors base their Laplace constructions on conditions involving unique minima and suitable Hessians, although they note that Laplace methods can also be applied without a unique minimum. They report that bias made the nested Laplace estimator ineffective in one electrical impedance tomography example at tolerance 0.2, and note that Gaussian importance sampling can generate samples outside a compact prior support.
limitations_unstated: The methods rely on local Laplace approximations, so results may be unreliable for strongly multimodal or poorly concentrated posteriors; the examples do not establish performance in such cases. The evidence is numerical and drawn from four simulated examples, rather than real experiments, and the 15-dimensional design optimization uses a greedy local procedure that does not establish a global optimum.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the estimators on real experiments and on models with multimodal posteriors, hard parameter bounds, or operational constraints on allowable designs. Further work could also develop sequential design updates and test alternative sampling or optimization strategies for the high-dimensional design problem.

summary: This paper develops methods for finding Bayesian experimental designs when there is a finite set of candidate samples and the goal is parameter estimation. It considers c-optimal designs, which target the precision of a specified linear combination of parameters, and L-optimal designs, which minimize a linear summary of parameter uncertainty. The authors reformulate these design problems as regression problems with squared sparsity penalties, then use the dual problem to derive safe rules for removing candidates that cannot receive positive design weight. They also adapt a Lasso homotopy algorithm to construct c-optimal designs in a finite number of steps. The examples show that screening can speed up design computations and that the homotopy method can be substantially faster than iterative alternatives.
key_results: In the MNIST handwritten-digit example, the c-optimal design for lambda equal to 0.4 used 10 supporting images, all showing the same digit as the target image. At lambda equal to 10 to the power of negative 2, the homotopy method found an exact solution in 3.16 seconds; Coordinate Descent took 29.00 seconds and Multiplicative Weight Updates took 204.67 seconds to reach the reported near-optimal tolerance of 10 to the power of negative 4. At lambda equal to 10 to the power of negative 4, homotopy took 44.66 seconds, while Coordinate Descent took 2012.15 seconds and did not reach that tolerance according to the authors’ discussion. In the random-field L-optimal example with 8192 candidates and 50 parameters, one new screening rule gave about a fivefold speed-up over running the design algorithm without screening, although both approaches required 18,738 iterations to reach the stated accuracy.

summary: The paper develops randomized designs for network A/B testing, where users connected in a social network are assigned to one of two treatments. It considers two response settings: network-correlated errors and network interference, and aims to reduce the variance of the estimated treatment effect. The design balances treatment-group sizes and user degrees, then rerandomizes assignments until a graph-cut objective meets a specified threshold. The paper derives asymptotic distributions to help choose those thresholds and assess rerandomization rates. Simulations and sampled Facebook networks show that the method can produce designs with lower treatment-effect estimation variance than complete random assignment.
key_results: For synthetic networks, the proposed designs under Scenario I had variance percentiles below 0.004 among 1,000 balanced random designs, and their reported optimality gaps were below the median-design gaps in every setting. Under Scenario II, synthetic-network percentiles ranged from 0.0037 to 0.0153; for network sizes 1,000 and 2,000, the reported gaps to the lower bound were 0.0000. For ten sampled Facebook networks ranging from 52 to 1,034 users, percentiles were below 0.0025 for Scenario I and below 0.015 for Scenario II; the gap comparison was similar to the synthetic-network results. The rerandomization calculations used a maximum of 5,000 attempts, with target probabilities of 0.005 for Scenario I and 0.1 for Scenario II.

limitations_unstated: The evaluations compare the method mainly with complete random balanced designs and their median variance, rather than with a broad set of competing optimization algorithms. summary: This paper develops a general equivalence theorem for locally D-optimal crossover designs under generalized linear models (GLMs). The designs are constructed for repeated observations on subjects, with period, direct treatment, and carryover effects represented in the model. The authors use generalized estimating equations (GEEs) and consider two objectives: minimizing the variance determinant for all parameters or for direct treatment effects alone. Their theorem gives conditions on sequence allocations that can identify or verify optimal designs without relying solely on constrained optimization. In both examples, the allocations found from the equivalence conditions matched those found through constrained optimization. The supplementary dairy example used 80 subjects and reported corresponding four-sequence allocations of 0.3540, 0.2108, 0.2726, and 0.1626 for the full-parameter objective, and 0.1725, 0.2482, 0.2225, and 0.3586 for the treatment-effect objective; the paper does not report numerical efficiency comparisons against other design methods.

summary: The paper introduces variational Bayesian design methods for geophysical experiments, where the objective is to choose an experiment that maximizes expected information gain about model parameters or a particular target. The methods approximate either the probability distribution of possible data or the model parameters after observing data, learning these approximations from samples generated using the prior and forward model. The authors test the methods in synthetic seismic source-location and amplitude-versus-offset problems, and in a simplified design problem for estimating carbon dioxide saturation. They compare the methods with sampling-based and covariance-based alternatives, and also demonstrate optimizing designs directly with stochastic gradients. The results show that variational methods can achieve competitive designs with lower computational demands, and that the best receiver arrangements can depend substantially on the scientific question being asked.
key_results: For seismic source location, variational estimates approached the results from nested Monte Carlo with reused samples at around 1×10^4 samples; the covariance-based DN method could improve on median and evenly spaced designs with as few as 10 samples. In the amplitude-versus-offset case, the ordinary nested Monte Carlo estimate showed no convergence at 1×10^5 samples, while the reused-sample version needed around 1×10^3 inner samples to converge; the authors estimate that the ordinary version could require about 1×10^9 total samples for a comparable inner sample count. For a two-receiver amplitude-versus-offset design, direct stochastic-gradient optimization used 1×10^5 forward evaluations, compared with 8×10^8 for grid search and 8×10^6 for sequential construction, reductions by factors of 8000 and 80, respectively. summary: This paper develops methods for allocating units among treatment combinations in factorial experiments with two levels per factor. It targets precise estimation of finite-population factorial effects using randomization-based inference, rather than relying on a specified outcome distribution. The authors derive allocation rules by optimizing a covariance-matrix upper bound, then extend the results to randomized block designs and cost constraints. summary: This paper develops practical sample-size calculations for randomized online experiments, or A/B testing, with the objective of adequately powering treatment-effect tests while controlling false positives. It addresses experiments where observations are correlated within the randomized unit, such as multiple sessions from the same user, by using user-level aggregates and the Delta method. It also derives sample-size calculations for relative treatment effects and relates the anticipated treatment effect to the minimum observed difference expected to be statistically significant. The authors support their methods with mathematical derivations, examples, and simulations, and discuss practical design choices such as allocation balance and metric selection. Their simulations show that the proposed calculations generally attain their target error rates and power, while standard independent-observation sizing can substantially understate the required sample size for correlated data.
key_results: In five simulated correlated-data cases, the proposed method produced type I error rates from 0.0447 to 0.0561 and power from 0.8026 to 0.8223. In the first correlated-data example, it required 448 users per arm, corresponding to 2,246 sessions, and achieved 80.9% power; the independent-observation calculation required 1,472 sessions and achieved 75.8% power in one comparison scenario, with type I error inflated to 11.4%. For an independent binary-outcome example with a 10% relative lift and a control rate of 0.6, the relative-lift formula required 1,124 observations per arm and achieved 81.3% simulated power, compared with 1,017 observations and 77.1% power using the absolute-lift sizing method. The authors estimate that, at 80% power and a two-sided 5% type I error rate, the minimum observed difference is about 70% of the anticipated treatment effect; at 90% power, the ratio is about 60%.
key_equations:
Variance for the clustered user-level mean: \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\approx\frac{h}{k},\quad h=\frac{1}{\mu_N^2}\left(\sigma_S^2-2\frac{\mu_S}{\mu_N}\sigma_{SN}+\frac{\mu_S^2}{\mu_N^2}\sigma_N^2\right)\] X̄ is the overall outcome mean, k is the number of independent randomized users, h is the user-level variance factor, μS and μN are the means of user-level outcome sums Sᵢ and observation counts Nᵢ, σS² and σN² are their variances, and σSN is their covariance.

Required users per arm for an absolute effect: \[k=2h\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2}{\delta^2}\] k is the required number of randomized users per arm, h is the clustered-data variance factor, z is a standard normal percentile, α is the type I error rate, β is the type II error rate, and δ is the absolute treatment effect to detect.

Required observations per arm for a relative effect: \[n_{\mathrm{rel}}=2\left(1+\frac{\mu_y^2}{\mu_x^2}\right)\sigma^2\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2}{\delta_{\mathrm{rel}}^2}\] nrel is the required observations per arm, μx and μy are the control and treatment means, σ² is their assumed common variance, z is a standard normal percentile, α and β are the type I and type II error rates, and δrel is the relative treatment effect.

Minimum observed difference and anticipated effect: \[|\Delta_{\mathrm{MOD}}|\approx\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta}}|\Delta_{\mathrm{ATE}}|\] ΔMOD is the minimum observed difference expected to be statistically significant, ΔATE is the anticipated treatment effect used for sample-size planning, z is a standard normal percentile, α is the type I error rate, and β is the type II error rate.
limitations_stated: The clustered-data calculation depends on assumptions including a constant treatment effect on user-level means and no treatment effect on the number of observations per user. The authors note that the clustered-data variance factor depends on the experiment’s duration, so historical data should be collected over a duration matching the planned experiment; they also report that relative-effect simulations can exceed the target power when the anticipated relative effect is large and the control mean is estimated imprecisely.
limitations_unstated: The validation is primarily simulation-based, supported by examples, and does not report a systematic evaluation across real experiments; the reported simulation settings therefore may not represent the full range of traffic patterns or outcome distributions in practice. The calculations may also be unreliable when users are not independent or when treatment changes session counts or has heterogeneous effects, conditions that can occur in online experiments.
future_work_stated: The authors identify sequential experiments, more complex user behavior, temporal heterogeneity, and percentile outcomes as future directions. They also suggest that the methods may be applicable to these settings.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the sizing procedures against outcomes from deployed experiments and assess calibration across different user-level count distributions and degrees of clustering. It could also develop practical adaptations for constraints such as limited treatment traffic, changing session counts, and unequal treatment effects across users.
