glossary: SF-SFD = Stochastic Fourier space-filling design, the method introduced in the paper.|L2 = The order-two discrepancy measure used to assess how well a design fills the space.|DFT = Discrete Fourier transform.|LHS = Latin hypercube sampling.|n, d, m = The design run size, the number of dimensions, and the number of cells in the discretized one-dimensional distribution, respectively.|P_d, p, x, x_k = The d-dimensional sampling distribution, its one-dimensional marginal distribution, a design point, and the kth coordinate of that point, respectively.|p_i, q_i, c_i, C = The probability mass in cell i, its square root, the ith Fourier coefficient, and the vector of Fourier coefficients, respectively.|D_c, X_n, E = The centered L2 discrepancy, a sample of n design points, and expectation over samples, respectively.
summary: The paper introduces stochastic Fourier space-filling design (SF-SFD), a method for creating non-adaptive designs in high-dimensional, simply bounded spaces. Its objective is to reduce the expected centered L2 discrepancy of a sample, which the authors use to measure poor space coverage associated with concentration of measure. The method discretizes a one-dimensional probability distribution, transforms the square roots of its cell probabilities into Fourier coefficients, and optimizes those coefficients using repeated random samples. It assumes the same one-dimensional distribution in every coordinate and draws coordinates independently. In comparisons with Latin hypercube sampling, Sobol sequences, and uniform random sampling, SF-SFD performs best more often as dimension rises, while the paper also notes that the discrepancy approximation becomes unreliable for highly clustered samples.
key_results: The study compared run sizes of 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 in dimensions 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30, averaging results over 10 random seeds. In dimension 30, SF-SFD had the lowest reported discrepancy at every run size: 3.7137 at 100 runs and 1.2504 at 500 runs, compared with uniform random sampling at 7.9939 and 1.5952, respectively. At dimension 25, SF-SFD was best at run sizes 100 through 400, while Sobol was best at 500 runs; at dimension 20, SF-SFD was best at 100 runs, while Sobol was best at the larger tested run sizes. In dimensions 5 through 15, Sobol had lower discrepancies than SF-SFD at all tested run sizes, and the authors report that SF-SFD is preferable for run sizes in the low hundreds when dimension is approximately 20 or greater.
key_equations:
Shared-coordinate distribution assumption: \[P_d(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{d}p(x_k)\] P_d is the d-dimensional sampling distribution, p is the shared one-dimensional marginal distribution, x is a design point, x_k is its kth coordinate, k indexes coordinates, and d is the number of dimensions.

Fourier representation of cell probabilities: \[q_i=\sqrt{p_i},\quad C=\operatorname{DFT}(q),\quad \sum_{i=1}^{m}|c_i|^2=1\] For each cell i, p_i is its probability mass and q_i is the square root of that mass; C is the discrete Fourier transform of the vector q, c_i is its ith coefficient, and m is the number of cells, with the coefficients constrained to unit squared norm.

Coefficient optimization objective: \[\min_C\; E[D_c(X_n)\mid X_n\sim P_d(C)]\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_i|c_i|^2=1\] The method chooses the Fourier coefficient vector C to minimize the expected centered L2 discrepancy D_c of a sample X_n of n points drawn from the distribution P_d determined by C, subject to the coefficients having unit squared norm; E denotes expectation.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the centered L2 discrepancy approximation can become extremely inaccurate when samples bunch near the origin and leave the corners empty, and that SF-SFD is affected too, though it mitigates the problem relative to the comparisons. Their experiments cover run sizes of 100 to 500 and dimensions of 5 to 30, and they note that finite samples will become sparse in sufficiently high dimensions.
limitations_unstated: The method restricts the joint sampling distribution to independent coordinates with identical one-dimensional marginals, so it cannot directly tune coordinate-specific distributions or dependence among factors. The reported evidence measures discrepancy only; the paper does not demonstrate that the generated designs improve surrogate-model accuracy or downstream engineering outcomes. The study also fixes the discretization at 10 cells and compares against only the stated sampling approaches, leaving sensitivity to discretization and broader benchmark performance untested.
future_work_stated: The authors propose adding A-, E-, and D-optimality, as well as maximin and minimax distance criteria, to the objective. They also propose proving a slower rate of measure concentration more rigorously and empirically testing whether the designs improve approximation performance in real-world applications.
future_work_unstated: Future work could relax the identical, independent coordinate assumption to handle factor-specific distributions, dependence, and practical constraints on allowable factor settings. It could also evaluate the designs in sequential or adaptive experiments and validate them against downstream prediction and optimization outcomes across a broader range of design methods.

design_type_evidence: Global D-optimal designs are obtained by accumulating the frequencies of the design points in local D-optimal designs, where the parameters are sampled from the prior

glossary: QQ = Quantitative-qualitative, referring to a system with both continuous and binary responses.|GLM = Generalized linear model.|D-optimal = A design criterion that maximizes information about model parameters, commonly through a determinant of an information matrix.|Y and Z = The paper's continuous response and binary response, respectively.|x and f(x) = The experimental input settings and the vector of model effects evaluated at those settings.|eta = The coefficient vector in the logistic model for the binary response.|beta(1), beta(2), mu0, sigma squared = The coefficient vectors for the continuous response conditional on each binary outcome, its intercept, and its error variance.|Q(X) = The paper's design criterion for design matrix X.|W0, W1, W2, R1, R2, rho = Model-based weight matrices for the binary and conditional continuous responses, prior correlation matrices, and the noise-to-prior-signal variance ratio.|n, q, B = The total number of experimental runs, the number of modeled effects, and the number of parameter values sampled for global design construction.
summary: The paper develops a Bayesian D-optimal design method for experiments that measure one continuous response and one binary response in a quantitative-qualitative system. It models the binary response with logistic regression and models the continuous response with separate linear regressions conditional on the binary outcome. The criterion combines information for the binary model and both conditional continuous models, using either noninformative priors or conjugate informative priors. A point-exchange search constructs local designs for fixed parameter values, and a global design is formed by combining the frequencies of points selected across local designs. In two numerical examples, the proposed designs generally outperform designs made for each response separately and then combined, as well as a fractional factorial comparison in the manufacturing example.
key_results: In the artificial example, the run size is 66 and the model has 22 effects. For two prior settings, the proposed local design has reported efficiency ratios of 1.08 and 1.10 against the continuous-response-only design, 1.11 and 1.14 against the binary-response-only design, and 1.05 and 1.07 against the naively combined design. Across 500 sampled parameter values, every reported local comparison with the combined design favors the proposed method; on a separate set of 100 parameter values, the global proposed design is reported to outperform the global combined design throughout. In the etching example, the proposed global design uses 126 runs, compared with 135 for the replicated minimum-aberration fractional factorial design, and the paper's efficiency plots favor the proposed design; almost every local comparison with the combined design also favors the proposed method.
key_equations:
Joint response model: \[\Pr(Z=1\mid x)=\pi(x)=\frac{\exp(f(x)^T\eta)}{1+\exp(f(x)^T\eta)},\quad Y\mid Z=z,x\sim N\!\left(\mu_0+z f(x)^T\beta^{(1)}+(1-z)f(x)^T\beta^{(2)},\sigma^2\right)\] Here Z is the binary response, Y is the continuous response, x is the input setting, pi(x) is the probability that Z equals one, f(x) is the model-effect vector, eta is the binary-model coefficient vector, z is a binary outcome, beta(1) and beta(2) are the continuous-model coefficient vectors for the two outcomes, mu0 is an intercept, and sigma squared is the error variance.

Bayesian D-optimal criterion upper bound: \[Q(X)=\mathbb{E}_{\eta}\!\left[\log\det(F^T W_0F)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\log\det(F^T W_iF+\rho R_i^{-1})\right]\] Here Q(X) is the design criterion for design matrix X, the expectation is over eta, F is the model matrix, W0 weights binary-model information, W1 and W2 weight observations expected in the two binary outcome groups, rho is the noise-to-prior-signal variance ratio, and R1 and R2 are prior correlation matrices for the conditional continuous-model coefficients.

Global design construction: \[d(x)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} I\{x\text{ is selected in local design }b\}\] Here d(x) is the global design probability assigned to candidate point x, B is the number of sampled parameter values and resulting local designs, and I is an indicator equal to one when x is selected in a local design and zero otherwise.
limitations_stated: The authors describe their global continuous design construction as heuristic and say that a rigorous method for finding the optimal continuous design remains to be developed. They also note that handling multiple binary responses can make the model and construction algorithm substantially more complicated, particularly when there are many binary responses.
limitations_unstated: The proposed method relies on a specified logistic model and conditional linear Gaussian models with a common variance, so misspecification of these assumptions could change which design is preferred. The evidence is based on numerical examples and simulated parameter values rather than experiments actually conducted in the etching process, and the point-exchange search can depend on its initialization and candidate-set filtering. The method also requires choices of prior ranges and variance or correlation settings, while the paper does not quantify how sensitive the recommendations are to those choices or to operational restrictions on feasible runs.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing a rigorous method for the optimal continuous design. For multiple binary responses, they identify development of an alternative model and corresponding design method for larger numbers of responses as future research. They also discuss possible extensions to multiple quantitative responses and binary responses.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method prospectively in a real manufacturing experiment and compare predicted information gains with observed parameter-estimation performance. Further work could incorporate practical constraints such as restricted factor combinations, blocking, or run costs, and assess robustness to prior misspecification and alternative conditional-response models. Reproducible implementation and benchmarking against other search strategies would also help engineers evaluate computational effort and deploy the method.

glossary: SP-GIES = Skeleton-Primed Greedy Interventional Equivalence Search, the hybrid network-learning method proposed in the paper.|GIES = Greedy Interventional Equivalence Search, the joint observational-and-interventional learner used in SP-GIES.|OED = Optimal experimental design, the selection of experiments to maximize an expected utility.|AUC-PR = Area under the precision-recall curve, a network-recovery metric.|SHD = Structural Hamming Distance, the paper’s measure of graph difference from the reference network.|SID = Structural Interventional Distance, a measure based on incorrect interventional distributions.|DREAM4 = The name of the synthetic gene-network benchmark used in the paper.|Equation notation: X, G, Pa, D, I, U, E, p, i, and hats = X denotes variables; G a graph; Pa the parent set of a variable; D observed data; I a candidate intervention; U utility; E the graph’s edge set; p the number of variables; i an index; and a hat marks an estimated quantity.
summary: The paper presents Skeleton-Primed Greedy Interventional Equivalence Search (SP-GIES) to recover causal gene-regulatory networks from observational and interventional data. It is designed for genome-scale networks, where the number of variables corresponds to the number of genes, and aims to improve network recovery speed and accuracy. The method first estimates an undirected skeleton from observational data, then limits Greedy Interventional Equivalence Search (GIES) to that edge set while learning from both data types. The authors also apply optimal experimental design (OED) to choose gene interventions using information gain or expected edge orientation as design objectives. In simulations, SP-GIES reaches networks of 2,000 nodes and improves recovery on some benchmarks, while its performance on the real RegulonDB network is weaker than some observational methods.
key_results: In the 1,000-node simulated small-world network, SP-GIES achieved an area under the precision-recall curve (AUC-PR) of 0.91, compared with 0.84 for GIES and 0.82 for the PC learner. The paper reports that SP-GIES was 3.87 times faster than GIES at 1,000 nodes and 2.39 times faster at 2,000 nodes; it completed the 2,000-node study, while the 1,000- and 2,000-node IGSP runs exceeded the 72-hour quota. On DREAM4 network 1, SP-GIES had an AUC-PR of 0.63 versus 0.51 for GIES. On the 1,146-node RegulonDB network, SP-GIES achieved an AUC-PR of 0.10, below CLR’s 0.30 and the no-edge reference’s 0.50; the authors note that CLR’s threshold used knowledge of the reference network. In the small-network OED comparison, edge-orientation selection performed better than information-gain selection, while SP-GIES gave a stronger initial estimate but tended to stagnate as interventions accumulated.
key_equations:
Bayesian network factorization: \[P(X_1,\ldots,X_p)=\prod_{i=1}^{p}P(X_i\mid\mathrm{Pa}(X_i))\] X_i is variable i, p is the number of variables, and Pa(X_i) is the set of parents of variable X_i; the equation expresses the network’s joint distribution as a product of conditional distributions.

Expected-utility intervention criterion: \[\hat I=\arg\max_I\mathbb{E}_{G\mid D}[U(G,I)]\] The estimated intervention I maximizes expected utility U over graphs G given data D.

SP-GIES search restriction: \[E_{\mathrm{search}}=E_{\mathrm{skeleton}},\qquad \hat G=\mathrm{GIES}(D_{\mathrm{obs}},D_{\mathrm{int}};E_{\mathrm{search}})\] The edge set searched by GIES is restricted to the observationally estimated skeleton; D_obs and D_int are the observational and interventional data, and the output is the estimated graph.
limitations_stated: The authors state that fixing the skeleton can restrict the search, cause SP-GIES to stagnate during sequential interventions, and potentially leave GIES in a local minimum. GIES uses a score based on a linear Gaussian assumption, which may not fit nonlinear real data such as RegulonDB. SP-GIES remains bottlenecked by GIES: a 10,000-node run did not complete within 24 hours.
limitations_unstated: The results do not establish that the method will recover networks as well when the observational skeleton is estimated from noisy or sparse measurements: edges omitted at that stage cannot be considered by the restricted GIES search. Evidence for practical intervention selection is also narrow, since the OED comparison uses a 10-node DREAM4 network and the real RegulonDB network is an estimated reference rather than a fully verified causal graph.
future_work_stated: The authors propose distributed parallel implementations of SP-GIES and incorporating it into an autonomous experimental-design loop. They also identify modeling environmental condition variables and incorporating nonlinear structure-learning approaches into joint learners as future directions.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test SP-GIES prospectively in laboratory experiments, comparing selected interventions with random choices under the same intervention budget. Further studies could also evaluate how robust the results are to realistic intervention constraints, such as limits on which genes can be perturbed or on the number of perturbations run at once.

summary: This paper develops a design framework for screening with two-level supersaturated designs, where there are more factors than runs can support through ordinary least squares. It assumes a sparse main-effects model with normally distributed errors and aims to improve the probability that the lasso recovers the signs of the active effects. The authors define sign-recovery criteria and use them to study target correlation structures for cases where active-effect signs are known or unknown. Their Heuristic-Initiated Lasso Sieve procedure first creates candidate designs using simpler criteria and then ranks those candidates with the sign-recovery criterion. The main finding is that orthogonality is the target when signs are unknown, whereas small positive correlations can be preferable when signs are known.
key_results: The theory shows that, for the completely symmetric correlation structures studied, orthogonality is suboptimal for nearly all positive tuning-parameter values when active signs are known; small positive common correlations can improve sign recovery. With unknown signs, orthogonality is a local maximum over a stated range of tuning-parameter values, supporting the use of orthogonality-based design criteria. In the reported examples, the procedure took about 6 minutes for 9 runs and 10 factors with unknown signs, about 4 minutes for the same run and factor counts with known signs, and about 1 hour and 21 minutes for 14 runs and 20 factors with known signs. In the 14-run example, the selected design performed comparably to the constrained-positive variance and Dantzig-based consistency designs, and all three performed better than the unconditional orthogonality-based design; constructing the Dantzig-based consistency design took dozens of hours.
key_equations:
Assumed sparse main-effects model: \[y=\beta_0\mathbf{1}_n+X\beta+e,\qquad e\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n)\] The response is y, the intercept is beta-zero, the all-ones vector has length n, X is the design matrix, beta is the sparse effects vector, e is the error vector, sigma-squared is the error variance, and I is the identity matrix.

Local sign-recovery design objective: \[\phi_\lambda(X\mid\beta)=P(\hat z=z\mid X,\beta,\lambda)\] The criterion phi is the probability that the estimated sign vector z-hat equals the true sign vector z, conditional on design X, effects beta, and tuning parameter lambda.

Target correlation structure: \[C^*=(1-c^*)I_p+c^*J_p\] The target correlation matrix C-star has p rows and columns, identity matrix I, all-ones matrix J, and common off-diagonal correlation c-star.

HILS candidate selection: \[X_{\mathrm{HILS}}=\arg\max_{X\in\mathcal{P}}\Phi_{\max}(X\mid k,\beta)\] The selected HILS design is the candidate X in Pareto set P that maximizes the summarized sign-recovery criterion Phi-max for k active factors and effect size beta; the candidate set is generated using the trace of V and the Frobenius distance between C and C-star.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the exact sign-recovery criteria can be computationally intensive to evaluate, especially when many active-factor sets and sign patterns must be considered. The completely symmetric target correlation matrices cannot be achieved by supersaturated designs, and even the candidate-screening approach can be too computationally demanding in some settings.
limitations_unstated: The demonstrations cover only a small number of design configurations and numerical scenarios, so the comparisons do not establish how the procedure performs across the broader range of screening experiments. The framework also relies on a sparse main-effects model with normally distributed errors and a specified effect size; performance under interactions, nonnormal errors, or unknown effect magnitudes is not validated with real experiments.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying criteria based on worst-case rather than average sign-recovery probabilities, constructing exact designs with positive correlations more directly, and developing faster design-search algorithms. They also propose incorporating prior uncertainty in active-effect magnitudes and allowing inactive factors to have small nonzero effects.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the designs in real screening experiments and test robustness to interactions, nonnormal errors, and practical restrictions on factor combinations or randomization. It would also be useful to develop a sequential version that updates the design after early runs provide evidence about which factors are active and their likely signs.

summary: This paper develops and explains Gaussian process regression as a surrogate for expensive likelihood or forward-model evaluations in Bayesian inverse problems. It studies how to choose computer-experiment training points so the surrogate is accurate where the posterior distribution places substantial probability, rather than uniformly across the parameter space. The authors derive bounds connecting posterior error to surrogate error measured with the true posterior as a weight, and give conditions under which posterior-focused training points achieve near-optimal convergence rates. The construction is theoretically motivated but requires knowledge or an approximation of the posterior, creating a practical circularity. Simple numerical examples support the recommendation to place more points in high-posterior-density regions.
key_results: The theory shows that the expected prediction error weighted by the posterior can decrease at a rate arbitrarily close to N raised to minus tau divided by d_u for the stated smoothness and domain assumptions, even when a region of negligible posterior mass is excluded from training. In a one-dimensional example with a Gaussian posterior and the function f(u)=u, the error was lowest when the design distribution's variance was near the posterior variance; a uniform-posterior example likewise showed lower error as design support covered more of the posterior range. In a subsurface-flow timing example, a forward-model evaluation took 2.6 × 10^-1 seconds, compared with 3.6 × 10^-5 seconds for surrogate-mean evaluation with 10 training points; computing the surrogate coefficients took 3.2 × 10^-3 seconds. For a cited climate-model application, the paper reports that comparable inference accuracy could be reached with on the order of 10^2 forward-model evaluations using emulation, versus on the order of 10^5 without it.
key_equations:
Observation model: \[y=G(u)+\eta,\qquad \eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Gamma)\] The observed data y equal the forward map G applied to parameter u plus Gaussian noise eta with covariance Gamma.

summary: This paper develops a method for choosing sensor locations in large nonlinear inverse problems governed by partial differential equations when the model contains uncertain parameters that are not being estimated. It combines the Bayesian approximation error approach with a Gaussian approximation to the posterior and an A-optimal objective that seeks to reduce average posterior variance. The design is represented by a binary selection of candidate sensors, and the authors use a greedy procedure that adds one sensor at a time. They also develop trace-estimation and low-rank eigenvalue methods to evaluate the objective, with computational cost in PDE solves that does not grow with the discretized parameter dimensions. In a simulated three-dimensional elliptic model, accounting for model uncertainty produced better sensor designs and more reliable parameter estimates than ignoring it, especially when few sensors were available.
key_results: The demonstration used 100 candidate sensor locations, 9,600 tetrahedral elements, 2,205 basis functions, and an inversion parameter with dimension 441. The approximation-error statistics were estimated from 1,000 samples; designs were computed using 5 training data samples and evaluated using 100 validation samples. For designs with 10, 15, and 20 sensors, the uncertainty-aware designs generally had lower expected posterior variance and lower expected relative error than random designs and designs computed while ignoring model uncertainty, with the clearest advantage at smaller sensor counts. The differences between uncertainty-aware and uncertainty-unaware designs became small at 30 or more sensors, and increasing the training sample count beyond 10 yielded diminishing improvements in the reported 10-sensor study. The low-rank eigenvalue approach avoids the additional Hessian solves required by the randomized trace approach, and both objective-evaluation approaches have PDE-solve costs independent of the discretized parameter dimensions.
key_equations:

Approximation error and its statistics: \[\epsilon(m,\xi)=G(m,\xi)-F(m),\quad \epsilon_0=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon],\quad \Gamma_\epsilon=\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon)\] The symbol epsilon is the difference between the full model G and nominal-parameter model F, epsilon zero is its mean, and Gamma epsilon is its covariance, with expectation and covariance taken over the parameter distributions.

Approximate posterior covariance: \[C_{\mathrm{post}}^y=\left(F_m(m_{\mathrm{MAP}}^y)^*\Gamma_\nu^{-1}F_m(m_{\mathrm{MAP}}^y)+C_{\mathrm{pr}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\] C posterior for data y is the approximate posterior covariance, F sub m is the derivative of the nominal-parameter model F with respect to m at the maximum a posteriori point, Gamma nu is total-error covariance, and C prior is prior covariance.

A-optimal sensor selection: \[\min_{w\in\{0,1\}^{n_s},\,\mathbf{1}^T w=K}\;\mathbb{E}_y[\operatorname{tr}(C_{\mathrm{post}}^{y,w})]\] The design vector w selects sensors from n sub s candidates, K is the required sensor count, the expectation is over likely data, and the trace of the design-dependent posterior covariance C post measures total posterior variance.
limitations_stated: The method relies on Gaussian approximations for both the posterior and the approximation error, and either approximation may fail to represent the relevant distribution adequately. The greedy search can become expensive when the number of candidate locations or selected sensors becomes very large. The numerical study uses an academic, application-driven model problem, and the authors identify more challenging problems with multiple types of modeling uncertainty as an area needing further examination.
limitations_unstated: The computational evidence comes from one simulated elliptic model with a regular candidate-sensor grid, so performance under real measurement conditions, different physical models, or irregular placement constraints is not established. The method also depends on estimated approximation-error statistics and a small set of training samples; sensitivity to sampling variability in those statistics is not separately quantified in the reported design comparisons.
future_work_stated: The authors propose examining more challenging inverse problems with multiple types of modeling uncertainty. They also suggest extending the framework to approximate forward models, replacing the greedy search with relaxation or stochastic optimization methods, and investigating fixed MAP points to reduce computational cost. For problems with several sources of secondary uncertainty, they propose using sensitivity analysis to identify the most influential uncertainties.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the designs in physical experiments and assess whether their benefits persist with sensor access, placement, and operating constraints found in practice. Further work could also study sequential design, in which new sensor locations are selected after earlier measurements update the parameter and uncertainty estimates.

summary: This paper studies how to construct screening designs for estimating main effects, interactions, and quadratic effects, including designs with nuisance block effects. It compares the determinant-based D-criterion with the variance-sum A-criterion and their Bayesian versions, which account for possible effects omitted from the fitted model. The authors derive how these criteria respond when one factor setting is changed and use coordinate-exchange algorithms to construct designs for continuous factors restricted to the range from minus one to one. They show that D-optimal designs can be tied across many factor settings even when their individual variances differ, while the A-criterion can distinguish among such choices. Across the examples, A-based Bayesian designs often offered better variance and aliasing trade-offs, although the preferred trade-off depended on the model and prior settings.
key_results: For main-effect designs with 3 to 20 factors and run counts from one more than the number of factors through 24, the continuous coordinate-exchange search found an A-optimal design in every case after using up to 1,000 starting designs; the discrete search failed in the 11-run, 10-factor and 19-run, 18-factor cases even after 10,000 starts. In those two cases, the continuous designs improved the A-criterion by only 0.28% and 0.08% over the best discrete designs reported or found, respectively; another comparison showed a 0.35% improvement over a two-level design. For scenarios where the run count was three more than a multiple of four, 78% of paired main-effect variances from A-optimal designs were smaller than those from D-optimal designs, while 16% were larger. In a blocked example with 6 factors and 8 blocks of 4 runs, the selected design gave all main effects variance 1/32 and zero aliasing of those effects with block and interaction effects; 5 of 15 interactions also had optimal variance, while the others had variances of 0.047 or 0.063. The authors report that the Bayesian A-based design in that blocked example was also best under the non-Bayesian A and D criteria, and that coordinate-exchange searches for those criteria did not find it even with 100,000 starts.

Variance and A-criterion for effects of interest: \[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta)=\{F^T(I-P_Z)F\}^{-1},\qquad A_s=\operatorname{tr}[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta)]\] F is the model matrix for effects of interest, I is the identity matrix, P_Z projects onto the nuisance-effect matrix Z, beta-hat is the least-squares estimate of beta, and the A criterion sums the diagonal variances.

limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons examine selected models, run sizes, and prior-precision settings, so they do not establish that the reported advantages hold across all screening situations. future_work_stated: The authors propose further work on more flexible weighting of primary effects, comparisons of Bayesian A-criteria with direct variance-and-bias optimization, and differences between A- and D-optimal designs when higher-order interactions are included. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate these designs in real screening experiments and quantify their effects on active-factor identification and follow-up decisions. summary: This paper derives K-optimal designs for first-order and second-order Scheffé mixture models, with the goal of estimating model parameters while reducing multicollinearity. The designs are constructed on the simplex, the region where component proportions are nonnegative and sum to one. For the first-order model, the design places equal weight on every simplex vertex. For the second-order model, it places one common weight on the vertices and another common weight on the midpoints of all edges. The authors give analytical solutions and illustrate the second-order design in a constrained color photographic dispersion formulation example.
key_results: For the first-order model, the K-optimal design assigns weight 1/q to each of the q vertices, giving an information matrix condition number of 1. For the second-order model, the design uses q vertices and q(q−1)/2 edge midpoints, with per-point weights (8q−7)/(q(16q−15)) and 16/(q(16q−15)), respectively. In the three-component example, this gives six support points: each vertex receives weight 17/99 and each midpoint receives weight 16/99. For q=3, the paper reports 99.95% D-efficiency for the K-optimal design relative to the D-optimal design, and 99.98% K-efficiency for the D-optimal design relative to the K-optimal design.

limitations_unstated: The analytical results are derived for first- and second-order Scheffé models on a simplex and rely on symmetry across components, so their direct applicability to asymmetric models or more complex feasible regions is not established. future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating K-optimal designs for other mixture models, including the Becker and Draper-John models. They also identify algorithms for searching for K-optimal designs in mixture experiments as a future research problem.
future_work_unstated: Further work could develop designs for asymmetric constraints and assess robustness when the assumed model is misspecified. It could also provide a practical run-allocation and randomization procedure, software implementation, and validation in real formulation experiments.

summary: This paper develops a model-free method for selecting a small subset from a large dataset while preserving the distribution of the original data. It defines the generalized empirical F-discrepancy (GEFD) to quantify how well a subsample represents the full dataset, then constructs data-driven subsampling (DDS) by mapping a space-filling uniform design into the data space. For correlated data, the procedure rotates the data using principal component analysis (PCA), maps the design into that space, and replaces design locations with nearby observed points. The authors also give an accelerated version and a parallel strategy for data held in separate locations. Their simulations and real-data example show that DDS often improves on random sampling and is more robust across the tested models, although it is not the best method in every comparison.
key_results: For a ten-dimensional example with a subsample size of 2,000 and full-data sizes from 10^4 to 10^7, the accelerated data-driven subsampling (ADDS) time at 10^7 points was 27.6287 seconds, compared with 143.5468 seconds for DDS. In the borehole simulation with a misspecified linear regression model and a subsample size of 50, DDS had mean squared prediction error (MSPE) 38.37, compared with 43.54 for uniform random sampling (URS), 55.73 for information-based optimal subdata selection (IBOSS), and 34.31 for support points; at size 400, the respective values for DDS, URS, IBOSS, and support points were 34.48, 35.20, 41.58, and 34.22. In the borehole simulation using the transformed generalized regression model at size 400, DDS had MSPE 5.426 × 10^-2, compared with 5.598 × 10^-2 for URS, 6.672 × 10^-2 for IBOSS, and 5.312 × 10^-2 for the full-data fit. In the protein dataset study, DDS generally performed better than URS for linear regression, while support points were better at some subsample sizes; for Gaussian process regression, DDS and URS were similar at larger sizes, and DDS was slightly better at smaller sizes.

Generalized empirical F-discrepancy: \[D^2(P;X,K)=\int K(T_X(x),T_X(z))\,d(F_X-F_P)(x)\,d(F_X-F_P)(z)\] D^2 is the squared GEFD, P is the selected subsample, X is the full reference dataset, K is a reproducing kernel, T_X maps each point to marginal empirical distribution coordinates, and F_X and F_P are the empirical distributions of the full dataset and subsample.

Empirical distribution transform: \[T_X(x)=(F_{X^{(1)}}(x_1),\ldots,F_{X^{(s)}}(x_s))^T\] T_X maps point x from the original data space to the unit cube, F_{X^{(j)}} is the empirical marginal distribution for coordinate j, x_j is that point's value in coordinate j, and s is the number of coordinates.

summary: This paper designs an adaptive exploration method for policy identification in linear Markov decision processes. Its objective is to identify a policy whose value is close to optimal while reducing the number of environment episodes required. The method, called Pedel, eliminates inferior candidate policies and uses online experiment design to focus data collection on feature directions needed to compare the policies that remain. It constructs the design by using a regret-minimization algorithm to approximate experiment-design updates, without knowing the transition dynamics. The authors prove instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees and give a constructed example where Pedel improves on low-regret methods.
key_results: The authors bound Pedel’s episode count using a sum of design costs: for each time step, the cost depends on the candidate policies’ feature directions, attainable covariances, and their value gaps. For a general linear Markov decision process, the reported worst-case sample complexity has dimension dependence of order d squared divided by epsilon squared, matching the stated dimension dependence of the lower bound, with additional horizon and logarithmic factors. On a constructed easy instance with horizon 2, Pedel’s leading instance-dependent term is of order log of 2d divided by delta, divided by epsilon squared; the paper contrasts this with a worst-case lower bound of order d squared divided by epsilon squared. On that same instance, any low-regret algorithm used with the described online-to-batch protocol requires expected episode count of at least order d times log of 1 divided by delta, divided by epsilon squared, giving a factor-d separation from Pedel’s instance-dependent rate. These are theoretical results; the paper reports no empirical experiment or real-world application.

summary: The paper develops a way to allocate units across strata in a prospective randomized controlled trial (RCT) when the planned analysis will combine trial estimates with estimates from a completed observational study. Its goal is to reduce squared error in estimates of treatment effects for each stratum, using an Empirical Bayes shrinkage estimator that pulls trial estimates toward observational estimates. The authors derive a way to calculate the estimator’s risk and propose allocation approaches based on Neyman allocation, an assumption of no residual observational bias, and a sensitivity analysis for possible unmeasured confounding. They also describe design constraints intended to keep the RCT useful on its own if the observational estimates are not used. In simulations, shrinkage-focused designs generally had lower risk than equal allocation and often lower risk than Neyman allocation, including when the observational study had unmeasured confounding.
key_results: The simulations used 5,000 repetitions, a prospective RCT of 1,000 units, an observational sample of 20,000 units, and 12 strata. With no unmeasured confounding, the best non-oracle shrinkage-design results left risk at 26% to 43% of the equal-allocation trial-estimator baseline across the treatment-effect settings. With unmeasured confounding, the best non-oracle shrinkage-design results left risk at 65% to 75% of that baseline. In the confounded simulations, the authors report that sensitivity-based robust designs generally performed best with shrinkage, while the design assuming no residual bias also performed well; Neyman allocation was generally less effective for the shrinkage estimator.

Risk criterion: \[R(\kappa_2)=E_r\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\tau_k-\hat{\tau}_{k})^2\right]\] Risk is the expectation over the future experiment of the sum of squared errors across strata; kappa squared is the estimator, tau sub k is the true effect in stratum k, tau hat sub k is its estimate, k indexes strata, and K is the number of strata.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their treatment-effect heterogeneity model is rigid: effects vary according to a known stratification on observed covariates. They also note that exact risk calculation relies on knowing stratum variances and observational-estimate errors, so they use heuristics when these quantities are unknown.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on a single simulated setting with a rare binary outcome, 12 strata, and a particular construction of unmeasured confounding, so it does not establish how the designs perform across a broad range of practical trial settings. The proposed greedy optimization can stop at a local optimum, and its performance may depend on the starting allocations and on whether the stated transportability and common-moment assumptions hold.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method beyond a fixed, known stratification, including estimating strata from observational data in one stage and using remaining data for shrinkage in another. They also suggest modeling treatment effects as a function of covariates and shrinking toward estimates for nearby covariate values.
future_work_unstated: Further work could compare the allocation strategies across more trial sizes, numbers of strata, outcome types, and patterns of unmeasured confounding, and validate them using data from real experiments. It could also study sequential allocation and develop accessible software that implements risk calculation, sensitivity-based constraints, and the design search.

summary: The paper develops constructions for computer experiments that combine qualitative and quantitative factors. Its objective is to pair an orthogonal array for the qualitative factors with a Latin hypercube for the quantitative factors, while ensuring marginal coupling and avoiding cascading quantitative designs. The construction uses subspaces over finite Galois fields, selects vectors that meet specified orthogonality conditions, and then replaces levels to form the quantitative design. The authors give two construction approaches and prove when their designs have guaranteed low-dimensional stratification. They also tabulate designs with three qualitative levels for several run sizes.
key_results: The constructions produce designs with s^u runs for prime-power s, with the available numbers of qualitative and quantitative factors determined by the selected construction parameters. The paper proves that, when the number of quantitative columns is at most (s^(u-1) minus 1)/(s minus 1), the transformed quantitative array can be made stratified on an s-by-s grid in every pair of dimensions. For two-level qualitative factors, one construction guarantees stratification on a 2-by-2-by-2 grid for any three quantitative dimensions under the stated parameter conditions. Three-level designs are tabulated for u from 2 through 5; the paper provides theoretical guarantees and tables rather than numerical efficiency comparisons with competing designs.

limitations_stated: The authors do not give a formal limitations section. limitations_unstated: The method requires a prime-power number of qualitative levels and uses a run size that is a power of that number, which may not fit a practical experiment’s run budget. future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating low-dimensional space filling for the quantitative factors within each qualitative-factor level, improving three- and four-dimensional coverage when two-dimensional projections are already uniform, and constructing designs with good coverage when perfect space filling is not expected.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to develop software that automates vector selection and tests feasibility under run-budget and factor-level constraints. summary: The paper develops multivariate tie-breaker designs for estimating treatment effects when subjects have covariates and treatment allocation must also account for priority or resource constraints. It assumes a linear regression in which the response has one set of coefficients for control subjects and another for treated subjects. A tie-breaker design assigns treatment to subjects with high running scores, control to those with low scores, and randomizes subjects in the middle; the authors also choose treatment probabilities by convex optimization for fixed covariates. The design can include constraints such as a treatment budget, monotonicity in a priority score, expected gain, and covariate balance. The authors show that random assignment is optimal under their unconstrained prospective criterion, while constraints allow a tradeoff between statistical efficiency and short-term gain.
key_results: The authors prove that a randomized controlled trial with treatment probability one half is prospectively D-optimal, and that it is the unique optimum among the specified three-level tie-breaker designs. For Gaussian covariates, the determinant-based efficiency of the randomized controlled trial relative to the regression discontinuity design is about 7.57; the authors report the same ratio for all numbers of covariates in their model. With a monotonicity constraint and a fixed average treatment probability, an optimal design has at most (d+2 choose 2)+2 distinct treatment-probability levels, where d is the number of covariates. In a semi-synthetic emergency-department example, the authors select 200 patients from a database containing 448,972 entries; designs with an average treatment rate of 0.2 and a minimum gain fraction of 0.7 illustrate how constraints push probabilities toward zero for low running scores and higher probabilities for high scores.

limitations_unstated: The emergency-department example is semi-synthetic: it uses acuity scores to construct a priority direction because the authors do not have treatment outcomes, so it does not validate treatment-effect estimates or real-world patient outcomes. summary: The paper develops a graphical extension of the Friedman test for comparing treatments in a randomized complete block design. For each treatment, it calculates a squared standardized rank contribution and plots those contributions against a common decision limit. The limit comes from a gamma approximation derived by matching moments, with a Bonferroni adjustment for the number of groups. The method aims to show both whether treatment effects are present and which groups contribute to the differences, using fewer tests than the overall Friedman test followed by pairwise comparisons. Simulations and an example using recorded question counts across eight days support the method's usefulness, while showing that the gamma approximation is weaker for some moments with very few blocks.
key_results: The paper reports a reduction from G(G − 1)/2 + 1 tests to G tests; for the four-group example, this means four group contributions rather than one overall test plus six pairwise comparisons. In that example, the Friedman test had a p-value of 0.0003, and the plot at the 0.05 level identified groups A and D as outside the decision limit. The error-rate simulation used 10,000 replications, group counts of 5, 10, and 20, block counts of 8, 15, 25, and 50, and normal and exponential data at nominal levels of 0.05 and 0.01; the authors report that both the proposed method and the Friedman test met their chosen robustness criteria and had similar error-rate behavior. For the gamma approximation to the group contributions, the reported first four moments were not well approximated at three blocks, especially variance and kurtosis, while the authors describe the approximation as very good for all four moments at five or more blocks.

summary: The paper develops an experimental-design method for nonlinear dynamical systems where model errors make a planned trajectory difficult for a feedback controller to track. It uses hyper-differential sensitivity analysis to identify model perturbations that would require the greatest additional control effort. The method combines those sensitivities with user estimates of model error and expected information from candidate experiments, then chooses experiments under a cost budget. The authors demonstrate the approach on the Zermelo boat-navigation problem and on a hypersonic trajectory-control problem using an aerodynamic surrogate based on X-43 flight-test data. In both demonstrations, the selected data locations reduce the observed demand on feedback control, although the method does not guarantee the minimum actual control effort.
key_results: For the Zermelo problem, the design selected 3 model-evaluation points, and the authors report that the resulting updated model brought the open-loop path closer to its reference and notably reduced feedback effort. They compared this design with 100 random 3-point designs, averaging tracking error and feedback effort over 100 perturbed high-fidelity models; the proposed design outperformed the majority of the random designs, but was not the best possible design by actual feedback effort. For the hypersonic case, the method selected 8 aerodynamic-evaluation points, after which the closed-loop trajectory improved and feedback no longer violated the controller bounds. The paper reports these improvements qualitatively and gives no numerical percentage reduction in effort or tracking error.

summary: The paper develops an online sequential test for qualitative treatment effects, where a new treatment may improve outcomes for some covariate-defined subgroups even if it does not improve outcomes for everyone. It models each treatment's conditional mean reward with a linear combination of basis functions and tests whether the treatment effect is positive anywhere in the covariate space. At successive analyses, the method estimates the treatment effects, uses a studentized supremum statistic, and determines stopping boundaries with a bootstrap and an error-spending rule. The method supports adaptive treatment assignment and can update its calculations as batches of observations arrive. The authors show theoretically that the procedure controls type-I error under stated assumptions and report simulations and a user-click-log example in which the test can stop early when evidence is present.
key_results: In simulations of qualitative treatment effects, the proposed test's type-I rejection rates were generally close to the nominal 5 percent level; reported null rejection rates were about 5.5 to 6.2 percent across the displayed settings. With nonzero effects, power increased with effect size and reached 99.8 percent in one reported setting; average stopping time also fell as effect size increased. In the same comparisons, the law-of-iterated-logarithm test had zero rejections across the qualitative-effect alternatives shown. The Yahoo! click-log analysis used 405,888 visits for two articles; the authors report that the test rejected after collecting about the first third of the observations in the A/B analysis and did not reject in the A/A analyses. The authors report an average computation time of 1 to 2 seconds per simulated test and several seconds for the real-data analysis.

Qualitative treatment-effect null hypothesis: \[H_0:Q_0(x,1)\le Q_0(x,0)\ \forall x\in\mathcal X\quad\text{vs.}\quad H_1:\exists x\in\mathcal X:Q_0(x,1)>Q_0(x,0)\] The null says the treatment's conditional mean reward Q0 at treatment 1 is no greater than at treatment 0 for every covariate value x in the covariate space X; the alternative says it is greater for at least one such value.

Studentized supremum test statistic: \[S(t)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\frac{\phi(x)^\top\{\widehat\beta_1(t)-\widehat\beta_0(t)\}}{\widehat{se}[\phi(x)^\top\{\widehat\beta_1(t)-\widehat\beta_0(t)\}]}\] At time t, S is the largest over covariate values x of the estimated treatment-minus-control mean contrast, using estimated coefficient vectors and dividing by the estimated standard error of that contrast.

Sequential stopping rule: \[\text{Reject }H_0\text{ at }t_k\text{ if }\sqrt{N(t_k)}S(t_k)>z_k\] At analysis k and time t_k, reject the null if the square root of the number of observations N collected by that time multiplied by the statistic S exceeds the stage boundary z.
limitations_stated: The main procedure uses the same basis functions at every interim analysis; the authors describe allowing the basis dimension to grow across analyses as desirable. They also note that this varying-basis extension is substantially more computationally intensive, and discuss a two-sided test as an extension rather than the main procedure.
limitations_unstated: The theoretical guarantees depend on assumptions including sequential randomization, adequate assignment probability to both treatments, a sufficiently accurate basis approximation, and conditions on the outcome distribution and adaptive allocation. Practical validation is limited: the simulations cover selected settings, and the real-data illustration uses one historical click-log subset with constructed A/A and A/B comparisons rather than a prospective operational deployment.
future_work_stated: The authors propose allowing the number of basis functions to increase across interim analyses to reduce approximation error, while noting the added computational burden. future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method prospectively in live experiments with operational constraints such as minimum traffic per arm, delayed outcomes, and limits on how frequently results can be checked. Further work could also provide a maintained software implementation and assess robustness when the conditional-mean model or adaptive assignment mechanism differs from the assumptions.

summary: The paper develops a Bayesian optimal-design method for experiments in which controllable variables can change during a run. It treats a scalar response as depending on time-varying profile variables through a scalar-on-function linear model, representing both the profiles and model parameters with finite basis expansions. This representation turns the problem into a standard linear-model design problem, with profile coefficients chosen to reduce expected estimation loss while respecting feasible operating ranges. The method is demonstrated in numerical examples and in a 12-run Ambr250 bioreactor study with dynamic feed volume and three static variables. The method produced implementable feed profiles, but the fitted bioreactor model did not find a significant effect of feed volume on titre.
key_results: In the illustrative examples, the authors evaluated squared-error and weighted squared-error criteria for 4 and 12 runs, two model complexities, and profile expansions ranging from 2 to 100 basis functions where estimable. For the Ambr250 study, the 12-run design used 4 basis functions for feed profiles and had an objective value of 69.802; the reported values were 68.085, 66.505, and 65.304 for 8, 16, and 100 basis functions, while 3 basis functions gave 128.802. Thus, increasing profile complexity beyond 4 gave limited gains, whereas using 3 basis functions gave a substantially worse objective value. After one run failed and one titre response was censored, the selected model retained effects for initial cell concentration, acidity, and temperature, including a quadratic temperature term; the dynamic feed effect was not significant.
key_equations:
Standard linear-model representation: \[y=Z\theta+\varepsilon\] The response vector y equals the model matrix Z multiplied by the coefficient vector θ, plus the random-error vector ε.

Bayesian squared-error design objective: \[\Psi(\Gamma)=\operatorname{tr}\left[(Z^{T}Z+\Sigma^{-1})^{-1}\right]\] The objective Ψ for design coefficients Γ is the trace of the inverse of the sum of the transposed model matrix Z times Z and the inverse prior covariance matrix Σ; the superscript T means transpose and the superscript −1 means inverse.
limitations_stated: The authors state that Bayesian optimal design requires assumptions about the data-generating process before responses are observed and may be sensitive to those assumptions. They also note that model complexity must be specified before the experiment.
limitations_unstated: The real study had only 12 planned runs, and only 11 returned titre responses, limiting the amount of information available to assess model adequacy and the feed effect. The reported design comparisons are primarily objective-function comparisons within the proposed framework; the paper does not report a head-to-head experimental comparison with a conventional static design or another design method.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to non-normal responses and scalar-on-function generalized linear models, where expected-loss objectives may not have closed forms. They also identify extensions to profile variables with multiple inputs, such as spatio-temporal studies, and exploration of Gibbs optimal design.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare this design prospectively with static or alternative dynamic designs under the same experimental budget, including validation of prediction and parameter-estimation performance. Further work could also evaluate designs under practical constraints such as restricted feed schedules, process safety limits, and sequential adaptation after observing early runs.

summary: This paper develops a design-based framework for bounding and estimating the variance of linear estimators in randomized finite-population experiments. It covers estimators including contrasts of means, Horvitz-Thompson estimators, ordinary least squares, and weighted least squares, across a broad range of assignment designs. The method uses a first-order Taylor approximation to express the variance of many estimators through a common design matrix, then constructs identified variance bounds using bounding matrices. A plug-in estimator applies these bounds to observed data. The paper shows that this framework includes familiar heteroskedasticity-robust and cluster-robust standard errors as special cases.
key_results: The paper derives an exact quadratic-form variance for Horvitz-Thompson estimators and for first-order Taylor approximations of general linear estimators, and gives conditions for consistency of the point and variance-bound estimators. In a comparison with 4 units, the eigenvalues of the difference between the complete-randomization and pair-randomization design matrices are 2.67, 0, and negative 1.33; the example shows that either design can be more precise depending on the potential outcomes. For that pair-randomized example, the paper’s iterative bounding algorithm produces a tighter bound than the Aronow-Samii bound, as their difference has eigenvalues 2 and 0. The paper also establishes that, under independent Bernoulli assignment, its ordinary least-squares bound estimator reduces to the canonical heteroskedasticity-robust estimator, and under independent cluster assignment it reproduces cluster-robust standard errors.
key_equations:
Linear estimator: \[\hat{\delta}_c = c^{\mathsf T} W R y\] Delta hat c is the linear estimate, c is the contrast vector, W is the estimator matrix, R is the assignment-indicator matrix, y is the potential-outcome vector, and the superscript T denotes transpose.

Variance of a Taylor approximation: \[V(\hat{\delta}_c) = z^{\mathsf T} d z\] V is the variance operator, delta hat c here denotes a first-order Taylor approximation to the linear estimator, z is its outcome-related vector, d is the first-order design matrix, and the superscript T denotes transpose.

Variance bound: \[z^{\mathsf T} d z \leq z^{\mathsf T} \widetilde{d} z\] z is the outcome-related vector, d is the first-order design matrix, d tilde is a bounding matrix, and the superscript T denotes transpose; the inequality states that the quadratic form from the bounding matrix is at least as large as the variance quadratic.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the generalized Neyman bound requires particular design and contrast conditions, so it does not apply to every design. They describe the general iterative bounding algorithm as a proof of concept. For estimators other than the Horvitz-Thompson estimator, the proposed plug-in variance-bound estimator is generally not unbiased because its inputs include quantities that must be estimated.
limitations_unstated: The paper provides theoretical derivations and illustrative matrix comparisons, but no empirical study or broad numerical evaluation of the accuracy or practical value of the bounds. The iterative algorithm operates on matrices whose dimensions grow with the number of units and treatment arms, but its computational cost, convergence behavior in practice, and feasible experiment sizes are not evaluated.
future_work_stated: The authors say that point estimation, consistency, and causal identification will be addressed in the third and fourth papers of their series. They do not state a separate future research program for the variance-bound method itself.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the bounds and algorithm across more assignment designs, including realistic restrictions such as unequal allocation, blocked or clustered assignment, and limited randomization. The framework could also be tested in real experiments and extended to sequential designs or alternative inferential criteria, with software and computational benchmarks to assess practical scalability.

summary: This paper is a tutorial and review on using Bayesian optimization to choose experiments for expensive black-box problems, with a focus on additive manufacturing. It explains the method using a probabilistic surrogate model, most often a Gaussian process, and an acquisition function that selects the next setting or batch of settings. It reviews applications in additive manufacturing, surveys open-source software, and provides coding examples for batch, multi-objective, constrained, and preference-based optimization. The examples use manufacturing data and illustrate how different software packages suggest experiments. The authors conclude that Bayesian optimization can help search large design spaces with relatively few trials, while software choice depends mainly on the problem features practitioners need.
key_results: The authors found eight papers applying Bayesian optimization to additive manufacturing, all published in the five years preceding their review. They compared software packages across nine practical features and provided batch-optimization examples using seven libraries, starting from 27 experimental settings and requesting batches of two. The paper also describes a prior study in which simulations suggested nearly a 60-fold reduction in the number of experiments, and another system that produced near-ideal geometry within 100 experiments. The software examples return different next settings; the paper presents them as demonstrations rather than a controlled comparison of predictive performance or efficiency.
key_equations:
Noisy black-box observation model: \[y=f(x)+\epsilon,\quad \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\] The observed output y at setting x is the unknown objective f evaluated at x plus noise ε, which follows a normal distribution with mean zero and variance σ².

Next-setting selection: \[x_{n+1}=\arg\max_{x\in X}\alpha(x;D_{1:n})\] The next setting x at observation n plus one maximizes acquisition function α over design space X, using collected data D through observation n.

Expected improvement: \[\alpha(x;D_{1:n})=\mathbb{E}[\max(0,f(x)-\hat f)\mid D_{1:n}]\] The expected improvement α at setting x is the expected positive difference between the unknown objective f at x and the best value observed so far, f̂, conditional on data D through observation n.
limitations_stated: The authors describe research applying Bayesian optimization in additive manufacturing as being at an early stage and report finding only eight papers. They also note that their software feature comparison reflects the state of the packages as of October 2021, and that some acquisition-function lists were incomplete.
limitations_unstated: The paper does not conduct a consistent, head-to-head validation of the software packages on common real manufacturing experiments; its package examples mainly show how to obtain recommendations. The illustrative run showing optimization progress uses a degree-two polynomial fitted using all 108 experimental results, so it is not an independent real-world validation of performance during a sequential campaign.
future_work_stated: The authors do not propose a specific future study. They note the trend toward autonomous and digitalized additive manufacturing and expect Bayesian optimization to be an important technology for intelligent manufacturing.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a prospective comparison of the methods on real manufacturing campaigns, with consistent budgets, constraints, noise handling, and outcomes such as product quality and experiment cost. Further work could also test how well the methods handle model mismatch and practical restrictions on settings, and validate preference-based optimization in real production studies.

summary: This paper studies whether experimental designs can improve estimation of the precision matrix, which represents relationships among response variables, in a Gaussian chain graph model. The regression effects of experimental predictors are treated as nuisance parameters, and the design objective is to improve precision-matrix inference. The authors derive a Laplace approximation to the marginal posterior precision and compare four prior choices: flat, Normal-Wishart, Normal-MGIG, and general independent priors. The approximation is independent of the design under the flat and Normal-Wishart priors, while the other two prior settings allow design information to affect inference but impose a theoretical upper bound on that gain. Simulations and a human gut microbiome example indicate that experiments are most helpful when prior knowledge about their effects is both accurate and sufficiently certain.
key_results: The simulations used 50 response variables, 50 predictors, six covariance structures, sample sizes from 200 to 2,200 in increments of 50, and 100 repetitions per setting. Compared with a null design, the clearest sustained improvement in information gain and precision-matrix estimation occurred with the Normal-MGIG prior at the certain setting, where Lambda was 10 to the power of negative 3 times the identity matrix; the improvements changed little as sample size increased. For the other main prior settings, the differences from the null design generally approached zero as sample size increased, while biased certain priors could produce less accurate estimates. The real-data example used fecal microbiota from 178 elderly subjects, but the experiment comparison was simulated from fitted model estimates; only the Normal-MGIG prior showed reduced posterior uncertainty under the hypothetical experiment, compared with Normal-Wishart.
key_equations:
Gaussian chain graph model: \[Y_i\mid X_i,B,\Omega\sim\mathcal{N}(\Omega^{-1}B^{\mathsf T}X_i,\Omega^{-1})\] Y_i is the response vector for observation i, X_i is its predictor vector, B is the regression coefficient matrix, Omega is the response precision matrix, and the distribution is multivariate normal.

Marginal posterior precision approximation: \[J_{\Omega}=A-GD^{-1}C\] J_Omega is the Laplace-approximated marginal posterior precision for Omega, and A, G, C, and D are blocks of the joint posterior precision matrix for the regression coefficients and Omega.

Design-dependent information and its bound: \[\Omega^{-1}B_0^{\mathsf T}[\Lambda^{-1}-\Lambda^{-1}(X^{\mathsf T}X+\Lambda^{-1})^{-1}\Lambda^{-1}]B_0\Omega^{-1}\preceq\Omega^{-1}B_0^{\mathsf T}\Lambda^{-1}B_0\Omega^{-1}\] Omega is the response precision matrix, B0 is the prior mean of the regression coefficients, Lambda is their prior uncertainty matrix, X is the design matrix, and the matrix inequality states that the design-dependent information is bounded by the expression on the right.

D-optimal design criterion discussed for the Normal-MGIG setting: \[\max_X\det(X^{\mathsf T}X+\Lambda^{-1})\] X is the experimental design matrix, Lambda is the prior uncertainty matrix for regression coefficients, and det denotes the determinant being maximized.
limitations_stated: The authors note that a broad comparison of priors for Gaussian chain graph models is beyond the scope of this paper. They also state that the Laplace approximation is valid only for log-concave posterior densities, so their derivations require conditions that ensure log concavity.
limitations_unstated: The simulation comparisons use random designs, specific diagonal designs, and a null design rather than numerically optimizing and testing the designs suggested by the derived criteria. The simulations fix both the number of responses and predictors at 50 and assume a particular design context, while practical constraints such as treatment availability, costs, and restrictions on allocation are not modeled. The microbiome analysis is not a prospective experiment: its hypothetical comparison uses simulated observations generated from parameters estimated from already collected data.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying whether the need for prior knowledge of treatment effects also arises in general Gibbs models, including the auto-logistic or Ising model, when designing experiments to infer networks. They note that approximations to the partition function may help connect that problem to their Gaussian results.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate genuinely optimized designs under realistic treatment, cost, and allocation constraints, and compare them with the random and specific designs used here. Further work could assess robustness of the design conclusions to prior misspecification and to non-Gaussian data, and test the recommendations in prospective experiments rather than simulations based on fitted observational data.

summary: This paper extends Bayesian Evidential Learning (BEL) to predict a wellhead protection area (WHPA) and to choose informative locations for tracer injection wells. It studies a simulated, single-layer groundwater aquifer in which hydraulic conductivity influences both the protection-area shape and tracer breakthrough curves measured at a pumping well. The method learns a predictor-to-target relationship from forward-simulated examples, reducing the data dimensions with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and learning correlations with Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA). It estimates a posterior distribution of protection areas directly from the tracer data, then evaluates candidate well locations by comparing posterior predictions with known targets. In the simulations, the downstream injection wells were more informative overall, with well 6 ranked highest, and cross-validation indicated that larger test sets were needed for stable design conclusions than for prediction.
key_results: A training set of 400 simulated cases was sufficient for prediction; the average image-similarity results stabilized at about that size. For the predictor, 50 principal components retained 99.87% of its variance, while 30 target components retained 98.81%. The modified Hausdorff distance (MHD) and structural similarity index (SSIM) gave similar rankings: wells 4, 5, and 6 were more informative than wells 1, 2, and 3, with well 6 the strongest overall and well 1 the weakest. Five-fold cross-validation showed that 100 test cases gave inconsistent rankings, while a dataset of 1,250 cases split into 1,000 training and 250 test cases gave consistent results. The authors report a forward-modeling time of 37 minutes per simulated pair and state that their approach avoids the thousands or more forward-model evaluations associated with some alternative design approaches, while retaining a full posterior prediction.
key_equations:
Posterior target distribution: \[p(\mathbf{h}^{c}\mid\mathbf{d}^{c}_{obs})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{h\mid d},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h\mid d})\] The equation states the assumed conditional Gaussian distribution of the target in canonical space, where p is probability, h is the target, d is the observed predictor, obs marks the observed value, mu is the conditional mean, Sigma is the conditional covariance, and N denotes a multivariate normal distribution.

Modified Hausdorff distance: \[\operatorname{MHD}(P,Q)=\max\left\{\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p\in P}\min_{q\in Q}D_{pq},\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\min_{p\in P}D_{pq}\right\}\] P and Q are the contour-point sets being compared, |P| and |Q| are their point counts, p and q are individual points, D_pq is the Euclidean distance between them, and MHD is the larger of the two directed average nearest-point distances.

Candidate-location design score: \[S(\ell)=\sum_{r=1}^{N_{test}}\sum_{j=1}^{\zeta}\operatorname{MHD}(h_r,\widetilde{h}_{\ell,r,j}),\qquad \ell^{*}=\arg\min_{\ell}S(\ell)\] S is the summed prediction discrepancy for candidate location ell, N_test is the number of test cases, r indexes a test case, zeta is the number of posterior samples, j indexes a sample, h_r is the true target, h-tilde is a posterior target sample for that location and test case, and ell-star is the location with the smallest score.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the canonical-correlation learning approach relies on linear relationships in reduced dimensions and can be biased when relationships are highly nonlinear. Training-set size, retained component counts, posterior sample counts, and the utility function require practitioner choices. They also note that their prior hydraulic-conductivity fields are smooth simulations, which may not represent more complex geological structures.
limitations_unstated: The design comparison tests only six predefined injection-well locations and optimizes one location at a time, so it does not establish how the method performs for combinations of wells or broader operational constraints. The evidence is entirely simulated and uses a single-layer aquifer; performance and rankings are not validated with field measurements. Each candidate design still requires forward simulations across prior cases, so the total computational burden could remain substantial when many locations or configurations are considered.
future_work_stated: The authors indicate that the framework can be extended to all possible spatial configurations involving one or more wells. They also state that additional uncertain model parameters, such as boundary conditions or spatial-correlation parameters, can be included, and discuss kernel density estimation or iterative prior updates as options when the assumed relationships are inadequate.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the design on field tracer tests and determine whether the recommended locations remain informative with measurement noise and practical well-placement constraints. Further work could compare multiwell combinations and alternative prediction-focused utility criteria, and assess whether the design can be updated sequentially as new tracer measurements arrive.
