summary: The paper characterizes variable-permutation symmetries in the linear programming relaxation of an integer linear program used to enumerate two-level orthogonal arrays. The objective is to identify symmetries that can help remove equivalent cases when arrays are classified up to isomorphism. The authors express the array constraints using J-characteristics and identify the symmetry group through transformations that preserve the row space of the constraint matrix. They prove exact group characterizations for strength one and for strength two when the number of factors is at least four. The strength-two result reveals symmetries beyond the natural group generated by factor and level permutations.
key_results: For a two-level orthogonal array of strength one, the authors prove that the relaxation's symmetry group is the wreath product of the two-element symmetric group with the factor-permutation group, with order 2^k k!. For strength two and k at least 4, they prove the group is the semidirect product of a group of order 2^k with the symmetric group on k+1 objects, with order 2^k(k+1!), equivalently 2^k times (k+1)!. This is larger by a factor of k+1 than the natural symmetry group of order 2^k k!. For k=3, the paper reports a different group of order 1152, isomorphic to (S4 times S4) semidirect product S2. The paper also notes that exploiting the newly identified strength-two symmetries had enabled results on arrays with 160 and 176 runs in related work; it does not report a comparative benchmark of design methods.
key_equations:
Frequency-vector formulation and its relaxation: \[Mf=J,\qquad f\ge 0\] M is the constraint matrix, f is the nonnegative frequency vector, and J is the target vector of J-characteristics; this is the equality-constraint portion of the linear programming relaxation.

Characterization of the relaxation's symmetry group: \[G_{LP}=\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{Row}(M))\cap S_{2^k}\] G_LP is the group of variable permutations preserving the relaxation; Aut denotes the invertible transformations preserving the row space, Row(M) is the row space of M, and S_{2^k} is the symmetric group on the 2^k frequency-vector entries.

Strength-one symmetry group: \[G_{LP}\cong S_2\wr S_k\] G_LP is the relaxation's symmetry group, S_2 is the symmetric group on two objects, S_k permutes the k factors, and the wreath product describes their combined group.

Strength-two symmetry group: \[G_{LP}\cong S_2^k\rtimes S_{k+1},\qquad k\ge 4\] G_LP is the relaxation's symmetry group, S_2^k is the direct product of k copies of the two-object symmetric group, S_{k+1} is the symmetric group on k+1 objects, and the semidirect product gives the group structure for k at least 4.
limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a formal limitations section. They state that the strength-two characterization applies when k is at least 4 and does not hold for k=3; their proposed characterizations for other strengths and level counts remain conjectures.
limitations_unstated: The proven results cover the specified two-level cases, not the general range of levels and strengths used in practice. The strength-two proof also uses R code to check possible linear combinations, and the paper does not report empirical benchmarks quantifying the computational benefit of the additional symmetries.
future_work_stated: The authors propose settling their conjectures: for two levels, that the group is the natural wreath product at odd strengths and the stated semidirect product at even strengths; for more than two levels, that it is the natural wreath product. They leave these characterizations as open problems for the stated formulation and equivalent formulations obtained by elementary row operations on the equality constraints.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to benchmark the additional symmetries in array-enumeration problems, reporting changes in solver time and search-tree size against the natural symmetry group. Further work could also test how the symmetry characterization and pruning perform when practical design constraints are added, and provide a reusable implementation of the group calculations.

summary: The paper introduces a way to conduct approximate Bayesian inference when likelihood evaluations are costly or noisy. It models the log-likelihood with a GP and uses that model to emulate the decisions made by an MH sampler. When the model is not sufficiently certain about an accept-or-reject decision, the method selects another likelihood evaluation to reduce uncertainty about that decision. The authors derive a sequential evaluation-location criterion and study both an iterative sampler and a two-stage variant. In their examples, the method often approximates posterior distributions with a few hundred likelihood evaluations, while its use depends on suitable smoothness and noise assumptions and careful initialization.
key_results: In three six-parameter synthetic examples, EPoE generally used evaluations more efficiently than the simple baseline; with a decision tolerance near 0.3, it produced reasonable approximations using at most a few hundred evaluations. For the five-parameter theta-Ricker example, a tolerance of 0.35 gave reported total variation distances at or below 0.1 with about 300–500 synthetic-likelihood evaluations. The cell biology example also produced reasonable approximations with a few hundred evaluations, although some individual decisions needed around 30–70 evaluations. The iterative sampler and its two-stage variant gave similar results; EPoE was generally competitive with the earlier integrated median interquantile range design, though that earlier design was slightly more efficient in the Ricker example.

Noisy log-likelihood model: \[y_j=f(\theta_j)+e_j,\qquad e_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_n^2(\theta_j))\] Here y_j is a noisy evaluation at parameter theta_j, f is the unknown log-likelihood, e_j is the evaluation noise, and sigma_n is its location-dependent standard deviation.

summary: The paper develops a design-based account of regression analysis for full factorial experiments with binary factors, focusing on estimating treatment effects. It defines general factorial effects as weighted averages of conditional effects, allowing the weights to reflect the target population or scientific question. The authors show how location-shifted factor-based regressions can estimate these effects and establish the sampling properties of their robust covariance estimates under complete randomization. For more than two factors, saturated regressions directly target effects under product weighting schemes; in the absence of three-way interactions, they extend to all coherent weighting schemes. Unsaturated regressions can be more precise, but may be biased when omitted interactions are present.
key_results: For an experiment with K binary factors, the saturated model includes 2^K minus 1 non-intercept terms and its coefficients equal the moment estimates of general factorial effects under the product weighting scheme induced by the location shifts. The robust covariance from this regression is asymptotically conservative for the design-based sampling covariance, supporting large-sample Wald-type inference. Under the no-three-way-interactions condition, the product-weighting restriction no longer limits inference to product-weighted effects. Under constant treatment effects, unsaturated regression estimates have smaller sampling covariance than the corresponding saturated estimates; without the no-nuisance-effects condition, however, the unsaturated estimates can have non-diminishing bias.
key_equations:
Location-shifted saturated regression: \[Y_i \sim 1+\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\}}\prod_{k\in S}(Z_{ik}-\delta_k)\] The observed outcome for unit i is regressed on an intercept and all nonempty products of shifted factor levels; K is the number of factors, S selects the factors in a term, Z_ik is unit i's level of factor k, and delta_k is that factor's location shift.

Coefficient and factorial-effect estimator correspondence: \[\hat{\gamma}=\hat{\tau}_{\delta_\times}\] The saturated regression coefficient vector equals the moment estimator of the general factorial effects under the product weighting scheme determined by the location shifts.
limitations_stated: The authors focus on complete randomization and note that Wald-type inference must be modified for other assignment mechanisms. They also caution that the zero-nuisance-effects assumption for unsaturated models cannot be verified exactly in practice, and that omitting nonzero effects can cause non-diminishing bias.
limitations_unstated: The paper gives no quantitative sample-size or run-allocation guidance for deciding when the saturated model's number of terms is impractical. Its theoretical bias-variance results and supplementary numerical examples do not establish how well the proposed approach performs in real experiments with uncertain interaction structure.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying data-driven model selection and post-selection inference under the design-based framework. They also suggest extending the theory to experiments with non-constant treatment probabilities using inverse-probability-weighted least squares.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to develop practical run-size and allocation recommendations that account for the number of factors and uncertainty about nuisance interactions. Software and validation on real factorial experiments would also help assess whether the theoretical precision gains translate into reliable applied analyses.

summary: This paper presents IsoCheck, an R package for checking whether two-level, multi-stage factorial designs with randomization restrictions are equivalent or isomorphic. It represents factorial effects as points in projective geometry over the field with two elements, and represents randomization defining contrast subspaces using spreads or covering stars. The package searches for relabelings through collineation matrices and speeds up equivalence checks with bitstring representations. The authors also show how the package can support catalogs of non-isomorphic designs and ranking by a design criterion. The paper's examples demonstrate the package's functions, but do not report runtime benchmarks or propose new designs or ranking criteria.
key_results: The package identifies the two illustrated one-spreads of P4 as isomorphic and reports 360 isomorphism-establishing collineations. It also finds isomorphisms for the illustrated spreads of P6 and for two designs in a 64-wafer example with six factors and nine subspaces of size seven. In an illustrative catalog search, the authors examined over 5 million random permutations and found almost 110 isomorphic spreads; they note this search was not exhaustive. The example design criterion values were 0.22 for the initial design and 0.44 for another design found by the search, with the lower value preferred under that criterion.

limitations_unstated: The paper provides worked examples but no timing, memory, or scaling results, so the practical computational limits of the isomorphism search are unclear. The methods also assume the specified spread or star structure and do not demonstrate how they handle practical randomization constraints that fall outside those structures.
future_work_stated: None stated.

summary: This paper applies optimal experimental design (OED) to reduce the number of isotherms needed to fit a liquid-density correlation model. The model is a Schilling-type equation of state (EOS) with eight terms, applied to real density data for ethylene glycol and propylene glycol. For the fixed-exponent model, the authors rank candidate isotherms by how much information they provide about the model coefficients, using an A-criterion that minimizes parameter uncertainty. They compare fits using the five most informative measured isotherms with fits using all measured isotherms, and also examine models with freely fitted exponents. The five-isotherm fits have density deviations close to the all-isotherm fits, suggesting that OED can support accurate modeling with fewer measurement series.
key_results: For ethylene glycol, the fixed-exponent model fitted to the five selected isotherms had a greatest relative deviation of 0.02542%, compared with 0.02243% for the fit using all eight measured isotherms. For propylene glycol, the corresponding deviations were 0.01571% using five selected isotherms and 0.01434% using all nine. Each ethylene glycol isotherm plan had nine pressure values, and each propylene glycol plan had eight; the five-isotherm designs therefore use five of the available isotherms, not five individual measurements. The A-criterion value for the five-isotherm measured selection was 78.82 for ethylene glycol and 90.86 for propylene glycol; the authors also calculated candidate selections on a freely chosen temperature grid spaced at 2 K but could not compare those selections using new measurements.
key_equations:
Schilling-type density model: \[\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}=\sum_{j=1}^{I_{\mathrm{Pol}}} n_j\,\sigma^{t_j}\,\pi^{p_j}\] Density rho is scaled by reference density rho_0; the sum runs over model terms j through I_Pol; n_j is the coefficient, sigma is reduced temperature, pi is reduced pressure, and t_j and p_j are their respective exponents.

Reduced temperature and pressure: \[\sigma=\frac{T}{T_0}-1,\qquad \pi=\frac{p}{p_0}+1\] Temperature T and pressure p are scaled by reference values T_0 and p_0 to give reduced temperature sigma and reduced pressure pi.

Information matrix for a series: \[I=\sum_i I_i,\qquad I_i=j(\pi_i,\sigma_i)^{\mathsf T}j(\pi_i,\sigma_i)\] The series information matrix I is the sum of the information matrices I_i from independent measurements i; each I_i is the outer product of the elementary Jacobian j evaluated at that measurement's reduced pressure pi_i and reduced temperature sigma_i.

A-criterion for selecting isotherms: \[\Psi_A(I)=\operatorname{trace}(I^{-1})=\sum_{k=1}^{8}\frac{1}{\lambda_k}\] The A-criterion value Ψ_A is the trace of the inverse series information matrix I, equivalently the sum of the reciprocals of its eight eigenvalues lambda_k; the design selects isotherms to minimize this value.
limitations_stated: Because the analysis used only already measured data, the authors could not compare a model fitted to the five best freely selected isotherms with one fitted to the five best measured isotherms. limitations_unstated: The design criterion is calculated for the linear fixed-exponent model, so its ranking does not establish that the same isotherms are optimal when exponents are also estimated. future_work_unstated: A prospective study could apply the selected isotherms to new fluids and independent measurement campaigns, checking whether the predicted reduction in effort holds under practical constraints and measurement variability. Further work could compare alternative design criteria that account for predictive accuracy or extrapolation and provide a usable software workflow for selecting and updating measurement plans.

summary: This paper designs a sequential sampling strategy for accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The strategy learns, from each current reconstruction, which Cartesian column of k-space to measure next, using policy-gradient methods and a fixed, pretrained reconstruction model. Its objective is to maximize final reconstruction quality, measured by the structural similarity index measure (SSIM), with reward defined as the quality improvement after each new measurement. The authors compare a greedy policy, which learns from immediate improvement, with non-greedy policies that account for later rewards, using knee and brain data from the fastMRI dataset. The greedy policy performs close to or better than the tested non-greedy alternatives and takes less time to train; the authors associate its performance with better adaptation to individual images.
key_results: On the knee data, the greedy method achieved SSIM scores of 0.7230 for the base horizon and 0.7442 for the long horizon, compared with 0.7223 and 0.7421 for the fully non-greedy method; the method with a discount factor of 0.9 scored 0.7232 and 0.7449. For knee data, the base and long settings made 16 and 28 further acquisitions and ended at an acceleration factor of 4; for brain data, the same acquisition counts were used, but the final acceleration differed because the images were larger. Approximate training times were 1.0 and 1.5 days for the greedy knee models versus 1.5 and 2.0 days for the fully non-greedy models, and 2.0 and 4.5 days for greedy brain models versus 3.0 and 5.0 days for fully non-greedy models.

future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method with multiple reconstruction architectures and alternative objectives that reflect diagnostic needs, not just image similarity. summary: The paper develops a computational method for choosing sensor locations to maximize expected information gain in Bayesian inverse problems governed by partial differential equations. key_results: In the linear example with 9 candidate sensors, the swapping greedy algorithm found the best design for 6 of the 7 tested sensor budgets; for the remaining budget it found the second-best design, while standard greedy selection found the best design for 3 of the 7 budgets. limitations_stated: The authors state that their framework assumes a Gaussian prior and additive Gaussian observation noise. They also identify the approximations used for nonlinear problems and the limitations inherent in greedy algorithms as drawbacks.
limitations_unstated: The validation consists of simulated examples rather than real experiments, and the candidate locations and sensor budgets are prescribed rather than subject to deployment constraints such as access, sensor cost, or correlated noise. summary: The paper introduces Bayesian truncated additive optimization (BTAO) to find machine-learning hyperparameter settings that minimize validation error while reducing training time. summary: This paper develops a sequential Bayesian method for choosing experiments to estimate the probability of structural failure when parts of the model are uncertain or expensive to evaluate. It addresses both hierarchical models with expensive subcomponents and models with uncertain parameters or costly function evaluations. At each step, the method selects an experiment expected to reduce uncertainty in the failure probability, while accounting for experiment cost. It approximates epistemic uncertainty with the unscented transform and uses Monte Carlo importance sampling to estimate rare failure probabilities; surrogate models are often Gaussian processes. In simulated examples, the method produced useful estimates with substantially fewer function evaluations than some reported comparison methods, while its one-step decision strategy also showed a potential stopping problem.
key_results: For the four-branch benchmark, the method used 35, 48, or 65 evaluations and reported failure-probability intervals of 4.163–4.547, 4.288–4.470, and 4.347–4.444, respectively, in units of 10 to the power of minus 3; each interval contained the Monte Carlo reference value of 4.416 in the same units. The table reports 124 and 126 evaluations for two active-learning comparison variants and 1,000,000 for Monte Carlo. In the seven-input hierarchical benchmark, the procedure converged after 10 iterations, with 2 additional evaluations of one expensive subcomponent and 8 of another; the reference failure probability was approximately 8.1 times 10 to the power of minus 3. In the pipeline example, the target-based stopping condition was reached after 25 iterations; across 100 runs, the expected-input initial design averaged 23 additional finite-element evaluations, 10 model-discrepancy observations, and 2 defect-depth measurements. These are simulated examples, not results from field experiments.
key_equations: Myopic experiment-selection criterion: \[d_k^* = \arg\min_d \lambda(d)\,E_k\!\left[H_{i,k+1}\mid d\right]\] Here d is a candidate experiment, k is the current experiment index, lambda is its cost, E_k is expectation given information available at that step, H is residual uncertainty after the next experiment, and i selects among the paper's three uncertainty measures.
limitations_stated: The authors describe their finite-dimensional approximation as crude: its simplest form treats uncertainty across input locations as fully correlated. They also report that the unscented-transform implementation uses few, predetermined points and can overestimate variance. They state that the one-step strategy can fail to reach a stopping condition and may keep requesting experiments at potentially unbounded cost; a fuller dynamic-programming solution is computationally difficult because of the curse of dimensionality.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence comes from four simulated examples, and the direct method comparisons are concentrated on one benchmark using results reported in earlier work; performance on real infrastructure experiments is not established. The uncertainty approximation and sampling strategy may be sensitive to the chosen surrogate model, importance-sampling proposal, and model assumptions, so the reported run counts may not transfer to other failure regions or cost structures.
future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating alternative unscented-transform methods and tuning the points used by the transform. They also identify multi-step look-ahead and approximate dynamic programming, buffered failure probabilities, and uncertainty objectives based on asymmetric risk measures as directions for further research.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the approach on real engineering experiments and quantify how errors in surrogate models and cost estimates affect the selected experiment sequence. Further work could also test explicit practical constraints on available experiment locations and budgets, and provide implementation tools that make those constraints easier to specify.

They report faster computation than prior methods and better edge discovery than simple passive-learning heuristics in their simulations.

summary: The paper develops two sequential sample-selection methods for Gaussian process regression when the data include uncertainties, and applies them to predicting composite fuselage shape under actuator forces. The authors test the methods using a simulated composite-fuselage system and compare them with four sampling benchmarks. The variance-based method gives the best reported mean and maximum deviation results, while the information-based method gives the best cross-validation error results.
key_results: The initial design contains 11 samples, and the candidate pool contains 200 inputs generated by a space-filling design. The variance-based method has the smallest mean and maximum mean absolute deviations once the sample count exceeds 17, compared with the no-active-learning design, random selection, maximum-distance selection, and expected improvement. limitations_unstated: The validation uses a computer-generated oracle based on finite-element simulation, rather than a prospective run of the active-learning procedure on physical fuselages, so the reported benefits are not directly confirmed in production experiments. summary: The paper develops tests for comparing the multivariate coefficient of variation (MCV) and its reciprocal, the standardized mean, across groups in general factorial designs. The authors report that permutation-test power was generally comparable to the alternatives when comparisons were fair, and higher in some cases where other tests were very conservative. summary: This paper develops a two-wave design for experiments in which treatment can affect connected units and outcomes can be dependent across network neighbors. key_results: For the real-world network study, the paper uses 832 units, with 416 main-experiment participants and a pilot of 70 units. Across the reported real-world network comparisons, the authors find lower variance for the proposed design than for the conventional competing designs; the advantage generally grows with heteroskedasticity. The paper reports that matching ELI’s variance could require up to 40 percentage points fewer total units than the best-performing alternative in the comparisons shown. limitations_stated: The main analysis assumes local interference and a sufficiently sparse network, and the paper notes that its sparsity condition fails for dense networks such as a star network. future_work_stated: The authors propose further theoretical work on partially observed networks, including selection of the model used to impute missing edges. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate how robust the design is when the exposure mapping, variance model, or estimated covariances are misspecified, using field experiments as well as simulations. summary: The paper develops Gaussian prepivoting, a way to construct randomization tests for treatment effects in finite populations. At sample size 50 under the sharp null, the randomization tests had error rates near 0.05, while the large-sample test’s rate was 0.110. In the multivariate simulations at sample size 5,000 under the weak null, the pooled Hotelling test’s randomization error rate was 0.951, compared with 0.005 after prepivoting; the prepivoted procedure was conservative in that setting. key_results: The authors compare their expected information gain estimate with uncertainty sampling for statistical expectations, variances, and percentiles, and with expected improvement for minimum finding. On the five-dimensional numerical example, they report convergence near the 35-sample mark for the proposed method on three quantities of interest, compared with almost 50 samples for uncertainty sampling; the two methods perform similarly for finding the minimum. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to recommend multiple experiments in one iteration so computational or laboratory resources can be used in parallel. They also suggest that this could be useful for problems with more than five input dimensions.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on physical experiments with realistic measurement noise, since the paper fixes the noise variance in its studies. summary: The paper develops R-optimal designs for multi-response regression, where several potentially correlated responses are measured at each experimental unit. The objective is to reduce the volume of a parameter-estimation rectangle based on Bonferroni intervals. The authors derive properties of the criterion, including convexity, an optimality check, scale invariance, symmetry results, and how designs depend on error correlations. They also provide an interior-point algorithm for computing designs on discrete candidate spaces and extend its use to nonlinear models when parameter values are specified. Numerical examples show that the method can compute designs for models with many factors and can outperform a multiplicative algorithm in some more difficult cases.
key_results: In the two-factor, three-response example, the reported optimal designs have 9 support points; computation took about 23 seconds on the smaller grid, while the multiplicative algorithm took about 27 seconds, and the authors report about 95 seconds for their method on the larger grid. In the five-factor example, the candidate space reached 16,384 points, symmetry reduced the number of weight variables to one eighth of that space, and the design had 32 support points; computation took about 1,801 seconds. For the nonlinear two-response example, designs had either 2 or 3 support points, included the upper boundary point, and the algorithm took from about 4 to 119 seconds in the reported cases. The paper establishes that the criterion is convex and gives a condition for verifying optimality; it also shows that when response functions differ, the design depends on the error covariance only through the correlation matrix.

limitations_stated: The authors note that the error covariance matrix is often unknown and that designs can be inefficient if the covariance or correlation matrix is misspecified. limitations_unstated: The reported computations use approximate design weights; the paper does not evaluate the effect of rounding those weights to an integer number of experimental runs. The numerical evidence is based on a small set of constructed examples and one stated computer setup, rather than comparisons across real experiments or a broad range of competing methods.
future_work_stated: The authors identify robust R-optimal designs as an important direction, with a minimax approach as one possible response to misspecified error covariance or correlation. They note that developing this approach is challenging because its resulting optimization problem is nonconvex and may be nonsmooth.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to study how to round approximate designs into fixed run plans while preserving their estimation performance, including under practical constraints on runs or factors. Further work could also evaluate sequential design updates and validate the method on real experiments, especially when nonlinear-model parameter values or error correlations are uncertain.

summary: The paper develops randomization-based estimation and variance estimation for treatment contrasts in possibly unbalanced split-plot experiments. The usual unbiased contrast estimator remains applicable, but a direct extension of the balanced-design variance estimator can remain biased even under additive treatment effects. For the school example with 40 units in 4 whole-plots of sizes 8, 8, 12, and 12, the construction procedure produced a matrix with largest eigenvalue 192. The simulations generated 200 potential-outcome sets in each of 8 scenarios; in the first two scenarios, the revised estimator's bias was zero while the earlier estimator's bias was 0.0133. summary: The paper develops a sequential experimental design method for identifying the best item when measurements can be taken only from a specified set that may differ from the items being compared. It assumes expected responses follow a linear model with an unknown parameter vector and independent sub-Gaussian measurement noise. The method, called Randomized Adaptive Gap Elimination (RAGE), allocates measurements using an optimal design over differences between currently active items, then removes items that appear clearly inferior. The authors prove instance-dependent lower and upper bounds and show that the method nearly achieves the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Simulations compare the method with existing adaptive and static allocation approaches.

In simulations at confidence level 0.05, the reported empirical failure probability was zero; each experiment was repeated 20 times. RAGE performed competitively with the oracle and other methods on the benchmark example, and its sample use grew less than LinGapE’s as the number of duplicate arms increased. In the transductive simulation, RAGE substantially outperformed the static allocation as dimension increased; the paper reports plotted simulation results rather than a table of exact sample counts.

Gap-based elimination: \[\widehat Z_{t+1}=\widehat Z_t\setminus\{z:\exists z'\in\widehat Z_t,\ (z'-z)^T\widehat\theta_t\ge 2^{-(t+2)}\}\] The next active set Zhat at round t plus one removes any current item z for which another active item z' has an estimated response advantage of at least the round threshold, using the least-squares estimate thetahat_t.

limitations_unstated: The method relies on a correctly specified linear response model and on the measurement vectors spanning the parameter space; performance under model misspecification or a restricted span is not evaluated. future_work_stated: The authors propose developing anytime algorithms and exploring whether the method’s ideas extend to instance-based regret bounds for linear bandits. They also propose studying regret and fixed-budget settings.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method with real experimental data and response models that depart from linearity, including robustness to measurement constraints and unequal measurement costs. summary: This paper develops an empirical Bayes shrinkage estimator for estimating average treatment responses in randomized experiments with multiple arms, especially online experiments. It starts from each arm’s sample mean and standard error, then shrinks estimates toward the across-arm average, with more shrinkage for estimates that are more extreme relative to the observed spread. The authors also give a variance estimate that accounts for uncertainty in estimating the shared average and the spread of arm effects. They report lower overall estimation error and improved typical sequential decisions compared with using unshrunk sample means.
key_results: Across the 17 experiments, the authors report that compound mean squared error fell in every experiment, with an average reduction of around 15%; experiments 14 and 15 had reductions on the order of 50%. They report that 85% of arms had reduced error in one analysis and that around 90% improved in another; 90% of arms had at least 90% coverage for nominal 95% intervals. In sequential simulations, empirical Bayes estimates gave typical end-of-experiment regret gains of around 10% compared with maximum likelihood estimates, while gains were smaller but nonzero early in the experiment. The typical increase in the chance of playing the best arm was between 5% and 10%, and experiments 1 and 5 showed increases of as much as 30% to 40% by the end.

limitations_stated: The authors assume normally distributed sampling errors and equal variances across arm means; they note that unequal variances are not addressed in this paper. They also warn that simple James-Stein shrinkage may perform poorly when the effect distribution is non-normal, such as when most effects are near zero but some true effects are outliers. limitations_unstated: The evaluations draw on 17 operational experiments from one company and a particular class of full-factorial messaging tests, so they provide limited evidence about how the method performs in other industries, experiment types, or effect distributions. future_work_stated: The authors propose adapting shrinkage to factorial designs by shrinking toward a simpler main-effects-only model. They also suggest multivariate shrinkage across outcome variables to use their correlation structure.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test the estimator prospectively in operational experiments across different application areas and compare its decisions with other estimation and sequential allocation methods. summary: The paper introduces an edge-based analysis for estimating treatment effects in one-to-one messaging experiments, where messages between treated and control users can violate the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA). In real LinkedIn experiments, the corrected estimates were generally larger than standard estimates, and the Active Status example showed that the correction could account for strong treatment affinity.
key_results: The evaluation used 43 iterations from 21 distinct LinkedIn experiments, each with an experimental population of at least 1 million members; no more than seven days of data per experiment were included. At a 50% treatment ramp, the corrected lift averaged 1.56% (standard deviation 2.20%), compared with 1.0% (standard deviation 1.62%) for standard lift; the paired comparison was statistically significant, with t(19) = 3.23 and a reported p-value below 0.01. Of 12 experiments with multiple iterations, seven had overlapping confidence intervals across all iterations for both methods, four had non-overlapping intervals for both, and one had non-overlapping intervals for the corrected estimate but overlapping intervals for the standard estimate. In the Active Status experiment, standard estimates were +2.3% and +3.0% at the 50% and 85% ramps, while corrected estimates were +4.4% and +4.6%, respectively.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the method’s assumptions and estimates may fail when an experiment does not primarily affect the message sender; they give an example in which the manipulation mainly changed message receipt. summary: The paper develops a rerandomization method for controlled experiments that uses kernel discrepancy to balance covariate distributions across treatment groups. In the New York schools example, the design assigned 1,376 schools to 32 treatment settings, with 43 schools per setting and 496 pairwise treatment comparisons; the composite rerandomization had substantially smaller and less variable discrepancies than complete randomization. summary: This review examines how optimal design ideas can be used to select smaller subsets from large datasets for parameter estimation. It describes methods for ordinary linear models, models with bias, and models with unobserved confounders, and develops a general formulation that includes both bias and confounders. The general model is linear in its terms, and the authors derive a determinant-based optimality result for its information matrix. The review compares existing selection methods and presents numerical examples, including a million-row mortgage dataset and simulated data. The authors conclude that current methods are better suited to tall datasets than to genuinely large datasets, and that efficient selection methods accounting for bias and confounders remain to be developed.
key_results: The review covers sequential utility-based selection, the deterministic Information-Based Optimal Subdata Selection method, robust design methods for model bias, and methods that account for confounders. The authors prove that maximizing the determinant of the information matrix is equivalent to minimizing the maximum variance function in their general formulation. Their experiments include a dataset with 1,000,000 observations and four predictors, from which a final subset of 6,200 was selected after starting with 5,000 observations; parameter estimates converged to similar values across different initial samples. Prediction was assessed on 10,010 held-out observations, and the authors report that the selected subset improved random-forest and neural-network performance relative to random training samples, while those prediction methods performed better when trained on the selected subset. They also report that the deterministic selection method was cost-effective in tests up to 1,000,000 points and four variables, but that the compared methods and examples do not establish efficient performance for genuinely large datasets with both bias and confounders.

Determinant-based design criterion: \[\xi^*=\arg\max_{\xi}\det M(\xi)\] The design measure xi-star maximizes the determinant of the information matrix M over the candidate design measures xi.

limitations_stated: The authors say that the reviewed approaches are currently more suitable for tall datasets than for genuinely large datasets and that efficient algorithms for selecting subsets in the presence of bias and confounders are still needed. They also note that one robust-design algorithm requires a high-dimensional QR decomposition and large matrices in memory, while the general results need refinement and do not yet provide an efficient large-data selection algorithm.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence is limited to a small set of examples and simulations, so it does not establish how the methods perform across varied data distributions, predictor counts, or practical sampling constraints. The general formulation relies on a linear representation of the bias and confounder effects and does not validate whether those terms can be specified or randomized adequately in real passive datasets.
future_work_stated: The authors propose integrating the bias and confounder ideas with existing selection algorithms to develop efficient subsampling methods for known and unknown confounders. They also propose refining the general theory and linking it to the algorithms reviewed in the paper.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the methods on real datasets with independently assessed selection bias and confounding, and compare estimation and prediction performance against full-data analyses and established sampling methods. It could also extend the approach to nonlinear bias or confounder structures and practical restrictions such as subgroup quotas or limited access to confounder measurements.

summary: This paper extends indicator-function methods for classifying fractional factorial designs from two-level factors to designs with factors having multiple levels. It represents a design by a polynomial that equals one at included treatment combinations and zero elsewhere, then derives algebraic equations that characterize such polynomials. It also constructs a contrast representation that expresses design size and orthogonality directly, with contrast coefficients that do not depend on the factor-level coding. The method is used with algebraic software to enumerate orthogonal fractions in two specific mixed-level design families. The paper reports complete classifications for both families at the stated strengths.
key_results: For designs with three two-level factors and one three-level factor, the authors found 44 solutions for strength 2 at size 12, grouped into 3 equivalence classes. For designs with four two-level factors and one three-level factor, they found 56 solutions for strength 3 at size 24, also grouped into 3 equivalence classes. The reported Groebner-basis calculation to identify compatible sizes took 0.1 seconds for each of these cases using the stated level codings. Changing the coding for the first design family to zero-and-one and zero-through-two levels made the calculation fail to finish in one week; the authors also report that a strength-2 calculation for the second family did not finish in one week.

limitations_unstated: The classifications cover only two specific mixed-level design families, so the results do not establish how well the approach works for broader factor structures or practical constraints. The work classifies exact orthogonal fractions rather than evaluating how designs perform with noisy responses, restricted randomization, or other real-experiment requirements.
future_work_stated: The authors identify quantitative evaluation of the contrast representation's computational effect and comparison of their method with brute-force search as open problems. They also note that larger or different design-classification problems remain computationally difficult.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to incorporate practical restrictions such as forbidden treatment combinations, blocking, and randomization limits into the classification. Applying the resulting designs in real experiments, and testing whether the approach can support sequential or constrained design selection, would also assess its practical value.

summary: The paper designs sequential methods for randomized A/B tests that balance two goals: reducing the cost of assigning units to an inferior option and reaching a reliable decision quickly. For independent rewards, it introduces a family of upper confidence bound methods whose exploration allowance is inflated by a tunable factor, alpha. The family ranges from a regret-focused method toward an explore-then-commit-style method, while providing a finite high-probability decision-time bound when alpha is greater than one. The paper also extends the approach to settings where users, patients, or servers generate repeated noisy observations, using a mean-of-means estimator. The authors prove performance guarantees and report simulations showing the trade-off in both the independent-reward and repeated-unit settings.
key_results: For the independent-reward setting, the paper reports that as alpha approaches one, the leading regret bound is 8 times the variance proxy times log of one over delta, divided by Delta, while the decision-time bound grows without limit. As alpha grows without bound, the leading regret bound becomes 32 times the variance proxy times log of one over delta, divided by Delta, and decision time is of order 64 times the variance proxy times log of one over delta, divided by Delta squared; explore-then-commit has corresponding leading bounds of 16 and 32. In simulations averaging 1,000 runs with two Gaussian options of means zero and one and variance one, alpha values of 1.5 and 2 produced lower regret but longer decision time than explore-then-commit; the authors report that the regret for alpha 1.5 was almost half that of explore-then-commit, which in turn was about half that of ETC-prime. In the repeated-unit simulation, with unit-performance and observation-noise standard deviations both equal to one, the methods again showed a trade-off between regret and decision time; the paper reports a factor of four between the regret of ETC-prime and UCB.

Inflated exploration allocation and stopping rule: \[i_t=\arg\max_i(\hat r_i+\alpha\epsilon_i),\qquad \text{stop if }\hat r_i-\epsilon_i>\hat r_j+\epsilon_j\text{ for }j\ne i\] The symbol i with subscript t is the population assigned next, arg max selects the population with the largest score, r-hat is its estimated mean, alpha inflates the exploration allowance, epsilon is the confidence radius, and i and j index populations.
limitations_stated: The authors note that dynamic user assignment can be difficult in production, for example because a returning user's assigned population must be retained. Their repeated-unit guarantees rely on assumptions such as independent unit arrivals and sub-Gaussian rewards and noise; they warn that arrivals correlated with the data can violate the needed assumptions and lead to poor performance. They also state that the results can be extended to bounded outcomes with unknown variance using empirical Bernstein bounds, but do not develop that analysis in the paper.
limitations_unstated: The empirical comparisons use two-option Gaussian simulations, with the reported repeated-unit simulation using equal variance proxies, so the practical performance of the method under more varied reward distributions and population structures is not established. The paper gives theoretical bounds but does not report validation in a real experiment, and adaptive allocation may be difficult to implement while preserving the stated assignment and causal assumptions.
future_work_stated: The authors identify modeling unit outcomes conditionally on arrival time as a direction for handling arrivals that are correlated with the data. They also suggest applying their proof approach to other per-unit processes, such as mean-reverting or cyclic processes, when suitable concentration bounds are available, and mention bounded rewards with unknown variance as an extension using empirical Bernstein bounds.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the methods in real A/B tests and clinical studies, including settings with delayed outcomes, unequal group sizes, and operational constraints on assignment. Further work could also compare alternative decision criteria and develop sequential monitoring or software tools that make the trade-off easy to configure and audit.

summary: The paper extends locally D-optimal design methods to nonlinear multiple regression models whose information depends on the linear predictor, including binary-response models with logit and probit links. It considers a design region that is a ball and uses rotation invariance to reduce the multidimensional design problem to a marginal problem along one coordinate. The resulting optimal designs are supported on the ball’s surface and have two marginal support points, which generate one or two rotational orbits. key_results: The derived designs use two marginal support points; when a support point is at a boundary, the authors give formulas for the other point and the weights, and otherwise give a system of equations for both points and their weights. limitations_unstated: The designs are local, so performance may be poor if the assumed parameter values are inaccurate; the paper does not quantify that sensitivity. summary: The paper introduces ridge rerandomization, a design for randomized treatment-versus-control experiments that seeks better covariate balance before treatment is assigned. Its objective is to improve estimation of the average treatment effect by reducing imbalances in covariates related to the outcome. The method replaces the standard Mahalanobis balance score with a regularized version that weights directions of covariate variation differently, using the covariates’ eigenstructure to set an automatic hierarchy of importance. Researchers choose an acceptance probability and tune the regularization parameter, then repeatedly randomize until an assignment meets the balance threshold. The authors’ theory and simulations indicate that the method can improve covariate balance and treatment-effect precision, especially with many or highly correlated covariates, although it is not always superior to standard rerandomization for treatment-effect estimation.
key_results: The simulations used 100 units, with 50 assigned to each group, and compared randomization, standard rerandomization, and ridge rerandomization at an acceptance probability of 0.1. They examined covariate counts from 10 to 90, correlations from 0 to 0.9, and 1,000 repetitions for each setting; the regularization parameter selected by their procedure was 0.01 in most settings and occasionally 0.02. Ridge rerandomization generally reduced average covariate-imbalance variance more than standard rerandomization, with its advantage increasing as the number of covariates or their correlation increased. For equally outcome-related covariates, it also generally reduced treatment-estimator mean squared error and confidence-interval width more than standard rerandomization in high-dimensional or high-correlation settings; reported interval coverage was near 95%. The paper gives these comparisons mainly in plots rather than reporting a single numerical improvement, and shows that standard rerandomization can do better when the outcome relationship is concentrated in a low-variation principal-component direction.

Acceptance probability calibration: \[\Pr(M_\lambda\le a_\lambda\mid x)=p_a\] The probability that the ridge distance is at most its threshold, conditional on the covariate data, is set equal to the prespecified acceptance probability.

Additive treatment-effect assumption: \[Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)+\tau\] For each unit i, the potential outcome under treatment equals the potential outcome under control plus the common additive treatment effect.
limitations_stated: The authors do not provide asymptotic inference results for ridge-rerandomized experiments, and state that developing them is future work. Whether ridge rerandomization improves treatment-effect estimation over standard rerandomization depends on the covariate-outcome relationship, which is typically unknown before the experiment.
limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence focuses mainly on 100 units, equal group sizes, and covariates with an equicorrelation structure, so performance in other sample sizes and more varied correlation structures is not established as broadly. The procedure also requires numerical calibration and a search over the regularization parameter; the paper does not report a practical runtime study for these steps or for repeated assignment screening in large experiments.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring other classes of rerandomization criteria and using prior information about outcome relationships to select criteria. They also identify asymptotic results for inference after ridge rerandomization as a promising direction.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method under practical assignment constraints, such as blocking, restricted allocation, or uneven treatment costs, and compare its performance using additional outcome models and balance objectives. Sequential implementations and validation in real experiments would also help establish how reliably the simulation findings transfer to practice.

summary: This paper develops a sequential design method for estimating the statistical expectation of an expensive black-box response under uncertain inputs. It models the response with a Gaussian process and selects each new experiment to maximize expected information gain about that expectation. The method measures information gain using the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the current and hypothetical updated distributions of the expectation. The authors derive tractable expressions for this criterion and use Bayesian global optimization to select experiments. key_results: For the three-dimensional synthetic problem, the authors report that the proposed method's estimate converged after 20 samples, while uncertainty sampling took almost 30, a saving of about 10 samples. In the five-dimensional problem, the estimate converged as early as the addition of the 45th sample for the proposed method, compared with 65 samples for uncertainty sampling. In the one-dimensional tests, the methods performed similarly overall, and uncertainty sampling reached the answer sooner for the sharply peaked function. For the steel wire drawing simulation, the study used 20 initial observations and added 80 samples; the expectation reference value was approximated as 0.2694 using 6,000 Latin-hypercube evaluations, and the proposed method was reported to converge with fewer samples than uncertainty sampling.

future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the framework under model misspecification, practical allocation restrictions, and additional design criteria, and validate design quality in real experiments. Its objective is to maximize cumulative reward while limiting the loss relative to the best version in each segment of time. The model assumes that rewards are independently and identically distributed within each segment, while the reward distribution may change between segments. The authors report theoretical regret guarantees and experiments in which FTBI often performs better and runs faster than AdaNormalHedge (ANH).

They report an update time of order log T and find FTBI to be approximately 10 times faster than ANH in their synthetic timing comparison. Synthetic results are averaged over 20 replications, and FTBI generally has lower regret than ANH across the tested reward gaps, numbers of shifts, and segment lengths. On the public time-series tasks, the reported reward improvement over FTL reaches up to 85%; on auction data, FTBI beats ANH in the reported comparisons, with revenue lift exceeding 4% in some cases, but it does not always outperform FTL.

summary: This paper develops GATE, an active learning method for binary classification with logistic regression. It aims to reduce the number of labels needed while also building a compact predictive model. The method first screens unlabeled subjects for uncertainty near the current classification boundary, then chooses from that candidate set using a locally D-optimal criterion. It selects variables greedily using a likelihood-gradient score and alternates subject and variable selection until its information-based stopping rule is met. Simulations and an artificial wave benchmark show that it can obtain classification performance close to full-data approaches using fewer labeled subjects and fewer variables.
key_results: In simulations with 100 predictors, an initial set of 100 subjects, and batches of 30, GATE used an average of about 314 to 528 labeled subjects across the three cases, compared with 15,000 subjects in the full-data approach. Its test accuracy ranged from 0.821 to 0.980 and its test AUC ranged from 0.886 to 0.998; the full-data approach had test accuracy from 0.832 to 0.982 and AUC from 0.898 to 0.999. In the wave benchmark, GATE used an average of 743.5 of the 10,000 training subjects, with test accuracy 0.920, test AUC 0.980, and an average of 22.45 selected variables, compared with 121 variables for the full-variable approach. Randomly selected subjects with all variables performed worse in the reported comparisons, including test accuracy 0.759 to 0.856 in the simulations and 0.857 in the wave benchmark.

Logistic regression model: \[p_i=\frac{\exp(\beta^T x_i)}{1+\exp(\beta^T x_i)}\] For subject i, p_i is the probability of response Y_i equal to one, x_i is its predictor vector, and beta is the vector of logistic regression coefficients.

Uncertainty-filtered D-efficiency selection: \[C_h=\{x_t:|\hat F(x_t\mid\hat\beta)-\alpha|\le d_{(h)}\},\quad R(x)=\frac{|M_{n+1}(x)|^{1/p}-|M_n|^{1/p}}{|M_n|^{1/p}},\quad x^*=\arg\max_{x\in C_h}R(x)\] C_h is the candidate set within the h-th ordered uncertainty distance d_(h) of threshold alpha; x_t is an unlabeled subject; F-hat is the fitted probability using estimated coefficients beta-hat; R is relative D-efficiency; M_n and M_(n+1)(x) are the information matrices before and after adding x; p is the number of active variables; and x-star is the selected subject.

limitations_stated: The authors state that GATE requires users to set the batch size, maximum tolerance distance, uncertainty candidate-set size, and stopping tolerance, and that choosing these values can be time-consuming. They also note that greedy forward selection can over-select variables; a stepwise approach could remove redundant variables but would substantially increase computation.
limitations_unstated: The method depends on a logistic regression model, but the paper does not test how its selection strategy performs when the true relationship is nonlinear or otherwise misspecified. Its evaluation uses simulations and an artificial benchmark rather than a real production experiment, and it does not assess practical labeling constraints or compare monetary costs. The reported tuning settings and comparisons cover a limited set of scenarios, so performance under different batch sizes, candidate-set sizes, or class balances remains uncertain.
future_work_stated: The authors identify stepwise selection, including backward removal of redundant variables, as a natural way to address over-selection. They caution that this approach would increase computational time.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the procedure on real quality-engineering studies and under logistic-model misspecification, class imbalance, and variable labeling costs. It could also evaluate operational constraints such as batch capacity and restricted randomization, and investigate sequential updating or alternative predictive criteria.

summary: This paper develops elastic I-optimality (EI) for generalized linear models (GLMs) when the goal is accurate prediction over a region or distribution of interest. The criterion minimizes an approximation to the average squared error in predicting the mean response, with the probability distribution allowing some parts of the region to receive more emphasis than others. The authors construct designs sequentially: they add a candidate point that most reduces the criterion and then update the weights on the selected points with a multiplicative algorithm. They establish optimality conditions and convergence results for the weight updates and the sequential procedure on a discrete candidate set. Numerical examples show that the method can be faster than a Newton-based comparator while producing designs with high relative efficiency, though its advantage shrinks for large candidate pools.
key_results: For the linear-model example, the proposed algorithm was about 4 times faster than Newton's method, and its relative efficiency was always above 99.7%. For the logistic examples, the proposed method reached the target efficiency lower bound in all reported scenarios; Newton's method did not reach that target within 100 iterations for one three-variable case. In a two-variable logistic example, candidate pools ranging from 102 to 1180 squared points produced relative efficiencies above 0.999 compared with the design from the largest pool. In the potato-packing example, the coefficient-estimation designs had relative EI-efficiencies of 80.64% and 85.44% compared with the EI-optimal design; the EI-optimal design had relative efficiencies of 88.76% and 81.12% under the determinant- and average-variance-based criteria, respectively.

limitations_stated: The method constructs local designs and therefore depends on specified regression coefficients. The authors note that computational efficiency can decline for very large candidate pools and that design support points may lie outside the prediction region of interest.
limitations_unstated: For continuous experimental regions, the algorithm searches a discretized candidate pool, so an inadequate pool can omit useful support points; the convergence result for the sequential algorithm is stated for a discrete region. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying robust EI designs for GLMs, potentially using an upper bound on integrated mean squared error to reduce dependence on the regression coefficients. future_work_unstated: A useful extension would address practical run constraints, such as integer replication counts, restricted factor combinations, and blocks, and evaluate how well the approximate designs can be converted to feasible experiments. Further work could also assess sequential updating when coefficient estimates change as data arrive and validate prediction performance in additional real experiments.

summary: The paper develops a method for generating orthogonal arrays (OAs) of a specified size and strength from a finite Hilbert basis. It focuses on comparing fractional factorial designs using the generalized word-length pattern (GWLP) and the generalized minimum aberration (GMA) criterion. The authors represent arrays as nonnegative integer combinations of basis arrays and show how counting functions can be added to calculate the GWLP of a union. They demonstrate the approach for five binary factors at strength two, examining designs with 16 and 20 runs. The examples show how the method narrows the search for GMA-optimal arrays, while the authors note that computing the Hilbert basis becomes expensive as designs grow.
key_results: For five binary factors at strength two, the computed Hilbert basis contains 26,142 arrays, with sizes from 8 through 36 runs. For 16 runs, the authors classify 1,932 distinct arrays and find 12 with third-order aberration equal to zero; two of these are GMA-optimal, with the first four GWLP entries after the constant term equal to zero and the fifth equal to 1. For 20 runs, they classify 10,752 distinct arrays and find 192 GMA-optimal arrays, all formed as unions of an 8-run and a 12-run array; their reported GWLP has entries 0, 0, 0.4, 0.2, and 0 for orders one through five. The paper reports design counts and aberration patterns rather than a comparison of estimation efficiency or prediction performance.

future_work_unstated: Future work could test the approach on larger arrays, mixed factor levels, and strengths beyond those in the examples, while developing ways to reduce the cost of Hilbert-basis computation. summary: This paper develops sequential experimental designs for predicting the output of two deterministic computer codes linked in a nested structure, where the first code supplies an input to the second. It models each code with a Gaussian process and uses information from the intermediate output rather than treating the pair as one opaque code. The authors propose an analytical method for calculating prediction moments under specific conditions and a linearized method that is faster and can extend to longer code chains. Their sequential designs reduce integrated prediction variance, with one design also choosing which code to evaluate after accounting for the codes' computational costs. In the examples, using the intermediate information and selecting evaluations sequentially improved prediction accuracy relative to the blind-box and space-filling comparisons.
key_results: In the moment-calculation comparison, the reported times were 5.33 seconds for Monte Carlo integration with 1,000 points, 0.78 seconds with 100 points, and 0.02 seconds for the linearized method. The analytical and linearized methods had similar prediction-mean accuracy in the examples, and both improved on the blind-box method, which ignored the intermediate output. The sequential designs generally improved prediction-mean accuracy over maximin LHS; the best I-optimal design was most accurate at a given computational cost in the analytical example, while the sequential methods were similar in the hydrodynamic example except that the best I-optimal design did better for the first added points. The best I-optimal design initially allocated more evaluations to the first code, and the results showed better accuracy at a fixed budget when that code was less costly.

limitations_stated: The exact analytical moment calculation requires particular forms for the second code's mean and covariance functions and cannot be extended to more than two codes. The linearized method relies on the first-code prediction uncertainty being small enough for the approximation to be valid. The authors focus on a scalar intermediate output and identify a functional intermediate output as a direction for future work.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers two numerical examples rather than real experimental deployments or a broad range of nested-code structures, so performance under different model behavior and operational constraints remains uncertain. The designs assume known evaluation costs that do not vary with input, and the paper does not establish how well the linearized approximation or its design choices work when that assumption or the Gaussian-process model is poor.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying nested codes with a functional intermediate output.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs on real engineering workflows and assess robustness when Gaussian-process assumptions or cost estimates are inaccurate. It could also develop and validate practical handling of input constraints and more complex evaluation costs, and compare sequential use with alternative prediction or uncertainty-reduction objectives.

summary: The paper develops a way to assess the power of an A/B test when actors can receive a treatment different from their original assignment because of interference. It studies tests of differences in means for normal outcomes and differences in proportions for Bernoulli outcomes. The authors express power in terms of the number of assignments retained and changed, then use a central limit theorem for independent Bernoulli switching to estimate those counts. For network applications, they estimate switching probabilities from actors’ neighbors and use those estimates to calculate expected power. Their results show that interference can reduce power, while the normal-outcome result finds specificity unchanged under the stated conditions.
key_results: Under the normal-outcome model, the authors derive an exact power expression showing that power decreases as more assignments change; under the stated balanced-group setup, specificity is unchanged by label misspecification. For Bernoulli outcomes, they derive an approximate power expression and show that power tends to zero when the net number of correctly assigned actors grows more slowly than the square root of the sample size, while it tends to one when that net number grows at least on the order of the square root of the sample size. The network applications use a Facebook friendship network with 561 nodes and 16,750 undirected edges, and a Twitter follower network with 81,306 nodes and 2,420,766 directed edges. Under the authors’ neighbor-based switching model, estimated power is higher for Twitter than Facebook across the plotted conditions; the paper attributes this in part to Twitter having more than 100 times as many nodes.
key_equations: Power under normal outcomes: \[\beta_{c|d}=1-\Phi\left(Z_{\alpha}-\frac{(n_S-n_D)\delta}{2\sigma\sqrt{n}}\right)\] β is test power, c and d denote the original and true group labels, Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, Zα is the upper normal critical value for significance level α, nS is the number of retained assignments, nD is the number of changed assignments, δ is the treatment effect, σ is the common standard deviation, and n is the total sample size.
limitations_stated: The theory covers normal and Bernoulli measurements, while other outcome distributions remain to be analyzed. The central limit theorem result is for independent Bernoulli switching and does not directly account for network dependence; the authors identify generalizing it to network interference as future work.
limitations_unstated: The exact normal-outcome result relies on balanced groups and a common known variance, and the power tests presented use a one-sided alternative. In the network applications, switching probabilities are based on a specified neighbor rule, and the reported power estimates do not include uncertainty in those probabilities or validation against outcomes from an actual experiment.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the results to other parametric outcome distributions and deriving central limit theorems for network interference, including models on configuration and stochastic block networks. They also identify intermediate or multiple treatment groups, and contagion models that allow more than complete switching, as open directions; they suggest that user behavior could inform more accurate models.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess how power estimates change when group sizes are unequal or when variance is estimated rather than known, and quantify uncertainty in the estimated network switching probabilities. Testing the method prospectively in real A/B experiments and comparing it with network bucketing or other interference-aware designs would help establish its practical value.

summary: This paper develops a method for finding approximate and exact designs on a finite design space when the objective is a compound Bayes risk criterion (CBRC). The criterion covers several weighted prediction risks and includes a linear criterion used for random coefficient regression (RCR). The authors construct an artificial design problem with an expanded design space and linear constraints, so that minimizing an ordinary A-optimality criterion solves the original problem. This reformulation makes tools such as second-order cone programming (SOCP) and mixed-integer second-order cone programming (MISOCP) applicable. A numerical example uses integrated mean squared error (IMSE) for predicting individual responses in a straight-line RCR model, including designs with spacing constraints. The results show how the method obtains both approximate and exact designs and accommodates those constraints.
key_results: In the straight-line example, the authors used 100 individuals, 10 trials per individual, and a design space of 51 points. Without added constraints, the exact design puts between 5 and 9 trials at the endpoint x = 1 as the rescaled slope variance increases; for example, it uses 5 trials for values from 0 to 0.005 and 9 for values from 0.136 to 1. With the constraint that no three neighboring points can together receive more than one trial, exact designs use 10 support points, with one trial at each support point. Mean computing times were 0.2977 seconds for approximate and 4.7918 seconds for exact designs without the added constraints, and 0.3320 and 3.4027 seconds, respectively, with them; these are timings for the authors’ example, not a comparison of competing optimization algorithms.

limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a dedicated limitations discussion. They note that constrained approximate designs are difficult to visualize across the full range of slope variance and therefore show one such design at a fixed variance value.
limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstration is restricted to a straight-line regression model on a one-dimensional grid, with specified population-variance structure and a uniform integration measure; it does not establish performance across other models or design spaces. future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the conversion on nonlinear, multivariable, and other hierarchical models, and on practical constraints beyond the illustrated spacing rule. summary: The paper develops experimental-design methods for dimensional analysis problems with multiple responses. It extends the Buckingham Pi theorem and states the conditions under which responses and factors can be represented by dimensionless groups. For design construction, it develops a multivariate criterion based on integrated prediction variance and describes both polynomial-model optimal designs and nonparametric space-filling designs. It also presents a robust design that seeks useful performance both in dimensionless-factor space and in the original-factor space. In the heat exchanger example, a 100-run design for two responses achieved about 97% efficiency for both response models at a selected weighting, while a robust design achieved efficiencies of 83% and 85% for its two objectives.
key_results: For the heat exchanger example, the authors reduced nine base variables to five dimensionless factors and constructed a 100-run design for full third-order models. The selected weighted design had about 97% I-efficiency for each response model; using the design optimized for the larger model alone still gave 92% efficiency for the other model. The 100-point nonparametric uniform design had 29% efficiency relative to the design for the larger model. The robust-DA design used a weight of 0.35 and achieved 83% efficiency for the dimensionless model and 85% for the empirical model in the original factors. The paper also gives a 20-point pump example and reports that the authors provide R code on the journal website; their nonparametric construction uses a modified Fast Flexible Filling procedure based on a candidate set.

In the TELEMAC-2D case, the authors compared 40-run adaptive designs, each built from 20 initial runs plus 20 additions, with a 40-run maximin design and a 500-run reference design; the ECD posterior approximation was closer to the reference than the WIMSE approximation.
