The construction uses an energy-distance decomposition to link the quality of the complete design and its slices, and gives one-shot and sequential optimization algorithms. The authors prove distributional convergence under stated conditions and show that the algorithms converge to stationary solutions. In their numerical examples, the proposed energy-distance methods generally provide better space-filling and prediction performance than the compared existing methods.
key_results: In uniformity comparisons repeated 50 times, the hybrid energy-distance one-shot method generally performed best, with its sequential version also substantially better than the compared existing methods on the reported criteria; the coset decomposition method had better minimum separation in one standard-simplex comparison. In prediction tests using 15 runs in each of three slices and a test set of 1,000 points, the energy-distance methods substantially outperformed the existing methods across three simulated response models, with the two hybrid-criterion methods performing best. In the drug-combination example, the design used seven dose levels and a test set of 1,400 points; the proposed methods performed better than other methods when dose was treated as continuous, while the compared energy-distance designs had broadly similar performance with the qualitative-level Gaussian process models. The paper reports these findings in figures rather than giving exact numerical error values in the text.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the number of required runs grows exponentially as the number of process variables and their levels increases. They also note that Euclidean distance may produce suboptimal uniformity in low-dimensional projections, and that partitioning a full design can be challenging to optimize accurately.
limitations_unstated: The algorithms use a finite collection of sampled points to approximate expectations, so the resulting design can depend on the quality and size of that approximation. future_work_stated: The authors propose combining their energy-distance decomposition with marginal coupled and double coupled design approaches to address growth in the number of process-level combinations. They also propose developing metrics and algorithms that improve uniformity in low-dimensional projections.
future_work_unstated: Further work could benchmark computation time and sensitivity to starting points and sample approximation size, alongside design quality, across larger constrained mixture regions. Validation in physical mixture experiments and testing how well the sequential designs support real early-stopping decisions would also clarify their practical performance.

summary: The paper develops optimal-design results for multivariate crossover trials, in which several responses are measured for each subject in each period. summary: The paper introduces the factorial-design optimal transport test (FDOTT), a method for testing relationships among probability distributions observed across factorial-design groups. It extends the analysis-of-variance idea of testing linear effects to discrete distributions on metric spaces, using optimal transport (OT) to quantify differences between distributions. The authors derive large-sample distributions for the test statistic and study plug-in, bootstrap, and permutation approaches for obtaining critical values. They report good performance in simulations and illustrate the method with cellular biophysics and fingerprint data.

Simulations used equal sample sizes of 50, 100, and 500 in hypothesis-testing comparisons, with 250 repetitions and 1,000 draws from limiting distributions; the authors report that FDOTT and the barycenter method had stronger power than rank-based and distance-based competitors when distributions shared a mean but had different covariances, while the rank-based method had higher power in some Poisson-distribution comparisons. In the fingerprint analysis, the overall comparison, interaction, and main effects had p-values below 0.001; the real-versus-synthetic whorl comparison was not significant, with p-value 0.666, whereas the other reported pairwise comparisons were significant.

Its goal is to add samples while retaining one-dimensional bin coverage and good space-filling properties. The method regrids the parameter space, selects empty bins, and places a new Latin hypercube design within those regions before combining it with the initial design. Across initial sizes of 10, 100, and 1000 samples and dimensions of 2, 4, and 8, the degree was largely independent of dimension and followed a similar trend with the ratio of added to initial samples, with perfect designs at additions that were multiples of the initial size. Compared with repeated one-at-a-time expansion, the direct expansion had a higher degree; repeated expansion was also reported to increase computation time by a factor proportional to the number of additions. limitations_unstated: The LHS degree measures only one-dimensional bin occupancy, so it does not by itself establish low correlation, good multidimensional projection behavior, or strong performance on a particular response model. summary: The paper introduces Bayesian experimental design with large language models (BED-LLM), a method for choosing questions adaptively in multi-turn information-gathering tasks. It is designed for settings where an agent wants to learn an unknown target, such as an entity in 20 Questions or a user's film preferences. At each turn, the method generates possible questions, estimates how much each is expected to reduce uncertainty about the target, and asks the question with the highest expected information gain (EIG). It builds and updates candidate beliefs by generating diverse hypotheses and filtering out those inconsistent with the interaction history. In the tested tasks, BED-LLM outperformed direct prompting and other adaptive question-selection approaches, including when the questioner and answerer used different models.
key_results: In 20 Questions, the paper reports that BED-LLM improved success by an average of 37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; its success rate more than doubled in over half of the evaluated setups and did not decrease in any. Across the reported model and dataset combinations, final success rates for BED-LLM ranged from 26% to 95%, compared with 8% to 45% for direct prompting, and BED-LLM was the strongest method in the table. For Qwen2.5-72B on the Animals dataset, BED-LLM took 2 hours, 28 minutes, and 43 seconds, while the data-estimation alternative took 1 day, 17 hours, 13 minutes, and 34 seconds. In preference elicitation, BED-LLM produced higher-rated film recommendations than direct prompting and the entropy-based comparison across the evaluated models, with results measured over 200 user profiles and five question turns.
key_equations: Expected information gain: \[\operatorname{EIG}(x)=H[p(\theta)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(y;x)}[H[p(\theta\mid y;x)]]\] Here, EIG is expected information gain, x is a candidate question, theta is the target, y is the response, p denotes the probability distributions in the model, H is entropy, and the expectation averages over possible responses.
limitations_stated: The authors note that selecting each question by its immediate information gain is myopic and can be suboptimal compared with planning for the final uncertainty after several turns. They also explain that full Bayesian updating can require too many costly language-model evaluations, and that the preferred model formulation depends on the relative complexity of the target and response spaces.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses language models to generate answers or judge recommendation quality rather than testing the method with actual users or a physical process, so performance in operational experiments is not established. Results also depend on generated candidate questions and hypotheses, filtering thresholds, and limited benchmark sets; the candidate pool may omit useful designs.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest that BED-LLM's model formulation, belief updates, and information-gain estimates could support policy-based experimental-design methods that plan beyond the next question. They also discuss using the data-estimation formulation when responses are more complex than the target, and updating the likelihood with interaction history when the target does not capture all information needed to predict responses.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method in real user studies and controlled engineering experiments, comparing its chosen questions with measured outcomes rather than language-model-generated answers or ratings. Further work could examine constrained or costly questions, broader response formats, and whether sequential use remains effective when candidate designs must meet practical operational restrictions.

summary: This paper develops a measure-based approach to optimal sensor placement for continuous-time stochastic filtering. It represents the observation budget as a probability measure over time, so discrete measurement schedules and continuously varying sensor strength fit within the same framework. The filtering equations depend on that schedule, and the authors derive utility gradients using a backward adjoint equation. They demonstrate the approach with a logistic-growth parameter-estimation example and a linear Gaussian filtering example. The examples show schedules concentrating observation effort at informative times, although the paper does not report a numerical comparison against competing optimization methods.
key_results: In the logistic-growth example, projected gradient descent began with a uniform schedule over the time interval from 0 to 6 and used 15 iterations with one Monte Carlo sample per gradient estimate; the schedule concentrated near time 3 and produced greater posterior contraction than the initial uniform schedule. In the linear Gaussian example, a two-dimensional Brownian signal was observed through one component before time 3 and the other afterward, over a time interval from 0 to 6. Over 100 minimization iterations, the optimized schedule concentrated observation effort just after times 0 and 3, and the plotted integrated covariance utility decreased. These are illustrative simulation results; the paper reports no numerical efficiency comparison with greedy, discrete-selection, or other gradient-based design methods.
key_equations:
Scheduled observation model: \[dZ(t)=\xi(t)g(X(t))\,dt+\sqrt{\xi(t)}\,\Gamma^{1/2}(t)\,dW(t)\] At time t, Z is the cumulative observation, xi is the sensor-schedule density, g is the observation map, X is the hidden signal, Gamma is the observation-noise covariance, and W is standard Brownian motion.

Expected-utility design criterion: \[\min_{\xi\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}\,[U(p_{\xi})]\] The design minimizes expected utility over schedules xi in the set P of probability measures; U is the utility and p indexed by xi is the filtering density obtained under that schedule.

Utility derivative from the adjoint: \[\eta(t)=\mathbb{E}\int \lambda_t(x)\left[-g(x)^\top\Gamma(t)^{-1}g(X(t))+\tfrac12\|g(x)\|_{\Gamma(t)^{-1}}^2\right]dx\] Eta is the derivative of expected utility with respect to the schedule at time t; the expectation is over signal and observation paths, lambda is the adjoint solution, x is a signal-state location, g is the observation map, X is the hidden signal, and Gamma is the observation-noise covariance; the superscript negative one denotes a matrix inverse, the superscript T denotes transpose, and the weighted norm uses the inverse covariance.
limitations_stated: The authors say that most calculations are formal and that rigorous justification, including well-posedness of the adjoint equation, is omitted. They also report that solving the filtering equation becomes infeasible at high dimensions and note that their simple projected gradient descent does not account for the stochastic nature of the utility.
limitations_unstated: The demonstrations use only low-dimensional simulated examples, so they do not establish how well the approach performs in real experiments or in larger, more complex filtering problems. The paper also does not benchmark its method against discrete sensor-selection or greedy methods, leaving practical comparative efficiency untested.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring stochastic optimization methods, including simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation, and gradient flows based on Wasserstein or Rao-Fisher geometry. They also identify adjoints for particle filters, the relationship between smooth schedules and discrete measurement locations, adaptive sensor placement, and extension to spatial sensor placement as future directions.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test robustness when the assumed signal or observation model is misspecified and assess performance using real experimental data. They could also evaluate schedules under operational constraints such as minimum spacing, sensor availability, and limits on how sharply observation effort can concentrate.

summary: The paper develops designs for group testing studies that estimate disease prevalence and diagnostic assay sensitivity and specificity when the assay is imperfect and study resources are limited. It uses a pooled-test probability model and constructs designs under several estimation criteria, as well as maximin designs that balance multiple criteria. For large studies, the authors compute approximate designs by convex optimization and verify their properties with optimal-design theory. For smaller studies, they propose rounding procedures to produce implementable exact designs subject to sample-size or budget constraints. In the Chlamydia examples, the designs retain high efficiency, while a numerical downstream example shows that sufficiently inaccurate parameter assumptions can increase the expected number of tests.
key_results: For the Chlamydia parameter values used in the main examples, maximin designs for two objectives had minimum efficiencies above 0.90, and designs balancing three objectives had minimum efficiencies above 0.81 across the reported settings. The proposed exact designs for individual criteria achieved efficiencies above 0.96 in the reported budget examples; exact multi-objective efficiencies approached their approximate-design benchmarks as sample size or budget increased, with a reported discrepancy of about 0.018 in small cases. Compared with optimizing one criterion at a time, a design can perform poorly on competing criteria: for maximum group size 61 and cost parameter 0.2, the determinant-optimal design had efficiencies of 0.568 under the least-information criterion and 0.536 for the selected sensitivity-specificity combination. The determinant-optimal and prevalence-focused designs reproduce results reported by earlier methods, while the paper adds other criteria and multi-objective designs. In the downstream example with 10,000 subjects, the oracle choice required an expected 5,108.374 tests; severe parameter misspecification increased this by up to 461.348 tests, or 9.031 percent.
key_equations:
Pooled-test positive probability: \[\pi(x\mid\theta)=p_1-(p_1+p_2-1)(1-p_0)^x\] The probability pi of a positive pooled test depends on group size x and parameter vector theta, whose components p0, p1, and p2 are prevalence, sensitivity, and specificity.

Information matrix: \[I(\xi,\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_i\lambda(x_i)f(x_i)f(x_i)^\top\] The information matrix I for design xi and parameters theta sums the contributions from k group sizes x_i, with allocation weights w_i, information factor lambda, and probability-derivative vector f.

Maximin design: \[\max_{w\in\Delta_M}\min_{j=1,\ldots,K}\operatorname{Eff}_j(w)\] The design weights w over the allowable group sizes in set Delta_M are chosen to maximize the smallest efficiency Eff_j across K objectives.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the approximate-design theory may not apply when sample sizes are small, and that approximate designs may not be implementable as exact designs. They also describe the designs as locally optimal, so their performance depends on the nominal parameter values; the proposed rounding procedures are practical constructions rather than direct proofs of exact-design optimality.
limitations_unstated: The main model and numerical examples do not establish performance when pooled outcomes have dependence, group-specific prevalence, or assay behavior that differs from the assumed model. Evaluation is primarily numerical and centered on specified Chlamydia parameter values, so the paper does not provide prospective validation in an operating screening program.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to multiple assays, more complex cost structures, and closer integration with fully sequential or adaptive testing procedures.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test these designs in field screening studies and assess how sensitive their performance is to dependence among subjects, prevalence heterogeneity, and pooling-related changes in assay accuracy. It could also optimize the first-stage estimation design and downstream testing rule jointly under a single total-resource constraint.

summary: This paper introduces Stepwise Deep Adaptive Design (Step-DAD), a method for sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED). It is designed for probabilistic models with unknown parameters and aims to maximize expected information gain (EIG) over a full sequence of experiments. The method first trains a policy-based BED (PB-BED) policy before the experiment, then uses observed outcomes to update the posterior and fine-tune the policy at selected points during the experiment. The authors evaluate the method in simulated source-location, temporal-discounting, and economic-preference problems. Across these problems, Step-DAD generally achieves higher information gain than the fully amortized Deep Adaptive Design (DAD) baseline, and can remain more robust when the prior used for training differs from the test-time prior.
key_results: For source location with 10 experiment steps and refinement at step 6, Step-DAD’s reported lower-bound total EIG was 7.759 ± 0.114, compared with DAD’s upper-bound estimate of 7.089 ± 0.013; these are conservative estimates using different bounds. With 10K DAD training steps followed by 2.5K refinement steps, Step-DAD matched or exceeded the 50K-step DAD baseline for refinement steps later than step 3. For hyperbolic temporal discounting, Step-DAD at step 10 achieved a lower-bound total EIG of 6.711 ± 0.040, versus DAD’s lower-bound 4.778 ± 0.013. For the constant elasticity of substitution problem, the corresponding lower-bound estimates were 13.879 ± 0.352 for Step-DAD and 10.181 ± 0.021 for DAD. In a source-location test with shifted priors, the paper reports that DAD’s information gain fell to essentially zero at larger shifts, while Step-DAD retained positive information gain.
key_equations:
Generative model: \[p(\theta, y \mid \xi)=p(\theta)p(y\mid\theta,\xi)\] The symbol p denotes a probability distribution, theta is the unknown parameter, y is the outcome, and xi is the experimental design.

Total information-gain objective: \[I_{1\to T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(h_T\mid\pi)}\left[H[p(\theta)]-H[p(\theta\mid h_T)]\right]\] The symbol I is total expected information gain, pi is the design policy, T is the total number of experiment steps, h_T is the resulting history, E is expectation, H is entropy, and p denotes a probability distribution over the unknown parameter theta.

Decomposition at a refinement step: \[I_{1\to T}(\pi)=I_{1\to\tau}(\pi)+\mathbb{E}_{p(h_\tau\mid\pi)}[I_{\tau+1\to T}^{h_\tau}(\pi)]\] The symbol I is total expected information gain, pi is the policy, T is the experiment horizon, tau is the refinement step, h_tau is the history observed by that step, and the superscript indicates information gain conditional on that history.

Conditional policy refinement: \[\pi_\tau^*=\arg\max_{\pi_\tau} I_{\tau+1\to T}^{h_\tau}(\pi_\tau)\] The symbol pi_tau star is the refined policy selected at step tau, arg max denotes the policy maximizing the objective, and I is the remaining expected information gain through step T conditional on the observed history h_tau.
limitations_stated: The authors note that Step-DAD requires computation during the experiment, which can be difficult when design decisions must be made very quickly. It also requires posterior inference and policy refinement, and the paper’s results show that performance can depend on the available inference and fine-tuning budgets.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated experiments and model-based information-gain estimates, so it does not establish how the method performs with real experimental data or substantial model error beyond the tested prior shifts. The comparisons cover a limited set of benchmark problems, and practical use depends on having enough time and computational resources to obtain a useful posterior and refine the policy between experiment stages.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate Step-DAD in real experiments and under broader forms of model misspecification, including errors in the outcome model and constraints on available designs. Further work could also test refinement schedules and compute budgets in constrained deployments, and develop reusable software or procedures for choosing when to update the policy.

summary: This paper develops a method for testing whether a new strategy improves outcomes in a randomized online experiment, with particular focus on detecting small average treatment effects. Its weighted two-armed bandit statistic combines a mean component and a volatility component, while a policy chooses subsequent arms based on the statistic’s running value. Because the statistic depends on observation order, the authors also propose calculating it across multiple reordered datasets and combining the resulting p-values. Counterfactual outcomes are estimated with doubly robust methods, using cross-fitting and machine-learning outcome and propensity models. The paper reports theoretical error control and higher power in simulations and analyses of operational data from a ride-sharing company.
key_results: In simulations with a sample size of 20,000, the paper compares the proposed method with the unweighted bandit statistic, a normal-score doubly robust test, a covariate-adjusted test, and a difference-in-means estimator; it reports controlled type I error rates and generally higher power for the permuted method. In semi-synthetic experiments based on real data, its reported power was 0.758 with one gradient-boosted model and 0.764 with a stacked model, compared with 0.738 and 0.732 for the corresponding unpermuted bandit results; type I error was 0.052 for the permuted method in both cases. On real dataset B, the permuted method’s p-values were 0.044 with either of two individual models and 0.032 with stacking, compared with 0.053 for the covariate-adjusted test. The authors used 25 reorderings and report that using more did not substantially improve power.
key_equations:
Average treatment effect: \[\mu=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]\] Mu is the average treatment effect, the expectation is over the study population, and Y(1) and Y(0) are the potential outcomes under treatment and control.

Weighted bandit statistic: \[T_{n,\lambda}(\theta_n)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}\bar R_n^{(\theta_i)}+\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{R_i^{(\theta_i)}}{\hat\sigma}\] The statistic is T; n is the sample size; lambda is the weight; theta_i is the arm chosen at step i; R_i is the reward at that step; bar R is the corresponding mean reward; and sigma-hat is the estimated reward standard deviation.

Bandit arm-choice policy: \[\theta_i^*=\begin{cases}1,&T_{i-1,\lambda}(\theta_{i-1}^*)\geq 0,\\0,&T_{i-1,\lambda}(\theta_{i-1}^*)<0,\end{cases}\quad i\geq2\] Theta-star is the chosen arm, with arm 1 selected when the preceding weighted statistic is nonnegative and arm 0 otherwise; i indexes the step and lambda is the statistic weight.

Cauchy combination of reordered p-values: \[C_B=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\tan\!\bigl(\pi(0.5-p_b)\bigr),\qquad p_a=0.5-\frac{\arctan(C_B)}{\pi}\] B is the number of reorderings, p_b is the p-value from reordering b, C_B is the combined statistic, and p_a is the aggregated p-value; pi is the mathematical constant.
limitations_stated: The authors state that machine learning provides a general way to capture data patterns but is not sufficiently refined compared with explicit models for the ride-sharing company’s data. They leave explicit modeling of the data distribution to future work.
limitations_unstated: The theoretical results center on an oracle statistic, while the operational method substitutes estimated counterfactual outcomes; the paper’s guarantees therefore rely on boundedness and doubly robust specification assumptions. The evaluation uses simulations and data from one company, and it does not report runtime or assess how the method performs when operational data have time dependence or other constraints that make arbitrary reordering unsuitable.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring explicit models of the ride-sharing company’s data distribution, rather than relying only on machine-learning methods.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method across organizations and outcome types, and assess performance when treatment assignment, allocation ratios, or data order are constrained by operational practice. They could also report computational costs and validate the method prospectively in field experiments.

summary: This paper designs a way to assign treatments under a fixed resource budget while retaining each unit’s intended treatment probability. It applies swap rounding to convert fractional assignment probabilities into binary decisions, with exactly B units treated and the original marginal probabilities preserved. The resulting assignments are negatively correlated, which the authors show can reduce the variance of the inverse propensity weighting (IPW) estimate of the average treatment effect compared with independent assignment. They also describe pairing units with similar covariates before rounding to seek further variance reduction. Simulations and semi-synthetic studies generally support the approach, though which version performs best varies by dataset.
key_results: The theoretical results show that swap rounding preserves the assignment probabilities and gives an unbiased IPW estimator; under the paper’s assumptions, its variance is no greater than that under independent assignment. The synthetic experiments use sample sizes of 50, 100, 250, 500, 1,000, and 5,000, with 100 scenarios replicated 100 times; the authors report that covariate-matched swap rounding has the lowest empirical variance across the three synthetic settings. The semi-synthetic infant health dataset contains 747 individuals, and the public housing dataset contains 3,163; covariate-matched swap rounding is reported as competitive in the infant health study, while regular swap rounding performs best in the housing study. The paper presents variance plots and comparisons with independent IPW, limited Bernoulli assignment, rerandomization, uniform random assignment, and self-normalized IPW, but does not state exact numerical variance reductions in the text.
key_equations:
Fixed-budget feasibility and preserved assignment probabilities: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i=B,\quad A_i\in\{0,1\},\quad \sum_{i=1}^{n}A_i=B,\quad \mathbb{E}[A_i]=p_i\] Here i indexes units, n is the number of units, p_i is unit i’s target treatment probability, B is the fixed treatment count, A_i is its binary treatment assignment, and the expectation states that the assignment probability is preserved.

Inverse propensity weighted treatment-effect estimator: \[\hat{\tau}_{IPW}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{A_iY_i(1)}{p_i}-\frac{(1-A_i)Y_i(0)}{1-p_i}\right)\] Here tau-hat is the estimated average treatment effect, IPW denotes inverse propensity weighting, n is the number of units, i indexes units, A_i is the assignment, Y_i(1) and Y_i(0) are potential outcomes, and p_i is the target treatment probability.

Assignment covariance under swap rounding: \[\rho_{ij}=\begin{cases}-p_ip_j,&p_i+p_j\leq 1,\\-(1-p_i)(1-p_j),&p_i+p_j>1.\end{cases}\] Here rho_ij is the covariance between assignments for units i and j, and p_i and p_j are their target treatment probabilities; the formula shows the covariance is nonpositive.

Variance comparison with independent assignment: \[\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{swap}\mid Y_{1:n}(0),Y_{1:n}(1))\leq\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{IPW}\mid Y_{1:n}(0),Y_{1:n}(1))\] Here tau-hat with the swap subscript is the estimate using swap-rounded assignments, tau-hat with the IPW subscript is the estimate using independent assignments, and the conditioned vectors contain all units’ potential outcomes.

Their semi-synthetic evaluations cannot use true propensities and both potential outcomes for each person, so they use estimated propensities and simulated counterfactual outcomes.
limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence is limited to synthetic and semi-synthetic studies, rather than a prospective experiment with real treatment assignments and observed outcomes. The paper does not report computational costs or quantify the practical effort needed to order units by covariates and run the rounding procedure.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method under outcome models and assignment constraints beyond those studied, including practical restrictions on which units may be paired. Prospective evaluations could also compare estimation accuracy and computational effort in operational experiments, alongside variance.

summary: The paper develops optimal experimental designs for drug-combination studies that aim to identify dose combinations producing a specified proportion of the maximum response. It considers nonlinear response-surface models, including an additive model and the Greco model, and defines effective combinations as response contour sets. The proposed design places observations to reduce prediction variance along the contour sets, using a selected L q norm; a Bayesian version averages the criterion over uncertainty in model parameters. The authors derive optimality conditions and an efficiency bound, then evaluate the method using a real oncological data set and simulations. In the reported examples, tailored designs estimate the target contours more precisely than common factorial and ray designs, while Bayesian designs help when interaction effects are uncertain.
key_results: For the case study’s target levels of 10% and 50%, the tailored design has efficiency 1.00 by definition, compared with 0.60 for the determinant-optimal design, 0.34 for the original design, 0.04 for the factorial design, and 0.06 to 0.07 for the ray designs. summary: This paper studies how many simulations are needed to train neural networks to extract cosmological information from simulated dark matter data. key_results: The authors generated a 32,768-simulation Big Sobol Sequence suite and used 16,600 simulations in the training, validation, and test analysis. For the power-spectrum task, the test loss scaled approximately as the number of training simulations to the power of negative 0.39 for the Latin hypercube data and negative 0.36 for the Sobol data. The original 2,000-simulation Latin hypercube set did not reach the information bound; the neural summary approached information saturation near 4,000 Sobol simulations, with little improvement beyond that point. future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare these designs under practical constraints such as parameter-dependent simulation costs, restricted parameter regions, or required marginal coverage, rather than uniform coverage alone. summary: The paper proposes a method that combines sequential Bayesian experimental design with online learning of model discrepancy. At each stage, it selects a measurement design to estimate parameters in a physics-based model, then uses the resulting data to update a neural-network correction. An ensemble-based indicator estimates whether the data are informative enough to justify updating that correction. Simulations of contaminant-source inference show that the approach can reduce parameter bias and improve model predictions while using far fewer forward evaluations than a full Bayesian analysis in the parametric-error comparison.
key_results: In the parametric-error example, the full Bayesian design evaluated a grid of 51 by 51 by 31 points, requiring 80,631 forward-model evaluations per stage; the hybrid method used a 51 by 51 grid and 2,601 evaluations per stage, while obtaining similar source-location and error-parameter results. For structural error, the neural-network correction improved field agreement: the good design achieved a mean squared error of 0.005 and relative error of 0.297, compared with 0.032 and 0.665 for a poor design and 0.142 and 1.553 for the uncorrected baseline. The ensemble indicator ranked the better correction data above the poorer data in the examples, and using the better data improved subsequent source-location estimates. In the ill-posed example, the method improved source-location inference even though the jointly optimized convection-rate parameter did not converge to its true value.

Sequential design criterion: \[d_i=\arg\max_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\mathrm{EIG}_i(d)\] At stage i, the design d is selected from the candidate design space D to maximize expected information gain EIG.

Discrepancy update: \[\theta_{\mathrm{NN}}^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta_{\mathrm{NN}}}p(y\mid d,\theta_G^{*},\theta_{\mathrm{NN}})\] The updated neural-network parameters θNN are chosen to maximize the likelihood of observation y at design d, with the physics-model estimate θG held fixed.
limitations_stated: The authors note that neural-network corrections can compensate for or obscure physics-based terms, making parameters difficult to identify; the paper mitigates this in its main structural-error example through restrictions on what the network learns. Averaging multiple posterior modes can be harmful when the posterior is genuinely multimodal, and the numerical studies use only measurements at the selected design point for model correction. The authors also report less satisfactory performance when relying only on simulated data to estimate design information gain.
limitations_unstated: The evidence is primarily from controlled numerical examples, so the results do not establish performance with noisy measurements, operational constraints, or real engineering systems. The structural-error demonstration uses a small, pre-trained network and a tailored constraint; its performance may not carry over to more general discrepancy patterns or substantially larger models. The method also has to solve both the design problem and repeated network optimization, but the paper does not quantify total runtime or sensitivity to optimization settings.
future_work_stated: The authors propose using the ensemble-based information-gain approximation to select designs that are directly informative for discrepancy calibration and extending it to non-Gaussian prior and posterior distributions. They also discuss mode-specific networks for multimodal parameter posteriors, post-training decomposition of learned model terms, and further work on estimating design value from simulations alone.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the method in physical experiments and under practical limits such as sensor relocation, measurement cost, and safety constraints. It would also be useful to develop stopping rules and sequential validation procedures that test whether a correction improves predictions beyond the locations used for calibration.

summary: The paper introduces Qualitative factors via Integer Programming (QuIP), a method for designing experiments when an expensive simulator has many categorical inputs. It uses a Gaussian process (GP) with an exchangeable covariance model and addresses both initial design and sequential selection for prediction or optimization. Initial runs are chosen to maximize the minimum Hamming distance between design points, and the resulting optimization is formulated as an assignment problem. For sequential work, the authors reformulate active-learning and upper-confidence-bound criteria as assignment problems that can be solved with an integer-programming solver. In path-planning simulations and a rover trajectory application, QuIP generally performed better than the compared design methods under limited evaluation budgets.
key_results: For initial designs with 50 runs, 10 to 30 levels, and factor counts from 5 to 25 above the number of levels, QuIP generally produced better maximin designs than differential evolution after a warm-up period of at most 15 seconds; with 30 levels it reached the stated upper bound in every tested case. In the maze experiment, QuIP improved prediction error over random and candidate-set sampling, and found lower-cost paths than random sampling, candidate-set sampling, and the latent-variable GP approach. In the greedy-snake experiment, QuIP found paths with greater reward than the compared methods; for the 10th sequential point, the solver's estimated optimum was close to the oracle optimum, and the stopping rule required the objective gap to be within 10% of the estimate. In rover optimization, all methods began with 30 runs and added 200 sequential points, and QuIP achieved lower current-best path costs than the random, candidate-set, and latent-variable GP comparisons.
key_equations:

Maximin initial-design criterion: \[\max_{x_1,\ldots,x_n\in[M]^d}\;\min_{i< i'} d_H(x_i,x_{i'})\] The design selects n points x_i from the space with M levels for each of d factors to maximize their minimum pairwise Hamming distance d_H.

Initial-design feasibility formulation: \[\text{find }I\in\{0,1\}^{n\times d\times M}:\quad d-\operatorname{tr}(I_iI_{i'}^{\mathsf T})\ge q,\quad\sum_{k=1}^{M}I_{ijk}=1\] The binary variable I_ijk assigns run i and factor j to level k; I_i and I_i' are the corresponding run slices, q is the required minimum distance, the trace term counts matching levels, and the sum constraint assigns each factor exactly one level in each run.

Upper-confidence-bound sequential criterion: \[x_{n+1}=\arg\max_x\{\mu_n(x)+\lambda\sigma_n(x)\}\] The next point x_n+1 maximizes the posterior mean mu_n plus lambda times the posterior standard deviation sigma_n, where lambda controls the balance between exploiting predicted response and exploring uncertainty.
limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a separate limitations section. They specify that QuIP uses a categorical-factor Gaussian process with an exchangeable covariance function, and identify broader models and objectives as possible extensions.
limitations_unstated: The method depends on the exchangeable covariance structure and maximum-likelihood estimation of its parameters, so performance may be weaker when factor effects or interactions do not fit that structure. The evidence comes from a limited set of path-planning simulations and one rover simulator, rather than trials across a broad range of real engineering simulators; large assignment problems may also require substantial solver resources.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the integer-programming design approach to broader Gaussian process models, including models for order-of-addition experiments and hierarchically sparse Gaussian processes. They also propose studying other sequential objectives, such as fault localization and multi-armed bandits, and applications to public-policy decisions.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method under model misspecification and compare its predictive and optimization performance on real simulator studies with engineering constraints. It could also develop constrained or batched sequential versions and assess how solver time and optimality gaps scale as the number of factors, levels, and requested runs grows.

summary: The paper designs experiments for estimating direct and spillover treatment effects when outcomes can depend on treatments received by other units and on prior treatments. Its method is for multi-unit experiments over time: at selected decision times, the design chooses between two population treatment probabilities, then independently assigns units to treatment or control and holds assignments fixed until the next decision time. It chooses decision times to minimize the worst-case weighted mean squared risk over bounded potential outcomes. The authors also study Horvitz–Thompson estimators, provide conservative variance estimates, and examine what happens when the carryover order is specified incorrectly. Their theory and numerical studies indicate that the proposed schedules can reduce risk relative to common schedules, while supporting asymptotic inference under the stated assumptions.
key_results: The authors provide a polynomial-time algorithm with time complexity O(T²) for finding the minimax design. In simulations, the selected minimax designs reduced the combined risk by an average of 19.7% compared with the design that randomizes every time period, and by 3.7% compared with the design using intervals of length p plus one. In simulations with correctly specified or over-specified carryover order, reported coverage probabilities for nominal 95% confidence intervals were generally close to 95%; single-center experiments with short observation periods had poorer coverage. In an analysis using synthetic outcomes fitted to trading data from 10 markets in 2016, the preferred schedule had combined risk 0.368, compared with 1.106 for randomizing every time period and 0.388 for the interval-length comparison design.

limitations_unstated: The exposure model represents interference through a common population treated probability, so it may not capture network-specific exposure, heterogeneous peer effects, or effects driven by the realized treated proportion. Numerical comparisons focus on a small set of alternative schedules, and the trading-data application evaluates synthetic outcomes rather than a new randomized field experiment.

future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to adapt the optimization to practical restrictions such as fixed treatment counts, limited switching, unequal assignment probabilities, or network-based exposures, and assess how those constraints affect risk. The method could also be implemented in publicly available software and validated prospectively in real multi-unit experiments, with sequential procedures for updating the design as outcomes accrue.

summary: This paper develops a multi-fidelity estimator for expected information gain, the objective used in Bayesian optimal experimental design to choose experiments that are expected to reduce uncertainty about model parameters. The method applies an approximate control variate framework, combining a high-fidelity utility estimate with estimates from cheaper models to reduce variance under a fixed computational budget. It first rewrites the information-gain expectation in terms of model parameters and data noise, so sampling the expectation does not require running each data model. The authors demonstrate the approach on a nonlinear benchmark and on simulated turbulent flow, where a pressure-probe location is selected to learn turbulence-model parameters. The estimates preserve the high-fidelity utility mean, and the examples show substantial variance reductions compared with a single-fidelity nested Monte Carlo estimator.
key_results: In the nonlinear benchmark, multi-fidelity estimates with inner-loop sample reuse reduced empirical variance by about 17 to 23 times relative to the single-fidelity nested Monte Carlo estimator; optimizing low-fidelity inner-loop sample sizes gave a more modest additional improvement. In the simulated flow study, under the same computational budget, the empirical variance reduction averaged across 875 candidate designs was 61.48 times for the fixed inner-sample setting and 70.19 times for the optimized setting. At the selected best design, the corresponding reductions were 94.24 times and 233.12 times. The authors report that estimated means align with the high-fidelity utility mean; this does not remove the finite inner-sample bias in the underlying nested Monte Carlo utility calculation.
key_equations:
Expected information gain: \[U(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_{Y,\Theta\mid\xi}\left[\log\frac{p(\Theta\mid Y,\xi)}{p(\Theta)}\right]\] Here, U is expected utility, xi is the experimental design, Y is observed data, theta is the uncertain parameter vector, the expectation averages over data and parameters conditional on the design, p denotes a probability density, and log is the natural logarithm; the quantity is the expected posterior-to-prior density ratio on a logarithmic scale.

Noise-based reparameterization: \[U(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_{Z}[u_E(\xi,Z)],\qquad Z=(E,\Theta)\] Here, U is expected information gain, xi is the design, Z is the pair of random inputs consisting of data noise E and parameters theta, and u_E is the reparameterized utility evaluated at those inputs.

Multi-fidelity estimator: \[\widetilde U=\widehat U_0+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\alpha_m\left(\widehat U_m(z_m)-\widehat U_m(z_m^*)\right)\] Here, U with a tilde is the multi-fidelity estimate, U with a hat and subscript zero is the high-fidelity sample mean, U with a hat and subscript m is the sample mean from auxiliary utility model m, alpha with subscript m is its control-variate weight, z_m and z_m star denote the allocated sample sets used for the paired estimates, and M is the number of auxiliary models.

Budgeted variance criterion: \[\min_{A}\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde U)\quad\text{subject to}\quad W(w,A)\leq w_{\mathrm{budget}}\] Here, A is the sample allocation, Var is estimator variance, W is the total evaluation cost computed from model costs w and allocation A, and w budget is the permitted computational budget.
limitations_stated: The method requires cheaper lower-fidelity models that are sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity model, and the models must share the same parameterization and random inputs. The paper also notes that finite inner-loop sampling leaves bias relative to the exact information gain, and that using one design-averaged covariance matrix can make the estimator suboptimal at particular designs.
limitations_unstated: The numerical validation covers only a one-dimensional benchmark and one simulated flow-calibration application, so it does not establish performance across other experimental domains or against a broad range of information-gain estimators. The flow example also depends on a particular set of nested numerical grids and pressure-probe candidate locations, which may not represent practical constraints such as probe access, measurement costs, or physical experiment variability.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying low-fidelity utility models created by changing inner-loop sample sizes and extending the method to models that share only some parameters. They also propose embedding the estimator in the overall design optimization, adapting estimator structure across the design space, and improving pilot sampling and the sharing or prediction of correlation information across designs.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the estimator with physical experiments and quantify how measurement errors or model misspecification affect the chosen design. It would also be useful to incorporate practical constraints on probe placement and experiment execution, and to test sequential design strategies that update the information-gain estimate as data arrive.

summary: The paper presents raxpy, a Python package for designing, evaluating, and running space-filling experiments on computer models with optional and hierarchical inputs. It uses Python type annotations and code introspection to derive a model's input space, then generates experiment points under a user-specified run budget. The authors introduce design measures for optional and hierarchical dimensions and propose several design-generation methods, including methods that construct designs separately within feasible full-subspaces. They compare these methods with random designs and with versions improved by maximum-projection optimization. In their numerical study, the full-subspace Latin hypercube method with value pools and maximum-projection post-optimization performs especially well on minimum interpoint distance, while the strongest method depends on the metric being considered.
key_results: The study compares 12 algorithms across four input spaces and three design sizes, using 30 replications per setting; the paper reports 360 designs evaluated. Lower average rank is better: the full-subspace Latin hypercube method with value pools and maximum-projection post-optimization ranks 1.0 for minimum interpoint distance, 2.5 for average single-dimension projection distance, 2.5 for star discrepancy, and 4.25 for weighted discrepancy. future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test the package on real simulation and engineering studies, measuring whether its designs improve surrogate prediction or engineering decisions as well as geometric space filling. summary: This software paper introduces MOODE, an R package for finding designs for quantitative-factor experiments. The package targets response-surface experiments where researchers want to estimate a chosen polynomial model, detect lack of fit, and reduce estimation bias if additional polynomial effects are present. It combines estimation, lack-of-fit, and robustness criteria using user-selected weights, and searches for designs with point-exchange or coordinate-exchange algorithms. Its examples show that compound criteria can produce compromises among competing objectives. In the reported comparisons, compound designs often retain useful estimation and lack-of-fit performance while providing replicated runs for estimating experimental error.

The three designs optimized for just one objective each performed poorly on at least one of the other objectives. In comparisons of 12-run designs for 3 to 9 two-level factors, compound designs achieved at least 50% efficiency for inference and typically did better, while retaining four pure-error degrees of freedom when possible. For four factors and 12 runs, the compound design used 8 distinct treatments, compared with 5 for the inference-optimal design and 12 for the mean-squared-error-optimal design.

future_work_unstated: Further work could test the criteria under alternative error and prior assumptions and with practical constraints on feasible treatments and randomization. summary: The paper develops collaborative designs for multiple controlled experiments that share the same subjects and have subject covariates. Its objective is to improve the precision of each experiment’s treatment-effect estimates by modeling the shared subject-specific random effect and maximizing a D-optimality criterion. The authors propose a randomized greedy method that solves a sequence of semi-definite programs and a faster method that solves one semi-definite program and uses random orthogonal vectors to create allocations. The design seeks to balance covariates within experiments while making allocations orthogonal across experiments. Simulations show that the proposed methods outperform covariate-agnostic allocation methods when the number of covariates is large.
key_results: The simulation used 96 subjects, 4 or 8 experiments, and either 10 or 70 covariates; the subject-specific random-effect standard deviation was 0.25 or 2, and each experimental-error variance was 1. Each randomized method was replicated 100 times per covariate matrix, and optimization times were capped at 50 seconds. With 70 covariates, the proposed methods generally had higher D-efficiency and lower treatment-effect variances than fully random allocation and Plackett-Burman designs. The greedy method using deterministic binary programming performed best in the comparisons and nearly reached the Hadamard-based D-efficiency upper bound with 10 covariates, but it does not randomize assignments. With few covariates, covariate-agnostic methods could outperform the single-design randomized method.

summary: The paper develops a way to construct augmented row-column designs for unreplicated trials, particularly trials in plant breeding where each test line has only one plot. It considers a square field with controls appearing once in every row and column, and constructs the control positions by converting an equireplicate incomplete-block design into a square array. The authors evaluate designs by the average variances of test-line and control-to-test-line comparisons, under a fixed-effects model with independent normal errors. They show that the construction works for cyclic and non-cyclic auxiliary designs, and that minimizing the auxiliary design’s average variance also minimizes the two principal comparison metrics. Their examples identify practical designs with control proportions in a range they recommend, and show that some non-cyclic designs can improve on cyclic alternatives.
key_results: For a 12-by-12 design with 3 controls, the best cyclic design reported has an average variance of 4.0341 for test-line comparisons and 2.0910 for control-to-test-line comparisons; controls occupy 25% of plots. The paper examines 147 cyclic designs with array sizes from 10 to 30 and control counts from 3 to 9, reporting that for a fixed array size the test-line comparison variance decreases as more controls are used. limitations_stated: The authors state that the designs presented are appropriate only for square fields. They also note that complete enumeration becomes computationally challenging as the number of treatments and controls grows.
limitations_unstated: The results rely on the stated fixed-effects model and independent, equal-variance errors, so they do not establish performance when field errors are spatially correlated or variances differ across the field. future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate these designs under spatially correlated errors, unequal variances, and practical field constraints such as unavailable plots or irregular field layouts. summary: This paper develops a method for optimal experimental design when measurement choices vary continuously and the model is nonlinear. In a Lorenz reconstruction comparison using 63 measurements for each strategy, strategic sampling converged faster and reached better final parameter-error and loss values than uniform sampling. The authors estimate a cost of O(dNT′) per outer iteration for the accurate-inner-loop method and O(d³ + d²N) for the streamlined method; these are complexity estimates, not measured run times. In the Schrödinger simulations, the designs concentrated measurements near the source-detector diagonal; A-optimal sampling also favored locations where the true potential was larger, while D-optimal sampling showed no similarly favored locations along the diagonal. The reported particle counts include 10,000 for uniform-start Schrödinger tests and 1,000 for warm-start tests.

future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method on real experiments and under deliberate model mismatch, noise variation, and limits on feasible measurement times or locations. summary: This paper reviews exact optimal designs for spherical harmonic regression on the unit sphere in three dimensions. For model orders 1 through 7, the smallest listed Hardin and Sloane designs have 4, 12, 24, 36, 60, 84, and 108 points, respectively; the corresponding designs from Dette and colleagues have 6, 20, 42, 81, 143, 221, and 345 points. The paper therefore recommends the Hardin and Sloane designs over those compared designs for their lower run counts and, where possible, manageable numbers of polar angles. limitations_unstated: The examples compare design sizes using published catalogues rather than evaluating estimation precision or prediction on simulated or real responses. summary: The paper presents a practical method and open-source software for choosing seismometer locations to improve estimates of earthquake locations at volcanoes. It uses Bayesian experimental design to maximize expected information gain about source location, with travel-time, amplitude, and seismic-array measurements considered together. The design is built from a prior distribution of likely source locations, a forward model and data likelihood, and a genetic algorithm that searches locations allowed by terrain and other constraints. They find that optimized layouts can reduce expected location uncertainty compared with random layouts, and that the software can produce an initial design quickly.
key_results: For the Etna example with three nodal stations and one array, the reported design has an expected information gain of 5.7 nats and an approximate posterior standard deviation of 545 meters. With a population of 64 candidate designs, the genetic algorithm needed about 200 generations to converge, with only slight improvements through about 600 generations; the authors report that this example can be computed in minutes using the DN method, compared with tens of minutes for the nested Monte Carlo method using the same number of samples. Across designs with up to 10 receivers, optimized layouts had the lowest expected uncertainty; Sobol space-filling layouts performed better than uniformly random layouts and approached the optimized results, while optimized designs could match the mean Sobol uncertainty using one fewer receiver when more than two receivers were used. In the velocity-model comparison, the homogeneous, layered, and heterogeneous designs scored 5.08, 5.10, and 5.26 nats, respectively, with approximate standard deviations of 667, 662, and 628 meters when evaluated using the heterogeneous model.

limitations_stated: The authors identify simplifying assumptions: a homogeneous velocity model in the basic workflow, Gaussian data likelihoods, and independent errors across data. They note that these assumptions can affect design quality and can be relaxed with additional scenario-specific information, but that more complex velocity models increase computation. The paper does not model full waveforms or optimize the full source solution including moment tensor, and the authors say an efficient extension to the latter remains unclear.
limitations_unstated: The main worked comparison uses simulated events and one volcano, Etna, so the reported gains do not establish performance in real deployments or across diverse volcanoes. future_work_stated: The authors identify extending the methods and software to optimize networks for the full source solution, including moment tensor, as a possible direction, while noting that an efficient implementation is not yet clear. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation against actual seismic deployments and observed event locations across several volcanoes, including tests of how misspecified priors and noise assumptions affect performance. It covers functional linear models and functional generalized linear models, including binomial responses with a logit link and Poisson responses with a log link. The method restricts otherwise infinite-dimensional functions using basis expansions, principally B-splines, and optimizes the resulting basis coefficients with coordinate exchange. For linear models it offers Bayesian A- and D-optimality, with roughness penalties available to encourage smooth parameter functions. For generalized models it uses prior information and either quadrature or Monte Carlo approximation to form pseudo-Bayesian criteria. The examples demonstrate varied designs for profile and scalar factors, but are demonstrations rather than comparisons against competing methods.
key_results: The package implements the coordinate exchange algorithm, supports repeated searches from multiple starting designs, and uses C++ components for computational work. In the four-run functional linear example, the Bayesian D-optimal design had an objective value of 0.4051947 and required 4 iterations. The 12-run linear example with two profile factors and an interaction reported an A-optimal objective value of 13.33739, 12 iterations, and 10 seconds; the bioreactor example produced four distinct feed-volume profiles in a 12-run design. The 12-run logistic example reported a pseudo-Bayesian D-optimal objective value of 847.976, 31 iterations, and 1 second, while the 12-run Poisson example reported a pseudo-Bayesian A-optimal objective value of 2.212573, 4 iterations, and 34 seconds. summary: The paper introduces an information-matching method for optimal experimental design and active learning. It is intended for models where the goal is precise downstream predictions, even when many model parameters are poorly identifiable. The method compares the information supplied by candidate training data with the information required to meet a specified prediction uncertainty, then uses a convex optimization problem to select and weight data. The authors demonstrate the method in simulated power-system sensor placement, underwater source localization, and interatomic-potential development. Their examples show that small selected data sets can meet the specified prediction-precision targets.
key_results: For the IEEE 14-bus power-system example, the method selected buses 2, 6, and 9 for full observability, consistent with prior studies; for the IEEE 39-bus example, its full-network placements were also reported as broadly consistent with earlier findings. In the main underwater-acoustics case, selected receivers were 5% of candidate locations, and across the tested sediment and frequency scenarios no more than 8% were needed to meet the source-location targets of plus or minus 2.5 meters vertically and plus or minus 100 meters horizontally. For the molybdenum disulfide potential, 7 of 2,000 candidate configurations met a target uncertainty set at 10% of predictions from the full-data-trained potential. For silicon, designs used at most 5 of 400 candidate configurations; the reported uncertainties for lattice constant, cohesive energy, and three elastic constants were each below their stated target uncertainties. The paper does not provide a quantitative head-to-head performance comparison with conventional parameter-focused design criteria; it contrasts their objectives conceptually.
key_equations:
Information from selected training data: \[I=\sum_{m=1}^{M} w_m I_m\] The combined Fisher information matrix I is the sum over m from 1 to M of each candidate datum's information matrix I_m weighted by its design weight w_m.

Information required for target prediction precision: \[J=J_g^{T}\Sigma^{-1}J_g\] The required information matrix J is formed from the prediction Jacobian J_g, its transpose, and the inverse of the target covariance matrix Σ.

Information-matching design criterion: \[\min_{w}\|w\|_1\quad\text{subject to }w_m\ge 0,\;\sum_{m=1}^{M}w_m I_m\succeq J\] The method minimizes the sum of absolute design weights w, requires every candidate weight w_m to be nonnegative, and requires the weighted information from M candidate data to be at least the required information matrix J in the positive-semidefinite ordering.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the optimization can be infeasible if the candidate set lacks data informative about parameters relevant to the predictions. The information matrix is local and can vary with parameter values; initial parameter choices can also change selected data, weights, and estimates, although the target uncertainty is met when the problem is feasible.
limitations_unstated: The prediction guarantee relies on local information matrices and a linearized uncertainty argument, so it may not hold accurately for strongly nonlinear behavior or substantial model misspecification. The demonstrations use a limited set of simulated scientific examples and do not establish real-world acquisition costs or compare performance quantitatively against competing design algorithms.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to larger models and machine-learning applications, including machine-learned interatomic potentials. They also propose deeper theoretical analysis of the optimization's limiting behavior to better understand robustness and broaden applicability.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the selected designs in physical experiments and compare their prediction accuracy, total acquisition cost, and robustness with established design methods. Further work could incorporate practical constraints such as limited sensor locations, variable measurement costs, and sequential decisions after new observations arrive.

summary: The paper presents CDsampling, an R package for choosing constrained samples in paid research studies and clinical trials. It finds allocations for generalized linear models (GLMs), including linear and logistic regression, and multinomial logistic models (MLMs), with the goal of improving parameter estimation by maximizing the determinant of the information matrix. Its construction uses a lift-one algorithm that optimizes allocation proportions one at a time within user-specified constraints, then converts the proportions to integer sample counts. The package also provides expected weighted designs that use parameter priors and uniform allocations for settings with limited model information. In the paper’s simulation example, the D-optimal approaches had lower estimation errors than simple random and constrained uniform sampling, though the full-data estimates had the lowest errors.
key_results: For the simulated trial example, 200 people were sampled from 500 available volunteers across six gender-and-age groups. The local D-optimal exact allocation was 50, 40, 10, 100, 0, and 0; the expected weighted allocation was 48, 40, 10, 43, 19, and 40. Across 100 simulation runs, both D-optimal methods had slightly higher root mean square errors (RMSEs) than using all 500 people, but lower errors than simple random sampling without replacement (SRSWOR) and constrained uniform sampling; constrained uniform sampling also performed better than SRSWOR. In the trauma-data example, the package allocated a sample of 600 from 802 patients across eight treatment-and-severity groups, with counts of 155, 0, 0, 100, 168, 0, 0, and 177. The paper reports no numerical RMSE values or broad benchmark timings, so the comparison is qualitative rather than a quantified efficiency ranking.
key_equations:
GLM Fisher information: \[F=n\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i X_iX_i^{\mathsf T}\] F is the Fisher information matrix, n is the total sample size, m is the number of design points, wi is the allocation proportion at point i, vi is its information weight, and Xi is its predictor vector.

Constrained D-optimal allocation criterion: \[w^*=\arg\max_{w\in S}\det F(w)\] w* is the optimal allocation-proportion vector, w is a feasible allocation-proportion vector, S is the feasible set, and F(w) is the Fisher information matrix for w; det means its determinant.
limitations_stated: The authors note that a D-optimal allocation may omit some subgroups and produce extreme designs, which could increase overfitting risk; they suggest allocating some participants to omitted groups to improve robustness. For local designs, model parameter values must be supplied, while expected weighted designs depend on chosen parameter priors.
limitations_unstated: The reported estimation comparison uses one simulated logistic model and one set of population subgroup sizes, with 100 replications; it does not establish performance across a wide range of models, priors, or practical sampling constraints. The paper gives no numerical RMSE table or runtime comparison, and exact allocations may depend on custom constraint-boundary and feasibility functions that users must define correctly.
future_work_stated: The authors propose adding other optimality criteria, such as A-optimality and E-optimality, and supporting models beyond GLMs and MLMs.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the package across a broader set of simulated models and real studies, including sensitivity to misspecified parameter values and priors. It could also provide ready-made support for common operational restrictions and evaluate sequential updates when enrollment or subgroup availability changes.

summary: This paper studies how to estimate the global average treatment effect (GATE) in A/B testing when one unit’s outcome can depend on other units’ treatment through a network. Rather than proposing a new treatment assignment rule, it uses data from existing ramp-up experiments that tested different treatment proportions. The method stacks those stages’ data to train a regression model, then predicts average outcomes under global treatment and global control. The authors derive bias and variance results for ordinary least squares under a general linear interference model and also evaluate graph neural network estimators in simulations. Their main finding is that variation in treatment proportions can reduce bias and improve estimation, while repeating experiments at one fixed proportion mainly reduces variability rather than bias.
key_results: Under the paper’s regular-interference assumptions, the one-stage linear regression estimator has bias of constant order and variance of order one over the number of units, so bias is the dominant error as the network grows. In the two-hop simulation, merging four stages reduced the graph neural network estimator’s MSE from 1.963 to 0.025 under unit-level randomization and from 0.904 to 0.008 under cluster-level randomization, compared with the single-stage baseline. Merging five stages gave MSE values of 0.026 and 0.010, respectively, so adding a stage did not always improve on four stages. Repeating the 50 percent treatment stage did not reduce bias: under unit-level randomization, MSE rose from 1.968 for one round to 2.214 for five rounds, despite lower standard deviation.
key_equations:
General linear interference model: \[Y(z)=\beta_0\mathbf{1}+\beta_1 z+Bz+\epsilon\] Here Y(z) is the vector of potential outcomes under treatment vector z, beta zero and beta one are baseline and direct-effect coefficients, 1 is the all-ones vector, B is the interference matrix, and epsilon is random noise.

Global average treatment effect: \[\tau=\beta_1+\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\top}B\mathbf{1}\] Here tau is the GATE, beta one is the direct-effect coefficient, n is the number of units, 1 is the all-ones vector, and B is the interference matrix; the superscript T denotes transpose.

Regression counterfactual estimator: \[\hat{\tau}(f)=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\left[f(\mathbf{1},A)-f(\mathbf{0},A)\right]\] Here tau-hat is the estimated GATE, f is the fitted prediction function, n is the number of units, 1 and 0 are the all-treated and all-control vectors, and A is the network adjacency matrix.

Leading bias for merged stages: \[\operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\tau}^{(T)})=-\frac{\sum_{i,j}B_{ij}}{n}\left[1-\frac{T\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_t^2-(\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_t)^2}{(\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_t)(T-\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_t)}\right]+O(1/n)\] This is the leading bias expression for the merged-stage linear regression estimator: tau-hat is the estimate, T is the number of stages, c sub t is the treatment proportion in stage t, B sub ij is an element of the interference matrix, n is the number of units, and O(1/n) is the smaller-order remainder.
limitations_stated: The theoretical results concern static GATE and assume potential-outcome parameters remain fixed across stages; they exclude cross-round spillovers. The authors note that a traffic cap can leave substantial bias, and their results for nonlinear interference and changing graphs are simulation evidence rather than general theoretical guarantees.
limitations_unstated: The simulations use a small number of network datasets and specified synthetic outcome models, so the reported improvements may not transfer to other networks, outcome processes, or real platform data. The evidence for the more flexible estimator also comes from one lightweight graph neural network setup and 100 Monte Carlo repetitions; performance with other model choices and operational constraints is not established.
future_work_stated: The authors identify extending the analysis to carryover effects and adaptive rollout decisions as important future work. They also recommend that stage selection account for exposure diversity as well as sample size, subject to operational risk and traffic constraints.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the approach using real platform outcomes and additional networks, while testing sensitivity to heterogeneous treatment effects, misspecified network structure, and other prediction models. Further work could develop practical stage-selection procedures that incorporate traffic, clustering, and business constraints, then validate them in sequential experiments.

summary: This paper develops a deterministic rounding method for experimental design using interlacing polynomials. It addresses D-design, A-design, and E-design, where the goal is to select a fixed-size multiset of vectors that optimizes a matrix-based measure of information. The method first solves a convex relaxation, then uses a polynomial family built from repeated random sampling to choose vectors one at a time. For E-design, the authors derive a new guarantee that also applies when the selection budget is close to the vector dimension. The framework also recovers established guarantees for D-design and A-design and extends to a generalized ratio objective.
key_results: For E-design, the deterministic algorithm has approximation factor equal to one divided by the square of one minus the square root of the dimension-minus-one divided by the budget. It is a near-one approximation when the budget is sufficiently large relative to the dimension and the inverse square of the desired accuracy; when the budget equals the dimension, its factor is the dimension squared, and when the budget is twice the dimension, the factor is constant. For D-design, the factor is the budget times the d-th root of the ratio of the budget-minus-dimension factorial to the budget factorial; this is at most the budget divided by the budget-minus-dimension-plus-one, and at budget equal to dimension it is at most e. For A-design, the factor is the budget divided by the budget-minus-dimension-plus-one. For all three objectives, the rounding stage takes order k times m times d raised to the matrix-multiplication exponent plus one; the generalized ratio objective also receives a stated approximation guarantee and the same rounding runtime.
key_equations:
Fractional information matrix: \[X=\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_i v_i v_i^{\mathsf T}\] X is the fractional information matrix, m is the number of available vectors, i indexes those vectors, x_i is the fractional weight for candidate i, and v_i is its input vector; the superscript T denotes transpose.

E-design approximation factor: \[\rho_E=\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{d-1}{k}}\right)^{-2}\] rho_E is the E-design approximation factor, d is the vector dimension, and k is the selection budget.

D-design and A-design approximation factors: \[\rho_D=k\left(\frac{(k-d)!}{k!}\right)^{1/d},\qquad \rho_A=\frac{k}{k-d+1}\] rho_D and rho_A are the D-design and A-design approximation factors, k is the selection budget, d is the vector dimension, and the exclamation mark denotes factorial.
limitations_stated: The authors do not know how to extend the interlacing-polynomial method to selection without repetitions, because they do not yet know how to define suitable probability distributions and expected polynomials. They also identify an open gap for E-design when the budget equals the dimension: their factor is the dimension squared, while the known integrality gap of the relaxation is only the dimension.
limitations_unstated: The guarantees depend on the stated matrix objectives and on the fractional convex relaxation; the paper does not evaluate how sensitive the method is to departures from those assumptions in real experiments. The reported runtime covers the rounding stage, while the paper does not quantify the practical cost of solving the convex relaxation or demonstrate performance on a real data set.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying whether the method can be adapted to selection without repetitions. They also identify closing the gap between the dimension-squared E-design guarantee and the dimension-sized relaxation integrality gap at budget equal to dimension as an open question.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate implementations on real experimental-design problems and report end-to-end runtime, including the convex optimization step. Further work could also test the method under practical constraints on which candidates may be selected and examine whether related guarantees hold for other design objectives.
