summary: This paper extends a nonparametric method for comparing a subpopulation with a full population, or comparing two subpopulations, while controlling for multiple covariates. It turns each vector of covariates into a one-dimensional score using the Hilbert space-filling curve, then applies cumulative comparison graphs and summary statistics to the responses. The method is intended for discrete responses and can also use sampling weights. The paper tests it on synthetic data and on public marketing and household-survey datasets. The author reports that results are generally less sensitive to the order of covariates than to which covariates are included.
key_results: In synthetic examples with 1,000 full-population observations and 100 subpopulation observations, the number of covariates ranges from 2 to 4,096; for examples with a constructed response difference, the reported maximum-deviation statistic divided by its estimated scale is 15.66 with 2 covariates and about 8.7 to 9.0 in examples with 2,048 to 4,096 covariates. Reversing the covariate order gives similar results in these examples, while null-response examples produce graphs described as consistent with random fluctuation. In the marketing dataset, which contains 47,117 people, the folding-card-only versus normal-card-only comparison has a reported normalized maximum-deviation statistic of 4.509 with two covariates and 4.332 with three covariates. In the household survey analysis, the full California sample contains 134,094 households; for San Joaquin County, the normalized statistic is 6.706 when controlling for income and move duration, 1.165 when controlling for income and number of children, and 1.371 when controlling for all three covariates. The paper does not report efficiency or run-size comparisons against competing design methods; it evaluates a method for analyzing existing data rather than constructing an experiment.

Deviation summaries: \[G=\max_{1\le k\le n}|F_k-\widetilde F_k|,\quad H=\max_{0\le k\le n}(F_k-\widetilde F_k)-\min_{0\le k\le n}(F_k-\widetilde F_k)\] Here G is the largest absolute cumulative difference, H is the range of cumulative differences, F_k and F̃_k are the cumulative responses being compared, k is the cumulative position, and n is the subpopulation size.
limitations_stated: The author states that the Hilbert curve does not fully account for the dataset's intrinsic geometry, except insofar as the positions of observations reflect data density. An alternative ordering based on an approximate traveling-salesperson solution can degenerate into analyzing discrete strata separately in some examples, so the author notes that better ways to account for intrinsic geometry may be needed.
limitations_unstated: The method reduces a multivariate covariate vector to one ordering, so different local patterns in covariate space can be obscured even when the ordering is stable. The evaluation does not compare the method systematically with regression, binning, or other adjustment approaches, and it does not establish performance across a broad range of response types or real experimental settings.
future_work_stated: The author suggests exploring alternative orderings, including approximate traveling-salesperson solutions, to represent intrinsic data geometry more fully, particularly for many covariates or sparse datasets. The paper also suggests that future work may develop better ideas for this purpose because the traveling-salesperson ordering can degenerate in examples.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate error rates and uncertainty calibration across more simulated response structures and compare results directly with established adjustment methods. It would also be useful to investigate how the method handles practical experiment constraints, such as categorical covariates, missing measurements, and sequential data collection, and to validate its findings in prospective experiments.

summary: This tutorial shows how Design and Analysis of Experiments methods can be used to plan, run, and interpret simulation studies. It presents a five-stage workflow, using cause-and-effect diagrams to identify factors and factorial or fractional factorial designs to select simulation runs. Analysis uses analysis of variance, effect plots, and Taguchi Robust Parameter Design to assess both performance and robustness. Examples reanalyze a study of hypothesis-test type I error and design a new comparison of two prediction methods. The examples show that structured designs and analyses can reveal important interactions and, in some cases, preserve the main findings with fewer runs.
key_results: In the hypothesis-testing example, the original full factorial had 432 runs; excluding the poorly performing asymptotic normality method left 324 runs, and a reduced 72-run analysis recovered the same main conclusions and the five largest effects. The paper’s new statistical-learning example used a 32-run quarter fraction instead of the 128-run full factorial, completed in under 30 minutes using two processor cores. In that example, lasso had higher predictive accuracy than random forests throughout the tested settings, although its performance varied more across some noise-factor settings. The chosen fractional design was resolution IV and prioritized estimation of effects involving the model factor; the paper does not present minimum aberration or orthogonality as an optimality criterion.

limitations_stated: The authors note that their treatment assumes independent and identically distributed errors across runs, and they identify randomization restrictions, blocking, and random effects as issues not addressed in their main treatment. Their illustrations use two-level fractional factorial designs; they note that designs with more than two levels are available but are not covered in the examples.
limitations_unstated: The evidence for the general workflow comes from two illustrative simulation settings, so its performance is not demonstrated across a broad range of applications or real experiments. In the 32-run learning example, some effects are aliased, which limits how confidently the results can distinguish specific effects beyond the effects the design was chosen to prioritize.
future_work_stated: The authors identify randomization restrictions, blocking, random-effects models, fair calibration of competing methods, and reproducibility as open issues for further consideration. They also note that additional runs can be added when aliasing is problematic.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the workflow across more population models, response measures, and practical constraints to determine how widely its conclusions about run savings hold. It would also be useful to evaluate sequential design augmentation, where early results guide which additional simulation runs are most informative.

summary: The paper introduces implicit Deep Adaptive Design (iDAD), a method for choosing experiments adaptively when a model can be simulated but its likelihood cannot be evaluated. It targets Bayesian optimal experimental design by learning a policy to maximize the expected information gained across a sequence of experiments. The policy and an auxiliary critic are trained together offline using simulated data and likelihood-free information bounds. At experiment time, the policy selects each new design from the data already collected, and the critic can also support likelihood-free parameter inference. Across three simulated applications, the method outperformed the likelihood-free comparison methods and, in models where a likelihood was available, came close to the likelihood-based adaptive method.
key_results: In the location-finding experiment with four parameter dimensions and ten experiments, iDAD with InfoNCE achieved an expected-information lower bound of 7.750 ± 0.039, compared with 5.547 ± 0.028 for static stochastic-gradient BOED and 7.967 ± 0.034 for DAD. For the two-dimensional location-finding case, design proposal took 0.0167 seconds for iDAD with NWJ and 0.0168 seconds with InfoNCE, versus 2256.0 seconds for the sequential variational method and 0.0070 seconds for DAD. In the pharmacokinetic experiment with five measurements, iDAD with InfoNCE achieved 3.200 ± 0.024, compared with 2.985 ± 0.027 for static stochastic-gradient BOED and 3.234 ± 0.023 for DAD. In the simulated epidemic experiment with five measurements, the InfoNCE lower bound was 3.915 ± 0.020, exceeding 3.752 ± 0.020 for the best reported static baseline.
key_equations:
Differentiable simulator and policy: \[xi_t=pi(h_{t-1}),\qquad y_t=f(\epsilon_t;\xi_t,\theta,h_{t-1})\] At step t, the policy pi maps the history h from earlier steps to design xi, and simulator f maps noise epsilon, design xi, parameter theta, and that history to outcome y.

Total expected information objective: \[I_T(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta)p(h_T\mid\theta,\pi)}\left[\log p(h_T\mid\theta,\pi)-\log p(h_T\mid\pi)\right]\] The total expected information I for T experiments under policy pi is the expectation over parameters theta and resulting history h, comparing the history density conditional on theta with its marginal density.

InfoNCE training bound: \[\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{NCE}}_T(\pi,U;L)=\mathbb{E}\left[\log\frac{\exp(U(h_T,\theta_0))}{\frac{1}{L+1}\sum_{i=0}^{L}\exp(U(h_T,\theta_i))}\right]\] The InfoNCE lower bound uses critic U to score history h against a parameter theta drawn with that history, theta zero, and L contrastive parameter samples; the expectation is over those samples and the simulator-generated histories.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the upfront training can be computationally expensive, although its cost can be amortized across experiment instances. Because the method uses gradients, they restrict it to continuous design settings. They also note that NWJ can have high variance, while InfoNCE is biased for finite numbers of contrastive samples.
limitations_unstated: The learned policy is trained for a specified simulator, prior, and experiment horizon, but the paper does not establish how well it transfers if these change or if the simulator differs from the real process. The experiments use a limited set of simulated models, and the paper does not validate the proposed policies in physical or operational experiments with practical constraints on allowable designs.
future_work_stated: The authors identify extending the method beyond continuous design settings as a direction for future work.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test policy robustness to simulator mismatch and changing parameter priors, and evaluate iDAD in real experiments with engineering constraints on feasible designs. It would also be useful to study whether policies can be updated sequentially as new operational data arrive, rather than being trained only for a fixed setup.

summary: This paper adapts Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) for simulator models of human behavior whose likelihoods are intractable. It studies three models of choices in multi-armed bandit tasks and aims to choose reward probabilities that improve either model discrimination or parameter estimation. The method trains a neural network to estimate a lower bound on mutual information (MI), using separate subnetworks to learn summary statistics for each block of behavioral data. It searches for designs with Bayesian optimization and uses the trained network to estimate posterior distributions. In simulations, the selected designs improved model recovery and parameter recovery compared with a commonly used baseline design.
key_results: The simulations used three-arm bandit tasks with 30 trials per block; model discrimination used two blocks, and parameter estimation used three. The optimized model-discrimination designs were [0, 0, 0.6] and [1, 1, 0]; their confusion-matrix diagonal values were 0.84, 0.88, and 0.90, compared with 0.57, 0.73, and 0.65 for the baseline. For parameter estimation in the Win-Stay Lose-Thompson-Sample model, the selected block designs were [0, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1], and [1, 0, 1]; the paper reports sharper posteriors around the true parameter values than for the baseline, based on 1,000 observations. The method used 400 design-utility evaluations, with 50,000 simulated samples at each design; the baseline reward probabilities were sampled from a Beta(2, 2) distribution.
key_equations:
Simulator model: \[y \sim p(y\mid\theta,d)\] The observed data y are generated from the probability distribution p, conditional on model parameters theta and experimental design d.

Design criterion: \[d^{*}=\arg\max_{d} I(v;y\mid d)\] The optimal design d star maximizes the mutual information I between variable of interest v and data y, conditional on design d.

Neural mutual-information lower bound: \[U(d;\psi)=\mathbb{E}_{p(y\mid v,d)p(v)}[T_{\psi}(v,y)]-e^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{p(y\mid d)p(v)}[e^{T_{\psi}(v,y)}]\] The utility lower bound U at design d and network parameters psi is the expectation of network T under the joint distribution of data y and variable v, minus the exponential-weighted expectation under the product of the data distribution given d and the prior distribution of v; e is the base of the natural exponential function.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their experiments use only synthetic data and no real-world data or participants. They also report that the transition parameters of the generalized latent-state model are not well estimated under either design, attributing this to uninformative priors and the small number of trials in the behavioral blocks.
limitations_unstated: The optimized designs often use reward probabilities at the boundaries, such as zero or one, so their practical value may depend on whether such settings are feasible and acceptable in a real behavioral study. The evaluation covers three simulated models and one baseline-design approach, and does not establish how well the designs work when the assumed models are misspecified or participant behavior differs from the simulators.
future_work_stated: The authors propose adapting the approach to sequential BOED with intractable models. They also propose applying it to experiments with real participants.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test designs that remain informative when reward probabilities are constrained away from zero and one, or when there are limits on how reward schedules can vary across blocks. It could also evaluate robustness to model misspecification and differences between participants and validate the resulting designs in real experiments.

summary: This paper develops sequential optimal experimental design (sOED) for choosing a fixed number of experiments to learn unknown model parameters. Its objective is to maximize expected information gain, measured by the Kullback–Leibler divergence between prior and posterior distributions, while allowing each design to respond to earlier observations and to account for later experiments. The authors formulate the problem as a finite-horizon decision process and use policy gradient (PG) learning, with deep neural networks (DNNs) representing the policy and its value function. They demonstrate the method on a linear-Gaussian benchmark and simulated contaminant-source inversion in a convection-diffusion field. The reported results show agreement with the benchmark’s analytic solution, lower computation time than an approximate dynamic-programming baseline, and higher mean rewards than batch and greedy designs in the contaminant cases.
key_results: On the linear-Gaussian benchmark, both the policy-gradient method and the approximate dynamic-programming baseline achieved a mean reward of 0.775 plus or minus 0.006, compared with an analytic optimum of approximately 0.783. For the reported timing comparison, policy-gradient training took 24 seconds and used 3.1 × 10^6 forward-model evaluations, while the baseline took 837 seconds and used 5.3 × 10^8 evaluations; testing took 4 seconds versus 24,396 seconds, respectively. In contaminant case 1, the mean reward was 0.615 plus or minus 0.007 for the proposed method and 0.552 plus or minus 0.005 for greedy design. In case 2, the means were 1.344 plus or minus 0.008 for the proposed method, 1.264 plus or minus 0.007 for batch design, and 1.178 plus or minus 0.010 for greedy design; in case 3, they were 3.435 plus or minus 0.016, 2.856 plus or minus 0.012, and 3.057 plus or minus 0.015, respectively. The contaminant comparisons evaluated 10,000 simulated episodes per design policy.
key_equations:
Bayesian update: \[p(\theta\mid I_{k+1})=\frac{p(y_k\mid\theta,d_k,I_k)p(\theta\mid I_k)}{\int p(y_k\mid\theta,d_k,I_k)p(\theta\mid I_k)\,d\theta}\] The posterior density p of parameter θ after stage k is proportional to the likelihood of observation y_k under design d_k and the previous record I_k, multiplied by the previous parameter density.

Expected total information utility: \[U(\pi)=E\left[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g_k(x_k,d_k,y_k)+D_{KL}\!\left(p(\theta\mid I_N)\Vert p(\theta\mid I_0)\right)\right]\] U is expected total utility under policy π over N experiments, g_k is the stage reward, x_k is the state, d_k is the design, y_k is the observation, and the terminal reward is the divergence between the final and initial parameter distributions.

Policy-gradient update direction: \[\nabla_w U(w)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}E_{x_k}\left[\nabla_w\mu_k(x_k)\left.\nabla_{d_k}Q_k(x_k,d_k)\right|_{d_k=\mu_k(x_k)}\right]\] The gradient of expected utility with respect to policy parameters w sums, over stages, the expected product of the policy's parameter gradient and the action gradient of the value function Q_k, evaluated at the design selected by policy rule μ_k.
limitations_stated: The authors identify high-dimensional inference as the main limitation: estimating the terminal information reward still requires Bayesian inference, and their grid method grows exponentially with the number of parameters. They state that alternative inference methods will be needed to improve scalability.
limitations_unstated: The evidence is from simulated examples rather than validation in a real environmental monitoring campaign, so performance under operational measurement conditions is not established. The contaminant demonstration relies on surrogate models trained from samples of the assumed prior; the paper reports low test error within the modeled setting but does not show how design quality changes if the forward model or prior differs in practice.

summary: The paper introduces GeneDisco, an open benchmark for testing batch active learning methods that select genetic interventions for drug-discovery experiments. Its intended model predicts an experimental outcome for an intervention, and the main benchmark objective is to improve prediction accuracy while also measuring how efficiently methods find interventions with large effects. The benchmark combines three sources of intervention descriptors with four published genetic-screen datasets, and compares nine acquisition methods using Bayesian neural networks and random forests. The experiments show that acquisition methods based on diversity often improve prediction relatively well, especially with smaller batches, while those methods tend to find fewer of the selected high-effect interventions. The authors conclude that there is a trade-off between improving a predictor and finding promising experimental hits.
key_results: The benchmark evaluates 9 acquisition methods across 4 experimental assays, 3 intervention-descriptor sets, 2 model types, and 6 batch sizes, using more than 20,000 central processing unit hours and 5 random seeds per experiment. The tested batch sizes range from 16 to 512, and the plots extend to cumulative selections of 5,120 interventions. For prediction accuracy, random selection and data-space k-means selection perform relatively well, particularly at smaller batch sizes; uncertainty-based methods do not consistently outperform them. For hit discovery, random and k-means data selection generally find fewer of the interesting interventions, defined as the top 5 percent by absolute measured effect, indicating a trade-off rather than one method winning on both outcomes.

limitations_stated: The authors caution that rankings may not transfer to settings with different datasets, models, hyperparameters, or experimental conditions. They also note that active learning assumes enough representative labeled data for model training and validation, which can be difficult early in a study or with noisy measurements; the benchmark does not address the trade-off between replicates and collecting more interventions.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation retrospectively replays published experimental datasets rather than testing a design policy in a new laboratory campaign, so its results do not establish prospective experimental savings or biological discoveries. future_work_stated: The authors propose expanding GeneDisco to support multimodal learning and simultaneous optimization across multiple output phenotypes.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test the methods prospectively, include multiple cell systems and donors, and incorporate experimental constraints such as replicate budgets and assay capacity. summary: The paper introduces GaussED, a probabilistic programming language and design engine for sequential experimental design with Gaussian process models. It selects experiments to improve an approximation of a specified quantity of interest, such as a function, an integral-based reconstruction, or an optimum. The method uses a decision-theoretic criterion based on expected loss, so users specify the quantity of interest and loss rather than an acquisition function. A finite spectral approximation of the Gaussian process, reparameterized sampling, and stochastic optimization are used to construct designs, with model hyperparameters estimated during the sequence. Demonstrations cover a partial differential equation, tomographic reconstruction, and optimization using gradient data; the reported results are promising but illustrate a methodology rather than broad real-world validation.
key_results: For the partial differential equation example, GaussED selected 150 experiments in 9 central processing unit hours, and the measured fill distance followed the reported optimal space-filling rate proportional to the inverse square root of the experiment count. In tomography, the nonlinear-quantity design improved the displayed reconstruction over a random design at 270 observations; the experiment required 2.5 central processing unit hours, although no numerical reconstruction score was reported. In the Lotka–Volterra optimization example, gradient-based Bayesian optimization outperformed gradient ascent and limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno after a small number of likelihood evaluations; the methods were run for 30 iterations, and the GaussED example required 1.5 central processing unit hours. The examples used 8, 32, and 17 lines of code, respectively, as reported by the authors.

limitations_stated: The authors state that GaussED is restricted to Gaussian process models and continuous linear functional data, limiting the flexibility of the statistical models it can use. limitations_unstated: The evaluations are illustrative computational examples rather than validation on real quality-engineering experiments, and most comparisons do not report a numerical accuracy measure. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess the method on real experiments with practical constraints such as cost, safety, and restricted or batchable experiment choices. summary: The paper develops a method for Bayesian inverse problems that use Gaussian process (GP) priors and large grids, where observations are linear functionals such as integral measurements. key_results: For a discretization of roughly 2 × 10^5 cells, the paper reports that an explicit posterior covariance matrix would require about 160 GB of storage. In tests using five simulated ground truths, the wIVR strategy detected 70–80% of the large excursion sets by volume after 450 observations; reported average false-positive percentages were 5–15%. summary: This paper proposes local Latin hypercube refinement (LoLHR), a sequential sampling method for multi-objective reliability-based robust design optimization (MORRDO). key_results: In the first analytical example, using 64 model evaluations, LoLHR achieved average hypervolume indicator (HVI) values of 2.831 with GP and 2.863 with SVR, compared with 2.532 and 2.628 for their stationary-sampling counterparts. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test LoLHR on physical experiments and manufacturing problems with measured uncertainty distributions, practical parameter constraints, and multiple failure targets. summary: The paper develops Bayesian I-optimal designs for discrete choice experiments in which each alternative is a mixture of ingredients. It uses a multinomial logit choice model with first-order, second-order, or special-cubic Scheffe models to represent how ingredient proportions affect utility. The design criterion minimizes the prior-averaged prediction variance of utility over the mixture region, and the designs are constructed with a mixture coordinate-exchange algorithm. In two computational examples, the resulting designs have substantially lower predicted-utility variance than Bayesian D-optimal designs. The paper also provides an R package for generating these designs.
key_results: For the cocktail example, the authors compare designs with 16 pairwise choice sets under a special-cubic Scheffe model. The median prediction variance was about 1.55 for the Bayesian I-optimal design, compared with about 3 for their Bayesian D-optimal design and 3.2 for the earlier benchmark design. In the artificial-sweetener example, which used 7 pairwise choice sets, the I-optimal design had lower prediction variance than both D-optimal comparisons at each of the four prior-uncertainty settings tested; the advantage increased as prior uncertainty increased. They used 128 Halton draws to approximate Bayesian criteria and recommend 80 random starts for the examples, while noting that more complex problems call for more draws and starts.

limitations_stated: The authors assume that the model form is known when the experiment is planned, so model misspecification can bias predictions. They also note that the multinomial logit model assumes homogeneous respondent preferences, which may be unrealistic.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison covers two three-ingredient examples and a limited set of prior specifications, so it does not establish the same performance advantage for higher-dimensional mixtures or other preference settings. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to other mixture models, adding process variables, and modeling heterogeneous preferences. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a prospective consumer experiment that compares the predicted utility precision and the selected preferred mixture against observed responses. The method could also be studied for sequential experimentation, where early choice data update the prior and guide later choice sets.

summary: This paper designs a non-reactive exploration policy for stochastic linear contextual bandits, where actions receive rewards that depend on known features and an unknown parameter. The objective is to collect data that supports a near-optimal decision policy on average over future contexts. The method first uses historical contexts to plan a sequence of reward-free uncertainty-reducing policies, then samples among those policies to collect online rewards. It estimates the reward parameter from the collected data and uses a greedy policy based on that estimate. The analysis gives sample-complexity guarantees, and experiments on a simulation and Yahoo! summary: This paper is a tutorial on using micro-randomized trials (MRTs) to develop just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs), especially digital health interventions that make repeated treatment decisions. It explains how to choose intervention components, decision points, feasible options, randomization probabilities, and proximal outcomes, with attention to participant burden and the way trial restrictions shape the resulting intervention. The authors define causal excursion effects and review weighted and centered least squares (WCLS) as a method for estimating them. Three case studies—HeartSteps, SARA, and BariFit—illustrate the design choices, and the HeartSteps data demonstrate overall and context-dependent activity-suggestion effects. The paper’s main methodological conclusion is that MRTs can support intervention optimization, but their findings concern effects under the trial’s prior treatment schedule and do not by themselves establish improvements in long-term outcomes.
key_results: The tutorial covers three trials: HeartSteps, a 42-day study with 37 participants and five daily activity-suggestion decision points; SARA, a 30-day study of engagement and reporting; and BariFit, a 120-day hybrid trial with both baseline and repeated randomization. In HeartSteps, the estimated average effect of an activity suggestion on the log-transformed following 30-minute step count was 0.131, corresponding to an estimated 14% increase; the reported p-value was 0.060 and the 95% confidence interval ranged from -0.006 to 0.268. The estimated effect decreased by 0.018 per study day, with a reported p-value of 0.005; the walking-suggestion effect also differed by location, with a reported interaction estimate of 0.377 and p-value of 0.049, while the corresponding anti-sedentary interaction was not statistically significant. The paper reviews the WCLS estimator, explains how to obtain it using standard statistical software, and illustrates its use with HeartSteps data; it also includes theoretical discussion, a simulation study, and code examples.

limitations_stated: The authors state that improving individual components does not necessarily optimize the intervention as a whole, because component costs and effects may not be additive. limitations_unstated: The numerical illustration of the primary effects relies on the HeartSteps sample of 37 participants, so the paper provides limited direct evidence about how reliably those estimates generalize to other populations and settings. The contextual findings are exploratory and include several moderation questions, while the proposed linear effect models may not capture more complex patterns in when effects change.
future_work_stated: The authors call for research on using MRT results to optimize the intervention as a whole, rather than only its separate components. They also propose continual optimization during deployment, extending MRTs to pull components, and developing personalized decision rules that differ between individuals.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test MRT findings in larger and more varied real-world populations, and check whether effects on the measured proximal outcomes lead to lasting improvements in distal health outcomes. Methods and practical guidance could also be developed for nonlinear effect patterns, competing participant-burden constraints, and sequentially updating decision rules while preserving credible evaluation.

summary: The paper develops a framework for Bayesian experimental design (BED) with implicit models, where data can be simulated but its likelihood is unavailable. It optimizes a neural-network-parameterized lower bound on mutual information (MI) with respect to both the network and the experimental design, using stochastic gradient ascent. The framework covers parameter estimation, model discrimination, joint estimation and discrimination, and improvement of future predictions. The authors test three lower bounds on simulated toy models and apply the Jensen-Shannon divergence approach to simulated epidemiological models. The results show that the method finds useful designs and that the Jensen-Shannon divergence approach generally gives estimates closer to reference values and posterior distributions in the toy experiments.
key_results: On the toy models, the Jensen-Shannon divergence approach, evaluated through the Nguyen-Wainwright-Jordan bound, estimated MI as 3.48 ± 0.05 for parameter estimation, 0.730 ± 0.007 for model discrimination, 3.95 ± 0.08 for joint estimation and discrimination, and 1.34 ± 0.01 for future prediction; the corresponding reference estimates were 3.55 ± 0.04, 0.737 ± 0.007, 3.97 ± 0.02, and 1.34 ± 0.02. Its average posterior divergences from reference distributions were 0.028, 0.009, 0.026, and 0.005 across those tasks, respectively, compared with 0.079, 0.016, 0.728, and 0.009 for the Nguyen-Wainwright-Jordan bound and 0.107, 0.018, 0.053, and 0.012 for the information noise-contrastive estimation bound. In the susceptible-infectious-recovered epidemic model, the authors report that the information gain begins to saturate at 10 measurements; at that budget, the average maximum a posteriori estimates were 0.59 ± 0.15 for the infection rate and 0.07 ± 0.01 for the recovery rate, against ground-truth values of 0.60 and 0.15. key_equations: Joint design and lower-bound optimization: \[d^*=\arg\max_d\max_{\psi}L(\psi,d)\] Here d is an experimental design, d* is the selected optimal design, ψ denotes neural-network parameters, and L is the parameterized mutual-information lower bound being maximized.
limitations_stated: The method requires gradients of the simulator's sampling path with respect to the design, either available directly or computable through automatic differentiation. limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation relies on simulated toy models and one simulated epidemiology application, so it does not establish performance or practical savings in real experiments. future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating scalable ways to handle cases without sampling-path gradients, including gradient approximations, and extending the framework to sequential design. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method in real experiments and quantify the costs of simulation, optimization, and measurement against established design strategies. summary: This paper develops exact and heuristic methods for finding orthogonal arrays (OAs) that are good under generalized minimum aberration (GMA), a criterion intended to reduce aliasing and support information extraction when the model is uncertain. The methods focus mainly on two-level OAs and extend earlier enumeration algorithms that use integer linear programming (ILP) with pruning of equivalent designs. The exact methods direct the enumeration toward designs with low aliasing, while heuristic searches seek GMA or near-GMA designs when exhaustive computation is too costly. The authors also compile a catalog of GMA design results and test their heuristics against it. They report 16 previously unreported GMA arrays and show that the heuristics recover most of the cataloged results while finding additional good designs in computationally difficult cases.
key_results: The directed enumeration methods established GMA designs for the first time for 28-run two-level arrays with 8–15 factors and 36-run two-level arrays with 3–10 factors; the paper reports 16 new GMA arrays overall. The authors report that their combined heuristic searches matched 92 of the 99 cataloged GMA distance distributions. For an example extension from a 24-run, 5-factor array to a 24-run, 6-factor array, enumeration took 1.52 minutes with isomorphism pruning and 4.45 minutes without it. The exact calculations could still be very demanding: enumerating 36-run, 8-factor arrays took about 1,797 hours and 41 minutes.

future_work_unstated: Future studies could extend the directed criteria to mixed-level designs, practical run restrictions, and objectives beyond the generalized word-length pattern. summary: This paper develops a method for finding the symmetry group of a feasible linear program (LP), including cases where equality constraints hide symmetries from methods based only on the written constraints. The method first puts the LP into a form without redundant constraints, then uses an orthogonal projection matrix and graph-based group computations to identify symmetries. The authors apply the method to integer linear programs (ILPs) that enumerate orthogonal arrays (OAs), and use the larger symmetry groups in branch and bound (B&B) with isomorphism pruning. For binary OAs of even strength, the additional symmetries include operations that relate arrays under orthogonal-projection equivalence (OD-equivalence), allowing direct enumeration of these equivalence classes. The method reduces reported enumeration times for two demanding OA classifications, while also showing that the added variables and group computations can increase costs in some cases.
key_results: For OA(160, 8, 2, 4) and OA(176, 8, 2, 4), the authors report that their method reduced enumeration time relative to the fastest previously known method by factors of 2.16 and 1.36, respectively. Their method enumerated 11,712 non-isomorphic solutions for OA(160, 8, 2, 4) in 32,880 seconds, compared with 99,618 solutions in 123,180 seconds using the smaller formulation symmetry group; for OA(176, 8, 2, 4), it enumerated 129,138 solutions in 1,067,822 seconds. Across many tested cases, using the LP-relaxation symmetry group reduced the number of solutions explored, sometimes substantially, but could be slower for individual cases because computing the group and handling the formulation cost time. The authors also report that adding slack variables and exploiting the resulting LP-relaxation symmetries can reduce enumeration times by several orders of magnitude in some settings.

summary: The paper develops treatment variant aggregation (TVA) to choose an effective policy from a large factorial experiment with multiple interventions and dosage levels. The method is designed for policy selection and treatment-effect estimation when many combinations are possible and sequential experimentation may not be practical. It represents effects as increments across treatment dosages, selects nonzero increments using a Puffer-transformed least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), then pools equivalent variants and removes ineffective policies. It estimates the remaining policy effects with ordinary least squares (OLS) and adjusts the selected best policy estimate for winner’s curse. In an experiment on immunization in Haryana, India, the authors find that combinations involving information hubs and other interventions outperform the status quo, with distinct best policies for immunizations and immunizations per dollar spent.

After adjustment for winner’s curse, the best policy for increasing immunizations—information hubs, sloped incentives, and reminders—increased monthly measles vaccinations by 3.26 per village relative to a control mean of 7.32, a reported 44% increase; its 95% hybrid confidence interval was [0.32, 6.25]. For cost effectiveness, information hubs with reminders and no incentives increased immunizations per dollar by a reported 9.1%; the adjusted effect was 0.004 against a control mean of 0.0435. In simulations, TVA achieved over 90% minimum-dosage best-policy inclusion at a sample size of 3,000 in two of the studied sparsity-relaxation regimes, whereas direct OLS selected the minimum-dosage best policy at about 36.67% in the reported comparison.

summary: This paper studies sequential designs that approximate a target probability measure by minimising the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) for a specified kernel. It compares kernel herding (KH), greedy MMD minimisation (GM), and Sequential Bayesian Quadrature (SBQ), including versions with different constraints on the weights. The methods select points from a finite candidate set and construct a discrete measure, either with uniform or optimised weights. The author derives finite-sample error bounds and computational costs, then illustrates performance for a uniform measure used in space-filling design and for a Gaussian mixture. The analysis gives inverse-run-size bounds for squared discrepancy in several methods, while the examples show that some bounds are pessimistic and that simpler methods can be preferable for larger designs.
key_results: The theoretical bounds show squared MMD decreasing at an inverse rate in the number of selected points for SBQ and for KH and GM with suitable step sizes; standard KH and GM with uniform weights have a logarithmic factor in their general bounds. For a fixed candidate set, KH and GM require work that grows linearly with the number of selected points, whereas SBQ and integrated weight optimisation have costs that grow quadratically. In the two-dimensional space-filling example, the candidate set had 131,072 points and the study compared designs through 1,000 selected points; uniform-weight KH performed better in practice than the alternatives with predefined nonuniform or optimised step sizes, despite some alternatives having tighter bounds. In the Gaussian-mixture example, the candidate set had 16,384 points and designs were evaluated up to 200 points; the authors report broadly similar discrepancy performance for standard KH and GM, with optimised-weight methods sometimes improving discrepancy at greater computational cost. For a 25-point space-filling design, the reported covering radii were about 0.1625 for GM, 0.1685 for standard KH, and 0.2024 for the unconstrained integrated-weight variant, illustrating that lower weighted discrepancy does not necessarily mean better unweighted coverage.
key_equations:
Squared discrepancy: \[\mathrm{MMD}_K^2(\mu,\xi)=\iint K(x,x')\,d(\xi-\mu)(x)\,d(\xi-\mu)(x')\] The squared MMD between target measure μ and discrete measure ξ is the kernel energy of their difference, with K the kernel and x and x′ points in the input space.

Design criterion: \[\min_{\xi\ \mathrm{a\ probability\ measure}}\mathrm{MMD}_K^2(\mu,\xi)\] The design seeks a probability measure ξ that minimises squared MMD from target measure μ using kernel K, with ξ supported on eligible candidate points.

Sequential measure update: \[\xi_{\mathrm{new}}=(1-\alpha)\xi_{\mathrm{current}}+\alpha\delta_x\] The updated measure ξ_new combines the current measure ξ_current with a point mass δ_x at selected point x, using step size α.
limitations_stated: The paper restricts its main analysis to finite candidate sets and to constructions that add one point at a time. It notes that extensions to continuous search and to selecting multiple points per iteration merit further study, and that avoiding the combinatorial growth of multi-point selection is a challenge.
limitations_unstated: The numerical illustrations are limited to two-dimensional examples and a small number of target distributions, so they do not establish how the comparisons transfer to higher-dimensional or more varied engineering problems. The finite candidate set can exclude useful design points, while the discrepancy objective depends on the chosen kernel and weights and may not align with unweighted coverage or other practical design constraints.
future_work_stated: The author proposes extending the results to methods that select several points at each iteration and developing computationally efficient approaches that avoid the combinatorial explosion of considering all possible subsets. Extension of the analysis to continuous candidate spaces is also identified as possible.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate these methods on higher-dimensional computer experiments with practical constraints such as prohibited regions, costs, or required design locations. It could also test sensitivity to kernel choice and tuning, and assess whether discrepancy improvements lead to better prediction or integration performance in real experiments.

summary: The paper presents a method for selecting binary sensor placements for Bayesian inverse problems governed by mathematical models, with the goal of reducing uncertainty in estimated parameters. It focuses its numerical examples on A-optimal design, which minimizes the trace of the posterior covariance, while also allowing penalties for sparse designs or sensor budgets. The method assigns each candidate sensor an activation probability and minimizes the expected objective over the resulting independent Bernoulli design distribution. A policy-gradient algorithm estimates the objective gradient by sampling designs, avoiding design-variable derivatives and a continuous relaxation followed by rounding. In simulated examples, a baseline to reduce gradient-estimator variability improved the method's ability to find globally optimal or near-optimal designs.
key_results: The advection-diffusion example used 14 candidate sensor locations, giving 16,384 possible binary designs for comparison by exhaustive search. Without a sparsity penalty, the global minimum selected all sensors, and the authors noted that adding sensors beyond 8 provided little additional information. With the optimal baseline, the sampled designs in that unpenalized experiment had objective values within 1% of the global optimum; with an L0 sparsity penalty of 1.0, the method found the global optimum with 3 active sensors. For the tested learning rates, 0.5 performed best in the budget-constrained experiment, although larger rates risked divergence; computationally, the method avoids evaluating the objective gradient separately for every candidate sensor, but the paper gives no measured runtime speedup.
key_equations:
Expected stochastic design objective: \[\theta_{\mathrm{opt}}=\arg\min_{\theta\in[0,1]^{n_s}}\Upsilon(\theta),\qquad \Upsilon(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim P(\zeta\mid\theta)}[J(\zeta)]\] Theta is the vector of sensor-activation probabilities, theta_opt is its minimizing value, n_s is the number of candidate sensors, Υ is the expected objective, E denotes expectation, ζ is a sampled binary design, P is its probability distribution given theta, and J is the objective including any penalty.

Independent Bernoulli design distribution: \[P(\zeta\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n_s}\theta_i^{\zeta_i}(1-\theta_i)^{1-\zeta_i}\] P is the probability of binary design ζ given probabilities theta, n_s is the number of candidate sensors, and i indexes a sensor whose activation decision is ζ_i and whose activation probability is theta_i.
limitations_stated: The authors identify selection of the learning rate as an open issue: decreasing rates can ensure convergence but may require many iterations. They also note that the gradient estimator can have high variance without a baseline, and that their numerical experiments use linear forward models even though the approach is intended to extend beyond them.
limitations_unstated: The independent Bernoulli policy cannot directly express dependencies among sensor choices, and the budget is enforced through a penalty rather than guaranteed for every sampled design. The principal design comparison uses only 14 candidate locations in simulated data, so performance at larger scales and in real deployments is not established by these experiments.
future_work_stated: The authors propose further work on learning-rate selection and on comparing the policy-gradient approach with other sample-based methods, including sample average approximation. They also indicate that analysis in nonlinear settings will follow in separate work.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could incorporate correlated or constrained sensor-selection policies that satisfy exact deployment requirements by construction, and evaluate scaling on substantially larger candidate sets. Testing the selected designs with real environmental measurements and assessing sensitivity to model and noise misspecification would also strengthen evidence for practical use.

summary: This paper studies randomized experimental designs for estimating parameters and controlling prediction error in linear regression. It considers E-optimality, which controls the largest covariance eigenvalue, and G-optimality, which controls the worst predicted variance. The authors first solve a convex relaxation to obtain probabilities over the available experiments, then analyze sampling experiments independently from that distribution. They derive finite-sample bounds and introduce refined measures of matrix dimension to sharpen a concentration bound for G-optimality. Their simulations show that randomized designs can compare favorably with greedy designs, including in a best-arm identification example for linear bandits.
key_results: The theoretical bounds establish an inverse-square-root convergence rate for randomized E- and G-optimal designs; the G-optimal bound holds with probability at least one minus twice the failure-probability parameter. In a synthetic E-optimal study with 500 candidate experiments and 10 parameters, the randomized method outperformed the greedy method as the number of selected experiments increased; with 500 experiments selected, its advantage diminished as the dimension increased. These synthetic comparisons were averaged over 100 random seeds. In the bandit study, the randomized G-optimal method performed similarly to the greedy method at low dimensions and better on average as dimension increased, and both methods returned the correct best arm in every repetition.

Information matrix for a relaxed design: \[M(\mu)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_k x_kx_k^\top,\qquad \mu\in\Delta_K\] Here, the information matrix is the sum over the available experiments; each experiment vector is weighted by its probability, and the probabilities belong to the simplex of distributions over the K experiments.

Randomized sampling construction: \[\Pr(X_i=x_k)=\mu_k^*,\qquad S_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\] Here, each sampled experiment is drawn with the probability assigned to it by the optimal relaxed design, and the sampled information matrices are summed over the n draws.
limitations_stated: The authors do not explicitly state limitations. They note that the convergence rate depends on a characteristic of the sampling covariance matrix and that the theoretical results are for randomized E- and G-optimal designs.
limitations_unstated: The analysis relies on a linear model and independent sampling from an optimal relaxed distribution; performance under model misspecification, dependent sampling, or reward-adaptive choices is not established. The empirical comparisons cover a synthetic Gaussian experiment pool and one specially constructed bandit example, rather than real industrial experiments or a broad range of design constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating batch or parallel bandits, using random sampling to select a batch of arms before observing their rewards.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method with practical restrictions such as costs, limited availability, or required balance among experiment types, and to validate it in real quality-engineering studies. Further work could also establish guarantees for sequential or adaptive use and compare the method across additional models and design criteria.

summary: The paper forecasts how accurately cluster weak lensing combined with cluster counts can estimate the amplitude of matter clustering, sigma 8, under a model with other cosmological parameters held fixed. Its proposed analysis uses the mean number of clusters and their mean lensing profile above one observed-mass-proxy threshold in each redshift bin. It treats the proxy-to-true-mass scatter as a key nuisance parameter and combines count and lensing information with a prior on that scatter using Fisher calculations. The authors assess forecast performance for survey assumptions resembling the Dark Energy Survey, Roman’s High Latitude Survey, and Rubin’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time, using theoretical calculations and simulation-based covariance estimates. They find that very precise constraints are possible, but only if mass-proxy scatter and observational systematics are controlled well.
key_results: With uncertainty in the mass-proxy scatter of 0.01, the forecast aggregate precision on sigma 8 is 0.26% for the Dark Energy Survey-like case, 0.24% for the Roman High Latitude Survey-like case, and 0.10% for the Rubin survey-like case. Scatter uncertainty of 0.05 degrades the aggregate precision by about 20% for the first two cases; for the Rubin-like case, scatter uncertainty must be 0.016 to produce a similar degradation. At redshift 0.7, a one-month targeted Roman observing program of about 2,600 clusters is forecast to constrain sigma 8 to about 0.5% on its own, or 0.33% when combined with the Roman survey. The wider survey generally outperforms a deeper, smaller-area survey when the cluster threshold is the same and scatter is well constrained; the authors also find little or no precision gain from dividing the sample into two mass bins under their general mass-proxy model.

Marginalized parameter uncertainty: \[\sigma(p_i)=\sqrt{(F^{-1})_{ii}}\] The uncertainty in parameter p_i is the square root of the corresponding diagonal element of the inverse Fisher information matrix.
limitations_stated: The authors emphasize that these are statistical forecasts and that achieving them requires accurate external knowledge of mass-proxy scatter and stringent control of systematics, including selection bias, miscentering, shear calibration, and baryonic effects. Their forecasts hold other cosmological parameters fixed and assume independent parameter estimates across redshift bins when forming aggregate constraints.
limitations_unstated: The forecasts do not demonstrate that the required scatter calibration or systematic-error control can be achieved with real survey data. They also do not optimize practical observing allocations under operational constraints; the survey comparisons rely on illustrative assumptions about source populations, cluster thresholds, and survey areas.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring combinations of cluster weak lensing with galaxy-galaxy lensing and cosmic shear across multiple redshift bins and clustering regimes. They also say they will investigate whether combinations of cluster-galaxy and galaxy-galaxy correlations can help calibrate scatter and selection-related projection effects.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the forecasts with real cluster samples and report how departures from the assumed mass-proxy scatter model change the estimates. Further work could also optimize the number of clusters observed at each redshift and mass threshold, while including feasible observing and calibration constraints.

summary: This software paper documents gonogo, an R implementation for conducting, analyzing, and simulating sequential sensitivity tests with binary responses and one stress factor. The software also provides confidence calculations, plots, batch and console workflows, and simulation tools, with options for normal or lognormal analysis. The paper documents the package through worked examples and reproductions; it does not establish that one procedure is more efficient than the others.
key_results: The documented program contains 118 functions and two constants and supports simulated, batch, and interactive testing. In a reproduced 30-run 3pod example, the estimated mean was 10.1707909, the estimated standard deviation was 0.9344091, and the estimated stress for a response probability of 0.9 was 11.36828. A described simulation example used 2,000 tests and had 1,894 qualifying outcomes, or 0.947; its selected computation took 260.62 seconds. summary: The paper develops a way to design physical experiments for calibrating a computer model when the model may not fully represent the physical system. With no added discrepancy, the pure computer-model design had the lowest prediction error, while the proposed design was comparable to the fractional factorial design with two replicates. With added discrepancy of variance 6, the proposed design had the lowest prediction error among the three designs; the figure reports values of 2.14 for the proposed design, 4.08 for the pure computer-model design, and 2.77 for the fractional factorial design.

future_work_unstated: Further work could establish principled ways to choose the replication count and balance calibration against discrepancy estimation for different experiment budgets and setup costs. With correlation length scale 3 and regularization parameter 0.001, the reported root-mean-squared error for the standard formulation with 8 sensors was 0.04279, compared with 0.01279 for the proposed sigmoid-weighted formulation with 8 sensors; using all sensors gave 0.0239. The study also compared product, exponential, and sigmoid weighting kernels, and reports that results varied with kernel and regularization settings. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method using measured environmental-monitoring data and covariance models estimated from repeated measurements, including tests of robustness to covariance misspecification. summary: The paper develops optimal experimental design for large Bayesian linear inverse problems governed by partial differential equations when both the parameter of interest and additional model parameters are uncertain. They apply the method to simulated contaminant transport, designing sensor placements to estimate a time-varying source while accounting for uncertainty in the initial condition. In this example, designs that account for the initial-condition uncertainty reduce posterior uncertainty more effectively and produce better estimates than designs that ignore it.
key_results: For the simulated transport problem, the discretization used 257 time steps for the source and 1,529 spatial degrees of freedom for the uncertain initial condition. The authors report that preprocessing the design matrices requires 3 times the number of candidate sensors in forward PDE solves and 2 times that number in adjoint PDE solves; after preprocessing, objective and gradient evaluations require no further PDE solves and their arithmetic cost grows cubically with the number of candidate sensors. For a 20-sensor design, the marginalized design gave lower marginal posterior standard deviation over the full time interval than the design that ignored initial-condition uncertainty. Greedy placement and regularized sparsification produced similar design objective values; sparsification required nearly constant numbers of objective evaluations as the design size increased, while greedy evaluation counts increased with sensor count. Across 200 draws of the secondary parameter and 500 noise samples, marginalized designs gave substantially better estimates than designs that used random secondary-parameter draws, although using the true secondary parameter gave slightly better estimates than marginalization.

The objective is to find and spread input combinations whose outputs are close to specified targets, measured by a weighted squared-error loss. The framework begins with a space-filling design, fits a feasibility classifier, and then uses minimum energy design (MED) to sample promising regions; surrogate models can reduce the need for costly simulator evaluations. Proposed points are screened for feasibility, checked with the actual simulator, and used to update the models. In simulations and two reactive force field (ReaxFF) applications, the method found improved parameter combinations and, unlike a global-optimum-focused comparator, also sought multiple well-performing points.

Across 100 simulation repetitions, the proposed design found a lower minimum loss than a uniform design in 71 cases, a lower median loss in every case, and usually a smaller loss variance. In the molybdenum-sulfur application, 5,000 initial combinations included 3,846 infeasible runs, and the best validated point improved the loss by 17% over the best of the 1,154 feasible initial points. In the nickel-chromium application, the best loss was 2,316.17, an 18% improvement over the initial-design best of 2,812; the conventional method did not find a loss below 5,614.26, and the authors report about two minutes for their approach versus two weeks for the conventional method.

limitations_stated: The authors note that the number of simulator evaluations can become prohibitive as input dimension increases, motivating surrogate models. limitations_unstated: The application evidence is limited to two ReaxFF systems and one family of simulation test functions, so performance in other physical systems or with different target and weight choices is not established. future_work_stated: The authors identify finding Pareto-optimal solutions under unknown constraints and high input and output dimensions as an interesting direction for future research. They also note that the framework could be extended to handle noisy responses.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the framework on additional engineering systems and compare it systematically with more constrained global-search and multiresponse design methods. It could also develop sequential run selection that explicitly balances predicted feasibility, surrogate uncertainty, and the value of sampling across distinct good regions.

summary: The paper develops batch greedy methods for choosing a limited subset of observations to maximize information about unknown parameters. Its main design application is a linear Bayesian inverse problem with Gaussian parameters and observation noise, where the objective is mutual information, equivalent in this setting to determinant-based optimality. The methods select several observations at once, using individual marginal gains or modular bounds that can be optimized more cheaply than evaluating every possible batch. The authors also analyze distributed and randomized versions and derive performance guarantees using measures of submodularity and supermodularity. In experiments, the methods performed well on simulated inverse problems and a climate-model sensor-placement example; modular-bound methods were often competitive with or better than standard batch greedy at larger batch sizes in the simulations.
key_results: For a uniform batch size, the standard batch-greedy method has a theoretical approximation factor of at least one minus the exponential of the negative product of the submodularity and supermodularity ratios. The batch method reduces the number of objective evaluations by a factor equal to the batch size compared with ordinary greedy selection. In synthetic tests, the authors evaluated 1,000 random forward models with 20 parameters and 100 candidate observations; for correlated observation errors, modular-bound methods generally did better than standard greedy at larger batch sizes, while single-index standard greedy was marginally better. In the climate application, there were 1,642 candidate locations, and the parameter dimension was reduced from 47 model inputs to 10; the compared methods had similar information-capture performance, and reducing batch size did not yield significant gains. In the synthetic comparison with random selections, even one-shot greedy selections had a higher median performance than random selection, and the median results for the two modular-bound methods exceeded the 90th percentile of random selection.
key_equations:
Linear Gaussian observation model: \[Y=GX+\varepsilon\] Y is the observation vector, G is the linear forward matrix, X is the unknown parameter vector, and ε is observation noise; the paper assumes Gaussian parameters and noise that are independent.

Mutual information for selected observations: \[I(X;Y_S)=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\det(\Gamma_{Y_S})}{\det(\Gamma_{Y_S|X})}\] I(X;Y_S) is the information shared by parameters X and observations selected by S, while Γ_Y_S and Γ_Y_S|X are the selected observations' marginal and conditional covariance matrices.

Modular bounds on a set's incremental gain: \[\eta\sum_{\nu\in A}\rho_\nu(B)\leq\rho_A(B)\leq\frac{1}{\gamma}\sum_{\nu\in A}\rho_\nu(B)\] ρ_A(B) is the objective gain from adding set A to B, ρ_ν(B) is the gain from adding individual index ν to B, and η and γ are the supermodularity and submodularity ratios.

Batch greedy approximation guarantee: \[F(A)\geq\left(1-e^{-\eta_{V,q}\gamma_{V,k}}\right)\max_{B\subseteq V,\,|B|\leq k}F(B)\] F is the non-decreasing objective, A is the returned selection, V is the candidate set, k is the selection-size limit, q is the uniform batch size, η_V,q is the supermodularity ratio for that batch size, and γ_V,k is the submodularity ratio for the selection limit.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their batch-greedy guarantee does not incorporate curvature, which could make the bound more informative. They report no theoretical approximation guarantee for the reverse-greedy method for minimizing information loss. They also note that the matrix-log calculations in their modular-bound methods are computationally demanding and that their asymptotic computational complexity does not improve on batch greedy based on incremental gains.
limitations_unstated: The climate sensor study builds a linear Gaussian approximation from an empirical cross-covariance estimate, so its conclusions may not carry over to the original nonlinear climate model or to non-Gaussian parameter uncertainty. The comparisons focus on cardinality limits and a single climate application; they do not establish how the methods perform under deployment constraints such as sensor costs, inaccessible sites, or required geographic coverage.
future_work_stated: The authors propose incorporating curvature into the theoretical guarantees and adapting batch size across selection steps to better use computational resources. They also suggest using the supermodularity ratio to analyze greedy minimization of non-increasing set functions and further investigating the connections between their modular bounds and polyhedral combinatorics.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the methods with practical placement constraints and costs, then validate selected locations using climate-model runs beyond the linearized approximation. Further work could also develop a reusable implementation and investigate sequential redesign in which new measurements update the model and subsequent sensor choices.

summary: This review explains optimal experimental design (OED) for Bayesian inverse problems with function-valued parameters governed mainly by partial differential equations (PDEs). It focuses on choosing measurement locations, especially sensor locations, to reduce uncertainty in estimated parameters. The review develops the mathematical framework for infinite-dimensional Bayesian inference and describes how common design criteria are formulated and discretized. It surveys computational approaches for linear problems, including randomized trace and determinant estimates, low-rank methods, sparsity penalties, and greedy sensor selection. For nonlinear problems, it reviews Bayes-risk objectives and criteria based on a Laplace approximation to the posterior. The paper synthesizes existing methods rather than reporting a new experimental comparison.
key_results: The paper is a review, so it reports methods and results from cited studies rather than a new benchmark or a single best design. For linear inverse problems, it describes A-optimality, c-optimality, and D-optimality, together with randomized methods and low-rank approximations intended to reduce the computational cost of objective and gradient calculations. It notes that discretized parameter dimensions can reach thousands or hundreds of thousands, and that greedy sensor placement requires a number of objective evaluations proportional to the number of sensors to be selected times the number of candidate locations. For nonlinear inverse problems, it describes Bayes-risk minimization and Laplace-based uncertainty criteria, while emphasizing that each approach entails computationally challenging repeated inverse-problem solves. The review cites applications including contaminant identification, subsurface flow, tomography, and electromagnetic imaging, but does not provide a common numerical comparison across methods.
key_equations:

A-optimal design objective: \[\Phi_A(w)=\operatorname{tr}\left(C_{\mathrm{post}}(w)\right)\] Phi_A(w) is the A-optimal objective for design weights w, tr is the trace, and C_post(w) is the posterior covariance for that design.
limitations_stated: The authors describe the review as non-exhaustive and focus primarily on selecting measurement locations, particularly sensor placement. They note that more complicated designs, such as choosing both sensor locations and sensor types, are not treated in detail.
limitations_unstated: The review does not establish how the surveyed methods compare under common models, budgets, or evaluation metrics, so it cannot support a general ranking for practitioners. Many formulations depend on assumptions such as a specified prior and measurement-noise model, and the sensor-selection setup with candidate locations may not directly represent experiments where locations or measurement conditions are constrained differently.
future_work_stated: The authors propose further work on computationally tractable design criteria for nonlinear inverse problems and on including uncertainty in model components that are not being estimated. They also identify goal-oriented design and the design of switching or mobile sensor networks for time-dependent problems as research directions.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a comparative evaluation of the reviewed approaches on shared benchmark problems, including sensitivity to prior and noise misspecification and to practical sensor constraints. Further work could also translate these methods into reproducible software and validate their recommended designs in real measurement campaigns.

summary: This paper develops and evaluates sequential sampling procedures for stochastic optimization, with the goal of finding a high-quality solution and assessing its optimality gap. It combines antithetic variates (AV) and Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) with a stopping rule that compares an estimated gap with its estimated variability. The authors give conditions under which the procedures stop in a finite number of iterations and yield asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Their computational study uses eight two-stage stochastic linear programs and compares the sampling methods with ordinary random sampling. Both AV and LHS often reduce confidence-interval widths; LHS is generally stronger outside the sequential setting, while AV can be especially effective for sequential intervals.
key_results: Across eight test problems, LHS reduced the average, variance, and bias of the optimality-gap estimate more than random sampling in all eight non-sequential comparisons; AV was compared with a two-observation random-sampling baseline. In the non-sequential confidence-interval comparisons, LHS produced a greater average-width reduction in seven of eight problems, while AV did so in one; in the sequential comparisons, each method produced the greater average-width reduction in four of eight problems, and AV produced the greater variance reduction in six. For APL1P, the reported confidence-interval width ratios were 2.31 for LHS versus random sampling and 2.50 for AV versus its baseline with the single-replication procedure. The authors recommend the averaged two-replication procedure because it reduces false identifications of optimal solutions; for PGP2, its reported coverage was 0.84 with random sampling, 0.84 with LHS, and 0.86 with AV, compared with 0.74, 0.76, and 0.76, respectively, for the single-replication procedure.
key_equations:
Stochastic optimization model: \[\min_{x\in X} E[f(x,\xi)]\] The decision x is chosen from feasible set X to minimize the expected value E of objective function f under random input xi.

Sequential stopping rule: \[T=\inf\{k\ge1:\ GAP_{n_k}(x_k)\le h'\sqrt{SV_{n_k}(x_k)}+\epsilon'\}\] The procedure stops at iteration T when the estimated gap for candidate x at sample size n is no greater than threshold h-prime times the square root of estimated sample variance, plus tolerance epsilon-prime.

Sublinear sample-size schedule: \[n_k\ge\frac{c_p+2p\ln^2 k}{(h-h')^2};\quad \text{for AV, }\frac{n_k}{2}\ge\frac{c_p+2p\ln^2 k}{(h-h')^2}\] At iteration k, sample size n must satisfy the schedule using constants c-sub-p and p and thresholds h and h-prime; for AV, the condition applies to half the observations, corresponding to the number of independent antithetic pairs.
limitations_stated: The theoretical results require assumptions that restrict the problem class, including compact feasible sets and independent random-input components with invertible distribution functions. The LHS results also require bounded objective values, and sublinear sample-size growth requires additional conditions such as monotonicity or additivity; without these conditions, the paper uses a superlinear schedule. The confidence-interval validity established is asymptotic.
limitations_unstated: The computational evidence comes from eight two-stage stochastic linear programs, so performance may differ for other optimization models and real engineering experiments. LHS requires a completely new sample at each iteration, which may add practical sampling and computation overhead; the larger sample-size schedule may also make the procedure costly. Coverage for the large problems was assessed using an approximate reference based on 50,000 LHS observations rather than known exact optimality gaps.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying sequential sampling for other problem classes and other variance-reduction methods, particularly for risk-averse optimization. They also suggest research on adaptive LHS partitions and other adaptive stratified sampling methods.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the procedures on real quality-engineering experiments and on models with practical constraints on sampling, such as dependent inputs or limited experimental budgets. It could also investigate sample reuse or sequentially updated LHS designs to reduce the cost of generating a fresh design at every iteration, and provide software and validation guidance for practitioners.

summary: The paper develops a Bayesian method for choosing observation times and animal counts in perturbation experiments on hematopoiesis. Its mechanistic model uses ordinary differential equations to describe hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and multipotent progenitors (MPPs), including feedback and feedforward regulation. A hierarchical model represents the unobserved starting cell counts and links each animal’s single measurement to its modelled trajectory. Designs are compared by their expected information gain about model parameters, with utility based on the change from prior to posterior distributions. Simulations show that the timing and allocation of observations affect parameter estimation, while the small real dataset provides little information about most parameters.
key_results: In simulations, 60 synthetic datasets were evaluated for each design; the 7-day-by-7-mice-per-day design used 49 mice, and reported 95% credible-interval coverage across parameters ranged from 0.86 to 1.00. The authors searched 70 candidate designs, using observation days from day 0 through day 6 and 3 to 7 mice at each observed time; the highest displayed overall utility was 4.8 times the baseline utility. With a fixed total number of mice, designs using more observation times and fewer replicates per time generally had higher utility than designs with fewer observation times. Earlier observations were more informative for the HSC division rate, while later observations, including day 6, better informed the HSC self-renewal feedback gain. In the real experiment, 13 mice were measured on days 0, 2, and 6, with 7, 4, and 2 mice at those times; the Bayes factor comparing models with and without feedback was 1.18, and the data shifted the estimate of initial HSC counts but provided little information about the other parameters.

Expected information gain for a design: \[u(d)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta,y}[U(y,d)]\] u(d) is the expected utility of design d, averaging over model parameters theta and possible data y.

Information-gain utility: \[U(y,d)=\int \log\!\left(\frac{p(\theta\mid y,d)}{p(\theta)}\right)p(\theta\mid y,d)\,d\theta\] U(y,d) is the utility for data y under design d; theta denotes the model parameters; p(theta) is their prior distribution and p(theta given y,d) is their posterior distribution.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their method can require substantial computation because it uses Monte Carlo averaging, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and bridge sampling. They also note that the preliminary real dataset provides little information about most parameters, and that adding cell types or branching would require more data to constrain the model.
limitations_unstated: The design search is performed on a finite grid and its utility depends on the assumed model and prior distributions, so a misspecified feedback structure or prior could favor a design that is not informative in the real system. The comparison of candidate designs is primarily simulation-based; the paper does not experimentally implement a selected optimized design to verify its predicted estimation gains.
future_work_stated: The authors propose faster sampling, more efficient differential-equation solvers, and more efficient design-space exploration. They also suggest stochastic hematopoiesis models, adding more differentiated cell types and perturbations, repeated measurements of covariates and cell counts, and lineage-tracking data from barcoded single cells.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess robustness of the selected observation schedules to alternative biological models and prior choices, especially because the proposed feedback loops are hypotheses. The method could also be extended to incorporate practical constraints such as limits on sacrifice days, assay capacity, and separate control-group allocation, then tested prospectively against a simpler schedule in a real experiment.
