summary: This paper develops first-order optimization methods for optimal experimental design (OED) with a fixed total design weight and pointwise upper bounds on the design density. The objective is to select weighted experiments that optimize a criterion based on the Fisher information matrix, including D-, A-, and E-criteria, with optional quadratic regularization. The authors derive optimality conditions, discretize the design space into cells, and use projection-based algorithms; they also introduce simplicial decomposition and active-set approaches to reduce the size of the computational subproblems. In the numerical examples, the proximal extrapolated gradient method (PGMA) converges much faster than FISTA, and the active-set methods improve on the unaccelerated method in the tested large problems. The authors find that the heuristic active-set variant is fastest in their examples, while noting that this is not guaranteed for every problem.
key_results: For the Lotka–Volterra example with 27,000 cells and the logarithmic D-criterion, PGMA reached the stopping tolerance in about 5.6 seconds and fewer than 300 iterations; FISTA did not approach the tolerance within 5,000 iterations. For the same example, when the regularization parameter was zero, the reported solution support sizes across criterion parameters q of 0, 1/2, 1, 2, and 10 were 16, 16, 15, 16, and 16; with regularization 10^-3, the support was 16 for q=0 and 27,000 for each larger q tested. On a 125,000-cell problem, SDM and SDMH reached the stopping criterion in about 2.8 seconds and less than 1.5 seconds, respectively, compared with 62 seconds for PGMA; simplicial decomposition did not reach the tolerance. On the stationary diffusion example with about 430,000 cells, SDM took 2,400 seconds and SDMH took 1,300 seconds, excluding the 610 seconds of preprocessing.
key_equations:
Bound-constrained design problem: \[\min_w F_q(\Lambda w)+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|w\|_{L^2(X)}^2,\quad 0\le w\le1,\quad \int_X w(x)\,dx=C\] The design density w is chosen over design space X to minimize criterion F_q of the information map Lambda w plus quadratic regularization with parameter alpha, subject to pointwise bounds and total weight C.

Information matrix from a design: \[\Lambda w=\int_X \Upsilon(x)w(x)\,dx\] The information matrix Lambda w is the integral over design space X of the information contribution Upsilon at point x weighted by design density w.

Family of information criteria: \[F_q(I)=\begin{cases}(n^{-1}\operatorname{trace}(I^{-q}))^{1/q},&q>0\\ n^{-1}\ln\det(I^{-1}),&q=0\\ \max\operatorname{eig}(I^{-1}),&q\to\infty\end{cases}\] The criterion F_q of information matrix I is defined using its inverse powers and trace for positive q, the logarithm of the inverse determinant at q=0, and the largest inverse eigenvalue as q tends to infinity; n is the number of parameters.

Simplicial representation: \[w=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i s_i,\quad \lambda_i\ge0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i=1\] The design w is represented as a convex combination of r feasible vertices s_i, with nonnegative coefficients lambda_i that sum to one.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the global Lipschitz-gradient assumption used in the standard FISTA convergence result does not hold for their criterion gradient, which is only locally Lipschitz on its domain. Their simplicial-decomposition inner solver is restricted to the unregularized case and criterion parameters q in [0,1], and they do not claim that SDMH will always outperform SDM. They also identify preprocessing of the elementary information matrices as a significant cost for large problems.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence comes from two model-based examples, with information contributions computed at nominal parameter values and, in the examples, approximated using cell midpoints; it does not establish performance on real experiments or under model misspecification. Reported solver times exclude information-matrix preprocessing, and the comparisons use specific discretizations, hardware, and stopping settings, so practical total-run-time advantages may differ.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing adaptive discretization strategies for the design space to reduce the cost of computing elementary Fisher information matrices.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test these algorithms under alternative model assumptions, design constraints, and objective criteria, including constraints imposed by real experimental capacity or cost. Implementations could also be validated on physical experiments and extended to update designs sequentially as new measurements become available.

summary: The paper adapts fast flexible filling to create space-filling split-plot designs for experiments in which some factors are harder to change than others. The design is intended for prediction, particularly in deterministic or high signal-to-noise settings, while respecting the whole-plot structure of hard-to-change factors. It constructs the design by first clustering random points across all factors, then continuing the clustering using only whole-plot factors to assign runs to whole plots. The authors compare it with other space-filling designs and split-plot response-surface designs using design criteria and prediction tests on analytical examples. They find that the proposed designs retain useful space-filling properties and can often accommodate blocking without a large loss in design efficiency.
key_results: The design-criterion comparisons used 2- and 4-factor cases, run sizes from 20 to 50 in steps of 5, and 8, 12, or 16 whole plots where applicable. The authors report that split-plot response-surface designs were best under their corresponding I-optimal criteria, with the next-best alternative showing an efficiency loss of around 50%; scaled SPFFF designs were nevertheless not far behind in some larger-run cases. SPFFF performed better than the alternatives on the maximin and Phi criteria, while the fast flexible filling and SPFFF designs had comparable minimax results; scaling SPFFF to put points on the design-space boundary improved its results across the reported comparisons. Prediction tests used a validation set of 100,000 points, and prediction performance was reported as being more dependent on the prediction model and sample size than on design type, with SPFFF performing at a similar level to other space-filling designs.

summary: The paper studies Bayesian experimental designs that maximize Fisher information gain (FIG) for models in the exponential family. It shows that the expected FIG can be expressed using the prior expectation of the trace of the Fisher information matrix. For these models, the design can be constructed by maximizing a per-run objective over the controllable-variable space, rather than optimizing the full design at once. The simplification can lead to designs with too few distinct settings or other parameter redundancy. The examples show that FIG-optimal designs may therefore be non-identifiable, so the authors advise caution when FIG is used as a default objective.
key_results: For exponential-family models, the design search reduces from the full design space to maximizing a function of one run's controllable settings. In a normal second-order response-surface example with 2 controllable variables and 6 parameters, FIG-optimal designs use only the 4 corner settings and are under-supported. In the logistic-regression example with 5 parameters, numerical search found only 2 maxima, at settings given by plus or minus the vector with coordinates minus 0.8701, 1, 1, and 1; the resulting designs are parameter-redundant. In the compartmental model, the objective had one maximum at time 24, so all runs at that setting produce an under-supported design.
key_equations:
Expected FIG objective: \[U_{\mathrm{FIG}}(D)=E_{\theta}\left[\operatorname{tr}\{I(\theta,D)\}\right]\] U_FIG is expected Fisher information gain, D is the complete design, E_theta is expectation over the prior distribution of the parameter vector theta, tr is matrix trace, and I is the Fisher information matrix.

Fisher information for known scale: \[I(\theta,D)=M(\theta,D)^{\mathsf{T}}W(\theta,D)M(\theta,D)\] I is the Fisher information matrix, theta is the parameter vector, D is the complete design, M is the matrix of derivatives of the response mean with respect to the parameters, the superscript T means transpose, and W is the diagonal matrix of inverse response variances.

Per-run objective for known scale: \[\phi(d)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}E_{\theta}\left[\frac{1}{\operatorname{Var}(y\mid\theta,d)}\left(\frac{\partial\mu(\theta,d)}{\partial\theta_j}\right)^2\right]\] phi is the per-run objective, d is a controllable-variable setting, p is the number of parameters, j indexes a parameter, E_theta is expectation over the parameter prior, Var is response variance, y is the response, theta is the parameter vector, and mu is the response mean function.

Design construction and under-support: \[d_i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\phi(d),\qquad q< p\Rightarrow\operatorname{rank}\{M(\theta,D)\}< p\] d_i is the setting for run i, arg max means a setting that maximizes phi, d ranges over the allowable setting space calD, q is the number of global maxima of phi, p is the number of parameters, rank is matrix rank, M is the derivative matrix, theta is the parameter vector, and D is the complete design.
limitations_stated: The authors restrict their results to exponential-family models. For an unknown scale parameter treated as a nuisance parameter, their explicit derivation is for normal responses with an inverse-gamma prior. They also caution that identifying the number of maxima may require a numerical search.
limitations_unstated: The examples are theoretical or numerical illustrations rather than validation in real experiments, so the practical consequences for run costs and experimental constraints are not assessed. The numerical search for maxima can depend on its search procedure, and the paper does not establish that such searches will find every global maximum in more complicated settings.
future_work_stated: The authors advise checking whether a FIG-optimal design causes parameter redundancy when FIG is used as a default utility. They also point to a game-theoretic approach based on FIG as an alternative that circumvents the disadvantages discussed in the paper.
future_work_unstated: Future work could develop constrained design procedures that balance FIG with full-rank or minimum-support requirements while respecting practical restrictions such as allowable settings and run budgets. It could also test the predicted identifiability problems in real experiments and compare the resulting parameter estimates with designs optimized for other criteria.

summary: The paper develops locally determinant-optimal designs for multinomial probit choice models used to estimate preference parameters. It considers choice sets with two or three options and models with qualitative attributes, sometimes combined with a quantitative attribute. The construction assumes normally distributed utilities and compares independent utilities with a model in which equal attribute levels create dependent utilities across options. The authors derive designs analytically for paired comparisons and for selected three-option settings, and use numerical comparisons for other cases. They find that allowing utility dependence can produce more reasonable designs than assuming independence, particularly for qualitative-attribute choice sets.
key_results: For paired comparisons at indifference with qualitative attributes, every full-depth comparison orbit is D-optimal under Model I; under Model II, all positive comparison depths are D-optimal. For three-option qualitative designs under Model II, balanced comparison depths are optimal in the reported cases for 2 through 7 attributes, and the authors prove the equal-depth result when the number of attributes is a multiple of 3; designs with two identical options have efficiencies of about 0.593 to 0.610 in the tabulated cases. With one additional quantitative attribute, Model I selects designs with two identical options in the numerical search for up to 7 qualitative attributes. Under Model II with a sharp quantitative decision, the best designs in the reported cases with at least 2 qualitative attributes use options differing in only one qualitative attribute; for 2 attributes, the duplicate-option design has efficiency 0.540 compared with the best design.

Paired-comparison construction: \[\xi^*=\bar{\xi}_K\otimes\delta_{t^*},\qquad t_1^*-t_2^*=\sigma_{\max}z^*,\qquad z^*=\arg\max_z\lambda_2(z)^{K+1}z^2\] xi-star is the optimal product design, xi-bar-K is the uniform design on full comparison depth for the qualitative attributes, delta is a one-point design at the quantitative setting t-star, t-one-star and t-two-star are the quantitative levels for the two options, sigma-max is the maximum standard deviation of their utility difference, z-star is the optimal standardized difference, lambda-two is the quantitative-attribute probit intensity function, and K is the number of qualitative attributes.
limitations_stated: The authors note that designs derived for indifference may not be very important in many practical choice situations. Their development assumes respondents face the same choice sets, and the paper treats choice sets with two or three options.
limitations_unstated: The designs are local, so their performance depends on the assumed parameter values; the paper does not establish robustness when those values or the normal-utility assumptions are wrong. The three-option numerical comparisons cover up to 7 qualitative attributes, and the paper provides no validation on data from an actual choice experiment or guidance on converting approximate designs into practical run schedules.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending dependent-utility probit designs to more than two levels for discrete attributes and to multiple quantitative attributes. They also suggest investigating criteria other than D-optimality, such as integrated mean squared error optimality.
future_work_unstated: Future work could assess robust or Bayesian designs that account for uncertain preference parameters and departures from the assumed normal utility model. It could also develop exact, constrained designs for practical choice experiments and validate their estimation performance using real respondent data.

summary: The paper develops a method for selecting sensor locations for Bayesian linear inverse problems governed by partial differential equations, when the model contains uncertainty that cannot be reduced by the observations. Its objective is A-optimal: minimize the expected trace of the posterior covariance while encouraging a small, binary set of selected sensors. The method approximates uncertainty with sampled model realizations, rewrites the objective using operators in the observation space, and builds joint low-rank bases to avoid repeated forward and adjoint equation solves during optimization. The authors demonstrate the approach by estimating an initial contaminant concentration in groundwater, accounting for uncertain flow fields and release times. In this example, designs accounting for uncertainty generally reduce expected posterior uncertainty more than designs optimized for a single realization, especially when fewer measurements are available.
key_results: The groundwater example used 234 candidate sensor locations and 100 samples of irreducible uncertainty for the uncertainty-aware designs. With one cluster, the reduced model used 410 basis vectors at tolerance 0.002 and had reported relative error 6.876 × 10^-4; at tolerance 0.0001, it used 985 basis vectors and had error 2.335 × 10^-6. The approach removes repeated partial differential equation solves from the optimization iterations after the reduced bases are computed, although the paper does not report a wall-clock speedup. In comparisons evaluated on independent uncertainty samples, uncertainty-aware designs generally performed better on average than deterministic designs optimized for a single realization, with a clearer advantage when there were fewer sensors or only two observation times; the advantage was less pronounced as the number of sensors increased.
key_equations:
Posterior covariance for a chosen design: \[\Gamma_{\mathrm{post}}(\xi,w)=\left(\sigma^{-2}F(\xi)^*WF(\xi)+\Gamma_{\mathrm{pr}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\] The posterior covariance Γpost depends on the uncertain model realization ξ and design weights w; F is the forward operator, W is the design-weight matrix, σ is the noise standard deviation, Γpr is the prior covariance, and the asterisk denotes the adjoint.

Expected A-optimal objective with sparsity penalty: \[\min_{w\in[0,1]^s}\;\phi(w)+\gamma\psi(w),\qquad \phi(w)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma_{\mathrm{post}}(\xi,w))]\] The design selects weights w between zero and one to minimize φ(w) plus the penalty γψ(w); φ is the expected trace of the posterior covariance over uncertainty ξ, γ sets the penalty strength, and ψ promotes sparse, eventually binary designs.

Composite reduced-basis approximation: \[\widetilde F_i\approx QQ^T\widetilde F_i\widehat Q\widehat Q^T\] For sample i, the prior-preconditioned forward operator F̃i is approximated using observation-space basis Q and parameter-space basis Q̂; the transpose indicates the corresponding projection.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the formulation is limited to linear parameter-to-observation maps, Gaussian priors, and additive Gaussian noise, and that further work is needed for nonlinear inverse problems. They also note that Monte Carlo approximation may require many samples when high accuracy is desired.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence is from one simulated groundwater example, and the uncertainty distribution for flow fields is based on a Laplace approximation fitted using six synthetic pressure observations; performance in other applications is not tested. The sparse continuation uses nonconvex penalties, for which the authors cannot guarantee a unique solution, and the study does not quantify total runtime or the practical cost of the required upfront reduced-basis construction.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying Taylor expansions or stochastic approximation as alternatives to Monte Carlo sampling, and extending the approach to nonlinear inverse problems, potentially using Gaussian approximations at the maximum a posteriori point. They also identify reducible sources of model uncertainty as an aspect not explored in this work and discuss designing primarily for the parameters of interest when such secondary uncertainties are present.
future_work_unstated: The method could be tested with operational constraints such as sensor access, costs, reliability, and limits on where or how often measurements can be taken. Further work could also assess stability across alternative uncertainty distributions and real field data, and compare practical computation costs and design quality against other criteria or sensor-selection methods.

summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework for covariate-adaptive randomization in two-treatment clinical trials. It examines the power of a linear-model treatment-effect test and the predictability of treatment assignments, assuming independent covariates and normally distributed errors. The proposed design assigns each patient using a weighted measure of overall, marginal, and within-stratum treatment imbalance, with a tuning parameter controlling how strongly assignments respond to imbalance. The authors show that the tuning can make covariate imbalance small enough for asymptotically maximal test power while making selection bias tend to its minimum value. A simulation study illustrates the finite-sample trade-off between power and selection bias.
key_results: The theory shows that power loss depends on imbalance in covariates included in the testing model: balancing more of those covariates reduces the loss, and conventional covariate-adaptive designs can achieve maximal asymptotic power when their relevant imbalance conditions hold. For the new design with matching test and randomization covariates, the paper reports imbalance of order n to the power gamma, selection bias equal to one half plus a term of order n to the power negative gamma over two, and relative power loss of order n to the power gamma minus one. In the simulation, using 5,000 replications and sample sizes of 50, 100, 200, and 400, Type I error estimates were generally near the nominal 5% level; for sample size 200 and the reported alternative with delta 10, power was 0.6910 under complete randomization and 0.7160 under the new design with gamma 0.2 and rho 0.9. At sample size 400 with rho 0.9, selection bias was 0.8295 for the Pocock and Simon procedure, compared with 0.5743 for the new design with gamma 0.8 and 0.5000 for complete randomization.

limitations_unstated: The simulation examines one specified model with three independent normal covariates, a particular discretization, and selected design settings, so it does not establish performance across the range of clinical-trial conditions. The paper gives theoretical tuning choices but does not assess the practical consequences of choosing weights and gamma under operational constraints or validate the method in a real trial.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the theory and procedures to multiple treatments, dependent covariates, and general error distributions. They also identify response-adaptive and covariate-adjusted adaptive designs as topics for future research.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could compare tuning and weighting choices across a broader set of covariate distributions, prognostic strengths, and clinical-trial constraints, and provide practical guidance for selecting them. Software implementation and validation using real trial settings would also help assess how readily the method can be adopted.

summary: The paper compares ways to make inferences about the average treatment effect after rerandomization, a design that accepts assignments only when observed covariates are sufficiently balanced. It studies regression adjustment and model-based Bayesian imputation alongside an existing asymptotic method for the mean difference estimator. The design is constructed by calculating the Mahalanobis distance between treatment and control covariate means and randomizing among allocations below a chosen threshold. The authors evaluate the methods in simulations with different sample sizes, covariate settings, and outcome-generating processes. They find that some regression and Bayesian methods perform better than the existing asymptotic approach for small or moderate experiments, although the most efficient methods can under-cover in the smallest experiments.
key_results: The simulation covered 640 settings, with 20 data sets per setting and 2,000 rerandomized experiments per data set, for 12,800 data sets in total. For sample size 400, all methods produced intervals whose average lengths were just over 80% of the conservative mean-difference intervals for the first outcome process, and just under 80% for the second. In smaller experiments, regression with treatment-covariate interactions and conventional robust standard errors was generally most efficient, but at sample size 50 with 10 covariates its coverage was about 10 to 11 percentage points below the nominal 95% level; the existing asymptotic method was about 7 points below. The authors report that leverage-adjusted regression standard errors and regression without treatment-covariate interactions under the first Bayesian model were useful approaches for sample sizes of at least 100; they recommend a Fisher randomization test for sample size 50.

limitations_unstated: The simulation uses equal-sized treatment and control groups and considers only two outcome-generating processes, two covariate distributions, and the specified sample sizes and covariate counts. summary: This paper develops optimal experimental design for regression and prediction when observations lie on a lower-dimensional Riemannian manifold. It uses a Laplacian Regularized Least Squares model, combining the labeled responses with a penalty for lack of smoothness along the manifold. The authors prove that D-optimal and G-optimal designs are equivalent for this model and give a lower bound on maximum prediction variance that is attained by an optimal design. They propose the sequential Optimal Design of Experiments on Manifolds (ODOEM) algorithm, which selects points with high prediction variance and updates a continuous design. In simulations and an image dataset study, ODOEM generally predicts better than the compared designs and models.
key_results: The theoretical results establish equivalence of D-optimal and G-optimal designs for the manifold model, with the maximum prediction variance at an optimal design equal to the stated lower bound. The proposed algorithm increases the information-matrix determinant monotonically and is proved to converge to a global D-optimal design. In four simulated manifold examples, each method selected 100 labeled instances; ODOEM produced more dispersed selections and better fits than classical D-optimal kernel regression, both with and without added noise. On four objects from the COIL-20 dataset, which contains 1,440 images of size 32 by 32 pixels, ODOEM had lower mean squared error across the reported learning curves than the compared kernel-regression, uniform-design, random-sampling, and support-vector-machine approaches.

Prediction variance: \[d(z,\xi)=\sigma^2 g(z)^T M_{Lap}(\xi)^{-1}g(z)\] Here d is prediction variance at point z under design ξ, σ² is the error variance, g is the feature vector, and M_Lap is the design information matrix.

Sequential design update: \[\xi_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)\xi_k+\alpha_k\delta_{z_{k+1}},\quad z_{k+1}=\arg\max_{z\in X}d(z,\xi_k)\] Here ξ_k is the design at iteration k, α_k is the update step size, δ is a point mass, z_{k+1} is the selected point, X is the candidate region, and d is prediction variance.
limitations_stated: The authors say that the regularization parameters need a systematic selection procedure: cross-validation is impractical at the beginning of sequential learning, so their parameter choices are heuristic. They also note that evaluating every candidate point can be computationally exhausting for very large discrete candidate sets.
limitations_unstated: The theoretical results depend on the LapRLS model and its information-matrix formulation, so their guarantees may not hold if the response relationship or manifold representation is substantially misspecified. The empirical comparisons use simulated examples and one image dataset, with fixed kernel and regularization settings; they do not establish performance on physical industrial experiments or across a broad range of noise and graph-construction choices.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing a systematic, theoretically justified way to choose the ambient and manifold regularization parameters. They also suggest extending the theory to optimality criteria beyond D-optimality and G-optimality. For very large candidate sets, they propose first clustering the covariates and then evaluating representative points from the clusters.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method in real designed experiments, including cases with operational constraints such as costs, forbidden settings, and restricted randomization. Further work could test sequential performance when the manifold or its graph must be estimated and updated as new observations arrive.

summary: The paper develops input-uncertain reliable level-set estimation (IU-rLSE) to find operating inputs for which a machine's response is below a specified threshold with sufficiently high probability despite variation in the actual inputs. It models the unknown response function with a Gaussian process (GP) and estimates the probability of meeting the threshold at each candidate operating input. The procedure constructs credible intervals for these probabilities, classifies inputs using those intervals, and selects evaluations using an approximate expected classification improvement criterion, with random exploration also available. It addresses known input distributions and a case where parameters of the distribution are unknown. The authors report better classification performance than the compared methods in synthetic studies and a study using a power-plant dataset.
key_results: Theoretical results show that, under the stated conditions, the algorithm terminates after a finite number of evaluations with probability 1; a separate result bounds classification loss by the chosen tolerance with probability at least 1 minus the chosen failure probability. summary: The paper develops a method to identify model uncertainty by combining parameter estimation, optimal sensor selection, and statistical hypothesis testing. It applies the method to a mechanical component of the 3D Servo Press, with the objective of estimating two stiffness parameters and assessing alternative descriptions of friction and hysteresis. The design selects sensor locations to reduce uncertainty in the parameter estimates, then compares estimates from calibration and validation data using confidence regions. The authors demonstrate the method with measurements from the press under loading and unloading. The simple friction descriptions are rejected, while the more detailed learned hysteresis model is consistent with the tested data.

summary: The paper proposes an active experimental design method for learning causal structure among continuous variables with potentially nonlinear relationships. It assumes a structural causal model with an acyclic causal graph and additive noise, and uses Gaussian process priors for the relationships between variables. At each step, the method selects a single-variable intervention intended to maximize expected information about the causal graph. It estimates this objective with Monte Carlo sampling and uses Bayesian optimization to search over possible intervention values. The paper presents a small illustrative example, but does not report a systematic evaluation of the proposed optimization strategy.
key_results: The authors derive an expected information gain objective for choosing interventions and show how Gaussian process models make the relevant likelihoods and predictions available in closed form. Their bivariate illustration uses 15 samples: five observational samples and five intervention samples for each of the two variables. With intervention values chosen at random rather than by the proposed Bayesian optimization, the graph posterior identifies the correct graph with more than 99% confidence after ten interventions. The paper reports no comparison of the proposed design against alternative designs or methods.

limitations_stated: The authors note that the number of candidate acyclic graphs grows super-exponentially, so the approach in its current form is intended for settings with only a few variables. limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence is limited to a bivariate illustration, and the reported high-confidence result uses randomly selected interventions rather than the proposed Bayesian optimization procedure. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare the optimized intervention policy with random and established design strategies across broader simulated settings, including cases with model misspecification and constrained intervention values. summary: The paper proposes supervised randomization to collect experimental data for customer-level treatment effect models while reducing the cost of random targeting. It is designed for marketing experiments in which an existing scoring model can identify customers who are more likely to benefit from treatment. The design uses the score to assign different treatment probabilities to different customers, while retaining random assignment and recording each probability. The authors describe inverse probability weighting and doubly robust estimation to correct for the resulting selection bias. In a simulation based on bank telemarketing data, supervised randomization improved campaign returns during the experiment, while downstream treatment effect models remained competitive with models trained on fully randomized data.
key_results: In the simulation, targeting 50% of customers under supervised randomization produced a 14.3% conversion rate, compared with 13.5% under equal-probability full randomization; this matched the 14.3% rate from full randomization with a 66% treatment probability while targeting fewer customers. For 40,000 prospective customers, the authors report experimental campaign cost savings of 7.1% to 9.4% compared with full randomization and 2.9% to 8.2% compared with imbalanced full randomization. Treatment effect estimates remained unbiased after correction, though their variance increased; doubly robust estimates had significantly lower variance than inverse probability weighted estimates. For the causal forest, mean absolute error increased from 0.0276 under full randomization to 0.0295 under supervised randomization, and the Qini coefficient decreased from 0.0056 to 0.0047. The reported campaign profit decrease for models trained on supervised-randomization data was about 0% to 1.3%, depending on the model and profit setting.

limitations_stated: The evaluation is an offline simulation, and the authors state that further evaluation in real-world experiments is necessary to establish net cost savings in practice. They also note that supervised randomization increases uncertainty in treatment effect estimates and can reduce downstream model performance.
limitations_unstated: The results rely on one public bank marketing dataset with simulated treatment effects and potential outcomes, so they do not establish performance across other industries, outcomes, or real campaign mechanisms. The design also depends on an existing scoring model and usable treatment probabilities; in practice, very small probabilities may yield sparse observations and less stable effect estimates for some customer groups.
future_work_stated: The authors propose testing the design in real-world experiments and describe online testing as future work. They also leave a more in-depth comparison with reinforcement learning and bandit approaches for future research.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test score-to-probability mappings under operational constraints such as fixed treatment budgets, minimum group sizes, and limits on customer contact. They could also validate the method across real experiments and other outcome models, and study how to update the scoring model and randomization probabilities over time without losing reliable effect estimates.

summary: This paper develops flexible sliced Latin hypercube designs for computer experiments, where slices may have arbitrary run sizes rather than equal sizes. The designs preserve Latin hypercube structure both overall and within every slice, supporting experiments that are run in batches or at multiple levels of fidelity. The construction assigns lattice positions to slices and adds random jitter; an optimization procedure then improves space filling using a criterion that combines the whole design with its slices. The authors use the sliced enhanced stochastic evolutionary algorithm for optimization and propose a faster two-part algorithm for larger designs. Their simulations show improved criterion values over random designs and lower computation times for the two-part method, though the sliced evolutionary method often gives better criterion values.
key_results: For a design with slices of 4, 8, and 12 runs and 2 factors, the paper's text reports that optimization reduced the combined space-filling measurement from 14.4740 to 5.7958; the figure labels instead report 14.4223 and 5.6844. In 100,000 randomly generated designs of that size, the best reported criterion value was 6.8387, higher than the text's optimized value. For designs with 15- and 30-run slices, the average criterion was 8.3100 for the sliced enhanced stochastic evolutionary algorithm, compared with 9.1712 for the two-part algorithm; their average times were 406 seconds and 18 seconds. For designs with 5, 10, 15, and 30 runs across four slices and 6 factors, the corresponding average criterion values were 2.0823 and 2.2424, while average times were 1110 seconds and 71 seconds. Thus the two-part method was faster in both comparisons, while the sliced evolutionary method achieved better average criterion values.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the sliced enhanced stochastic evolutionary algorithm can converge slowly for designs with large run counts and many factors because the number of possible neighboring designs is large. limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation covers only a small number of design configurations and does not validate the designs in real computer experiments. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying orthogonal-maximin sliced Latin hypercube designs with arbitrary slice run sizes, combining orthogonality with space-filling properties.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method across more factor counts, slice-size patterns, and alternative space-filling criteria and weights, with consistent reporting of numerical results. summary: This paper presents a hands-on classroom exercise for teaching split-plot design of experiments using a boomerang tin toy. They describe how to plan a screening design, assess degrees of freedom, and analyze the data using a model that accounts for whole-plot and run-level errors. summary: This paper designs multidimensional diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) acquisitions for estimating tissue parameters in the Standard Model (SM). The authors seek b-tensor measurement sets that provide precise parameter estimates, using a D-optimal criterion based on the determinant of an averaged Fisher information matrix (FIM). They test two design constraint schemes for 60 measurements, with tensor orientations fixed and different freedoms for tensor shape and size. The resulting designs use linear tensor encoding (LTE) and planar tensor encoding (PTE), and simulations show lower estimation errors than a balanced LTE/PTE comparison protocol.
key_results: The optimized designs used only LTE and PTE, with LTE making up about 75% to 85% of measurements; the designs also grouped measurements at two diffusion weightings. For the comparison, the authors simulated 10,000 voxels with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 100 and compared the more flexible design against a balanced LTE/PTE acquisition. The optimized design improved estimation accuracy by 14% for the diffusion and second cumulant tensors and by 7% for the double-Watson Standard Model. The design used 60 b-tensor measurements, while the paper does not report a run-size comparison across alternative measurement counts.

limitations_stated: The authors use the fourth-order cumulant expansion rather than the analytical SM signal to compute information, and regard it as a reasonable surrogate only over the stated diffusion-weighting range. They also note the Gaussian noise approximation under optimistic SNR, approximations in integrating over the parameter space, and the possibility that the high-dimensional optimization may miss better solutions. Their search fixes tensor eigenvectors and assumes the same SNR across diffusion weightings.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated signals and does not establish performance on acquired clinical data or in the presence of experimental deviations from the assumed tissue model. The reported comparison is limited to a balanced LTE/PTE design, so it does not show how the method compares with a broader set of practical acquisition protocols or constraints imposed by gradient hardware.
future_work_stated: The authors propose in-silico studies with different numbers of measurements and different fiber orientation distributions, as well as designs focused on particular parameters. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the selected protocols using real acquisitions and assess robustness to deviations from the assumed signal and noise models. Further work could also incorporate explicit gradient-waveform and scan-time constraints, then provide software that lets practitioners generate and compare feasible protocols.

summary: This paper develops a sequential design method for predator-prey functional-response experiments. At each step, the method selects the initial prey density for the next experiment using the current parameter and model information, then updates that information after observing consumption. Across all four true models, sequential designs outperformed static and random designs for parameter estimation, and the authors report the same overall advantage for model discrimination. For the combined parameter-estimation and model-discrimination objective, sequential designs outperformed static designs on both components; the total-entropy design was only marginally less effective than the single-purpose designs in the additional utility comparison. limitations_unstated: The evaluation is simulation-based, and the simulated parameter settings were drawn from the posterior for a single cited dataset, so the comparisons do not establish performance across a broad range of real predator-prey systems. Its goal is to reduce uncertainty in the estimated parameters using an A-optimal design criterion, which measures the reduction in average posterior variance. The authors use randomized subspace iteration to approximate the objective and its gradient by exploiting low-rank structure, and construct sparse, nearly binary sensor selections with a reweighted penalty solved through majorization-minimization. They also introduce a modified A-optimal criterion intended to reduce computational work. In a simulated contaminant-source identification study, the methods produced sparse sensor layouts, and the modified criterion yielded designs with similar posterior variance to those from the standard criterion at lower computational cost.
key_results: The numerical study used 109 candidate sensor locations and measurements at three observation times, for 327 total observations. With 127 columns in the randomized approximation, the reported design objective, active-sensor count, and number of optimization subproblem solves matched the results obtained with larger approximations; at the reported penalty setting, the design used 30 sensors. A design with 18 sensors was also shown, and at 207 columns the reported A-optimal criterion approximation accuracy was on the order of 10^-7. Across the tested designs, those computed by the proposed method had lower exact A-optimal values than the random designs compared against them; designs from the modified criterion had similar posterior variance to standard A-optimal designs while requiring one fewer group of PDE solves per evaluation.

Binary-promoting penalty: \[P_{\epsilon}(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\frac{|w_i|}{|w_i|+\epsilon}\] The penalty Pε sums a softened indicator of nonzero weights; wi is the weight for sensor i, ε is a positive smoothing parameter, and ns is the number of candidate sensors.

Reweighting step: \[r_i^{(m)}=\frac{\epsilon}{(|w_i^{(m-1)}|+\epsilon)^2}\] At iteration m, the reweighting value ri is calculated from the previous weight wi, with ε controlling smoothing; these values weight the next convex optimization subproblem.
limitations_stated: The authors report that randomness can cause modest variation in the selected sensors: in additional, unreported experiments, designs differed by at most one or two sensor locations for a modest approximation size. They also describe the modified A-optimal criterion as suboptimal when the goal is to obtain a standard A-optimal design.
limitations_unstated: The numerical validation is limited to one simulated contaminant transport problem, so the reported performance may not carry over to different physical models or noise structures. future_work_stated: The authors propose adaptively choosing the target rank during optimization, investigating other low-rank approximations such as the Nyström method, and extending the estimators to traces of matrix functions. future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs on real environmental monitoring data and compare their performance under spatial access, budget, or sensor reliability constraints. It could also study sequential placement, where new sensors are selected as measurements arrive, and provide a reusable software implementation for practitioners.

summary: The paper develops a way to choose a rerandomization threshold for a non-sequential treatment-control experiment. It targets estimation of the treatment effect with a covariate-adjusted linear regression estimator, seeking protection against high estimation error caused by unobserved factors. The method starts with a large set of balanced random assignments, orders them by observed-covariate imbalance, and evaluates progressively larger sets using a tail quantile of the estimator’s mean squared error. The threshold is chosen where this tail criterion is minimized, balancing covariate balance against retaining enough randomness. Simulations and a bootstrap study based on an education experiment show that the resulting designs can improve tail error over unrestricted balanced randomization, while very restrictive deterministic assignment can have a much worse tail.
key_results: In a simulation with 100 subjects, 10 covariates, and 25,000 candidate assignments, the selected thresholds across six residual-distribution procedures ranged from 0.232 to 0.289; the three proposed designs retained 5,881, 5,601, and 6,901 assignments. In a separate simulation, the proposed designs had the lowest 95th-percentile error among the compared strategies, and their performance was similar to selecting the least imbalanced 0.5% of assignments. In the education-data bootstrap study, the two practical proposed procedures reduced mean squared error relative to balanced complete randomization by 4.6% and 6.2%, and reduced the 95th-percentile error by 5.7% and 4.9%. The deterministic design had slightly lower mean error in that study, but its 95th-percentile error was almost 300% larger than that of the proposed designs.

limitations_stated: The authors do not provide an optimized procedure for the difference-in-means estimator because its criterion depends on unknown treatment-covariate coefficients. They also note that the search is computationally intensive and that a sampled base set of assignments may fail to include sufficiently low-imbalance assignments or may be too small for accurate estimation and randomization-based inference.
limitations_unstated: Although the education study uses data from a real experiment, its design comparisons are conducted through a bootstrap with estimated conditional means and resampled residuals, rather than by implementing the new assignments in a fresh experiment. The main evaluations also use balanced assignments and a particular imbalance measure, so results may differ with unequal allocation, practical assignment constraints, or other measures of covariate balance.
future_work_stated: The authors identify the choice and construction of the base assignment set as the most pressing open question, including whether to supplement balanced random assignments with assignments from a pair-switching procedure. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a prospective experiment that applies the selected threshold and compares observed outcomes with the paper’s bootstrap-based performance estimates. Further evaluations could also test the method under operational assignment constraints and treatment-effect patterns beyond the constant-effect model used here.

The method models the two groups’ success rates with binomial distributions and compares hypotheses of no effect, a positive effect, a negative effect, or any difference. It uses normal priors on the grand mean of log odds and the log odds ratio, and lets users encode expert expectations by eliciting prior distributions from quantities such as absolute risk. The authors demonstrate the method with a fictitious business example and a reanalysis of a medical trial; they do not construct or optimize an experimental design.

summary: This paper studies whether methods for identifying mean-changing effects remain reliable when an unreplicated two-level factorial experiment also has effects that change response variance. The authors simulate four-factor experiments with one or two variance-changing effects and compare the Box–Meyer, Lenth, Berk–Picard, and Loughin–Noble methods. The simulated variance follows a multiplicative model, which can correlate estimated location effects even though the methods do not account for that correlation. The first three methods generally retain control of false detections, while the Loughin–Noble method can lose that control as variance effects become large. The paper also finds that variance effects can change the chance of detecting pairs of location effects together, depending on their relationship and signs.
key_results: The study used 1,825 simulated data sets per setting in a four-factor, two-level experiment, and calibrated methods to an individual error rate near 0.05. With no active location or variance effects, the individual error rates were 0.051 for Lenth, 0.051 for Box–Meyer, 0.050 for Berk–Picard, and 0.049 for Loughin–Noble; their experimentwise error rates were 0.414, 0.474, 0.459, and 0.274, respectively. The individual error rates of the first three methods stayed near their nominal level across the simulated variance-effect sizes, whereas the Loughin–Noble rate rose above 0.1 for the largest sizes, with the increase more pronounced when two variance effects were present. The Loughin–Noble method’s average power also increased with variance-effect size, alongside its elevated error rates; the other methods showed little power increase, and Box–Meyer sometimes had a small power advantage. Joint power for two location effects could rise or fall substantially when the variance effect induced correlation between their estimates, depending on whether the signs aligned.

The method, called WaterfallUCB1, uses optimistic estimates of acceptance probabilities and an optimization oracle to select each successive selling strategy, updating estimates from the networks observed in that sale. Its analysis gives a sublinear regret bound against an offline approximation, and its experiments test synthetic and public real-world data. summary: The paper develops a computational method for Bayesian experimental design with nonlinear models, especially when an experiment should teach us about selected parameters rather than every model parameter. Its objective is the expected information gain (EIG) in those parameters, averaged over possible experimental outcomes. The method, called layered multiple importance sampling (LMIS), reuses samples and model evaluations from earlier steps to build better importance-sampling distributions for estimating posterior normalizing constants. The authors assess it in linear Gaussian examples and in a nonlinear Mössbauer spectroscopy example. They find that LMIS estimates the design objective more accurately than prior-based sampling at the same computational effort.
key_results: In the four- and eight-dimensional linear Gaussian examples, LMIS reduced estimation error by several orders of magnitude compared with prior-based sampling; with 1,000,000 model evaluations, its mean squared error (MSE) was comparable to the method using exact posterior distributions as the sampling distributions. In the Mössbauer example, LMIS reduced MSE by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior-based sampling. For the three-velocity designs studied, the reported optimum for learning the peak center was minus 1.3, zero, and 1.3, while the optimum for learning the offset was minus 2, zero, and 2. The authors’ theoretical analysis gives an MSE rate proportional to computational work to the power of minus two-thirds under an asymptotically adjusted inner-to-outer sample ratio, compared with minus one-half for a fixed ratio; they caution that the adjusted ratio may not help at finite budgets when bias dominates.

limitations_unstated: The evidence is based on simulated examples, including a single nonlinear spectroscopy model, rather than validation in a real experiment. The method also requires many likelihood or model evaluations and a sequential sample-reuse procedure, while the paper does not demonstrate an end-to-end optimization workflow under practical experimental constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors propose using surrogate models to construct biasing distributions more cheaply, and combining surrogates or marginal-likelihood approximations with LMIS through control variates or multilevel Monte Carlo while preserving consistency. They also suggest using Laplace approximations when posterior gradients are available, pairing LMIS with stochastic design-optimization methods, and applying focused design to parameters representing model discrepancy.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test LMIS on real experiments and on higher-dimensional nonlinear models, measuring both computational cost and the quality of the selected design. It would also be useful to assess the method when run sizes, allowable settings, or randomization are constrained, and to compare alternative parameterizations and criteria for selecting or pruning reusable samples.

summary: The paper develops treatment-assignment designs for two-treatment A/B testing on social networks, where connected users may have correlated continuous responses. It models this correlation with a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model and seeks to estimate the treatment effect precisely using a D-optimal design criterion. The authors formulate the exact design problem and a modified version as mixed integer programming (MIP) problems. The modified formulation avoids needing a known correlation parameter and is designed to be faster to solve, though it does not guarantee the exact D-optimal design. Simulations and studies using real network structures show that the modified method often improves estimation precision over random assignment, especially when network correlation is not small.
key_results: For a simulated network of 50 nodes with density 0.1, D-efficiency for the random design fell from 0.98 at correlation 0 to 0.76 at correlation 0.3; the exact and modified designs had values from 1.00 to 0.90 across those settings. For the same network, at correlation 0.3 the reported empirical variance was 0.0037 for the modified design with alpha 0.6, compared with 0.0046 for random assignment with the CAR model. The exact MIP reached a 10.0863% optimality gap after the 24-hour time limit in one reported comparison, while modified-design runs on networks of 50 nodes took 13.26 to 24.80 seconds across the tested alpha values. On five Facebook ego networks, the modified design usually had lower empirical variance than random assignment at correlations 0.2 and 0.3, but its advantage was not substantial at 0.1. For networks of approximately 1,000, 1,500, and 2,000 nodes assembled from disjoint clusters, the modified design had the smallest median variance among the compared methods, and the reported rank-sum tests found that its median was significantly lower than random assignment in all three cases.
key_equations:
Continuous response model: \[y_i=\beta_0+x_i\beta+\delta_i\] The response y_i for node i is the intercept beta_0 plus its treatment assignment x_i multiplied by the treatment effect beta, plus its random error delta_i.

Simplified exact D-optimal criterion: \[\arg\min_{x_i\in\{-1,1\}}\left[\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\left(\sum_i m_i\right)\left(\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}x_ix_j\right)+\left(\sum_i m_ix_i\right)^2\right]\] The design minimizes this expression over assignments x_i, where rho is the network correlation parameter, m_i is the number of neighbors of node i, and w_ij indicates an edge between nodes i and j.

Modified design criterion: \[\min_{x_i\in\{-1,1\}}\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}x_ix_j\quad\text{subject to}\quad-c\leq\sum_i m_ix_i\leq c\] The modified design minimizes the sum of edge indicators multiplied by the assignments at both ends of each edge, subject to a bound c on the degree-weighted assignment total.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the exact MIP requires the correlation parameter to be known, while the modified formulation does not guarantee that the exact D-optimal design will be found. They also report that directly obtaining MIP-based designs for networks above 500 nodes is nearly impossible in their setting, motivating their approach of solving designs by cluster and combining them.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes an undirected network, continuous responses, positively correlated errors among connected nodes, and a linear model with one treatment factor and no covariates; performance under departures from these assumptions is not evaluated. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to categorical responses, incorporating covariates into network designs, and constructing sequential designs on networks.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate robustness when the CAR assumptions or network structure are misspecified, and assess design performance using actual responses from deployed experiments. It could also study practical assignment constraints and randomization procedures, and develop scalable software or solution strategies for large networks that are not separable into disjoint clusters.

summary: This paper studies space-filling designs generated by determinantal point processes and asks whether they remain regular when some coordinates are removed. The design objective is to retain repulsive point patterns in every coordinate projection, supporting experiments whose active factors may change. The authors derive the projected process’s pair correlation function when the original kernel separates across coordinates. They examine Gaussian, L1-exponential, and Dirichlet kernel examples, using a normalized Ripley function to compare their regularity. Their theory and simulations show that projections remain repulsive under the stated kernel conditions, and that the Dirichlet design performs especially well in the reported integration examples.
key_results: The theory shows that when the kernel separates across coordinates, every projected process has a pair correlation function bounded by one, although repulsion weakens as more coordinates are discarded. In the reported regularity comparisons at dimensions 6, 10, and 100, the Dirichlet designs were generally more repulsive and lost less repulsion under projection than the Gaussian designs; the L1-exponential designs were less favorable than the Gaussian designs. For numerical integration, the authors compared Poisson, Gaussian, and Dirichlet designs at intensities 200, 400, 600, 800, and 1000, using 10,000 replications in dimension 6 and test functions of dimensions 1 through 6. The empirical variance was lower than the Poisson reference for both determinantal designs, and the Dirichlet design had lower variance than the Gaussian design across the reported cases.
key_equations:

limitations_stated: The authors note that the Dirichlet model can perform poorly depending on how its intensity parameter factors, particularly when that parameter is a high prime number. They also state that broader comparisons with other point-process and standard design classes, and tests using functions with different regularity or support properties, are needed.
limitations_unstated: The theoretical guarantee depends on a separable kernel, so it does not directly establish the same projection behavior for kernels that model dependence across coordinates or for nonstationary designs. The numerical integration evidence uses one test-function form and one full dimension, so performance on other integration tasks and practical computer experiments is not established here.
future_work_stated: The authors propose comparing these designs with other point-process models, including Gibbs, Matérn, and multivariate orthogonal polynomial ensemble designs, as well as standard Halton, Sobol, and quasi-Monte Carlo designs. They also propose studying test functions with different regularity and with non-compact support.
future_work_unstated: Further work could investigate projection guarantees for nonseparable kernels and designs subject to practical constraints on factor levels or run selection. Sequential updating and validation on real computer experiments would also test whether the reported variance advantages persist beyond the simulated integration examples.

summary: The paper develops multilevel nonregular fractional factorial designs for screening and estimating effects of quantitative factors. key_results: For the proposed transformed designs, the authors prove that the third beta measure is zero for the shift specified by their formula; under stated conditions, this shift is the unique one with that property. In tables for 25-, 49-, and 121-run designs, the proposed designs have zero third beta measure and generally smaller fourth beta measures than the regular and linearly permuted comparisons. In a 25-run, three-factor example, estimated quadratic-term variances decrease by up to 14.9% and bilinear-term variances by up to 19.6% relative to the linearly permuted design, and the proposed design also has less bias in estimated linear effects under the examined omitted third-order terms. For the 121-run, 12-factor comparison, the proposed design has better reported space-filling values than the maximum-projection design and its collapsed version for projection dimensions up to 11; the collapsed design is marginally better at dimension 12. limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons cover selected designs and run sizes, with the space-filling benchmark focused on one 121-run, 12-factor example; they do not establish performance across a broad range of practical settings. summary: The paper designs battery experiments to estimate parameters of the Single Particle Model with electrolyte dynamics (SPMe), a reduced electrochemical model intended for battery control and state estimation. The objective is to make the parameter estimates more accurate by minimizing their estimated uncertainty. The method calculates how voltage outputs respond to the parameters, then optimizes the applied current using an A-optimal criterion that minimizes the trace of the estimated parameter covariance matrix. To reduce the computation required for long experiments, it designs an input in segments and combines them into a complete experiment. Simulations show that this approach estimates parameters faster than constant-current and multistep discharge procedures, and improves voltage prediction when the more detailed Pseudo-Two-Dimensional (P2D) model is treated as the simulated battery.
key_results: With the SPMe as the simulated plant, the optimized input produced low parameter-estimate error after the first 1,000-second experiment, while the standard approaches took longer to converge. After the first experiment, the reported parameter variances for the optimized design were between 0.00005 and 0.006; those for constant-current discharge ranged from 0.01 to 14.88, and those for multistep discharge ranged from 0.0166 to 0.8118. After 10 experiments, the sensitivity condition number was 577 for the optimized design, compared with 31,963 for constant-current discharge and 260 for multistep discharge; the corresponding collinearity indices were 152, 7,548, and 110. For a 200-second design problem, splitting the input into 4 segments reduced reported computation time from 68.51 seconds to 18.30 seconds, with the scaled covariance trace changing from 0.020 to 0.025. In the P2D simulation, the optimized design gave the best voltage-prediction result on the validation profile and produced physically meaningful parameter estimates sooner than the two standard approaches.

limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses a specific seven-parameter set, fixed sampling and operating settings, and simulated measurement noise, so performance may differ across cells and real test conditions. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the design on physical cells across multiple cell types and operating conditions, including practical limits on current, voltage, temperature, and test duration. summary: The paper introduces sequential randomized trials as a design for learning how to sequence, time, and personalize interventions in scaled digital learning environments. The trial included 8,681 learners in India and the United States. The findings suggest that email effects differed across learner groups and weeks, but many comparisons were uncertain, so the study provides exploratory evidence rather than a confirmed best intervention.
key_results: The Problem-based Email Reminder Coursera Study included 8,681 unique learners: 3,455 in India and 5,226 in the United States; 22,073 emails were sent. In India, emails in weeks two and three generally had positive effects on returning to the course, and no-problem emails were as effective as or more effective than problem emails; week two appeared to be a useful time to send reminders. For learners in the United States, effects were mostly not statistically significant, except for a cultural-problem email in week three, and some estimates suggested emails could reduce return activity. Email open rates were 41.7% for United States learners and 27.0% for Indian learners, with a reported p-value below 0.001, despite the greater apparent email benefit among Indian learners. Most sequence comparisons had overlapping confidence intervals, so the authors describe the differences as suggestive rather than significant; compared with assigning each learner once to a fixed condition, repeated randomization allowed comparisons of many more treatment sequences and time-specific effects.

They also note that the large number of possible treatment sequences makes sample-size and power planning important, and that their comparison with single randomization used only one example design.
limitations_unstated: The experiment was conducted in one course and included only learners identified as being in India or the United States, so its findings may not generalize to other courses, populations, or intervention types. future_work_stated: The authors propose using the exploratory findings to narrow the treatment options, running a second sequential randomized trial with fewer treatments, and then comparing a promising adaptive email sequence with no email in a confirmatory single-randomization trial. They describe combining sequential randomization with adaptive designs and using different randomization timing or trigger-based assignment as further possibilities.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the selected email strategy in other courses and learner populations, while measuring learning and completion outcomes in addition to clicks. summary: The paper presents a Bayesian experimental design method for implicit models, where the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated. Its objective is to choose designs that maximize expected information gain about model parameters. The method uses Likelihood-Free Inference by Ratio Estimation (LFIRE) to estimate density ratios and approximate mutual information from simulated data. It uses Bayesian optimisation (BO) to search for high-utility designs with fewer evaluations than grid search, including in higher-dimensional design problems. Tests on two simulated epidemiological models show that the approach identifies informative measurement times and produces parameter estimates with credible intervals containing the generating values in the reported examples.
key_results: For the Death Model, Bayesian optimisation using LFIRE selected a measurement time of 1.06 with utility 1.359; grid search using LFIRE selected 1.10 with utility 1.350, while analytic grid search selected 1.40 with utility 1.347. For an eight-dimensional Death Model design, the authors report reaching an optimum after around 20 utility evaluations, compared with 76,904,685 evaluations for a four-dimensional grid with 40 points per dimension. In the one-dimensional SIR Model, grid search and Bayesian optimisation selected times of 0.40 and 0.44, respectively; for the eight-measurement design, utility was 1.08 at equally spaced times and 1.10 at the optimized times, with convergence in around 15 evaluations. For that eight-measurement SIR design, posterior mean estimates were 0.13 for the infection rate and 0.05 for the recovery rate, and the reported 95% credibility intervals were 0.02 to 0.18 and 0.02 to 0.07, respectively; both intervals contained the generating values.
key_equations:
Optimal design: \[d^* = \arg\max_d U(d)\] The symbol d is a candidate design, d-star is the optimal design, U(d) is its expected utility, and arg max means to choose the design with the greatest utility.

Information objective: \[U(d)=I(\theta;y\mid d)\] U(d) is the expected utility at design d, I is mutual information, theta is the model parameter or parameter vector, and y is the data conditioned on the design.

Monte Carlo utility approximation: \[U(d)\approx\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\theta),\,y\sim p(y\mid d,\theta)}[\log r(d,y,\theta)]\] U(d) is the expected utility, the expectation averages over prior draws of theta and simulated data y at design d, p denotes the prior or simulator distribution, log is the natural logarithm, and r is the estimated density ratio.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the applicability of high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation in hundreds of dimensions remains to be investigated. Posterior estimates from LFIRE are approximate, and the authors say that a more general characterization of how this approximation affects mutual information would be informative.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated data from only two epidemiological models, so it does not establish performance on real experiments or on other application areas. The multi-measurement designs require ordered measurement times, and the reported eight-measurement examples do not test other practical constraints on when measurements can be taken.
future_work_stated: The authors propose applying the method to other implicit models, including temporal and spatial models from neurobiology, cell biology, and physics. They also identify incorporating experimental cost or time and developing sequential designs that update beliefs after each outcome as valuable directions for further work.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess robustness when the assumed simulator or prior is misspecified, and validate the selected designs in real experiments. It could also evaluate the method under practical scheduling or resource constraints and compare it with additional design criteria beyond information gain.

summary: The paper develops designs for experiments in which a treatment is an ordering of a fixed number of components, with the goal of estimating how the order of each component pair affects the response. summary: The paper develops iterative algorithms for finding continuous experimental designs for linear regression models. Its objectives are D-optimality (determinant-based) and A-optimality (average-variance-based), both aimed at estimating model parameters precisely. The algorithms update the design density directly over the continuous design space rather than first discretizing that space. The authors prove monotonic convergence and convergence to an optimal design for the D-optimal algorithm under a stated boundedness condition, while they support the A-optimal algorithm with numerical results and conjecture monotonic convergence. Four numerical settings illustrate the designs and compare their support points and weights with theoretical values and results from a randomized exchange method.
key_results: The paper reports that its algorithms converged in all four numerical settings, but it gives no numerical runtime or speedup measurements. In the quadratic model on a disk, the theoretical D-optimal allocation places 1/6 of the weight at the center and 5/6 uniformly on the boundary. For the quadratic model on a square, the reported design has 9 support points; the proposed D-optimal weights closely match the theoretical weights, such as 0.1457 versus 0.1457 at each corner. For the quadratic model on a three-dimensional cube, the proposed method identifies 27 support points, and its reported D-optimal weights are close to theoretical values; the comparison also shows that randomized exchange weights can vary across points and runs.
key_equations:
Linear regression model: \[y(w)=x(w)^T\beta+\varepsilon(w)\] The response y at design point w is the transpose of the regressor vector x at w multiplied by the unknown parameter vector beta, plus random error epsilon at w.

Design objectives and density constraint: \[\min_f\{-\log\det M(f),\ \operatorname{tr}(M(f)^{-1})\},\quad \int_E f(w)\,dw=1,\quad f(w)\ge0\] The first objective is minimized for D-optimality and the second for A-optimality, separately; f is the design density, M(f) is its information matrix, E is the design space, and w is a point in that space; the density is nonnegative and integrates to one.

Iterative density updates: \[f_{n+1}(w)=\begin{cases}f_n(w)x(w)^TM(f_n)^{-1}x(w)/p,&\text{D}\cr f_n(w)\{1+(p-1)\operatorname{tr}[M(f_n)^{-1}x(w)x(w)^TM(f_n)^{-1}]/\operatorname{tr}[M(f_n)^{-1}]\}/p,&\text{A}\end{cases}\] At iteration n, the next density f at point w is updated by the first expression for D-optimality or the second for A-optimality; x is the regressor vector, M is the information matrix for the current density, and p is the number of parameters.

limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation covers four polynomial-regression settings and comparisons with randomized exchange, so it does not establish performance across a broad range of models, design spaces, or competing algorithms. future_work_unstated: Future work could establish convergence conditions for the A-optimal update and compare computational cost and accuracy against more methods over varied models and design spaces. summary: The paper develops optimal test designs for estimating a person's ability in the generalized partial credit model, assuming item thresholds and discrimination parameters are already known. It first derives the design maximizing Fisher information for a known ability, then considers Bayesian criteria that average performance over a weight distribution for ability. The locally optimal probability pattern puts equal probability on the first and last response categories and zero probability on intermediate categories, making the model equivalent to the two-parameter logistic model. Because that pattern cannot be attained with finite thresholds when there are more than two categories, the authors also examine Bayesian optimality and its dependence on the weight distribution. Their examples show that the one-point design can be Bayesian optimal for fixed discrimination and sufficiently concentrated symmetric weights, but not in all cases when discrimination and threshold can both vary.
key_results: For a fixed number of more than two response categories, the locally optimal design does not exist at finite thresholds; it can only be approached as the thresholds move toward limiting values. In an illustrative four-category item comparison, the information of the limiting optimal design was about 2.86 times higher at medium ability and about 3.75 times higher at low or high ability than for the example item. With discrimination fixed at one, the reported critical scales for the expected-log-information and negative-expected-inverse-information criteria were, respectively, 2.5757 divided by J and 2.1773 divided by J for uniform weights, 1.683 divided by J and 1.177 divided by J for normal weights, and 1 divided by J and 0.603 divided by J for logistic weights. Numerical sensitivity checks for three-category items suggest that the necessary conditions are sufficient for both criteria under uniform and normal weights, and for the expected-log-information criterion under logistic weights; for the other logistic criterion, the necessary condition appears not to be sufficient. In numerical examples for the dichotomous model with both threshold and discrimination varying, the optimal one-point designs were not Bayesian optimal for the uniform, normal, or logistic weight distributions examined.

Bayesian design criteria: \[\psi_0=E_{\Pi}[\log M(\theta,\tau,\alpha)],\qquad \psi_{-1}=-E_{\Pi}[M(\theta,\tau,\alpha)^{-1}]\] Psi sub zero is expected log information, psi sub minus one is negative expected inverse information, E under Pi means expectation over the ability weight distribution, and M is Fisher information for ability theta under thresholds tau and discrimination parameters alpha.

limitations_stated: The authors note that the locally optimal design for a fixed number of more than two categories does not exist at finite thresholds, and that items engineered to make intermediate responses nearly impossible may be impractical and undermine the purpose of partial credit. They also identify unresolved cases, including asymmetric ability weights, optimal sampling designs, and Bayesian designs for alternative ordinal models.
limitations_unstated: The conclusions rely on the specified generalized partial credit model, known item parameters, and an asymptotically efficient estimator; they do not establish performance when those assumptions fail. Numerical sensitivity investigations are limited to items with up to three response categories, and the paper offers no validation using data from actual tests.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying designs under asymmetric ability weight distributions and deriving optimal sampling designs for the generalized partial credit model. They also call for further design work on alternative ordinal models, including Bayesian designs for the graded response model and designs for the sequential model.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare the theoretical designs with constrained designs whose thresholds and discrimination levels are feasible in real test development.
