summary: The paper develops approximation algorithms for choosing a fixed number of experiments to estimate an unknown parameter vector in a linear model with Gaussian measurement errors. It considers the determinant-based design objective, which corresponds to reducing the volume of the confidence ellipsoid for the estimation error. The algorithms first solve a continuous convex relaxation and then use randomized selection based on the relaxed weights, with separate methods for designs that allow repeated experiments and those that do not. The authors also derive deterministic versions of the randomized methods. Their main finding is that constant-factor guarantees hold for both variants, and stronger guarantees are available when the number of selected experiments is sufficiently large relative to the parameter dimension.
key_results: For designs with and without repetitions, the proposed methods guarantee an objective value of at least one divided by Euler's number times the optimum; deterministic implementations retain the same guarantees. Without repetitions, the asymptotic sampling method guarantees a factor of one minus the target tolerance when the run size is at least four times the parameter dimension divided by the tolerance, plus twelve times the inverse squared tolerance times the logarithm of its inverse. With repetitions, the corresponding guarantee holds when the run size is at least the parameter dimension minus one divided by the target tolerance. These are theoretical results, not empirical comparisons; the paper reports randomized implementations with running times of order n squared or linear in n for the main methods, and more costly deterministic implementations.

summary: This paper develops approximation algorithms for selecting a fixed number of measurement vectors to minimize average estimation variance, the A-optimal design objective. It studies designs both with and without repeated selections, using a convex relaxation to obtain fractional selection weights. The authors introduce proportional volume sampling, which weights candidate sets using a hard-core probability measure and the determinant of their information matrix. They show how approximate independence properties of the measure yield approximation guarantees and give efficient randomized and deterministic implementations for the proposed sampling methods. Theoretical results establish improved guarantees in several run-size regimes, as well as limits on the relaxation and a hardness result when the number selected equals the vector dimension.
key_results: Without repetitions, the method gives a dimension-factor approximation when the number selected equals the dimension, and a factor of one plus epsilon when the number selected is at least on the order of dimension divided by epsilon plus the logarithm of one over epsilon divided by epsilon squared. The paper compares this latter threshold with prior work requiring a run size on the order of dimension divided by epsilon squared for a factor of one plus epsilon. With repetitions, the guarantee is the number selected divided by the number selected minus the dimension plus one; the authors prove this matches the convex relaxation's integrality gap, and the factor becomes one plus epsilon when the run size is at least the dimension plus dimension divided by epsilon. For the extension with fewer selected vectors than the dimension, they prove a factor equal to the number selected; they also establish that A-optimal design is hard to approximate within a fixed constant when the run size equals the dimension.

summary: The paper develops ascent with quadratic assistance (AQuA), a method for converting approximate designs into high-quality exact designs for linear regression and related design problems. It targets several information objectives, including D-optimality, A-optimality, and I-optimality, and permits linear constraints on the design. The method approximates the criterion quadratically near an optimal or estimated approximate information matrix, then optimizes that approximation over integer-valued run counts. A low-rank property enables a mixed-integer conic quadratic formulation that avoids storing a large quadratic matrix. In the reported examples, this formulation produced designs with efficiency close to competing methods and substantially reduced computation time in large or constrained problems.
key_results: For the constrained three-component mixture model with 861 candidate points, the D-optimal exact design had efficiency 0.98374 and took 8.56 seconds with the proposed conic formulation, compared with efficiencies 0.98377 and 0.98373 and times of 616.91 and 625.53 seconds for the mixed-integer second-order cone and direct integer quadratic approaches. For the same model under I-optimality, the conic formulation achieved efficiency 0.99647 in 4.54 seconds, compared with 0.99627 in 602.96 seconds for the mixed-integer second-order cone approach and 0.98928 in 636.16 seconds for the direct integer quadratic approach. The authors report that the conic reformulation can reduce computation time by as much as two orders of magnitude while producing designs of similar efficiency. In a wine-review data example with 111,534 records, the method selected 42 records under a USD 1,000 price limit and a minimum average quality of 90 points; each of five random starts converged to the same solution in as few as four steps, with each step taking less than four seconds.

summary: This paper develops space-filling designs for computer experiments that aim to identify control settings robust to variation in noise factors. It models the response with a Gaussian process and focuses on accurately estimating control-by-noise interactions, which matter for finding robust settings. The proposed design starts with a cross array, then jitters its points using a maximum projection criterion to improve coverage while preserving the interaction-estimation structure. For normally distributed noise, a double transformation based on a beta distribution with shape parameters of two-thirds spreads design points more than a direct probability transformation. Simulated and manufacturing examples show improved identification of robust settings and clearer estimation of an important interaction, though the reported prediction improvements are mixed.
key_results: In the simulation study, the authors tested 200 cases and used 100 test samples per case to compare designs with 54 runs. Applying the double transformation improved prediction performance for both the maximum-projection Latin hypercube and the jittered cross array; for estimating the robust setting, the double-transformed jittered cross array performed best among the compared designs. In the manufacturing packing-line example, the new design and the existing design each used 91 runs, and their prediction errors were reported as close. The new double-transformed jittered cross array estimated the most significant control-by-noise interaction more accurately than the transformed maximum-projection Latin hypercube; the paper reports no numerical prediction-error or interaction-error values.

summary: The paper develops Bayesian D-optimal designs for pharmaceutical dose-response studies that compare multiple dosing-frequency groups while allowing some model parameters to be shared. The objective is to estimate all parameters accurately while accounting for uncertainty in their values and choosing doses and sample allocation across groups. The authors derive analytical characterizations of saturated designs, which use the minimum number of dose levels needed to estimate the parameters. They treat shared location parameters separately from shared location and scale parameters, and give results for Emax, exponential, and linear-in-log dose-response models. In a numerical example, the saturated design has estimation efficiency close to that of an unrestricted Bayesian design and the locally optimal benchmark across the parameter combinations examined.
key_results: For models with a common location parameter, the authors show that the group with the smallest error variance is used to estimate that common parameter, and derive saturated designs from the optimal designs for the individual models. For two models with common location and scale parameters, they characterize the saturated designs by cases determined by the ratio of group variances and functions of the prior distributions. In the example with two Emax groups and 25 parameter combinations, the saturated design's efficiencies range from 94.25% to 99.81% relative to the locally D-optimal design; the unrestricted Bayesian design's efficiencies range from 96.59% to 99.94%. The saturated design uses four dose levels in total in the example, compared with five for the unrestricted candidate design, while retaining efficiency close to that candidate.
key_equations:
Dose-response model: \[Y_{ij}=f_i(d,\theta)+\epsilon_{ij},\qquad \epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma_i^2)\] The response Y for observation j in group i has mean given by the group-specific function f at dose d and parameter vector theta, with random error epsilon that is normally distributed with mean zero and variance sigma squared for group i.

Bayesian D-optimality criterion: \[\max_{\xi}\int_{\Theta}\log\det\{M(\xi,\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta)\] The design xi is chosen to maximize the prior average of the logarithm of the determinant of information matrix M, with theta ranging over parameter space Theta and pi denoting the prior distribution.

Weights for a saturated design: \[\lambda_i=\frac{m_i}{m},\qquad \omega_{ij}=\frac{1}{m_i}\] In a saturated design, lambda is the fraction of total observations assigned to group i, m_i is the number of dose levels in that group, m is the total number of parameters, and omega is the within-group weight at dose level j.
limitations_stated: The authors show that the saturated design in their numerical example is not globally Bayesian D-optimal. They also note that finding a design optimal among all possible designs is computationally intensive, even with only two administration-frequency groups.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison is limited to two Emax groups, equal variances, a shared design interval, and 25 parameter combinations; it does not establish comparable performance for other settings or models. The methods also rely on the specified nonlinear regression forms, normally distributed errors, and prior distributions, and the paper does not assess how sensitive practical designs are to violations of those assumptions or to operational constraints on dose assignment.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the saturated designs under additional dose-response models, unequal or restricted dose ranges, and practical allocation constraints, and quantify sensitivity to model and prior misspecification. Prospective validation in real dose-finding studies and software that constructs the designs and checks their optimality would also help assess practical use.

summary: The paper develops optimal experimental design methods for linear inverse problems with constraints on the unknown state, using tomographic image reconstruction as its main application. It aims to reduce measurement costs while limiting reconstruction error. One design approach uses a fine grid of candidate measurement settings and a sparsity penalty; another directly optimizes the locations of a fixed number of measurements. The methods use Bayes risk when distributional information is available and empirical Bayes risk when training examples are used instead. The authors derive efficient calculations for the unconstrained case and use interior point methods and implicit differentiation to optimize designs with inequality constraints.
key_results: In simulations using four image datasets, each with 20 training images, adding non-negativity or box constraints generally produced lower reconstruction error and required fewer projections than unconstrained or equality-constrained designs. For rectangles, the non-negativity and box-constrained designs selected projections at 0 and 90 degrees; for pentagons, their selected angles were 25, 64, 99, 136, and 171 degrees, and 27, 62, 99, 134, and 171 degrees, respectively. In the fixed-size design comparison, the authors optimized two projection angles and found that box constraints gave the lowest errors overall across the tested datasets. The paper also shows that increasing the sparsity penalty reduces the number of selected projections, with constrained designs often achieving lower error even with fewer projections; it does not report a single numerical efficiency gain across all cases.
key_equations:
Design objective: \[J(p)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{2}\|\hat f(p)-f_{\mathrm{true}}\|_2^2\right]+R(p)\] Here, p is the design vector, J is the design objective, the expectation is over the uncertain true state and measurement noise, fhat is the estimated state, f_true is the true state, and R is the measurement-cost term; the norm measures squared reconstruction error.

Constrained state estimate: \[\hat f(p)=\arg\min_f\left\{\frac{1}{2}\|M(p)f-d(p)\|_2^2+\frac{\alpha^2}{2}\|L(f-\mu)\|_2^2\right\},\quad C_e f=c_e,\ C_i f\ge c_i\] Here, fhat is the estimate that minimizes the data-fit and regularization terms, f is a candidate state, M(p) is the measurement operator, d(p) is the data, alpha is the regularization weight, L is the regularization operator, mu is the prior mean, and C_e and c_e and C_i and c_i specify equality and inequality constraints.

Sparse design penalty: \[R(p)=\beta\|p\|_1,\quad p\ge 0\] Here, R is the design-cost penalty, beta controls its strength, p is a nonnegative vector of design weights, and the one-norm penalty encourages some weights to be zero.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the empirical-risk approach based on a sample average may not be feasible when the training dataset is very large. Their simplified Bayes-risk formulation is for unconstrained state problems; the empirical formulation is used to incorporate inequality constraints.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation is limited to simulated tomography images and does not validate the selected designs in physical scanning experiments. The fixed-size design examples use only two projection angles, and the empirical studies use small training sets, so performance for larger or more varied real-world datasets is not established.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying integer or binary constraints on design settings, extending the methods to nonlinear inverse problems, and applying them to other domains.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be testing the designs with practical acquisition restrictions, such as minimum spacing between projection angles, measurement-time limits, or dose limits, and validating them with real tomographic data. Further work could also assess how designs behave when training images are unrepresentative and explore sequential selection of measurements as data arrive.

summary: This review examines how to choose simulation or experiment inputs for fitting polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs) by least-squares approximation (LSA). It covers standard random sampling, space-filling designs, quadrature-based sampling, and optimal design of experiments (ODE), including designs aimed at estimating coefficients or improving predictions. The authors propose alphabetic-coherence-optimal sampling, which selects runs using D-, A-, or E-optimal criteria from a candidate set generated by coherence-optimal sampling. They compare methods in three numerical examples: manufactured expansions, a nonlinear oscillator, and lithium-ion battery life prediction. The proposed hybrid approach generally gives the most accurate results, particularly for high-order expansions and when the number of runs is close to the number of coefficients.
key_results: The numerical comparison averages results over 60 independent replications for the manufactured-function example. For a ninth-order oscillator expansion with 220 coefficients, the authors compare 242, 440, and 660 runs; alphabetic-coherence-optimal designs have smaller prediction errors than the other compared methods, especially at 242 runs, and D- and A-optimal variants perform slightly better than the E-optimal variant. In the battery example, a third-order expansion uses 121 runs and its predicted remaining useful life distributions coincide with Monte Carlo results based on 20 × 10^6 solution runs. The authors report that standard Monte Carlo and Latin hypercube sampling can be adequate for low-order expansions when runs number about three to four times the coefficient count, but may perform poorly for high-order expansions even with that oversampling.
key_equations:
Truncated polynomial representation: \[\hat u(\xi)=\sum_{j=1}^{P}\hat c_j\psi_j(\xi)\] The predicted output u-hat at input xi is a sum of P terms, where c-hat-j is the estimated coefficient and psi-j is the jth polynomial basis function.

Weighted least-squares fit: \[\hat c=\arg\min_c\|W(u-\Psi c)\|_2^2\] The estimated coefficient vector c-hat minimizes the squared Euclidean norm of the weighted difference between sampled outputs u and basis predictions Psi c, with W containing sample weights.

Coherence-optimal sampling: \[f_Y(\xi)=c^2f(\xi)B^2(\xi),\qquad w(\xi)=c^{-1}B^{-1}(\xi)\] The sampling density fY is proportional to the input density f times the squared basis bound B, and the weight w is the reciprocal of c times B, where c is a normalization constant.

Sequential alphabetic design selection: \[\xi_{n+1}=\arg\min_{\xi_i\in C\setminus S_n}\phi\!\left(\Psi(S_n\cup\{i\},J)\right)\] The next input xi at step n plus one is selected from candidate set C excluding previously selected points S-n to minimize criterion phi evaluated on the resulting basis matrix Psi using column set J.
limitations_stated: The authors state that current algorithms for alphabetic-optimal design become computationally expensive for large numbers of polynomial coefficients, limiting their use to relatively low-order or low-dimensional expansions. They identify scalable optimization methods for these designs as an open problem.
limitations_unstated: The empirical comparison covers three numerical examples and a selected subset of the reviewed sampling methods, so it does not establish that the reported ranking holds across other models or practical constraints. The hybrid designs also require generating a candidate set and carrying out an optimization procedure, adding design-generation work that may matter when model evaluations are inexpensive or operational constraints restrict allowable runs.
future_work_stated: The authors identify developing scalable optimization techniques for alphabetic-optimal designs as an open research problem. They also mention multi-element generalized polynomial chaos as a possible way to address increasing error over time in the oscillator example, while leaving its discussion outside the paper’s scope.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the hybrid method on real experiments and on constrained run plans, such as designs with bounds, discrete factors, or restricted combinations of settings. It could also evaluate adaptive or sequential use in which new runs are selected using observed model outputs, and provide software that makes the design construction practical at larger coefficient counts.

summary: The paper develops design guidelines for stochastic kriging, a method for predicting the mean response of a noisy computer simulation. It separates prediction inaccuracy into nominal error, numeric error, parameter estimation error, and numeric error in parameter estimation. The authors derive bounds that connect each source of error to design features, including how well distinct sites cover the input space, how far apart they are, and how many runs are replicated at each site. The guidelines also address non-stationary response patterns, changing noise levels, and regression functions. The main finding is that designs should balance space coverage with replication, with more replication favored when noise is large relative to process variation. ࠀ
key_results: In simulations with a fixed total of 72 runs, the preferred balance shifted toward more replication as noise increased and toward more distinct, space-filling sites as noise decreased. For example, at noise variance 0.5, the MaxPro design with four replications had average maximum squared prediction error 0.192; at noise variance 0.01, its lowest reported error was 0.010 with one replication. In the input-varying noise study, with 18 distinct sites, parameter-estimation-guided allocation had error 0.113 when replications varied by location, compared with 0.141 with constant replication; the corresponding values were 0.125 versus 0.170 with 24 sites and 0.125 versus 0.190 with 36 sites. The study used 300 simulated Gaussian-process draws for its prediction-error comparisons, and the authors report that the proposed bounds gave useful guidance for choosing replication levels.

Stochastic output model: \[y(x)=f(x)+\epsilon(x)\] The observed output y at input x is the underlying mean response f plus random noise epsilon.

limitations_stated: The paper provides upper bounds rather than exact comparisons of expected error, and two designs with the same bound may perform differently. The authors do not analyze error from model misspecification, and they do not explicitly develop projection-design properties. They also note that characterizing non-stationarity across the input space and optimizing designs under complex criteria can be challenging.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons use simulated Gaussian-process responses in a small number of two-dimensional settings, so they do not establish how well the guidelines transfer to high-dimensional or real simulation studies. The bounds and example allocations also depend on assumed covariance and noise structures; the paper does not test how sensitive the recommendations are when those structures or their parameter values are wrong.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest using localized residual resampling when the Gaussian noise model fits poorly, and adapting the non-stationary model to represent changes in process variability. They also suggest using the numeric-error bounds to identify and remove design points that cause ill-conditioning, and using projected space-filling designs when some inputs are inactive.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the design guidelines in real engineering simulations and across higher-dimensional problems, including sensitivity to misspecified covariance and noise models. Further work could develop software that automates the replication and site-selection trade-off, and assess sequential updates as simulation results arrive.

summary: This software paper presents acebayes, an R package for finding Bayesian optimal experimental designs. The package applies approximate coordinate exchange (ACE) to maximize expected utility for goals including parameter estimation, model selection, and prediction. It builds a Gaussian process (GP) approximation to expected utility for one design coordinate at a time, then searches for a promising value of that coordinate while holding the others fixed. The package supports user-defined utility functions as well as tailored functions for generalized linear and nonlinear models. Its examples show that the approach can improve design objectives in problems with more design coordinates than methods discussed as existing in the paper.
key_results: For the compartmental pharmacokinetic example, the final design had 13 unique sampling times rather than 18, and its reported relative D-efficiency was 103.0255 percent compared with the Phase I design. In the logistic-regression example, the normal-based parameter-estimation design had mean approximate utility of -8.056569, compared with -10.61123 for the pseudo-Bayesian A-optimal design; the reported relative A-efficiency between the selected and first-run designs was 118.4983 percent. For chemical model selection, the estimated probability of selecting the data-generating model rose from about 81 percent for the starting design to about 88 percent for the optimized design. In the prediction example, approximate utility increased from 92.41169 to 95.86214 while total placement cost fell from 6.653732 to 3.081133; these are illustrative examples rather than a broad comparative benchmark.

summary: This paper studies an extensible randomized design for numerical integration, formed by mapping scrambled van der Corput sequence points through a Hilbert space-filling curve. The objective is to estimate integrals over a multidimensional unit cube and to establish when the standardized estimation error is asymptotically normal. The authors show that the method acts as a stratified design, with one random point in each curve-defined region. They prove normality for continuously differentiable functions and for certain discontinuous functions, under stated conditions. For smooth nonconstant functions, the variance rate matches the previously established upper-bound rate.
key_results: For smooth nonconstant functions, the paper establishes a variance lower bound of order n to the power negative one minus two divided by d, matching the upper-bound rate reported from earlier work. The numerical study used 1,000 independent replications and sample size 16,384 for its standardized-error density comparisons; the Hilbert-curve method appeared nearly normal for the tested smooth, piecewise-smooth, and indicator functions. limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons cover only a small set of constructed functions and dimensions 2 and 8, so they do not establish how well the theoretical results describe a broad range of practical integration problems. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method on real engineering simulation models and compare practical confidence-interval coverage, not only error-density shapes. summary: This paper develops algebraic tests for deciding whether a qualitative fractional factorial design can be made regular by permuting factor levels. It studies symmetric orthogonal arrays with a prime number of levels, rather than optimizing a response model or a design criterion. One approach represents level permutations with polynomials and uses polynomial algebra to test whether two fractions are equivalent. A second approach represents strength-two arrays with Latin squares and checks whether suitable level permutations make the square rank one. Examples show that the methods can identify arrays equivalent to regular fractions and rule out arrays that cannot be made regular.
key_results: For five-level, three-factor arrays with 25 runs, the paper examines three examples: one is regular, a second can be transformed into a regular array by level permutations, and a third cannot. In the five-level permutation search, the authors reduce the candidates on the third factor from 120 permutations to six relevant ones. A polynomial-algebra calculation for one example took 29 seconds and produced a Gröbner basis with 91 elements; the calculation recovered permutations establishing equivalence to a regular fraction. The authors also give a seven-level strength-two array constructed to remain nonregular under level permutations.

limitations_stated: The methods are developed for symmetric designs with a prime number of levels. The authors say that nonprime-level and mixed designs require a different approach because several properties used for roots of unity do not hold for those cases.
limitations_unstated: The worked examples are limited, mainly involving five-level arrays, and the paper gives little evidence about computational performance as the number of factors or levels grows. The tests classify exact arrays under level permutations, but do not evaluate how the resulting regularity relates to response-model adequacy or practical restrictions on which permutations can be used.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the methods to nonprime-level and mixed designs, developing the concept of mean aberration for permutations compatible with a design matrix, and providing efficient software packages for symbolic and statistical software.
future_work_unstated: Further work could benchmark the polynomial and Latin-square procedures over larger sets of arrays and report how computation scales with the number of factors and levels. It could also address practical restrictions on level relabeling and test the methods on real experiments, including whether the recovered regular structure improves subsequent analysis.

summary: This paper introduces MIMIX, a Bayesian model for analyzing high-dimensional microbiome count data from designed experiments. It aims to test whether treatments affect the microbiome as a whole, estimate effects on individual operational taxonomic units (OTUs), quantify sources of variability, and identify groups of taxa with related responses. The model conditions on each sample’s total read count and uses a multinomial likelihood, factor analysis to represent dependence among taxa, and sparse Bayesian priors for treatment effects. The authors evaluate it in simulations and in a replicated two-by-two nutrient-supplement and herbivore-exclusion experiment on grass-associated fungi. They report improved detection and estimation of sparse treatment effects compared with methods that do not model cross-taxon dependence, and identify a nutrient-supplement effect in the real experiment.
key_results: In simulations covering 18 combinations of signal density and variance, with 50 replications per combination, MIMIX and its version without factors generally had greater power for global treatment tests than PERMANOVA, with type I error usually at or below 0.05. For local treatment effects under medium error variance, MIMIX’s true positive rate ranged from 81.6% to 97.0%, compared with 59.6% to 87.4% without factors; MIMIX also generally had lower estimation error when treatment effects were present. In the real experiment, five-fold cross-validation favored MIMIX over the version without factors for 69% of the test-data log-likelihood differences. For the 166 samples and 2,662 fungal OTUs, MIMIX found strong evidence for a nutrient-supplement effect on overall composition, no detected herbivore-exclusion or interaction effect, and 84 OTUs (3.2%) with nutrient-effect credible intervals excluding zero.

Conditional multinomial model: \[Y_i\mid m_i,\phi_i\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(m_i,\phi_i),\quad \phi_i=\operatorname{softmax}(\theta_i)\] Y_i is the taxon-count vector for sample i, m_i is its total read count, phi_i is its vector of expected taxon proportions, theta_i is its latent log-abundance vector, and i indexes samples.

Global treatment-effect decision rule: \[\Pr(\boldsymbol{\beta}\ne\mathbf{0}\mid\mathbf{Y})>0.9\] Beta is the vector of treatment-effect coefficients, 0 is the zero vector, Y is the observed count data, and 0.9 is the posterior-probability threshold used to reject the global no-effect hypothesis.
limitations_stated: The authors note that using the same factor loadings for fixed effects, random effects, and residual variation is a strong assumption. They also state that MIMIX is not suited to longitudinal studies with repeated measures and that substantially larger taxon counts could make computation time and memory more pressing concerns, potentially requiring a reconstructed sampling scheme. The taxonomic assignments in the motivating data are preliminary.
limitations_unstated: The real-data demonstration concerns one fungal microbiome, one plant species, four central United States sites, and samples collected at one time, so it provides limited evidence about performance across other organisms, settings, or experiment types. The comparisons are also narrow: simulations compare against PERMANOVA and a version of MIMIX without factors, while the real-data comparison is primarily between the two MIMIX versions and PERMANOVA.
future_work_stated: The authors say that MIMIX’s features will need to scale as microbiome experiments become more complex. They specifically note that larger taxon collections may require rebuilding the posterior sampling scheme, and that the current model does not handle longitudinal repeated-measures studies.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the model on independent experiments involving different organisms and treatment structures, including practical constraints such as unequal replication or restricted randomization. Comparisons with additional joint and taxon-specific models, alongside validation of predicted treatment responses in new experiments, would clarify when the factor model is most useful.

summary: The paper introduces rotated sphere packing designs for computer experiments that need points spread through a multidimensional input region. The construction starts with a lattice based on known sphere coverings, then scales, rotates, translates, and crops its points to obtain the requested design size. In two dimensions, the authors use a particular rotation angle; in higher dimensions, they try random rotations and retain the design with the best projective uniformity. The designs aim to support prediction and numerical integration, and the paper gives theoretical properties, simulations, and R code. The results show strong distance-based performance in low dimensions, but weaker performance at higher dimensions and near the region’s boundaries.
key_results: In simulations with dimensions from 2 through 10 and a run size of 10 times the number of dimensions, rotated sphere packing designs had the best minimum pairwise distance through 5 dimensions, the best integrated prediction error through 3 dimensions, and the best prediction error over the inner region through 7 dimensions. For 8 dimensions and 80 runs, their projected distance performance was poor for one- and two-dimensional projections but comparable to other methods for projections of at least 3 dimensions; maximum-projection Latin hypercube designs generally performed best on the projected-distance measure. In two dimensions, the paper proves a discrepancy rate of order the inverse of the run size times its logarithm, and gives one-dimensional projection gap bounds of at least 0.289 divided by the run size and at most 2.155 divided by the run size. For higher run sizes, the method was best for integrated prediction error at 5 dimensions with at least 400 runs; generation was fast through 7 dimensions in the reported timing study, but took substantially longer above 8 dimensions.

limitations_stated: The authors state that boundary and especially corner prediction distances are not controlled and can be poor, reducing prediction accuracy over the full input region. limitations_unstated: The comparisons are simulation-based and use a correctly specified Gaussian process correlation model with selected parameter values, so performance under model misspecification is not established. future_work_stated: The authors propose improving boundary uniformity, finding useful rotation angles for dimensions above two, and studying designs built from densest packings. They also propose adapting the construction to design regions other than the unit cube.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the designs under misspecified prediction models and across a broader range of response functions and practical constraints. It could also develop sequential versions that add runs over time and assess performance in real computer experiments.

summary: This paper develops theoretical consistency results for sequential experiments guided by Gaussian process models. The construction treats the uncertainty measure after each observation as a supermartingale, which allows the authors to derive general conditions for convergence. The main finding is that these strategies consistently reduce their stated uncertainty measures under the paper’s assumptions, including expected improvement with continuous Gaussian process sample paths.
key_results: For quasi-stepwise-uncertainty-reduction designs, the paper proves almost-sure convergence of the uncertainty measures for all four studied strategies; the results also establish convergence in the integrable-mean sense for the estimators and optimization quantities considered. For excursion estimation, integrated Bernoulli variance yields consistent estimation of both the excursion set and its measure, while excursion-volume variance guarantees consistency for the volume but not generally for the set itself. For optimization, the knowledge-gradient strategy consistently identifies the maximum, and expected improvement consistently drives its uncertainty to zero and its estimated maximum and current best value to the true maximum. The expected-improvement result removes the earlier no-empty-ball covariance restriction; the paper presents its excursion-estimation consistency proofs as the first for these Gaussian-process strategies.

limitations_unstated: The guarantees assume that the function being studied is generated by the Gaussian process model used to construct the design, with compact input space and continuous sample paths; model misspecification is not evaluated. The paper gives asymptotic proofs rather than finite-budget performance evidence, and it does not assess the computational or practical effects of constrained experiment locations or imperfect criterion optimization beyond allowing increasingly accurate quasi-minimization.
future_work_stated: The authors propose further study of convergence rates for stepwise uncertainty reduction strategies.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test these guarantees when the assumed Gaussian process model is misspecified and in real experiments with restrictions on feasible locations, cost, or replication. summary: The paper develops a finite-population approach to estimating causal treatment contrasts in randomized experiments with multiple treatments. It covers general assignment mechanisms, including stratified and split-plot randomization, unequal replications, and other restrictions on assignment. The method uses unbiased estimators of treatment means and known assignment probabilities, then uses a matrix-based variance decomposition to identify conditions under which the variance can be estimated without bias. Those conditions can be weaker than strict additivity of treatment effects. The authors also show that the conventional Neymanian variance estimator minimizes the worst-case bias under the stated criterion when all second-order assignment probabilities are positive.
key_results: The theory shows that a variance estimator can be unbiased under generalized additivity, a condition that may be weaker than strict additivity, provided the assignment mechanism also meets the required second-order probability condition. When all second-order assignment probabilities are positive, the Neymanian choice of matrix minimizes the maximum possible bias among the considered choices. In simulations, the authors generated 100 populations for each of six models with 50 units; under the model with within-stratum additivity but not strict additivity, the strict-additivity estimator had a median positive bias of 0.176, while the stratum-based estimator had zero bias. limitations_unstated: The variance results depend on the assumed potential-outcome conditions and on known assignment probabilities; in practice, the generalized additivity condition involves outcomes that are not all observed and may not be verifiable. summary: The paper develops a method for designing finite-sample experiments to estimate regression parameters when observations have correlated Gaussian errors. It first derives the best linear unbiased estimator for a continuous-time model, focusing on triangular covariance kernels that can be transformed to Brownian motion. It then chooses discrete estimator weights to make the finite-sample estimator approximate the continuous-time estimator, and selects design points by minimizing a trace-based error criterion. In the examples, the new estimator and its designs are close in efficiency to the finite-sample best linear unbiased estimator. The method also performs substantially better than the earlier approach used for comparison, especially in the multi-parameter examples.
key_results: In the one-parameter examples with five observations and a uniform design, the new estimator's efficiencies were 99.798 percent for the quadratic function, 99.783 percent for the shifted quadratic function, and 98.416 percent for the fourth-power function; the corresponding earlier-method values were 99.582, 99.346, and 92.662 percent. In the three-parameter examples, the new estimator's efficiencies under optimal designs were 96.71 and 96.65 percent for the two kernels, close to the best linear unbiased estimator's 96.77 and 96.72 percent; the earlier method achieved 82.14 and 79.60 percent. For the four-parameter examples, optimal-design efficiencies for the new estimator were 83.40 and 82.95 percent, compared with 70.91 and 71.57 percent for the earlier method. The paper reports that uniform designs are already highly efficient in the one-parameter examples and for the three-parameter examples, while multi-parameter designs were obtained numerically using particle swarm optimization.

limitations_stated: The authors note that the standard formulas become degenerate when the covariance kernel gives zero variance at the lower endpoint, so that case requires a separate treatment. limitations_unstated: The construction depends on a correctly specified regression function and covariance kernel, and the paper does not investigate how misspecification affects the weights or designs. Numerical comparisons are limited to selected models and five-observation examples; the multi-parameter optimal designs require numerical optimization, whose practical stability and computational burden are not assessed.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess robustness when the covariance kernel or regression functions are estimated rather than known, and evaluate designs under practical constraints such as restricted sampling times. Testing the method in real experiments and studying sequential updates to the design would also extend the paper's theoretical and numerical evaluation.

summary: The paper constructs optimal choice designs for two-level experiments under the multinomial logit model, assuming that the options are equally attractive before their attributes are considered. Its objectives are to estimate main effects while allowing for two-factor interactions, and to estimate main effects together with selected two- or higher-order interactions. The constructions use Hadamard matrices, complements, and generators to balance the information for the effects of interest. The paper gives designs for different numbers of alternatives per choice set and factors, including constructions that need relatively few choice sets. It establishes universal optimality theoretically rather than evaluating the designs with experimental data.
key_results: The authors show that their designs are universally optimal under the stated model and are therefore also optimal under several standard estimation criteria. Their table reports that choice sets of size four use the fewest choice sets among the listed sizes for each model setup shown. For a four-factor example, they give a design with four choice sets of size four for estimating all main effects and specified two- and higher-order interactions; the paper contrasts this with a cited design using 80 choice sets of size two for all main effects and all two-factor interactions, so the effect sets differ. The paper also reports that, for the broader main effects model, odd-sized choice sets require twice as many choice sets as the main effects model in the cases described in its discussion.

limitations_unstated: The constructions rely on two-level factors, equally attractive options, and the multinomial logit model, so the results may not carry over to other choice models or unequal baseline attractiveness. summary: The paper introduces privacy sets as a way to express hard constraints for space-filling experimental designs. It presents the Privacy Sets Algorithm (PSA), a heuristic that searches for designs while allowing temporary violations of those constraints during design changes. The authors apply the method to Bridge designs for linear regression models, using D-optimality for parameter estimation, and to constrained regions using the average reciprocal distance (ARD) criterion. The algorithm starts with a permissible design, then tests candidate changes and uses greedy additions to restore a full, permissible design. In the reported numerical comparisons, PSA found higher D-criterion values than the competing Bridge-design algorithm in all four tested cases.
key_results: For two factors and 21 runs, the paper reports that the competing algorithm’s relative efficiencies versus PSA’s designs were 0.79, 0.82, 0.96, and 0.96 across the four tested combinations of regression model and minimum spacing. In a further comparison for dimensions 2, 4, 6, and 8, with 21, 41, 61, and 81 runs respectively, PSA significantly outperformed the competing algorithm in all four cases; the paper does not give exact criterion values in the text. For six factors and 32 points, the competing designs were slightly better on the reported nearest-point distance space-filling measure, while PSA designs had better D-criterion values. The constrained-region examples use 100 runs and demonstrate PSA designs optimized for different ARD projection settings; the paper reports the resulting criterion values in a table.

D-optimality criterion: \[\Phi_D(\xi)=\det(M(\xi))^{1/m},\qquad M(\xi)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in\xi}f(x)f(x)^\top\] The D-criterion Phi_D is the determinant of the standardized information matrix M raised to the power one over m; m is the number of regression-function components, N is the run count, f(x) is the regression vector at design point x, and the superscript top denotes transpose.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the choice of grid density involves a compromise: a smaller grid can accelerate the algorithm but may reduce design quality. They also note that rejection sampling can become less effective depending on the constrained region and the number of dimensions, and that the grid must be chosen so a full permissible design exists.
limitations_unstated: The algorithm is a heuristic local search and the paper gives no guarantee that it will find a globally optimal design or a reproducible level of solution quality. future_work_stated: The authors identify extensions to the MaxPro criterion and other useful extensions as subjects for future research.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess the method on physical experiments and on constraints that arise in practical operations, including run-order or resource restrictions. summary: This review surveys experimental designs and analysis methods for screening input variables, with particular attention to numerical models whose outputs may depend on many variables. It describes factorial and fractional factorial designs, group screening, space-filling samples, and model-free methods based on elementary effects, alongside linear and Gaussian process models. The authors compare six screening approaches on two test functions with 20 inputs, one having six active variables and the other ten. In those examples, elementary-effect screening was the most effective and robust overall, while the highly economical supersaturated and definitive screening designs performed poorly. The study also shows that effective screening can require substantially more runs when the model is less sparse or has complex effects.
key_results: In the comparison of two functions with 20 inputs, the authors conclude that at least 40 runs were needed for effective screening, with more runs needed when factor sparsity did not hold. The elementary-effects method identified all active variables in the second example with 84 runs; systematic fractional replicate designs identified all active variables in both examples at a sensitivity-index threshold of 0.01 using 42 runs, with no type I errors in those reported results. Gaussian process methods generally performed well at 84 or 200 runs, but were unreliable at 16 runs; for the second example, one method had sensitivity 0.80 at 84 runs and both reached 1 at 200 runs. The supersaturated design using 16 runs had sensitivity 0.50 and false discovery rate 0.40 for the first example, and sensitivity 0.60 and false discovery rate 0.60 for the second; the 41-run definitive screening design also had low sensitivity for the second example.

Elementary-effect screening summaries: \[\mu_i=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{j=1}^{r}EE_i(x_j),\qquad \mu_i^*=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{j=1}^{r}|EE_i(x_j)|\] Mu_i is the mean elementary effect, mu_i* is the mean absolute elementary effect, r is the number of trajectories, and x_j is the starting setting for trajectory j.

limitations_stated: The comparison uses only two test functions, and the authors note that changing the functions can substantially reduce the effectiveness of some methods. They caution that small screening experiments can fail when factor sparsity does not hold or when the assumed surrogate model is too simple; they also identify cancellation and aliasing as risks for factorial methods.
limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison uses deterministic functions and a single generated data set for each design, so it does not quantify run-to-run variation in performance across a broader collection of models. Some results depend on visually selected variables or chosen thresholds, and the comparisons do not establish how those decisions would transfer to noisy physical processes or practical operating constraints.
future_work_stated: The authors identify further research on design choices for Gaussian process screening and on extensions of Gaussian process models for high-dimensional inputs. They also recommend sequential screening where practical: use a small initial experiment, such as elementary-effects screening, followed by targeted experiments and Gaussian process model building on the retained variables.
future_work_unstated: A broader benchmark could evaluate the methods across many simulated and real engineering systems, including noisy responses and different levels of nonlinearity, while repeating designs to measure variability. Further work could also compare prespecified decision rules and practical constraints on factor settings, and test sequential follow-up strategies in real experiments.

summary: This paper surveys online and sequential experiment design using stochastic multi-armed bandits, where each treatment or option is an arm and only the selected arm's outcome is observed. Its objective is to balance exploration of uncertain arms with exploitation of arms expected to give better outcomes, usually by maximizing reward or reducing regret. The authors organize algorithms for the basic finite-arm setting and for extensions involving adversarial rewards, covariates, changing environments, continuous choices, and multiple simultaneous selections. They explain how the methods work and collect their known regret guarantees in a comparison table. The main finding is that guarantees and suitability depend on the problem assumptions, and reward optimization alone may not ensure precise estimates of treatment effects.
key_results: The survey reports logarithmic regret for several stochastic finite-arm methods, including UCB1, Thompson sampling, and BESA, under their respective assumptions. It reports that BESA has a finite-time logarithmic regret result, while a naive implementation requires 2 to 20 times the computation of Thompson sampling. In a cited real-world redundant-content-routing problem, POKER is reported to outperform epsilon-based methods by about a factor of 3; the authors note that no finite-time regret analysis for POKER was known. For nonstationary bandits, discounted UCB and sliding-window UCB have regret of square-root order in the horizon under the cited assumptions; these guarantees are not directly comparable to the stationary results.
key_equations:
Bandit observation process: \[X_{S_t,t}\sim P_{S_t}\] At time t, the policy selects arm S_t, observes reward X with that arm's reward distribution P.

Expected regret: \[R_H=\sum_{t=1}^{H}\left[\max_i E(X_{i,t})-E(X_{S_t,t})\right]\] R is cumulative expected regret through horizon H; t indexes time, i indexes arms, X is an arm reward, S is the selected arm, and E denotes expectation.

Generic upper-confidence-bound choice: \[S_t=\arg\max_i\left(\bar X_i+P_i\right)\] At time t, the selected arm S maximizes its empirical mean X bar plus uncertainty padding P, over arms indexed by i.
limitations_stated: The authors state that regret is not always the most important design measure: estimator variance and accurate effect-size estimation may matter more in experiments. They also note that feedback delay is under-considered in the bandit literature, and that several algorithms lack known regret properties or have bounds that may not be tight.
limitations_unstated: The survey compiles results obtained under different assumptions, regret definitions, and evaluation settings, so its table cannot be read as a controlled, like-for-like ranking of algorithms. It gives limited evidence about whether the reviewed reward-focused methods deliver valid treatment-effect estimates or meet practical experimental constraints such as ethical allocation, delayed outcomes, and required sample sizes.
future_work_stated: The authors propose combining regret minimization with constraints that require sufficiently precise estimates of parameters of interest. Their example is a medical-trial design that minimizes regret while ensuring, with high probability, a desired confidence level for each estimator.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be systematic comparisons on shared experimental-design benchmarks that report both cumulative reward and estimation quality, with realistic delays, allocation constraints, and sample-size limits. Further work could also evaluate sequential stopping and provide accessible software implementations so quality engineers can reproduce and validate the reviewed approaches in real experiments.

summary: This paper studies how to define and relate resolution and strength for simple nonregular fractional factorial designs. It extends the Box-Hunter idea of resolution by defining effects as contrast subspaces and assessing aliasing after restricting those contrasts to the fraction. The authors prove that a design's maximum Box-Hunter resolution equals its maximum strength plus one. Together with an established result for generalized wordlength, this shows that the maximum resolution also equals the minimum interaction order with a nonzero generalized wordlength value.
key_results: The main theorem establishes that the maximum Box-Hunter resolution of a simple fraction is its maximum strength plus one, and therefore equals its minimum generalized wordlength order. The paper illustrates this with a 64-run, four-factor, four-level fraction that has strength 2 and maximum resolution 3. It also describes a 9-run, three-factor, three-level regular fraction with resolution 3, illustrating how effects can be aliased after restriction to the fraction.
key_equations: Maximum resolution and generalized wordlength: \[R_{\max}=t_{\max}+1=\min\{i:A_i>0\}\] R_max is the maximum Box-Hunter resolution, t_max is the maximum strength, i is interaction order, and A_i is the generalized wordlength value at that order.
limitations_stated: The authors' result and aliasing definition apply to simple fractions, or to equireplicate designs under the stated framework. They say it is unclear how to extend their definition of aliasing to non-simple designs, and note that a comparable theory explaining the aliasing information in generalized wordlength patterns is not yet available.
limitations_unstated: The paper provides a theoretical relationship rather than a procedure for generating or choosing a fraction, so it gives no practical guidance on run-size tradeoffs or implementation. Its conclusions also depend on the specified contrast-subspace definition of aliasing and do not establish how the result performs under alternative aliasing definitions or model-based criteria.
future_work_stated: The authors identify extending the theory to non-simple designs as a larger goal, which would require extending their definition of aliasing. They also point to the need for a theory that explains what aliasing structure is represented by generalized wordlength patterns for nonregular designs.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to develop computational tools that calculate the proposed aliasing relations and resolution for candidate fractions, including designs with practical restrictions. Further work could compare the definition with model-based bias measures and validate its usefulness in real experiments.

summary: The paper derives F tests for strip-split-plot experiments, in which two factors are assigned to intersecting strips and a third factor is applied to subplots within their intersections. Their central message is that the actual field layout and randomization determine the appropriate analysis.

future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess the actual error rates and power of the proposed tests through simulation across different numbers of blocks, factor levels, and variance components. summary: This paper develops combinatorial results for space-filling point sets and sequences, rather than a statistical response model or a conventional experimental design. It studies generalized nets and sequences, which control how evenly points occupy specified regions of a multidimensional unit cube. The authors connect these nets to mixed orthogonal arrays, whose columns can use different alphabet sizes, and extend the connection to ordered arrays. They use these relationships and bounds for orthogonal arrays to derive restrictions on which net and sequence parameters can exist. The main finding is an equivalence between nets and a particular class of mixed ordered orthogonal arrays, along with necessary parameter bounds.

summary: This paper adapts response surface methodology (RSM) to optimize an unknown, costly-to-evaluate function whose input is high-dimensional or functional. It assumes the response can be approximated locally by a first- or second-order model, and constructs experiments by projecting multivariate design points onto selected directions in a Hilbert space. The directions can come from a fixed basis or from data-driven principal component analysis (PCA) or partial least squares (PLS). Properties of the multivariate design, including orthogonality, carry over to the resulting functional design. The method is studied on simulated functional data and applied to a nuclear-safety simulation to seek operating curves that increase the margin factor.
key_results: For the first simulated objective, the first descent step reduced the response from 70.4 ± 0.1 to 6.33 × 10⁻³ ± 10⁻⁵ using 280 experiments; after a second-order step, the response was 5.45 × 10⁻³ ± 10⁻⁵, with 557 experiments reported in total. For the second simulated objective, the first step reduced the response from 2.88 ± 0.01 to 1.99 ± 0.01, an improvement of about 31%. In comparisons over 50 training samples of size 500, PLS performed better than PCA for the first descent step, while the comparison between PLS and a Fourier basis was less clear. The nuclear-safety design combined functional designs for temperature, pressure, and heat transfer into 128 design points; the estimated ascent primarily changed the temperature transient, especially between 500 and 2000 seconds and between 3000 and 4000 seconds.

summary: PopED lite is software for designing preclinical drug studies using fixed-effect pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) models. Its objective is to improve parameter-estimation accuracy by selecting practical dose amounts and sampling times. The software calculates a Fisher information matrix from model predictions, parameter guesses, measurement error, and quantification limits, then scores designs using determinant-based criteria. It accounts for uncertain parameter guesses by evaluating randomly generated values within user-specified ranges, and searches discretized design options with stochastic algorithms. Three drug-discovery case studies illustrate reduced estimation uncertainty, fewer observations or less compound in some designs, and rapid design calculations.
key_results: In the first case study, a design using one dose of 2.8 micromoles per kilogram and five observations had predicted coefficients of variation of 36% and 44% for two potency parameters, compared with 52% for each parameter in the manual design; it also used one dose and five observations rather than two doses and ten observations. In the second case study, the software proposed a dose of 0.04 micromoles per kilogram, with a predicted coefficient of variation of 10% for the potency estimate; the experiment produced 7%, whereas the preceding uninformative experiment had uncertainty above 400%. In the third case study, the predicted coefficient of variation for clearance fell from approximately 38% for the standard schedule to 4% for the proposed schedule, and the estimate from three mice had a coefficient of variation of 2%. The authors report calculation times of around ten seconds for models without ordinary differential equations and around one minute for models with stiff ordinary differential equations.

limitations_unstated: The evaluation consists of three project-based case studies, without a broad, controlled comparison against other design software or a systematic assessment of how often the stochastic search reaches the best possible design. future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess the software prospectively across a larger range of experimental settings and compare its designs and calculation time with other available tools. summary: This paper designs Refined Stratified Sampling (RSS), a sequential sampling method for Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification (UQ) of model outputs from independent input variables. The method begins with a stratified design and extends it by dividing an existing stratum, then sampling in the newly created empty region and updating sample weights. The authors compare stratified sampling (SS) with simple random sampling (SRS) and Latin hypercube sampling (LHS), emphasizing how their space-filling and projection properties suit different models. They prove that balanced refinement reduces estimator variance compared with adding samples to an existing stratum, and demonstrate RSS on a stochastic function and a simplified structural response to underwater shock. In the examples, RSS often reaches the reported convergence criteria with substantially fewer model evaluations than SRS and hierarchical Latin hypercube sampling (HLHS), while allowing samples to be added one at a time.
key_results: For the stochastic-function study, the authors ran 1,000 calculation sets per input-distribution case, starting with 20 samples and recording the sample count needed for 95% of sets to meet the convergence criterion. Across the ten cases, RSS required 942 to 125,842 samples, compared with 12,880 to 236,090 for SRS and 2,560 to 163,840 for HLHS; the paper reports that RSS gave a 10–20% greater sample-size reduction than HLHS. For low-kurtosis outputs, RSS reduced sample size by as much as 90% or more relative to SRS, and its empirical-distribution convergence was comparable to HLHS while permitting finer-grained extensions. In the structural-response example, 4,000 RSS analyses were compared with 90,000 SRS analyses; the estimated mean met a 0.1% convergence threshold after 300 RSS samples versus 84,900 SRS samples. The authors also report that RSS needed 2,920 samples for 15% convergence of kurtosis, while SRS did not reach that threshold in 90,000 samples.

summary: This paper compares three sampling designs for numerical integration of functions over high-dimensional spaces: Monte Carlo, Latin hypercube sampling, and quasi-Monte Carlo using Sobol’ sequences. The results generally favor Sobol’ sequence sampling, especially when the function’s effective dimension is low. Latin hypercube sampling can outperform the other methods for some low-interaction functions at smaller run sizes, but the authors recommend quasi-Monte Carlo as the safer general choice when the function type is unknown.

For type C functions at 10 dimensions, quasi-Monte Carlo had exponents of 0.64 and 0.68, versus about 0.5 for both alternatives. The authors report that, for one type A example, the quasi-Monte Carlo estimate reached the theoretical integral value at about 2^4 points, while Monte Carlo and Latin hypercube estimates did so at about 2^9 points; they describe quasi-Monte Carlo as about 30 times faster in that example. summary: This paper develops determinant-optimal designs for experiments with ordered categorical responses modeled using cumulative link models. The candidate experimental settings are fixed, and the method allocates runs among them to improve parameter estimation. In the toxicity example, the approximately uniform original design had 52.6% efficiency relative to the proposed design. For odor removal under parameter uncertainty, the expected-information design took 5.43 seconds to find, versus 313 seconds for the Bayesian design, and achieved 99.99% relative efficiency by the Bayesian criterion; the uniform allocation achieved 87.67%. summary: The paper develops optimal experimental designs for regression with correlated errors observed over an interval, covering both one-parameter and multi-parameter models. key_results: For the Brownian-motion model with regression function f(t) = t squared plus 1 on the interval from 1 to 2, the continuous-time best variance is approximately 0.075004, and the proposed weighted least-squares estimator is reported to have almost the same precision as the best linear unbiased estimator. It considers approximate designs on the unit cube and the unit Euclidean ball, with the goal of maximizing the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix. summary: The paper designs compressive measurements to estimate a structured signal when both the signal and the pre-measurement clutter have known statistical structure. The measurement model includes the signal and clutter before sensing, followed by post-measurement noise. The design uses mixture-model prior information summarized by covariance matrices and chooses a sensing matrix under an energy constraint. Because the full prior distributions are not known, the authors optimize the error of the best linear estimator, using a Bayesian A-optimal criterion. Their iterative construction alternates between a water-filling update and a choice of covariance-related eigenvectors; in synthetic experiments it performs better than the tested alternative designs.
key_results: The simulations use signals of dimension 100, with 10 signal models and 10 clutter models, each having covariance rank 6; the authors report 1,000 trials. They examine 20, 40, 60, and 80 measurements and compare the proposed design with random compressive measurements, a low-rank Wiener-filter design, and a design that treats clutter as signal. The proposed design has higher reconstruction signal-to-noise ratio than each alternative across the plotted energy budgets and all four measurement counts. The paper gives no exact numerical improvement values in the text.

limitations_stated: The authors restrict the estimator to be linear for analytical tractability and use only first- and second-order prior statistics. limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses synthetic covariance models and does not establish performance on real experimental data or under inaccurate prior covariances. future_work_stated: The authors call for further investigation of whether cancellation should be built into the sensing matrix rather than left to the estimator. They also defer a more thorough comparison with mutual-information-based design approaches to subsequent work.

summary: This paper develops first-order algorithms for the A-optimal experimental-design problem in a general linear model. The goal is to choose weights on a finite set of candidate regression points to minimize the mean dispersion of parameter estimates. The method uses a dual ellipsoid formulation to derive optimality conditions, then updates the weights by moving toward selected candidate points; one algorithm also allows away steps that reduce existing weights. The paper proves convergence and complexity bounds, and tests the algorithms on randomly generated regression-point sets. The results show that away steps and a more selective initialization can substantially improve computation time, while the first-order approach can be much faster than a semidefinite-programming solver on the tested instances.
key_results: The authors prove that each update can be computed with a number of arithmetic operations proportional to the product of the model dimension and the number of candidate points. Under their stated bounded-distance assumption, the first algorithm reaches an approximate solution in a number of iterations proportional to the logarithm of the candidate-point count plus the inverse of the tolerance; modified versions with a D-optimal initialization have bounds involving the logarithm of the model dimension instead. In the simulations, the away-step algorithm was generally faster than the algorithm without away steps, and the modified initialization was advantageous on large problems; tests included 50,000 candidate points. For instances solved to a tolerance of 10 to the power of negative 7, the reported comparison showed speed-ups above 300 on some cases, and the authors report solving an instance with model dimension 500 and 10,000 candidate points to tolerance 10 to the power of negative 4 in under 30 minutes. The tested first-order method and semidefinite solver produced solutions whose distance was below 10 to the power of negative 7, while the first-order method was reported to be more than 300 times faster in some comparisons.
key_equations:
Information matrix: \[M(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_i x_i x_i^T\] The information matrix M(u) is the sum over candidate points i of each weight u_i times the regression vector x_i and its transpose.

A-optimal design criterion: \[\max_{u}\ -\operatorname{Trace}(M(u)^{-1})\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_i=1,\ u_i\geq 0\] The design chooses nonnegative weights u_i that sum to one to maximize the negative trace of the inverse information matrix M(u).

Weight update: \[u^{+}=(1-\tau)u+\tau e_j\] The updated weight vector u plus is formed from the current weight vector u, step size tau, and unit vector e_j selecting the chosen candidate point j.
limitations_stated: The complexity bounds depend on a bounded-distance assumption whose constant depends on the geometry of the design points and the iterates. The authors note that this constant can be large when points are concentrated near a proper subspace, and that their local linear-convergence bound depends on problem-specific data.
limitations_unstated: The method optimizes weights for a finite candidate set and an approximate, large-sample design; the paper does not establish that rounding those weights yields a good exact design for a specified finite run size. The computational comparisons use randomly generated regression points rather than real experiments, and the semidefinite-solver comparison covers only a limited set of instances.
future_work_stated: The authors note that hybrid update rules that compare a small set of promising points, and methods using active-set strategies, may perform better on some instances. They also observe that related algorithms for other design criteria are possible, though their step sizes and convergence analyses would need to be tailored to each criterion.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the algorithms on applied experiments with practical constraints such as restricted candidate settings, costs, or required replication counts, and to assess how well approximate weights convert to exact run plans. Further work could also compare criteria and sequential updating strategies on the same applied problems.

summary: This paper develops methods for checking whether two multi-stage, two-level factorial designs with randomization restrictions are isomorphic. The designs are represented through randomization defining contrast subspaces (RDCSSs), using finite projective geometry to express the restrictions at each stage. The authors define design equivalence and isomorphism, then use binary representations and a structured search over factor relabelings to avoid testing every possible relabeling. They give separate algorithms for designs built from disjoint spreads and from stars whose subspaces share a common overlap. The algorithms are illustrated on manufacturing examples, and the paper reports that they substantially reduce the search space and classify several families of small designs.
key_results: The proposed search reduces the candidate space by 7 orders of magnitude for 2-spreads of P6, 13 orders for 1-spreads of P10, and 12 orders for 4-spreads of P10, compared with exhaustive relabeling. The two silicon-wafer designs are shown to be isomorphic, while the two plutonium-alloy designs are non-isomorphic because their shared-overlap structures have different nucleus sizes. The paper reports 131044 isomorphism classes of 1-spreads of P6, but the cyclic construction method reaches only one of those classes. The algorithms and supporting functions are implemented in the R statistical computing language and made available in a public repository.

limitations_stated: The paper focuses on balanced designs constructed from spreads and stars; it does not provide a complete treatment of unbalanced designs. limitations_unstated: The paper does not report broad runtime benchmarks, so the practical cost of the search for larger or difficult non-isomorphic cases is unclear. The method's demonstrations and comparisons are focused on particular geometric design families and examples, rather than a wide range of applied experiments or alternative design-quality criteria.
future_work_stated: The authors identify construction and classification of unbalanced spreads and stars as areas needing further work. They also say that some results and algorithms can be extended to designs with more than two factor levels, and that the relabeling approach can help find designs meeting specified randomization restrictions.
future_work_unstated: Further work could benchmark run time and memory use across larger problems, especially when the designs are non-isomorphic and the search cannot stop at the first match. It could also test the methods on real industrial experiments with additional practical constraints and connect isomorphism checking to explicit design-ranking criteria.

summary: This paper adapts the group lasso, a method for selecting groups of variables, to construct experimental designs. It considers finite-level factors and a specified regression model, then selects candidate design points to estimate chosen model coefficients with low total estimator variance while limiting the number of runs. The authors formulate this as a group-lasso optimization problem with unbiasedness constraints, and propose a distance-based procedure for choosing penalty weights that breaks symmetries among candidate points. The approach can also accommodate repeated measurements and, with a relaxed formulation, confounding among factors.

summary: This paper develops a way to identify saturated fractions in factorial experiments for a specified linear model. A saturated fraction uses the minimum number of design points needed to estimate all model parameters, so it has no residual degrees of freedom for estimating error. The authors characterize saturation using circuits, which are combinatorial descriptions of linear dependencies among design points. Their method computes the circuits for the full model once, then checks whether a candidate fraction contains the support of any circuit. They also use Markov-basis methods to sample saturated fractions subject to specified projections. The paper proves the circuit characterization and demonstrates the approach on several factorial models.

The authors compute 140 circuits for this model, and report that checking circuit supports identifies nonsaturated fractions without calculating each fraction's determinant. They report generating 5,000 random saturated fractions in about one second. With the same one-way projections specified, they report generating a sample of 5,000 saturated fractions in less than one minute using the Markov-chain approach.

summary: The paper presents a method to guide decisions about continuing or stopping searches for saturated designs under determinant-based optimality (D-optimality). A saturated design has as many experimental runs as the number of model parameters, and the method seeks designs that estimate those parameters efficiently. It repeatedly runs a design-search algorithm from randomized starting designs, treats distinct criterion values as species, and estimates the chance that another run will discover a previously unseen species. The search stops when that estimated chance falls below a user-chosen threshold or a maximum number of iterations is reached. In the example, the approach found many different designs, and the best reported design was found using the exchange algorithm.
key_results: For a model with 7 two-level factors, including the overall mean, main effects, and all two-factor interactions, the paper searched for saturated designs with 29 runs. With the exchange algorithm and a discovery-probability threshold of 0.10, the search stopped after 493 runs with 103 different designs; their D-efficiencies ranged from 78.9605 to 85.6265. Continuing to a threshold of 0.05 brought the total to 1,764 runs and 191 designs, with the same maximum D-efficiency of 85.6265 and a minimum of 78.1134. With the Fedorov algorithm, the search stopped after 18 runs with 4 designs, whose D-efficiencies ranged from 82.4212 to 83.9844; the authors describe it as more stable but slower than the exchange algorithm, and its first sample did not find the best exchange-algorithm design.

Stopping rule: \[\text{stop at iteration }s\text{ if }\widehat U_{s+0}(0)< p^\star\] At iteration s, the search stops if the estimated probability of discovering a new species is below the chosen threshold p star.

future_work_unstated: The method could be evaluated across more models, candidate sets, search algorithms, and practical restrictions on allowable runs, with comparisons of both design quality and computational effort. summary: The paper develops computational methods for optimal design of multiresponse experiments, where each experiment can produce several measurements.
