summary: This paper develops an algebraic method for finding the support points of locally optimal designs for nonlinear models with two parameters. The method is applied to four binary-response models, a Poisson count model, and the Michaelis–Menten model, including constrained design regions. The main finding is that many design problems can be reduced to optimizing over two support points, with a third point sometimes needed for particular binary-response models or regions.
key_results: For logistic and probit models on symmetric design regions, the paper proves that a design based on two symmetric points has an information matrix at least as good as that of any design in the region; double exponential and double reciprocal models may also require the point zero. For the four binary-response models on regions lying entirely on one side of zero, a two-point design suffices, with one point at the relevant boundary. For the loglinear Poisson and Michaelis–Menten models on the stated bounded regions, a two-point design suffices, with one point at the upper boundary. The paper reports theoretical support reductions rather than numerical efficiency percentages, estimates, or prediction results.

limitations_unstated: The designs are locally optimal and therefore depend on assumed parameter values, but the paper does not assess how sensitive the proposed support points are to incorrect parameter guesses. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to nonlinear models with more than two parameters. They also identify complete results for complementary log-log and skewed logit models as an open question.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test how much the selected supports and resulting efficiency change when the locally assumed parameters are inaccurate. summary: This paper is a review of nonregular fractional factorial designs used mainly for economical factor screening and, in some settings, for detecting interactions. limitations_unstated: The paper is a broad narrative review rather than a systematic comparison using a common set of models, evaluation measures, and datasets, so readers cannot infer a consistent ranking of the reviewed criteria. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method under prior misspecification and practical constraints such as limited experiment capacity or unequal resource availability. summary: This paper proposes regression-tree models for analyzing designed experiments and predicting mean responses. It applies the approach to replicated and unreplicated factorial experiments, as well as Poisson count data and logistic proportion data. The construction recursively partitions the factor space and fits simple or multiple main-effects regression models within the resulting leaves, so interactions are represented through changes in conditional main effects across leaves. The GUIDE algorithm selects split variables using tests of residual patterns, chooses split values to reduce residual error, and uses cross-validation to select a tree. Simulations and real-data examples show that these models can provide interpretable predictions and often balance overfitting against underfitting better than the traditional methods considered.
key_results: For replicated factorial experiments, the paper reports 10,000 simulation trials per model, with 96 observations per trial: 6 replicates at each of the 16 combinations in a four-factor, two-level design. Across four simulated response models, the GUIDE methods had relatively low prediction mean squared error (PMSE) across scenarios; the experimentwise error rate method controlled false positives better but had higher PMSE in non-null cases, while individual error rate and Akaike information criterion methods tended to overfit under the null. For unreplicated experiments, the simulations also used 10,000 trials, with 16 observations per trial; GUIDE generally overfit less than the individual error rate version of Lenth’s method, while Lenth’s experimentwise error rate version controlled false positives at the cost of underfitting non-null cases. In the 720-observation soldering example, the GUIDE piecewise main-effects model fit slightly better than the compared Chambers–Hastie model. The seed-germination example shows how a five-leaf logistic tree displays the effects of storage temperature and moisture level, including their interaction.
key_equations:

Piecewise main-effects model: \[\hat{y}=\hat{\beta}_{0,r}+\sum_{j\in S_r}\hat{\beta}_{j,r}x_j\] yhat is the fitted response, r identifies the tree leaf, betahat zero r is that leaf’s intercept, S_r is its predictor set, betahat j r is the coefficient for predictor j in that leaf, and x_j is predictor j.

GUIDE split construction: \[j^*=\arg\min_j p_j,\qquad c^*=\arg\min_c\{RSS_L(c)+RSS_R(c)\}\] The algorithm first selects variable j with the smallest chi-squared test p-value p_j, then selects split value c that minimizes the combined residual sums of squares RSS_L and RSS_R in the left and right child nodes.
limitations_stated: The authors say that more simulation results are needed to assess how well the trees estimate the true response surface. They also note that it remains useful to formalize how to distinguish tree complexity caused by interactions from complexity caused by main effects, and that methods for unordered nominal responses were limited.
limitations_unstated: The simulation comparisons cover a small set of specified response models and factorial settings, and the paper reports relative PMSE plots rather than absolute prediction-error values. Because the approach uses recursive splits and cross-validation, the selected tree may depend on the particular data and validation procedure; this stability is not evaluated in the paper.
future_work_stated: The authors propose formalizing an algebraic way to distinguish interaction-driven trees from trees that represent main effects, and using trees to identify potentially important high-order effects for subsequent traditional regression analysis. They call for further simulation studies, extensions to unordered nominal responses, and investigation of applications to unbalanced or sequential response-surface experiments.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could measure how stable the selected partitions and predictions are under repeated sampling, alternative cross-validation choices, and practical restrictions on allowable factor combinations. The paper would also benefit from a reproducible software implementation and prospective validation on new manufacturing experiments.

summary: The paper develops experimental designs for switching measurements on a Josephson junction (JJ), where each current pulse produces a binary switching outcome. It models the probability of switching with a complementary log-log response curve and seeks to estimate its unknown slope and intercept. The authors derive a two-point design using determinant-based optimality (D-optimality), then propose a sequential procedure that first searches for usable starting points and subsequently updates estimates and measurement settings. The method is tested in both a laboratory experiment and simulations against a theoretical design that already knows the optimal measurement points. The authors report that the sequential procedure becomes close to that theoretical benchmark as the number of measurements grows and can be used for faster data acquisition in the tested setup.
key_results: The derived two-point design uses linear-predictor values of 0.979633 and −1.33774, corresponding to switching probabilities of about 0.930295 and 0.230826. In the laboratory test at 20 millikelvins, a 50-stage experiment used 117,288 pulses and took 8 minutes 16 seconds, including 1 minute 30 seconds for estimation; the authors report that practically sufficient accuracy was reached after 20–30 stages, or about 6,000–17,000 pulses. In 500 simulation runs, the sequential design was compared with the theoretical D-optimal design, whose optimal points were assumed known from the start; the paper says their performance was reasonably close once the run size exceeded 200 observations. At 20,000 observations, the reported mean squared errors for the slope estimate were 0.000007 for the sequential design and 0.000006 for the theoretical design, while those for the intercept estimate were 0.473926 and 0.399793, respectively.
key_equations:
Binary switching model: \[P(Y=1\mid x)=1-\exp\left[-\exp(ax+b)\right]\] P is the probability, Y is the binary switching outcome, x is the applied-current covariate, and a and b are the unknown slope and intercept parameters.

D-optimal information criterion: \[\det(J)=\sum_{i< j}g(z_i)g(z_j)(x_i-x_j)^2,\quad g(z)=\frac{e^{2z}}{e^{\exp(z)}-1}\] J is the information matrix, det denotes its determinant, i and j index observations, x_i and x_j are their covariate values, z_i and z_j are their linear predictors, and g is the model weight function.

Optimal two-point predictor values: \[z_1^*\approx 0.979633,\quad z_2^*\approx -1.33774\] The two values are the optimal linear predictors for the two measurement points, and the asterisk marks their optimal values.

Sequential choice of current points: \[x_k=\frac{z_k^*-\hat b}{\hat a},\quad k\in\{1,2\}\] x_k is a selected covariate, z_k^* is one of the two optimal predictor values, and the hatted a and b are the current parameter estimates used to calculate the next measurement points.
limitations_stated: The authors say the complementary log-log model may be too inflexible for complicated junction structures and that more flexible models may be needed. They also describe their choice of measurements per stage as empirical and say a systematic method for minimizing total experiment time is a non-trivial problem.
limitations_unstated: The design relies on the assumed complementary log-log response and on the approximation that the current itself is the covariate, so departures from that model could shift the selected measurement points and affect estimates. The practical demonstration uses one laboratory sample and one measurement setup, while the simulation comparison uses a single motivating parameter setting and a theoretical benchmark with optimal points known in advance.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying criteria other than D-optimality, systematically choosing the number of measurements per stage to minimize time to a target accuracy, and performing estimation and measurement simultaneously. They also suggest more flexible models for complicated junctions and adaptive designs to track parameter changes with environmental conditions.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the procedure across multiple junctions, environmental conditions, and deliberately misspecified response curves, including how such changes affect the recommended points and uncertainty. It could also evaluate practical constraints such as allowable current ranges and instrument limits, and compare stopping rules based on estimation precision and total experiment time.

summary: The paper develops multi-level supersaturated designs (SSDs) for experiments that screen many factors with too few runs to estimate every main effect. It assesses designs using generalized minimum aberration (GMA), which first minimizes overall pairwise aliasing and then considers higher-order aliasing. The authors derive a tighter lower bound and give explicit constructions using linear and quadratic polynomials evaluated over finite fields. The construction yields balanced designs, including classes without fully aliased columns, and the paper also treats mixed-level designs. The authors report that many constructions attain the lower bound and are GMA-optimal, while comparisons show tradeoffs among measures of pairwise aliasing.
key_results: For a multi-level SSD, the paper derives a new lower bound on the second generalized wordlength value; it is attained when the numbers of shared levels between every pair of rows differ by at most one, and such designs are GMA-optimal. For prime-power level counts greater than two, the half Addelman–Kempthorne construction has s to the n runs, 2 times (s to the n minus 1) divided by (s minus 1), minus 1 columns, and overall A2 equal to s to the n minus s; it has no fully aliased columns. In the reported comparisons, designs with 27 runs and 26 factors from the construction in Theorem 7 have average f of 3.77 and maximum f of 12, compared with 3.78 and 16 for Fang and colleagues and 4.26 and 16 for Aggarwal and Gupta. The paper says the gains are marginal for run sizes up to 25, and that its designs can perform better on one comparison criterion but worse on another.
key_equations:
Assumed effects model: \[Y=X_0\alpha_0+X_1\alpha_1+\cdots+X_m\alpha_m+\epsilon\] Y is the observation vector, X_j is the contrast matrix for effects involving j factors, alpha_j is the corresponding effect vector, and epsilon is the vector of independent random errors.

GMA criterion: \[\operatorname{GMA}(D)=\operatorname{lexmin}\bigl(A_1(D),A_2(D),A_3(D),\ldots\bigr)\] D is a design, A_j(D) is its jth generalized wordlength value, and lexmin means to minimize these values in order, starting with the first.

Lower bound on pairwise aliasing: \[A_2(D)\geq\frac{m(s-1)(ms-m-N+1)}{2(N-1)}+\frac{(N-1)s^2\eta(1-\eta)}{2N},\quad\eta=\frac{m(N-s)}{(N-1)s}-\left\lfloor\frac{m(N-s)}{(N-1)s}\right\rfloor\] A_2(D) is the second generalized wordlength value for design D, m is the number of factors, s is the number of levels, N is the number of runs, and eta is the fractional part of m times (N minus s) divided by (N minus 1) times s.

Polynomial construction: \[H_n=\{c_1X_1+\cdots+c_nX_n:c_i\in F_s,\ c_n\ne0\text{ is the last nonzero coefficient and equals }1\},\quad Q_1^*=\{X_1^2+aX_1+h:a\in F_s,\ h\in H_{n-1}\},\quad D=[H_n\mid Q_1^*]\] H_n is the set of normalized nonzero linear functions in n variables, c_i are their coefficients, X_i are the variables, F_s is the finite field with s elements, Q*_1 is the set of quadratic functions formed using coefficient a and linear function h from H_(n−1), and D is the design formed by juxtaposing the two column sets.
limitations_stated: The authors state that for run sizes up to 25 the benefits of their designs are marginal, and that a design may be better under one comparison criterion but worse under another. They also state that it is not known whether mixed-level designs attaining their lower bound are optimal under GMA.
limitations_unstated: The main explicit polynomial constructions require a prime-power number of levels, with the stated construction section assuming more than two levels, which limits direct use for other level counts. The paper provides theoretical properties and tabulated comparisons rather than validation in real screening experiments, and it does not establish how its designs perform when the assumed effect structure is inaccurate or practical run-order constraints apply.
future_work_stated: The authors call for further work to determine whether mixed-level designs that attain the derived lower bound are also GMA-optimal. They do not state another specific future-work program.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to develop comparable constructions for level counts outside the stated prime-power setting and for practical restrictions such as blocks or constrained factor settings. Real-experiment studies could test screening performance under interaction effects and assess whether the theoretical aliasing advantages translate into reliable identification of important factors.

summary: This theory paper develops a framework for connecting Bayesian data analysis with experimental design through a logic of questions. It treats an experimental question as relevant when its answers help resolve a scientific issue. The proposed design approach chooses the experimental question with the greatest relevance to that issue. If the paper’s relevance-entropy conjecture is true, this is equivalent to maximizing mutual information between the experiment and the issue. The paper gives a theoretical derivation rather than a particular experimental design, application, or empirical evaluation.
key_results: The paper derives a relevance-based criterion for selecting an experimental question and shows that maximizing this criterion reduces to maximizing the relevance of the common question shared by the experiment and scientific issue. Under the conjecture that relevance can be expressed using entropy, the criterion is equivalent to mutual information. In that form, a useful experiment has high entropy in its possible results and low average conditional entropy of results given the scientific scenario. The paper reports no numerical efficiency, run-size, prediction, or estimation results, and makes no empirical comparison of designs.
key_equations:
Relevance of an experimental question: \[b(E|S\vee H)=\frac{b(E\vee S|H)}{b(S|H)}\] The relevance of experimental question E to scientific issue S in background context H equals the relevance of their common question divided by the relevance of S in that context; b denotes relevance and the vertical bar means given.

Information-gain criterion: \[I(E;S)=H(E)-H(E|S)\] Mutual information I between experimental question E and scientific issue S equals the entropy H of E minus the conditional entropy of E given S.

Design construction: \[b(E\vee S|H)=b(E|H)+b(S|H)-b(E\wedge S|H)\] The relevance of the common question for E and S in context H equals the relevance of E plus the relevance of S minus the relevance of their joint question; b denotes relevance, the vertical bar means given, and the conjunction symbol denotes a joint question.
limitations_stated: The author states that the conjecture connecting relevance to entropy has not been proven. The relationship between the spaces of questions and assertions is not fully understood, including whether those spaces are isomorphic, and the author notes that reasoning directly with questions can be difficult.
limitations_unstated: The paper gives no worked design example, numerical calculation, or empirical validation showing how the proposed criterion performs in practice. It also does not specify an operational procedure for choosing among feasible experiments when run costs, practical constraints, or a particular response model must be considered.
future_work_stated: The author calls for further investigation into the structure and relationship of the spaces of questions and assertions. The paper also suggests deriving prior relevance and performing calculations directly in question space, without translating everything back into assertions.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the relevance-based criterion in real experiments and compare its selected designs with established information-gain methods. Further work could also develop an implementable selection procedure that accounts for run cost and practical design constraints.
